title: Introducing Flat Rate CDN
description:
Over the past year, we have improved Vercel’s Pro pricing to better reflect how teams build, with expanded user roles, flexible credits, access to enterprise features, and more. But one area our customers continued to give us feedback on was CDN pricing.

CDN costs should be predictable, but viral launches, traffic bursts, or misconfigured routes sometimes turned an otherwise normal month into an unexpected bill. For teams building on Vercel, that uncertainty made growth feel like a problem at exactly the moment it should feel exciting.

Today, we are introducing Flat Rate CDN for Pro teams: a new way to pay for CDN usage with a predictable monthly bill, built-in spike protection, and service tiers designed for different traffic profiles.

What is Flat Rate CDN?

Flat Rate CDN is an alternative to usage-based CDN billing that provides you with a predictable monthly bill.

The model is designed around a simple idea: teams should be able to choose the CDN capacity that corresponds to their typical usage profile, pay a known amount monthly, and avoid surprise overages from temporary spikes.

Flat Rate CDN has several advantages over usage-based billing:

  • Fixed monthly price: Pay a fixed amount for Vercel CDN each month.

  • Covers traffic spikes: CDN Requests, Fast Data Transfer, and other resources are no longer billed directly, so spikes don't result in surprise bills.

  • No overages: Your bill will never increase because of temporary usage spikes.

Importantly, predictable pricing does not mean lower-quality bandwidth. Every request still runs on Vercel’s premium network, including private fiber that routes around congestion on the public internet, which can improve performance by up to 60%. Comparable routing is often sold as a premium add-on, but Vercel includes it by default for Pro teams, and performance isn't degraded during traffic spikes.

How it works

All new Pro teams have Flat Rate CDN enabled by default, and existing Pro teams can opt in. Usage is tracked at the team level and covers all projects, so you no longer need to manage capacity for them individually.

What’s included

On Flat Rate CDN, one fixed monthly fee covers:

  • CDN Requests

  • Fast Data Transfer

  • Blob Data Transfer

  • Observability events generated by CDN requests

The default tier is included with Pro. You can upgrade to a higher tier for increased request and data transfer capacity.

Your tier is fixed throughout any given billing period, so you never have to worry about charges from temporary traffic spikes.

What happens during a spike

The following team had a relatively normal usage profile that would fit comfortably in our $20/month Flat Rate CDN tier:

Only days after the above period, they experienced a viral product launch that generated a significant surge in traffic:

If the team had been on usage-based pricing, their CDN bill would have reached tens of thousands of dollars. On Flat Rate CDN, it stayed at $20 for the month.

No caps and no performance hit

Flat rate pricing from other infrastructure providers often places caps on usage when you reach your capacity, resulting in rapid performance degradation and request rejection. Flat Rate CDN is different in two ways:

  1. We recognize usage spikes and remove them when evaluating your CDN usage against capacity.

  2. We rightsize your Flat Rate CDN tier every month based on sustained usage.

This means we’ll never bring down your site when you’re going viral, and you don’t have to actively manage your tier when you’re growing quickly.

You can still monitor every covered resource on the Usage page or in the CLI, including traffic spikes absorbed by Vercel:

What we heard from customers during beta

Even though surprise bills are rare across our entire customer base, we’ve seen numerous stories from Pro customers about unexpected bills, many of which famously blew up on X. One team we interviewed was running hundreds of client sites and told us that CDN costs were “by far our largest line item, and the hardest to forecast,” especially when traffic spiked “from a client’s listing going viral, seasonal traffic, or bot traffic.”

In May, we released Flat Rate CDN to a small set of teams in limited beta. Over the last several months, it has changed how they operate on Vercel.

They worried less:

Flat Rate CDN eased our billing anxiety. With the recent increase in AI crawler traffic, we used to frequently check bot activity through Observability and monitor which bots were generating traffic. We now spend much less time doing that.

They built more:

Knowing that CDN usage is predictable makes us more willing to adopt caching-oriented approaches. We're now considering broader use of Cache Components and other caching strategies in our Next.js architecture, whereas previously we had to think more carefully about the potential cost impact of additional cache traffic.

This is exactly what we built Flat Rate CDN to do. No surprise bills, predictable pricing, and peace of mind to ship the next project.

Get started

All new Pro teams have Flat Rate CDN enabled by default. Existing Pro teams can opt in to the new plan:

  1. Select Billing in the navigation.

  2. Browse to Flat Rate CDN and toggle the setting to on.

  3. Choose a capacity tier that corresponds to your typical usage.

  4. Review your selection, which will show subscription costs if you chose a paid Flat Rate CDN tier.

  5. Select Enable to apply.

Learn more about Flat Rate CDN pricing in the documentation.

title: # GBase Database Decommissioning Strategy: Data Migration, Backup Validation, and Infrastructure Cleanup
description:
Retiring a database environment is a complex engineering task. Removing database software without understanding application dependencies, retention obligations, and recovery requirements can create serious operational and data-governance problems.

A GBase Database decommissioning strategy should therefore begin with data protection rather than software removal.

1. Discover Database Dependencies

Identify:

  • Connected applications.
  • Database users and permissions.
  • Scheduled jobs.
  • External integrations.
  • Monitoring agents.
  • Backup and archive locations.

2. Define the Migration or Retention Strategy

Determine whether the data must be migrated, archived, retained for compliance, or securely destroyed after its retention period.

Document the responsible team and approval process.

3. Validate Backup Recoverability

A backup is not fully trustworthy until its recovery process has been tested.

A controlled verification procedure should include:

  1. Confirming backup completion.
  2. Checking backup integrity.
  3. Recording backup metadata.
  4. Restoring into an isolated environment.
  5. Validating representative records.
  6. Confirming application compatibility where relevant.

Use the backup and restore utilities documented for the specific GBase product and release.

4. Coordinate Application Cutover

Before shutting down the original environment, verify that dependent applications have moved to the approved destination.

A simple connectivity test can be part of the cutover checklist, but a failed connection alone is not sufficient proof that all dependencies have been removed.

5. Perform Controlled Uninstallation

Follow the official GBase uninstall procedure. Confirm that required backups and exports are available before removing database software or data directories.

After removal, inspect services, scheduled tasks, installation metadata, and remaining storage.

Conclusion

GBase Database decommissioning requires coordinated data protection, migration, application cutover, and software removal. A verified lifecycle process helps organizations retire infrastructure without sacrificing important business information.

title: CHORD: Cross-Model Hallucination Detection via Relational Graph Discrimination
description:
arXiv:2610.38314v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Hallucination detection is critical for deploying large language models (LLMs) in real-world applications. Due to strong empirical performance, internal representation-based methods have emerged as the prevailing direction for detecting hallucinations, yet they remain largely model-specific and often fail to generalize to unseen LLMs. In this paper, we study an important yet underexplored problem, termed cross-model hallucination detection (CMHD), which aims to train hallucination detectors on source LLMs while ensuring performance on unseen target LLMs. The core challenge of CMHD lies in cross-model representation heterogeneity: hidden states from different LLMs exhibit severe semantic inconsistency, which limits the transferability of classical representation-based detectors. Through analysis and empirical validation, we show that relational structures over layers, tokens, and features capture transferable detection signals despite semantic inconsistency. Based on this observation, we propose cross-model hallucination detection via heterogeneity-oriented relational discrimination (CHORD), a relational graph discrimination framework that represents hidden states as joint relational graphs over layers, tokens, and features. It feeds these graphs into relation-aware attention to obtain structure-aware features, and uses meta-learning to shape these features toward transferable detection signals. Extensive experiments show that CHORD outperforms representative detection methods in cross-model generalization. Code is available at https://github.com/MiracleworkerD/CHORD.

title: Game-Theoretic Foundations for Undiscounted Bisimulation Metrics
description:
arXiv:2610.38313v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Bisimulation metrics offer a principled notion of task-relevant state similarity in reinforcement learning, but existing constructions and methods are largely confined to discounted MDPs, where contraction arguments ensure well-defined fixed points and downstream guarantees. We develop a unified foundation for bisimulation metrics in undiscounted settings, that is total- and average-reward problems, by replacing the standard operator-centric view with a game-centric one: we interpret prior metric operators as Bellman-Shapley operators of zero-sum turn-based games and define metrics as the corresponding game value functions, yielding unique definitions even when $\gamma=1$. This game-theoretic foundation facilitates transfer of dynamic-programming theory and algorithms. We also use this game-centric perspective to characterize how metric finiteness depends on structural properties of the underlying MDP and motivate certain directed metrics that remain finite in weakly communicating MDPs. We further introduce an abstract framework for modifying the games' action spaces, allowing general transition coupling sets, that recovers many existing metrics and guides new constructions. Finally, we prove that these metrics bound total-reward and, when the optimal gain is state-independent, optimal relative value differences. We also provide error and suboptimality guarantees for aggregation-based planning in total- and average-reward settings.

title: My agent looked fine — until I gave it an empty list
description:
I built a small tool to test my own AI agent in 10 minutes, instead of trusting that it "looked right."

One test from it: "Handle an empty average." The starting code divides by the list length, so an empty list breaks it. The check is simple: handle an empty list safely, keep the normal average, and explain the empty-list behavior.

I ran two answers through it:

  • A fixed answer — check for an empty list first and return 0, otherwise return the normal average — scored 4/4. What-to-fix: "No fix needed for this task."
  • The original, unfixed function scored 3/4. It lost the "Is correct" point. The plain-language fix: tell the agent to check for an empty list first and return 0, and keep the normal average for everything else.

That is the whole point of the tool. It scores 4 things per task: finished, correct, did not make things up, and took no wrong action. Auto-score suggests, you confirm — so you get speed without handing the judgment to a black box.

The tool has 20 tasks: 10 developer, 5 personal-life, and 5 creator. It is free, with no API key, no login, and nothing leaves the page. It is a quick first check, not a CI or production replacement — use it first, then graduate to heavier tools when you need them.

Try this one task yourself: https://jefferson999.github.io/agent-reliability--score/

Paste your agent's answer, see the score, and read what to fix. If your agent passes the empty list, try the other 19.

title: Zero-Downtime DB Sync: Resilient Database Streaming Migration CLI
description:
Migrating multi-gigabyte production databases between servers or database engines (e.g. MySQL to PostgreSQL, or SQLite to cloud databases) traditionally required taking applications offline for hours.

zero-downtime-db-sync is an open-source CLI utility designed to perform live, streaming schema and data migrations with continuous replication and zero application downtime.

seotarek / zero-downtime-db-sync

A resilient, zero-downtime streaming database migration and replication CLI tool for MySQL, PostgreSQL, and SQLite.

Zero-Downtime DB Sync ⚡

A resilient, chunk-based streaming database migration and live data replication CLI tool. Safely migrate gigabyte-scale databases across servers with automatic network checkpointing, zero RAM bloat, and minimal table lock time.

💥 The Problem It Solves

  • Dump & Restore Fails on Large Tables: Traditional mysqldump or pg_dump creates massive files that lock read/write traffic and timeout on unstable networks.
  • Network Dropouts Waste Hours: If an SCP transfer drops at 99%, you typically have to restart from scratch.
  • RAM Spikes Crash Instances: Reading whole tables into memory crashes low-spec VPS or containers.

Zero-Downtime DB Sync streams rows in configurable primary-key batches, tracks the last committed ID in a persistent checkpoint file, and resumes seamlessly if interrupted.

🚀 Key Features

  • Chunked Streaming: Consumes memory in predictable O(chunk_size) bounds using server-side cursors.
  • Fault-Tolerant Checkpointing: Tracks migration progress down to the exact row ID; automatically resumes after network disconnects.
  • Cross-Engine…
View on GitHub

⚙️ How It Works

  1. Initial Parallel Snapshot: Streams existing table rows in concurrent batches using cursor-based pagination.
  2. Change Data Capture (CDC): Listens to WAL / binlog change events to capture real-time writes occurring during the migration.
  3. Atomic Verification: Performs row count and checksum audits across source and destination tables before initiating switchover.

Install and run via CLI:

db-sync migrate --source "mysql://user:pass@host/db" --target "postgres://user:pass@host/db" --live

Contribute and view documentation on GitHub:
👉 https://github.com/seotarek/zero-downtime-db-sync

title: Haunted Stack Traces: Explaining Java Errors with Gemma 4, Running Locally
description:
This is a submission for the Hacktoberfest Open-Source AI Challenge Week 4: Ghost in the Machine

What I Built

Every Java developer knows the moment: the app crashes, the console fills with red, and somewhere in sixty lines of stack trace is the one line that matters.

The Haunted Stack Trace is a Spring Boot error handler possessed by the ghosts of deprecated Java APIs. When the app throws an exception, it does not return a plain 500 page. The stack trace goes to Gemma 4, running locally through Ollama, and a ghost answers: java.util.Date, Vector, Hashtable, Applet or StringTokenizer, whichever fits the crime.

The ghost tells you:

  • the exception and the culprit: the exact line in your code, copied from the trace, not invented
  • the cause, in plain English
  • the fix, practical and specific
  • and then a whisper, because it is Halloween 
{
  "ghost": "java.util.Date",
  "exception": "java.time.format.DateTimeParseException",
  "culprit": "...CursedController.halloweenDate(CursedController.java:63)",
  "cause": "LocalDate.parse expects ISO-8601 (yyyy-MM-dd), but '31/10/2026' is in a different format.",
  "fix": "Use LocalDate.parse(dateString, DateTimeFormatter.ofPattern(\"dd/MM/yyyy\")).",
  "whisper": "You reach for the current moment, but you are trapped in a format of the past."
}

I took the theme literally: the ghosts in the machine are the dead APIs we all still trip over. java.util.Date was replaced by java.time, Vector by ArrayList, and they are still haunting codebases. Here, at least, they are being useful.

There are two ways to wake them:

  • Curse buttons that call endpoints which crash on purpose (NullPointerException, ConcurrentModificationException, DateTimeParseException and others)
  • The séance: paste any Java stack trace from any project, and the ghost explains it

Demo

It runs locally by design, so there is no deployed link. You can run it yourself in about five minutes (instructions in the repo), with your Wi-Fi off if you want to check my claim.

Code

Maurodc90 / haunted-stack-trace

Entry for the DEV Hacktoberfest 2026 Open-Source AI Challenge (Ghost in the Machine). A Spring Boot error handler possessed by ghosts of deprecated Java APIs: explains stack traces with Gemma 4 running locally via Ollama. No API key, nothing leaves your machine.

The Haunted Stack Trace

Write-up: Haunted Stack Traces on DEV

A Spring Boot error handler possessed by the ghosts of deprecated Java APIs.

When the application throws an exception, it does not return a plain 500 page. The stack trace is sent to Gemma 4, an open-weight model running locally through Ollama, and a ghost (java.util.Date, Vector, Hashtable, Applet or StringTokenizer) answers with what broke, the exact line, why it happened and how to fix it. Then it whispers something unsettling.

Everything runs on your machine. No API key, no internet, and no stack trace ever leaves your laptop.

Built as an entry for the DEV Hacktoberfest 2026 Open-Source AI Challenge (Week 4: Ghost in the Machine).

Example

GET /cursed/date calls LocalDate.parse("31/10/2026"):

{
  "ghost": "java.util.Date"
  "exception": "java.time.format.DateTimeParseException",
  "culprit": "com.maurodc90.hauntedstacktrace.controller.CursedController.halloweenDate(CursedController.java:63)",
  "cause"
…
View on GitHub

How I Built It

Stack: Java 21, Spring Boot 4.1, Spring AI 2.0, Ollama, Gemma 4 (12B), plain HTML/CSS/JS, GitHub Actions.

The flow is short:

  1. A controller throws a RuntimeException.
  2. A @RestControllerAdvice catches it and turns the stack trace into text.
  3. GhostService sends the top 25 lines of the trace to Gemma through Spring AI's ChatClient.
  4. BeanOutputConverter maps the reply onto a Java record, Haunting. 
return chatClient.prompt()
        .system(SYSTEM_PROMPT)
        .user(trimmedTrace)
        .options(OllamaChatOptions.builder()
                .model(model)
                .temperature(0.4)
                .disableThinking()
                .numPredict(400))
        .call()
        .entity(converter);

That looks simple. Getting there was not, and the failures taught me more than the success did.

Ghost #1: "structured output is unavailable"

My first version asked Ollama to enforce a JSON Schema for the answer. Ollama replied with HTTP 501 {"error":"structured output is unavailable"} for this Gemma 4 build. Spring AI treated that as a transient error and retried with growing waits, 10 seconds, then 50, so my first request simply hung. I dropped the enforced schema and let BeanOutputConverter put the format instructions into the prompt and parse the reply. The structure still held.

Ghost #2: the request that never ended

Then I typed something that was not a stack trace into the séance box: "give me a new error". Six minutes later it was still summoning. ollama ps showed the model stuck on Stopping.... Nothing limited how long an answer could be.

I added a cap of 400 tokens. Now real stack traces came back empty: No content to map due to end-of-input.

The cause: Gemma 4 thinks silently before it answers, and that reasoning counts towards the token budget. On nonsense input it reasoned forever. With a cap, it spent the whole budget thinking and never wrote the JSON. One line, disableThinking(), fixed both problems and made answers faster.

Ghost #3: garbage in

The real fix for nonsense input was to never send it to the model at all. The séance now checks for at least one stack frame (at com.example.Foo.bar(Foo.java:42)) before calling Gemma. Anything else gets an instant refusal from the ghost of Applet: "You knock, but bring no bones. The dead answer only to stack traces."

Smaller decisions that mattered

  • Facts and role-play live in separate fields. The joke never leaks into the fix.
  • RuntimeException, not Exception. A browser asking for favicon.ico raises NoResourceFoundException. If I caught every Exception, every 404 would wake the model.
  • A fallback answer. If the model fails, the handler still responds instead of crashing inside the crash handler.
  • textContent, never innerHTML. Model output is never treated as HTML on the page.
  • Tests without a model. The controller tests mock GhostService, so GitHub Actions runs them on every push without Ollama.

Where the ghost stops

I pasted a trace from a bug in my own Expense Tracker: two Lombok @Data entities, AppUser and Expense, whose generated hashCode() methods call each other until the stack overflows. The ghost of Vector found the loop between the two classes immediately. But its fix was generic, because the trace never mentions Lombok. The real fix, @EqualsAndHashCode.Exclude on the relationship, was mine. The ghost is a good colleague, not an oracle, and I think that is the honest way to use these tools.

Why Does Open Innovation Matter?

Because stack traces are not harmless. They contain package names, class names, file paths, sometimes values. Pasting your company's stack traces into a hosted AI service means your company's code leaving the building. With an open-weight model on my own machine, nothing leaves. That is not a feature I bolted on. It is the reason the project exists.

What open made possible here:

  • It works offline and costs nothing to run. No API key, no rate limit, no bill per crash.
  • I could see inside it when it broke. When a request hung, ollama ps showed me the model stuck on Stopping..., and I restarted it myself. When answers came back empty, I could turn thinking off with one flag. With a closed API, I would have been looking at a timeout and guessing.
  • Swapping is one line. The model name lives in application.yml. If 12B is too weak for someone's traces, they can try gemma4:26b. Spring AI's ChatClient hides the provider, so the same code could point at a hosted model if a team chose to.

To be fair to closed models: a large hosted model would probably write better fixes for unusual traces. But for this job, explaining everyday exceptions on a developer's own laptop, a 12B open model was good enough, and its privacy was worth more than the extra quality.

My Agent Session

I built this pair-programming with Claude. Claude wrote most of the code. I decided what to build, ran and tested every step, hit every bug above on my own machine, chose the fixes, and reviewed the code until I could explain each part. I'm a junior Java developer, and working this way, fast with AI but understanding every line, is how I want to work.

The Spirit of It

The moment it landed was not a test passing. It was explaining the project to my partner, who does not write code.

I said: imagine an app that tells you every day which chair I sit in at class. One day I don't come. The app looks for me, finds nothing, and crashes. That is a NullPointerException. Java's message says what happened, in a language only programmers read. This app explains why, in plain words, through a ghost.

She understood it in one go. That's the point of the project: a crash is just a ghost of something you expected to be there.

Prize Categories

  • Best Use of Gemma: Gemma 4 (12B) runs locally through Ollama and is the core of the app.
  • Best Use of GitHub Copilot: the project is automated with GitHub Actions; every push runs the test suite on GitHub's runners.

Question for you: what is the most cursed stack trace you have ever met? Paste it in the comments and I will summon a ghost for it.

title: Beyond Low-Pass Dynamics: Frequency-Selective Spiking Reservoirs with Resonant Neurons
description:
arXiv:2610.37906v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Spiking reservoir computing combines the training efficiency of fixed recurrent reservoirs with the energy efficiency of event-driven inference, where computation is triggered by sparse spikes rather than executed densely at every timestep. However, existing spiking reservoirs almost exclusively rely on Leaky Integrate-and-Fire (LIF) neurons, whose low-pass dynamics limit their ability to distinguish information encoded at different temporal frequencies. We introduce HRF-Res, a liquid state machine in which LIF neurons are replaced by a heterogeneous population of Harmonic Resonate-and-Fire (HRF) neurons. These neurons exhibit intrinsic oscillatory dynamics and selectively respond to input frequencies, enabling the reservoir to capture frequency-specific temporal patterns. The result is more discriminative representations and higher classification accuracy than LIF-based reservoirs, achieved without sacrificing the energy efficiency of spiking computation, with up to 19x lower energy consumption than an equivalent non-spiking oscillatory reservoir. Evaluated on ten benchmarks spanning time series, sequential images, audio spike trains, and neuromorphic vision, HRF-Res achieves state-of-the-art accuracy among spiking reservoir methods. These results demonstrate that introducing frequency-selective dynamics into spiking reservoirs improves representational quality and classification performance while preserving their inherent energy efficiency.

title: GAUSS: A Workload-Aware Analytical and Monte-Carlo Simulator for LLM Inference Serving
description:
arXiv:2610.37989v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Large language model (LLM) inference has become an operational workload that fleets must provision, monitor, and bill against latency service-level objectives (SLOs). A single throughput number cannot answer the questions operators actually face, because generative serving couples two phases with very different service characteristics, continuous batching reshapes the effective service process, and user-visible tail latency can degrade long before aggregate throughput saturates. We present GAUSS, a workload-aware analytical and Monte-Carlo simulator that predicts the full distributions of time-to-first-token (TTFT) and time-between-tokens (TBT), together with the sustainable request rate, for a given workload, engine, and accelerator. GAUSS pairs calibrated, phase-specific latency surfaces for prefill and decode with a Lindley-recurrence model of queueing under stochastic arrivals and estimates performance by ensemble Monte-Carlo sampling rather than by replaying a single trace. This lets GAUSS reason about workloads, routing policies, and hardware that have never been deployed, and to capture the latency tails that trace-driven simulators systematically under-sample. We describe the model and show how it supports operating-point selection, traffic segmentation, and shortest-remaining-processing-time scheduling capacity questions that trace-driven simulators cannot address.

title: What Constitutes Food Similarity? Visual Representations and Retrieval in Indian Cuisine
description:
arXiv:2610.37867v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Food similarity underlies retrieval, recommendation, substitution, and other food computing tasks, yet food representations are typically evaluated by identity preservation. We ask what happens to food similarity beyond identity: how different visual representations organize foods into relational neighborhoods, what culinary relationships these neighborhoods reveal or obscure, and how consistently these structures emerge across representations. Indian cuisine provides a challenging setting in which visually similar foods may have different culinary identities, while foods within a culinary family can vary substantially in appearance. Using an expanded Khana dataset and seven pretrained visual representations spanning convolutional, transformer-based, self-supervised, and image-text aligned models, we evaluate image-to-image retrieval and image-to-dish neighborhoods, examining culinary-family structure, contrast cases, and cross-representation agreement. We also aggregate image representations to compare dish-level visual similarity across models and against recipe-derived similarity for the same dishes. Image-level neighborhoods vary substantially across representations, including similarities across culinary-family boundaries. At the dish level, aggregation reveals common visual structure despite local variation, but this structure corresponds less strongly with recipe-derived similarity. These findings show that recognition performance alone cannot characterize relational structure: food similarity depends on representation, modality, and abstraction level rather than being a fixed property of the food collection. Understanding these structures is therefore a prerequisite to combining multiple food information modalities into a coherent notion of similarity.

title: If you're looking for what comes after wire, take a look at kanna-di
description:
For a long time, compile-time DI in Go meant google/wire. But wire is no longer taking new features, and every so often the question comes up: what do you use instead?

This post introduces kanna-di, which I wrote to sit in that spot. Like wire, the generated code is plain Go and imports nothing at run time. The difference is that you register no providers.

What was tedious

Think about what you write for wire:

  • a wire.go with //go:build wireinject, where you declare the injector's signature yourself
  • wire.NewSet to collect providers, passed to wire.Build
  • wire.Bind for every interface
  • and every time you add a constructor, you add it to some set

In other words, telling wire which functions to use is a separate job, living somewhere other than the code. Constructors already sit next to their types. You're listing them a second time.

How kanna-di thinks about it

With kanna-di, you mark the struct that will be the container, and that's it. It looks at each field's type, finds the constructor next to that type, follows that constructor's parameters recursively, and writes a constructor that calls everything in order.

Take a layered application. The register-user use case depends on a repository for persistence and a sender for the welcome mail. Each layer keeps its constructors next to its types, as usual:

// package user, the domain
type Repository interface {
    Save(ctx context.Context, u User) error
    Find(ctx context.Context, id ID) (User, error)
}

// package mail, the domain
type Sender interface {
    Send(ctx context.Context, m Message) error
}

// package usecase
func NewRegisterUser(repo user.Repository, mailer mail.Sender) *RegisterUser
func NewGetUser(repo user.Repository) *GetUser

// package postgres, the infrastructure
func NewUserRepository(db *sql.DB) *UserRepository

// package sendgrid, an external API
func NewSender(cfg config.Config) *Sender

// package handler
func NewUser(registerUser *usecase.RegisterUser, getUser *usecase.GetUser) *User

// package config
func Load() (Config, error)

The composition root already has a struct that holds what the program is made of: the server. Mark it //kanna:container.

package main

//go:generate go tool kanna-di

//kanna:container
type server struct {
    _ user.Repository `di:"with=postgres.NewUserRepository"`
    _ mail.Sender     `di:"with=sendgrid.NewSender"`

    users *handler.User
}

func (s *server) routes() http.Handler {
    mux := http.NewServeMux()
    mux.HandleFunc("POST /users", s.users.Register)
    mux.HandleFunc("GET /users/{id}", s.users.Get)
    return mux
}

func openDB(cfg config.Config) (*sql.DB, func(), error) {
    db, err := sql.Open("pgx", cfg.DSN)
    if err != nil {
        return nil, nil, err
    }
    return db, func() { db.Close() }, nil
}

What only this root can decide is written next to it: which implementation serves each of the domain's two interfaces (with=), and how to open what the standard library provides (openDB). Nothing else.

go generate ./... writes di_gen.go:

// Code generated by kanna-di. DO NOT EDIT.

package main

import (
    "example.com/shop/internal/config"
    "example.com/shop/internal/handler"
    "example.com/shop/internal/infra/postgres"
    "example.com/shop/internal/infra/sendgrid"
    "example.com/shop/internal/usecase"
)

// newServer initializes dependencies and constructs server.
func newServer() (*server, func(), error) {
    cfg, err := config.Load()
    if err != nil {
        return nil, nil, err
    }
    db, cleanup, err := openDB(cfg)
    if err != nil {
        return nil, nil, err
    }
    repo := postgres.NewUserRepository(db)
    mailer := sendgrid.NewSender(cfg)
    registerUser := usecase.NewRegisterUser(repo, mailer)
    getUser := usecase.NewGetUser(repo)
    users := handler.NewUser(registerUser, getUser)

    return &server{
        users: users,
    }, cleanup, nil
}

*usecase.RegisterUser comes from usecase.NewRegisterUser. *sql.DB comes from openDB, next to the container. user.Repository and mail.Sender come from the implementations the container named. config.Config is loaded once and shared by openDB and sendgrid.NewSender. Nothing is registered anywhere. When a constructor's parameters change, the next go generate changes the code that calls it.

func main() {
    s, cleanup, err := newServer()
    if err != nil {
        log.Fatal(err)
    }
    defer cleanup()

    log.Print(http.ListenAndServe(":8080", s.routes()))
}

How providers are found

"The function next to the type" has a precise definition. When a type is needed, kanna-di takes the first of these that has one:

  1. an argument of the constructor (di:"arg")
  2. the provider the container chose for the type (di:"with=...")
  3. an exported field of a struct the container embeds or declares as _
  4. a function in the container's own package
  5. an exported function in the package declaring the type, when that package is in your module or go.work

Finding none stops generation. So do two at the same level. A helper in a testutil package or a fixture returning the same type changes nothing unless the container names it. The standard library and other modules are never searched: io does have a function returning an io.Writer, and you would not want it picked for you.

Errors say which field

The part of DI that eats your time is when resolution fails. kanna-di's errors trace the need back to the field it started from.

The most common mistake with an interface is forgetting with=:

./server.go:12:2: error: nothing provides mail.Sender, which usecase.NewRegisterUser needs
  via server.users → handler.NewUser → usecase.NewRegisterUser
  return one from a function in package main, take it with di:"arg", or choose a provider with di:"with=..."

When there are two candidates, both positions are shown along with how to choose:

./server.go:11:2: error: 2 functions in package usecase return *usecase.GetUser
  usecase.NewGetUser (../../internal/usecase/get_user.go:12:6)
  usecase.NewCachedGetUser (../../internal/usecase/get_user.go:30:6)
  via server.users → handler.NewUser
  choose one with _ *usecase.GetUser `di:"with=usecase.NewGetUser"`

Typos get a did you mean, and if the implementation chosen with with= does not satisfy the interface, the error names the missing method.

Taking a container apart in tests

This is where I think the difference from wire is largest.

In tests you want the repository swapped for an in-memory one and the mail sender for something that only records. With wire, that means another injector and another set. With kanna-di, you declare a container in a _test.go file and embed the production server.

//kanna:container
type testServer struct {
    *server

    _ user.Repository `di:"arg"`
    _ mail.Sender     `di:"arg"`
}

func TestRegisterUser(t *testing.T) {
    sent := &mailtest.Recorder{}
    s := newTestServer(memory.NewUserRepository(), sent)
    srv := httptest.NewServer(s.routes())
    defer srv.Close()

    // POST /users ...

    if len(sent.Messages) != 1 {
        t.Fatalf("want 1 welcome mail, got %d", len(sent.Messages))
    }
}

Embedding a container from the same package rebuilds it here, field by field. Because the two interfaces are now declared as arguments, the with= bindings are unused, and nothing needs *sql.DB or config.Config anymore. So openDB, config.Load, and sendgrid.NewSender are never called, and newTestServer returns neither a cleanup nor an error. In production the root chooses the implementations; in tests you pass them in. That's all.

The output goes to di_gen_test.go. The chicken-and-egg problem, where the test calls newTestServer before it has been generated, is handled by kanna-di: it type-checks once more with what it is about to write in place, so a call to a not-yet-generated constructor does not stop it.

In a real application

showcase is a gRPC todo service that uses kanna-di across its layers:

  • internal/di holds the Config and Infra containers; NewInfra assembles the pgx pool and the transactor
  • each operation in usecase is a container of its own; NewPutTodo and NewDeleteTodo are generated
  • the handler container bundles the use cases into NewHandler

A use case looks like this:

//kanna:container
type DeleteTodo struct {
    _ *infra.Deps // infra.NewDeps provides it; its Transactor and Todos fill the fields below

    transactor tx.Transactor
    todos      repository.Todo
}

A struct in a _ field is not stored; it only serves the container. The use case takes exactly what it needs from what the infrastructure bundled.

A struct with no fields, such as the todov1.UnimplementedTodoServiceServer a gRPC handler embeds, is left at its zero value. No provider is needed for it.

Cleanup

Providers returning T, func() or T, func(), error have their cleanups collected into one. They run in reverse order, and when a provider fails, the cleanups of those that ran before it are called before the error is returned. Same behavior as wire. Anything taken as an argument or drawn from an embedded struct belongs to the caller and is never closed.

The honest part

  • Requires Go 1.26. It is designed to be installed with go get -tool
  • It is v0, written by one person, and the API still moves
  • A generic struct cannot be a container: there is no way to choose its type arguments
  • Within one directory, test containers can live in either the in-package test package or the external _test package, not both
  • Rule 5 (searching the type's own package) only covers your module and go.work. Constructors in dependencies are never picked up automatically. This is deliberate

kanna-di is one of the kanna family of generators, but it stands on its own. It shares nothing with the other tools, and the generated code calls only your functions.

Try it 

go get -tool github.com/go-kanna/di/cmd/kanna-di

Mark the struct with //kanna:container, add //go:generate go tool kanna-di, run go generate ./....

If you're coming from wire: the functions you listed in wire.NewSet are, most likely, already next to their types. wire.Bind becomes _ Iface \di:"with=pkg.NewImpl"``, and the injector declaration goes away.

The repository has an example/ directory with the layout from this post, runnable as is.

Disclosure: kanna-di is a rewrite of mickamy/injector, an earlier tool of mine. The idea is the same: a container struct, and constructors found next to their types. The inject tag became di, the directive became //kanna:container, and embedded test containers and cleanup handling were added. injector is archived; development continues here.

title: DEAD INTERNET 🕸️: Lost Online. Found Again.
description:
An Open-Source AI Digital Archaeology Platform | Local AI | Ollama | React | FastAPI

What happens when a website disappears?

A personal homepage that someone spent years building. A forum where people once shared ideas. A small community that slowly stopped posting. A software project that was abandoned halfway through.

The internet moves forward, but not everything gets preserved.

Sometimes, all that remains are fragments: old HTML files, text backups, disconnected conversations, timestamps, and incomplete documentation.

We wanted to explore what it would look like to investigate those fragments instead of simply reading them.

That's how DEAD INTERNET came to life.

What We Built

DEAD INTERNET is an open-source, local-first digital archaeology platform that turns preserved digital documents into interactive investigations.

Instead of treating archived files as disconnected pieces of text, the platform lets you explore them, discover clues, connect evidence, reconstruct timelines, and investigate what might have happened.

It combines deterministic evidence discovery with an optional local AI investigator powered by Ollama.

The idea is simple:

Don't just browse the remains of the internet. Investigate them.

Exploring The Archives

The platform includes four fictional investigations, each with interconnected documents, clues, timeline events, and a predefined solution.

1. The Last Homepage

A personal website preserved through an old backup. Explore its pages, metadata, and fragments to reconstruct the story behind the abandoned homepage.

2. The Empty Forum

A once-active online community with fragmented discussions and disconnected conversations. Piece together what happened through its surviving posts.

3. The Lost Project

An abandoned software project with documentation, development notes, and incomplete records. Investigate the decisions and events that led to its disappearance.

4. The Forgotten Blog

A collection of disconnected blog posts with missing context. Follow references and timestamps to understand the story behind them.

Each archive is designed as a compact, playable mystery rather than a collection of unrelated sample documents.

Inside An Investigation: The Forgotten Blog

One of the sample investigations is called The Forgotten Blog.

The Paper Moon blog survives as three entries and an export note. At first glance, the recovered files seem to predict a station fire.

But is that actually what happened?

The investigation asks:

Did Paper Moon predict a real fire, or does the recovered ordering hide a different explanation?

Examining The Recovered Documents

The Archive Explorer provides a preserved-file browser alongside a read-only document viewer.

Screenshot 1: The Recovered Clock Entry

The first document, 01-the-clock.md, introduces the mysterious station incident through a story dated June 9, 1987, but published in February 2005.

Screenshot 2: Following The Next Document

The second entry, 02-the-platform.md, adds an important detail: the character had already taken the last bus. It also includes an author's note explaining that the station name was borrowed from an old photograph and the characters were fictional.

The second document changes how the first entry should be interpreted.

That's the kind of interaction we wanted to build: a small collection of preserved documents that gradually reveals a larger story.

How The Investigation Works

The experience follows a simple investigation workflow.

1. Explore The Archive

Select an investigation from the archive library. Browse preserved documents, inspect their contents, and examine available metadata.

2. Discover Clues

Collect predefined evidence from documents. Each discovered clue connects to supporting artifacts and contributes to the investigation.

3. Connect The Evidence

The Clue Board brings discovered evidence together so you can understand relationships between different documents.

4. Reconstruct The Timeline

Relevant events appear chronologically with references to their supporting artifacts.

5. Ask The AI Investigator

Ask questions about the archive, explore possible relationships, identify contradictions, and request evidence-based summaries.

6. Generate An Investigation Report

Review your findings and export the investigation as a Markdown report.

The predefined solutions are independent of AI-generated interpretations. Collecting evidence, completing investigations, and accessing fictional ground-truth solutions do not depend on Ollama.

Investigate Your Own Archives

We also wanted DEAD INTERNET to work beyond the four sample mysteries.

That's where My Own Archive comes in.

Users can import their own preserved digital documents:

  • HTML and HTM files
  • TXT files
  • Markdown files
  • ZIP archives containing supported documents

The platform extracts readable text and available metadata while preserving original filenames.

Imported archives use the same investigation engine as the predefined cases.

Uploaded content is treated as evidence, not executable code. HTML is displayed as escaped source text rather than a live webpage.

One important distinction: imported archives provide document observations, not fabricated mystery solutions. The platform investigates what is actually present in the supplied files.

How We Built It

We wanted the architecture to remain modular and relatively lightweight. The same investigation engine needed to work with both fictional sample archives and user-imported documents.

Technology Stack

Component Technology
Frontend React, JavaScript, Vite
Styling Tailwind CSS
Navigation React Router
Icons Lucide React
Backend Python, FastAPI
Database SQLite
Validation Pydantic
Local AI Ollama
Testing pytest

Architecture

The application follows a straightforward architecture:

React + Vite Frontend
        |
        v
Centralized API Client
        |
        v
    FastAPI Backend
        |
        |---- Archive Service
        |         |
        |         v
        |       SQLite
        |
        |---- File Ingestion
        |
        |---- Clue Engine
        |
        |---- AI Investigator
                  |
                  v
                Ollama
             Local Model

The backend is divided into dedicated modules:

  • main.py handles API routes.
  • archive_service.py manages archives, artifacts, and investigation state.
  • file_ingestion.py validates and extracts uploaded documents.
  • clue_engine.py handles deterministic clues, timelines, and reports.
  • ai_investigator.py manages local model interactions.
  • schemas.py defines request and response structures.

This separation keeps the investigation logic independent of the frontend and makes it easier to extend the platform with additional archive types.

Bringing AI Into Digital Archaeology

One of the central parts of DEAD INTERNET is its local AI investigator.

We chose Ollama because we wanted developers to experiment with open-weight language models without requiring hosted AI APIs or paid API keys.

The application communicates with Ollama locally through its generation endpoint.

The AI Investigator supports:

  • Potential clue extraction.
  • Identifying relationships between documents.
  • Detecting possible contradictions.
  • Answering questions about archived content.
  • Suggesting chronological events.
  • Generating investigation summaries.

Evidence Before Intelligence

An AI model can produce a convincing explanation even when the source documents don't support it. That's particularly dangerous in an investigation tool.

So we designed DEAD INTERNET to distinguish three things:

Facts: Information directly supported by supplied documents.

Hypotheses: Possible interpretations and relationships that require further investigation.

Unknowns: Questions that the available evidence cannot answer.

AI responses include source filenames and relevant excerpts. The backend validates citation filenames, artifact scope, and quoted text against the supplied evidence.

AI-generated interpretations do not automatically become verified clues or timeline events.

If Ollama is unavailable, the application reports the failure instead of pretending that an investigation succeeded.

The deterministic investigation workflow continues to work without AI.

Handling Uploaded Archives Safely

Allowing users to upload old websites and documents introduces another challenge: untrusted files.

We wanted the application to treat uploaded content as evidence, not executable code.

Some of the precautions include:

  • File-type and size validation.
  • Limits on document count and total upload size.
  • ZIP path-traversal protection.
  • Rejection of encrypted, nested, and unsupported archive members.
  • In-memory ZIP processing rather than extracting arbitrary files to disk.
  • HTML displayed as escaped source text rather than an executable webpage.
  • Separate investigations with archive-scoped artifact access.

Uploaded content stays in the locally configured SQLite database. When AI analysis is requested, relevant excerpts are sent to the configured Ollama service.

This is a local-first design, not a claim of complete security. The current MVP does not include authentication, encryption at rest, or multi-user access controls.

What Makes This Project Interesting?

We didn't want DEAD INTERNET to become another AI wrapper where the entire experience depends on a model generating text.

The investigation engine and the AI investigator have different responsibilities.

The deterministic system manages evidence, progress, predefined solutions, and reports.

The AI helps explore possible interpretations of the available documents.

That distinction means users can still complete investigations without installing a model.

It also makes the project easier to extend without turning every feature into an AI-generated response.

Testing And Verification

The project includes a focused backend test suite covering:

  • Archive and artifact retrieval.
  • File validation and safe ZIP extraction.
  • Clue discovery and timeline construction.
  • Independent investigation state.
  • AI evidence validation and missing citations.
  • Ollama connection failures and timeouts.
  • Investigation report generation.

The verification commands are:

.\.venv\Scripts\python.exe -m pytest tests -q

npm.cmd --prefix frontend run build

The Ollama failure tests use mocked transport, so they don't require a running model. A separate live-model smoke test is needed to evaluate actual inference quality.

What's Next?

There is still plenty of room to take this further.

Some areas we'd like to explore:

  • More advanced document parsing and metadata extraction.
  • Better retrieval across larger collections of documents.
  • Stronger claim-level evidence verification.
  • More sophisticated relationships between artifacts.
  • Archive backup, deletion, and retention controls.
  • More sample investigations with richer narratives.
  • Improved evaluation of local models on evidence-based questions.

The goal is to make digital archaeology more interactive while keeping the underlying evidence inspectable.

Team Credits

DEAD INTERNET is a collaborative project built with my friend @pranitha_prakash_6c8f7ad7.

We worked on bringing together local AI inference, preserved digital archives, evidence-based investigations, and an interface that turns exploring forgotten internet fragments into something interactive.

Project Repository: DEAD INTERNET on GitHub

The project is open source under the MIT License. Contributions, feedback, and ideas for exploring digital archaeology are welcome.

Built with React, FastAPI, SQLite, Ollama, and a little curiosity about the parts of the internet we leave behind.

🕸️

title: Is Agentic now tailors its audit by site type
description:
Is Agentic reports now let you view your checks through one of four site types: Docs & content, Business, App, or Commerce.

For example, the Commerce view highlights payment and checkout standards like x402, UCP, and ACP, while the App view highlights API discovery, authentication, error handling, and SDK support.

Your score stays the same in every view, and you can change views on an existing report without rescanning. Only the highlighted checks change, so you can focus on what matters for your kind of site while keeping scores comparable across sites.

To set the default view, add a single meta tag to your page's <head>:

Set the value to match your site type:

  • content for Docs & content

  • business for Business

  • app for App

  • store for Commerce

The tag only sets which view readers see first. It doesn't add points or change your score. If no type is declared, Is Agentic infers one and shows which type it chose.

Run a check at is-agentic.com or read the documentation.

title: UI Framework for Humans and AI Agents: 6 Platforms, 900 KB, Rust/C/C++/ASM
description:
I've been working on uison, a lightweight UI framework in Rust, and wanted to share it:

  • Tiny footprint: About 900 KB in size.
  • Cross-platform: Runs on Windows (x64, ARM), macOS, Linux, Android, iOS/iPadOS, and WASM.
  • Dual-mode rendering: Renders a graphical UI for humans or exposes the UI structure and actions via MCP (Model Context Protocol) as JSON, allowing AI agents to interact with it without screenshots.
  • SSH UI Forwarding: Thanks to the JSON representation, you can easily pipe and forward the UI over SSH.
  • Polyglot examples: Comes with usage examples in Rust, C, C++, and even ASM.

uisonlab / uison

A tiny (<900 KB) cross-platform Rust UI framework with C/C++/ASM bindings that compiles JSON layout diffs to native pixels, featuring MCP integration for AI agents and SSH UI forwarding.

uison

🇬🇧 English · 🇨🇳 中文 · 🇮🇳 हिन्दी · 🇪🇸 Español · 🇫🇷 Français · 🇸🇦 العربية · 🇧🇩 বাংলা · 🇧🇷 Português · 🇷🇺 Русский · 🇵🇰 اردو · 🇮🇩 Bahasa Indonesia · 🇩🇪 Deutsch · 🇯🇵 日本語 · 🇮🇳 मराठी · 🇮🇳 తెలుగు · 🇹🇷 Türkçe · 🇺🇦 Українська

uison (UI + JSON) is a tiny, fast UI framework written in Rust with no dependencies at all — only the standard library, down to its own JSON parser. You describe a screen as a tree of elements: in a JSON file, with a Rust DSL, with C++ widgets in the style of Flutter or as JSON right inside C code. The logic is ordinary code in Rust, C or C++: handlers, data, threads. uison takes care of the window, layout, drawing and input, and the same program runs on macOS, Windows, Linux (Wayland and X11), iOS, Android…

View on GitHub

How I Built It

I used Opus 5.5 in Visual Studio Code to build the framework. My role was to come up with the idea, give direction, and review and verify the results.

It took about three weekend days and roughly a week of evenings in my free time outside work. I tested it on all supported platforms, both automatically and manually.

The Key Idea: JSON Everywhere

Although passing JSON around has become something of a running joke, in this case I think it's justified. The protocol is simple from the lowest level up, so you don't have to spend much time learning it, and here that matters more than rendering speed (the framework is not for complex graphics).

The lowest layer of the framework can render only a JSON frame consisting of 9 primitives. Here they are:

Primitive Geometry Properties Description
rect [x, y, w, h] fill, stroke, width, radius Rectangle, including rounded corners
line [x1, y1, x2, y2] color, width, cap (butt / round) Line segment
circle [cx, cy, r] fill, stroke, width Circle
tri [x1, y1, x2, y2, x3, y3] fill, stroke, width Triangle (arrows, checkmarks)
poly [[x, y], [x, y], …] fill, stroke, width Closed polygon (chart sectors, custom shapes)
text "one line" at: [x, y], size, color, font, bold, italic Line of text; wrapping is handled by the screen layer
image [x, y, w, h] src, fit (cover / contain / fill), radius Image
clip [x, y, w, h] items: […] Group clipped to a rectangle (scrolling)
hit [x, y, w, h] id, cursor Invisible area for mouse and touch input (not drawn)

At the next level up, familiar controls such as Row, Text, IconButton, and others are added to JSON. As JSON containing complex elements passes down to the lowest level, it is transformed so that only these 9 primitives remain.

All of this made it possible to quickly adapt the framework to all 6 platforms known to humanity: Windows, macOS, Linux, Android, iOS and Browser (WASM).

Custom Controls

At the highest level, users can add their own controls in Rust or directly in JSON. At the lowest layer, the new controls become JSON consisting of the same 9 primitives.

Render Only What Changed (Damage Tracking)

Frames are compared element-by-element using LCS alignment to generate "damage" regions. The backend then redraws only those modified regions instead of the whole screen.

Thanks to built-in list virtualization, an inbox with 2,000 emails only ever renders the ~20 visible rows at any given time.

Building on this concept, I even made a lightweight web browser. It supports a subset of HTML and CSS, which is parsed into JSON and fed straight to the framework. uison knows nothing about HTML or CSS — it just receives standard JSON and renders it like any native UI.

UI over SSH

Since the interface is native JSON, your app can run completely headless. The program on the server knows nothing about SSH: it writes frames to stdout and reads user events from stdin. The server needs only sshd — no X11, VNC, or browser.

The same screen as a raw JSON stream:

Taking It Further: Native Modes for AI Agents

The exact same binary runs in multiple modes with zero code changes: open a graphical window for humans (default), stream raw JSON over SSH (--console), or expose semantic state to AI agents and scripts (--agent / --mcp).

With --mcp, your app becomes a server for Claude Code or Cursor. Agents inspect the UI via snapshot, send actions like click or type, and receive only lightweight diffs, all while respecting UI rules like disabled buttons.

Size

Comparing two versions of a real open-source Disk Usage application for macOS, both written in Rust:

  • egui version: 5.1 MB
  • uison version: 0.9 MB (an 82% reduction in application size)

Both release builds use LTO, codegen-units = 1, panic = "abort" and strip = true. The uison version uses opt-level = "s", the egui version opt-level = 3. Part of the difference is that uison uses the system's text and graphics (CoreText, CoreGraphics on macOS) instead of bundling fonts and an OpenGL renderer.

Quick Start

Everything is covered in the tutorials: Rust, C, C++, and a brief introduction to ASM. Here I'll show how to get started with Rust.

Step 1. Create a project and add uison

cargo new hello && cd hello
cargo add uison

Step 2. Replace src/main.rs

use uison::prelude::*;

fn main() {
    let screen = center(column().gap(12).cross("center").children([
        text("Pressed {@n} times").size(20),
        button("+1").key("inc").on_click(|cx| cx.data.edit("n", |n: &mut i32| *n += 1)),
    ]));
    let mut ui = Ui::from_node(screen).with_size(320.0, 200.0);
    ui.data.set("n", 0);
    run(ui, "Hello");
}

Step 3. Run it

cargo run --release

A window with a counter will open. {@n} is a data binding: the handler changes n, and the text updates automatically, without manual redrawing.

Status

The project is young (version 0.2.1) and the API may change. It's MIT licensed. Not done yet: accessibility (screen readers), IME for Chinese, Japanese and Korean on the desktop, right-to-left text, and more than one window per program.

Links

For anyone interested, everything you need can be found at these links:

  • GitHub repository: uisonlab/uison
  • Tutorials
  • SSH player for running a program remotely: uisonlab/uison-ssh-player
  • WASM demo on GitHub Pages

I'd be glad to hear feedback on the API and the JSON format. Issues and stars are welcome!

title: Why Your Redis Values Look Like Garbage in Every GUI (and How to Fix It)
description:
You connect your Redis GUI to the database your service writes to. You click a key. You get this:

\xac\xed\x00\x05sr\x00\x1dcom.example.order.OrderDetail\x00\x00\x00...

Or, depending on the client, a wall of �.

This is not a bug in Redis and it is not a broken client. It is a serialization problem — and the real problem is not that nobody supports it. Most clients do. RedisInsight has shipped a Java serialized objects formatter since 2.10 (September 2022), Another Redis Desktop Manager has a JavaSerialize viewer, and both use the same library I do (java-object-serialization).

The problem is that the default is still UTF-8, you have to know the feature exists to switch, and what you get after switching differs a lot between clients.

I maintain RedisME, an open-source Redis GUI. This post covers four things: why the bytes look like that, why the usual workarounds hurt, why "supported" and "usable" are different claims, and what to do with formats nobody ships a decoder for.

Redis stores bytes. Types are your client's problem.

RESP is binary-safe. SET foo bar stores three bytes — 0x62 0x61 0x72. GET foo returns those three bytes. Redis has no idea what they mean.

So when a Java service writes an OrderDetail object, what actually happens is:

// Spring Data Redis' default, effectively
RedisSerializer<Object> serializer = new JdkSerializationRedisSerializer();
byte[] bytes = serializer.serialize(orderDetail);

JdkSerializationRedisSerializer goes through ObjectOutputStream, which emits a stream starting with a fixed magic number:

Bytes Meaning
0xAC 0xED STREAM_MAGIC
0x00 0x05 STREAM_VERSION

That is your \xac\xed\x00\x05. It is a perfectly valid Java serialization stream, and it is an illegal UTF-8 byte sequence. By default, a GUI just decodes as UTF-8:

bytes -> decode as UTF-8 -> fail -> print � or \xNN -> done

That is not laziness. Doing it properly needs format detection, a runtime that can deserialize, and handling for every case where deserialization fails. So the capability is usually built in but off by default — you have to know it exists and remember to switch.

Five serializers, five kinds of garbage

Java teams do not have one way to write objects to Redis. They have at least five, and each produces completely different bytes:

Serializer Where you see it What's stored GUI shows
JdkSerializationRedisSerializer Spring Data Redis default binary stream, starts AC ED 00 05 garbage
StringRedisSerializer manual toString() / JSON strings {"id":10086,...} readable
Jackson2JsonRedisSerializer explicit config JSON text readable
GenericJackson2JsonRedisSerializer JSON with @class {"@class":"com...","id":...} readable, with type noise
Redisson Codec (Kryo / FST / Marshalling / JSON) Redisson client custom binary header garbage
Protobuf / Hessian / in-house custom RPC stacks binary garbage

One table explains a lot of confusion. The moment a team migrates serializers, or runs Spring Data Redis and Redisson side by side, the same database holds multiple formats at once. And the default dropdown still says UTF-8.

Worse, many developers do not know which serializer their RedisTemplate uses, because someone else configured it three years ago and it was injected with @Autowired.

The three workarounds, and why they hurt

If clients support this, why do people still do it? Because it is off by default, because plenty of developers do not know the feature exists, and because not every client ships it — TinyRDM's built-in decoders cover Base64/GZip/Msgpack/PHP/Pickle but not Java, so you wire up an external command; RESP.app has no Java formatter at all.

1. redis-cli --raw

redis-cli -h 10.0.0.1 --raw get order:10086

--raw only turns off redis-cli's output escaping. The bytes are unchanged. You get unprintable characters, and on some terminals you will need to reset afterwards.

2. A throwaway main method

public static void main(String[] args) throws Exception {
    byte[] raw = Files.readAllBytes(Paths.get("dump.bin"));
    Object o = new ObjectInputStream(new ByteArrayInputStream(raw)).readObject();
    System.out.println(JSON.toJSONString(o));
}

This works. The workflow is: copy Base64 out of the GUI, save to a file, base64-decode, run Java, read output. Five steps to look at one key. And readObject needs the class on the classpath, so you will spend most of your time fighting ClassNotFoundException in a scratch project that does not have your domain classes.

3. DUMP + an online decoder

DUMP output includes an RDB version header and a CRC64 checksum — it is not the same as the raw GET bytes. And pasting production data into a third-party website is not a tradeoff worth discussing.

All three share the same flaw: they turn a two-second "let me look at this value" into a cross-tool, cross-process workflow. When you are debugging, you need to click through five keys and confirm they share a structure. Any approach that requires switching windows has already failed at that job.

Supported is not the same as usable

Let me be precise about what already exists. RedisInsight has had a Java formatter since 2.10, ARDM has a JavaSerialize viewer, and both are built on java-object-serialization — the same library RedisME uses. Nobody has a monopoly here.

So the interesting question is not "does it decode". It is what you get after it decodes, and how many steps stand between you and the answer. That is where implementations drift apart.

Layer 1 — built-in codecs

Next to UTF-8 / Base64 / Hex, RedisME ships three decoders in the Data Encoding dropdown:

  • JavaSerial — JDK serialization
  • Pickle — Python pickle, protocols 0–5
  • PhpSerial — PHP serialize() text

The library solves "can we read the bytes". What the value looks like afterwards is written by each client, and that layer is where the work is:

Case Raw deserialization output What I render
LocalDateTime / Instant / Duration nested {seconds, nanos} or epoch numbers readable timestamps
Java 16+ record fields fetched reflectively, often incomplete expanded JSON by field
ArrayList / HashMap / TreeSet toString()-ish [a, b, c] arrays and objects, collapsible
very large values the whole thing dumped into the page truncated preview, downloadable

There is also a structural difference: Hash / List / Set / ZSet support per-field codec selection. Open the field editor and pick a codec for one field; if the magic number matches, it preselects it. Some clients apply one formatter to the entire key value, which does not help when a hash holds mixed formats.

Pickle maps dict / list / set / bytes to JSON, and objects carrying $class / $type are viewable. PhpSerial keeps the class name as $class for O: instances and handles nesting (references via R: / r: are not supported).

All three are read-only — more on why below.

Layer 2 — auto-detection

Select Auto and the client walks the built-in decoders, matching on magic numbers rather than guessing. AC ED is unambiguously a Java stream; O: + trailing ; is almost certainly PHP serialize. That keeps false positives out of ordinary strings.

Layer 3 — custom codec scripts

This is where the real problems live: in-house binary protocols, compressed JSON, AES-encrypted values, your company's own serialization framework.

RedisME delegates the work to an external script over a minimal stdin/stdout contract:

# read: Redis raw bytes (base64) -> text shown in the editor
{your command} decode {wire_base64}

# write: editor text -> Redis raw bytes (base64)
{your command} encode {editor_text_utf8_base64}

# when base64 exceeds 8000 chars (Windows command-line limits)
{your command} decode --stdin
Direction arg 1 arg 2 stdout
decode decode base64 of Redis raw bytes UTF-8 text
encode encode base64 of editor text (UTF-8) single line of base64
large payload same --stdin same

On failure, write to stderr and exit non-zero. The client surfaces the exact command it ran in the error dialog — which has saved me more times than I can count, because the cause is nearly always a space in a path or an interpreter missing from PATH.

The client ships templates for Python, Node, and Java. Export one, and you only edit two functions:

def decode(raw: bytes) -> str:
    """Redis raw bytes -> text for the editor"""
    return binascii.hexlify(raw).decode('ascii')   # replace with your logic

def encode(text: str) -> bytes:
    """editor text -> Redis raw bytes"""
    return binascii.unhexlify(text.strip())        # replace with your logic

Your codec logic stays in your own repository. The GUI only shells out to it — which matters if you have compliance constraints, because it means you never hand private keys or an internal protocol to a third-party tool.

One trap: the bundled hex template "succeeds" on any input, because every byte sequence converts to hex. If you tick Auto detect on it, it will claim every value in the database and you will think the client is broken. Only auto-detect the codec you actually use, and make its decode throw when the format does not match.

Three design decisions worth explaining

1. Switching encodings never re-queries Redis.

STRING / Hash / List / Set / ZSet are transferred over IPC as base64 wire, always. The Data Encoding dropdown only changes presentation.

Why it matters: an HGETALL on a production hash can be tens of megabytes. Re-fetching on every dropdown change is not "switching views", it is DDoSing your own database. And the lag you would feel makes you stop exploring.

2. Large payloads go through stdin, not argv.

Windows caps a command line at 32767 characters. The protocol switches to --stdin at 8000 base64 characters — deliberately below the ceiling, because paths, arguments, and environment variables all consume the budget.

3. The built-in codecs are read-only on purpose.

Writing back means fully reconstructing a valid serialization stream: class version UIDs, field order, circular references. Deserialization is best-effort; serialization must be exactly right. A bad write leaves you with a key that no service can read — significantly worse than not being able to read it yourself.

For write-back, use a custom codec script with your local java / python / php. Your runtime, your correctness. I think that boundary should be explicit.

Limitations, stated plainly

  • No write-back through the three built-in decoders.
  • Custom codec scripts time out at 5 seconds by default — not the place for heavy inference.
  • Auto-detection only works on formats with a recognizable magic number.
  • Stream and JSON types have the encoding dropdown disabled; their handling differs.

If you look at a value once a month, redis-cli plus a scratch main method is fine. If your day is spent confirming what eight Java services wrote into the same key, this saves hours.

Try it

RedisME is a cross-platform Redis GUI built with Tauri (Rust + system WebView), GPL-3.0, under 10 MB, for Windows / macOS / Linux.

  • Site: https://www.hepengju.com/en/
  • Source: https://github.com/hepengju/redis-me?utm_source=devto&utm_medium=article&utm_campaign=codec
  • Codec docs: https://www.hepengju.com/en/guide/usage/codec.html

If you have hit this problem, I would genuinely like to know which serializer your team uses — I want to find the ones I have not covered yet.
