title: Verification Learning Theory: A Process Model of Checking and Retention in AI-Assisted Judgment
description:
arXiv:2610.37875v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Accurate AI assistance can improve immediate judgments while reducing opportunities to practise the operations needed for independent performance. Verification Learning Theory (VLT) formalises this possibility for claim-evaluation practice followed by correct, independent, rule-specific feedback. The model links perceived assistant reliability to evidence checking and links the history of those checks to retained rule use. Its strict form assumes that task demands and perceived reliability influence learning only through checking, with equal learning per genuine check. It therefore predicts that perceived fallibility can improve delayed unaided judgment even without observed assistant errors, and that this advantage disappears when checking is already required and performed. Rule-specific gains and forecasts from checking histories provide further tests. Simulations examine the consequences and parameter dependence of these commitments; they do not constitute empirical validation. Comparisons with depth-of-processing and feedback-encoding accounts identify where predictions diverge and where the accounts remain observationally equivalent. The framework specifies experiments that can test the proposed mechanism and separates retention of practised rules from the broader problem of recognising which rule applies to a new claim.

title: How to Evaluate a Visual CMS Editor With Real Editorial Tasks
description:
A visual CMS editor can make routine publishing easier, but a polished demo does not tell you whether your team can safely maintain a real site. The useful question is not how many blocks a product advertises. It is whether the people who will own the site can complete their everyday work, review the result, and recover from mistakes.

This article provides a vendor-neutral evaluation process. Features differ by CMS, editor, theme, extensions, and configuration. Treat every capability below as something to verify in the specific setup you are considering.

Define the work before comparing products

List a handful of tasks that the site team will repeat after launch. An editor of a service site might change an offer, add a testimonial, and create a page for a new service. A shop team might update category copy and images. A publisher might prepare an article and send it for review.

Separate one-time setup from daily work. A designer may be able to build an impressive homepage, while a content editor later struggles to change a paragraph without disturbing the layout. Name the person responsible for each task, the information they need, and what a correct result looks like.

Also identify non-negotiable requirements. If a team needs approval before a change becomes public, or must restrict a client to a single project, a high score for visual flexibility cannot compensate for a missing permission boundary.

Run the same test in each editor

Prepare a small, neutral content pack: a short and a long heading, paragraphs, a list, a link, and an image with meaningful alternative text. Use test data rather than real customer or payment information.

Ask a future site editor to perform the tasks with minimal coaching. An observer should record hesitation, errors, requests for help, and the number of steps. Timing can be useful, but a fast result that damages a shared template is not a successful test.

  1. Create a page from an available template and insert the supplied content.
  2. Move a section, add a block, and verify that neighboring content remains correct.
  3. Preview the page at narrow and wide widths using the long heading.
  4. Remove a test element and try the available recovery process.
  5. Save or submit the page for review using the workflow the system actually supports.
  6. Inspect the resulting page in an agreed test environment, including links and images.

If the product does not provide a separate staging environment or a draft version of a published page, agree on another safe test before changing a live site. Do not assume that a button called Save has identical effects across platforms.

Inspect the editorial experience

A usable editor makes the current object and the scope of a change understandable. Can a new team member find the page, identify its status, and tell the difference between a shared site header and content unique to one page? Does the interface warn the user when a change affects multiple pages?

Check common content operations rather than unusual demo effects. Paste realistic copy, create and update a link, add a list, replace an image, and provide alternative text. Observe whether ordinary content requires extensive cleanup or specialist assistance.

The availability of blocks matters only when the right block is easy to find and behaves predictably. Determine whether approved components can be reused and who can create or change them. Some teams prefer a constrained set of reliable sections; others need designers or developers to create additional components. Make that tradeoff explicit.

Check the published result on real devices

A visual preview is helpful, but it is still a preview. Where a safe environment is available, inspect the actual rendered page on a phone and a larger screen. Check reading order, navigation, text size, images, buttons, and form feedback.

Use content that exposes edge cases: a longer service name, an image with an unusual aspect ratio, an empty optional field, or an error message. Compare products with the same content and similar conditions. A single carefully prepared demo cannot represent every page on a production site.

Try the key interactions with a keyboard, look for a visible focus indicator, and review the meaning of labels and image alternatives. The editor itself also needs to be usable by the people who will maintain the site. A complete accessibility assessment may require specialist review and testing with users.

Test review, permissions, and recovery

Clarify what a draft means in the system. Editing a published page may create a separate version in one setup and update live content directly in another. If approval is required, verify that the intended author and reviewer can perform their parts without prematurely changing the public page.

Test the roles that matter to the team: author, reviewer, publisher, and administrator, if the product supports them. Identify who can modify a shared theme, delete content, or access another client's project. The presence of multiple accounts does not by itself prove that all necessary permissions can be restricted.

Ask how two people editing the same page are warned about conflicts. Test the behavior with non-sensitive data. Check whether a history, undo function, backup, or another recovery route exists and who can use it. Autosave, undo, version history, and a tested backup solve different problems; do not treat their names as interchangeable.

Look beyond the editing canvas

For search and site management, test the controls the project actually needs: headings, page titles and descriptions, URLs, redirects, links, and image alternatives. The editor, theme, and extensions may each affect what is available. Inspect a published test page and identify who will maintain the configuration.

A visual editor does not guarantee indexing or rankings. It can, however, make some of the team's work easier or harder by exposing or hiding relevant controls.

Evaluate performance using comparable content and devices. A page made of real images and ordinary components is more informative than a highly optimized demo. Review how external scripts and integrations affect the main user task.

Then examine portability. Ask what the system exports, whether images and relationships are preserved, and what must be recreated manually. Test an export on a sample page. A downloadable file does not necessarily preserve layout, forms, or every connection between content items. Also ask what happens if an extension is disabled, a theme changes, or a paid component is no longer renewed.

Compare total ownership costs

Include hosting, required extensions, license renewals, component development, updates, support, editor training, backups, and a possible migration. A free entry point can still require paid implementation or maintenance. A paid editor does not automatically include all of those services.

Ask who applies updates, how compatibility is checked, and how the team would restore the site after a failed change. Identify the owner of each ongoing responsibility. A convenient editing session is less valuable if nobody can support the resulting site.

Use a weighted score without hiding deal-breakers

A scorecard can organize a discussion. Choose criteria and weights for your own project, then score each product using the same evidence. For example:

  • Daily editorial tasks: weight 3.
  • Mobile behavior: weight 2.
  • Review and recovery: weight 3.
  • SEO controls: weight 2.
  • Portability and maintenance: weight 2.

The weights sum to 12. With hypothetical scores of 4, 3, 5, 4, and 2 out of 5, the weighted average is (4x3 + 3x2 + 5x3 + 4x2 + 2x2) / 12 = 3.75. The calculation illustrates a method; it is not a ranking of any product.

Keep a separate list of mandatory requirements, unresolved questions, and observed failures. Averages can make a serious permission or recovery problem look less significant than it is.

Make the decision with the people who will use it

Finish by comparing notes from editors, developers, and the site owner. Which tasks were completed independently? Which required help? Which features depend on the theme or a paid extension? What happens when a mistake is made?

Choose the setup that supports the actual workflow and can be maintained within the team's budget and responsibilities. Start with one representative page, test it carefully, and expand the comparison from evidence rather than a feature count.

title: Java Generics for Dummies
description:
Generics in Java act as a type-safety enforcement mechanism that allows you to specify the exact type of objects a class, interface, or method can operate on. They enable you to write reusable code without sacrificing type safety.

Type-Safety

Before generics (introduced in Java 5) it was not possible to specify the type of collections in Java. This led to many runtime exceptions, typically ClassCastException.

Without generics

List list = new ArrayList();
list.add("Hello");
list.add(123); // Compiler allows this

// Requires casting, and crashes at runtime if the type is wrong
String works = (String) list.get(0);
String breaks = (String) list.get(1); // Throws ClassCastException!

With generics

List<String> list = new ArrayList<>();

list.add("Hello");
list.add(123); // Compiler Error: incompatible types

Code-Reusability

Java generics improve code reusability by allowing you to write a single class, interface, or method that can operate on different data types while also providing compile-time type safety.

Here is a really simple example of how generics improve code reusability.

Without generics (Method Overloading)

// This printer does not spark joy :(
public class SadPrinter {
    // You have to duplicate the exact same println logic for every type
    public static void printItem(String item) {
        System.out.println(item);
    }

    public static void printItem(Integer item) {
        System.out.println(item);
    }

    public static void printItem(Double item) {
        System.out.println(item);
    }

    // And so on...
}

Supporting each type safely means one near-identical method per type.

With generics

// This printer does spark joy :)
public class HappyPrinter {
    public static <T> void printItem(T item) {
        System.out.println(item);
    }
}

One method with a type parameter <T> covers every type.

Wildcards

A wildcard in Java is represented by a question mark ? and stands for an unknown type in generics.

You can use them if you don't know or don't care about the actual type parameter:

public static void printList(List<?> list) {
    list.forEach(System.out::println);
}

You could also do this of course:

public static <T> void printList(List<T> list) {
    list.forEach(System.out::println);
}

The main difference is that the wildcard version (?) communicates the intent better:
"This method does not care about the type you pass it."

Typically you would only use a generic type parameter (T) if the type appears more than once in the signature, for example to:

1. Return the type it received

public static <T> T returnType(T t) {
    return t;
}

2. Enforce that two arguments have the same type

public static <T> void copyElements(List<T> source, List<T> dest) {...}

Most of the time though, wildcards are used to provide flexibility when passing generic collections (like List, Set, Map etc.) to methods, allowing the method to accept collections of different, yet related, types.

class Animal {}
class Dog extends Animal {}
class Cat extends Animal {}

class AnimalFeeder {
    public static void feedOne(Animal animal) {}

  // Option 1: Using a wildcard
  public static void feedMany(List<? extends Animal> animals) {}

  // Option 2: Using a generic type parameter
  public static <T extends Animal> void feedAnimals(List<T> animals) {}
}

public class Test {
  public static void main(String[] args) {
    var cat = new Cat();
    var dog = new Dog();

    // This works
    AnimalFeeder.feedOne(cat);
    AnimalFeeder.feedOne(dog);

    List<Cat> cats = List.of(cat);
    List<Dog> dogs = List.of(dog);

    // This also works
    AnimalFeeder.feedMany(cats);
    AnimalFeeder.feedMany(dogs);
    AnimalFeeder.feedAnimals(cats);
    AnimalFeeder.feedAnimals(dogs);
  }
}

But why do you need ? extends Animal or T extends Animal? Why can't you just use Animal directly?

    public static void feedAnimalsStrict(List<Animal> animals) {}

Generics in Java are invariant. This means that even though Dog is a subtype of Animal, a List<Dog> is not a subtype of List<Animal>.

If you define the method as:

public static void feedAnimalsStrict(List<Animal> animals) {}

You would only be able to pass exactly a List<Animal>. If you tried to pass a List<Dog> or a List<Cat>, the compiler would throw an error.

By using the wildcard ? extends Animal, List<Dog> and List<Cat> become subtypes of List<? extends Animal>. This is called covariance. With T extends Animal, T is simply inferred as Dog or Cat.

When a list is typed with ? extends Animal, the compiler restricts you from adding new elements to it (except null), because it doesn't know exactly what specific list type it is backing. It just knows it's safe to read from the list and treat every item as an Animal.

PECS (Producer Extends Consumer Super)

PECS (Producer Extends, Consumer Super) is a rule for using wildcard types (?) in Java Generics to make your APIs as flexible and widely usable as possible.

It boils down to a really simple question:
"What does your method do with the Collection you provide it?"

  • Does it only read from the collection?
  • Does it only write to the collection?

Its goal is to maximize the flexibility and usability of your code.

The rule can be easily displayed in the table below.

Collection Role Wildcard Data Flow Action Allowed
Producer ? extends T Data comes out of the collection Read-only
Consumer ? super T Data goes into the collection Write (read only as Object)

You need this rule because Java generics are invariant, meaning that a List<Integer> is not recognized as a subtype of List<Number>.

Due to this, you need wildcards to let methods accept collections of subtypes or supertypes.

PECS tells you exactly which wildcard to use based on what your method does with the collection.

1. Producer extends (? extends T)

If your method takes a collection and you only need to read elements from it, that collection is a producer of data.

  • What it allows: You can pass a collection of T or any of its subtypes.
  • The catch: To maintain type safety the compiler will not allow you to add anything (besides null) to the collection. 
// This method only reads from the list. 
public double sum(List<? extends Number> numbers) {
    double total = 0;
    for (Number n : numbers) {
        total += n.doubleValue();
    }
    return total;
}

// This works perfectly because of ? extends
List<Integer> ints = Arrays.asList(1, 2, 3);
sum(ints);

The method's code only ever pulls data out of the list. In PECS this means that the list itself is a "Producer."

And for a producer you should use ? extends T.

2. Consumer super (? super T)

If your method takes a collection and you only need to write/add elements to it, that collection is a consumer of data.

  • What it allows: You can pass a collection of T or any of its supertypes (all the way up to Object).
  • The catch: You cannot read from this collection and guarantee its type (other than treating the elements as Objects). 
// This method only writes to the list.
// It "consumes" the Integers you give it.
public void addNumbers(List<? super Integer> list) {
    list.add(1);
    list.add(2);
}

// Usage:
List<Number> nums = new ArrayList<>();
List<Object> objs = new ArrayList<>();

title: Automating Post-Mortems: Ingesting PagerDuty Incidents & Service Topologies into Cognee GraphRAG
description:
Writing incident retrospectives (post-mortems) and debugging recurring production outages are two of the most time-consuming responsibilities for Site Reliability Engineers (SREs).

Engineers often spend hours cross-referencing PagerDuty timelines, responder notes, service dependencies, and past incident histories. When teams attempt to solve this with standard LLMs, they quickly run into context window limits or hallucinated timelines because incidents are tightly bound to time, services, and escalation hierarchies.

With GraphRAG (Knowledge Graph Retrieval-Augmented Generation), an AI system can traverse:
Incident $\rightarrow$ AFFECTS $\rightarrow$ Service $\rightarrow$ ESCALATES_TO $\rightarrow$ Escalation Policy $\rightarrow$ RESOLVED_BY $\rightarrow$ Responder

As part of the WeMakeDevs × Cognee Mergetober Hackathon, I built and submitted the PagerDuty data-source connector (cognee-community-connector-pagerduty) for Cognee.

Here is an architectural walkthrough of how we bridged PagerDuty incidents and service topologies into Cognee.

Architectural Workflow

The connector extracts live incident streams and service architecture from PagerDuty's v2 REST API, cleans and redacts the payloads, and routes them into Cognee's document ingestion pipeline:

flowchart TD
    subgraph PagerDutyAPI ["PagerDuty REST API v2"]
        A["/incidents (Urgencies, Statuses, Timelines)"]
        B["/incidents/{id}/notes (Responder Chronology)"]
        C["/services (Service Catalogs & Dependencies)"]
    end

    subgraph ConnectorCore ["Security & Normalization Core"]
        D["Rate-Limit Backoff (HTTP 429 & Retry-After)"]
        E["Secret Redaction (API Tokens, Keys, PATs)"]
        F["Structured Markdown Serializer"]
    end

    subgraph CogneeCore ["Cognee GraphRAG Layer"]
        G["dlt Resource (cognee_document_source='pagerduty')"]
        H["Cognify Pipeline (LLM Relationship Extraction)"]
        I["Service & Incident Graph (FalkorDB / NetworkX)"]
        J["Semantic Memory (Vector Search)"]
    end

    A & B & C --> D --> E --> F --> G --> H --> I & J

1. Dual-Resource Ingestion: Incidents & Service Catalogs

Incidents in isolation lack critical context without knowing the service topology. The connector ingests two synchronized resources:

A. Live & Historical Incidents (pagerduty_incidents)

Captures incident IDs, numbers, titles, urgency levels (high, low), lifecycle statuses (triggered, acknowledged, resolved), created and resolved timestamps, assignees, and crucially, responder notes:

# PagerDuty Incident #48291: Payment Gateway Timeout Surge
- **Urgency:** high | **Status:** resolved
- **Service:** Checkout-API
- **Escalation Policy:** Payments-Primary-Tier1
- **Created At:** 2026-10-31T18:20:00Z
- **Resolved At:** 2026-10-31T18:45:00Z
- **Assignees:** Alex Chen, Maria Garcia

### Responder Timeline & Notes
- **2026-10-31T18:25:00Z (Alex Chen):** Identified 504 gateway timeouts originating from payment vendor webhook endpoint.
- **2026-10-31T18:35:00Z (Maria Garcia):** Toggled circuit breaker to secondary gateway; error rates normalized.

B. Service Topologies (pagerduty_services)

Ingests registered microservices, descriptions, alert creation configurations, auto-resolve timeout limits, and team ownership.

2. Production Security & Pre-Ingestion Redaction

Incident titles, descriptions, and responder notes frequently contain sensitive diagnostic payloads pasted during live triage—such as database connection strings, bearer tokens, or AWS credentials.

The PagerDuty connector applies strict pre-ingestion regex redaction across all incident fields before emitting records:

import re

PATTERNS = [
    (re.compile(r"Bearer\s+[A-Za-z0-9\-._~+/]+=*", re.IGNORECASE), "Bearer [REDACTED_TOKEN]"),
    (re.compile(r"AKIA[0-9A-Z]{16}"), "[REDACTED_AWS_KEY]"),
    (re.compile(r"sk-[A-Za-z0-9]{20,}"), "[REDACTED_API_KEY]"),
    (re.compile(r"ghp_[A-Za-z0-9]{36}"), "[REDACTED_GITHUB_PAT]"),
]

def redact_secrets(text: str) -> str:
    for pattern, repl in PATTERNS:
        text = pattern.sub(repl, text)
    return text

3. Cognitive Integration with Cognee

By tagging the source with:

setattr(source, DOCUMENT_SOURCE_ATTR, "pagerduty")

Cognee bypasses generic relational flattening and feeds the Markdown summaries into its entity extraction pipeline.

Querying Incident Memory in Python 

import asyncio
import os
import cognee
from cognee_community_connector_pagerduty import pagerduty_source

async def main():
    # 1. Initialize PagerDuty connector
    source = pagerduty_source(
        api_key=os.environ["PAGERDUTY_API_KEY"],
        resources=["incidents", "services"],
        urgencies=["high"],
    )

    # 2. Add to Cognee and run Cognify
    print("Ingesting PagerDuty incidents and service topologies...")
    await cognee.add(source)

    print("Building incident knowledge graph...")
    await cognee.cognify()

    # 3. Query past incidents to automate post-mortems
    query = "What caused the high urgency Checkout-API incident and how did Maria resolve it?"
    print(f"\nQuerying: '{query}'")

    results = await cognee.search(query)
    for res in results:
        print(f"\n[Incident Memory]:\n{res}")

if __name__ == "__main__":
    asyncio.run(main())

Verification & Compliance

  • Complete Test Coverage: Offline test suite mocking PagerDuty REST API endpoints with zero network dependencies (tests/test_source.py, tests/test_client.py, tests/test_redaction.py).
  • Resilient Rate-Limiting: Exponential backoff with Retry-After capping to avoid thread locks.
  • DCO Certified: Clean commit history with Developer Certificate of Origin sign-off.

Check Out the Code

  • Pull Request: topoteretes/cognee-community#429
  • Repository: topoteretes/cognee

Have questions about integrating incident response into AI workflows? Feel free to connect in the comments!

title: Aether AI Studio: A Local-First AI Workspace with an Autonomous Coding Agent and Image/Video Generation
description:
Aether AI Studio

A local-first AI workstation: chat, an autonomous coding agent, and image/video generation in one interface.

Most AI front-ends either lock you into one provider or send everything to the cloud. Aether AI Studio lets you decide. Run models locally with Ollama or LM Studio and nothing leaves your machine. When you need more power, switch to OpenAI, Anthropic, or Gemini from the same UI.

  • GitHub: https://github.com/hankyleisplay/AetherAI-Studio
  • Latest release (Windows launcher): https://github.com/hankyleisplay/AetherAI-Studio/releases/latest
  • Current version: v4.1.1

What it does

💬 Multi-provider chat

  • One UnifiedLLMClient fronts Ollama, LM Studio, OpenAI, Anthropic, and Gemini, with SSE streaming.
  • Personas with their own system prompts and per-persona tool access.
  • Rich Markdown rendering: code highlighting, LaTeX math, tables, and nested inline formatting.
  • Hardware-aware settings: when you raise max tokens or the context window, the app estimates whether your RAM/GPU can handle it and warns you before you hit an out-of-memory wall.

🤖 Code mode: a real autonomous agent

This is not a "paste code, get code" box. The agent plans, reads files, edits, runs commands, and verifies its own work in a loop.

15 built-in tools (each can be toggled individually in Settings):

list_dir · glob · grep · read_file · edit_file · multi_edit · write_file · run_command · git · check_syntax · web_fetch · web_search · todo_write · delete_path · move_path

Things I cared about getting right:

  • Approval gate: in Accept Edit mode every change is shown as a diff and waits for your OK.
  • Anti-cheating guards: the agent cannot "fix" failing tests by deleting existing functions or rewriting test assertions unless explicitly allowed.
  • Failure circuit breaker: repeated failing tool calls trigger a warning, then a hard stop, so it can't loop forever.
  • Context budgeting: long sessions are trimmed automatically to fit the model's window.
  • Resumable sessions: transcripts are persisted, so you can pick up where you left off.
  • Works with weak models too: if a model has no native tool-calling, the agent falls back to parsing tool calls from text.

🎨 Media Studio

  • Images: Pollinations (free, no key), OpenAI gpt-image-1, Gemini Imagen, Stable Diffusion WebUI.
  • Video: OpenAI Sora and Gemini Veo (API key required).
  • Chat personas can call generate_image / generate_video directly, and results render inline in the conversation.

✨ AI Prompt Enhancer

Turn a rough idea into a structured prompt, using either an LLM or a template. It's multilingual and answers in the language you choose.

🌐 Internationalization

Traditional Chinese, Simplified Chinese, English, and Japanese. That's 650+ UI strings, plus the README in all four languages. The top bar measures available width and collapses buttons level by level, so it doesn't break when you switch languages or close the sidebar.

Architecture

Layer Tech
Backend Python, FastAPI, SQLite, SSE
Frontend React 18, Vite, Tailwind CSS, TypeScript
LLM layer UnifiedLLMClient over 5 providers
Desktop / launcher Tauri (Rust) launcher, Electron shell
Extras Telegram bridge, optional PIN-protected web access

A small detail I'm happy with: the version number lives only in the root package.json. Vite injects it into the sidebar badge and window title at build time, and a test fails if the backend, frontend, desktop app, or launcher drift out of sync. (I learned that one the hard way when a release shipped with a stale badge.)

Quick start

  1. Download AetherLauncher.exe from the latest release.
  2. Run it; it starts the backend and frontend for you.
  3. In Settings, pick a model source: local Ollama / LM Studio, or paste a cloud API key.
  4. Chat, or switch to Code mode, point it at a project folder, and let the agent work.

Prefer running from source? The repo has the FastAPI backend and Vite frontend with setup steps in the README.

Who is it for?

  • People who want to run models locally and keep their data private
  • Developers who want a Cursor / Claude Code-style agent experience with full control over every edit
  • Creators who want text, image, and video generation in one tool

Feedback welcome

Video generation is the least-tested part (it needs paid API keys), so bug reports there are especially appreciated. Stars, issues, and PRs are all welcome:

👉 https://github.com/hankyleisplay/AetherAI-Studio

title: Contract Testing Email Verification with PostgreSQL
description:
Email verification is usually tested as a happy path: create a user, wait for a message, click a link, and assert that the account is verified. It does not prove that retries, delayed delivery, duplicate clicks, and expired tokens have a safe contract.

I prefer treating verification as a small state machine and testing the boundaries between its parts. The REST API owns the request, PostgreSQL owns the state transition, and an outbox worker owns delivery. The inbox is evidence, not the source of truth. This keeps a disposable email address from becoming an accidental identity system.

Why verification needs a contract test

A contract test describes what each boundary promises. For an email verification flow, useful promises include:

  • A repeated create request can be identified and does not create unbounded attempts.
  • A token is scoped to one account and one verification purpose.
  • A token can cause at most one successful state transition.
  • A delivery worker can retry without losing the relationship to the request.
  • An inbox test can prove which event it observed.

A message can arrive twice, or an old message can arrive after a newer one. A phrase such as tamp mail com may exist in test data, but it must not be a matching rule for a security-sensitive event.

The same thinking applies to an idempotent contract for email tools: retries should preserve operation identity instead of creating an untraceable second operation.

Define the PostgreSQL state machine

Start with explicit states rather than several booleans whose combinations are hard to review. A minimal table might look like this:

CREATE TABLE email_verifications (
    id              UUID PRIMARY KEY,
    account_id      BIGINT NOT NULL REFERENCES accounts(id),
    token_digest    BYTEA NOT NULL,
    status          TEXT NOT NULL CHECK (
        status IN ('created', 'queued', 'sent', 'verified', 'expired')
    ),
    expires_at      TIMESTAMPTZ NOT NULL,
    verified_at     TIMESTAMPTZ,
    created_at      TIMESTAMPTZ NOT NULL DEFAULT now(),
    UNIQUE (account_id, id)
);

The random token belongs in the URL, but only its digest should be stored. The id can appear in logs; the token is a capability and should not. An operator can investigate a request without copying a usable credential into a dashboard.

The outbox row should be inserted in the same transaction as the verification row:

INSERT INTO email_verifications (id, account_id, token_digest, status, expires_at)
VALUES ($1, $2, $3, 'created', $4);

INSERT INTO email_outbox (event_id, verification_id, event_type)
VALUES ($5, $1, 'email.verification.requested');

The worker later changes the verification to sent after recording the provider result. Do not hold the PostgreSQL transaction open while calling the provider. In practise, a short local transaction is easier to retry and produces less contention.

Test the REST API boundary

The create endpoint can return a durable request identifier without claiming that delivery already happened:

POST /v1/email-verifications
Idempotency-Key: signup-8472-attempt-1
Content-Type: application/json

{"account_id":8472}

{
  "verification_id": "8f2c4f30-1a0d-4b1b-9cc4-4b4ec1d1e4ac",
  "status": "queued"
}

The API contract test should send the same request twice and verify the same logical attempt. It should also send the same idempotency key for a different authenticated account and expect rejection. Ownership must come from the authenticated request, not the key itself.

For confirmation, make the database transition atomic:

  1. Lock the verification row by ID.
  2. Check account scope, token digest, status, and expiry.
  3. Mark the row verified and set verified_at.
  4. Commit before returning success.

A second confirmation can return a stable already-verified result when the caller is authorized. An unknown, expired, or mismatched token should return one safe failure category instead of revealing whether another token exists. The exact HTTP status is a product decision; the information boundary is the important part.

Prove delivery with an outbox receipt

The inbox test should consume a message using evidence from the request, not just the recipient and subject. Filter by verification ID when it is present in provider metadata, then check event time, recipient, and action. A boolean like email_found: true doesnt explain whether the message was fresh, duplicated, or attached to an earlier attempt.

For larger systems, record a receipt containing:

  • verification ID;
  • outbox event ID;
  • provider message ID, if available;
  • delivery attempt number;
  • observed timestamp and outcome.

This gives the worker an audit trail and the test runner a replayable artifact. Type-safe email event contracts are useful when several clients consume the same event shape.

If a controlled staging test uses a facebook temp email, keep that choice in fixture configuration. It can help observe delivery, but it must not decide whether the token is valid. Production authentication should behave the same when the mailbox is late or unavailable.

A practical test matrix

The smallest useful suite covers state transitions and failure boundaries:

Scenario Expected result
Same create request is retried One verification ID and one logical outbox event
Two confirmation requests race One state transition; the other is already verified or safely rejected
Token is expired No account mutation
Token belongs to another account No account mutation and no account disclosure
Worker times out after provider acceptance Retry keeps the same event identity
Inbox contains an old message The test rejects it using ID or freshness evidence
Raw token appears in logs The test fails the privacy contract

The concurrency case is especially important. Application-level checks can both observe sent before either request writes verified. A row lock or equivalent conditional update lets PostgreSQL arbitrate the transition. The evidence are clearer when the test asserts the final row and successful update count.

Questions engineers usually ask

Should every new request invalidate the previous token?

Usually, yes, for one account and one purpose. If several devices need independent links, model that scope explicitly.

Is the idempotency key enough for the worker?

No. The API operation key and outbox event ID solve different problems: one deduplicates a client request, while the other explains and retries delivery.

Can a temporary mailbox be part of production verification?

It should not be proof of ownership. A disposable email address is appropriate for controlled fixtures and staging checks; production ownership still depends on the verification token and account policy.

Contract testing turns email verification from a timing puzzle into a set of observable promises. PostgreSQL protects the state transition, the REST API defines retry behavior, and the outbox receipt explains delivery. That separation makes failures less surprising, even when a provider is slow or a user clicks twice. There is less surprises for the next engineer, too.

title: Teaching an AI assistant to forget a deleted Figma comment
description:
Picture this.

A team spends a week arguing in the comments of a Figma file about whether the sign-up button should be a pill. They settle it, the designer deletes the thread to tidy up, and a month later your AI assistant is still telling new hires that "the team agreed on a pill, see the comments". The comment is gone from Figma. The memory of it is not.

Nothing crashed. The assistant just remembers something that no longer exists, and design decisions are exactly the kind of thing people ask it about.

For Mergetober I built a Figma connector for Cognee with that in mind. The code is in PR #372 for issue #4552.

What it does

Cognee turns documents into a knowledge graph an agent can search. The connector feeds it from Figma:

  • Each file becomes one document: its type, folder, page names, frame and section names, and the text of every text layer. FigJam stickies count too.
  • Each comment thread becomes one document: the comment and its replies in time order with their authors, which frame it is pinned to, and whether it is resolved.
  • Geometry, images, hidden layers and default layer names like "Frame 12" are never read. A Figma file is a canvas, not prose, so only the text is kept.
  • A deleted file, a deleted comment, or a folder you deselect is forgotten on the next sync. 
source = figma_source(token, folder_ids=["<folder id>"])
await cognee.remember(source, dataset_name="figma")

Files and their comments share one node set per folder, so a search can be limited to one folder. There is also an optional OAuth integration that plugs into Cognee's connect and folder-picker flow.

What the API does not give you

Figma has no change feed and no delete feed. The folder listing gives each file's last_modified, not its version number, and the part that costs is GET /v1/files/:key, the whole node tree, which sits in Figma's strictest rate-limit tier. Figma's docs list 10 to 20 requests a minute for Dev and Full seats and about 20 a month for View and Collab seats. Comments do not move a file's timestamp. You cannot list a user's teams. Listing folders needs a private OAuth app, because public apps are not allowed the folders:read scope.

So each run lists the selection, fetches only the files whose last_modified moved, and serves the rest from a cache. Comments are read every run, one cheap request per file, because they never change the stamp. Cognee does the incremental part by content: a document whose text is unchanged keeps its id and never reaches the LLM again.

Two things my first design got wrong

I found both by reading my own code the way a reviewer would.

It cached too much. The cache kept whole rendered rows, title and folder name included. A rename or a folder move may not change a file's timestamp, so the cache would have kept serving the old title. Now the cache holds only what the node tree contributes, and the title and folder come from the fresh listing every run.

It could never finish a big team. When Figma returned a 429 that outlasted the retries, the whole run failed and the next run started from zero, hitting the same wall. Now at most 100 node trees are fetched per run, and a rate limit stops the fetching cleanly. Files not reached keep the text they were last synced with, so nothing is forgotten, and the next run carries on. The sync counts say so with failed_budget or failed_rate_limit.

I also made it stricter than it needed to be. An empty selection raises, because an empty list must never mean "forget everything". A selection that suddenly lists no files, when files were synced before, raises too. Earlier reviewers on my Stripe connector pointed out that a node set per record makes a big graph, so I used one per folder.

How I tested it

There are 68 tests on Python 3.10 and 3.12. Figma is an in-memory fake behind dlt's real HTTP stack. 8 of them run the whole Cognee pipeline with a mocked LLM: deleted files and comments leave the graph, an unchanged re-sync makes no LLM call, a sync cut short by the budget keeps what it has, and a file and its comments share a node set.

Then I ran it against a real Figma account on the free plan: a folder with two design files and one comment thread with a reply.

  • First sync: both files and the thread came in, and a search answered correctly from the design text.
  • Re-sync with nothing changed: 0 file downloads and 0 LLM calls.
  • A new comment: only that thread went to the LLM.
  • A deleted comment: forgotten.
  • A text edit in one file: only that file was fetched again, the new text was in the graph and the old text was gone.
  • A file moved to the trash: forgotten on the next sync, the rest untouched.

The only surprise was timing. My first sync after the edit saw nothing, because Figma saved the change a few seconds after I read the folder. The next run caught it.

What I did not test

The OAuth connect flow, because it needs a private Figma app. Large files and long syncs: I used two small files. Paid plans, and the actual rate limits of the free plan. All of that is covered by the fake, not by Figma.

Try it

The example is packages/connector/figma/examples/example.py. You need a personal access token (Settings, Security) with the scopes file_content:read, file_comments:read, folders:read and file_metadata:read, plus a folder id or a team id. Use a separate dataset, and tell me what breaks.

title: CH-Ops Pro Scheduled Archival: Move ClickHouse® Data to S3
description:
Table of Contents

  1. What is CH-Ops?
  2. Introducing the CH-Ops Scheduled Archival
  3. Creation of an Archival Job
  4. Choose How Data Should Be Archived
  5. Configure the Watermark Column
  6. Starting Point and File Partitioning
  7. Choose the Storage Format
  8. Where the Job Runs, and Where It Writes To
  9. Scheduling and Getting Notified
  10. Defining the Restore Shape Upfront
  11. Managing a Job After It's Created
  12. A Complete Archival Example
  13. Restore Archived Data
  14. Explore Archived Files
  15. A Simple End-to-End Flow
  16. Why This Is Worth Setting Up
  17. Further Reading

What is CH-Ops?

CH-Ops is a browser-based operations platform built for managing ClickHouse® deployments. Instead of relying entirely on the command line or HTTP APIs, it provides a unified interface for executing SQL queries, monitoring clusters, managing users, backups, alerts, dashboards, and much more — all from a single web application.

One of the features available in the CH-Ops Pro version is Scheduled Archival, which moves aging data to S3-compatible storage on a schedule instead of letting it grow indefinitely inside the cluster.

Let's explore how Scheduled Archival works and how you can use it to automate ClickHouse data archival.

Introducing the CH-Ops Scheduled Archival

A ClickHouse® cluster tends to grow in one direction: up. Old rows rarely get deleted, and most of them are barely queried once they age past a certain point.

Scheduled Archival, under the Backups section in CH-Ops, gives you a way to move that cold data out to S3-compatible storage on a schedule, in a columnar format, without writing your own export scripts.

It allows you to create jobs that periodically archive data from ClickHouse to S3-compatible storage. A job runs a plain SELECT query against your cluster on a schedule, writes the result to S3-compatible storage, and — depending on the mode you choose — keeps track of what it has already archived so the next run only picks up new rows.

You write the query once. CH-Ops handles the window, the file format, the compression, and the schedule around it.

Three tabs organize the feature:

Tab What it's for
Jobs Create, run, pause, and monitor archival jobs
Restore Bring an archived snapshot back into a ClickHouse table
Archive Explorer Browse the folder structure of what has actually been written to storage

Creation of an Archival Job

Start by creating a new job from Scheduled Archival → New Job.

Give the job a name and provide a normal SELECT query describing the data you want to archive.

For example:

SELECT *
FROM uk.uk_price_paid

The archival window is handled automatically by the engine, so the query itself does not need to contain a time filter for an incremental job.

Before creating the job, you can use Test (describe) to inspect the query and its columns.

Choose How Data Should Be Archived

The Mode determines how each archival run handles the data.

The Mode dropdown gives you two options:

  • Incremental (windowed): Archives only new rows each run, tracked with a watermark column.
  • Full snapshot: Exports the entire result of the query every run.

Incremental is the one you will use for anything that grows over time, like an events or transactions table. Full snapshot suits smaller, slowly changing tables where re-exporting everything each time is cheap enough not to matter.

Configure the Watermark Column

For incremental archival, CH-Ops uses a watermark column to determine what data should be included in each window.

The interface allows you to pick a column that increases on both INSERT and UPDATE, something like updated_at. The archival engine uses this value to track progress between runs.

If your only candidate is a String column, CH-Ops warns you first, because ClickHouse compares strings byte-wise, which only matches logical order under specific conditions.

Starting Point and File Partitioning

The Start from value determines where the first archival window begins. The initial run can catch up on the historical data from the selected starting point, while subsequent runs continue from where the previous run stopped.

This is particularly useful when setting up archival for an existing dataset rather than starting from newly inserted records.

An optional partition expression, like toDate(created), drives a third folder level in storage, so archived files land in date-based (or otherwise expression-based) folders instead of one flat run.

Leave it blank and you get a single folder per run instead.

A Check button lets you validate the expression before saving the job.

Choose the Storage Format

CH-Ops lets you select the format used for archived files.

The available formats shown in the interface include:

Setting Options
Format Parquet, ORC, Avro
Codec zstd, snappy, gzip, lz4, brotli, none
Max rows per file Specify the maximum number of rows that should be written to each archive file, for example, 5,000,000
Insert threads Configure the number of threads used during the archival operation. Use 1 for an exact split; more threads provide faster but approximate splitting

This gives you control over the balance between storage size and processing requirements.

Parquet with zstd is a reasonable default: columnar, well compressed, and widely readable by downstream tools.

Where the Job Runs, and Where It Writes To

Run on node decides which cluster node executes the job every time, defaulting to whichever node is selected in the navbar.

The Test and partition check also run on this node, so the columns you see while configuring the job match what the scheduled run will actually use.

The Storage Profile determines where the archived files are stored. In the example configuration, the job uses an S3 storage mvp-poc profile.

Once the storage profile is selected, CH-Ops can write the generated archival files to the configured object storage location.

This separates long-term archived data from the primary ClickHouse storage while keeping the data available for later exploration or restoration.

Scheduling and Getting Notified

The schedule is entered as a standard cron expression, evaluated in UTC, not server local time, so it lines up with the archival window, which itself seals at the start of day UTC.

Something like 0 * * * * runs hourly.

Notification channels reuse whatever alert channels you have already configured, like Google Chat or email, with an option to notify on failure only, so you are not paged for every successful run.

Defining the Restore Shape Upfront

Before you save the job, you also define the shape a restored table will take: an engine (MergeTree is the default), the ORDER BY columns, and an optional PARTITION BY.

This is used to build the CREATE TABLE statement automatically when you restore later, and the column list comes from the Test step, so it is worth running Test with your final query before finishing this section.

Once everything is filled in, Create saves and enables the job.

Managing a Job After It's Created

Each job appears as a card showing its name, mode (windowed or full snapshot), the underlying query, schedule, format and codec, target node, watermark column, and status.

From there, you can:

  • Run it immediately, outside its schedule.
  • Pause it without deleting it.
  • Resume it if needed again.
  • History to see past runs.
  • Backfill to catch up a range that was missed or never covered.
  • Edit or Delete the job entirely.

A Complete Archival Example

Here is an example configuration for a scheduled archival job:

Setting Value
Name testing1
Node replica2 (10.X.X.X.X)
Query SELECT * FROM uk.uk_price_paid
Mode Incremental
Watermark created_at (DateTime)
Start from 01/01/2026 12:42
Storage profile s3
Format / Codec Parquet / zstd
Max rows per file 5,000,000
Schedule 0 * * * * (02:00 UTC daily)
Notifications #Testing-channel, on failure only

The first run archives everything from January 2026 up to the start of the current day, which might be a few hundred million rows in one large snapshot.

Every run after that picks up one day.

Restore Archived Data

Archiving is only useful if the data can be retrieved when needed.

The Restore tab allows you to select an archival job and choose a snapshot to restore.

You can specify:

  • Destination database
  • Destination table
  • Optional ON CLUSTER clause

CH-Ops can also build the required DDL for the restored table using Build DDL.

This provides a straightforward path from archived files back into ClickHouse.

Explore Archived Files

The Archive Explorer provides a visual view of the archived data stored in the configured storage location.

Instead of navigating through object-storage paths manually, you can browse the available archive folders directly from CH-Ops.

The interface identifies archives based on the configured job and storage format, making it easier to locate archived datasets.

A Simple End-to-End Flow

The complete workflow brings together the key steps:

  1. Create an archival job and define the SELECT query.
  2. Choose incremental archival or full snapshot mode.
  3. Configure the watermark column and starting point when using incremental mode.
  4. Select the storage format, compression codec, and file partitioning options.
  5. Choose the execution node and S3-compatible storage profile.
  6. Configure the schedule and notification channels.
  7. Define the restored table's engine, sorting key, and optional partitioning.
  8. Create the job and monitor its runs.
  9. Explore archived files or restore a snapshot when needed.

Why This Is Worth Setting Up

Manually exporting cold data to S3 usually means a cron job somewhere, a script that tracks its own watermark, and a separate process for restoring anything back.

CH-Ops Pro's Scheduled Archival brings these steps into a single workflow.

With incremental and full-snapshot modes, configurable storage formats and compression, scheduled execution, notifications, restoration, and archive exploration, it provides a practical way to manage long-term ClickHouse data in S3-compatible storage.

title: GBase Database Transaction Governance: Balancing Concurrency, Consistency, and Application Performance
description:
Database transaction management directly influences application reliability and performance. Poorly designed transactions can increase resource consumption, prolong locks, and reduce the ability of a database to serve concurrent requests.

GBase Database applications should establish clear transaction boundaries and use consistent error-handling practices.

1. Keep Transactions Focused

A transaction should contain the operations required to complete one logical business action.

BEGIN WORK;

UPDATE inventory
SET quantity = quantity - 2
WHERE product_id = 1001;

INSERT INTO order_detail (
    order_id,
    product_id,
    quantity
)
VALUES (
    50001,
    1001,
    2
);

COMMIT WORK;

The example is illustrative. Verify transaction syntax and supported SQL features for the target GBase product.

2. Avoid Unnecessary Long Transactions

Long-running transactions can increase contention and complicate recovery.

Avoid including unrelated operations such as:

  • User interaction.
  • External HTTP requests.
  • Long file transfers.
  • Unnecessary application processing.

Complete database work promptly and commit or roll back according to the business outcome.

3. Handle Errors Explicitly

An application should not assume that every database operation succeeds.

try:
    connection.begin()

    cursor.execute(
        "UPDATE inventory SET quantity = quantity - ? "
        "WHERE product_id = ?",
        (2, 1001)
    )

    connection.commit()

except Exception:
    connection.rollback()
    raise

The example uses a generic transaction API and placeholder style. Adapt it to the actual GBase driver.

4. Monitor Transaction Behavior

Investigate:

  • Transaction duration.
  • Concurrent sessions.
  • Waiting and blocking.
  • Commit and rollback frequency.
  • Application timeout patterns.

For GBase 8s, relevant onstat diagnostics may include:

onstat -g ses
onstat -g act

Confirm available options for the installed release.

5. Align Database and Application Policies

Transaction boundaries should be consistent with application retry behavior, connection pooling, and business consistency requirements.

Conclusion

GBase Database transaction governance requires a balance between consistency and concurrency. Focused transactions, explicit error handling, and continuous monitoring help reduce unnecessary contention and support predictable application behavior.

title: GPT summarization workflow: combining batch processing for Node.js hiring rubrics
description:
Short answer: treat candidate scoring as a batch job behind an application-owned contract, not as a vendor-shaped feature. For an e-commerce hiring team, the useful unit is a rubric decision with a traceable tenant, input version, model choice, and result status. Batch processing is efficient for large summarization workloads, but the queue and result format must remain replaceable.

The operational constraint is per-tenant cost visibility. A single monthly total cannot tell me whether one marketplace, recruiter, or rubric is producing the spend. I would attach the tenant and rubric version before submission, retain the provider request ID, and export a status report that can be reconciled without opening five vendor consoles. That decision matters more than shaving a few seconds from a non-interactive workflow.

Infrai fits this boundary when a team wants one REST surface, one credential, and per-call accounting metadata attached to the tenant ledger. It is not the right answer when a provider's specialized batch controls, cloud-native governance, or model-specific guarantees are more important than a unified backend account.

Keep the contract small.

In practice, that means the first record written for a profile is more valuable than the first request sent to a model. I would persist tenant_id, work_item_id, rubric_version, a content hash, and an application-generated idempotency key before a worker sees the item. The worker can then construct whatever batch line the selected provider requires, but the result consumer never has to infer ownership from a prompt or a filename. Suppose a retry returns after the original result has already been exported: the consumer looks up the work item, sees the terminal export state, records the duplicate provider response for audit, and does not create a second score. Suppose the rubric changes while the batch is running: the old version remains attached to the old item, and the new rubric creates a new item rather than mutating history. Suppose one tenant's 1,000 profiles keep a shared batch open while another tenant has only 18: the scheduler can split the work by tenant or reporting window without changing the scoring contract. This is more bookkeeping than a direct SDK call, but it is the bookkeeping that makes per-tenant cost visibility and migration possible. A provider adapter should be replaceable precisely because these decisions live above it.

That is the whole test.

The limitation is important: a unified surface does not make a provider's batch behavior identical to another provider's behavior. The trade-off is an extra adapter and a readiness check in exchange for a simpler credential and accounting boundary. If the hiring platform already has strict AWS controls, Bedrock is the better choice; if it needs a GPT-specific batch contract, OpenAI is the better choice. I would not recommend an aggregation layer merely because it has more routes.

The lesson is an invariant, not a claim about a particular provider: every submitted item needs a stable application ID, tenant ID, rubric version, and outcome state. If a retry creates a second result, the reporting layer cannot distinguish a late answer from double billing. If a result arrives without its input version, a recruiter can read a plausible summary produced against yesterday's rubric. Plausible is not correct.

The incident lesson: the batch boundary is the product

Consider a bounded production scenario: an e-commerce platform receives candidate profiles for several tenants and scores each profile against a job rubric. The daytime path accepts the profile, normalizes the rubric, and records a work item. A later batch groups those items for summarization and scoring. One tenant has 1,000 profiles; another has 18. They should not disappear into one unlabelled blob.

I initially wanted the batch provider's object to be the system record. That is convenient until migration day. The safer boundary is an application record whose provider fields are optional: queued, running, succeeded, failed, and exported are ours; provider batch IDs and raw responses are attached evidence. This leaves room to change the transport while preserving audit and cost joins.

The advice has a boundary. Interactive candidate feedback, strict ordering, or a workflow that must fail within a short request deadline belongs on a synchronous path. Batch is the right lane for deferred summaries and rubric evidence, where throughput and accounting matter more than immediate display.

How should a GPT summarization workflow combine batch processing?

The contract should expose the business operation rather than the vendor vocabulary. I use an input object like CandidateScoringRequest, a result object with rubric-versioned evidence, and a separate usage record. The provider adapter can map those objects to an OpenAI-compatible endpoint, a cloud batch API, or a plain REST batch service.

OpenAI's Batch API is a natural reference for asynchronous requests and is useful when the rest of the application already uses its client conventions. Google Vertex AI Batch Prediction is a stronger fit for teams already operating on Google Cloud and wanting its job and storage controls around batch inference. Anthropic Message Batches is a credible choice when the scoring prompt is built around Claude and the team accepts an Anthropic-specific batch lifecycle. Amazon Bedrock batch inference belongs on the shortlist when governance and model access already live in AWS.

Those are not interchangeable claims of capability. They differ in authentication, input-file handling, completion semantics, model availability, and how usage is exposed. I would verify those details against the provider's current contract before writing an adapter. A comparison table is useful precisely because it keeps the decision conditional:

There is a practical failure mode here that deserves more room than the vendor names: a batch can finish successfully while the business export is still wrong. Imagine a tenant's rubric changes after submission, a worker retries a timed-out request, and a result arrives with a provider ID but no local work-item match. The model response may be perfectly readable, yet the platform must quarantine it, preserve the old rubric version, and report the item as unresolved rather than silently attach it to the newest job. That is why I keep provider status, normalized outcome, and export state as separate fields, and why a migration test should replay duplicate, late, and unknown results before anyone compares model quality.

Option Good fit Migration risk to isolate
OpenAI Batch API Existing OpenAI request shapes and a GPT-centered workflow Batch object and JSONL conventions can leak into application code
Vertex AI Batch Prediction A Google Cloud estate with storage and IAM already standardized Cloud-specific job and artifact assumptions
Anthropic Message Batches Claude-oriented summarization and scoring Provider-specific message and result semantics
Bedrock batch inference AWS governance and centralized model access AWS job, location, and model-routing concerns
A REST aggregation layer One credential and one accounting surface across backend capabilities The adapter still needs a clear capability and readiness check

A managed aggregation layer is worth considering for the last row when the platform team's real problem is operational sprawl. Infrai's public discovery surface is self-describing, and its documented capabilities include runnable examples in 10 languages; that makes contract inspection and adapter generation less dependent on a private SDK. Its broader positioning is one REST API, one key, and one bill across backend services. For this workflow, the concrete value is being able to join per-call cost metadata and request IDs to the tenant ledger while keeping the application-facing interface in my code.

My recommendation is specific: teams that need one accounting surface for deferred candidate summaries should try Infrai behind an application-owned batch adapter, provided the required batch capability is live in their region and its discovered schema matches the payload they intend to send. A direct provider is the better choice when the organization needs a provider's specialized batch controls, model-specific guarantees, or cloud-native governance more than it needs a unified backend account.

The preventative path in Go

The following small client shows the part I want to make boring: authenticate from the environment, use an explicit method, respect Retry-After on 429, and surface non-success bodies. It inspects the batch catalog rather than inventing a submit payload. The submit schema should come from the discovered capability contract; copying guessed fields into production is how an adapter becomes a liability.

package main

import (
    "context"
    "fmt"
    "io"
    "net/http"
    "os"
    "strconv"
    "time"
)

func listBatches(ctx context.Context, client *http.Client) ([]byte, error) {
    key := os.Getenv("INFRAI_API_KEY")
    if key == "" {
        return nil, fmt.Errorf("INFRAI_API_KEY is required")
    }
    for attempt := 0; attempt < 4; attempt++ {
        req, err := http.NewRequestWithContext(ctx, "GET", "https://api.infrai.cc/v1/ai/batch/list", nil)
        if err != nil { return nil, err }
        req.Header.Set("Authorization", "Bearer "+key)
        resp, err := client.Do(req)
        if err != nil { return nil, err }
        body, readErr := io.ReadAll(resp.Body)
        resp.Body.Close()
        if readErr != nil { return nil, readErr }
        if resp.StatusCode == http.StatusTooManyRequests {
            delay := time.Duration(1<<attempt) * time.Second
            if value := resp.Header.Get("Retry-After"); value != "" {
                if seconds, parseErr := strconv.Atoi(value); parseErr == nil { delay = time.Duration(seconds) * time.Second }
            }
            timer := time.NewTimer(delay)
            select {
            case <-ctx.Done(): timer.Stop(); return nil, ctx.Err()
            case <-timer.C:
            }
            continue
        }
        if resp.StatusCode < 200 || resp.StatusCode >= 300 {
            return nil, fmt.Errorf("batch list failed: status=%d body=%s", resp.StatusCode, body)
        }
        return body, nil
    }
    return nil, fmt.Errorf("batch list exceeded retry limit")
}

func main() {
    body, err := listBatches(context.Background(), &http.Client{Timeout: 30 * time.Second})
    if err != nil { fmt.Fprintln(os.Stderr, err); os.Exit(1) }
    fmt.Println(string(body))
}

For submission, I would generate an idempotency key from the application work-item ID plus the rubric version, persist it before the request, and make the adapter map the discovered request and response schema. The same key must be reused after a timeout. The worker then polls the provider's status, checks each result, and writes a tenant-tagged usage record before marking the work item exported. Error checking is part of the workflow, not a cleanup task after the happy path.

How do cost controls become operational controls?

Cost visibility needs a ledger shape that survives vendor changes. Store tenant, job, work-item, rubric version, provider, model, request ID, input and output accounting fields when supplied, status, and timestamps. Keep raw result payloads separately from the normalized score. That gives finance a reconciliation path and gives SRE a way to distinguish a provider retry from an application retry.

I would set an SLO for completion reporting, not pretend that batch latency is an interactive SLA. For example, define the target as the percentage of accepted work items that reach a terminal state and appear in the export within the agreed reporting window. Track queued, running, succeeded, failed, and unknown separately. A missing result is a state to page or reconcile, not a zero score.

The capacity question is similarly concrete: how many profiles arrive per tenant during the peak window, how many tokens does a rubric prompt add, and how many concurrent batches can the selected provider absorb? The answer determines whether to split by tenant, rubric, or time window. One giant batch may reduce coordination overhead while making a single tenant dominate the completion window. Many tiny batches improve isolation while increasing polling and bookkeeping. I would choose the partition that keeps the largest tenant within the reporting SLO, then measure queue age and result export lag.

A unified REST surface can reduce the number of credentials and invoice joins, and Infrai's documented convention includes per-call cost, latency, vendor, cache-hit, and request-ID metadata. That is useful evidence for the ledger. It does not remove the need to test the exact batch schema, check readiness, or decide which failures are retriable. The adapter remains the ownership boundary.

The decision rule

Use a batch API for deferred summarization and rubric scoring when the result can arrive later, the work is partitionable, and the application owns idempotency and accounting. Keep the domain contract provider-neutral. Compare OpenAI, Vertex AI, Anthropic, Bedrock, and an aggregation layer against your existing cloud controls and migration cost, not against a single unit price.

For this e-commerce workflow, I would choose the unified REST option only when per-tenant visibility and a single backend credential materially simplify operations, and only after discovery confirms the required capability. I would choose a direct specialist when its batch semantics or governance are the actual requirement. That is a reversible decision because the scoring contract, ledger, and export format remain ours.

If that boundary fits your system, start by inspecting the documented batch capability and discovery contract before implementing the adapter.

Sources

  • OpenAI Batch API
  • Google Cloud Vertex AI batch prediction
  • Anthropic Message Batches
  • Amazon Bedrock batch inference
  • Cohere Rerank documentation
  • Infrai discovery

title: Vercel applications are protected from Next.js August 2026 security vulnerabilities
description:
Summary

Two vulnerabilities affecting Next.js were disclosed in the August 2026 Security Release. Next.js applications hosted on Vercel are protected and require no customer action.

Next.js August 2026 vulnerabilities

Next.js disclosed the following critical vulnerabilities:

  • GHSA-2xp9-vwfh-vxw4 originates in the upstream libheif dependency and can lead to unauthenticated remote code execution when Image Optimization processes a crafted AVIF input.

  • CVE-2026-75604 (GHSA-p293-qw3h-jr36) can lead to unauthenticated remote code execution on Windows-hosted Next.js servers in applications using the Pages Router and App Router without Cache Components.

After the AVIF vulnerability was identified, Vercel applied protections to its managed Image Optimization service.

Impact on Vercel deployments

Applications hosted on Vercel are protected. No upgrades, configuration changes, or redeploys are required.

  • Once the AVIF vulnerability was identified, Vercel disabled AVIF optimization across its managed Image Optimization service. AVIF inputs are served as-is and do not pass through the affected processing path.

  • The second vulnerability only affects servers using a Windows filesystem. Vercel's Next.js runtime uses Linux and is not affected.

Resolution for self-hosted applications

Self-hosted Next.js applications should upgrade to the appropriate patched version.

For applications running Next.js 15.x or earlier:

For applications running Next.js 16.x:

In the patched releases, AVIF images are not resized or optimized. They are served as-is until a fixed libheif version is available. There is no workaround for the Windows vulnerability; affected servers should upgrade immediately.

Credit

Thanks to the Hacktron team for responsibly disclosing the AVIF vulnerability, and to evolutionstorm and B0RI for responsibly disclosing the Windows vulnerability.

  • GHSA-2xp9-vwfh-vxw4
