title: Prospero’s useful timeout trick: keep the command, return a handle
description:
A build takes longer than the agent expected. The tool says “timeout.” The agent starts the build again.

Except the first build is still alive. Now both are writing into the same directory. Excellent. A distributed system, accidentally. 🫠

That failure is why the part of Prospero that caught my attention is its command lifecycle. Chris Wellons’s new native coding harness describes a specific transition: when a foreground command outlasts its wait, it becomes a background job the agent can still identify.[1]

Original explanatory diagram of the documented lifecycle. This is not a captured Prospero session.

The wait ended. What happened to the work?

“Timeout” is an incomplete answer. It could mean the process was terminated, the caller stopped waiting, or a request failed while the remote work continued.

Those outcomes need different next actions. Retrying makes sense after a confirmed failure. It can duplicate work when the original process is merely slow.

Prospero’s shell-tool description makes that distinction explicit. A running command becomes a job after its foreground timeout. The agent is told when that job ends; it can read output or stop the job through separate tools.[2] 🔎

The useful object is the handle: a continuing reference to the work already started. A transcript that says only “timed out” loses that reference at precisely the moment it becomes valuable.

This also changes the meaning of progress. “Still running, attached to this job” is an actionable result. It should not be turned into “failed” merely because the tool call has returned.

There is an inspectable contract behind the announcement

I followed the announcement into the shell-tool source and its tests. The source names job_output and job_kill; the latter is described as stopping the job and the processes it started.[2]

The test file includes expected messages for a command moved into a job, a user moving it into the background, and the failure case where there is no room for another job.[3] That last case matters: background execution has capacity limits too.

These are source observations. I have not run Prospero or its test suite, and I am not claiming that reading a test proves process cleanup on every supported platform.

💡 The design gives the model a more precise vocabulary: running, completed, failed, or stopped. “The tool returned” is not itself one of those process outcomes.

Stopping needs its own meaning

Wellons also describes keeping the process tree together when stopping a command.[1] That addresses the other half of the problem: terminating a wrapper while its compiler, test worker or development server survives.

The practical review question is therefore broader than “does the stop button respond?” It is: which descendants still exist after cancellation, and can they keep modifying the workspace?

That is a question to test in a disposable project. A successful exit in the transcript is not a census of surviving processes.

⚠️ The common mistake is to treat a wait limit as a cleanup guarantee. Prospero’s documented promotion to a job deliberately means the work continues. Explicit cancellation and natural completion are separate paths.

Why this is more interesting than another interface debate

Prospero has a native GUI and connects to a separately supplied model provider.[4] Those choices explain its packaging. The command contract explains how an agent might recover from an ordinary slow build without starting a competing copy.

The same concern appears in Danil Galeev’s DEV article about agent cleanup: command limits, session deadlines and workspace lifetime are separate responsibilities.[5] That distinction helped frame my reading here. Preserving a job handle solves one ownership problem; it does not decide when an entire workspace should expire.

✅ My takeaway from the source is a small acceptance criterion for coding tools: after a wait expires, the next action should operate on the existing command, with its identity and outcome still visible.

The interesting unit is the piece of work that survives the conversation turn.

References and figure

  1. Chris Wellons: Prospero announcement.
  2. Prospero shell and job tools, inspected revision.
  3. Prospero tool-result tests, same revision.
  4. Prospero README.
  5. Danil Galeev: The agent finished. Who turns off the VM?.

Lifecycle diagram: original illustration; arrows describe documented states, not measured timings.

AI disclosure

AI was used to draft the article.

title: Deep Dive into WPF — Style
description:
Style is used to share properties, resources, and event handlers across different instances of a type. You can think of a Style as a shortcut for applying a set of property values to multiple elements.

That is MSDN’s description of Style—fairly conventional, as translations go. Put simply, Style is a batch operation on property values. Much like CSS on the web, it lets you apply a whole set of property values to UI elements at once.

Example

The simplest Style example:

<Window>
    <Grid>
        <Grid.Resources>
            <Style TargetType="{x:Type Button}" x:Key="ButtonStyle">
                <Setter Property="Height" Value="22"/>
                <Setter Property="Width" Value="60"/>
            </Style>
        </Grid.Resources>
        <Button Content="Button" Style="{StaticResource ButtonStyle}"/>
        <Button Content="Button" Style="{StaticResource ButtonStyle}" Margin="156,144,286,145" />
    </Grid>
</Window>

For Resources, see MSDN. Here we create a ButtonStyle whose target type is Button. The two Buttons find this Style through static resource (StaticResource) lookup. The Style defines the Button’s Height and Width. Once the Style is applied, neither Button needs manual sizing—they automatically take the preset values 22 and 60 from ButtonStyle.

As a batch mechanism for properties, resources, and events, Style provides a shortcut for configuring controls quickly. There are two main benefits:

  1. Extract common settings into a Style so those controls share a consistent look; changing property values in the Style conveniently affects every control that uses it.
  2. Define multiple Styles for the same control type and switch looks by swapping the Style.

Style Elements

In the Style example above, Setter was used inside Style to define preset property values. Style not only batches property values but can also share resources and event handlers:

<Window>
    <Window.Resources>
        <Style TargetType="{x:Type Button}" x:Key="ButtonStyle">
            <Style.Resources>
                <SolidColorBrush x:Key="brush" Color="Yellow"/>
            </Style.Resources>
            <Setter Property="Height" Value="22"/>
            <Setter Property="Width" Value="60"/>
            <EventSetter Event="Loaded" Handler="Button_Loaded"/>
        </Style>
    </Window.Resources>
    <Grid>
        <Button x:Name="button1" Style="{StaticResource ButtonStyle}" Background="{DynamicResource brush}"/>
        <Button x:Name="button2" Style="{StaticResource ButtonStyle}" Background="{DynamicResource brush}" Margin="156,144,286,145" />
    </Grid>
</Window>

The Button_Loaded handler lives in the code-behind:

void Button_Loaded(object sender, RoutedEventArgs e)
{
    MessageBox.Show((sender as Button).Name + " Loaded");
}

The Style defines the SolidColorBrush resource, sets Height and Width, and uses EventSetter to attach the Loaded handler.

Trigger

Style uses Setter and EventSetter to set a control’s properties and event handlers respectively—the word “setter” simply means “to set.” After designing those two kinds of settings, Style introduces a more advanced idea: conditional setting.

For a plain Setter such as <Setter Property="Height" Value="22"/>, the meaning is obvious: set height to 22. Conditional setting means assigning a value only when some condition holds.

WPF introduces the Trigger to express that condition, written like this:

<Style TargetType="{x:Type Button}" x:Key="ButtonStyle">
    <Setter Property="Width" Value="60"/>
    <Style.Triggers>
        <Trigger Property="IsMouseOver" Value="True">
            <Setter Property="Width" Value="80"/>
        </Trigger>
    </Style.Triggers>
</Style>

Here the Trigger means: when the Button’s IsMouseOver property is set to True, set the Button’s Width to 80.

Inside a Style you do not need to specify the Setter’s TargetName; the default target is the control using the Style. As a trigger, when it fires it sets width to 80; when IsMouseOver becomes False—i.e. the condition is no longer met—width returns to the default Setter value of 60.

WPF defines five kinds of Trigger as conditions: Trigger, DataTrigger, MultiTrigger, MultiDataTrigger, and EventTrigger. Their conditions are:

  1. Trigger: a control property is the condition—for example, the earlier case when IsMouseOver is True.
  2. DataTrigger: a property on the control’s DataContext is the condition.
  3. MultiTrigger: multiple control properties form the condition.
  4. MultiDataTrigger: multiple DataContext properties form the condition.
  5. EventTrigger: a RoutedEvent is the condition; it fires when the specified routed event is raised.

For detailed usage of these five Triggers, see MSDN; they are not described further here.

Implicit Style

In the examples above, Style was always set with StaticResource. You can of course also use DynamicResource. Both approaches require an explicit reference in XAML or code-behind. For convenience, WPF offers an Implicit Style that can be applied to controls automatically:

<Window>
    <Grid>
        <Grid.Resources>
            <Style TargetType="{x:Type Button}">
                <Setter Property="Height" Value="22"/>
                <Setter Property="Width" Value="60"/>
            </Style>
        </Grid.Resources>
        <Button x:Name="button1" Style="{x:Null}"/>
        <Button x:Name="button2" Margin="156,144,286,145" />
        <Button x:Name="button3" Margin="196,144,0,145" />
    </Grid>
</Window>

When the Style is defined in the Grid’s Resources without a Key, it is applied automatically to every child Button of the Grid. If a Button explicitly sets a Style—like button1, which sets it to Null—the implicit Style does not apply.

Digging Deeper into Style

Style is a good concept. For a presentation framework, separating structure, style, and behavior of UI objects is a solid design. Style is also easy to pick up; even Implicit Style feels like a natural idea. In practice, however, problems appear. WPF often follows this pattern: a nice concept, a simple description, a bright future—and bizarre bugs. To explain those issues clearly, we need to start from the root: what exactly is a Style?

By the usual intuition, Style should be something like a Dictionary<string, object> of setters—pre-stored property names and preset values that are then applied to UI objects. WPF’s ambitions for Style go much further. It packs in a great many features around several key technologies. Let’s walk through them in detail.

Style and Dependency Property

The Dependency Property (DP for short) is at the heart of WPF, and Style is built on Dependency Properties. For the internals of DPs, see Deep Dive into WPF — Dependency Property (Part 1). A Style’s Setter acts on DPs; if you define a plain CLR property on a control, Style cannot set it. The essence of Dependency Property design is to peel field storage away from the object (DependencyObject). A single property value is stored across multiple internal fields, and the current value is decided by the priority of the value sources.

The priority of Dependency Property value sources (lowest to highest from top to bottom) is:

public enum BaseValueSource
{
    Unknown,
    Default,
    Inherited,
    DefaultStyle,
    DefaultStyleTrigger,
    Style,
    TemplateTrigger,
    StyleTrigger,
    ImplicitStyleReference,
    ParentTemplate,
    ParentTemplateTrigger,
    Local
}

A concrete example:

<Window>
    <Window.Resources>
        <Style TargetType="{x:Type Button}" x:Key="ButtonStyle">
            <Setter Property="Width" Value="60"/>
            <Style.Triggers>
                <Trigger Property="IsMouseOver" Value="True">
                    <Setter Property="Width" Value="80"/>
                </Trigger>
            </Style.Triggers>
        </Style>
    </Window.Resources>
    <Grid>
        <Button x:Name="button1" Style="{StaticResource ButtonStyle}" Background="{DynamicResource brush}" Width="20"/>
    </Grid>
</Window>

Line 4 uses the Style’s Setter to set Width=60; this priority is Style. Line 6 sets Width=80 when IsMouseOver is True; this priority is StyleTrigger. Line 13 defines Width=20 directly on the Button that uses the Style; this priority is Local. Local has the highest priority, so even when the mouse is over the Button, the Trigger on line 6 does not take effect because its priority is not high enough. Remove Width="20" from line 13, and hovering the Button makes Width become 80; when the mouse leaves, it returns to the 60 set on line 4.

Style and FrameworkElement

Style is a property defined on FrameworkElement, so every control that inherits from FrameworkElement can use Style. FrameworkElement defines several styles: Style, ThemeStyle, and FocusVisualStyle.

  1. FocusVisualStyle: the dashed rectangle shown around a control when it receives keyboard focus. This style is not applied directly to the corresponding FrameworkElement. When the control gets keyboard focus, the AdornerLayer creates a new Control, FocusVisualStyle is applied to that Control, and it is overlaid on the original FrameworkElement to form the dashed frame.
  2. Style: the Style we have been setting all along.
  3. ThemeStyle: this introduces the concept of a theme—let’s talk about it.

Windows defines many themes, and you can switch themes in Control Panel:

The top two rows belong to the Aero theme. Switching from Aero to Windows Classic changes the appearance of the taskbar, windows, and the controls inside them. To support theme switching more cleanly, WPF introduced ThemeStyle. When you generate a custom control from a VS2010 template, it automatically adds a Themes folder and a Generic.xaml file:

The Aero.NormalColor.xaml file here was added by hand; set that aside for a moment and talk about default control styles.

WPF ships many controls—Button, ListBox, TabControl, and so on. When we use them we do not specify a Style; WPF provides a default Style that is tied to the Windows theme. For example, if you switch Windows from Aero to Classic, the look of controls inside WPF windows changes as well. Those default Styles are stored as ResourceDictionaries in DLLs such as PresentationFramework.Aero.dll and PresentationFramework.Classic.dll. The naming convention is: assembly name + theme name + .dll.

How does WPF find the matching ThemeStyle for the current Windows theme? WPF introduces the ThemeInfo attribute to specify theme information. ThemeInfo is usually defined in Properties/AssemblyInfo.cs:

[assembly: ThemeInfo(
    ResourceDictionaryLocation.SourceAssembly,
    ResourceDictionaryLocation.SourceAssembly)]

ThemeInfo has two parameters. The first refers to ThemeResource and the second to GenericResource; their type is ResourceDictionaryLocation:

public enum ResourceDictionaryLocation
{
    None = 0,
    SourceAssembly = 1,
    ExternalAssembly = 2,
}

For ResourceDictionaryLocation: None means there is no corresponding resource; SourceAssembly means the resource lives in this assembly; ExternalAssembly means the resource lives in an external assembly, found by the rule we already saw: assembly name + theme name + .dll.

For any control—whether built-in or custom—when WPF starts, it looks up the ThemeStyle matching the current Windows theme. The lookup rules are:

  1. First, find the assembly for the control’s Type, then read its ThemeInfo to see where ThemeResource and GenericResource live. If ThemeResource is not None, the system reads the corresponding ResourceDictionary and looks for TargetType={x:Type controlType}. If found, that Style becomes the control’s ThemeStyle.
  2. If the first step fails, GenericResource comes into play—“generic” meaning general. WPF looks at ThemeInfo’s second parameter, GenericResource, using the same rules as step one. On success, that Style becomes the control’s ThemeStyle.

Any control that does not explicitly set Style and cannot find a default ThemeStyle has no visual appearance. For convenience, when you add a custom control via VS, VS generates Generic.xaml by default. If you want the custom control to track system theme changes as well, add a corresponding ResourceDictionary under Themes—such as the Aero.NormalColor.xaml above—and set ThemeInfo’s first parameter to SourceAssembly, indicating that this assembly supports system theme changes and that the resource files live in it. The ResourceDictionary must sit under the Themes folder, because WPF locates it with something like:

string relativePackUriForResources = "/" +
        themeAssemblyName.FullName +
        ";component/themes/" +
        themeName + "." +
        colorScheme + ".xaml";

Style and ResourceDictionary

We have mentioned ResourceDictionary many times; the WPF resource system will be covered in more detail later. The resource system stores resources in a ResourceDictionary. As the name implies, it is a dictionary—key/value pairs. When we created a Style in a Window’s Resources earlier, we gave the Style a key (x:Key) and later referenced that key with StaticResource.

If you add a Button object to a ResourceDictionary without a key (x:Key), the code will not compile. Yet the Implicit Style we introduced earlier only specified TargetType={x:Type type} and no key—why does it compile?

When you add a Style to a ResourceDictionary without specifying x:Key, WPF generates a key for you. That key is not a string; it is of type object—specifically a Type instance. So it is equivalent to:

<Style TargetType="{x:Type Button}" x:Key="{x:Type Button}">

The trailing x:Key can be omitted.

Both Application and FrameworkElement define a Resources property, each holding a ResourceDictionary. Resource lookup follows a nearest-wins principle:

<Window>
    <Window.Resources>
        <Style TargetType="{x:Type Button}">
            <Setter Property="Background" Value="Yellow"/>
        </Style>
        <Style TargetType="{x:Type ToggleButton}" x:Key="toggleBtnStyle">
            <Setter Property="Background" Value="Red"/>
        </Style>
    </Window.Resources>
    <StackPanel>
        <StackPanel.Resources>
            <Style TargetType="{x:Type Button}">
                <Setter Property="Background" Value="Blue"/>
            </Style>
            <Style TargetType="{x:Type ToggleButton}" x:Key="toggleBtnStyle">
                <Setter Property="Background" Value="Green"/>
            </Style>
        </StackPanel.Resources>
        <ToggleButton Width="80" Height="20" Style="{DynamicResource toggleBtnStyle}"/>
        <Button Width="80" Height="20"  Content="button2" Click="Button_Click"/>
    </StackPanel>
</Window>

Both Window and StackPanel Resources define toggleBtnStyle and an implicit Style for Button. By nearest-wins, the ToggleButton and Button inside StackPanel use StackPanel’s resources rather than Window’s.

Style Merge

This brings us to the focus of this article—a topic that is easy to overlook and yet frequently a source of bugs: Style merging.

We have mentioned many styles: ThemeStyle, Style, Implicit Style. Style is a batch of property values. For any single property there can be only one preset value, not many. At runtime these styles must be merged and then applied to the FrameworkElement.

Merging Styles happens in two steps:

  1. Find all relevant Styles.
  2. Determine their priority and merge by that priority.

For a Button:

  1. If the current Windows theme is Aero, after startup the corresponding ThemeStyle is found in PresentationFramework.Aero.dll.
  2. If the Button uses StaticResource or DynamicResource to specify a Style, that Style is found in the resource system by key.
  3. If no Style is set explicitly on the Button, the resource system looks for an Implicit Style (x:Type Button).
  4. Steps 2 and 3 are mutually exclusive—they identify at most one Style. That Style is then merged (Merge) with the ThemeStyle to produce the Button’s final look.

Start with the merge itself. Explicit and Implicit styles have higher priority than ThemeStyle. If both a Style and a ThemeStyle set the same property via Setter, the Style’s Setter wins and ThemeStyle is ignored. EventSetter is special: it uses a RoutedEvent. If both styles’ EventSetters handle the same RoutedEvent, both are registered on that RoutedEvent.

As we saw, explicit and Implicit styles are mutually exclusive—only one applies. In real projects, however, it is common to define a global base style for Button and then apply special handling on top of that base at the point of use. To support that, Style has a BasedOn property to express inheritance:

<Window>
    <Window.Resources>
        <Style TargetType="{x:Type Button}">
            <Setter Property="Width" Value="80"/>
            <Setter Property="Height" Value="20"/>
            <EventSetter Event="Click" Handler="btnBase_Click"/>
        </Style>
        <Style TargetType="{x:Type ButtonBase}" x:Key="toggleBtnStyle">
            <Setter Property="Width" Value="80"/>
            <Setter Property="Height" Value="20"/>
            <Setter Property="Background" Value="Red"/>
        </Style>
    </Window.Resources>
    <StackPanel>
        <StackPanel.Resources>
            <Style TargetType="{x:Type Button}" BasedOn="{StaticResource {x:Type Button}}">
                <Setter Property="Background" Value="Blue"/>
                <EventSetter Event="Click" Handler="btn_Click"/>
            </Style>
            <Style TargetType="{x:Type ToggleButton}" x:Key="toggleBtnStyle" BasedOn="{StaticResource toggleBtnStyle}">
                <Setter Property="Background" Value="Green"/>
            </Style>
        </StackPanel.Resources>
        <ToggleButton Style="{DynamicResource toggleBtnStyle}"/>
        <Button Content="button2"/>
    </StackPanel>
</Window>

To explain more clearly, I used an uncommon example. Line 16 creates an Implicit Style for Button whose BasedOn is itself an Implicit Style for Button. The resource system walks up and finds the Implicit Style for Button in Window.Resources, then merges the two. A single ResourceDictionary cannot have duplicate keys; StackPanel and Window each have their own ResourceDictionary, so their keys do not clash, and nearest-wins finds the highest-priority resource during lookup. The ToggleButton example on line 20 is the same as Button. The difference is that the toggleBtnStyle found on line 8 has TargetType ButtonBase—ButtonBase is the base class of ToggleButton—so BasedOn still works.

WPF’s Style mechanism is a sealing (Seal) mechanism. Its authoring model is flexible and supports merging, but once merging is complete the Style is sealed, and its Setters and other members can no longer be modified. That sealing design has its reasons, but it falls short on Style dynamism.

Consider a custom control. Suppose you custom-derive a Button named MyButton that inherits from Button. In custom controls you often see code like:

static MyButton()
{
    DefaultStyleKeyProperty.OverrideMetadata(typeof(MyButton), new FrameworkPropertyMetadata(typeof(MyButton)));
}

Here DefaultStyle appears—another name WPF uses for ThemeStyle. ThemeStyle is what determines the default Style; later, BaseValueSource also uses DefaultStyle to mean ThemeStyle. Overriding the internal metadata of DefaultStyleKeyProperty in MyButton’s static constructor tells the WPF system that the key used to look up MyButton’s ThemeStyle has changed from {x:Type Button} to {x:Type MyButton}.

If you change DefaultStyleKeyProperty as above, you must define MyButton’s default (Theme) Style in Themes/Generic.xaml; otherwise MyButton has no appearance, because the ThemeStyle lookup key has changed and assemblies such as PresentationFramework.Aero.dll do not define {x:Type MyButton}.

That covers ThemeStyle usage. Back to Implicit Style: even if you define an Implicit Style for Button (TargetType={x:Type Button}) in Application.Resources, every MyButton control will not use that Implicit Style unless you also define, below the Button Implicit Style in Application.Resources:

<Style TargetType="{x:Type local:MyButton}" BasedOn="{StaticResource {x:Type Button}}"/>

This brings us back to Style merging. Style’s merge is very basic (rather dumb)—it is not automatic. Specifically:

  1. An Implicit Style for a base control type does not apply to derived control types.
  2. If Implicit Styles for Button are defined separately in Window and StackPanel as above, they are not intelligently merged and then applied to the Button; nearest-wins picks only one.
  3. Style’s BasedOn only supports StaticResource references, because Style inherits from DispatcherObject rather than DependencyObject, and DynamicResource only supports DPs.

All of these must be solved through BasedOn. Because BasedOn uses a static reference, updating Implicit Styles at runtime becomes painful.

Theming / Skinning

Skinning a UI can look very slick. There are two kinds: (1) replace the entire control Style; (2) replace the color brushes inside the Style. The second is simple: define color brush resources in a ResourceDictionary, bind with DynamicResource when using the brush, and when re-skinning just swap the brush resource dictionary.

Many companies maintain their own skin libraries. Those libraries are usually Implicit Styles—Implicit Styles for all controls—and at use time the skin resource is merged into Application.Resources. To change skins, remove the old skin resource from Application.Resources and replace it with the new skin’s ResourceDictionary.

That approach is easy to understand, but it breaks down with BasedOn. BasedOn uses StaticResource—a one-shot static reference. After a new skin library is added to Application resources, if Application resources already define an Implicit Style such as <Style TargetType="{x:Type Button}" BasedOn="{StaticResource {x:Type Button}}"/>, the controls will not update their skin. If you have that requirement, you must merge Styles manually, something like:

public static void Merge(this Style style, Style otherStyle)
{
    foreach (SetterBase currentSetter in otherStyle.Setters)
    {
        style.Setters.Add(currentSetter);
    }

    foreach (TriggerBase currentTrigger in otherStyle.Triggers)
    {
        style.Triggers.Add(currentTrigger);
    }

    foreach (object key in otherStyle.Resources.Keys)
    {
        style.Resources[key] = otherStyle.Resources[key];
    }
}

You still need additional condition checks here, and a decision about whether to recursively merge otherStyle’s BasedOn chain. Returning to the earlier point: the application needs DynamicResource to watch for Implicit Style changes in Application resources. An attached property can solve that:

public static readonly DependencyProperty AutoMergeStyleProperty =
    DependencyProperty.RegisterAttached("AutoMergeStyle", typeof(Type), typeof(Behavior),
        new FrameworkPropertyMetadata((Type)null,
            new PropertyChangedCallback(OnAutoMergeStyleChanged)));

private static void OnAutoMergeStyleChanged(DependencyObject d, DependencyPropertyChangedEventArgs e)
{
    if (e.OldValue == e.NewValue)
    {
        return;
    }

    FrameworkElement control = d as FrameworkElement;
    if (control == null)
    {
        throw new NotSupportedException("AutoMergeStyle can only be used in FrameworkElement");
    }

    Type type = e.NewValue as Type;
    if (type != null)
    {
        control.SetResourceReference(Behavior.BaseOnStyleProperty, type);
    }
    else
    {
        control.ClearValue(Behavior.BaseOnStyleProperty);
    }
}

SetResourceReference is the code form of DynamicResource in XAML—equivalent to Behavior.BaseOnStyle="{DynamicResource type}". Applying SetResourceReference to a control watches the key type on a custom attached property BaseOnStyleProperty. When re-skinning replaces Application’s resource dictionary, the BaseOnStyle property is updated. In BaseOnStyleProperty’s Changed handler you can read the control’s Style and the new ThemeStyle, call Merge on the two, and set the result back on the control’s Style.

Conclusion

WPF’s Style design is fairly conventional. Separating an object’s style from its structure was the original goal, and the design also includes good ideas such as Trigger. In practice, though, problems still appear; Style is neither as smart nor as perfect as one might hope. I hope readers will look at Style from the inside out and get more out of it.

Aside

This “Deep Dive into WPF” series has grown to several posts. Writing articles takes more patience and care than talking through something out loud. There are many levels of explanation: making simple things complicated; making complicated things complicated; making complicated things simple; and making complicated things simple while adding poetry and philosophy. I cannot claim to reach that highest level. I hope instead to explain the technical main line directly and without avoidance, and I hope to hear more feedback so I can keep expanding and improving the series.

Thank you for your support—and for clicking the upvote button. ^_^

title: The Anatomy of Socio-Demographics in Pluralistic Offensiveness Modeling: When and Where It Helps, and the Role of Reasoning
description:
arXiv:2610.37896v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Subjective judgments such as offensiveness often vary substantially across individuals, motivating pluralistic modeling approaches that incorporate annotators' socio-demographic information to capture this variation. However, prior findings on the benefits of socio-demographic information for pluralistic modeling are mixed, calling for a systematic analysis of both its effectiveness and the mechanisms through which it improves prediction. In this work, we study $\textbf{when}$ and $\textbf{where}$ socio-demographics benefit pluralistic offensiveness modeling, as well as $\textbf{the role of explicit reasoning}$ in leveraging this information. Across three multi-annotator datasets with prompted and trained LLMs, we first show that demographic gains are small and inconsistent for individual predictions but become clearer at the group and population levels, because aggregation attenuates the idiosyncratic variation that masks small but systematic demographic signals. Second, using a reasoning and prediction format that explicitly decomposes individual judgment into an overall baseline and a demographic-specific deviation, we show that the gains arise from both components: demographic information improves baseline estimation and enables meaningful demographic-specific shifts, and interventions show that better component estimates improve final predictions. Finally, comparing direct demographic conditioning with explicit reasoning about how the text interacts with annotator demographics, we find that reasoning yields more accurate baseline and shift estimates as well as final predictions, whereas conditioning alone rarely produces informative shifts. These results suggest that the mixed evidence in prior work may partly stem from individual-level evaluation, and that the value of socio-demographic information depends on both how it is evaluated and how models are guided to use it.

title: Rebuilding this site as an F1-style dashboard
description:
My old portfolio was a long page you scrolled down, like most people's.

At that size the page is almost four screens tall. It had also broken quietly: the Xbox card said 0 games, next to a picture that no longer loaded.

I rebuilt it twice in a few days. The first rebuild was a gamer profile, and it didn't survive my own laptop. The second is the F1-style dashboard at siddharthabbineni.in. After that I moved the blog out to a site of its own, the one you're reading now.

I built all of it with Claude Code running Opus. I decided what I wanted and Opus did most of the typing.

The player profile, and why it went

The first version was a character sheet: a character build, a campaign timeline for my jobs, and a trophy cabinet with certifications and live Xbox and Steam achievements. On my 1440p monitor it looked great.

Then I opened it on a 1080p laptop with Windows set to 125%. That leaves the browser about 1536×730 pixels, and the page turned into a wall of text.

Three columns were all talking at once, and every panel was packed with small labels, chips and bullets. Nothing on the screen was more important than anything else. Making the text smaller to fit only made it worse.

Trying ideas before writing code

This time I didn't touch the code first. I asked Opus for rough screens of very different ideas: game menus, a magazine spread, a metro map, an F1 pit wall. I liked the metro map and the pit wall, so I mashed them together and drew my career as a line on the Nürburgring GP circuit.

I got a second opinion on that concept, and it made two points I agreed with. The section menu shouldn't be part of the career track, and the track shouldn't be a closed lap with a finish line, because my career hasn't finished yet. So the route became an open stretch of the circuit with the road carrying on past my current job.

The F1 dashboard

The site shows one section at a time, with F1 names and a plain line under each: Seasons (where I've worked), Driver profile, Podiums, Garage and Press. It uses the real F1 colours, and every button, tab and card has the same slanted cut as the nameplate.

On the track, grey is life before work, black is work, and red is my current job and the road after it. When you pick an older job, it and the stretch up to the next job turn teal. One job shows at a time, with a short summary, up to three numbers, a few bullets and the tools I used with their logos. That's far less text than before.

The buttons for moving between jobs took two goes. At first "Earlier" sat on the right and disappeared on the oldest job, so "Later" slid under the mouse. Clicking Earlier a few times in a row took me back to the newest job. Now each button has its own fixed spot and keeps it, even when the other one is hidden.

The header copies a driver's TV graphic: a picture on a red panel, with my first name small and my surname big, the way F1 shows "Max / VERSTAPPEN". It started as my photo. It's now a drawing of me in a helmet with SA on the side, which is also the little icon in your browser tab on both sites.

The Garage has my side projects, with my pull requests to other people's projects in a column that looks like a timing tower. One that hasn't been merged yet is marked "Under review", which is what the stewards say about an incident they haven't ruled on. The footer is a single "Team radio" line that flips between my two newest posts and two newest merged PRs.

You can get around without the mouse. The keys 1 to 5 open a section, and ↑ and ↓ change job. On a desktop the page never scrolls, so the mouse wheel steps through the jobs and then on to the next section. The animations use Motion, the library that used to be Framer Motion.

I worried that the logos would make the site heavy, since Simple Icons has 3,466 of them. I checked the production build: only the 14 I use reach the browser, about 15 KB in all.

Fitting on one screen

The whole design is 96 by 45.6 rem, and one line of CSS sets the size of a rem:

html {
    font-size: min(100vw / 96, 100dvh / 45.625, 20px);
}

At 1536×730 that's 16px, and at 1920×1080 it's 20px, where it stops. On bigger screens the page sits in the middle of a dark backdrop with a faint outline of the circuit.

I asked Opus for a Playwright script that opens every section at five laptop sizes, from 1280×600 to 1920×1080, and fails if anything scrolls or gets cut off. It checks all five jobs too, because each one has a different amount of text.

The track outline comes from Pitlane02's Nürburgring drawing on Wikimedia Commons (CC BY-SA 3.0).

Moving the blog home

My two posts lived on dev.to, and the site pulled them in through its API. I moved them into my repo as markdown files, so a new post is a commit, a draft gets a staging preview, and the pages are built ahead of time.

At first the posts lived inside the dashboard, under Press. Next.js 16 with Cache Components surprised me a few times along the way:

  • dynamicParams isn't allowed any more. Unknown slugs call notFound() instead.
  • With Partial Prefetching on, you have to read params inside a <Suspense> boundary so the page can show its outline straight away.
  • Typed routes won't accept `/blog/${slug}` for a plain string. A small postHref() helper fixed it in one place.
  • The standalone build doesn't copy files you read with fs, so the posts folder has to go in outputFileTracingIncludes.
  • Running next build while next dev was still running confused the dev server, and every page started reloading itself about five times a second. Restarting it fixed that.
  • A 'use cache' function caches whatever it returns, failures included. My Xbox and Steam data is cached for six hours, so one rate-limited request would have emptied the Podiums section until the next refresh. Failures now call cacheLife('minutes') and get retried soon after.

Sharing a link

When I pasted a link into LinkedIn, the preview had a title and no picture. X was worse, showing the wrong title. Each page set its own Open Graph tags, and those replaced the site-wide ones, image included.

Now every section of the dashboard gets its own card, made at build time with Next's opengraph-image files and next/og. It has the same tab, slashes and nameplate as the site. The fonts had to be TTF files, because the renderer behind next/og can't read the WOFF2 files the site uses.

Digging up 2005

I had a blog long before dev.to. It started on Blogger, moved to WordPress on thesid.net, and died when my hosting ran out while I was moving countries. Luckily the Wayback Machine had saved it.

Its API lists every address it saved for a domain. For my two old domains that was about 1,300 addresses, and most were junk: client sites I used to host, and the crawler going round in circles. After removing duplicates I had 145 posts. Opus wrote a scraper that fetched them slowly, then a second script went looking for the images. Most image hosts from 2006 are gone (RIP echo.cx and ImageShack), so some pictures are lost for good.

I kept the posts exactly as I wrote them, typos and all. They're under Earlier sessions on this blog, one page per year. Reading 2006 me go on about BSNL and the new Iron Maiden album made the whole thing worth it.

The blog gets its own site

With 150 posts in it, the blog didn't fit the dashboard any more. The dashboard is built to fit on one screen, and a long post doesn't. I kept making the reader tighter, with smaller text, Older and Newer up in the tab row, and the title moving into the tabs once you scrolled past it, and it was still a long article in a box.

So the blog moved to blog.siddharthabbineni.in. Press on the dashboard is now a short feed of the three newest posts, and each one opens here. It reads a posts.json file the blog publishes at build time and caches it with 'use cache'. If the blog doesn't answer, Press says so and gives you the link.

I wanted it to feel like racing without copying the dashboard. Opus drew a few directions on a canvas. The first name was Night session, which I didn't like, so I picked Free practice. That's the session where drivers try things out, and that's most of what I write about. The look I picked is wet tarmac: dark asphalt with grain and puddles, worn white paint, and a chequered line under the title. New posts line up on a starting grid with the newest in P1. Inside a post, each heading is a lap, and the bar at the top lights them up as you read.

A few things changed after I lived with it for a day:

  • The header was far too tall. On a 1080p screen the title, blurb and tags took up most of the first screen, so I drew red lines on screenshots where I wanted them to stop. The home header is now about 256 pixels tall, and the tags moved to the end of each post.
  • The light mode background was too dark. Now it's pale concrete, and the white paint became charcoal, because white lines don't show up on concrete.
  • Search came back after I noticed it had gone missing in the redesign. It's a box in the header. Press / on any page to jump to it, and it searches titles, tags and the full text from an index made at build time. On the search page the footer stays put, since the results changing height made it jump up and down.

The blog is a plain static site. Next.js exports it as files, so route handlers like the RSS feed and the search index need dynamic = 'force-static'. Each post's share card gets drawn at build time into an og.png next to the post.

One repo, two sites

The repo is now split into apps/portfolio and apps/blog. Each has its own package.json and lockfile, and I skipped npm workspaces, since the two apps share nothing. Each one has its own GitHub workflow that only runs when its folder changes, so fixing a typo in a post doesn't rebuild the dashboard.

Both run on Azure Static Web Apps. My first apps were in West Europe for no good reason, so I deleted them and made new ones in East Asia, which is a lot closer to India. There are four now: the portfolio and the blog, each with a staging copy. Everything goes to staging first, and the staging sites tell search engines not to index them. Opus handled the Cloudflare DNS records through the API with a token that can only edit DNS for this one domain. Adding another subdomain later, like one for NuPrint, is one more app and one more record.

Phones, again

  • The Email button is gone. My resume has my email on it anyway. Resume and Blog moved to the end of the page, and a small pen icon next to the theme toggle opens the blog.
  • The Team radio line is now a bar stuck to the bottom of the screen.
  • Swiping used to work only on the tab row. Now a sideways swipe anywhere on the page moves to the next section, and the tabs scroll to keep the open one in view.
  • On a 360-pixel phone the pen and theme buttons wrapped onto their own line, so the photo, name and slashes shrink a little on small phones.

Seasons on a phone took the most work. Tapping a job used to open it in place while the old one stayed open, so the page jumped around and the job you tapped ended up somewhere different every time. I wanted an accordion: the open job folds up, the tapped one opens, and the page scrolls so the tapped one sits just under the tabs.

My first version did nothing at all. The fold animated height: 'auto' with Motion, and to measure that, Motion saves the scroll position, measures, and puts the scroll back with window.scrollTo. That cancelled my smooth scroll every time. I swapped Motion for a CSS grid row that goes from 0fr to 1fr, which folds just as well without measuring anything.

Then the tapped job landed anywhere from 16 to 19 pixels off. There were two causes. The page wasn't tall enough yet to scroll that far while the new job was still opening, so it now gets a temporary minimum height. And the browser's scroll anchoring was nudging the page as content above it folded away, so that's turned off until the fold finishes. Now it lands in the same spot every time. The first fold took 350ms, which was too quick to see what happened, so it takes 550ms now.

What I'd tell myself

  • Look at your site on the laptop people actually use, at the scaling they actually use.
  • Draw the screens before writing code. Throwing away a mockup takes seconds.
  • Less text on screen beats smaller text.
  • A dashboard and a blog want different layouts. Give long reading its own site.
  • If an animation fights your scrolling, find out what the library does when it measures.
  • Keep your writing somewhere you own.

First posted on my blog, Free practice.

title: ThinkJev: One Thought, Every Budget for Calibrated Typed Decisions
description:
arXiv:2610.37732v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Many uses of language models end in a typed decision: a choice among a closed set of options, whose probabilities code can act on. Reading those probabilities from one forward pass is fast but often wrong on decisions that take several steps, such as arithmetic, counting, and date comparison. Letting the model think first fixes most of these errors, but costs seconds per decision instead of milliseconds. To pay for thinking only where it helps, ThinkJev builds a fast and a slow system from one open hybrid-thinking model that can answer directly or after a thought. System 1 reads the model's probabilities for the option letters when it answers directly; System 2 reads the same letters after the model has thought on the same cached prompt, so escalating repeats no work and both systems give probabilities over the same options. Because the letters can be read after any number of thought tokens, one sampled thought also gives the answer under every thinking budget. Without training, ThinkJev lets System 1 answer alone only where a statistical test on labeled dev data guarantees that its accepted answers stay under a target error rate. At a 5% target, Qwen3.5-27B answers 24.5% of 8359 test decisions this way with a realized error of 3.9% (Qwen3.5-4B and 9B: 6.5% and 0.0%). For the rest, stopping each thought as soon as its answer is confident reaches 81.6% accuracy, against 82.7% for always thinking, with 72% of the thought tokens. Choosing when to think from System 1's confidence alone saves less, because the decisions System 1 is least sure of are often not the ones thinking fixes. On the public items of JevBench, an independent benchmark of typed-decision services, Qwen3.5-27B thinks on 29.4% and is not distinguishable in accuracy from the two thinking APIs listed (exploratory). Code and data generators are available at https://github.com/ding-xiaolu/ThinkJev.

title: Designing Time-Bound Financial Operations: An Engineering Checklist
description:
Model the lifecycle explicitly
A time-bound operation has more states than a button and a timer. A robust design describes creation, validation, reservation, active monitoring, expiry, settlement and exceptional review. The exact vocabulary depends on the product, but the allowed transitions should be defined before the UI is built.

The server must be authoritative. A browser timer can show a useful estimate, yet it cannot decide that an operation has expired or that funds may be released. Each transition needs a durable event, an allowed previous state and a clear financial effect. If a request arrives after the state has changed, the server should return a conflict or the existing result rather than applying a second transition.
Start with invariants
Write down what must always remain true. A ledger transaction must balance. A reserved amount must not be available for a second trade. A settled operation must not be settled again. A withdrawal must not debit more than once. A user should not see another user's record through a route parameter.

These invariants guide both schema design and testing. They also make incident response less dependent on guesswork. When a page reports a surprising balance, an operator can compare the projection with durable entries, reservations and source records. If the invariant is broken, the incident is financial and should be handled as such.
Make repeated requests safe
Idempotency keys, unique constraints and transaction boundaries are practical tools, not abstract vocabulary. A user can double-click. A mobile client can retry after a timeout. A worker can be restarted after writing one side of a process. The same logical command must produce one durable outcome.

The key should be bound to the actor, operation and relevant parameters. Store the result or conflict outcome so that a retry can return it. Do not allow a client to reuse the same key with a different amount or destination. Test two concurrent requests and a response that is lost after the server commits.

For background tasks, idempotency must include the claim or lease. A queue message can be delivered twice. A worker needs an atomic way to claim an item and a safe way to discover that a prior attempt already completed.
Separate market data from decision logic
A feed adapter should normalize external prices, timestamps, symbol names and source metadata. Downstream settlement logic should receive a well-defined input with a freshness decision, not a raw network response. This makes it possible to reject stale data consistently.

A chart may continue to display a last-known value while the settlement path remains pending. That is not a contradiction. It is an important distinction between information for orientation and data authorized for a financial decision. If the source is unavailable, the system should preserve the operation and surface the exception.

Price sources also need observability. Record the source identifier, timestamp and decision context without logging credentials or personal data. Keep the raw response only when retention and privacy rules permit it. Otherwise retain a safe digest and the fields needed for reconciliation.
Use a double-entry ledger
A balance column is not enough for a financial system. Double-entry accounting creates offsetting records for each movement and supports a balance check independent of the dashboard. Deposit credit, trade reservation, settlement, withdrawal reservation and release should each have explicit transaction types and references.

Ledger entries should be append-only after posting. Corrections should be new, auditable transactions rather than edits to old history. A reconciliation job can compare accounts, transaction totals and business records. It should flag negative balances, orphan entries and a transaction whose debits and credits do not net to zero.

The ledger does not remove the need for controls. Access to manual adjustments requires strong authorization, a reason, an audit trail and an idempotent operation. A review workflow should not turn a single account into two pretend approvers.
Design settlement as recoverable work
A separate worker can process due operations without keeping an HTTP request open. The worker should use leases or atomic claims, handle transient provider failures and write durable checkpoints. Restarting it should resume pending work without repeating a settlement.

Define interruption points. What if the process stops after reserving funds but before publishing a notification? What if it writes the settlement result and crashes before acknowledging the queue message? The answer should be a recovery path based on the durable record, not a manual guess.

For uncertain outcomes, prefer pending or review. This is especially important for blockchain payout verification. A TXID supplied by an operator is only an input to verification. The verifier needs the correct chain, token contract, recipient, amount, transaction status and confirmation threshold. If the provider is absent or unavailable, approval must remain blocked.
Protect boundaries and private data
A financial platform has multiple boundary types: public onboarding, authenticated user routes, administrative APIs, private uploads and external providers. Each route should enforce authorization on the server, not only through hidden navigation. Object identifiers must be checked against the current user or role.

Private documents need access checks, safe content headers and storage outside public directories. Logs should exclude passwords, session cookies, MFA seeds, recovery codes and full identity documents. Build artifacts should not contain local databases, test fixtures or production credentials.
Test the unhappy paths
A meaningful test suite exercises concurrency, retries, stale data, worker restarts, provider timeouts, duplicate callbacks and partial failures. Test both the response and the durable state afterward. A green toast is not evidence if the ledger did not change, and an error response is not acceptable if the database already committed the operation.

Use disposable PostgreSQL and Redis for financial integration tests. A mock market or chain provider belongs only in the test environment and must be impossible to activate accidentally in production. Production-like tests should include migration rehearsals, schema compatibility and recovery checks.
Observability and independent review
Useful telemetry includes queue depth, overdue operations, repeated idempotency requests, settlement exceptions and balance reconciliation results. It should exclude session cookies, private API keys, authentication seeds and personal recovery codes.

Technical writing can explain design intent, but it cannot certify production security or regulatory compliance. The right conclusion is a repeatable engineering methodology: model the lifecycle, define failure states, reconcile funds, isolate test environments and maintain evidence for important changes. ASTREON provides a concrete architectural example of these broader practices.
