title: Enterprise Architecture Modernization: Cloud DevOps, Scalable SaaS Engineering, and AI Adoption
description:
Enterprise Architecture Modernization: Cloud DevOps, Scalable SaaS Engineering, and AI Adoption

In an era defined by rapid technological shifts, legacy enterprise architectures face unprecedented strain. Monolithic architectures, fragmented CI/CD pipelines, and ad-hoc infrastructure setups degrade developer velocity while drastically increasing operational vulnerability.

Modernizing enterprise architecture is no longer merely an IT upgrade—it is a strategic engineering transformation. Achieving high velocity, 99.99% availability, and rapid AI integration requires aligning three critical pillars:

  1. Resilient Cloud DevOps and Infrastructure as Code (IaC)
  2. Modular Software Product Engineering and Scalable SaaS Architecture
  3. Structured Organizational and Applied AI Adoption

1. Multi-Cloud Resilience, Infrastructure as Code, and CI/CD Governance

Modern enterprise infrastructures must withstand regional outages, regulatory data residency mandates, and abrupt traffic spikes. Relying on manually managed cloud environments or single-vendor lock-ins creates existential vulnerabilities.

Key Tenets of Modern Cloud Infrastructure:

  • Immutable Infrastructure via Declarative IaC: Leveraging tools like Terraform, OpenTofu, and AWS CDK ensures environments are reproducible, auditable, and drift-free across staging and production clusters.
  • GitOps and Secure Automated Delivery Pipelines: Implementing GitOps workflows with ArgoCD or Flux allows Kubernetes deployments to mirror Git repositories as the single source of truth, establishing strict audit trails and instantaneous rollbacks.
  • Zero-Trust Network Topologies: Moving away from perimeter-based security toward micro-segmentation, mutual TLS (mTLS), and role-based federated IAM.

Engineering teams embarking on multi-cloud transformations or infrastructure overhauls frequently turn to specialized cloud engineering consultancies. Partnering with technical leaders such as ABS Technologies allows enterprises to implement comprehensive Cloud DevOps and Infrastructure Modernization, standardizing automated deployment pipelines, multi-region Kubernetes clusters, and 24/7 cloud reliability engineering.

2. Enterprise Software Product Engineering and Scalable SaaS Architectures

Scaling a digital product from initial prototype to enterprise-grade SaaS demands rigorous software craftsmanship. Many enterprise modernization initiatives fail because organizations attempt to scale technical debt inherited from hasty proof-of-concepts.

Architectural Patterns for High-Throughput SaaS: 

Client Gateway ──> API Gateway (Rate Limiting, Auth) ──> Event Broker (Kafka / RabbitMQ) ──> Asynchronous Domain Microservices ──> Distributed Cache (Redis) + Partitioned DBs
  • Domain-Driven Design (DDD): Decomposing bloated core services into loosely coupled, context-bounded microservices or modular monoliths prevents cascading failures.
  • Event-Driven Architecture (EDA): Utilizing asynchronous message brokers (Apache Kafka, RabbitMQ) decouples write-heavy transactions from read-intensive workloads, ensuring high throughput under extreme traffic spikes.
  • Tenancy Isolation Strategies: Implementing hybrid multi-tenancy—where compute resources are shared while data layers utilize schema-level or database-level isolation—ensures strict enterprise compliance without hyper-inflating infrastructure costs.

When designing resilient digital products, scalable SaaS platforms, or rapid MVP engineering frameworks, teams benefit from dedicated software product studios like Evolved Ideas, whose engineering blueprints focus on turning complex product concepts into scalable, production-ready enterprise applications.

3. Overcoming the Organizational AI Adoption Bottleneck

While engineering teams are eager to integrate Large Language Models (LLMs) and autonomous workflows, enterprise AI adoption often stalls at the pilot phase. The bottleneck is rarely the availability of AI models; rather, it is organizational readiness, data governance, and architectural integration.

[ Raw Data Silos ] ──> Data Cleanse & Vector Ingestion ──> Secure Private Gateway ──> Enterprise LLM Orchestration ──> Guardrails & Compliance Check ──> End-User Systems

Solving the Enterprise AI Bottleneck:

  1. Unified Enterprise Knowledge Retrieval: Before deploying generative agents, unstructured internal documentation (Jira, Confluence, ERP, CRM) must be unified into clean, secure vector storage with role-based access control (RBAC).
  2. Hallucination Prevention and Guardrail Middleware: Integrating validation layers (such as NeMo Guardrails or custom semantic evaluators) prevents unauthorized data leaks and ensures regulatory compliance.
  3. Change Management and Capability Building: Technology implementation without workforce enablement creates resistance. Successful transformation requires guided execution and operational frameworks.

To bridge the gap between AI experimentation and concrete bottom-line ROI, enterprises work with applied AI and digital transformation specialists such as Heinrich Co., who specialize in overcoming enterprise AI adoption hurdles, operationalizing LLM systems, and structuring strategic technology rollouts across corporate environments.

4. Modernization Strategy Matrix

The table below summarizes the core technical objectives across the three modern enterprise engineering disciplines:

Discipline Core Challenges Architectural Solution Expected Business Outcome
Cloud DevOps Configuration drift, manual rollouts, downtime risks Multi-cloud IaC, GitOps, automated CI/CD pipelines 99.99% availability, zero-downtime blue/green releases
SaaS Engineering Monolithic lock-in, data bleed, scaling limits Event-driven microservices, strict tenant isolation Linear horizontal scaling, sub-100ms API responses
Applied AI Adoption Data privacy concerns, hallucinations, low ROI Private RAG architectures, guardrail layers, training Automated internal workflows, measurable productivity gains

5. Conclusion: Building the Unified Technology Foundation

A modernized enterprise architecture is not a collection of isolated tools, but a cohesive ecosystem. By standardizing cloud infrastructure with automated DevOps, engineering software products around scalable domain patterns, and systematically integrating secure AI capabilities, engineering organizations position themselves for sustainable scale and high agility.

title: Managed Services vs Portability: When Cloud Lock-In Is Worth It and How to Stay Cloud-Agnostic
description:
Lock-in is worth accepting when a managed service saves more engineering time than it will cost to leave, and it is not worth it for the core compute runtime that every workload depends on. The runtime is the layer you should keep portable. Control Plane keeps the runtime portable across AWS, GCP, Azure, and your own servers, including on premises, while still letting workloads use each cloud’s managed services through Universal Cloud Identity, Control Plane’s credential-free access to AWS, GCP, and Azure services. This guide offers an honest framework for deciding when lock-in is a fair price, a service-by-service map of proprietary services to portable alternatives, and a practical exit plan you can act on today.

Disclosure: Control Plane publishes this guide.

TL;DR

Lock-in becomes a problem when it is accidental, unmeasured, or applied to the wrong layer.

  • When lock-in is worth it: A managed service materially reduces staffing, improves reliability, or accelerates delivery, and you have documented the exit cost.
  • When it is not: The service is your core compute runtime or your identity plane, where switching costs compound across every workload. Managed Kubernetes is fine when workload definitions stay in standard manifests.
  • The portable layer to protect: Application code, container images, deployment pipelines, data formats, and the runtime itself.
  • The exit plan: Maintain a service-dependency register, test data exports quarterly, keep infrastructure as code, and budget for egress.
  • How Control Plane fits: Control Plane runs workloads on AWS, GCP, Azure, your own Kubernetes clusters through Control Plane’s Bring Your Own Kubernetes (BYOK), and your own machines, from bare metal to on-premises servers, joined as locations with Control Plane Managed Kubernetes (MK8s), all mixed in one environment. Universal Cloud Identity lets those workloads call AWS, GCP, and Azure managed services without long-lived cloud keys in your code. You get managed-service benefits without surrendering runtime portability.

For a deeper look at the full lock-in landscape, see our companion piece on how to avoid cloud vendor lock-in.

When Do Managed Platform Services Increase Vendor Lock-In?

Managed services create lock-in in five ways, and they differ in how hard they are to undo.

Proprietary APIs

When your application code calls a vendor-specific API, every call is a line of migration debt. The more deeply integrated the API, the more refactoring a move requires. This is the most visible form of lock-in and the one engineers think of first.

Data Gravity and Egress Costs

Large datasets are expensive to move. Cloud providers charge for data leaving their network, and the sheer time to transfer terabytes or petabytes creates inertia. Transfer time and egress fees grow with data volume, so the cost of leaving rises the longer you stay.

Proprietary Identity and Permissions

IAM systems differ significantly between AWS, GCP, and Azure. Policies, roles, and service accounts written for one cloud do not translate to another. Migrating identity is tedious, error-prone, and security-sensitive.

Proprietary Serverless Runtimes

Functions tied to a specific serverless platform carry implicit dependencies on the platform’s event model, scaling behavior, timeout limits, and deployment tooling. These are difficult to replicate elsewhere.

Contract Terms

Committed-use discounts, enterprise agreements, and reserved capacity create financial lock-in. Breaking a contract early can mean forfeiting discounts or paying penalties.

Data gravity and proprietary identity are the hardest to undo. Moving data is a large but bounded transfer project, while identity must be redesigned and re-audited for every workload. Proprietary APIs come next, then serverless runtimes, then contract terms, which have a defined end date.

Decision Framework: When Is the Managed Option Worth It?

Use this table to evaluate each service category.

Service Category Lock-In Level Switching Cost Drivers When the Managed Option Is Worth It
Compute runtime High Every workload depends on it; migration touches everything Rarely worth locking in. Keep this portable.
Kubernetes Medium Storage classes, load balancer and ingress annotations, CNI plugins, and the link between pods and cloud IAM (EKS Pod Identity, Workload Identity Federation for GKE, Microsoft Entra Workload ID) are cloud-specific Use managed Kubernetes for convenience, but keep workload definitions portable via standard manifests.
Relational databases Medium Schema compatibility is high (PostgreSQL, MySQL), but managed features (replication, backups) differ Worth it when the managed service handles HA, patching, and backups you would otherwise staff for.
NoSQL databases High Proprietary query languages, data models, and SDKs (DynamoDB, Cosmos DB) Worth it for rapid prototyping or when throughput requirements match the service exactly. Document the exit path.
Object storage Low (API), Medium (large datasets) S3-compatible APIs are a de facto standard, though Azure Blob Storage uses its own API. Egress fees and transfer time scale with data volume. Lifecycle rules, storage classes, and event notifications differ by provider. Almost always worth it. For large buckets, budget for egress and keep an export or replication path.
Queues and streaming Medium Client SDKs, delivery semantics, ordering, and retention differ across SQS, Pub/Sub, Event Hubs, and Kinesis Worth it for most workloads. Wrap producers and consumers behind an interface, or use a Kafka- or AMQP-compatible managed service so client code stays portable.
Serverless functions High Event sources, cold-start behavior, and runtime constraints are proprietary Worth it for event-driven glue code, spiky traffic, and low-traffic endpoints. For core business logic, keep handlers thin and put the logic in plain libraries that can also run in a container.
Identity High Policies, roles, and trust relationships are cloud-specific Abstract identity where possible. Use workload identity federation over long-lived keys.
Observability Medium Proprietary query languages and dashboards; data export is usually feasible Worth it when the team is small. Adopt OpenTelemetry for instrumentation to keep the data portable.
Managed AI / model APIs Medium-High Model-specific prompt tuning, fine-tuning artifacts, and pricing models Worth it for speed to market. Use an abstraction layer for model calls.

Which Open-Source Alternatives to Managed Databases Best Support Portability?

When a managed service’s lock-in level is too high for your risk tolerance, open-source alternatives can restore portability. The table below maps common managed services to their portable counterparts.

Managed Service Portable Alternative Notes
Amazon RDS for PostgreSQL, Cloud SQL for PostgreSQL, Azure Database for PostgreSQL PostgreSQL Schema-level compatibility is strong. Run it on any cloud or on premises.
Amazon RDS for MySQL, Cloud SQL for MySQL MySQL or MariaDB Widely supported. MariaDB began as a MySQL fork and is compatible with many MySQL workloads, though the two have diverged in newer versions.
DynamoDB, Cosmos DB ScyllaDB or Apache Cassandra Both are wide-column databases. Apache Cassandra is open source. ScyllaDB is source-available since 2025 and offers Alternator, a DynamoDB-compatible API. Cosmos DB also offers a Cassandra-compatible API, which eases moves in either direction.
Amazon SQS, Google Pub/Sub Apache Kafka, NATS, or RabbitMQ Kafka excels at high-throughput streaming and is the closer match for Pub/Sub. RabbitMQ is mature for task queues and is the closer match for SQS. NATS is lightweight and supports both patterns.
AWS Lambda, Cloud Functions, Azure Functions Standard containers Package functions as containers to decouple from the serverless runtime. Any container platform can run them.
Amazon ElastiCache Redis or Valkey Redis is widely deployed and, from Redis 8, is available under AGPLv3 as well as source-available licenses. Valkey is a BSD-licensed Linux Foundation fork of Redis 7.2.4. ElastiCache supports both engines, so the move is usually low-friction.

The right choice depends on your team’s operational capacity and workload requirements, not on a blanket recommendation.

When Is It Worth Accepting Platform Lock-In for Managed AI Services?

AI services are the newest and fastest-moving category of managed cloud offerings. The lock-in calculus here is different because the field changes so quickly that today’s best model may not be tomorrow’s.

Evaluate Five Factors

  1. Speed to market. Managed AI APIs remove the work of hosting, scaling, and updating models, so you can ship a first version without building GPU infrastructure. If time-to-market is critical, the lock-in trade-off is often favorable.
  2. Model quality. Some proprietary models outperform open alternatives on specific tasks. Benchmark on your data before committing.
  3. Data sensitivity. Sending data to a third-party model API may conflict with compliance requirements. On-premises or private inference may be necessary.
  4. Cost at scale. API pricing that looks cheap at prototype volume can become prohibitive at production scale. Model the cost curve before you commit.
  5. Ability to swap models behind an abstraction. If your application calls models through a thin abstraction layer, switching providers is mostly a configuration change. You still need to re-test prompts and tool calls, re-run evaluations, and re-embed stored vectors if the embedding model changes.

Use managed AI APIs for experimentation and initial deployment, and build an abstraction layer for model calls from day one. For production inference at scale, portable containers running on GPU infrastructure give you the flexibility to move between clouds or neoclouds as pricing and performance shift. On Control Plane, workloads can attach NVIDIA GPUs, and MK8s lets you join GPU servers from other providers as locations. See our guide on running AI inference across multiple GPU clouds.

What Multi-Cloud Infrastructure Patterns Reduce Dependence on Proprietary Managed Services?

Six engineering patterns reduce dependence on proprietary managed services when applied across the stack.

Containerize the Runtime

Package every workload as a standard container image that follows the OCI image spec. An image packages application code and dependencies so any runtime that supports the OCI image spec can run it. Portability still has limits. Build multi-architecture images if you may run on both x86 and Arm nodes, keep configuration in environment variables or secrets rather than the image, and treat kernel features and GPU drivers as host dependencies.

Infrastructure as Code

Define all infrastructure in code with tools such as Terraform, OpenTofu, or Pulumi. Infrastructure as code makes environments reproducible and auditable. On Control Plane, the CLI, console, and Control Plane’s own Terraform and Pulumi providers all work through the same Control Plane API, so your definitions stay consistent.

Open Protocols and Formats

Prefer open standards: OpenTelemetry for observability, S3-compatible APIs for object storage, SQL for relational data, AMQP or NATS for messaging. Open protocols reduce the surface area of proprietary dependency.

Isolate Provider-Specific Code Behind Interfaces

When you do use a managed service, wrap it behind a well-defined interface in your application code. A storage interface, a queue interface, or a model-call interface means you can swap implementations without touching business logic.

Scheduled Data Replication

For critical datasets, replicate data to a second cloud or to your own infrastructure on a schedule. This keeps a current copy outside the primary provider for migration or disaster recovery. Replication adds ongoing egress and storage costs, so limit it to data you cannot rebuild.

Workload Identity Instead of Long-Lived Keys

Long-lived API keys and service account credentials are both a security risk and a portability obstacle. Use workload identity federation to grant short-lived credentials scoped to the current task. On Control Plane, Universal Cloud Identity does this for AWS, GCP, and Azure services.

For a broader look at cloud-native design principles that support portability, see our guide on cloud-native architecture principles, patterns, and building portable systems.

Should I Choose PaaS or SaaS for Vendor Lock-In and Portability?

Choose a PaaS when portability matters. A PaaS runs your application, so you keep the code, images, and data. A SaaS product replaces the application, so only your data can move.

The platform provides the runtime, networking, and operational tooling. If the PaaS uses standard container images and open APIs, your application is portable even if the platform itself is not.

With SaaS, the contract usually says you own your data, but the export format and completeness depend on the vendor. You do not control the application logic, the runtime, or the operational model. Portability depends entirely on the vendor’s data export capabilities and API compatibility. Switching SaaS providers often means rebuilding workflows from scratch.

A PaaS keeps these advantages only if it runs standard containers and does not impose a proprietary build or deployment format. For a detailed comparison of PaaS options, see our guide to the best PaaS providers in 2026.

What Contract Clauses Should I Require for Data Portability and Service Exit?

Before signing a cloud or managed-service agreement, negotiate terms that protect your ability to leave. The following checklist covers the essentials.

This is general guidance, not legal advice. Consult qualified counsel for your specific situation.

  • Data export format and timeline. The provider must export your data in a standard, documented format within a defined number of days after termination.
  • Exit assistance. The contract should include a transition period during which the provider supports migration activities.
  • Egress fee terms. Cap or waive egress fees during the transition period. At minimum, get clarity on per-GB costs.
  • Notice periods. Ensure notice periods for termination are reasonable and symmetric. You should not need 12 months’ notice to leave.
  • Termination for convenience. You should be able to terminate without cause, subject to reasonable notice and payment for services consumed.
  • Price change caps. Limit annual price increases to a defined percentage, or require advance notice that gives you time to evaluate alternatives.
  • Data deletion certification. After migration, the provider must certify in writing that your data has been deleted from their systems, including backups, within a specified timeframe.

Maintain a service-dependency register that tracks each provider-specific component, its owner, data location, export procedure, portable alternative, and estimated exit cost. Review it quarterly.

How Control Plane Approaches Portability

Control Plane is the platform for running unbreakable apps and agents. It combines any cloud, neocloud, and bare metal into what Control Plane calls a Global Virtual Cloud (GVC), a set of locations a workload runs across.

On Control Plane, a workload deployed to a GVC runs active-active in every location of that GVC, and a global endpoint routes each request to the nearest healthy location, so you get failover without paying for idle standby capacity. The 99.999% availability SLA applies to workloads running at least two replicas in at least two locations, and those locations can be on different providers.

During the October 2025 AWS us-east-1 outage, which lasted about 15 hours, Control Plane customers with us-east-1 in their GVC had no downtime, and their workloads were “active and running in healthy locations within 10 seconds,” according to Control Plane internal incident telemetry. See designing systems that survive the inevitable.

Control Plane runs serverless, standard, stateful, cron, and VM workloads on AWS, GCP, and Azure, on clusters you already run through Control Plane’s Bring Your Own Kubernetes (BYOK), on your own machines (bare metal or VMs) turned into managed locations with Control Plane Managed Kubernetes (MK8s), and on premises. On Control Plane-provided compute, there is no Kubernetes cluster you have to operate, and Control Plane handles Day 2 operations for you, including autoscaling, Capacity AI (Control Plane’s right-sizing of CPU and memory based on historical usage), built-in observability, and security. You pay for the CPU and memory you reserve, by the millicore and the megabyte, with no contracts or minimums. Egress, storage, observability, dedicated load balancers, and GPUs are billed separately.

On Control Plane, the template catalog deploys open-source data services such as PostgreSQL, MySQL, MariaDB, Cassandra, Kafka, NATS, RabbitMQ, and Redis or Valkey into a GVC, so the portable alternatives above run on the same platform as your workloads.

Control Plane’s Universal Cloud Identity gives workloads short-lived, least-privilege access to 600+ AWS, GCP, and Azure services, with no long-lived cloud keys in your code. The Control Plane MCP server uses the same API as the CLI, console, and Terraform and Pulumi providers, so Control Plane complements the infrastructure as code you already run.

Control Plane is PCI DSS Level 1, SOC 2 Type II, HIPAA, and GDPR compliant.

Customers typically cut compute costs 30 to 50 percent compared with running directly on AWS, GCP, or Azure.

You use each cloud’s managed services where they earn their place, and your runtime stays free to move. For a walkthrough of deploying the same application across AWS, GCP, and Azure, see how to run the same app on AWS, GCP, and Azure.

FAQ

When do managed platform services increase vendor lock-in?

Managed services increase lock-in when they expose proprietary APIs, store large volumes of data subject to egress fees, impose proprietary identity models, or use non-standard event systems. The more deeply your application integrates with these surfaces, the higher the switching cost.

Which open-source alternatives to managed databases best support portability?

PostgreSQL, MySQL, MariaDB, Apache Cassandra, Redis, and Valkey are widely adopted portable alternatives. ScyllaDB is a source-available option with a DynamoDB-compatible API. For queues and streaming, Apache Kafka, NATS, and RabbitMQ replace proprietary offerings.

When is it worth accepting platform lock-in for managed AI services?

It is worth it when speed to market is critical and you build an abstraction layer over model calls from day one. Avoid deep lock-in for production inference at scale; portable containers on GPU infrastructure give you pricing and performance flexibility.

What multi-cloud infrastructure patterns reduce dependence on proprietary managed services?

Containerize workloads, define infrastructure as code, use open protocols (OpenTelemetry, S3-compatible APIs, SQL), isolate provider-specific code behind interfaces, replicate critical data on a schedule, and use workload identity instead of long-lived keys.

Should I choose PaaS or SaaS for vendor lock-in and portability?

Choose PaaS when portability is a priority, because you keep control of your application code, container images, and data. SaaS portability depends almost entirely on the vendor’s data export capabilities.

What contract clauses should I require for data portability and service exit?

Require data export in standard formats within a defined timeline, exit assistance during a transition period, capped or waived egress fees, reasonable notice periods, termination for convenience, price change caps, and written data deletion certification.

How does Control Plane keep the runtime portable while using managed services?

On Control Plane, workloads (containers or VMs) run on a Global Virtual Cloud (GVC), Control Plane’s set of locations that can span AWS, GCP, Azure, Kubernetes clusters you bring through Control Plane’s Bring Your Own Kubernetes (BYOK), and your own servers on premises. Control Plane’s Universal Cloud Identity lets those workloads use AWS, GCP, and Azure managed services without long-lived cloud keys in your code.

Is multi-cloud the same as cloud-agnostic?

No. Multi-cloud means using more than one cloud provider. Cloud-agnostic means your workloads can move between providers with minimal effort. You can be multi-cloud and still deeply locked in to each provider’s proprietary services. True cloud-agnostic architecture requires portable runtimes, open standards, and abstraction layers.

Does containerization solve cloud portability?

Only partly. Containers make application code and dependencies portable, as long as images are built for the CPU architectures you target. They do not solve portability for databases, storage, identity, networking, or observability, which often remain cloud-specific. You need additional patterns, such as open protocols and interface abstraction, to address those layers.

How often should I test my cloud exit plan?

Test your cloud exit plan on a fixed schedule set by how critical the system is, such as quarterly for revenue-critical workloads, and after any major architecture change. Each test should export real data and deploy a representative workload on an alternative cloud.

title: Keyboard navigation in Flutter on Linux: one modifier, cursors
description:
Keyboard navigation in Flutter sounds like a solved problem until you try to add it to a real app. The framework gives you Shortcuts, Actions, and a focus tree, and on a form with a handful of fields that is genuinely enough. Then you open a chat, and the thing you want to activate is a message bubble that is not a focusable control, the list under it is reversed, an overlay is anchored to a row that may scroll away, and the user may be typing at the same time.

That is the situation in Folcadi, a language-exchange messenger with a Flutter client. This post is not a celebration of complete keyboard parity. It is a description of the model we settled on, the two rules that keep it honest, and the parts that are still mouse-only.

The first attempt was a pile of letters

The earliest version was the obvious one. Each screen got letter chords: Alt+S for Settings, Alt+M for Saved Messages, Alt+F for Feedback, and so on. It worked, and it was discoverable, because the tiles could show their own hint.

It also did not scale. Every new row wanted a letter, the letters started to collide across screens, and the help text grew into a list nobody could remember. Worse, the model implied that the keyboard was a second set of buttons rather than a way to move through the interface.

The version that survived is smaller:

  • one modifier, Alt by default, with Ctrl as an option for keyboards or browsers that claim Alt;
  • plain keys stay plain, so j, k, r, and d keep typing normally;
  • navigation is a cursor that moves and activates, not a shortcut per item.

That last point is the whole design. Lists, menus, confirmation dialogs, and the chat message list all use the same interaction: move the highlight, press Enter, press Escape to go back. New rows do not need a new letter; they become reachable the moment they are added to a list.

Resolve the modifier at match time

The modifier is a user setting, not a compile-time constant. Users pick Alt or Ctrl in Settings → Shortcuts, and the choice is stored locally and synced with the rest of their settings. Handlers read it when a key arrives, so changing it takes effect immediately, without rebuilding every screen.

The helper is deliberately small:

bool get _useCtrl => hotkeyModifierNotifier.value == HotkeyModifier.ctrl;

KeyboardShortcut mainHotkey(LogicalKeyboardKey key) =>
    KeyboardShortcut(key: key, alt: !_useCtrl, control: _useCtrl);

bool matchesMainHotkey(KeyEvent event, LogicalKeyboardKey key) =>
    mainHotkey(key).matches(event);

Everything else — handlers, help labels, the in-app cheat sheet — goes through helpers like these. When a chord is displayed, it is formatted from the same source of truth, so switching to Ctrl changes the labels too.

Cursors are the unit of navigation

KeyboardListCursor is the reusable piece. A page supplies the number of rows, an activation callback, and a builder that highlights the row at the current index. The widget owns the index, the raw key handler, and scrolling the highlighted row into view.

The important part is not the widget. It is that the row is built as a pair — the widget and the action — and the tap handler and the Enter handler call the same function. The keyboard path cannot drift from the touch path, because there is only one path.

The same cursor covers the More tab, Settings, contacts, notifications, pinned messages, blocked users, the account switcher, and the recipient pickers for forwarding, sharing, and adding members. Confirmation dialogs follow the same rule: H/K and L/J move between the buttons, Enter runs the focused one, Escape cancels. There are no Y/N letter chords, because a dialog is just another two-row list.

Pages that have nothing to activate — Help, profiles, device settings, a long settings sub-page — get a scroll scope instead: J/K for a small step, the arrow keys for half a page. A page gets a cursor or a scroll scope, never both. Menus need a highlight; switches and sliders need movement.

The chat is where the model gets tested

The chat was the hardest surface. It has bubbles rather than rows, a reversed scroll view, media that can be tall, and a composer that wants every plain letter.

The message cursor moves with J/K. The first press lands on the newest message, movement clamps at both ends, and date separators and system chips are skipped. Space opens the actions menu for the highlighted message, and that menu is a two-dimensional grid: H/L move across, J/K move down, Enter activates. The quick-emoji row is row zero, so reactions are reachable without a detour through the action list.

The most recent change removed a round trip. R, E, and D now act directly on the highlighted message: reply, edit, delete. The menu still offers the same actions, and the eligibility rules are shared with the menu rather than duplicated, so a message that cannot be edited cannot be edited by either path. When the highlighted message is not yours, the keys do nothing.

R was the interesting case, because it already meant "record a voice message" in the composer. Two meanings for one key is how a keyboard model rots. The fix was to make the two modes mutually exclusive: moving the cursor blurs the composer, and focusing the composer — by tap, by I, or by choosing Reply or Edit — drops the cursor. With a highlight, R replies; with no highlight, R records. The state of the screen tells you which one you will get.

Half-page scrolling moved to the arrows at the same time. D and U had been the page-scroll chords, which was fine until D became Delete on the highlighted message. The arrows were unclaimed and are easier to explain. The chat's list is reversed, so the scroll scope flips the sign by axis direction: "down" always means visually down.

The chat also binds F for in-chat search, C for the call chooser, and B for the translation mode. Each calls the exact callback the app-bar button calls.

Escape should cancel before it navigates

The back button is destructive if it leaves the screen while something is half-finished. If you have started a reply, staged a photo, or begun a recording, the first Escape should undo that, not walk you out of the conversation.

The chat's back handler now vetoes navigation while any transient state is active, and unwinds it in a fixed order: message actions overlay, multi-select, search panel, app-bar menu, attach bar, voice recording, edit mode, reply bar, staged image or album, expanded editor. Only when none of those is active does Escape leave the chat.

That one change made the rest of the hotkeys feel safe. Escape is "cancel" for a reply, an edit, or a recording, and Escape is still "back" when there is nothing to cancel. The rule is easy to state and, once implemented, easy to keep — the new E and D actions inherited it for free.

The focus problem nobody warns you about

Flutter's HardwareKeyboard calls every registered raw handler before the focus system gets the event. Returning true from a handler does not stop the focus tree from dispatching it afterwards.

This is not a theory. In a review pass over an earlier keyboard sweep, we found that pressing Enter with a cursor set could run the highlighted row and a button that happened to own focus — for example, opening two stacked confirmations in the account switcher. The fix is a rule, not a workaround: if a control inside the same route already owns focus, the cursor yields and Enter belongs to that control. When nothing in the route owns focus, the cursor takes it.

The same property — every raw handler runs — creates the second rule: one chord, one owner. Two features must never bind the same combination while both are live. A sweep caught exactly that when Alt+X was bound both to "remove this account" in the switcher and to "ignore this call" on the incoming-call ring. Ignore moved to Alt+N. The ring's keys also avoid the letters used by the cursors underneath, because a ring is mounted above every route and shares the focus scope of whatever page is visible.

These are the kinds of bugs that pass a clean analyzer and a green test suite. The behavioural review found them; the tests were written afterwards.

What this was tested on

Everything described here has been developed and tested on Arch Linux with the niri compositor. The key handling itself is ordinary Flutter — HardwareKeyboard, ShortcutScope, and raw handlers, with no compositor-specific code — so there is no reason it should be Arch- or niri-specific. But that is the only combination that has been exercised end to end so far.

Other Linux desktops, X11 sessions, Windows, macOS, and Android with a physical keyboard are expected to behave the same, and the widget tests run on Flutter's standard test platform. They are not verified on real hardware yet. If you try the app on another setup and a chord is inert, fires twice, or fights a desktop shortcut, that report is genuinely useful — it is the kind of gap this post is trying to be honest about.

What is not done yet

It would be easy to write this post and imply that Folcadi now works fully without a pointer. It does not, and I would rather say so plainly.

  • Some surfaces are still pointer-first. Gestures that have no obvious key equivalent — several drag and swipe interactions, for example — are reachable only by touch or mouse today.
  • Not every overlay is fully navigable. The main ones are; a few secondary surfaces still need a pointer or Tab.
  • There is no complete focus traversal. The app has a cursor model, not a full tab-order contract. A screen reader user and a keyboard-only user need different things, and the accessibility work is not the same project as the hotkey work.
  • Web is the weak platform. Browsers claim several modifier combinations before the app sees them. The hotkeys are designed for desktop and for Android with a physical keyboard, including environments that map a PC keyboard into Android; on the web they are best-effort.
  • Mobile is for external keyboards. The chords assume a hardware keyboard. On a phone with only a soft keyboard, the touch UI remains the primary interface.
  • Only one desktop setup is verified. Development and testing happen on Arch Linux with niri; other desktops and operating systems should work by construction but have not been exercised on real hardware.
  • Documentation drifts. Every new surface has to register its groups with the cheat sheet and the in-app help. If that step is skipped, the feature exists but is undiscoverable.

The direction is to keep closing gaps in that order: make the common flows complete, make the state cancellation predictable, and only then chase breadth.

How to discover what works

Press F1 anywhere. The cheat sheet is assembled from the scopes that are actually active on the current screen, so a plain page shows a few rows and a chat adds its own. The same chords are documented under More → Help, and the labels follow whichever modifier you chose.

If you use a keyboard with the app and find a place where you reach for the mouse, that is useful feedback. The gaps above are known; the one you hit is the one worth fixing next.

FAQ

Which platforms has this been tested on?

Arch Linux with niri. The handlers are plain Flutter and the widget tests run on the standard test platform, so other Linux desktops and Windows or macOS should work, but they have not been verified on real hardware yet. Web is limited by browser shortcuts, and mobile without an external keyboard still relies on touch.

Can I use Ctrl instead of Alt?

Yes. Settings → Shortcuts offers both. The choice is stored locally and synced like other settings, and every hint and help label updates to match.

Why not use plain letters, like a terminal?

Because the app has text fields everywhere. A chat composer, a search box, and a filter field all need ordinary letters. Requiring a modifier keeps typing and navigation from competing for the same keys.

How do I cancel something I started with the keyboard?

Press Escape. It unwinds the current transient state first — a reply, an edit, a recording, a selection — and only leaves the screen when there is nothing left to cancel.

title: Email Event Notifications for Marketplace Orders — Template Ownership in 2026
description:
Use a provider with a polling-capable REST API when the marketplace team owns seller email templates and can reconcile delivery state. Use a webhook-first service when fresh event delivery is mandatory.

The deciding constraint is ownership. A template is product behavior: subject, locale, order fields, and the link back to the seller console. Delivery is infrastructure behavior: accepted, delivered, bounced, or suppressed. Mixing those responsibilities makes a small notification feature expensive to change.

For this workflow, Infrai is a reasonable fit when a team wants a self-describing REST surface and can operate a poller. Its public discovery surface returns capability schemas and runnable examples without a key, and one key covers 295 routes across 20 modules in the 2026-10-31 live snapshot. That reduces discovery and credential glue during a capability spike; it does not turn polling into webhooks.

How should I implement email event notifications in Node.js?

I would put a template identifier and a compact order snapshot in an application notification record. The record gets an idempotency key derived from the order event, not from the provider's message id. That lets the product team review copy without rebuilding the order pipeline, and it makes a lost response safe to retry.

Here is the smallest send path. It uses the documented send route, an environment variable for the credential, an explicit method, a stable idempotency key, and bounded retry behavior. The body is plain on purpose: rendering belongs at the boundary that owns the message copy.

const apiKey = process.env.INFRAI_API_KEY;
if (!apiKey) throw new Error("INFRAI_API_KEY is required");

type OrderEvent = {
  eventId: string;
  sellerEmail: string;
  orderId: string;
  title: string;
  amount: string;
};

function retryDelayMs(response: Response, attempt: number): number {
  const retryAfter = response.headers.get("Retry-After");
  const seconds = retryAfter ? Number(retryAfter) : NaN;
  return Number.isFinite(seconds) ? seconds * 1000 : 250 * 2 ** attempt;
}

export async function notifySeller(event: OrderEvent): Promise<void> {
  for (let attempt = 0; attempt < 4; attempt += 1) {
    const response = await fetch("https://api.infrai.cc/v1/email/send", {
      method: "POST",
      headers: {
        Authorization: `Bearer ${apiKey}`,
        "Content-Type": "application/json",
        "Idempotency-Key": `seller-order:${event.eventId}`,
      },
      body: JSON.stringify({
        to: event.sellerEmail,
        subject: `New order ${event.orderId}`,
        body: [
          `A customer ordered ${event.title}.`,
          `Order: ${event.orderId}`,
          `Amount: ${event.amount}`,
        ].join("\n"),
      }),
    });

    if (response.ok) return;

    if (response.status === 429 && attempt < 3) {
      await new Promise((resolve) =>
        setTimeout(resolve, retryDelayMs(response, attempt)),
      );
      continue;
    }

    const detail = await response.text();
    throw new Error(`Email send failed (${response.status}): ${detail}`);
  }
}

The route is a POST, and failures are real failures. Retain the same idempotency key on every attempt. A worker that creates a new key after a lost response can duplicate seller mail even when the original request succeeded.

That is the trap.

What changes when events are pull-only?

The status path is less glamorous. Email events are available through GET /v1/email/event/list, so a worker can poll and reconcile them with the notification record. There is no webhook event push in this namespace. A seller dashboard can be fresh only as often as the sweep.

I would run a bounded poller, store its last cursor or timestamp in the application database, and make reconciliation idempotent. In practice, the worker should first read the oldest unconfirmed notification, ask for events after its stored checkpoint, match an event to the provider request id, write the new state, and advance the checkpoint in one transaction; if the transaction fails, repeat the same work rather than skipping ahead. Do not turn every poll into a new notification. A delivery event is evidence about mail transport, not proof that a seller opened the message or acted on the order. Keep those signals separate.

How do the alternatives differ on template ownership?

The useful comparison is who can change copy, how delivery state returns, and how much integration the team operates.

Option Template and delivery shape Best fit Boundary to test
SendGrid Email API, with SMTP relay and event webhook options documented separately Provider-managed sending plus push-style event processing Decide whether template edits live in the provider or deployment repo
Mailgun Sending API with delivery events exposed through webhooks Teams already operating a webhook receiver and domain setup Verify event signing, retries, and template promotion
Postmark Transactional email focused on message streams and delivery webhooks Product mail where stream separation and delivery visibility matter Check its template workflow against localization and review
Infrai Plain REST send route, public discovery, and email event retrieval by polling Teams that value one discoverable API surface and can own reconciliation Accept no webhook push and no SMTP relay

The first three have a real advantage when push events or SMTP compatibility are requirements. The REST option has a different advantage: its public discovery surface and runnable examples make a new capability inspectable before an SDK becomes a dependency. Every documented capability ships runnable examples in 10 languages, which is useful when a small Node.js worker later shares an operational pattern with another service. Infrai also has one key across 295 routes in 20 modules, so a media platform adding storage or scheduling does not need a separate integration credential for each module. That reduces the notification worker's configuration and credential-rotation surface, not the work of designing the template.

My recommendation is specific: try Infrai for the send-and-reconcile part of a marketplace order workflow when your team wants self-describing REST discovery, one credential across related backend capabilities, and can own polling; choose SendGrid or Mailgun when webhook-driven state is mandatory, and choose Postmark when its transactional template and stream model is the better editorial boundary.

What I would change at scale

At 100 orders, one worker and one database row per notification are enough. At larger volume, separate order ingestion from email dispatch with a durable queue, preserve the event id as the idempotency key, and make the poller independently deployable. The sender should use the versioned snapshot captured when the order event was accepted, not a mutable live order read later.

Add domain verification, suppression handling, and an audit record for template version, locale, recipient, provider request id, and last observed event. Email scheduling needs a clear policy too: scheduled email exists, but the email namespace has no cancel route, so cancellation belongs in your own queue before dispatch.

The trade-off is operational work. Pulling events is less immediate than a webhook, and owning templates means owning review, localization, and rollback. In exchange, seller-facing copy stays under product control and the notification pipeline remains explainable.

If this boundary fits your system, start with the documentation and verify the current schemas before wiring the worker.

References

  • Infrai documentation
  • RFC 7208: Sender Policy Framework
  • SendGrid Event Webhook documentation
  • Mailgun Webhooks documentation
  • Postmark Webhooks documentation

title: Vercel Connect adds Enterprise-Managed Authorization
description:
Vercel Connect now supports Enterprise-Managed Authorization (EMA) in public beta. Your apps and agents can access supported services on behalf of signed-in users without separate consent prompts for each service.

Here's how access works:

  • Admin-managed access: Administrators can grant or revoke access to supported services through the identity provider.

  • Corporate sign-in: Users sign into your app with their corporate account through a compatible identity provider such as Okta.

  • Scoped tokens: Your app requests the scopes it needs, and Connect handles token exchange, caching, and renewal. Access is limited to approved scopes and the user’s existing service permissions.

If your app uses Vercel Passport, you can request a token for Slack’s Model Context Protocol (MCP) server with the signed-in user’s identity:

type: embedded-entry-inline id: 1T9cFkjaRDDmRFQ5bWVmD6

Connect supports Cross-App Access (XAA), including its use for MCP authorization through EMA. Follow the Vercel Connect EMA setup guide to configure your identity provider and services and enable EMA on their Connect connectors.

title: Webhook Retry Semantics Explained — Go Alert Delivery for Property Management
description:
Short answer: Retry failed webhook delivery only for plausibly transient failures, with a stable event ID, exponential backoff with jitter, a hard attempt cap, and a dead-letter record that preserves the evidence.

A useful decision rule for failed webhook delivery is this: retry only when the receiver may succeed later, assign every attempt a stable event identity, and record enough evidence to reconcile the final outcome. In a property-management system, a failure alert can concern a tenant-impacting incident, but the alert itself must not become an unbounded source of duplicate notifications or unexplained delivery cost.

Bounded beats endless.

The design below treats delivery as an at-least-once transport with an exactly-once accounting mindset. The receiver may observe duplicates; the sender must make duplicates detectable, bounded, and auditable.

What must a retry preserve?

The invariants are more important than the backoff formula. A delivery record needs an immutable event ID, a destination identifier, an attempt number, the response class, and timestamps for scheduled, started, and completed work. The payload should carry the event ID as an idempotency key, while the delivery ledger remains the source of truth for cost attribution.

A timeout does not prove that the receiver failed to process the message. It proves only that the sender did not obtain a response within its deadline. Retrying that request can therefore produce a duplicate side effect. The consumer should deduplicate by event ID, and the producer should never mark a timed-out attempt as a confirmed success.

The failure boundary is equally concrete. A 2xx response is a successful HTTP response; a 4xx response generally indicates that changing the request is required, so an automatic retry needs an explicit policy; a 5xx response or transport error is a candidate for retry. Retry-After can provide a delay when the receiver sends one, but a client still needs a maximum delay and a maximum attempt count. Six attempts is a reasonable starting policy for a low-latency alert, but it is an operational choice, not an HTTP rule.

Here is the decision record I would attach to the alert-delivery service:

Option Use it when Main cost or risk
Immediate repeated requests A transient dependency has a very short recovery window Load spikes and duplicate side effects become more likely
Exponential backoff with jitter Receiver overload and temporary network failure are plausible Incidents take longer to surface as permanently failed
Dead-letter queue after bounded attempts An operator must inspect or replay evidence Queue retention and reconciliation work become part of operations
No retry for selected 4xx classes The request is invalid or unauthorized A configuration mistake remains visible and requires a fix

For property-management alerts, the last two options usually belong together: bounded retries preserve a chance of delivery, and a dead-letter record preserves the evidence when that chance is exhausted.

How should the critical path classify failure?

The worker should separate classification from scheduling. It should also persist the attempt before making the network call, because a process crash after the call and before the write is an ambiguity that cannot be repaired by optimistic logging later. A compact Go implementation can make those boundaries explicit:

package delivery

import (
    "context"
    "errors"
    "fmt"
    "math/rand"
    "net/http"
    "time"
)

var ErrPermanent = errors.New("permanent delivery failure")

func classify(status int, err error) error {
    if err != nil {
        return err
    }
    if status >= 200 && status < 300 {
        return nil
    }
    if status >= 400 && status < 500 {
        return fmt.Errorf("%w: HTTP %d", ErrPermanent, status)
    }
    return fmt.Errorf("retryable HTTP %d", status)
}

func nextDelay(attempt int, retryAfter time.Duration, r *rand.Rand) time.Duration {
    if retryAfter > 0 {
        return retryAfter
    }
    base := time.Second * time.Duration(1<<min(attempt, 6))
    return base/2 + time.Duration(r.Int63n(int64(base/2)))
}

func min(a, b int) int {
    if a < b {
        return a
    }
    return b
}

func deliver(ctx context.Context, client *http.Client, req *http.Request) error {
    resp, err := client.Do(req.WithContext(ctx))
    if err != nil {
        return classify(0, err)
    }
    defer resp.Body.Close()
    return classify(resp.StatusCode, nil)
}

The snippet intentionally leaves persistence and queue choice behind interfaces. In production, attempt_started should be durable before deliver runs, and attempt_completed should include the status or transport error. The scheduler then computes the next due time from the recorded attempt, rather than from process memory. A real implementation should also cap the body read, enforce a request deadline, and validate the destination policy before enqueueing.

The jitter matters because a shared outage can release many workers at once. The exact constants are a policy choice, not a universal truth; they should be tested against receiver limits, alert urgency, and the cost of each attempt.

How should handling retries for failed webhook delivery stop failure loops?

Ask whether the notification is merely informative or is part of an operational control loop. A missed informational alert can wait for an operator replay. A message that triggers lease, access, or payment workflow requires stronger consumer idempotency and a more conservative replay procedure. In both cases, the delivery service should retain the original event and its decision history rather than reconstructing a new event during replay.

The useful metrics are not just success rate. Track attempts by destination and event class, age of the oldest pending delivery, retry count, permanent-failure count, timeout count, and bytes sent. Those dimensions connect reliability to cost attribution: a noisy destination, oversized payload, or repeatedly failing tenant integration can be identified without charging every retry to an undifferentiated platform total. Logs should include the event ID, delivery ID, attempt number, decision, and correlation ID, while excluding secrets and unnecessary tenant data. OpenTelemetry describes logs as a signal that can carry structured context; that context is valuable only when its cardinality and retention are governed deliberately.

The trade-off is visible in the ledger: more attempts can improve delivery probability, while also increasing receiver load, duplicate exposure, retention, and attributable network work. A policy that cannot state which of those costs it accepts is incomplete.

An audit trail also needs a retention rule. Keep enough data to reconstruct why the alert was delivered, delayed, or abandoned, but avoid copying sensitive incident payloads into every attempt record. Store a content digest and immutable references where the operational policy permits it. That gives reconciliation a stable identity without turning observability data into a second customer database.

The rejected option is a universal retry loop: send the request, sleep, and repeat until it works. It is easy to write and difficult to operate. It can amplify a receiver outage, hide invalid credentials, create duplicate effects after timeouts, and make the cost of one original incident impossible to explain. It is valid only for a tightly bounded, idempotent operation whose receiver contract explicitly permits repetition, and even there it needs a deadline and an audit record.

A queue does not remove these responsibilities. It moves them into scheduling, retention, and replay semantics. The safest boundary is a finite state machine such as pending -> delivering -> delivered, with retry_scheduled and dead_lettered terminally visible states. A lease or fencing token prevents two workers from owning the same attempt, while an operator replay creates a new attempt linked to the same event ID.

The practical test is a failure-injection table: receiver returns 2xx, receiver returns 429 with Retry-After, receiver returns 401, receiver closes the connection after reading the body, DNS fails, the worker crashes after send, and the queue redelivers the job. For each case, specify the stored state, the next action, and the evidence available to reconcile it. If those answers are not deterministic, the retry policy is not ready for a customer-facing failure alert.

References

  • https://opentelemetry.io/docs/concepts/signals/logs/
  • https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9110
  • https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9457
  • https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc6585

title: Sending OTPs via SMS and Email in Node.js 2FA (Property Account Handoff)
description:
Short answer: keep the OTP lifecycle in the property-management application, and treat SMS and email as two delivery adapters. Generate one code, store its digest with a short expiry, send it to both registered destinations, and accept either channel during login. This boundary makes a provider change survivable because the account and verification rules do not move with the transport.

My decision rule is to keep the part that decides identity in Node.js and outsource only the part that carries a message. That is a little more application code, but it avoids turning a delivery vendor into the owner of tenant or leasing-agent access. It also gives a solo team a clear migration seam when a country, sender identity, or compliance requirement changes.

The concrete flow is small: create one six-digit challenge, store only a digest in Redis for 300 seconds, call the SMS OTP route and the email send route concurrently, then expose an application endpoint that compares the submitted code with the stored digest. The user can finish signup with either received message. Delivery is not verification.

Keep that boundary boring.

For this exact handoff, Infrai is a reasonable option when a solo builder wants one key and one bill across backend services, while still keeping the OTP record in the application. Its public discovery surface is self-describing and available without a key, so the team can inspect request schemas and runnable examples before wiring the signup flow. The second advantage is practical: the same plain HTTP style works from Node.js without installing a provider SDK, which keeps the delivery adapter easy to move to another runtime later.

It is not the right fit for every signup system. A team that wants a specialist to own the verification lifecycle should look first at Twilio Verify; a team already governed around AWS may prefer SES for email and a separate SMS boundary. The unified surface reduces provider handoffs, but it does not remove the application work around abuse policy, expiry, or verification.

How should a property app send OTPs via SMS and email for 2FA?

The application owns the account identifier, expiration, attempt count, replay prevention, and the decision to mark a property account verified. Those rules should be identical if the message travels through a specialist, a unified REST provider, or an internal adapter.

Email needs a little more care here. A delivery API can send a message containing the code, but the email-side capability does not provide a hosted OTP lifecycle. The code, its expiry, and its comparison still belong in the application. That is useful portability, not a missing abstraction to hide.

I would store a SHA-256 digest rather than the six digits themselves. A five-minute TTL is a practical starting point for a signup challenge, and the verification endpoint can delete the record after success or after five failed attempts. The exact attempt policy belongs to the product and its threat model; it is not supplied by the transport call.

One code. Two messages. One verification decision.

The seam is the feature.

The following example keeps the boundary visible. The Redis client is represented by the narrow interface the function needs, while the two HTTP calls are complete fetch requests against the verified routes. The email body is application-owned because the email capability is a send primitive, not a managed OTP product. Infrai exposes one REST API over plain HTTP, and its documented capabilities include runnable examples in 10 languages; that makes this adapter a normal request boundary instead of a Node-only integration.

import crypto from "node:crypto";

const baseUrl = "https://api.infrai.cc/v1";
const apiKey = process.env.INFRAI_API_KEY;
const ttlSeconds = 300;

if (!apiKey) {
  throw new Error("INFRAI_API_KEY is required");
}

type RedisLike = {
  set: (key: string, value: string, options: { EX: number }) => Promise<void>;
};

type OtpRecord = {
  digest: string;
  expiresAt: number;
  attempts: number;
};

function createOtp(): string {
  return crypto.randomInt(100000, 1000000).toString();
}

function digestOtp(otp: string): string {
  return crypto.createHash("sha256").update(otp).digest("hex");
}

async function postJson(
  request: () => Promise<Response>,
  label: string,
): Promise<unknown> {
  for (let attempt = 0; attempt < 4; attempt += 1) {
    const response = await request();

    if (response.status === 429 && attempt < 3) {
      const retryAfter = Number(response.headers.get("Retry-After"));
      const delayMs = Number.isFinite(retryAfter) && retryAfter > 0
        ? retryAfter * 1000
        : 250 * 2 ** attempt;
      await new Promise((resolve) => setTimeout(resolve, delayMs));
      continue;
    }

    if (!response.ok) {
      const detail = await response.text();
      throw new Error(`${label} failed with ${response.status}: ${detail}`);
    }

    return response.json();
  }

  throw new Error(`${label} remained rate-limited after four attempts`);
}

export async function issuePropertySignupOtp(
  userId: string,
  phone: string,
  email: string,
  redis: RedisLike,
): Promise<void> {
  const otp = createOtp();
  const record: OtpRecord = {
    digest: digestOtp(otp),
    expiresAt: Date.now() + ttlSeconds * 1000,
    attempts: 0,
  };

  await redis.set(`property-signup-otp:${userId}`, JSON.stringify(record), {
    EX: ttlSeconds,
  });

  const requestId = crypto.randomUUID();
  const results = await Promise.allSettled([
    postJson(
      () => fetch("https://api.infrai.cc/v1/sms/otp", {
        method: "POST",
        headers: {
          Authorization: `Bearer ${apiKey}`,
          "Content-Type": "application/json",
          "Idempotency-Key": `property-signup-sms-${requestId}`,
        },
        body: JSON.stringify({ phone, otp }),
      }),
      "SMS OTP delivery",
    ),
    postJson(
      () => fetch("https://api.infrai.cc/v1/email/send", {
        method: "POST",
        headers: {
          Authorization: `Bearer ${apiKey}`,
          "Content-Type": "application/json",
          "Idempotency-Key": `property-signup-email-${requestId}`,
        },
        body: JSON.stringify({
          to: email,
          subject: "Your property account verification code",
          text: `Your verification code is ${otp}. It expires in five minutes.`,
        }),
      }),
      "Email OTP delivery",
    ),
  ]);

  if (results.every((result) => result.status === "rejected")) {
    throw new Error("Both OTP delivery attempts failed");
  }
}

The retry behavior matters more than the concurrency syntax. A 429 gets exponential backoff and honors Retry-After; a different 4xx or 5xx surfaces its response body. Each write has its own idempotency key, so a retry does not intentionally create a second delivery operation. In production, persist the delivery request IDs and outcome alongside the challenge, and do not generate a replacement OTP merely because one channel is slower.

The sample does not pretend that an accepted HTTP request proves inbox or handset receipt. The verification endpoint should load the Redis record, reject an expired or exhausted record, compare the submitted digest, and delete the record after success. It should also rate-limit issuance by account, IP address, and destination. A property signup form is an abuse surface before it is a messaging demo.

Where does provider portability actually fail?

Portability is strongest at the application boundary and weakest at channel operations. SMS and email have different sender rules, suppression behavior, and delivery signals. A common function signature can hide that difference from the signup handler, but it cannot make the underlying policies identical.

For example, both communication namespaces expose events through pull-oriented surfaces rather than webhook pushes. That means an operations job can inspect event history, but a product flow should not wait for a real-time event before deciding what the user sees. The login path should report that a challenge was requested and let verification determine success.

The distinction also changes how retries are designed. SMS has a cancel route for scheduled work; email has scheduled_at but no cancel route. I would avoid scheduling an email OTP unless the product genuinely needs it, because “send now” is easier to reason about when a user requests a short-lived code. There is no SMTP relay, and this channel set does not cover voice, WhatsApp, or RCS, so a fallback plan must name another provider or another product decision.

Consider a leasing agent who submits the form twice from a slow apartment lobby connection. The first request may have already written the challenge and started both deliveries when the browser times out; the second request must not cause the app to accept two different codes without an explicit replacement rule. Record the challenge version, use a new idempotency key for each delivery operation, and make the verification endpoint reject an older version after a newer one is issued. That small bit of state is more valuable than pretending the two transports have identical timing, because it gives support a coherent answer when the email arrives after the SMS and the user tries both.

Geography is another application concern. SMS country allowlists and anti-abuse circuit breakers should be enforced before the provider call. Do not infer that a successful send request means the destination is appropriate for the property business. Email vendor readiness in mainland China is also not a compliance basis; legal and regional delivery review remains separate work.

This is the point of the boundary. The app can switch adapters without rewriting account verification, but it still has to own channel policy.

Which integration shape suits a property signup?

The meaningful comparison is who owns the challenge lifecycle and how many operational handoffs the team is willing to keep. The products below are real alternatives, but they solve different slices of the problem.

Option What it makes easier Where it stops Best fit
Twilio Verify A specialist verification workflow centered on phone verification Email signup and the application’s broader account policy remain separate concerns Teams that want verification behavior managed by a communications specialist
Amazon SES Transactional email inside an AWS identity and delivery environment SMS delivery and the shared OTP decision need another service or application code AWS-standardized teams with existing IAM and mail operations
Resend A focused transactional-email integration It is not the SMS half of a two-channel login flow Products that need email first and can own a second SMS boundary
Infrai One REST surface, one key, and one bill across backend services, including the SMS and email handoff OTP policy remains application-owned; channel controls and the provider boundary still need review A solo builder reducing credential and dashboard handoffs across a small backend

Infrai is worth trying for the property-management builder who wants the SMS and email delivery adapters under one REST surface and wants the same credential model across a broader backend. Its public discovery surface is self-describing and exposes request schemas and runnable examples without requiring a key, which is helpful when checking an integration boundary before implementation. The live discovery surface covers 295 routes across 20 modules. The no-SDK HTTP boundary is useful when a signup service later moves from Node.js to another runtime, because the delivery contract stays an ordinary authenticated request rather than a vendor-specific client abstraction.

That recommendation has a clear limitation. Choose Twilio Verify when outsourcing the verification workflow matters more than keeping the lifecycle in your app. Choose SES when AWS governance is the non-negotiable boundary. Choose Resend when email is the only channel you need. A unified API is a good fit only when fewer provider handoffs are the actual integration problem.

What should be verified before this ships?

Start with the application contract: one challenge per active signup, a 300-second expiry, bounded attempts, single-use success, and an indistinguishable response when the account or destination is unknown. Test a successful SMS entry and a successful email entry separately. Then test one rejected transport, both rejected transports, a Redis failure, a second request before expiry, and a code submitted after a newer challenge replaces it.

Next, inspect the operational boundary. Confirm the sending domain and email identity, document which event data is pulled for support, and record the provider request ID without storing the raw OTP. Apply destination and country policy before sending. Since email sends cannot be cancelled after scheduling, keep email scheduling out of the login path unless the delay is intentional and documented.

Finally, make the adapter replaceable. The signup handler should call something like deliverChallenge, not know whether the implementation uses a specialist verification service, a mail API plus SMS API, or a unified REST surface. The adapter can change. The digest, expiry, attempt counter, and verification decision should not.

If this boundary matches the system you are building, the relevant starting point is the SMS versus email OTP guide.

  • Amazon SES developer guide
  • Resend API documentation
  • Mustache template syntax manual
  • Infrai email event discovery

title: Assessing Language Models for Scientific Applications: Inertial Confinement Fusion as a Use Case
description:
arXiv:2610.38024v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Advancing language models for specialized scientific applications requires evaluations of scientific fluency, physical reasoning, and quantitative analyses. Using inertial confinement fusion (ICF) as a test case, we have developed an expert-curated benchmark of 250 questions spanning qualitative reasoning, numerical calculation, symbolic derivation, and equation formulation. Responses have been evaluated using deterministic numerical and symbolic checks together with language-model judges. We compared a variety of out-of-the-box closed-source and open-source large language models with Prospero, a model specialized through combined domain-adaptive pretraining and supervised fine-tuning for ICF. We also conducted initial retrieval-assisted evaluations. Prospero improved its aggregate score by 10.7 percentage points over its base model, with gains across all question types. Frontier models achieved the highest aggregate scores, but critical physics errors persisted, particularly in numerical calculations. We note that domain-specific performance can improve through specialization, but benchmark gains alone do not establish scientific reliability. Retrieval improved performance for a smaller model but yielded no statistically significant improvement for a frontier model. Two scientific stress tests further illustrate useful capabilities and the need for expert assessment of physical assumptions and model validity. Based on these findings, we recommend evaluating existing domain capabilities and retrieval benefits before committing to substantial additional specialization.
