title: Mastering Security Headers
description:
Implementing security headers is crucial for protecting production websites, and it can be done by using headers like Content Security Policy (CSP), HTTP Strict Transport Security (HSTS), and secure cookie flags to prevent common web attacks, ensuring a secure user experience.

Key Takeaways

  • Implement Content Security Policy (CSP) to define allowed sources of content.
  • Use HTTP Strict Transport Security (HSTS) to enforce HTTPS connections.
  • Set secure cookie flags to prevent JavaScript access to sensitive cookies.
  • Configure security headers to prevent clickjacking and cross-site scripting attacks.

What are Security Headers?

Security headers are HTTP response headers that provide an additional layer of security for web applications. They help prevent common web attacks like cross-site scripting (XSS), clickjacking, and man-in-the-middle (MITM) attacks. By implementing security headers, you can significantly improve the security posture of your production website. For more information on security headers, you can visit the OWASP documentation.

How Does Content Security Policy (CSP) Work?

Content Security Policy (CSP) is a security header that helps prevent cross-site scripting (XSS) attacks by defining which sources of content are allowed to be executed within a web page. CSP works by specifying a set of sources from which content can be loaded, making it difficult for attackers to inject malicious scripts. You can implement CSP using the Content-Security-Policy header, like this:

Content-Security-Policy: default-src 'self'; script-src 'self' https://example.com;

This example allows content to be loaded from the same origin ('self') and from https://example.com. You can learn more about CSP and its directives on the MDN Web Docs.

Why is HTTP Strict Transport Security (HSTS) Critical?

HTTP Strict Transport Security (HSTS) is a security header that enforces HTTPS connections between a website and its users. HSTS works by instructing the browser to only connect to the website over HTTPS, even if the user types http:// in the address bar. This helps prevent man-in-the-middle (MITM) attacks and ensures that all communication between the website and its users is encrypted. You can implement HSTS using the Strict-Transport-Security header, like this:

Strict-Transport-Security: max-age=31536000; includeSubDomains

This example sets the maximum age of the HSTS policy to one year and includes all subdomains. For more information on HSTS, you can visit the RFC 6797 documentation.

How to Set Secure Cookie Flags?

Secure cookie flags are used to prevent JavaScript access to sensitive cookies. You can set secure cookie flags using the Set-Cookie header, like this:

Set-Cookie: session_id=1234567890; Secure; HttpOnly

This example sets a secure cookie with the name session_id and value 1234567890. The Secure flag ensures that the cookie can only be transmitted over HTTPS, and the HttpOnly flag prevents JavaScript access to the cookie. You can learn more about secure cookies and their flags on the MDN Web Docs.

What are the Best Practices for Configuring Security Headers?

To get the most out of security headers, it's essential to follow best practices for configuring them. Here are some tips:

  • Use a web application firewall (WAF) to help manage security headers.
  • Implement security headers for all production websites and applications.
  • Regularly review and update security headers to ensure they are effective.
  • Use online tools to test and validate security headers.
  • Consider implementing additional security measures, such as SSL/TLS certificates and secure protocols.

Why is it Important to Test and Validate Security Headers?

Testing and validating security headers is crucial to ensure they are effective and correctly configured. You can use online tools like Security Headers or SSL Labs to test and validate security headers. These tools can help identify vulnerabilities and provide recommendations for improving security headers. For more information on testing and validating security headers, you can visit the Security Headers documentation.

How Do Security Headers Impact Web Application Security?

Security headers can significantly impact web application security by preventing common web attacks and ensuring that all communication between the website and its users is encrypted. By implementing security headers, you can reduce the risk of XSS, clickjacking, and MITM attacks, and improve the overall security posture of your production website.

What are the Common Challenges of Implementing Security Headers?

Implementing security headers can be challenging, especially for complex web applications. Some common challenges include:

  • Configuring security headers for multiple domains and subdomains.
  • Ensuring that security headers are compatible with different browsers and devices.
  • Balancing security with functionality and usability.
  • Keeping security headers up-to-date with the latest security standards and best practices.

Related Guides

  • Email Authentication for Phishing Defense
  • Cloud Misconfiguration Prevention
  • Cloudflare DDoS Protection

Frequently Asked Questions

What is the purpose of the Content Security Policy (CSP) header?

The Content Security Policy (CSP) header helps prevent cross-site scripting (XSS) attacks by defining allowed sources of content, reducing the risk of malicious scripts being injected into a web page, and improving the overall security of a website.

How do I implement HTTP Strict Transport Security (HSTS) on my website?

You can implement HSTS by setting the Strict-Transport-Security header in your website's HTTP responses, which instructs the browser to only connect to the website over HTTPS, preventing man-in-the-middle (MITM) attacks and ensuring encrypted communication.

What is the difference between the Secure and HttpOnly cookie flags?

The Secure flag ensures that a cookie can only be transmitted over HTTPS, while the HttpOnly flag prevents JavaScript access to the cookie, providing an additional layer of security and protection against cross-site scripting (XSS) attacks and cookie theft.

title: Next.js 16 `use cache` Directive: Granular Caching at the Function Level and What It Replaces
description:
Next.js 16 use cache Directive: Granular Caching at the Function Level and What It Replaces

This article was written with the assistance of AI, under human supervision and review.

Next.js 16 eliminates the framework's most confusing aspect: implicit caching. Previous versions cached fetch requests automatically, left developers guessing when route segments became static, and buried cache configuration inside fetch options. The new use cache directive makes every cache decision explicit. Developers mark what to cache, set expiration with cacheLife(), and invalidate with cacheTag().

The old model failed because developers could not predict cache behavior. A fetch call with no options might cache forever or not cache at all, depending on whether the route contained dynamic functions. Route segments became static or dynamic based on heuristics the compiler inferred from your code. Production bugs emerged when a component that worked dynamically in development suddenly rendered statically in production, serving stale data for hours.

Problem: implicit caching causes unpredictable cache behavior and stale data

Next.js 16 solves this with use cache. When you add the directive to a function or component, the framework caches its return value. When you call cacheLife('hours'), the cache expires in one hour. When you call cacheTag(['products']), you can invalidate that cache entry on demand. The mental model becomes: mark what you cache, state when it expires, name it for invalidation.

Solution: explicit use cache directive gives predictable control

This post covers what use cache replaces, how function-level and component-level caching work, migration patterns from unstable_cache, the cache hierarchy Next.js now uses, and production gotchas around cache storage.

Key Takeaways

  • use cache replaces unstable_cache, fetch cache options, and all implicit caching; every cache decision is now explicit.
  • You can cache at the function level (data fetching) or component level (entire UI trees), with arguments and closures becoming part of the cache key automatically.
  • cacheLife() sets expiration windows; cacheTag() enables on-demand invalidation; both pair with use cache to control freshness.
  • Cache storage defaults to in-memory per instance; use cache: remote moves entries to a shared durable handler for high hit rates.
  • Migration requires converting unstable_cache wrappers to use cache directives and replacing fetch next.revalidate with cacheLife() calls.

What use cache Replaces: unstable_cache, fetch Options, and Implicit Caching

use cache supersedes three caching mechanisms from Next.js 15 and earlier.

unstable_cache: developers wrapped functions in unstable_cache(fn, keyParts, options) to cache database queries or API calls. The wrapper returned a new function that memoized results. The name signaled instability; the API never graduated to stable. Next.js 16 removes it entirely.

fetch cache options: developers passed { next: { revalidate: 3600 } } to fetch calls to cache HTTP responses. The framework intercepted fetch, stored the response in a data cache, and served cached data until expiration. This worked only for fetch calls. Database queries and third-party SDK calls required unstable_cache.

Implicit route caching: Next.js analyzed route segments at build time. If a segment contained no dynamic functions (cookies, headers, searchParams), the compiler marked it static and prerendered it. If any child component called a dynamic function, the entire segment became dynamic. Developers could not see this decision; they inferred it from build output or production behavior.

All three mechanisms are gone. use cache handles every scenario.

Diagram showing old caching mechanisms replaced by use cache

The removal creates a single model. You mark cacheable operations with use cache, set expiration with cacheLife(), and invalidate with cacheTag(). The compiler generates cache keys from function arguments and captured closures. No wrapper functions, no fetch-specific options, no implicit heuristics.

This unification matters because developers now reason about caching the same way everywhere. A database query, a fetch call, and a React Server Component all use identical syntax. The cache key derivation follows the same rules. The expiration model applies uniformly.

How use cache Works: Function-Level and Component-Level Caching

The use cache directive applies to async functions and React Server Components. When Next.js encounters it, the framework serializes the function's return value into an RSC payload and stores that payload in a cache.

Function-level caching targets data operations. Add use cache to the top of an async function that fetches from a database, calls a third-party API, or performs expensive computation:

import { cacheLife } from 'next/cache';

export async function getProduct(id: string) {
  'use cache';
  cacheLife('hours');

  const product = await db.query(
    'SELECT * FROM products WHERE id = $1',
    [id]
  );

  return product;
}

The compiler generates a cache key from the function identity and its arguments. In this example, the key includes getProduct and the id value. Calling getProduct('123') creates one cache entry; calling getProduct('456') creates another. The framework does not cache the function itself; it caches the result for each unique set of arguments.

Component-level caching targets UI trees. Add use cache to an async component that renders JSX:

import { cacheLife } from 'next/cache';

export default async function ProductList() {
  'use cache';
  cacheLife('minutes');

  const products = await db.query('SELECT * FROM products');

  return (
    <ul>
      {products.map(product => (
        <li key={product.id}>{product.name}</li>
      ))}
    </ul>
  );
}

The framework caches the entire RSC payload for the component. The payload includes the rendered JSX, serialized props, and any data the component loaded. When Next.js renders the same component again within the cache window, it returns the cached payload without executing the component body.

Content image showing cache key generation and payload storage

How use cache generates keys and stores payloads

The cache key includes arguments and any values captured from parent scopes. If a component reads a variable from a closure, that variable becomes part of the key. This ensures different inputs produce separate cache entries.

Arguments and return values must be serializable. You cannot cache functions, class instances with methods, or objects containing Symbols. The framework serializes primitives, plain objects, arrays, and React elements. Attempting to cache non-serializable values throws a runtime error.

Components marked with use cache cannot directly call cookies(), headers(), or access searchParams. These APIs provide request-time data that varies per request. Calling them inside a cached function creates a contradiction: the cache expects stable inputs, but runtime APIs return dynamic values. If you need runtime data, pass it as an argument to the cached function from a non-cached parent component.

Using cacheLife() for Granular Cache Control

cacheLife() sets the expiration policy for a cached function. Without it, Next.js applies a default profile. The default provides basic time-based invalidation, but production apps need explicit control.

The function accepts a named profile or a custom configuration object. Next.js 16 ships with four built-in profiles:

Profile Revalidate Expire Stale
seconds 15 seconds 15 seconds 1 minute
minutes 5 minutes 5 minutes 1 hour
hours 1 hour 1 hour 1 day
days 1 day 1 day 7 days

Revalidate determines when the cache entry becomes stale. After this window, Next.js marks the entry for refresh but continues serving the stale value while fetching a new one in the background.

Expire sets the hard limit. After this window, the cache entry becomes invalid. Requests cannot use it; Next.js must fetch fresh data synchronously.

Stale controls client-side caching. The browser keeps the RSC payload fresh for this duration when prefetching or navigating.

Use a built-in profile when the default windows fit your data freshness requirements:

import { cacheLife } from 'next/cache';

export async function getUser(id: string) {
  'use cache';
  cacheLife('hours');

  return await db.users.findUnique({ where: { id } });
}

Use a custom configuration when you need precise control:

import { cacheLife } from 'next/cache';

export async function getInventory(warehouseId: string) {
  'use cache';
  cacheLife({
    revalidate: 300,    // 5 minutes
    expire: 600,        // 10 minutes
    stale: 3600,        // 1 hour
  });

  return await inventoryApi.getStock(warehouseId);
}

The configuration accepts seconds as numbers. The example caches inventory for 5 minutes, expires it after 10 minutes, and allows the browser to use stale data for 1 hour during navigation.

Pairing cacheLife() with cacheTag() enables on-demand invalidation:

import { cacheLife, cacheTag } from 'next/cache';

export async function getProduct(id: string) {
  'use cache';
  cacheLife('hours');
  cacheTag('products', `product-${id}`);

  return await db.products.findUnique({ where: { id } });
}

When you call revalidateTag('products') from a Server Action, Next.js invalidates all cache entries tagged with products. The next request for any product executes the function and generates a fresh cache entry.

Migration Patterns: Converting Legacy Caching to use cache

Migrating from Next.js 15 caching requires three steps: remove unstable_cache wrappers, replace fetch cache options, and add explicit use cache directives.

Step 1: Remove unstable_cache wrappers

Old pattern with unstable_cache:

import { unstable_cache } from 'next/cache';

const getCachedUser = unstable_cache(
  async (id: string) => {
    return await db.users.findUnique({ where: { id } });
  },
  ['user'],
  { revalidate: 3600, tags: ['users'] }
);

export async function getUser(id: string) {
  return await getCachedUser(id);
}

New pattern with use cache:

import { cacheLife, cacheTag } from 'next/cache';

export async function getUser(id: string) {
  'use cache';
  cacheLife('hours');
  cacheTag('users');

  return await db.users.findUnique({ where: { id } });
}

The directive goes inside the function body. The cache key now derives automatically from the function identity and arguments. You do not specify key parts manually.

Step 2: Replace fetch cache options

Old pattern with fetch options:

export async function getProducts() {
  const response = await fetch('https://api.example.com/products', {
    next: { revalidate: 300, tags: ['products'] }
  });
  return response.json();
}

New pattern with use cache:

import { cacheLife, cacheTag } from 'next/cache';

export async function getProducts() {
  'use cache';
  cacheLife('minutes');
  cacheTag('products');

  const response = await fetch('https://api.example.com/products');
  return response.json();
}

The fetch call no longer carries cache options. The use cache directive controls caching for the entire function, including the fetch call and any subsequent processing.

Content image showing migration from old caching patterns to use cache

Step 3: Add explicit directives to previously implicit routes

Routes that relied on implicit static optimization need explicit use cache directives. If a page component performs data fetching that should cache, add the directive:

import { cacheLife } from 'next/cache';

export default async function ProductPage({ params }: { params: Promise<{ id: string }> }) {
  'use cache';
  cacheLife('hours');

  const { id } = await params;
  const product = await db.products.findUnique({ where: { id } });

  return <div>{product.name}</div>;
}

The migration flow moves all cache control to the function level. You see caching decisions in the code where they apply, not in build output or framework internals.

Migration flow from old caching patterns to use cache

use cache vs Data Cache vs Full Route Cache: Understanding the Cache Hierarchy

Next.js 16 maintains three cache layers: function-level cache (via use cache), prerendered HTML, and browser cache. Each serves a different purpose in the request lifecycle.

Function-level cache stores RSC payloads for individual functions and components. When you mark a function with use cache, Next.js caches its serialized return value. This cache applies during rendering. If a component calls a cached function multiple times in a single request, the framework returns the cached result after the first call.

Prerendered HTML stores complete pages generated at build time or during incremental static regeneration. When Next.js prerenders a page, it executes all cached functions, generates the RSC payload, renders HTML, and writes the HTML to disk. Subsequent requests serve the HTML directly without executing Server Components. The cacheLife expire window controls when the HTML becomes stale and triggers a background revalidation.

Browser cache stores RSC payloads the client receives during navigation or prefetching. When a user navigates to a new page, Next.js sends the RSC payload. The browser caches this payload according to the cacheLife stale window. During that window, navigating back to the page uses the cached payload without a server request.

Cache hierarchy showing function-level, HTML, and browser caches

These layers work together. A request hits the browser cache first. If the cached payload is stale, the browser requests from the server. The server checks for prerendered HTML. If the HTML is stale or missing, Next.js executes the page component. The component calls cached functions, which check the function-level cache. If a function's cached result is stale, the framework executes the function and updates the cache.

The distinction matters when you configure cacheLife. Setting revalidate to 5 minutes means the function-level cache refreshes every 5 minutes. Setting expire to 10 minutes means the prerendered HTML becomes invalid after 10 minutes. Setting stale to 1 hour means the browser uses its cached payload for 1 hour without checking the server.

Cache layer Storage location Invalidation trigger Controlled by
Function-level In-memory or remote handler revalidate window or revalidateTag() cacheLife() revalidate
Prerendered HTML Disk or platform storage expire window or deployment cacheLife() expire
Browser Client memory stale window or user action cacheLife() stale

The default cache handler stores function-level entries in memory per instance. This works for small apps but does not share cache across instances. For apps with multiple servers or serverless functions, use use cache: remote to store entries in a shared handler. The remote handler requires a network roundtrip for each cache hit, so it only pays off when the hit rate is high and the cached operation is expensive.

Production Gotchas: Cache Storage, Edge Runtime, and Common Mistakes

Production environments introduce cache storage constraints, edge runtime limitations, and developer mistakes that do not surface in local development.

Cache storage defaults to ephemeral in-memory per instance. When you deploy to a platform like Vercel, each serverless function instance maintains its own cache. Cache entries do not persist across cold starts. If an instance scales down and later scales up, the new instance starts with an empty cache. This differs from development, where next dev maintains a single long-running process with a persistent in-memory cache.

For durable shared caching, configure a cache handler in next.config.ts:

const nextConfig = {
  cacheHandlers: {
    default: {
      handler: './cache-handler.js',
    },
  },
};

export default nextConfig;

The cache handler must implement the Next.js cache handler interface. The official Redis handler provides a reference implementation. Using a remote cache introduces latency; each cache hit requires a network roundtrip to the cache store. Profile your cache hit rate before migrating. If the hit rate is low, the network overhead exceeds the benefit.

Edge runtime does not support all cache operations. Functions deployed to the edge can use use cache, but they cannot write to a durable cache handler that requires a persistent connection. The edge runtime allows only stateless HTTP requests. If your cached function must run at the edge, limit cache storage to the edge instance's memory. Cache entries do not persist across edge locations or instance restarts.

Common mistakes include caching non-serializable values, accessing runtime APIs inside cached functions, and misunderstanding cache key derivation.

Attempting to cache a class instance fails at runtime:

// This crashes when Next.js tries to serialize the cache entry
export async function getUserService(id: string) {
  'use cache';
  return new UserService(id);
}

The framework can only serialize plain objects, arrays, primitives, and React elements. Extract the data from the class instance and cache the data:

export async function getUserData(id: string) {
  'use cache';
  const service = new UserService(id);
  return await service.getData();
}

Accessing cookies() inside a cached function throws an error:

// This crashes because cookies() is a runtime API
export async function getSessionUser() {
  'use cache';
  const cookieStore = await cookies();
  const sessionId = cookieStore.get('session');
  return await db.sessions.findUnique({ where: { id: sessionId.value } });
}

Runtime APIs provide request-specific data. Caching request-specific data breaks the cache model. Move the runtime API call to a parent component and pass the value as an argument:

export async function Page() {
  const cookieStore = await cookies();
  const sessionId = cookieStore.get('session')?.value;

  if (!sessionId) {
    return <div>Not logged in</div>;
  }

  const user = await getCachedUser(sessionId);
  return <div>Hello {user.name}</div>;
}

async function getCachedUser(sessionId: string) {
  'use cache';
  cacheLife('minutes');

  const session = await db.sessions.findUnique({ 
    where: { id: sessionId },
    include: { user: true }
  });

  return session?.user;
}

The cached function receives sessionId as an argument. Different session IDs produce different cache entries. The cache key includes the session ID, so each user gets their own cached entry.

Production flow showing cache handler, edge limitations, and error paths

Cache key derivation includes function identity, arguments, and captured closures. If a closure captures a value from a parent scope, that value becomes part of the key. This can produce unintended cache misses if the captured value changes frequently:

export default async function ProductList({ category }: { category: string }) {
  const baseUrl = process.env.API_URL;

  // The cache key includes both category and baseUrl
  async function fetchProducts() {
    'use cache';
    const response = await fetch(`${baseUrl}/products?category=${category}`);
    return response.json();
  }

  return <div>{await fetchProducts()}</div>;
}

If API_URL changes between deployments, the cache key changes and all entries become invalid. For stable cache keys, pass environment variables as arguments or read them inside the cached function without capturing them from closures.

Frequently Asked Questions

When should you use use cache: remote instead of the default in-memory cache?

Use use cache: remote when your app runs on multiple serverless instances or containers and the cached operation is expensive enough to justify a network roundtrip. The remote cache shares entries across instances, but each cache hit requires fetching from the remote store. Profile your cache hit rate first; if it is below 80%, the network overhead likely exceeds the benefit.

Can you cache Server Actions with use cache?

Server Actions cannot use use cache directly because they are not idempotent operations; they mutate state rather than fetch data. You can pass Server Actions through cached components to Client Components without invoking them inside the cacheable function. The cached component treats the action as a serializable prop.

What happens when you call revalidateTag() with a tag that does not exist?

Calling revalidateTag() with a non-existent tag succeeds silently without invalidating anything. The framework does not track which tags exist; it only invalidates cache entries that match the tag. If no entries match, the call has no effect. This makes tag-based invalidation safe to call speculatively.

How does Next.js handle cache entries when you redeploy your app?

A new deployment generates a new build ID, which becomes part of the cache key for all use cache entries. When the build ID changes, all previous cache entries become inaccessible. This applies to both in-memory and remote caches. The new deployment starts with an empty cache, even if you use a durable cache handler.

Can you use use cache in Client Components?

Client Components cannot use use cache because they run in the browser, which has no server-side cache. The directive only works in Server Components and server-side async functions. If you need to cache data in a Client Component, fetch it in a Server Component, cache the Server Component with use cache, and pass the data as props.

Conclusion: Building a Mental Model for Next.js 16 Caching

The mental model for Next.js 16 caching reduces to three principles: mark what you cache, state when it expires, name it for invalidation. Every cache decision is explicit. No framework heuristics infer whether a route should cache. No fetch calls carry hidden cache options. No compiler analysis determines static versus dynamic rendering.

Add use cache to functions that fetch data or render UI. Call cacheLife() to set expiration windows. Call cacheTag() to enable on-demand invalidation. The compiler generates cache keys from function identity, arguments, and captured closures. Arguments and return values must be serializable. Runtime APIs like cookies() cannot be called inside cached functions.

Migration from Next.js 15 requires removing unstable_cache wrappers, replacing fetch cache options, and adding explicit directives. Production deployments need cache handler configuration for durable shared caching. Edge deployments limit cache to in-memory per instance. Cache entries do not persist across deployments because the build ID becomes part of the cache key.

The result is a caching model where developers control every aspect. You see caching decisions in the code where they apply. You reason about cache behavior the same way everywhere: functions, components, routes. You configure freshness requirements once, at the function level, rather than in multiple places with conflicting options. For teams managing complex data dependencies, this clarity eliminates an entire class of production bugs.

title: Google Adds Indexing Guidance for Shareable Pages and Generated Content
description:
Google has added a new section, "Only index content meant for Search," to its guidance on preventing user-generated spam. The update addresses a common issue for platforms, apps and AI-enabled tools: URLs may be created for a user to share, collaborate on or use directly, without being suitable destinations for organic search.

The October 26, 2026 documentation update does not create a new ranking signal. It is practical indexing guidance. Google is asking site owners to make an intentional distinction between pages designed to be discovered in Search and pages that exist primarily through a direct link. That distinction matters when a product can generate large numbers of public URLs.

What Google changed

In its updated guidance on preventing user-generated spam, Google discusses content created for direct sharing, collaboration or utility. Examples can include shareable pages, generated outputs and web applications.

The core recommendation is to consider whether this content is meant to be discovered through search results or accessed only by people with a direct link. For content that is not intended for Search, Google advises site owners to apply noindex by default, using either a robots meta tag or an X-Robots-Tag HTTP header. It also identifies blocking crawling with robots.txt as an option.

Google's October 2026 documentation updates record the addition to the spam guidance. Search Engine Journal also reported on the change in its coverage of Google's indexing advice for shareable pages.

This is especially relevant where a website's URL creation can outpace its editorial review. A collaborative document, a user profile, a generated report, a tool result or an AI-produced page may be useful to the person who created it without offering a distinct, durable search result for a broader audience.

Why shareable and generated URLs need an indexing decision

Search indexing is not simply a technical default. Indexed URLs can become part of a site's searchable footprint, consuming crawl attention and creating quality-control challenges at scale. Where users or software can create pages quickly, the number of URLs can rise far beyond the number of pages a site actually wants to surface in Search.

Google's wording is particularly important for products that mix public sharing with search visibility. A page can be accessible on the open web but still be inappropriate for indexing if it is intended only for recipients of a specific link.

For example, a platform might have two different kinds of output:

  • An evergreen, reviewed resource page intended to answer a searcher's question.
  • A one-off result page created for a user, collaborator or customer to access through a shared URL.

The first may warrant indexation if it provides useful search-facing content. The second may be better kept out of the index by default. The appropriate decision depends on the page's purpose, quality and intended discovery path, not merely on whether the URL is publicly reachable.

Noindex and robots.txt do different jobs

Google mentions both noindex and robots.txt, but they should not be treated as interchangeable if the goal is preventing a URL from appearing in search results.

A noindex directive tells search engines that can crawl the page not to show it in their results. It can be delivered in a robots meta tag in the HTML or through an X-Robots-Tag response header, which can be useful for non-HTML files or server-level rules.

A robots.txt rule controls crawling. Google specifically cautions that it is not a guaranteed way to prevent indexing. A URL blocked from crawling can still appear in search results if other sites link to it, because Google may learn about the URL without fetching its contents.

That caveat makes the objective important. If a site needs a strong signal that a crawlable page should not appear in Search, noindex is the directly relevant directive. If a page is blocked in robots.txt, Google may be unable to crawl it and see an on-page noindex tag. Teams should therefore avoid assuming that a crawl block alone solves an indexing problem.

A practical approach for platforms and AI-generated content

The new section is a prompt to review URL architecture and publishing defaults. It does not mean every generated page should be excluded from Search. It means sites should decide which classes of pages are genuinely search-facing before they scale.

A useful implementation process is:

  1. Map generated and shareable URL types. Identify URLs created by users, collaboration features, exports, AI tools, previews and application workflows.
  2. Define the purpose of each type. Separate pages built for direct access from pages intended to meet a search need.
  3. Set a default indexing policy. For direct-link-only output, use noindex by default where appropriate. Allow indexing only where a page type is deliberately designed for search discovery.
  4. Check technical consistency. Make sure templates, HTTP headers, canonical handling and crawl rules do not send conflicting signals.
  5. If a generated-page type becomes part of an SEO or GEO content strategy, establish standards for usefulness, uniqueness, access and quality before opening it to indexing.

For generative engine optimization, the same discipline helps avoid confusing availability with discoverability. A page intended to be cited or found through search should be an intentional, accessible publication asset. A private-style share link or a transient utility result serves a different role, even when it has a public URL.

Monitor indexation and creation spikes

Google also advises publishers to monitor indexation through Search Console, including the Page Indexing report and Search performance report. These reports can help teams spot unexpected changes, such as a new URL pattern appearing in indexed pages or generating impressions when it was not meant to be search-facing.

The guidance also calls for tracking platform-level content creation and indexing activity for spikes. This is important for marketplaces, community platforms and apps where an automated workflow, abuse event or product change can create many URLs quickly.

Monitoring should focus on changes in patterns, not just a single page. A sudden increase in created pages, crawl activity, indexed URLs or search impressions can indicate that a template or publishing default needs review. Search Console can reveal the search side of that issue, while internal platform metrics can show whether content creation itself has changed.

For teams managing AI-assisted publishing, this is a governance issue as much as a technical SEO task. The key question is whether a system has clear rules for what becomes a search destination and what remains a direct-use output.

If your site creates shareable reports, app pages or AI-generated URLs, GEO Search Leads can help you assess whether the pages you intend to make discoverable are structured around clear search-facing opportunities. Create a GEO Search Leads account to begin identifying website GEO readiness and prioritizing optimization opportunities without treating every generated URL as content that should be indexed.

Frequently Asked Questions

What is Google's new guidance for shareable pages?

Google says site owners should consider whether shareable pages, generated outputs and web-app content are intended for discovery through Search or only for direct linking. Content not intended for Search should generally be kept out of the index by default.

Does robots.txt guarantee that a page will not appear in Google Search?

No. Google notes that a URL blocked by robots.txt can still appear in search results if Google discovers it through links on other sites. Robots.txt blocks crawling, but it does not guarantee that a URL will not be indexed.

When should a site use noindex for generated content?

Noindex is appropriate for generated or shareable pages that are intended for direct sharing, collaboration or utility rather than search discovery. Pages intentionally built to serve searchers should be evaluated separately based on their purpose and quality.

Which Search Console reports does Google recommend monitoring?

Google points to the Page Indexing report and the Search performance report for identifying indexing anomalies. It also recommends tracking platform-level creation and indexing activity for spikes.

Conclusion

Google's update reinforces a basic but increasingly important publishing rule: not every URL a platform can create should become a search result. Sites that deliberately separate search-facing pages from direct-share and utility output will be better positioned to manage indexation, monitor anomalies and scale generated content responsibly.

title: Prototype-Guided Dynamic Domain Modulation and a Large-Scale Multi-SKU Benchmark for Shampoo Bottle Surface Defect Detection
description:
arXiv:2610.38194v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Industrial shampoo-bottle surface defect detection must operate across many stock keeping units (SKUs), where differences in bottle geometry, material, label layout, reflectance, and imaging conditions can substantially alter the appearance of the same defect. Existing industrial defect datasets rarely provide both instance-level defect annotations and product-variant identities, making it difficult to study SKU-aware detection under realistic manufacturing conditions. We introduce Bottle-SKU, a large-scale multi-SKU benchmark for shampoo bottle surface defect detection. Bottle-SKU contains 13,119 images, 20,419 instance-level bounding boxes, seven defect categories, and 48 bottle SKUs, enabling evaluation of both shared defect recognition and SKU-specific appearance variation. To address the challenge of SKU-specific appearance variation, we propose Prototype-Guided Dynamic Domain Modulation (ProDMM). ProDMM constructs a visual prototype for each SKU from training images and predicts a soft SKU distribution for each input. The resulting prototype-conditioned representation dynamically generates low-rank Query/Value modulation for the visual backbone and residual conditioning for defect-text-to-visual attention, while preserving the pretrained Grounding DINO detection pathway. The model is trained jointly with detection, SKU-domain classification, and modulation-regularization objectives. Experiments on Bottle-SKU and the public GC10-DET-SKU metallic surface defect dataset demonstrate the effectiveness of prototype-guided domain conditioning for industrial surface defect detection.

title: A free, beginner-friendly TypeScript course for JavaScript developers: 33 written sessions, from your first type to a complete Node.js API.
description:
What Is This Course?

TypeScript: Basics to Advanced is a free course that teaches TypeScript step by step, the way companies use it.

It is made for developers who already know JavaScript. You start with your first type and finish by building a complete REST API with Node.js, Express and MongoDB.

  • 33 sessions, each one a single page on GitHub
  • 1 to 2 hours per session, including practice
  • Completely free: no signup, no paywall, no videos to sit through

mohin-sheikh / typescript-basics-to-advanced

A beginner-friendly TypeScript course for JavaScript developers, from your first type to typed Node.js, Express and MongoDB APIs. 33 step-by-step sessions with tested examples, real tsc error messages, animated diagrams, exercises and interview questions. Uses TypeScript 7.

TypeScript: Basics to Advanced

A free, beginner-friendly TypeScript course for JavaScript developers. You know JavaScript. In 33 sessions you learn TypeScript the way companies use it: from your first type to generics, classes, validation, and a fully typed Node.js API. Everything runs with Node.js, and every example is tested.

Table of Contents

  • What Makes This Course Different
  • Who This Course Is For
  • What You Need
  • Quick Start
  • How to Use This Course
  • Course Outline
  • Find a Topic Fast
  • What You Will Be Able to Do
  • Before and After This Course
  • Repository Structure
  • Feedback

What Makes This Course Different
Built on TypeScript 7 Most tutorials online use TypeScript 5. This course uses the newest version, 7.0, and tells you when an older tutorial shows something different.
Backend from day one No web pages or browser code. You run everything with Node.js, with examples from real servers: users, orders, carts, logins and
…
View on GitHub

Is This Course for You?

This course is for you if:

  • You know JavaScript and want to learn TypeScript
  • Your team uses TypeScript and you want to understand it properly
  • You build backends or full-stack apps with Node.js
  • You are preparing for a TypeScript or Node.js interview

What you need before you start

  • Basic JavaScript: variables, functions, arrays, objects, classes and promises
  • Node.js 24 or newer
  • A code editor, such as VS Code

You do not need any TypeScript experience. If JavaScript is also new to you, start with the free JavaScript course first.

What Is TypeScript?

TypeScript is JavaScript with types. You describe what your data should look like, and TypeScript checks your code before it runs.

Here is a small example from Session 09. An order can have only four statuses, and someone makes a typo:

type OrderStatus = "pending" | "paid" | "shipped" | "cancelled";

interface Order {
  readonly id: number;
  status: OrderStatus;
}

const order: Order = { id: 1001, status: "pending" };
order.status = "shiped";

TypeScript catches the mistake before the code ever runs, and even suggests the fix:

error TS2820: Type '"shiped"' is not assignable to type 'OrderStatus'. Did you mean '"shipped"'?

In plain JavaScript, the wrong status would be saved without any warning, and someone would find the bug much later. TypeScript is built to catch mistakes like this early.

What You Will Learn

The course has 7 parts. Each part builds on the one before it.

Part Sessions What you learn
1. Getting Started 01 to 05 Setting up TypeScript, basic types, and reading error messages
2. Typing Your Data 06 to 11 Arrays, objects, interfaces, union types, and handling null safely
3. Functions 12 to 13 Typing functions, as const and satisfies
4. Generics and Type Tools 14 to 19 Generics, keyof, and utility types like Partial and Pick
5. Classes 20 to 22 Classes, inheritance, interfaces and decorators
6. Real Programs 23 to 29 Async code, modules, validation with Joi, tsconfig, testing with Vitest
7. TypeScript with Node.js 30 to 33 Node.js, Express and MongoDB with TypeScript, and a final project

See the full list of all 33 sessions

What Makes It Different

  • Up to date. Most tutorials online use TypeScript 5. This course uses the newest version, TypeScript 7, and tells you whenever an older tutorial shows something different.
  • Every example is tested. All the code was run. Every output and every error message in the course is real, so you can compare it with yours.
  • Easy to picture. 362 animated diagrams show what happens inside your code.
  • Learn from mistakes. Every session shows common beginner mistakes, with the real error and the fix.
  • Backend focused. No browser code. The examples come from real servers: users, orders, carts, logins and APIs.
  • One step at a time. A session only uses what earlier sessions have already taught.

What Every Session Contains

Part of a session What it gives you
Simple explanations One idea at a time, in plain words
Tested code examples Code to type and run, with the real output
Animated diagrams A picture of what is happening
Mini examples Small real programs that combine the session's topics
Beginner mistakes The wrong code, the error, and the fix
Practice exercises Tasks to try on your own
Interview questions Short questions with clear answers

Across the course, that adds up to 352 beginner mistakes, 261 practice exercises and 406 interview questions.

The Final Project

In the last session you build a complete Task Management API in TypeScript, using everything from the course:

  • Users register and log in (JWT tokens and hashed passwords)
  • Each user adds, updates and deletes their own tasks
  • Tasks can be filtered by status and loaded page by page
  • Admins can see all users
  • 25 automated tests check that everything works

How to Start

Step 1: Check that Node.js is installed. Open a terminal and run:

node -v

You need version 24 or newer. If you don't have it, install the LTS version from nodejs.org.

Step 2: Create a practice folder. Make a folder called ts-practice and open it in VS Code (File > Open Folder).

Step 3: Open Session 01. Read it and do the "Try It Yourself" part. Session 02 then installs TypeScript with you, step by step.

Tips to get the most out of it

  1. Go in order. Every session builds on the ones before it.
  2. Type the code yourself. Don't copy and paste. Typing helps you learn.
  3. Check and run. Run npx tsc to check your code and node to run it, then compare with the session.
  4. Do the exercises before you move on to the next session.

At one session a day, most learners finish in 6 to 7 weeks.

A Free Learning Path

This course is one of three free courses that work together:

Step Course What it teaches
1 JavaScript: Basics to Advanced The JavaScript language (25 sessions)
2 TypeScript: Basics to Advanced TypeScript (33 sessions, this course)
3 Node.js Learning Path Servers, APIs and databases (30 sessions)

All three use the same simple style and the same kind of examples, so moving from one to the next is easy.

FAQ

Is it really free?
Yes. No signup, no paywall, no email list.

Are there videos?
No. Everything is written, with animated diagrams for the hard parts, so you can learn at your own pace.

I have never used TypeScript. Can I follow it?
Yes. Session 01 starts from zero. You only need basic JavaScript.

My company uses an older version of TypeScript. Is this still useful?
Yes. The language is the same, and the course points out the places where older versions behave differently.

I found a mistake. What should I do?
Please open an issue on GitHub. Every report helps the next learner.

Thanks for Reading

If this course helps you, please give it a star on GitHub. It helps other developers find it. And if you know someone who wants to learn TypeScript, share it with them.

Are you learning TypeScript right now? Tell me in the comments what you find hardest.

title: Bounded Clinical Search Explained: Ranking Signals for Appointment Assistants
description:
Short answer: Use staged retrieval with explicit collections, bounded queries, and source context that survives reranking; a healthcare appointment assistant should not promote a result that an operator cannot trace to a URL or document ID. Choose the product only after writing that retrieval contract, its timeout budget, and its deletion procedure.

That order matters in B2B healthcare SaaS. A plausible appointment answer delivered from stale or untraceable context is harder to review than an empty result. The ranking layer has two jobs: improve relevance and preserve the evidence needed to inspect the answer later. Relevance alone isn't the acceptance criterion.

What retrieval architecture and ranking signals should a healthcare appointment assistant use?

Use three stages: retrieve from a named collection, reject candidates that violate the contract, then rerank the remaining bounded set. The contract should require a source URL or stable document identifier on every candidate. It should also define the query limit, total timeout, retry behavior, and what the assistant does when too few eligible records remain.

Keep the stages observable as separate decisions. Suppose retrieval returns 20 candidates and the eligibility gate removes 7 because their source reference is absent. The trace should say so; the reranker receives 13, rather than silently manufacturing confidence for all 20. Those numbers describe a test case, not a measured production result, but the invariant is firm: a candidate without reviewable source context cannot support a grounded answer.

Stop there.

The ranking signals should follow the same hierarchy. First gate on traceability and current collection membership. Then use the relevance order returned by retrieval as the input to reranking. Finally, apply deterministic tie-breaking so repeated requests do not reshuffle equivalent candidates. I'm not sure which domain-specific relevance signal will win for a particular corpus without an evaluation set; labeled appointment queries, expected documents, and reviewer judgments are what resolve that uncertainty.

This staged shape also gives the on-call engineer a useful failure boundary. A slow source cannot consume the entire user-flow budget because every query has an explicit timeout and limit. A transient HTTP 429 can be retried with backoff, while a response that fails the source contract is rejected rather than retried. Those are different events and should not share an alert.

Make provenance a ranking gate, not a footnote

Return source URLs or document identifiers with retrieved context. Carry that reference through reranking and into the answer record; otherwise, the system loses the join needed for review. A polished sentence without that join is operationally weak.

Freshness is a collection-maintenance property, not a clever scoring weight. Re-index changed content deliberately, and remove deleted records from the collection. If a clinic page or appointment policy disappears, lowering its score is insufficient — it must no longer be eligible for retrieval. This distinction belongs in the postmortem template: the index may have answered exactly as asked while the ingestion runbook failed to remove a record that no longer existed. That is a lifecycle failure, so tuning similarity cannot correct it.

The catch is that strict provenance can reduce recall when source metadata is incomplete. Don't loosen the gate invisibly. Route the request to a defined no-grounded-result response, record the rejection reason, and repair the ingestion path. This design is not suitable when the assistant must answer from undocumented knowledge; keep a human scheduling workflow for those cases until the knowledge has stable identifiers.

Choose the operational boundary before the product

The safest API combination implements the contract with the fewest unowned transitions. A web-search stage can discover external material, while a vector-query stage can retrieve from an explicit collection. Do not blend them into one opaque score: operators need to know which stage supplied each candidate, and the user-visible answer still needs its source reference.

Vendor choice follows from the boundary a team can operate. This table states decision conditions, not a synthetic benchmark; no runtime latency, uptime, or savings measurements are available here.

Option Prefer it when Main limitation to examine
Elasticsearch The existing deployment already has a tested retrieval contract, deletion procedure, and on-call runbook Its presence elsewhere in the company does not prove this corpus is grounded
Pinecone An evaluation verifies the required source fields and bounded-query behavior in the target deployment A vector database label does not substitute for source review
Weaviate The team can own its collection lifecycle and verify the same traceability contract A semantically similar demo result is not an operational acceptance test
Unified REST platform Search is one of several backend needs and broad production modules behind one consistent REST API reduce integration ownership Consolidation alone does not prove answer quality

Infrai fits the last condition because one key covers 295 routes across 20 modules, and its public self-describing discovery surface provides request and response schemas without requiring that key. That breadth behind a plain REST interface is the relevant advantage here: adding a backend capability is another endpoint under consistent conventions, not another required SDK. It is not the automatic choice for a team whose Elasticsearch, Pinecone, or Weaviate path already has evaluated relevance, source propagation, deletion handling, and practiced rollback. Stick with the system operators can verify when consolidation would add migration risk without improving the retrieval contract.

No vendor removes the need for a corpus-specific evaluation.

Implement the bounded query client in Go

The client below sends one validated request to POST /v1/vector/query. It deliberately reads the JSON body from standard input because the discovery schema, rather than an invented field list, is the authority for the current request shape. It sets an explicit method, keeps the key and API base in environment variables, checks status, honors a numeric Retry-After, and bounds 429 retries. Save it as main.go, set INFRAI_BASE_URL from the service configuration, provide a request body that conforms to the discovered schema, then run go run main.go < query.json.

package main

import (
    "bytes"
    "fmt"
    "io"
    "net/http"
    "os"
    "strconv"
    "strings"
    "time"
)

func retryDelay(response *http.Response, attempt int) time.Duration {
    if seconds, err := strconv.Atoi(response.Header.Get("Retry-After")); err == nil && seconds > 0 {
        return time.Duration(seconds) * time.Second
    }
    return time.Second * time.Duration(1<<attempt)
}

func main() {
    key := os.Getenv("INFRAI_API_KEY")
    if key == "" {
        panic("INFRAI_API_KEY is required")
    }
    baseURL := strings.TrimRight(os.Getenv("INFRAI_BASE_URL"), "/")
    if baseURL == "" {
        panic("INFRAI_BASE_URL is required")
    }
    endpoint := baseURL + "/v1/vector/query"

    body, err := io.ReadAll(os.Stdin)
    if err != nil {
        panic(err)
    }
    if !bytes.HasPrefix(bytes.TrimSpace(body), []byte("{")) {
        panic("stdin must contain a JSON object")
    }

    client := &http.Client{Timeout: 8 * time.Second}
    for attempt := 0; attempt < 3; attempt++ {
        request, err := http.NewRequest(http.MethodPost, endpoint, bytes.NewReader(body))
        if err != nil {
            panic(err)
        }
        request.Header.Set("Authorization", "Bearer "+key)
        request.Header.Set("Content-Type", "application/json")

        response, err := client.Do(request)
        if err != nil {
            panic(err)
        }
        responseBody, readErr := io.ReadAll(response.Body)
        response.Body.Close()
        if readErr != nil {
            panic(readErr)
        }

        if response.StatusCode >= 200 && response.StatusCode < 300 {
            fmt.Println(string(responseBody))
            return
        }
        if response.StatusCode == http.StatusTooManyRequests && attempt < 2 {
            time.Sleep(retryDelay(response, attempt))
            continue
        }
        panic(fmt.Sprintf("query failed: status=%d body=%s", response.StatusCode, responseBody))
    }
}

Keep reranking outside this transport client. After decoding a successful response according to its discovered response schema, enforce the source-reference gate, remove records not in current collection membership, preserve the bounded candidate set, and only then run the domain ranking policy. The separation is intentional: transport retry, eligibility rejection, and relevance ordering need different counters and different runbook actions.

The alternative route, POST /v1/web/search, belongs in a separate discovery stage when external material is required. Do not enumerate more endpoints or send both calls by habit. Map the user-visible answer back to a retrieval contract first, then enable only the stage that the contract requires.

Verify, degrade, and roll back

Ship with a verification matrix that runs before an index change and again after it. Test a normal query, a query with no eligible result, a candidate missing both source fields, a deleted record, a timeout, and a 429 response. Assert the candidate limit at the retrieval boundary and at reranker output. The second assertion catches accidental application fan-out even when the upstream request was bounded.

For each answer, retain enough trace data to reconstruct the path: collection identity, candidate count before and after gating, chosen document identifiers or URLs, and final ordering. Do not turn that into a dump of sensitive user text. The goal is an auditable decision trail, not broader data retention, and local policy must decide the permitted contents and lifetime of that trail.

Rollback should be boring. Keep the previous collection or index version addressable, stop writes to the version under review, switch queries back to the last accepted version, and verify a fixed set of appointment queries before reopening traffic. Re-index changed content deliberately instead of mutating records ad hoc. After deletion, test that the removed document cannot reappear in retrieval; after rollback, test that source references still resolve to the expected review records.

Use a degraded response when the source times out or the eligibility gate removes every candidate. This architecture is not suitable when the product requirement insists on an answer regardless of evidence. Change that requirement or route to a human workflow — don't hide the gap by widening the timeout indefinitely.

One last runbook rule: page on user-visible loss of grounded retrieval, not every individual retry. Aggregate bounded retry exhaustion and contract-rejection rates into signals an operator can act on. A single 429 is control flow. A sustained inability to return traceable appointment context is the incident.

References

  • Retrieval-Augmented Generation research paper: https://arxiv.org/abs/2005.11401

title: What SEBI's retail algo circular means for your order layer
description:
SEBI's 4 February 2025 circular, "Safer participation of retail investors in Algorithmic trading", is mostly a compliance document. But if you build trading software, most of it lands on one place in your code: the layer that sends orders to a broker. Here is what it changes in practice. I'm writing this as a developer, not as a lawyer, so read the circular itself before you design anything.

  1. No more open API keys The circular does not permit open APIs. A broker may give API access only through an API key that is specific to the vendor and the client, together with a static IP the broker has whitelisted. The aim is traceability: the broker should be able to say which algo provider and which end client sent any order.

For your system this means API keys and IPs are per client records, not global settings, and your order traffic has to leave from a fixed, known address.

  1. Orders need to be tagged Brokers have to detect and tag algo orders using identifiers the exchange specifies, and this also applies to algos a broker offers to its own clients. Where the broker's API has an order tag field, you can pass a compact tag yourself. Kite Connect, for example, accepts an optional alphanumeric tag of up to 20 characters that comes back in the order book.

A pattern that works: encode the strategy ID and version in the tag, so one look at the broker's order book tells you which rule set sent the order.

  1. Versions must be frozen
    An approved algo that changes needs fresh approval. In software terms, a strategy version should become immutable once it is approved, and a change creates a new version with a new record. If your strategies are edited in place, you cannot prove later what was running when an order went out.

  2. Keep an audit trail you can actually read
    For every order, store the client, strategy ID and version, the rule that triggered it, the request you sent and the broker's response. This is the record you will want when a client asks why an order fired.

  3. Login is OAuth and two-factor
    The framework asks for OAuth-based authentication and two-factor authentication. Most brokers already work this way. The practical effect is a daily login step: for example, Kite Connect's access token expires at 6 AM the next day. Plan for a re-login prompt and pause live strategies for any client whose token has lapsed, instead of letting orders fail silently.

What is still moving
Secondary sources disagree on when parts of this apply, and the exchanges have issued their own operational rules (for example on static IP changes). Check the SEBI and NSE notices for the current dates before you commit a launch plan.

Where we wrote this up in more detail
We build algo trading software for brokers, strategy providers and trading educators, and we keep a longer technical guide with the Kite Connect login and order flow table, the order-layer audit design and cost drivers: Algo trading software development in India. If you are planning an app around it, the trading app development guide covers the client side.

Sources: SEBI circular text (reproduced by TaxGuru), Zerodha Kite Connect documentation on user login and orders.

Reviewed by Ranjeet, Technical Reviewer at Brandzivio.

title: SciGame: Let Agents Play the Scientific Discovery Games in the Real and Counterfactual World
description:
arXiv:2610.37919v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Large language model agents are increasingly used for scientific discovery. However, existing benchmarks mix law inference with programming, score data fitting instead of prediction on unseen inputs, and do not separate empirical evidence from pretrained priors. We introduce SciGame, a controlled benchmark that converts scientific literature into structured scientific cards. Each card yields a pair of Original and dimensionally consistent Counterfactual environments with the same task interface. SciGame contains a Historical collection of canonical laws and a live Temporal collection curated from papers published after model knowledge cutoffs. It evaluates agents in candidate-guided Identification and open-ended Discovery settings. Each setting runs under Prior-only, Fixed, and Adaptive protocols. Experiments on five frontier models yield three findings. First, familiar priors hurt performance once the governing relation is altered. Second, adaptive experimentation helps the strongest models but harms weaker ones under limited budgets. Third, good explanations can hide quantitative failures. Recovering the exact symbolic form remains the main bottleneck, even when agents interpret evidence correctly. Current agents can investigate systems actively, but inducing exact laws in unfamiliar settings remains an open challenge.

title: Your Review Process Wasn’t Built for This Much Code
description:
Every year, analyst firms publish predictions, and most of us skim them and move on. One from Forrester’s 2027 cybersecurity and risk report stuck with me because it describes a problem developers are already living with. Forrester predicts that an AI-generated bug or regression will cause a global outage across multiple industries, on the same scale as the July 2024 outage.
forrester

The cause it names isn’t “AI writes bad code.” It’s the mismatch between how fast vulnerabilities are found and patched and how much testing capacity exists. That is a pipeline problem, and pipelines are something we can fix.
forrester

Generation got cheap, verification didn’t

AI assistants have made writing code very fast. A function that took twenty minutes now takes twenty seconds, and a patch for a newly disclosed vulnerability can be drafted before the coffee cools.

Reading, reviewing, testing, and deploying that code still happen at human speed. Review is still done by people with finite attention, and staging environments still differ from production in the ways that hurt.

Forrester’s framing is that the pace of AI-assisted development and patching will outstrip testing capacity, leading to a major outage from faulty AI-generated code. Press coverage of the report adds that the pressure to distribute patches quickly will overwhelm software engineers, creating a need to rely even more on AI. That’s a feedback loop. We use AI to keep up with the volume AI created.

technewsworld.com

Your throughput is now limited by how fast you can trust code, not how fast you can write it.

The 2024 comparison is worth reading carefully

The July 2024 outage Forrester points to was the CrowdStrike incident, where a faulty update crashed a huge number of Windows machines worldwide. As far as I know, AI had nothing to do with it. It was an ordinary software quality failure with a very wide blast radius.

That’s the point. Forrester isn’t predicting a new kind of failure. It’s predicting the same failure at higher frequency, because the volume of change keeps rising while the safety net stays the same size. Their advice is that organizations need to get better at rapidly rolling back unreliable vendor patches.
forrester

Notice that the recommendation is about recovery, not prevention. Prevention will never be perfect, so the question is how fast you can undo a mistake.

What I’d change on Monday

None of this requires exotic tooling.

1. Treat rollback as a feature, not an emergency procedure. If you’ve never rehearsed reverting a bad release, you don’t have a rollback plan. You have a hope. Practice it the way you’d practice a fire drill.

2. Stage everything that touches many machines. Canary releases, percentage rollouts, and kill switches exist because the worst bugs only show up at scale. A change that goes to everyone at once is an experiment on all your users.

3. Be honest about where AI code is flowing. Know which parts of your codebase were mostly machine-generated and which were reviewed line by line. You don’t need to ban anything. You need to know where your thinnest review coverage is.

4. Make tests the bottleneck on purpose. If your tests can’t keep pace with your generation speed, let the tests set the pace. A suite that catches regressions is worth more than a model that writes features faster.

5. Have a dependency story. Many of the outages that go global come from vendor updates, not your own code. Know which vendors can push changes to your production systems without your approval.

The other prediction: accountability

The same report makes a second prediction that developers should care about. It says an AI negligence lawsuit will force a CEO’s exit or a leadership change, with US accountability for AI still fragmented but heading toward the courts. One example from the broader conversation is the Mobley v. Workday case, where an age discrimination lawsuit over AI hiring software also named dozens of companies that used the tool as co-defendants.

Predictions 2027: It’s Going To Be Another “Hold My Beer” Kind Of Year For Security And Risk

Explore Forrester’s 2027 cybersecurity predictions, from AI accountability and outages to NIS 2 risk, and prepare for disruption.

forrester.com

The lesson for engineers is that “the model did it” won’t work as a defense. If you deploy a system, you own its behavior, and organizations will increasingly need documentation, logs, and decision records that show who approved what. Audit trails and design docs, which many teams treat as optional, start to look like legal infrastructure.

A fair caveat

Predictions are not forecasts you can bank on. Analyst firms make bold calls partly because bold calls get attention, and Forrester itself has urged leaders to focus on the operational disciplines needed for adoption rather than another cycle of AI alarmism. I’d take the same stance. Whether the big outage lands in 2027 or never, the underlying gap between how fast we generate code and how fast we verify it is already here.

Forrester urges firms to prioritise practical AI governance

Enterprises face mounting risks from AI outages and hidden governance costs as Forrester says day-to-day operational needs now outrank frontier fears.

itbrief.co.nz

The takeaway

Speed was never the hard part of software. The hard part is knowing that what you shipped does what you think it does, and being able to take it back when it doesn’t. AI made the easy half much easier. The teams that do well in 2027 will be the ones that put the saved time into the hard half.

So here’s a question to bring to your next retro: if the last change you shipped turned out to be wrong, how long would it take to undo it? If you can’t answer confidently, that’s your roadmap.

Sources:

Forrester, “Predictions 2027: It’s Going To Be Another ‘Hold My Beer’ Kind Of Year For Security And Risk” (Forrester blog). Basis for the AI-generated-bug outage prediction, the testing-capacity mismatch, the rollback advice, and the AI negligence lawsuit prediction.
https://forrester.com/blogs/predictions-2027-its-going-to-be-another-hold-my-beer-kind-of-year-for-security-and-risk

Forrester press release, “Forrester’s 2027 Technology And Security Predictions: AI Will Account For 20% Of All Business Technology Spend.” Basis for the claim that AI-assisted development and patching will outpace testing capacity.
https://www.forrester.com/press-newsroom/forresters-2027-technology-and-security-predictions-ai-will-account-for-20-of-all-business-technology-spend/

Professional Security, “AI, cyber predictions.” Basis for the point that patch-distribution pressure will push engineers toward relying more on AI.
https://professionalsecurity.co.uk/news/case-studies/ai-cyber-predictions/

IT Brief US, “AI lawsuits risk surges by 2027, warns XFactorAi CEO.” Basis for the Mobley v. Workday example.
https://itbrief.news/story/ai-lawsuits-risk-surges-by-2027-warns-xfactorai-ceo

IT Brief New Zealand, “Forrester urges firms to prioritise practical AI governance.” Basis for the “operational discipline over alarmism” caveat.
https://itbrief.co.nz/story/forrester-urges-firms-to-prioritise-practical-ai-governance
