title: Analyzing 454 Express Entry draws with pandas: what IRCC's own data says about Canada's CRS cut-offs
description:
Canada's Express Entry system publishes every "round of invitations" it runs: the date, the program or category, how many people were invited and the lowest Comprehensive Ranking System (CRS) score that got an invitation. IRCC puts this in a JSON feed behind its rounds of invitations page. I cleaned that feed into three CSV files and put them on GitHub, so I wanted to see what you can learn from it with a few lines of pandas.

Everything below runs as is against the public CSVs. The outputs are pasted straight from my terminal (pandas 3.0, data through round #453 on October 28, 2026).

1. Load the data 

import pandas as pd
pd.set_option("display.width", 120)
pd.set_option("display.max_columns", 10)

BASE = "https://raw.githubusercontent.com/izafar0999-gitup/canada-express-entry-draws/main/"

draws = pd.read_csv(BASE + "express_entry_draws.csv",
                    parse_dates=["date"], dtype={"round_number": "string"})
print(draws.shape)
print(draws["date"].min().date(), "to", draws["date"].max().date())
print(draws[draws["round_number"].str.contains("[a-z]", regex=True)]
      [["round_number", "date", "invitations"]])

(454, 9)
2015-01-31 to 2026-10-28
    round_number       date  invitations
362          91b 2018-05-30          200
363          91a 2018-05-30          500

First gotcha: round_number is not an integer. On May 30, 2018 IRCC ran two rounds on the same day and numbered them 91a and 91b. Reading it as string on purpose makes that explicit and stops anyone from casting it to int later and crashing on 91a.

2. Rounds and invitations per year 

draws["year"] = draws["date"].dt.year
yearly = draws.groupby("year").agg(
    rounds=("round_number", "size"),
    invitations=("invitations", "sum"),
    median_cutoff=("crs_cutoff", "median"),
)
print(yearly)

      rounds  invitations  median_cutoff
year                                    
2015      23        31063          469.0
2016      27        33782          482.0
2017      30        86023          438.5
2018      28        89800          442.0
2019      26        85300          459.5
2020      37       107350          471.0
2021      42       114224          712.0
2022      24        46539          692.0
2023      42       110266          486.0
2024      52        98903          524.5
2025      58       113998          533.5
2026      65       149409          514.0

2026 is not over, and it already has the most rounds (65) and the most invitations (149,409) of any year in the data.

Second gotcha: that median_cutoff column is misleading. Provincial Nominee Program (PNP) rounds only invite people who already have a provincial nomination, and a nomination is worth 600 CRS points on its own (see IRCC's CRS criteria page). In 2021 IRCC ran only program-specific rounds, 25 of the 42 of them PNP, so the median jumps to 712. Drop PNP rounds before you compare years:

no_pnp = draws[draws["category"] != "Provincial Nominee Program"]
print(no_pnp.groupby("year")["crs_cutoff"].median().loc[2019:])

year
2019    459.5
2020    469.0
2021    401.0
2022    510.0
2023    486.0
2024    499.0
2025    504.5
2026    475.0
Name: crs_cutoff, dtype: float64

Even this still mixes very different draws. The 2021 figure includes round #176 (February 13, 2021), a Canadian Experience Class round that invited 27,332 people with a cut-off of 75, which is still the largest and lowest round in the file. A median per year is a rough summary at best. Group by category if you want a number someone could plan around.

3. The end of the "general" draw

IRCC labels each round as General (all programs), Program-specific (one program, such as CEC or PNP) or Category-based (for example French speakers or healthcare workers). A pivot table shows how the mix changed:

share = (draws.pivot_table(index="year", columns="round_type",
                           values="invitations", aggfunc="sum", fill_value=0)
              .pipe(lambda t: t.div(t.sum(axis=1), axis=0) * 100)
              .round(1))
print(share.loc[2019:])

last_general = draws[draws["round_type"] == "General"].sort_values("date").iloc[-1]
print("Last general round:", last_general["round_number"], last_general["date"].date(),
      last_general["invitations"], "ITAs, cut-off", last_general["crs_cutoff"])

round_type  Category-based  General  Program-specific
year                                                 
2019                   0.0     98.8               1.2
2020                   0.0     63.4              36.6
2021                   0.0      0.0             100.0
2022                   0.0     76.8              23.2
2023                  23.5     69.6               7.0
2024                  42.9     14.6              42.4
2025                  59.0      0.0              41.0
2026                  54.1      0.0              45.9

Last general round: 294 2024-04-23 2095 ITAs, cut-off 529

In 2019 almost every invitation came from a general round. In 2025 and 2026, none did. The last general round was #294 on April 23, 2024. If you only look at the cut-off column without round_type, you will compare a French-language round with a CEC round and draw the wrong conclusion.

4. 2026 by category 

d26 = draws[draws["year"] == 2026]
summary = (d26.groupby("category")
              .agg(rounds=("round_number", "size"),
                   invitations=("invitations", "sum"),
                   min_cutoff=("crs_cutoff", "min"),
                   max_cutoff=("crs_cutoff", "max"))
              .sort_values("invitations", ascending=False))
print(summary)

                                               rounds  invitations  min_cutoff  max_cutoff
category                                                                                  
French language proficiency                        12        60500         382         435
Canadian Experience Class                          18        57750         507         523
Healthcare and social services occupations          3        11500         467         475
Provincial Nominee Program                         21        10814         697         805
Trade occupations                                   2         6500         476         477
Senior managers with Canadian work experience       3         1000         389         429
Physicians with Canadian work experience            3          891         169         223
Transport occupations                               2          450         470         477
Skilled military recruits                           1            4         368         368

The spread is the story: CEC cut-offs stayed in a tight 507 to 523 band all year, while French-language rounds closed between 382 and 435. Same system, same year, a gap of roughly 100 points depending on which door you are eligible for.

5. Where the pool sits

The second file is the CRS score distribution IRCC publishes with most rounds: how many profiles are in the pool in each score band.

pool = pd.read_csv(BASE + "express_entry_crs_score_distribution.csv",
                   parse_dates=["date", "distribution_as_of"])
latest = pool.sort_values("date").iloc[-1]
bands = ["candidates_601_1200", "candidates_501_600", "candidates_451_500",
         "candidates_401_450", "candidates_351_400", "candidates_301_350", "candidates_0_300"]
snap = latest[bands].astype(int)
print("Snapshot as of", latest["distribution_as_of"].date(), "total", int(latest["candidates_total"]))
print((snap / int(latest["candidates_total"]) * 100).round(1).to_string())

Snapshot as of 2026-10-25 total 228724
candidates_601_1200     0.3
candidates_501_600      9.0
candidates_451_500     31.1
candidates_401_450     27.8
candidates_351_400     20.9
candidates_301_350      7.5
candidates_0_300        3.3

Only 9.3% of the 228,724 profiles score above 500. CEC rounds in 2026 needed at least 507, so most of the pool is below the line for those rounds, and the biggest single band is 451 to 500 (31.1%). Two caveats if you use this file: IRCC often reuses the same snapshot for several rounds in one week, so drop_duplicates("distribution_as_of") before you plot a time series, and the bands are fixed by IRCC, so you cannot compute an exact count above, say, 519.

6. Draws come in clusters 

d26 = d26.sort_values("date")
weeks = d26["date"].dt.isocalendar().week
per_week = d26.groupby(weeks).size()
print("2026 rounds:", len(d26), "| weeks with at least one round:", per_week.size)
print(per_week.value_counts().sort_index().rename("weeks").rename_axis("rounds_in_week"))
gaps = d26["date"].diff().dt.days.dropna()
print("Longest gap:", int(gaps.max()), "days, ending", d26.loc[gaps.idxmax(), "date"].date())

2026 rounds: 65 | weeks with at least one round: 21
rounds_in_week
1     1
2     3
3    10
4     7
Name: weeks, dtype: int64
Longest gap: 25 days, ending 2026-06-22

The 65 rounds of 2026 fell in just 21 calendar weeks. In 17 of those weeks IRCC ran three or four rounds back to back (typically PNP, then CEC, then a category round). So "how many draws were there" is a less useful question than "how many draw weeks were there". If you are building any kind of "next draw" estimate, model the week, not the individual round.

Things to know before you build on this

  • PNP cut-offs include the 600 nomination points. Subtract 600 if you want to compare them with other rounds, or just keep them separate.
  • From November 3, 2026, IRCC changes how Canadian work experience and job offers are scored, and says it will pause rounds for up to two weeks while it recalculates every profile (source: IRCC's CRS criteria page and its October 2026 backgrounder on high-wage occupations). Cut-offs after that date will not be directly comparable with earlier ones, so add a rules_version column before you mix them.
  • Tie-breaking timestamps are ISO 8601. A trailing Z means IRCC gave the time in UTC.

Get the data

  • GitHub: https://github.com/izafar0999-gitup/canada-express-entry-draws (CSV files, data dictionary and the build script that regenerates them from IRCC's JSON feed)
  • Source: IRCC rounds of invitations, https://www.canada.ca/en/immigration-refugees-citizenship/services/immigrate-canada/express-entry/rounds-invitations.html, under the Open Government Licence â€“ Canada

If you would rather read the pool numbers than compute them, I keep a plain-English version on the Express Entry pool statistics page. And if you want to turn the scoring tables themselves into code, the step-by-step CRS calculation guide walks through every factor with a worked example.

Zafar Iqbal maintains crscalcu.ca, an independent site that is not affiliated with IRCC. Always confirm rules on canada.ca before making immigration decisions.

title: AWS + Snowflake: Building Modern Data and AI Workflows with Glue, S3, Iceberg, and Cortex
description:
Modern data platforms are no longer just about moving data from one database to another. Organizations need scalable data pipelines, governed data access, open table formats, real-time analytics, and AI-powered insights.

Two platforms that play an important role in this ecosystem are Amazon Web Services (AWS) and Snowflake.

AWS provides a broad ecosystem for storage, data integration, security, analytics, and machine learning. Snowflake provides a cloud data platform for data warehousing, data sharing, analytics, and AI-powered applications.

The interesting part is how these platforms can work together without forcing organizations to move all their data into a single environment.

In this article, we'll explore important AWS and Snowflake integration capabilities and build a practical mini-project that moves sales data from Amazon S3 through AWS Glue into Snowflake.

1. Why Combine AWS and Snowflake?

Many organizations already store large volumes of data in Amazon S3 while using Snowflake for analytics and business intelligence.

Combining these platforms can help teams:

  • Build scalable ETL and ELT pipelines.
  • Process data using AWS Glue and Apache Spark.
  • Store raw and curated datasets in Amazon S3.
  • Analyze structured data in Snowflake.
  • Improve data governance and access control.
  • Work with open table formats such as Apache Iceberg.
  • Build AI-powered analytics workflows.

A simplified architecture looks like this:

        Data Sources
             |
             v
        Amazon S3
       (Raw Data)
             |
             v
         AWS Glue
      (ETL Processing)
             |
             v
        Snowflake
     (Data Warehouse)
             |
             v
      SQL Analytics
      BI / AI Apps

Each service has a specific responsibility, allowing teams to build flexible data architectures.

2. AWS Glue Catalog Federation with Snowflake Horizon Catalog

One important development is the ability to access Snowflake Horizon Catalog metadata through AWS Glue catalog federation.

This is particularly useful when organizations work with Apache Iceberg tables and want to discover and query data across platforms.

Traditionally, integrating separate data catalogs can require additional metadata synchronization and operational complexity.

Catalog federation helps reduce that friction.

How it works

  1. Snowflake manages catalog metadata through Horizon Catalog.
  2. AWS Glue connects to the federated catalog.
  3. AWS Lake Formation can help manage permissions.
  4. Amazon Athena can query supported federated Iceberg data.

The key idea is that teams can access catalog metadata without treating every dataset as a separate copy that must be moved into another system.

Why it matters:

  • Less metadata duplication.
  • Better interoperability.
  • Centralized governance options.
  • More flexibility for analytics teams.
  • Easier access to Iceberg-based data.

Always verify the supported authentication method, catalog configuration, and table compatibility for your specific environment.

3. AWS Glue and Snowflake Connectivity

AWS Glue can connect to Snowflake to support ETL workloads.

A common pattern is:

  1. Read source data from Amazon S3.
  2. Transform records using AWS Glue and PySpark.
  3. Validate and clean the data.
  4. Write curated records into Snowflake.
  5. Run analytical SQL queries.

Authentication and credential management are important parts of this integration.

For production environments, prefer supported OAuth-based authentication or securely managed credentials over hardcoding passwords in scripts.

Keep credentials in an appropriate secret-management solution and grant only the permissions required by the job.

4. Amazon Quick and Snowflake Cortex AI

Another interesting direction is the integration of Amazon Quick with Snowflake Cortex AI through the Model Context Protocol (MCP).

This brings conversational analytics closer to business users.

Instead of manually writing every query, users can ask questions about their data using natural language.

For example:

  • Which products generated the highest revenue?
  • What were the monthly sales trends?
  • Which regions experienced declining sales?
  • Which customers contributed the most revenue?

Snowflake Cortex capabilities can support different AI workflows, including structured-data analysis, document search, and agent-based interactions.

Amazon Quick can provide a conversational interface for interacting with supported Snowflake capabilities.

This creates opportunities for more accessible analytics while keeping data access and governance important parts of the architecture.

5. Apache Iceberg: Connecting Open Data Across Platforms

Apache Iceberg is an open table format designed for large analytical datasets.

It provides capabilities such as:

  • Schema evolution.
  • Partition evolution.
  • Snapshot-based queries.
  • Time travel.
  • Reliable metadata management.

For organizations using both AWS and Snowflake, Iceberg can help reduce dependence on proprietary storage formats and improve interoperability.

A possible architecture is:

             Amazon S3
                 |
                 v
        Apache Iceberg Tables
                 |
          +------+------+
          |             |
          v             v
       AWS Glue      Snowflake
          |             |
          v             v
       Athena       Analytics

The exact integration pattern depends on catalog ownership, permissions, supported table features, and the query engine being used.

6. Hands-On Mini Project: Build an S3-to-Snowflake Sales Pipeline

Let's build a simple data engineering project.

Project objective: Read sales data from Amazon S3, transform it using AWS Glue, load it into Snowflake, and run analytical queries.

Architecture 

       sales.csv
           |
           v
       Amazon S3
           |
           v
       AWS Glue Job
       (PySpark ETL)
           |
           v
       Snowflake
       SALES_DB
           |
           v
       SALES_ANALYTICS

Step 1: Create a sample CSV file

Create a file named sales.csv:

order_id,customer,product,quantity,price,region
1001,Ali,Laptop,1,1200,Asia
1002,Sara,Mobile,2,600,Europe
1003,Ahmed,Tablet,1,400,Asia
1004,Ayesha,Laptop,2,1200,North America
1005,Usman,Mobile,1,600,Asia
1006,Hina,Monitor,2,300,Europe

Step 2: Upload the file to Amazon S3

Create an S3 bucket and upload the CSV file.

Example S3 path:

s3://my-data-engineering-bucket/raw/sales.csv

Your bucket should contain:

my-data-engineering-bucket/
    |
    └── raw/
         └── sales.csv

Step 3: Create a Snowflake database and table

Run the following SQL in Snowflake:

CREATE DATABASE SALES_DB;

CREATE SCHEMA SALES_DB.ANALYTICS;

CREATE TABLE SALES_DB.ANALYTICS.SALES (
    ORDER_ID NUMBER,
    CUSTOMER VARCHAR(100),
    PRODUCT VARCHAR(100),
    QUANTITY NUMBER,
    PRICE NUMBER(10,2),
    REGION VARCHAR(100),
    TOTAL_AMOUNT NUMBER(12,2)
);

Step 4: Configure AWS Glue

Before running the job:

  • Create an AWS Glue IAM role.
  • Grant the role access to the required S3 location.
  • Configure the supported Snowflake connector.
  • Provide Snowflake connection details securely.
  • Confirm network connectivity and permissions.
  • Ensure the Glue job has the required connector dependencies.

The exact connector configuration depends on your AWS Glue version and the Snowflake connector setup you choose.

Step 5: Transform the data using PySpark

The following example demonstrates the transformation logic.

from pyspark.sql import SparkSession
from pyspark.sql.functions import col

spark = SparkSession.builder \
    .appName("SalesETLPipeline") \
    .getOrCreate()

# Read CSV from Amazon S3
df = spark.read \
    .option("header", True) \
    .option("inferSchema", True) \
    .csv("s3://my-data-engineering-bucket/raw/sales.csv")

# Calculate total sales amount
df = df.withColumn(
    "TOTAL_AMOUNT",
    col("quantity") * col("price")
)

# Remove records with missing required values
df = df.dropna(
    subset=["order_id", "customer", "product", "quantity", "price"]
)

# Display transformed data
df.show()

# Inspect schema
df.printSchema()

This example focuses on the transformation itself. To complete the pipeline, configure the Snowflake connector's supported Spark write integration and connection options, then write the transformed DataFrame into SALES_DB.ANALYTICS.SALES.

Do not assume that a generic JDBC or connector configuration will work unchanged across every Glue runtime. Follow the connector documentation for the selected runtime.

Step 6: Run analytical queries in Snowflake

Once the transformed records are loaded, run:

Total revenue

SELECT
    SUM(TOTAL_AMOUNT) AS TOTAL_REVENUE
FROM SALES_DB.ANALYTICS.SALES;

Revenue by region

SELECT
    REGION,
    SUM(TOTAL_AMOUNT) AS REVENUE
FROM SALES_DB.ANALYTICS.SALES
GROUP BY REGION
ORDER BY REVENUE DESC;

Top-selling products by revenue

SELECT
    PRODUCT,
    SUM(TOTAL_AMOUNT) AS TOTAL_SALES
FROM SALES_DB.ANALYTICS.SALES
GROUP BY PRODUCT
ORDER BY TOTAL_SALES DESC;

Customer purchase analysis

SELECT
    CUSTOMER,
    COUNT(*) AS TOTAL_ORDERS,
    SUM(TOTAL_AMOUNT) AS TOTAL_SPENT
FROM SALES_DB.ANALYTICS.SALES
GROUP BY CUSTOMER
ORDER BY TOTAL_SPENT DESC;

You now have a basic cloud data pipeline using Amazon S3, AWS Glue, PySpark, and Snowflake.

7. Production Architecture Considerations

A working demo is only the first step. Production data platforms require additional planning.

Security

  • Use IAM roles with least-privilege permissions.
  • Store credentials securely.
  • Prefer supported OAuth-based authentication where appropriate.
  • Encrypt data at rest and in transit.
  • Apply Snowflake role-based access control.
  • Use AWS Lake Formation where applicable.
  • Avoid exposing credentials in Glue scripts or logs.

Data Quality

  • Validate incoming schemas.
  • Handle null and duplicate records.
  • Track rejected records.
  • Implement data reconciliation checks.
  • Monitor failed and incomplete loads.

Performance

  • Use appropriate file formats and partitioning.
  • Avoid unnecessary Spark shuffles.
  • Tune Glue worker capacity based on workload.
  • Use Snowflake warehouse sizing appropriate to query demand.
  • Monitor query execution and data transfer patterns.

Cost Optimization

  • Avoid running oversized Glue jobs.
  • Use appropriate Snowflake warehouse auto-suspend settings.
  • Monitor S3 storage and request costs.
  • Track data movement between AWS and Snowflake.
  • Use incremental processing instead of repeatedly loading entire datasets.

8. When Should You Use Each Integration?

Requirement Possible approach
Process data in S3 AWS Glue
Query S3 data Amazon Athena
Centralize AWS data permissions AWS Lake Formation
Enterprise data warehousing Snowflake
Open table interoperability Apache Iceberg
Conversational analytics Amazon Quick + Snowflake Cortex AI
Cross-platform catalog discovery Glue catalog federation

The best architecture depends on where your data lives, which platform owns the catalog, your governance requirements, and the workloads you need to support.

9. Final Thoughts

AWS and Snowflake are not necessarily competing choices. They can complement each other in a modern data architecture.

AWS provides scalable infrastructure, data ingestion, transformation, storage, and governance capabilities. Snowflake provides a powerful environment for analytical workloads, data sharing, and AI-powered data experiences.

With catalog federation, Apache Iceberg interoperability, and conversational analytics integrations, organizations have more options for building connected data platforms.

The practical takeaway is simple: choose the right service for each workload, keep governance at the center, and avoid unnecessary data movement.

Start with a small pipeline, measure its performance and cost, and expand the architecture as your data requirements grow.

References and Further Reading

  • AWS Big Data Blog: Access Snowflake Horizon Catalog Data Using Catalog Federation in AWS Glue
  • AWS What's New: Amazon Quick and Snowflake Cortex AI Integration
  • AWS Glue Documentation
  • Amazon Athena Documentation
  • Snowflake Documentation
  • Apache Iceberg Documentation

If you're building data pipelines with AWS and Snowflake, try the mini-project and extend it with incremental loads, data-quality checks, and automated orchestration.

title: VerifiedLab: Harnessing Knowns for Unknowns
description:
arXiv:2610.37923v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Across human history, knowledge has undergone several transitions, from orality to writing and then to digital archives. At each transition, humans established new conventions to preserve knowledge for the new era. Nowadays, as research agents are increasingly deployed for laboratory experiments, knowledge is crossing another boundary: from records written for humans to those for machines. In this work, we introduce VerifiedLab, a multi-agent harness framework for this human-to-machine transition of knowledge. VerifiedLab transforms research output from passive artifacts into active systems that accelerate downstream use, adoption and prediction of future trends. In VerifiedLab, a team of AI scientists with distinct roles reasons over records verified field by field: a principal investigator plans, a librarian computes the evidence directly from the records, specialists draft, and a gate and a critic check each claim against the measured reliability of its data before the harness decides whether to release or withhold it. We demonstrate the efficacy of VerifiedLab through extensive experiments on perovskite solar cells: VerifiedLab recovers known physical trends, anticipates devices reported a year later, and lets AI scientists inherit the literature together with a measure of how far it can be trusted. By scaling the inference-time verification compute, VerifiedLab introduces a new pathway for knowledge dissemination and machine harness for AI co-scientists.

title: Node.js SMS OTP: Verifying a Phone Number with 3 Reliable Routing Guardrails
description:
Short answer: Use /v1/sms/otp for the first challenge, verify the submitted code in your own endpoint, and make resend and queue publication idempotent. For a marketplace support form, a self-describing REST surface is useful when the same key must cross account, email, and SMS work; Infrai is a reasonable fit for that boundary, while a specialist remains better for provider-specific channel controls.

The right trade-off for a marketplace contact form is to make phone verification a bounded state transition, not a delivery assumption. Send one OTP, persist only a protected, expiring representation of its state, and make every retry safe to repeat. The contact form should enter a support queue only after the account and phone proof have been joined. That leaves a useful fallback when an SMS is late without turning a flaky carrier path into duplicate tickets.

I care about this boundary because missed jobs and duplicate deliveries are the same operational problem wearing different clothes: an uncertain handoff gets retried, and the receiver cannot tell whether the first attempt took effect. The implementation below keeps that uncertainty local.

The incident lesson: delivery is not verification

A production-shaped failure is easy to describe without inventing a vendor outage. A buyer submits a damaged-order contact form, requests an OTP, closes the tab, then tries again from a second device. The first message may arrive after the second request. The user may also press resend twice. If the service treats every request as a new truth, the support queue gets two cases or the older code remains valid longer than intended.

The invariant is narrower: one verification attempt has one server-owned expiry and one successful consumption. The SMS provider transports a challenge; it does not decide whether the form may be routed. Store a one-way representation of the code, its expiry, the account identifier, the phone reference, an attempt counter, and a client-supplied idempotency key. Never log the code.

For this workflow, the sending path is /v1/sms/otp; a user who did not receive it can use /v1/sms/resend/{id}. The validation endpoint belongs to the marketplace application. Rate-limit both code creation and guesses, and apply a geographic or per-country spend circuit in the business layer because that policy is not supplied by the SMS API.

How should Node.js code handle verifying a phone number with SMS OTP?

Resend is a state transition, not a second validation path. Keep the original attempt record, enforce a short resend interval, and invalidate or supersede the previous challenge according to a policy your support and fraud teams can explain. The response should not reveal whether a phone number belongs to an account. A failed guess should consume an attempt; a successful guess should atomically mark the challenge used before the contact form is published.

Here is the part worth putting in a runbook. The interface is deliberately small, so the storage and SMS adapters can be tested independently. The API's public discovery surface provides the request schema and runnable examples for the exact integration payload; read that schema before wiring the adapter rather than guessing from prose.

package otp

import (
    "bytes"
    "context"
    "crypto/rand"
    "crypto/sha256"
    "encoding/hex"
    "errors"
    "fmt"
    "strconv"
    "sync"
    "time"
)

var ErrRejected = errors.New("otp rejected")

// Sender is the narrow boundary around POST /v1/sms/otp.
// The concrete adapter must use the discovery schema and shared API key.
type Sender interface {
    Send(ctx context.Context, phone, idempotencyKey string) error
}

type record struct {
    digest string
    expires time.Time
    used bool
    attempts int
}

type Service struct {
    mu sync.Mutex
    sender Sender
    records map[string]record
}

func New(sender Sender) *Service {
    return &Service{sender: sender, records: make(map[string]record)}
}

func (s *Service) Start(ctx context.Context, accountID, phone string) (string, error) {
    raw := make([]byte, 4)
    if _, err := rand.Read(raw); err != nil {
        return "", err
    }
    code := fmt.Sprintf("%06d", int(raw[0])<<16|int(raw[1])<<8|int(raw[2]))[:6]
    attemptID := accountID + "-" + strconv.FormatInt(time.Now().UnixNano(), 10)
    digestBytes := sha256.Sum256([]byte(attemptID + "/" + code))
    rec := record{digest: hex.EncodeToString(digestBytes[:]), expires: time.Now().Add(5 * time.Minute)}

    s.mu.Lock()
    s.records[attemptID] = rec
    s.mu.Unlock()

    if err := s.sender.Send(ctx, phone, attemptID); err != nil {
        s.mu.Lock()
        delete(s.records, attemptID)
        s.mu.Unlock()
        return "", err
    }
    return attemptID, nil
}

func (s *Service) Verify(attemptID, code string) error {
    digestBytes := sha256.Sum256([]byte(attemptID + "/" + code))
    digest := hex.EncodeToString(digestBytes[:])

    s.mu.Lock()
    defer s.mu.Unlock()
    rec, ok := s.records[attemptID]
    if !ok || rec.used || time.Now().After(rec.expires) || rec.attempts >= 5 {
        return ErrRejected
    }
    rec.attempts++
    if rec.digest != digest {
        s.records[attemptID] = rec
        return ErrRejected
    }
    rec.used = true
    s.records[attemptID] = rec
    return nil
}

The example is a local state machine. In a multi-instance service, replace the mutex map with a transactional store and make successful consumption conditional on used = false, then publish the contact form using the same idempotency key. The sender adapter below sends the payload obtained from discovery. That avoids pretending an undocumented request field is stable while still showing the real HTTP boundary, explicit method, environment-based authentication, status handling, and retry pause.

package otp

import (
    "context"
    "fmt"
    "io"
    "net/http"
    "os"
    "strconv"
    "time"
)

func sendOTP(ctx context.Context, payload []byte, idempotencyKey string) error {
    req, err := http.NewRequestWithContext(ctx, http.MethodPost, "https://api.infrai.cc/v1/sms/otp", bytes.NewReader(payload))
    if err != nil {
        return err
    }
    req.Header.Set("Authorization", "Bearer "+os.Getenv("INFRAI_API_KEY"))
    req.Header.Set("Content-Type", "application/json")
    req.Header.Set("Idempotency-Key", idempotencyKey)

    resp, err := http.DefaultClient.Do(req)
    if err != nil {
        return err
    }
    defer resp.Body.Close()
    if resp.StatusCode == http.StatusTooManyRequests {
        if seconds, parseErr := strconv.Atoi(resp.Header.Get("Retry-After")); parseErr == nil {
            time.Sleep(time.Duration(seconds) * time.Second)
        }
        return fmt.Errorf("rate limited")
    }
    if resp.StatusCode < 200 || resp.StatusCode >= 300 {
        body, _ := io.ReadAll(resp.Body)
        return fmt.Errorf("otp request failed: %s: %s", resp.Status, body)
    }
    return nil
}

Add bytes to the import list in a complete implementation. The payload is deliberately an input from the live discovery schema, rather than a fabricated field map. In production, retry the request with the same idempotency key after a transient failure and use a bounded backoff around Retry-After; do not sleep inside a request handler without a deadline.

Why ownership matters more than the transport

Clerk, Resend, and Twilio are credible choices, but they put different boundaries in your hands.

Option Connection shape Best fit Main boundary
Clerk Hosted identity plus SDKs Sessions and identity are the center Less control over a marketplace-owned OTP state machine
Resend Email API Email-first contact workflows Your application still owns SMS fallback and OTP semantics
Twilio Communications APIs Provider-specific SMS and country controls More credentials and reconciliation when paired with separate identity and email services

Clerk is strongest when identity and session management should be the center of the system. Resend is a focused email delivery choice, so it fits when the contact workflow is primarily email and your team already owns OTP semantics. Twilio is a broad communications specialist and fits when SMS policy, country coverage, and channel controls need to be deeply provider-specific.

The three-service stack means three signups, three credential sets, and glue for account identity, welcome email, SMS fallback, suppression state, retries, and reconciliation. That glue is where an onboarding form can be accepted while its verification record is missing, or where a suppressed recipient is interpreted differently by each service. A single REST surface makes the handoff easier to reason about: the same key and base URL cover the account lookup, the welcome-mail side of the flow, and the SMS fallback. It still leaves one vendor to trust, one bill, and one outage surface. That cost is real.

The useful fit here is narrower than replacing every communications system. Try Infrai for the SMS verification and fallback boundary when the team wants public, self-describing discovery to expose the request schema and runnable examples before an integration is written, and wants the same credential convention across account, email, and SMS capabilities. Its discovery surface is the practical advantage: wiring a new capability starts by reading one endpoint instead of learning another SDK. The documented idempotency convention can also reduce integration glue, but it does not remove application-owned expiry, abuse controls, or queue idempotency.

Do not choose it as the sole answer if you need email-hosted OTP, SMTP relay, voice, WhatsApp, RCS, provider-specific geographic pricing controls, or push webhooks. Events are pull-based, email has no hosted OTP interface, and SMS geo-fencing or country-price circuit breaking remains application work. A communications specialist is the better boundary when those controls are the product.

The recovery contract for a support queue

After verification, write a durable routing record containing the account reference, contact-form id, queue decision, and the idempotency key.

That record is the handoff.

A worker can safely retry the enqueue operation because the consumer treats standard queue delivery as at-least-once. If the SMS request succeeds but the HTTP response is lost, retry with the same key; if the application crashes after verification but before enqueue, a reconciler can find verified, unrouted forms.

This is also where template ownership becomes an engineering decision. Keep the message template and queue-routing policy in the marketplace application if support needs reviewable, versioned language and deterministic escalation rules. Delegate transport delivery when carrier reach and delivery mechanics are the expensive part. Either way, the application owns the promise made to the buyer: one valid proof, one routed case.

The rule I would put in the runbook is simple: retry transport, never retry business effect without an idempotency key; expire challenges; cap guesses; and make resend observable as a distinct operation. That rule survives a late carrier message, a crashed worker, and a user with two browser tabs.

One valid proof. One routed case.

If this boundary fits your system, start with the SMS OTP and resend reference, then verify the live discovery schema before implementing the sender adapter.

Sources

  • RFC 6376: DomainKeys Identified Mail (DKIM)
  • Clerk documentation
  • Resend documentation
  • Twilio Verify documentation
  • Infrai API documentation

title: Decompose, Don't Expand: Capability-Independent AI Systems by Construction
description:
arXiv:2610.38144v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: A recurring design choice in building AI systems is whether, when a task is too hard for a model, to expand the model (make it larger, better-prompted, fine-tuned), or to decompose the task (extract the parts that admit a deterministic solution to a host, leaving the model only the irreducibly fuzzy residue). We make three claims. First, that many tasks commonly delegated whole to a model are in fact deterministic tasks with a small generative core. Second, and our central empirical result, that decomposing such a task yields a measurable and desirable property we call parity by construction: on the extracted sub-tasks the model-size performance curve becomes flat, because no model performs them at all. We measure this across nine models spanning a 494M-parameter local checkpoint to a frontier Opus-class model, a thirty-fold parameter range on the local family alone: once the host resolves the context, operation selection scores identically for all nine models and selector resolution for eight of nine, while the one task that does not decompose, labelling, remains sloped across the same range. Because the task leaves the model, a stock checkpoint suffices: no task-specific training and no fine-tuning. Third, that this is a general design discipline, not a domain trick: we show the same move recurring across physics setup, motion retargeting, and object-model editing, and in a Web-CLI tool family (same author, so not an independent replication). We give a method for locating the cut, the construction that makes a cut exist (a deterministic surface and a closed grammar over it), and a way to make the residue safe (resolve the deterministic context; verify the generative output), position the work against neuro-symbolic AI, tool-augmented language models, and generate-and-verify approaches, and are explicit about what is measured (one domain) versus illustrative (the rest).

title: The three things that break every Mercado Pago Pix webhook signature
description:
Mercado Pago has no stripe trigger. Here's what that costs you.

If you've integrated Stripe, you know stripe listen --forward-to localhost:3000/api/webhook and stripe trigger payment_intent.succeeded. You test webhooks locally, end to end, in seconds.

If you've integrated Pix, you know the other thing: there is no equivalent. There is no pix trigger. So you do what everyone does — deploy to a URL, generate a real Pix, pay yourself R$5 from another bank app, and read console.log in production to find out whether your webhook handler actually works.

This post is about the three specific things that break in that setup. All three fail quietly: your endpoint returns 200, Mercado Pago records a success, and nothing ever retries.

Trap 1: data.id is in the query string, not the body 

POST /api/webhook?data.id=123456&type=order

The signature is computed over data.id. Not the notification id, not the body — the resource id, which arrives in the query string.

If your framework hands you a parsed body and nothing else, you can never validate a signature. You need req.url. In Express that means reading the raw query, not req.body.data.id.

Trap 2: the manifest has a trailing semicolon

The header looks like this:

x-signature: ts=1704908010,v1=618c85345248dd820...

And the string you HMAC-SHA256 is:

${data.id};${x-request-id};${ts};

Three things bite here:

  • The trailing ; is part of the manifest. Drop it and every comparison fails.
  • x-request-id comes from the header, and it's absent in some test events — in which case it's an empty string, but the semicolons around it stay.
  • ts is in seconds, not milliseconds. 
import { createHmac, timingSafeEqual } from 'node:crypto';

const manifest = `${dataId};${requestId};${ts};`;   // trailing semicolon
const expected = createHmac('sha256', secret).update(manifest).digest('hex');

const valid = timingSafeEqual(
  Buffer.from(expected, 'hex'),
  Buffer.from(v1, 'hex'),
);

Compare with timingSafeEqual, not ===. And if the two buffers differ in length, timingSafeEqual throws — check a.length === b.length first.

Trap 3: order notifications use type=order, not type=payment

The Orders API sends type: "order" and action: "order.processed". The legacy Payments API used payment.

If you filter on payment — which most tutorials from 2023 and earlier do — every Orders event falls through your handler, your endpoint returns 200 anyway, and Mercado Pago marks the delivery as successful. It never retries.

This is the worst of the three because nothing errors. You find out when a customer says they paid and you have no order.

The smaller ones that still cost hours

notification_url doesn't exist on Orders. Per-order callbacks fail with
400 unsupported_properties: additionalProperties '$.notification_url' not allowed.
That's a legacy field. On Orders the webhook is configured once per application,
in the panel.

total_amount alternates between string and number. "5.00" in the create
response, 5.00 inside some webhook payloads. amount.split('.') on a number throws → 500 → infinite retries.

The webhook already contains the full order. data isn't just an id — it's the whole object. No follow-up GET needed. (The legacy API did send only an id, which is why older tutorials tell you to fetch.)

paidAt doesn't exist. There's no date_approved field on the Orders webhook. If you need exact settlement time, store your own.

Idempotency, and why the retry will bite you

Providers re-deliver webhooks. If your handler processes the same event twice, a customer gets charged once and shipped twice.

The ordering rule:

parseWebhook → markProcessed → onEvent

Dedupe before your business logic. If you run the handler first and mark afterwards, a crash halfway through leaves a half-applied event and the retry applies it again.

The HTTP codes matter just as much:

Situation Correct response
Valid, first time 200
Duplicate 200 (not 409 — the provider would retry)
Invalid signature or irrelevant event 200 (not 401 — the provider would retry forever)
Your handler threw (transient) 500 (so it retries)

Return 4xx on something the provider thinks is retryable and you get redelivery forever. Return 5xx on something it doesn't retry and you lose the payment silently.

Testing it without paying yourself R$5

I wrote a small CLI that does one thing: sends a correctly signed Mercado Pago webhook at any URL you point it at, including localhost.

npx pix-harness send --to http://localhost:3000/api/webhook

It reproduces all three traps above — data.id in the query string, the
ts=...,v1=... header, the manifest with the trailing semicolon. Zero dependencies, MIT, source on npm.
I built it because I got tired of the deploy-pay-check loop.

The flag worth knowing about:

npx pix-harness send --to http://localhost:3000/api/webhook --duplicate

It delivers the same data.id twice, with the same signature. If your handler
creates two orders, you've just found your idempotency bug in two seconds instead
of in a customer's bank statement. Mercado Pago's own "Simular notificação" panel
can't do this — it has no repeat/duplicate control.

Bonus: make Mercado Pago approve a Pix by itself

In the test environment, payer.first_name acts as a scenario switch:

payer.first_name Result
APRO Order created, then automatically approved
OTHE Stays pending
CANO Cancelled

Poll getCharge() and watch action_required become processed in about three
seconds. Full cycle, no scanning, no paying, no tunnel.

That's the whole map. The three traps are the part the docs don't spell out, and
now they're not going to cost you a weekend.

title: Investor's Last Exam: Can AI Agents Do Equity Investment Without Seeing the Future?
description:
arXiv:2610.38342v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Financial agents must form forecasts and investment judgments from decision-time evidence, with predictions evaluated against subsequent outcomes. Existing benchmarks assess financial knowledge, research workflows, or forecasting, but evaluating the full research process requires a strictly frozen information set and professional evaluation criteria. We introduce Investor's Last Exam (ILE), an equity-research benchmark led by experienced buy-side investors and fund managers. Its three components are a versioned financial database spanning 3.43 million document versions and nine source categories, supplemented by structured market data, with validated timestamps governing retrieval and computation; a task taxonomy organized around professional analyst deliverables; and an expert-led framework linking scoring criteria to sources, calculations, and assumptions through financial dependency graphs. Evaluation spans 86 assignments and jointly assesses research quality, forecast accuracy, and simulated investment performance. GPT-6 Astra and Claude Opus 5.5 lead overall at 68.1 and 66.9 out of 100, yet even Astra scores only 52.5 on Forecast & Model. Our results show that even state-of-the-art models fail to translate overall research capability into predictive performance. ILE shifts the evaluation unit from isolated capabilities to the evidence--assumption--judgment chain, allowing researchers to locate where analytical advantages fail to translate into forecasts and investment judgments, and providing a traceable, diagnostic foundation for training and evaluating financial agents.

title: Testing Webhook & Transactional Email Flows with Ephemeral Inboxes: A Practical Guide
description:
Testing Webhook & Transactional Email Flows with Ephemeral Inboxes: A Practical Guide

When developing features that trigger transactional emails—such as password reset tokens, purchase receipts, or magic login links—validating that emails actually reach inboxes and parse correctly is one of the most frustrating parts of testing.

Relying on staging trap systems like MailHog or Mailpit works inside local Docker networks, but falls short when third-party SaaS services (Stripe, Twilio, SendGrid, Auth0) need to deliver real webhooks and real SMTP messages to public internet domains.

Here is how modern engineering teams architect frictionless transactional testing using public ephemeral inboxes.

The Problem with Traditional Email QA

  1. Shared Team Inboxes: Testing with team-qa@mycompany.com causes test runs to overwrite each other. When two engineers trigger a reset flow simultaneously, race conditions occur.
  2. Plus-Addressing Limitations: While qa+user123@gmail.com routes to your personal inbox, many third-party auth platforms and payment gateways strip or reject plus tags.
  3. Domain Blocking in Staging: Mock mail servers running on localhost cannot receive emails sent by external third-party production webhooks.

Architecture: Ephemeral Inbound Webhook Pipelines

The optimal setup requires:

  • An internet-accessible domain with valid MX, SPF, and DKIM records.
  • High-concurrency edge ingestion that converts inbound SMTP to WebSocket / JSON streams.
  • Ephemeral mailboxes generated per test execution. 
[External SaaS / Auth0 / Stripe]
               │ (Real SMTP Delivery)
               ▼
[Edge MX Router (@mailfo.site)]
               │ (Sub-second Parse)
               ▼
[Real-Time WebSocket / In-Memory Queue]
               │
               ▼
[Test Runner / Mobile App / Web Client]

Key Verification Metrics

When running automated integration tests, your assertion library should verify:

  • Time-to-Delivery: Ensure transactional emails arrive in < 5 seconds.
  • Regex Extraction: Pull verification codes (/\b\d{6}\b/) immediately from HTML/plaintext payloads.
  • Header Integrity: Verify SPF and DKIM pass indicators to confirm delivery hygiene.

Instant Ephemeral Testing with Mailfo

Whether you are testing mobile app onboarding on an Android emulator or validating signups from a web browser, Mailfo offers instant, throwaway inboxes with sub-second delivery:

  • 📱 Native Android Client: Download Mailfo on Google Play Store — Features local SQLite/Room persistence, ensuring your OTP code isn't lost if Android backgrounds the app during signup.
  • 🤖 Telegram Integration: @mailfo_official_bot — Instant address generation and code viewing inside Telegram.
  • 🌐 Web Portal: https://mailfo.pages.dev/ & mailfo.xyz

Beam supports tool calling and structured outputs, with a 1M-token context window for code, documents, and conversation history. Reasoning effort is adjustable. title: Why a failed handler gets its payment back and a failed settlement does not
description:
A payment gate marks a payment spent before it knows whether the work succeeded. You don't get to pick that ordering: record the key after the handler returns and the entire run is open to a second presentation of the same signed payload. Record it first and you get the opposite failure, where a handler that fell over has burned a payment for a response nobody received. The fix is a release allowed on exactly one path, and the reasoning about which path carries more weight than the mechanism does.

The code here is paygate402, an x402 payment gate that wraps an http.Handler: an unpaid request comes back as 402 with the terms the server accepts, the client repeats it with an X-PAYMENT header, and the gate gets that payment verified and settled before the handler's response reaches anybody.

The ordering is not a choice

The replay key is a hash of the payment, not of the request:

// PaymentKey is the replay key for a payment.
func PaymentKey(payment Payment) string {
    sum := sha256.New()
    sum.Write([]byte(payment.Scheme))
    sum.Write([]byte{0})
    sum.Write([]byte(payment.Network))
    sum.Write([]byte{0})
    sum.Write(payment.Payload)
    return hex.EncodeToString(sum.Sum(nil))
}

That payload is what a client sends over the wire, and the server is not the only party that ever holds a copy of it. If the key went into the store after the handler returned, the gap between the two would be as long as the work takes (a report to generate, a model to call, a file to build), and the same payload could be spent again inside that gap, concurrently, as many times as the server has goroutines to serve it. A replay window as wide as your own p99 latency is not a window you get to reason about. It opens widest exactly when the endpoint is expensive.

So the key goes in first. One refinement is worth saying out loud, because it mirrors the whole problem: the key goes in after verification passes, not at first sight. Recording an unverified payment would burn a payload the facilitator rejected, and a rejection is often something the client can fix (an allowance, an approval) and then legitimately resend the same signed payment for.

store := g.Seen
if store == nil {
    store = defaultStore
}
if store.SeenBefore(PaymentKey(payment), window) {
    g.challenge(w, accepts, "this payment has already been used")
    return
}

// The handler runs into a buffer.
recorder := &recorder{header: http.Header{}, status: http.StatusOK}
next.ServeHTTP(recorder, r.WithContext(withPayer(r.Context(), verification.Payer)))

The handler writes into a recorder that buffers status, headers and body. Nothing has reached the client yet, and that is what makes the next decision possible at all.

Four exits, and only one of them is before the money

Once the key is recorded there are four ways out of the handler:

Exit What the client gets Key after
Handler answered outside 2xx the handler's own status and body released
Settle returned an error 502, settlement unavailable stays spent
Settlement.Success is false 402 with the facilitator's reason stays spent
Settled the buffered response plus X-PAYMENT-RESPONSE stays spent

The first exit is the only one you reach before any settlement was attempted:

if recorder.status < 200 || recorder.status >= 300 {
    // Nothing was delivered, so nothing is charged — and nothing was
    // settled either, so the payment is handed back rather than left
    // spent on a response the client never got.
    if releaser, ok := store.(Releaser); ok {
        releaser.Release(PaymentKey(payment))
    }
    recorder.flush(w, "")
    return
}

Notice what the flush does not carry: no X-PAYMENT-RESPONSE, because there is no settlement to report. The client sees its 500 and can retry with the identical header.

The other two failure exits look like they deserve the same treatment. They don't:

settling, done := context.WithTimeout(context.WithoutCancel(r.Context()), g.settleTimeout())
defer done()

settlement, err := g.Facilitator.Settle(settling, payment, terms)
switch {
case err != nil:
    g.log("settlement call failed", "error", err)
    http.Error(w, "payment settlement is unavailable", http.StatusBadGateway)
    return
case !settlement.Success:
    g.log("settlement declined", "reason", settlement.ErrorReason)
    g.challenge(w, accepts, orDefault(settlement.ErrorReason, "payment could not be settled"))
    return
}

A transport error is the unknown case, and it is the oldest trap in payments: a call that failed is not a transfer that did not happen. The request may have reached the facilitator, the facilitator may have broadcast, and all you know is that you did not hear back... Release the key there and the next presentation of the same payload gets settled again, on top of a transfer that may already be sitting on the chain.

The declined case is subtler, and it is the one I see people get wrong. Success: false with a reason reads like a definitive no, but it is the facilitator's account of what it observed, and the gate has no second witness. The gate does not read the chain, and it has no business doing so inside a request. So both of these keep the payment spent, and the client is told plainly that the payment was used. For an honest client that is a worse outcome than an automatic retry would be, and it is the only direction that cannot charge twice.

One detail keeps the unknown case from being manufactured on purpose: settlement runs on context.WithoutCancel with its own timeout. A client that hangs up the instant it would have received its response cannot abort the transfer mid-flight and leave the money in the one state nobody can act on.

The release is optional, and that is the safety property

Release is not part of the store interface. It is a second, narrower one:

// Releaser is a SeenStore that can forget a key.
type Releaser interface {
    SeenStore
    Release(key string)
}

A store that does not implement it keeps the payment spent, and there is a test pinning exactly that, using a wrapper that is a SeenStore and nothing more:

// keepingStore is a SeenStore and nothing more: it cannot take a payment back.
type keepingStore struct{ inner *MemoryStore }

func (s *keepingStore) SeenBefore(key string, ttl time.Duration) bool {
    return s.inner.SeenBefore(key, ttl)
}

func TestAStoreWithoutReleaseLeavesThePaymentSpent(t *testing.T) {
    g := releaseGate(&keepingStore{inner: NewMemoryStore()})
    signed := header(t, payment("1"))

    if failed := releaseRequest(t, g, handlerThatFails(), signed); failed.Code != http.StatusInternalServerError {
        t.Fatalf("status = %d, want the handler's 500", failed.Code)
    }
    retry := releaseRequest(t, g, paidHandler(), signed)
    if retry.Code != http.StatusPaymentRequired {
        t.Fatalf("retried request: status = %d, want 402; body %s", retry.Code, retry.Body)
    }
}

This is for whoever puts a shared store behind the interface, which any multi-replica deployment has to do: the bundled MemoryStore is one process's memory, and FileStore is one machine's disk. A Redis-style store implements Release in a line. A store that genuinely cannot delete, say an append-only audit log you do not control, or a third-party idempotency service with no revoke, does not have to pretend. Leave the method off and the gate takes the conservative branch, with no configuration flag anywhere and no way for a deploy to pick up the dangerous half of the behaviour by accident.

Forgetting in an append-only log

FileStore exists so a restart does not hand a captured X-PAYMENT header a second chance. Its file is an append-only log of expiry key lines, so forgetting cannot be a deletion. It has to be another line:

// releaseMarker stands where an expiry would be, on a line that takes a payment
// back. An append-only log forgets by appending, and the later line wins when
// the file is read again.
const releaseMarker = "-"

A release writes the key with - where its timestamp would be. On the way back in, the record parser turns that marker into the zero time, and the loader deletes any key whose expiry is zero. The tombstone survives the restart, which is the whole point: a release that lived only in memory would resurrect the spent key on the next boot and refuse a retry the client is entitled to. Releasing a key that was never recorded writes nothing, so a stray release does not grow the file, and the file gets rewritten once the dead records outnumber the live ones.

The free tier obeys the same rule from the other side. An allowance is spent before the X-PAYMENT header is even read, and a free request that answered outside 2xx comes back through Return on the allowance store: work that was not delivered is not charged for, whether the unit of charge is a stablecoin transfer or one of five courtesy requests.

What I would change

Release(key string) returns nothing. For a map behind a mutex, and for a file that keeps its own error for you to ask about later, that is fine. For a network store it is not: a release that fails against Redis is a payment silently left spent, with no log line and nothing for an operator to find. I would give it an error return and log the failure at the gate, while still treating it as non-fatal. The client already has its 500, and a release that did not take is the same conservative outcome as a store that cannot release at all.

The second change is about visibility. The gate asks whether the store is a Releaser per request, inside the failure branch, so the quiet, conservative behaviour is also the invisible one: an operator who swapped in a store without Release probably learns about it from a support ticket. I would resolve the capability once, where the gate is validated, and say so at startup.

What I would not change is the single-path rule. Everything above collapses into one sentence: record the payment before the work runs, and forget it only where nothing was attempted. The mechanism is the easy half of that. The part I had to sit with is that a declined settlement is not evidence of an absent transfer, and that the gate has to be the component which refuses to guess.

title: Can LLMs Faithfully Solve Ontology Engineering Tasks? A Mechanistic Interpretability Study
description:
arXiv:2610.38326v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Ontological knowledge underpins large language model (LLM) performance on knowledge-intensive tasks. However, existing evaluations of LLMs' ontological understanding largely rely on behavioral correctness, leaving the underlying mechanisms unexplained. Existing mechanistic interpretability work has largely focused on instance-level factual knowledge, leaving ontological knowledge under-explored. To bridge this gap, we introduce MIOE, a causal-abstraction benchmark that evaluates interchange interventions for two ontology engineering tasks: entity typing and subsumption prediction. MIOE tests whether learned internal intervention targets can change an ontology-level target answer while preserving class-specific auxiliary information. Across Qwen3-8B and Qwen3-4B, we evaluate SAE-, DBM-, and DAS-based methods, including multi-task and multi-layer variants. Distributed subspace methods give the strongest results and generalize across prompt settings, but the induced changes remain only partially separated from auxiliary class-specific information. Multi-task objectives and contiguous layer-window interventions improve this balance, while class-level analyses reveal substantial variation across ontology classes. These results suggest that ontological predictions are mechanistically accessible in LLMs, although current methods do not yet isolate a cleanly disentangled causal mechanism for ontological knowledge.

title: How to Get Every Open Job From a Company's Careers Page (Greenhouse, Lever & Ashby APIs)
description:
Most tech companies don't build their own careers page. They use an applicant tracking system (ATS), and the three big ones (Greenhouse, Lever, and Ashby) each publish a free, public JSON API for every company's job board. They exist so companies can show their jobs on their own sites, so there's no scraping, no login, and no API key.

If you know the company's board name (usually just the company name), one request gets you every open job.

ATS Public endpoint
Greenhouse https://boards-api.greenhouse.io/v1/boards/{company}/jobs
Lever https://api.lever.co/v0/postings/{company}?mode=json
Ashby https://api.ashbyhq.com/posting-api/job-board/{company}

How do you find the name? Open the company's careers page and click any job. The link will contain boards.greenhouse.io/airbnb, jobs.lever.co/spotify, or jobs.ashbyhq.com/ramp.

The script (standard library only)

It tries all three platforms, keeps the one with the most jobs, and saves a CSV.

"""Every open job at a company, from its public job-board API. Usage: python3 company_jobs.py airbnb"""
import csv
import json
import sys
import urllib.error
import urllib.request

BOARDS = {
    "greenhouse": "https://boards-api.greenhouse.io/v1/boards/{}/jobs",
    "lever": "https://api.lever.co/v0/postings/{}?mode=json",
    "ashby": "https://api.ashbyhq.com/posting-api/job-board/{}",
}


def get(url):
    try:
        with urllib.request.urlopen(urllib.request.Request(url, headers={"User-Agent": "jobs-script"}), timeout=30) as r:
            return json.load(r)
    except urllib.error.HTTPError:
        return None  # no board with that name


def rows(ats, data):
    if ats == "greenhouse":
        return [(j["title"], j["location"]["name"], j["absolute_url"]) for j in data["jobs"]]
    if ats == "lever":
        return [(j["text"], j["categories"].get("location", ""), j["hostedUrl"]) for j in data]
    return [(j["title"], j.get("location", ""), j["jobUrl"]) for j in data["jobs"]]


def jobs_for(company):
    # A company name can exist on more than one platform (often an old, nearly empty board), so keep the biggest
    found = [(ats, rows(ats, data)) for ats, url in BOARDS.items() if (data := get(url.format(company)))]
    return max(found, key=lambda f: len(f[1]), default=(None, []))


company = sys.argv[1]
ats, jobs = jobs_for(company)
if not ats:
    sys.exit(f"No Greenhouse, Lever or Ashby board found for {company}")
with open(f"{company}-jobs.csv", "w", newline="") as f:
    w = csv.writer(f)
    w.writerow(["title", "location", "url"])
    w.writerows(jobs)
print(f"{company} ({ats}): {len(jobs)} open jobs saved to {company}-jobs.csv")

Real runs (October 2026):

$ python3 company_jobs.py airbnb
airbnb (greenhouse): 201 open jobs saved to airbnb-jobs.csv
$ python3 company_jobs.py spotify
spotify (lever): 89 open jobs saved to spotify-jobs.csv

The gotcha: stale boards

My first version returned the first platform that answered. For Ramp, that was a Greenhouse board with exactly 1 job. Ramp's real board is on Ashby, with 170. Companies switch ATS and leave the old board up, so check every platform and keep the biggest. That's what the max() line does.

Other things to know:

  • Descriptions are in the full responses: Greenhouse needs ?content=true, Lever has descriptionPlain, and Ashby has descriptionPlain.
  • Salary shows up on Ashby (?includeCompensation=true) and Lever (salaryRange) when the company publishes it.
  • Lever EU companies live at api.eu.lever.co.
  • Be polite: cache results, and don't hammer the endpoints. Job boards change a few times a day at most.

Tracking new jobs (no code)

The script is enough for a one-off export. If you want many companies, more platforms, and only the jobs posted since yesterday, I packaged it as a Company Jobs Scraper on Apify. It covers Greenhouse, Lever, Ashby, Workable, SmartRecruiters, and Recruitee in one format, with title, location, remote, and date filters. It has a "only new jobs since the last run" mode for schedules, and costs $1.40 per 1,000 jobs with no subscription. People use it for job alerts, recruiting research, and hiring signals ("who's hiring ML engineers this week?").

Either way, the script above is yours to copy.

title: Measuring Where Intent Gets Lost in Agentic Smart Contract Synthesis
description:
arXiv:2610.37830v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: AI agents can now write software from a plain-English description, but code that runs is not the same as code that does what was asked. This gap matters most for smart contracts, the programs behind Web3 applications that move money on a blockchain and cannot be fixed once deployed. We ask how to check whether an AI-written contract behaves as it should, and where the requested behavior gets lost.
  We design an evaluation built on execution rather than opinion. We replay the same transactions on an AI-written contract and on the original it should reproduce and measure how often they agree. We test every grading tool on planted mistakes, compare against an answer key written without the description, and audit our own scorer until known wrong answers cannot pass. Common methods, such as AI judges and standard analysis tools, miss obvious mistakes, and scoring choices matter too. Checking only the functions every system includes hid about half the difference between pipelines.
  We then propose an elicitation-first architecture. Before writing code, the agent asks the client a short checklist of questions, checks the contract against an independently written executable answer key, and returns disagreements to the client instead of silently rewriting code. Asking first matters far more than reviewing or patching afterwards, across three AI models, while automated security fixes often break requested behavior. A few well-chosen questions recover much of what a short description omits, and their value can be estimated without the original contract. To our knowledge, this is the first study in smart contract synthesis to gather missing requirements before generation and check the result against an independently written executable model. The lessons extend to any setting where AI agents turn requests into programs. We release our tools, 600 tasks and all results.

title: What $99 a month proves about your AI agent
description:
When an AI agent spends money, two artifacts exist. The first is the transaction: a hash on a chain, visible to anyone. The second is the decision to allow it — and when the decision was no, almost nobody keeps the second one.

Ask a team what their agent refused last month and you usually get a dashboard, a screenshot, or a log where every row says allowed. A dashboard is a claim made by the same system that is being questioned. That is why the interesting artifact is not the allow list. It is the refusal, written down in a form someone else can check.

What a refusal record has to contain

The record has to answer four questions without help from the service that produced it: what was asked, which policy decided, who asked, and can this file be changed after the fact.

{
  "v": 1,
  "prev": "<sha256 of the previous record>",
  "ts": "2026-10-29T09:14:02+00:00",
  "decision": "deny",
  "reason": "payee not in allowlist",
  "policy_id": "E03-allowlist",
  "task_id": "task_7f21",
  "artifact_hash": "sha256:9c1e...",
  "actor": "agent:research-1",
  "meta": {"requested_amount": "12.50", "allowed_max": "0.05"},
  "hash": "<sha256 of this body>",
  "signature": "<Ed25519 signature>",
  "public_key": "<base64 key>",
  "algorithm": "ed25519"
}

Three properties do the work. prev chains each record to the one before it, so deleting a row breaks every row after it. The signature covers the body including prev, so a record cannot be rewritten and re-signed without the key. The public key is embedded, so verification needs no network call and no account with the vendor.

Writing one is a single request:

curl -X POST https://attest.rta.lat/deny \
  -H 'content-type: application/json' \
  -d '{"reason":"payee not in allowlist","policy_id":"E03-allowlist",
       "task_id":"task_7f21","artifact_hash":"sha256:9c1e","actor":"agent:research-1"}'

Reading them back is the other one: GET /deny?since=...&limit=100. Offline check is a function call against the exported log, not a login:

from attest.deny import read, verify_log
verify_log(read())

What it proves, and what it does not

This table is the reason the product exists, and it is more useful than any feature list:

Proves Does not prove
The record was not changed after issue That no other chain was shown to someone else
The chain has no gaps (each prev matches) That every refusal in your system reached this log
The signature verifies offline with the embedded key That the policy behind the refusal was correct

Read the right column twice. A signed refusal log is evidence that a specific decision happened and was recorded in a way that cannot be quietly edited. It is not a certificate of good judgement, and it is not a control: it records what was stopped, it does not stop anything. If you need enforcement before the action, that is a separate layer — a mandate checked against the proposed action, not a log written after it.

Anyone who sells you "compliance" as a single artifact is selling you the left column and hoping you do not read the right one.

Why it costs money at all

Recording a refusal is cryptography, not inference. There is no model in the path: Ed25519 signing and a SHA-256 chain cost nothing per record, which is why the price is flat rather than metered.

The paid plan is $99 for 30 days, unlimited records, one-time payment, no auto-renewal. A trial key starts at 0.01 USDC and covers 100 records over 7 days; free evaluation is 20 records a day. Payment is USDC on Base to the address on the page, and the page issues the API key after the transfer.

Now the honest part about the subscription: the price is not the proof. Paying monthly proves you had $99 and a reason. What proves something is the artifact, and the artifact does not expire with the subscription. Records you already hold keep verifying offline after the plan ends, because verification uses the public key inside the record, not a call to the vendor. If a service's evidence stops working when you stop paying, it was never evidence — it was a rented dashboard.

So what does $99 a month actually prove? That you decided the question "what did the agent refuse, and can I show it later" is worth a fixed line item rather than a screenshot. The rest is arithmetic: signing a record is Ed25519, not inference, so the five-hundredth refusal in a month costs the same as the first — zero.

Where it fits in a real conversation

An auditor asks for a refusal and gets a signed chain with the policy and the numbers. An incident review needs a timeline; the gap is usually exactly where the agent was stopped, and this is the file that fills it. A customer asks what your agent is not allowed to do; the answer is a set of policy ids with the records that applied them.

None of those conversations are won by a dashboard. They are won by a file the other side can check without trusting you.

The contract, the offline verifier and the pricing block are here: https://attest.rta.lat/deny-evidence

title: Vercel Connect now supports Secure Compute
description:
Vercel Connect now supports Secure Compute, allowing connectors to reach providers with IP allowlists, such as Salesforce and Snowflake.

With Secure Compute routing enabled, Connect’s provider requests use the selected network’s dedicated static IP addresses instead of Connect’s shared IPs. Requests to obtain and refresh access tokens follow that route; your app’s direct API routing is unchanged by this setting. Credential management stays the same, so you don’t need to store long-lived provider secrets in your app or build OAuth flows yourself.

To enable Secure Compute routing for a supported connector and all projects that use it:

  • Open your connector’s Settings in the Vercel dashboard.

  • Under Secure Compute Routing, choose an existing network.

  • If your provider uses an IP allowlist, add the selected network’s displayed IP addresses to it in the provider’s settings.

  • Save your changes in Connect.

Requests for initial connector creation and all provider discovery requests bypass the selected network and connect directly to providers. If the selected network is unavailable, routed requests fail instead of falling back to Connect’s shared IPs.

Read the Secure Compute routing documentation for configuration details.

Read more

title: Why Birthday Reminders Fail When They Only Remember the Date
description:
Remembering a birthday is useful.

Remembering it at the right time is better.

A simple birthday reminder can tell you that someone’s birthday is today.

But that may already be too late if you wanted to:

  • buy a gift
  • make a reservation
  • send something by post
  • plan a visit
  • organize a group message

That is why I think birthday apps should do more than store dates.

The date is only the final deadline

A birthday is a fixed date.

Planning around it is not.

Different people need different amounts of preparation.

For one person, a reminder on the same morning may be enough.

For another, you may need:

  • one week to order a gift
  • several days to arrange travel
  • time to coordinate with family
  • time to prepare something personal

A useful birthday planner should support that difference.

One reminder is rarely enough

A single notification creates a binary experience:

either you saw it or you did not.

A better approach can use multiple reminder points.

For example:

  • one month before
  • one week before
  • one day before
  • on the birthday itself

That gives the user time to act instead of simply informing them.

Context matters too

A birthday list becomes much more useful when it contains more than names and dates.

Depending on the user, useful context might include:

  • relationship
  • gift ideas
  • notes
  • age or birth year
  • previous plans
  • important preferences

The point is not to create a complicated CRM.

It is to reduce the mental load of remembering details every year.

Planning is different from remembering

This distinction changed how I think about birthday apps.

A reminder app answers:

When is the birthday?

A planner answers:

What do I need to do before it arrives?

Those are different product problems.

A good birthday app should reduce stress

The best birthday tools should make the user feel less rushed.

They should help turn a date into a manageable plan.

That can mean:

  • seeing upcoming birthdays early
  • organizing people clearly
  • keeping notes in one place
  • setting useful reminders
  • avoiding last-minute decisions

The value comes from preparation.

How this shaped Annum

Annum was designed around the idea that birthdays are easier to manage when they are treated as upcoming events, not just calendar dates.

The focus is on keeping important people organized, seeing what is coming next, and preparing before the birthday arrives.

That makes the app more useful than a simple “today is someone’s birthday” notification.

Final thought

Remembering a date is easy for software.

Helping someone prepare for that date is a better product challenge.

For birthday planning, the most useful reminder is often the one that arrives before you need it.

Learn more

Annum – Birthday Planner for Android

Visit the official Annum page
