title: Migrax vs Flyway: generated vs hand-written migrations
description:
Flyway and Migrax both keep a database schema in numbered SQL files, apply them in order and record what ran. The difference is where the SQL comes from. With Flyway you write every migration yourself. With Migrax you change your JPA entities and it writes the migration, which you then review.

This article makes the same change with both, on the same PostgreSQL database, and compares what each one does along the way. It also says where Flyway is the better choice.

Tested with: Flyway Community 13.12.0 (the open-source command line, released 2026-10-30), Migrax 0.17.1, Spring Boot 3.5.7, Hibernate 6.6.33, PostgreSQL 17. Compared on 2026-10-31. Statements about Flyway's editions come from Redgate's feature summary (last updated 2026-10-27). Every output below was copied from a real run.

The change

A customers table with two rows, and the change from Stop using ddl-auto=update in production: name becomes full_name, email gets longer, and every customer needs a country.

With Flyway

You write the migration. A correct version keeps the data by renaming the column, and adds the required column in three steps because the table has rows:

V2__rename_name_add_country.sql:

ALTER TABLE customers RENAME COLUMN name TO full_name;
ALTER TABLE customers ADD COLUMN country varchar(2);
UPDATE customers SET country = 'GB';
ALTER TABLE customers ALTER COLUMN country SET NOT NULL;
ALTER TABLE customers ALTER COLUMN email TYPE varchar(320);

$ flyway migrate
Current version of schema "public": 1
Migrating schema "public" to version "2 - rename name add country"
Successfully applied 1 migration to schema "public", now at version v2 (execution time 00:00.019s)

Flyway runs what you wrote, exactly as written. Whether the file matches the entities, and whether it keeps the data, is up to you and your reviewers. If you forget the UPDATE, or write DROP COLUMN name and ADD COLUMN full_name instead of a rename, Flyway runs that too.

There is no way back with the open-source edition:

$ flyway undo
ERROR: Flyway Redgate Edition Required: undo is not supported by OSS Edition

Undo scripts (U2__...sql) and the undo command are part of Flyway Teams and Enterprise, and you write each undo script yourself.

With Migrax

You change the entity (fullName, length = 320, a new country field) and run generate:

$ migrax generate --rename customers.name=full_name
warning: Adding NOT NULL column 'customers.country' without a default fails if the table has rows. Add a default in the SQL, or add it as nullable, backfill, then make it NOT NULL.
Created src/main/resources/db/migration/0002_rename_customers_name_and_more.sql:
  - rename column customers.name to full_name
  - add column customers.country
  - alter column customers.email
Rollback script written to src/main/resources/db/migration/rollback.
...

It writes the forward migration and a rollback script, and lints the migration before anything runs. The warning above is the UPDATE you would otherwise have to remember. You edit the file the same way as the Flyway one, and end up with the same five statements. Without --rename, Migrax sees a column go away and another appear, asks whether it was a rename, and refuses to drop the column without --allow-destructive. In CI, where no one can answer, it stops and prints the --rename option to use.

migrax rollback runs the generated rollback script:

rollback/0002_rename_customers_name_and_more.sql:

ALTER TABLE customers DROP COLUMN country;
ALTER TABLE customers ALTER COLUMN email TYPE varchar(255);
ALTER TABLE customers RENAME COLUMN full_name TO name;

So the work moves from writing SQL to reviewing it. You still read every migration; you no longer type it, or its undo script.

What both do

Much of the day-to-day is the same:

  • Plain SQL files in order. Flyway's V1__...sql, Migrax's 0001_...sql. Both also run Java migrations for changes SQL can't express.

  • A history table with checksums. Both refuse to continue when someone edits a migration that already ran:

    ```shell $ flyway validate Migration checksum mismatch for migration version 1 -> Applied to database : -328024399 -> Resolved locally : 1803351363 Either revert the changes to the migration, or run repair to update the schema history.

    $ migrax migrate error[MXE104]: Checksum changed for applied migration V1__create_customers.sql ```

  • Baselines for a database that existed before the tool: flyway baseline and migrax baseline.

  • Running at application startup, through Spring Boot's built-in Flyway support or the Migrax starter, and both have Maven and Gradle plugins.

Where they differ

Flyway Community Flyway Teams / Enterprise Migrax
Who writes the SQL You You; Enterprise can generate it from a schema model Generated from JPA entities, you review it
Undo / rollback No Teams and Enterprise: undo scripts you write Rollback script generated with each migration
Dry run script No Yes migrax migrate --sql prints the script without running it
Drift detection No Enterprise migrax drift, and a check at startup
Lint for risky statements No Not in the feature summary migrax lint, run on every generate
Throwaway-database check No Not in the feature summary migrax verify applies every migration and rollback
Databases About 30, including Snowflake, BigQuery and MongoDB (list) Same, with Redgate support 12 relational databases
Licence Apache 2.0 Commercial Apache 2.0, every feature

"Not in the feature summary" means Redgate's feature summary doesn't list it; Redgate's documentation describes the checks each edition has.

Where Flyway is the better choice

  • There are no JPA entities. Migrax generates migrations from Hibernate, JPA and a few other Java mappings (or a SQL schema file). A project that writes SQL by hand, or isn't on the JVM, gains less from it, while Flyway works the same for everyone.
  • The database isn't one of Migrax's 12. Flyway reaches warehouses and document databases such as Snowflake, BigQuery, Databricks and MongoDB.
  • You want a vendor behind the tool. Redgate sells support, a desktop application and compliance features. Migrax is an open-source project.
  • The team prefers writing every statement. Some teams want the migration to be the source of truth, not the entities. Flyway is built around that.

Switching from Flyway

Migrax reads Flyway's history table, so a project can switch without rerunning anything. Copy or keep the V*__ files in the migration folder and run:

$ migrax import flyway
Recorded 2 migration(s) as applied.
Next: disable Flyway (spring.flyway.enabled=false), then run 'migrax generate'; its first run uses the current database as the baseline.

$ migrax status
Migrations in src/main/resources/db/migration for jdbc:postgresql://localhost:5432/shop_fw
  [X] V1__create_customers.sql         applied 2026-10-31 11:45:20
  [X] V2__rename_name_add_country.sql  applied 2026-10-31 11:45:20
2 applied.

$ migrax generate
No snapshot yet: using the current database schema as the baseline.
No changes detected.
Saved the entity schema as the baseline snapshot: .migrax/snapshot.json

The old files keep working, and the next entity change becomes 0003_...sql. Each other environment needs migrax import flyway once. The guide Switching from Flyway or Liquibase has the details.

Summary

  • Flyway applies the SQL you write. Migrax writes the SQL from your entities, with a rollback script and lint warnings, and you review it.
  • Both keep a checksummed history, refuse edited migrations, baseline existing databases and run at startup.
  • Undo, dry-run scripts and drift detection are paid Flyway features; in Migrax they are part of the free tool.
  • Flyway is the better fit without JPA entities, for databases Migrax doesn't support, or when you want commercial support.

Originally published at migrax.org.

title: MCP Postgres Guard: Preventing SQL Injections and Slow Queries in AI Agents
description:
Giving an AI assistant access to a database through MCP can be transformative for data analytics, but executing raw LLM-generated SQL against production or staging databases carries severe risks:

  • Accidental DROP TABLE or DELETE WITHOUT WHERE clauses.
  • Expensive unindexed sequential scans locking the database.
  • SQL injection vulnerabilities.

mcp-postgres-guard is an audited, secure MCP server for PostgreSQL designed to act as a resilient safety firewall.

seotarek / mcp-postgres-guard

A secure Model Context Protocol (MCP) server for PostgreSQL: query auditing, slow-query analysis, and SQL injection prevention for AI agents.

MCP Postgres Guard 🐘🛡️

A security-first Model Context Protocol (MCP) server for PostgreSQL: query auditing, destructive command interception, and SQL injection prevention for autonomous AI agents.

Developed by Tarek Mohamed (@seotarek)

📌 Why MCP Postgres Guard?

Allowing AI agents (Claude, Cursor, LangChain agents) direct SQL access creates severe operational risks: accidental table dropping, unbounded deletions, or SQL injection. MCP Postgres Guard intercepts and audits all agent-generated SQL queries before they reach your database:

[ AI Agent / Claude / Cursor ]
               │
               ▼
 ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────┐
 │           MCP Postgres Guard Server          │
 │  • Destructive Query Blocker (DROP/TRUNCATE) │
 │  • Unbounded DELETE/UPDATE Prevention        │
 │  • Stacked Query & RCE Probe Detection       │
 └──────────────────────┬───────────────────────┘
                        │ (Only If Verified Safe)
                        ▼
             [ Production Database ]

🛠️ MCP Tools

  • pg_validate_query: Validates whether a SQL statement is safe to execute for an autonomous agent.
  • pg_check_read_only: Enforces a strict read-only policy…
View on GitHub

🔒 Security Features

  1. AST Query Validation: Parses incoming SQL statements using pglast / sqlparse to enforce read-only semantics (SELECT only, no INSERT/UPDATE/DELETE/TRUNCATE/ALTER).
  2. Transaction Timeouts & Statement Limits: Caps execution time at configurable thresholds (e.g. 3000ms) to prevent Denial of Service (DoS).
  3. Query Plan Cost Analysis: Runs EXPLAIN before executing heavy queries; rejects plans with estimated costs exceeding safety budgets.
  4. Data Masking (PII): Automatically masks sensitive columns (emails, phone numbers, password hashes) in result sets.

Check out the full repository and setup guide on GitHub:
👉 https://github.com/seotarek/mcp-postgres-guard

title: The end of credential sprawl for agents
description:
Every useful agent reaches beyond your codebase. It posts to Slack, opens pull requests, queries Snowflake, or calls an internal API. That reach is what makes it valuable, and it's also where the risk lives, because for years, granting it meant provisioning a long-lived token and hoping it never leaked.

Vercel Connect replaces long-lived tokens with ones your code requests at runtime, scoped to the task and expiring on their own.

During the public beta, we've grown the ecosystem past 100 connectors, unified how they work, and added the governance capabilities teams need in production.

Today, Vercel Connect is generally available.

Vaults don't fix long-lived tokens

Managing credentials has become its own workload. Teams write rotation scripts, copy secrets across environments, and share tokens between users. Putting a token in a vault made it harder to steal, but no less dangerous once stolen. It never expires, and no vault limits what a leaked credential can do.

Agents compounded the problem by touching more systems with greater autonomy, more often. Yet the tools to contain a secret haven't changed.

With Vercel Connect, your app never stores credentials. It requests one:

  • You register a connector once for a provider like Slack, GitHub, Snowflake, Shopify, or your own OAuth service

  • You attach it to the projects and environments that need it

  • Your code requests a token at runtime, and it refreshes automatically

  • Your app has no provider secret to commit by accident

Requesting a token doesn't require another secret. Every deployment on Vercel carries an OIDC identity, and the SDK uses it to prove who's asking.

What changes when access becomes a request

The difference shows up in the properties of the credential:

Property

Stored token

Vercel Connect

Lifetime

Never expires

Short-lived, refreshed automatically

Reach

Everything the agent could need

Scoped to the task in the request

Identity

One shared bot for every user

App or a specific named user

Rotation

Mint, update copies, redeploy

None to perform

Revocation

Rotate and redeploy

One command, per user or all tokens

Credentials that used to sit in environments long after the work finished now expire on their own. Nothing lingers for an attacker to find.

Scoping happens per request. One step of an agent might read a repository, the next opens an issue, and each asks for only that.

How fine-grained a token can be depends on the service, and GitHub is the clearest example. Requests can restrict a token to a single repository with read-only permissions, rather than trusting a standing grant organization-wide.

The open-source GitHub Tools SDK puts this into practice. Choose a preset like code-review, and it mints tokens with only the required scopes.

Identity is per request as well. Tokens act as the app by default, but pass a named user as the subject and the token acts on their behalf, scoped to what they authorized during a one-time consent flow.

Connectors for the services you already use

Vercel Connect now ships with 100+ preset connectors for developer tools and SaaS providers like Notion, Shopify, and Workday, as well as managed connectors for Slack, GitHub, Linear, Salesforce, and more.

Your own services follow the same model via custom OAuth and API Key authentication, and any OAuth-capable MCP server can serve as a connector.

Finding and creating them is faster, too. Browse the full catalog on the Vercel website, create a connector in fewer steps, and manage everything from the dashboard, CLI, or API.

Governance that scales with your team

Teams adopting Vercel Connect need more than scoped tokens. They need to control who manages connectors and to track how access is used.

GA adds three capabilities:

  • Fine-grained RBAC controls who can create and manage connectors

  • Audit logs record authorization and connector activity

  • Token and trigger observability shows usage across projects

Together with per-environment attachment and one-command revocation, access becomes something you can inspect and prove.

When an auditor asks who had access to a system and when, the answer is a query against the audit log, not an investigation across projects and Slack threads.

Wherever your agents run

Vercel Connect is available wherever you and your users are:

  • Custom Environments are supported, so a qa environment gets its own connector alongside production, preview, and development

  • eve supports Connect out of the box, with connections declared per agent

  • Chat SDK support brings the same model to conversational apps

Build connected apps in v0

Apps and agents built in v0 use the same model.

Tell v0 which service your app needs, and it sets up the connector during the build. Slack, GitHub, and other managed connectors need nothing on the provider's side, and since tokens are minted at runtime, the generated app has no secret to keep.

The KERNEL team shipped a voice-driven browser agent this way:

Events flow in, without a secret either

Requesting tokens is half the picture. Your agent also needs to hear about events.

Triggers handle this without putting a secret back in your app. When a user posts in Slack, the provider sends the event to Vercel Connect. It verifies the signature server-side, re-attests the event with an OIDC identity, and forwards it to your project. Forwarded events arrive even with Deployment Protection enabled.

Your app has no bot token to act with and no signing secret to verify webhooks, yet the full loop still runs.

Moonpig Group runs its internal legal agent on this loop in production:

Built around a single call

Underneath everything is getToken from the Vercel Connect SDK.

Whether your agent is built on eve or the AI SDK, runs as a background job in Vercel Workflows, or is a loop you wrote yourself, it asks for a credential the same way.

Around that call, adapters handle the wiring:

  • @vercel/connect/eve supplies the credentials behind an agent's connections

  • @vercel/connect/chat hooks Connect into Chat SDK adapters

  • @vercel/connect/betterauth and @vercel/connect/authjs produce provider configs for Better Auth and Auth.js

  • @vercel/connect/ai-sdk and @vercel/connect/mcp do the same for AI SDK tools and MCP clients, whether your agent calls tools directly or through a server

For eve agents and Chat SDK applications, the two secrets a Slack integration usually keeps in your environment, SLACK_BOT_TOKEN and SLACK_SIGNING_SECRET, are gone from your app entirely.

Pricing and availability

Vercel Connect is available on all plans, with pricing based on token requests and trigger events. The Hobby plan includes 500 token requests and 1,000 triggers per month at no additional cost. Pro plans are billed at $3 per 1,000 token requests and $0.95 per 1,000 triggers, with custom pricing on Enterprise.

If you used Vercel Connect during the beta, your current billing terms stay unchanged until September 25, 2026, when the updated pricing takes effect.

title: I gave my messy photo archive a spirit guide — an offline, open-weight AI that learns your family, names your places, and finds any memory
description:
This is a submission for the Hacktoberfest Open-Source AI Challenge Week 4: Ghost in the Machine

What I Built

Alebrije (github.com/JamesDBartlett3/Alebrije) is a local-first archive spirit-guide for your photos, videos, and audio clips. Alebrijes are the brightly colored creatures of Mexican folk art that guide souls where they need to go — this one guides you through thousands of memories that would otherwise sit in folders with names like DCIM_0947.

You point it at a messy directory. It then:

  1. Meets your people. You introduce a friend or family member from a sample photo (alebrije person add Abuela --photo abuela.jpg), and Alebrije builds a private people book: the face is embedded locally by open face models (SCRFD detection + AdaFace recognition via onnxruntime) and described in words by the vision model — no cloud, no face database handed to a third party.
  2. Recognizes them everywhere, and names every place. Every photo is scanned for faces; each becomes a 512-d vector stored locally. Faces close to someone in your people book are matched automatically, borderline ones are double-checked by Gemma, and recurring strangers cluster into "Unnamed" people you name with one rename. It also tags every photo and video with objects, clothing, animals, food, and the mood of the moment. If a photo carries GPS coordinates, it finds the closest point of interest (a park, museum, landmark — nearest by real haversine distance, via the OpenStreetMap Overpass API) and always appends the municipality chain: Civic Center Park — Denver, Colorado, USA, or with no landmark in range simply City of Golden, Jefferson County, Colorado, USA.
  3. Remembers by feeling, not filename. Everything is embedded with an open model into a local SQLite index, so you can search in plain language — "dog on the beach at sunset" — sorted by relevance, newest, media type, or name.

Everything runs on your machine: an open-weight multimodal model (Gemma 3 4B via llama.cpp) looks at your media, open face models (SCRFD + AdaFace via onnxruntime) recognize your people, an open embedding model (nomic-embed-text) indexes it, and a Día de los Muertos–themed local web app — papel picado banner, marigold glow — serves the whole collection to any phone or laptop on your network. Nothing about your family ever leaves your hardware (the only outbound calls, and only for GPS-tagged files, are the two open-data OpenStreetMap geocoders, which receive coordinates, never images).

I built this for the #GhostInTheMachine theme the way Día de los Muertos itself treats it: the dead stay alive as long as their stories are told. A hard drive full of untagged photos is a room full of ancestors waiting to be introduced. Alebrije is the marigold path through it.

Demo

Everything below is from a live run on an ordinary 4-core desktop, CPU only:

Six files went in named IMG_4031.png … IMG_4043.jpg. Alebrije tagged all six (captions, objects, clothing, mood), recognized and named a person across four of them from a single sample photo, and reverse-geocoded the two that carried GPS. Then, in plain language:

"dog on the beach at sunset" puts the three beach-dog photos on top — including one taken before the archive's newest party photos — because ranking is by meaning, not date.

The CLI speaks the same language:

And it's the same app on a phone, served from your own desk over the LAN:

Code

https://github.com/JamesDBartlett3/Alebrije

Install and run (Python 3.10+ and pipx are the only prerequisites — Alebrije installs everything else):

pipx install git+https://github.com/JamesDBartlett3/Alebrije.git@v0.2.0
alebrije setup        # downloads llama.cpp + the open-weight models, auto-detects your GPU
alebrije init ~/Pictures/family
alebrije up           # starts the two local model servers
alebrije scan         # index files, read EXIF dates + GPS
alebrije tag          # vision-tag everything (CPU: ~1 min/photo, GPU: seconds)
alebrije serve        # http://localhost:8799 — also on your LAN
alebrije update       # later: checks GitHub releases, upgrades in place

No pipx? git clone + python alebrije.py <command> works straight from the repo — friendliest option on Windows.

How I Built It

  • Vision + language: Gemma 3 4B IT (open weights, Gemma license) served by llama.cpp's llama-server with its multimodal projector. Every caption, object list, clothing item, animal, mood, person description, and gray-band identity double-check comes from this one local model.
  • Embeddings & search: nomic-embed-text v1.5 (Apache-2.0), via llama.cpp's OpenAI-compatible embeddings endpoint. Vectors live as float32 blobs in SQLite; cosine ranking is a few lines of Python.
  • Faces, without the cloud: v0.1 matched people by Gemma descriptions alone — we shipped it, watched it conflate lookalike relatives and miss people across decades, measured the failure, and rebuilt identity on real face embeddings. SCRFD-10GF detects every face (five landmarks each) and AdaFace ir101 — trained specifically to handle low-quality faces, i.e. old family photos — turns each aligned crop into a 512-d identity vector, both on onnxruntime (MIT) on CPU. Detection runs a letterboxed whole-image pass plus overlapping native-resolution tiles on large photos, so faces never get lost to downsampling; alignment crops are always warped from the full-resolution original. Matching uses measured thresholds (same person ≈ 0.56–0.95, different people ≈ 0.0), with Gemma confirming borderline cases and strangers auto-clustering into nameable "Unnamed" people.
  • The app itself is nearly all Python standard library — a scanner (with a hand-rolled EXIF parser that pulls capture dates and GPS coordinates out of JPEG APP1 segments), a tagging pipeline, a people book, a vector index, a CLI, and a threaded web server with an embedded single-page UI. The only pip dependencies are onnxruntime and Pillow. No framework, no account.
  • Fully self-installing, fully cross-platform. alebrije setup works on Linux, macOS, and Windows: it queries the llama.cpp GitHub releases API and downloads the prebuilt build matching your OS, CPU architecture, and accelerator — NVIDIA (nvidia-smi), AMD ROCm (rocm-smi), Vulkan (vulkaninfo), Apple Metal on any Mac, or plain CPU — then fetches the five open models (three GGUFs from Hugging Face, two face ONNXs from GitHub releases) with resume support. When a GPU is present, alebrije up launches the models with full layer offload (-ngl 999).
  • Tests: 182 offline tests (alebrije selftest) cover the scanner (including a synthetic JPEG with hand-built EXIF + GPS binary), the face pipeline (letterbox/tiling math, SCRFD decoding, similarity alignment, threshold bands, clustering, v0.1-database migration), tag coercion, people matching, vector math, search sorting, the bootstrap asset picker for every OS/GPU combo, server lifecycle, the web API (real HTTP on an ephemeral port), and the CLI — all against fake model servers, no network or GPU required.

Why Does Open Innovation Matter?

Your family photos are the last data you'd ever hand to a stranger, and the first data that gets uploaded without thinking the moment you use a cloud "AI photo assistant." Open weights flip that: the same Gemma model a giant cloud product would run is running on your desk, inspectable, with your files never leaving the room.

Openness also made this project possible at all. llama.cpp's OpenAI-compatible server meant the whole app is one urllib call away from vision and embeddings; the GGUF ecosystem meant a 4B model runs on an ordinary 4-core CPU; permissive licenses meant everything here ships without negotiation; and OpenStreetMap's open geodata meant place names without a paid maps API. If the models were closed, an offline family-archive assistant simply couldn't exist — and if they were free-but-closed, it couldn't be audited, fine-tuned, or trusted with something as personal as a memorial archive.

The Spirit of It

The moment it landed: I fed it six files named IMG_40xx and asked, out loud, "dog on the beach at sunset" — and the first three results were exactly the three photos I'd have picked, one of them taken years before the others. A folder became a memory. That's the whole ofrenda: the tech is just the marigold petals; what they guide home is your own past.

Prize Categories

  • Gemma (Featured) — Alebrije is built around Gemma 3 4B: every caption, tag, person description, and borderline identity double-check comes from the open-weight Gemma model running locally through llama.cpp.

title: FilingLoop: Evaluating and Evolving LLM Agents for Corporate Disclosure Review and Revision
description:
arXiv:2610.37905v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Public disclosure repositories such as SEC EDGAR support informed investment through web access to corporate filings. Supporting their review with language model agents requires discovering unstated deficiencies across related documents, acquiring missing company facts, and verifying that requested revisions satisfy evidence-backed requirements. Existing financial question-answering evaluations provide limited evidence of these interactive capabilities. We introduce \textbf{FilingLoop}, an interactive benchmark and a self-evolving agent framework for corporate disclosure review and revision. Grounded in historical U.S.\ Securities and Exchange Commission correspondence, FilingLoop reconstructs 380 predominantly IPO review tasks from 96 companies under distinct information constraints. An evaluator separate from the acting agents scores final filings and responses against 6,099 eligible requirements and audits unsupported claims and harmful revisions. Our framework couples iterative review and revision within each case with procedural learning across cases, converting requirement-level evaluation feedback into role-specific guidance without updating model weights. Updates affect only subsequent cases, allowing procedural adaptation to be assessed without retrying scored tasks. On the evaluated stream, evolution increases requirement fulfillment from 24.28\% to 27.96\% and full comment resolution from 16.90\% to 20.75\%, with a 5.8\% increase in total cost over the fixed-policy variant. FilingLoop connects the concerns an agent discovers with the company facts it obtains and the revisions it commits, providing requirement-level feedback for procedures used in later review tasks.

title: Node.js OTP Throttling: Delivery Guarantees for Logistics 2FA
description:
A rate limiter for SMS OTP requests is a delivery-control system, not a single counter. The useful trade-off is strict enough to stop abuse while leaving a legitimate driver a recovery path when a message is delayed. For a Node.js logistics portal, I would enforce limits at three scopes: account, verified phone number, and network signal. I would also count attempts and sends separately. That distinction keeps a slow carrier from turning retries into an SMS storm.

How do you rate-limit SMS OTP requests in a Node.js 2FA flow?

Option Pick this when Main boundary
Fixed window You need a small, easy-to-audit baseline A boundary reset can create a burst
Sliding window You need a smoother per-identity policy It needs shared, expiring state
Token bucket You need controlled bursts with a steady refill Capacity and refill units need careful tuning
Distributed counter Several Node.js instances serve the login flow Clock, atomicity, and key expiry become part of the design

For a single process or a first test, a fixed window can be enough. Pick sliding-window state when the abuse pattern is bursty and the user experience matters. Pick a token bucket when a brief burst is legitimate but the long-run SMS rate must stay bounded. For production traffic across instances, the decision is less about the algorithm name than about atomic updates and expiry in the shared store.

The limits should be policy, not magic. A useful starting shape is one code request per identity every 30 seconds, five requests per hour per phone number, and a daily ceiling that triggers a support path. Those values are examples to validate against carrier behavior, fraud data, and the risk of the account. They are not universal defaults.

How should Node.js separate sending from verification?

Think of the flow as a narrow pipe: request OTP -> reserve a send quota -> create a short-lived challenge -> enqueue delivery -> verify the code. The receipt email after a settled logistics payment sits beside this pipe, not inside it. Both workflows need delivery telemetry, but a receipt must never be a reason to relax an authentication limit.

The counter is the easy part.

The critical rule is to reserve the quota before the provider call. Otherwise two concurrent requests can both pass a read-then-write check. Imagine a driver tapping “send again” while a browser retry is still in flight: two workers read the same remaining quota, both call the SMS service, and the dashboard records an innocent-looking pair of successful requests. A retry from the delivery queue can multiply that effect unless the send operation has an idempotency key. The reservation must be atomic in the shared store, and a failed provider call needs a deliberate policy: release the reservation only when a retry is safe, or keep it consumed to protect the carrier. The code below keeps the limiter behind an interface so the application can use a Redis-like store, a database transaction, or another implementation with the same atomic contract.

type LimitResult = {
  allowed: boolean;
  retryAfterSeconds: number;
};

type QuotaStore = {
  consume(key: string, limit: number, windowSeconds: number): Promise<LimitResult>;
};

const policies = [
  { suffix: "identity", limit: 1, windowSeconds: 30 },
  { suffix: "phone", limit: 5, windowSeconds: 60 * 60 },
  { suffix: "network", limit: 20, windowSeconds: 60 * 60 },
] as const;

async function canRequestOtp(
  store: QuotaStore,
  identityId: string,
  phoneHash: string,
  networkKey: string,
): Promise<LimitResult> {
  const keys = [
    `otp:${policies[0].suffix}:${identityId}`,
    `otp:${policies[1].suffix}:${phoneHash}`,
    `otp:${policies[2].suffix}:${networkKey}`,
  ];

  const results = await Promise.all(
    policies.map((policy, index) =>
      store.consume(keys[index], policy.limit, policy.windowSeconds),
    ),
  );

  const blocked = results.find((result) => !result.allowed);
  return blocked ?? { allowed: true, retryAfterSeconds: 0 };
}

Do not use a raw phone number as a key. Normalize it first, then use a keyed digest with controlled access. Do not log the OTP, the full phone number, or a code that can be replayed. A challenge needs an expiry, a single-use state transition, and a maximum verification-attempt count. Rate-limit verification too; otherwise the send limiter protects the carrier while the guesser attacks the code.

What should the dashboard prove?

A 429 response is only the visible edge. Record counters for requests, allowed sends, blocked sends, delivery-provider accepts, delivery failures, verification successes, and verification lockouts. Add dimensions for policy scope and a coarse region, but avoid putting phone numbers, OTPs, or raw IP addresses into labels. High-cardinality labels make the dashboard expensive and can expose personal data.

The useful diagram in words is: request rate -> quota decision -> queue delay -> carrier acceptance -> handset delivery -> verification result. A fall in the last metric can come from a carrier delay, an expired challenge, or an attack. Those are different actions, so keep the stages separate.

Alert on ratios and persistence. For example, a sudden increase in blocked requests with stable successful verifications suggests abuse or an overly strict policy. A stable request rate with rising queue age points to delivery capacity. A high provider-accept rate with low verification success needs investigation, but it does not prove the SMS reached the handset.

For the logistics portal, trace one correlation ID across the payment-settled event, receipt dispatch, and authentication session, while keeping the OTP itself out of the trace. That lets an operator answer a practical question: did the user fail to authenticate, or did the message arrive after the challenge expired?

Where do common implementations break?

The first trap is an in-memory Map. It disappears on restart and each Node.js instance sees a different truth. The second is a non-atomic get followed by set; concurrent requests can both win. The third is returning a different message for an unknown account, which creates an account-enumeration oracle. Keep response timing and wording deliberately similar.

A limiter can also lock out a real user behind a shared office network. That is why network scope should be a backstop, not the only key. Conversely, phone-only limits can be evaded with many accounts. Use several signals, document their order, and give support a controlled recovery process with stronger identity checks.

This design does not guarantee delivery.

SMS carriers, handset state, and regional filtering remain outside the application. It also does not replace fraud detection, consent requirements, or a second authentication factor that is less dependent on a phone network. Test expiry boundaries, concurrent requests, restarts, clock skew, and queue retries before treating the counters as evidence.

Sources

  • https://nodejs.org/api/crypto.html
  • https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/HTTP/Status/429
  • https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc6585#section-4
  • https://opentelemetry.io/docs/specs/semconv/http/http-spans/
  • https://support.google.com/a/answer/81126

title: SaaS Backup & Disaster Recovery: RPO, RTO and PITR
description:
A nightly pg_dump to the same VPS is not a backup strategy. It is a file that disappears with the disk, the compromised root account or the provider incident that took the server down in the first place, and even when it survives it can only take you back to 2 AM. For a SaaS product, the real questions are how much data you can afford to lose (RPO), how long you can afford to be down (RTO), and whether anyone has actually restored from your backups recently.

At Loop Origin we run Laravel and Node SaaS platforms on VPS infrastructure for clients, and backup design is part of every server setup and maintenance engagement. This is the setup I deploy by default, with the configuration, restore commands and drill schedule.

What is a good backup and disaster recovery setup for a SaaS on a VPS?

Direct answer: Combine continuous database archiving for point-in-time recovery (PostgreSQL WAL with pgBackRest or WAL-G, MySQL binary logs) with periodic full backups pushed to versioned, write-protected object storage in a separate account and region. Define RPO and RTO per tier, encrypt everything, and run a timed restore drill every month.

RPO and RTO tiers: pick one per system, not per company

RPO (recovery point objective) is how much recent data you can lose. RTO (recovery time objective) is how long recovery may take. They drive cost, so set them per system rather than declaring "zero data loss" for everything.

Tier Typical RPO Typical RTO Mechanism Fits
Tier 0 Seconds Minutes Streaming replica plus WAL/binlog archiving, scripted failover Payments, orders, core tenant data
Tier 1 Minutes 1-4 hours Continuous WAL/binlog archive plus daily full backup, restore to new VPS Most B2B SaaS primary databases
Tier 2 24 hours 1 day Nightly full backup to object storage Analytics copies, internal tools
Tier 3 Rebuildable Days Infrastructure as code, no data backup Caches, queues, search indexes rebuilt from source

Most clients I work with land on Tier 1 for the primary database and Tier 2 or 3 for everything else. Redis queues and Elasticsearch-style indexes are usually Tier 3: rebuild them from the database instead of backing them up. My guide on running Laravel queues in production covers why failed jobs should live in the database rather than only in Redis.

Why dumps alone are not enough

A logical dump (pg_dump, mysqldump) is a consistent snapshot at one moment. If a bad migration or an accidental DELETE without a WHERE runs at 4:40 PM, a nightly dump takes you back to the previous night and you lose the day. Point-in-time recovery (PITR) closes that gap: restore the last full physical backup, then replay the database's change log up to the second before the mistake.

Dumps are still useful for moving individual tenants, seeding staging and long-term archives. They are just not the recovery mechanism for the primary.

PostgreSQL PITR with pgBackRest

postgresql.conf changes (restart required for archive_mode and wal_level):

wal_level = replica
archive_mode = on
archive_command = 'pgbackrest --stanza=main archive-push %p'
archive_timeout = 60          # force a WAL segment switch at least every 60s

/etc/pgbackrest/pgbackrest.conf:

[global]
repo1-type=s3
repo1-s3-bucket=acme-db-backups
repo1-s3-endpoint=s3.eu-central-1.amazonaws.com
repo1-s3-region=eu-central-1
repo1-path=/pgbackrest
repo1-retention-full=4
repo1-cipher-type=aes-256-cbc
repo1-cipher-pass=<from secrets manager>
compress-type=zst
start-fast=y

[main]
pg1-path=/var/lib/postgresql/16/main

Initialize, verify and schedule:

sudo -u postgres pgbackrest --stanza=main stanza-create
sudo -u postgres pgbackrest --stanza=main check          # confirms WAL archiving works
sudo -u postgres pgbackrest --stanza=main --type=full backup   # weekly via cron/systemd timer
sudo -u postgres pgbackrest --stanza=main --type=diff backup   # daily
sudo -u postgres pgbackrest --stanza=main info

archive_timeout = 60 is what makes the RPO roughly one minute on a quiet database: without it, a low-traffic system may not fill and ship a 16 MB WAL segment for a long time.

The restore you will run when someone drops a table at 16:40:

sudo systemctl stop postgresql
sudo -u postgres pgbackrest --stanza=main --delta \
  --type=time --target="2026-10-31 16:39:00+05" --target-action=promote restore
sudo systemctl start postgresql

In practice I restore to a new server first, verify the data, then cut over or copy the missing rows back. Restoring over the only production copy removes your ability to try again.

WAL-G is the main alternative: archive_command = 'wal-g wal-push %p', wal-g backup-push $PGDATA for base backups, and wal-g backup-fetch $PGDATA LATEST plus restore_command = 'wal-g wal-fetch %f %p' and recovery_target_time for PITR. I prefer pgBackRest for its built-in check, retention and parallel restore, and WAL-G where a team already uses it.

MySQL and MariaDB PITR with binary logs 

# my.cnf
[mysqld]
server_id = 1
log_bin = /var/lib/mysql/binlog
binlog_format = ROW
binlog_expire_logs_seconds = 1209600   # 14 days, longer than your full-backup interval
sync_binlog = 1

Take a consistent full backup with Percona XtraBackup for large databases, or mysqldump --single-transaction --source-data=2 for smaller ones (--source-data replaced --master-data in MySQL 8.0.26). Ship binlogs off the server continuously, for example with mysqlbinlog --read-from-remote-server --raw --stop-never running on a backup host.

Recovery: restore the full backup, read the binlog file and position recorded in it, then replay up to just before the incident:

mysqlbinlog --start-position=157 --stop-datetime="2026-10-31 16:39:00" \
  binlog.000412 binlog.000413 | mysql -u root -p

--stop-datetime is interpreted in the local time zone of the machine running mysqlbinlog, a detail that has caught more than one team restoring on a UTC server.

Object storage: where backups survive the incident

The repository must survive the loss of the server and of the credentials on it:

  • Separate account or project for the backup bucket, with a write-only key on the server. A stolen server key should not be able to delete backups.
  • Versioning plus object lock (S3 Object Lock, or the equivalent on S3-compatible providers that support it) with a retention period longer than your detection window.
  • A different region or provider from the primary VPS.
  • Client-side encryption (pgBackRest's repo1-cipher-type, or restic for file backups) with the passphrase stored outside the server.
  • File uploads (storage/app, user uploads) backed up with restic or rclone, or written directly to object storage in the first place.

Cost drivers, compared

Component What drives cost How to control it
Object storage Total stored size × retention Compression (zstd), differential backups, retention limits
Request and egress fees Restore downloads, frequent small uploads Choose providers with low egress; restore drills to the same region
Standby replica (Tier 0) A second always-on server Use only for systems that truly need minute-level RTO
Restore drill servers Hours of a temporary VPS per month Script the drill, destroy the server afterwards
Engineer time Setup, monitoring, drills Automate checks and alerts; document the runbook

For most Tier 1 SaaS databases the storage bill is small next to the replica and engineering time. My VPS vs managed PaaS cost comparison shows where managed databases with built-in PITR change the calculation.

Failure modes I have seen

  • Archiving silently broken. archive_command fails, WAL piles up in pg_wal and the disk fills. Monitor pg_stat_archiver.failed_count and the age of last_archived_time.
  • Backups nobody restored. Encryption passphrase lost, wrong PostgreSQL major version, missing extensions. Only a drill finds these.
  • Same blast radius. Backups in a bucket the compromised server can delete.
  • Binlog retention shorter than the backup interval. A gap makes PITR impossible past the last full backup.
  • Forgotten tenants' files. The database restores, but uploaded documents do not.
  • Shared-database multi-tenancy surprises. Restoring one tenant from a shared physical backup needs a side restore and a selective copy; plan it. My multi-tenant SaaS database architecture guide covers the trade-offs.

Monthly restore drill runbook

  1. Provision a clean VPS from infrastructure code.
  2. Restore the latest full backup plus WAL or binlogs to a target time from yesterday.
  3. Time it end to end; compare against your RTO.
  4. Run integrity checks: row counts on key tables, latest order or invoice timestamp, application smoke test.
  5. Restore a sample of uploaded files and open them.
  6. Record duration, issues and the backup set used in the runbook.
  7. Destroy the drill server and rotate any credentials it used.

Frequently asked questions

What is the difference between RPO and RTO?

RPO is the maximum acceptable data loss, measured as time between the last recoverable point and the incident. RTO is the maximum acceptable time to restore service. A system can have a one-minute RPO and a four-hour RTO, and the two are engineered with different tools.

Is pg_dump enough for a production SaaS database?

Not as the only mechanism. It restores to the moment the dump ran, so anything after that is lost. Use physical backups with WAL archiving for point-in-time recovery, and keep logical dumps for tenant exports, staging data and long-term archives.

pgBackRest or WAL-G?

Both provide base backups, WAL archiving to object storage, compression, encryption and PITR. pgBackRest has a built-in configuration check, retention management and parallel restore. WAL-G is lighter and common in container setups. Choose the one your team will monitor and drill.

How often should I test restoring backups?

At least monthly for production databases, and after any major version upgrade, storage change or backup configuration change. A drill should restore to a fresh server, be timed against your RTO and include an application-level check, not just a successful exit code.

Should backups be stored in the same cloud provider?

A different region at minimum, and ideally a separate account with write-only credentials from the server and object lock enabled. A different provider adds protection against account-level incidents at the cost of egress fees during restores.

Do I need to back up Redis?

Usually not, if Redis holds caches, sessions and queues that can be rebuilt or retried. Keep durable state such as failed jobs and anything business-critical in the main database. Back up Redis only if it is your primary store for data you cannot regenerate.

title: How to Uninstall GBase Database(GBase 8a): A 5-Step Clean Removal Guide
description:
Wrong software version, completed POC, or server migration? These situations often require a clean GBase Database(GBase 8a) uninstall.

GBase Database provides an uninstall script, but running it in the wrong order can leave services running, processes holding files, or installation directories behind.

Follow these five steps to safely uninstall GBase Database. Run the commands as the DBA user and prepare the required uninstall password in advance.

Step 1: Back Up All Database Data

Before uninstalling GBase Database, back up everything you need to retain. The uninstall script deletes database data and does not preserve it for recovery.

Make sure you back up:

  • Database tables and other required data
  • Configuration files
  • Installation and troubleshooting logs
  • External table definitions and source files
  • Any load files stored outside the database

Pay special attention to external tables and load source files. Confirm their actual storage paths and make separate copies if necessary.

Do not proceed until the backup is complete and verified.

Step 2: Check for Active Business Connections

Before stopping GBase Database services, confirm that no business connections, running queries, or data loading operations remain.

Stopping services while data loading is in progress may leave incomplete files or interrupt ongoing operations.

Even in a POC environment, check for active workloads before continuing.

Step 3: Stop GBase Database Services

Stop services in reverse startup order: stop GCluster first, followed by GCware.

gcluster_services all stop
gcware_services all stop

Stopping the compute and SQL service layer before the underlying cluster management service helps ensure an orderly shutdown.

For multi-node GBase Database clusters, verify that services have stopped on every node. Stopping services on the first node does not automatically guarantee that remote nodes are clear.

Step 4: Run the GBase Database Uninstall Script

Navigate to the gcinstall directory extracted from the original installation package.

Run the uninstall script in silent mode using the original demo.options configuration file:

cd /opt/gcinstall
./unInstall.py --silent=demo.options

The script uses the existing configuration rather than requiring you to enter all installation parameters again.

Be prepared to enter the required password when prompted. The exact interaction and supported parameters may vary by GBase Database version, so consult the corresponding installation manual.

Important: Do not interrupt the uninstall process. Stopping it midway may leave the cluster in a partially removed state and require manual cleanup.

Step 5: Verify the Uninstall and Clean Up Remaining Files

After the uninstall script finishes, verify that the GBase Database processes have exited and the installation directory has been removed.

Check running processes:

ps -ef | grep -E "gcluster|gcware" | grep -v grep

Check the installation directory:

ls -ld /opt/gbase

A clean result should show no remaining GCluster or GCware processes belonging to this cluster and no remaining installation directory.

If processes remain, identify which cluster they belong to before stopping or killing them. Other database instances or services may share the same host.

If the machine will be reused, also review:

  • Old environment variables and profile settings
  • Scheduled jobs and automatic startup entries
  • The DBA user and its associated configuration
  • Residual files and directories
  • System parameters modified during environment preparation

Only remove shared users, directories, or system settings after confirming that no other application depends on them.

Additional Notes: Preserve Configuration and Installation Records

The GBase Database uninstall script relies on demo.options. Archive this file together with the installation logs and backup records.

Also remember that system-level settings modified by environment preparation scripts may not be automatically restored during uninstall.

Whether these settings need manual restoration depends on the operating system and GBase Database version. Record all relevant changes in the deployment handover documentation.

For production environments, perform uninstall operations through the approved change management process. Uninstallation is irreversible, and a verified backup is the recovery path.

Final Checklist: GBase Database Uninstall

Before marking the uninstall as complete, confirm:

  • [ ] Database data and required files are backed up.
  • [ ] No active business connections or loading operations remain.
  • [ ] GCluster and GCware services are stopped on every node.
  • [ ] unInstall.py completes successfully.
  • [ ] No related service processes remain.
  • [ ] The installation directory is removed.
  • [ ] Environment settings and startup entries are reviewed.
  • [ ] demo.options and installation logs are archived.

The key takeaway: A clean GBase Database uninstall is more than running unInstall.py. Back up data, stop services in reverse startup order, execute the uninstall script, and verify every node before returning the machine to service.

Keep these five steps in your GBase Database deployment runbook to make future reinstalls, server replacements, and POC environment cleanup more predictable.
