title: Configuration Management in Markdown
description:
Introducing Korta: Configuration Management in Markdown

Managing servers should not require a complicated stack just to install packages, create users, or keep services running.

Those tasks are familiar to anyone who operates infrastructure. Yet the knowledge behind them often ends up scattered across shell scripts, internal wikis, configuration files, and someone’s memory. Over time, it becomes harder to answer a simple question: What is supposed to be running on this server?

Korta is our attempt to make that answer easier to write, review, and apply.

Korta is a command-line tool for configuration management in Markdown. You describe the desired state of your servers in a role, preview what would change, and apply it over SSH.

# Packages

- nginx, curl

# Users

- deploy added to apps group, shell /bin/bash

# Directories

- /opt/app owned by deploy:apps, mode 0750

# Services

- nginx started, enabled

Then run: 

korta plan role.md -i hosts.md
korta apply role.md -i hosts.md

The plan checks your hosts and shows the changes Korta would make. The apply command plans first, asks for confirmation, and then carries out the changes.

There is no agent to install on each server. Korta connects over SSH and uses root or passwordless sudo.

Configuration you can read

A role is a Markdown document organized around the things you want to manage. You can describe users, groups, packages, directories, files, services, kernel settings, firewall rules, updates, and custom commands.

Your hosts live in a Markdown inventory:

# Production

identity: ~/.ssh/prod_ed25519
- web1 deploy@web1.internal env=prod

# Staging

identity: ~/.ssh/staging_ed25519
- web2 deploy@web2.internal env=staging

You can use labels to select a subset: 

korta apply role.md -i hosts.md --limit env=staging

Markdown gives teams a familiar place to keep configuration alongside the context that explains it. A role can live in Git, be reviewed in a pull request, and be read by the next person responsible for the system.

Who Korta is for

Korta is for people who manage Linux servers and want a straightforward way to describe and maintain their configuration.

That includes developers running a few virtual machines, small teams maintaining their own infrastructure, platform engineers who want reviewable roles, and consultants managing servers across multiple environments.

It is especially useful when you want to keep control of your servers and use the SSH access you already have. The core CLI can run directly from your machine without a central manager.

Korta supports Ubuntu, Debian, RHEL, Rocky Linux, AlmaLinux, and CentOS Stream. Hosts need SSH and appropriate privileges; they do not need a Korta agent.

Why now

More teams are reexamining how they run software. Some want more control over infrastructure costs. Others want to run applications and databases on their own servers, or simply make existing systems easier to understand and maintain.

At the same time, teams are increasingly using AI to help write operational code. That makes review more important: generated configuration still needs to be understandable, validated, and approved by the people responsible for the machines.

Korta starts with a workflow built around those needs:

  1. Write the desired state.
  2. See what would change.
  3. Review and approve it.
  4. Apply it to the selected hosts.

The goal is to make routine server work easier to share and repeat, while keeping the operator in control.

Why open source

Server configuration is foundational. The tool that interprets it should be something people can inspect, understand, and improve.

We want Korta’s core to be open source so developers and operators can see how roles are parsed, how plans are produced, and what runs over SSH. We also want teams to be able to use the CLI in their own environments and contribute fixes, ideas, and support for real-world use cases.

Open source is also a practical way to build a better infrastructure tool. Servers, operating systems, and operational requirements vary widely. The people using Korta will encounter cases we have not, and the project will be stronger with their feedback and contributions.

The open-source core includes the korta CLI, Markdown role engine, inventory parser, SSH client, and operating-system detection.

Korta Enterprise builds on that core for teams that need a shared manager. It adds a web console and API, approval and audit workflows, an encrypted vault, an AI role assistant, and deployment features for databases and applications. The same CLI and role files work with the Enterprise manager.

Where to start

Write a small role for a staging server, add the host to an inventory, and run korta plan. Review the output, then apply it when you are ready.

The core project is at github.com/nexusrun/korta (https://github.com/nexusrun/korta). We’re looking forward to sharing it and hearing what you build with it.

title: Open weight takes 71.5% of tokens and 23% of spend
description:
AI Gateway Production Index — October 2026

Every month, AI Gateway routes tens of trillions of tokens between production applications and AI labs. That traffic gives us a view of what AI usage actually looks like in today's enterprise, and we publish it here monthly. See the Production Index reports from July, August, and September.

October 2026 summary

  • Open-weight models now process more than seven in ten gateway tokens and account for nearly one in four dollars. Their share of spend has more than quadrupled since June.

  • September’s gateway spend was about 13 times December’s, while the average price per token was 47% lower. Almost one in three teams changed their most-used lab in September, an index record.

  • Nearly 70% of September’s gateway spend on Chinese models went through US-based providers, up from less than 10% in December.

  • Jev was the fastest-adopted model in AI Gateway history, reaching 35% of paid teams in its first two weeks, but it accounted for just 0.27% of gateway spend over that same period. Opus 5.5 took more than one in ten gateway dollars in its own first two weeks, the largest spend share of any September model launch.

Frontier spend up 900%, spend share down 22%

In August, open-weight models processed the majority of AI Gateway token volume for the first time. The money is now following. Open weight’s share of spend has more than quadrupled over the last three months, from one in twenty gateway dollars in June to nearly one in four in September.

Open weight's growth is coming from both ends of its price range, and it mirrors the wider gateway. The cheapest models drive token growth, while the expensive models drive spend.

Led by Kimi K3, models priced at least four times the open-weight average cost per token accounted for about two-thirds of the increase in open-weight spend.

In contrast, DeepSeek-v4.1-Flash alone processed nearly half of all September tokens but took just 2.6% of spend. Its price per token was about a fifth of the open-weight average.

Customers are increasing budgets on both sides of the market. Since December, spend on frontier models has grown tenfold; spend on open-weight models has grown more than seventyfold.

In September, 68% of teams that put more money into open-weight models did the same for closed-weight models. And more than two in five teams already paying for frontier models spent more on them than in August, the highest share this year.

Spending on the frontier is still growing, but spending on alternatives is growing faster. A company can spend more with a frontier lab while relying on it for fewer workloads, so the lab gets more money, but a smaller part of the customer’s business.

AI spend increases 13x while the cost per token halves

Market share is changing hands inside a market that is getting much bigger and cheaper.

September's gateway spend was about 13 times December's, an increase of 1,180%, while the average price per token fell 47%. The median paid customer active in both December and September more than doubled its spend.

Teams are spending more, but labs have to keep winning their business. In September, nearly one in two teams changed their most-used model. And almost one in three changed their most-used lab, an index record.

Even teams with lower token volumes use a wide mix of models. Since December, teams that processed at least 10 million tokens over that period used an average of 15 different models. The average rose to 26 for teams processing at least 100 million tokens, and 42 for those processing at least a billion.

The model is becoming a replaceable part of a much larger investment. Companies can continuously improve their AI products and workflows while changing which models power them. They can spend more on AI without becoming more dependent on any one lab.

Chinese models are big business for American providers

More than two-thirds of September’s gateway spend on Chinese-origin models went to US-based providers, up from less than a tenth in December. The Chinese lab builds the model; the American provider runs it and sells access.

DeepSeek’s models processed 58% of all gateway tokens for 6.6% of spend. More than four in five of those tokens were served by DeepSeek itself, yet two in five dollars spent on its models went through US-based providers.

Moonshot AI, the Beijing-based lab behind Kimi, accounted for 3.6% of gateway tokens and 13.2% of spend in September. US-based providers served nine in ten of those tokens.

Z.ai, also based in Beijing and the creator of GLM, accounted for 7.2% of all tokens and 4.5% of spend. US-based providers served seven in ten.

Customers can use Chinese models through access sold by American providers. For teams that put more money into Chinese models in September, an average of 53% of their spending on those models went through US-based providers and 41% through China-based ones.

The same Chinese model can compete with US-based models while generating revenue for US-based providers.

September model launch scorecard: Jev, Opus 5.5, and GPT-6

Whether a model launch is successful depends on what you measure: how broadly it’s tried, how much usage and spend it receives, or what share of its initial users return. We ranked every model launch in September with at least two weeks of data by these metrics; the tables show the top ten for each. The full scorecard is at the end of the report.

Jev is the most-adopted and most-called model

In its first two weeks, Jev reached more than a third of paid teams, nearly double the reach of Sonnet 5.5 in second place. This is the fastest adoption of any model in AI Gateway history.

Jev also received the most requests of any model in September, even though it launched halfway through the month. Of the teams that tried Jev in week one, 55.6% returned in week two, the fifth-highest retention rate.

Jev is a decision model. Compared with typical language-model requests, a Jev request is faster, cheaper and uses a fraction of the tokens. So although its adoption was fast and broad, it accounted for just 1% of the month’s tokens and 0.15% of spend.

In September, Jev quickly became a popular model for production while remaining a tiny part of the inference bill.

Opus 5.5 takes more than one in ten gateway dollars

The launch that received the most dollars was Opus 5.5, with more than twice the share of any other September launch, followed by GPT-6 Astra and DeepSeek-v4.1-Flash.

Opus 5.5 caught on quickly, with almost nine in ten dollars coming from teams already using Opus 5. Existing customers were trying the new release while the wider Opus family was losing market share.

Across all versions, Opus accounted for almost a third of gateway dollars in September, down from one in two in August. Anthropic’s overall share fell below half of total gateway spend for the first time, dropping from 63.7% to 43.9%.

Luna brought users back; Astra brought spend

GPT-6 Luna reached nearly three out of every twenty paid teams in its first two weeks, in third place behind Jev and Sonnet 5.5. But its return rate was the highest of the month; almost two-thirds of the teams that tried it in its first week came back in the second.

GPT-6 Astra reached a smaller audience but took more budget. In its first two weeks, it accounted for about one in twenty gateway dollars; Luna accounted for less than one in a hundred. Luna reached almost three times as many teams while Astra captured more than five times the share of spend.

OpenAI is attracting more customers with Luna, but capturing far more money with Astra, even though fewer teams use it.

Full September scorecard

Previous AI Gateway Production Index reports

  • May 2026

  • June 2026

  • July 2026

  • August 2026

  • September 2026

About this report

This report uses anonymized, aggregate traffic routed through Vercel AI Gateway through September 2026.

A few notes on measurement:

  • Token volume includes input, output, reasoning, cached-input and cache-creation tokens.

  • Spending is estimated at published list prices; actual bills may differ. Average price per token is estimated spending divided by token volume.

  • Open-weight classifications follow the current AI Gateway model list, a broader definition than in earlier reports.

  • Switching rates compare paid teams with at least 10 million paid tokens in both months. “Most-used” is measured by paid tokens.

  • Provider location means company headquarters.

  • Launch metrics cover external paid teams during each model’s first 14 days. Reach uses paid teams active from the start of the launch month through the data cutoff. Spend share uses total paid gateway spending during the model’s window. Return rate is the share of first-week teams that used it again in week two.

  • Model counts cover December–September, with each version counted separately. Team-size thresholds use total input and output tokens over that period.

  • All figures use the most recent data and protocol available; prior months may be revised as methodology is updated.

Read more about our methodology, and explore or download the public data.

Read more

title: A contract scanner that refuses to guess
description:
Every AI contract tool I have tried answers with confidence. Ask about a clause that is not in the document, and you get a plausible paragraph with an article number that does not exist. The failure is not that the answer is wrong. The failure is that the wrong answer looks exactly like the right one.

Contract Scan is a small tool that does the opposite, and I want to describe precisely where it stops instead of what it promises. It takes a text PDF or a plain text file and returns two risk flags for free, then five flags with the exact wording to fix for $5 in USDC. That is the whole product. The interesting part is the refusals.

What happens when it cannot read

The file is the first thing that can be wrong, so the tool answers about the file before answering about the contract:

  • An image-only scan returns 422 with "the file looks like a scan, no extractable text". It does not run OCR and it does not guess at clauses it cannot see.
  • An empty file returns no text found. A whitespace-only file returns 422 as well.
  • A file over 8 MB returns 413 with the limit, not a 500 after two minutes of silence.
  • A PDF that is not a PDF returns the exception class in the message, so you know whether the problem is encryption, a broken stream or the wrong file entirely.

None of this is impressive engineering. It is just the difference between "I could not analyse this" and a confident paragraph about a contract the service never read.

The free pass is rules, not a model

The five risk types are fixed: auto-renewal, unlimited liability, penalties and forfeitures, unilateral change, and a distant forum or arbitration. The preview runs deterministic patterns over the extracted text. The same document produces the same flags on every call, in milliseconds: ten contracts take about 4 ms on the server.

Determinism matters for a boring reason. If a scanner is a model wrapped in a prompt, two runs on the same contract can disagree, and then the output is not a document you can attach to an email to the other side. It is a conversation you had with a service.

The paid report adds a model pass on top of the rules, because live contracts are written in wording no regex anticipates: "liable for all damages", "courts of Delaware", "indemnify". Every flag in the report carries source: rules or source: model, so you can see which mechanism produced it. A flag with no provenance is an opinion with a timestamp.

We published the accuracy, including the failure

This is the part that most tools skip. The rules were measured on ten contracts written as real documents, for a named reader: a tenant in Moscow, a client in New York, an employee in St Petersburg. Each contract had risks planted deliberately, and each flag was checked against the quoted wording rather than eyeballed.

The first measurement, before any of this was announced:

Metric Measured Target Verdict
Completeness (planted risks found) 25 / 34 = 73.5 % ≥ 80 % not met
False flags 4 / 29 = 13.8 % ≤ 10 % not met
Flags pointing at a real risk 25 / 29 = 86.2 % — —
Server errors on edge inputs 0 0 met

Both thresholds were missed, and the misses were not random. Russian contracts scored 11 of 18 (61 %) against 14 of 16 (88 %) for English ones, because the English rules were written from live contracts and the Russian ones from a dictionary of legal phrases. Nine of nine misses traced back to three holes: Russian morphology, English synonyms for a penalty, and the concept of a "home court", which is not a risk at all when you are the local party.

The same exercise found two ways the scanner could answer "clean" on a dangerous contract: a cp1251-encoded text file silently lost all Cyrillic, and a PDF longer than 40 pages was cut off at page 40. A silent clean is the worst output a scanner can produce, worse than an error.

Both are fixed, with tests, in the same day's commits. The rules now return 35 of 35 planted risks with 0 false flags on that corpus — and that sentence needs a caveat the size of the corpus: the fixes were written against these ten documents, so the second number is a regression baseline, not an accuracy promise. It says the holes are closed. It does not say the next hundred contracts will score the same, and it is pinned in the test suite precisely so that it cannot quietly drift.

If you count risks outside the declared five-type checklist — a five-year non-compete, "as is" with no warranty, termination without a cure period — the ceiling was 61 % on the original run. That is the honest limit of a five-template triage, and it should never be confused with a legal review.

What happens to the file

Files are processed in memory and discarded when the request ends. Only aggregate counters survive: how many operations ran, not the documents. There is no account, so there is no account to leak. Payment is 5 USDC on Base to the address shown on the page; you paste the transaction hash and the page says so when the hash is wrong instead of pretending it worked.

What it is not

It is a reading aid with quoted wording. It is not legal advice, it does not know which side of the contract you are on, and it does not promise an outcome. When the document cannot be read, it says so; when the rules miss, the published number says so for it.

Two free flags, five in the report, and the accuracy table above are all on the page:

https://ailegal.legal/contract-scan

title: Python Error Handling: try, except and finally Explained with Examples
description:
Originally published on CodingCush.

Python error handling uses a try block to run risky code, an except block to catch and handle any error that happens, and a finally block for code that must run no matter what, such as closing a file. Instead of letting your whole programme crash with a red error message, you catch the problem, show a friendly message, and keep the rest of your code running safely.

What Is Error Handling in Python?

Every programme meets problems sooner or later. A user types letters where a number should go. A file you expected is missing. A network connection drops halfway through a download. In Python, these problems are called exceptions, and when one happens Python normally stops the programme and prints a long traceback — helpful for you as the developer, terrifying for your user.

Error handling is simply your plan for those moments. You tell Python: "Try this code, and if something goes wrong, do this instead of crashing." It is a bit like wearing a seatbelt. You do not plan to crash, but you are very glad it is there on the one day you need it.

Python gives you four keywords for this job: try, except, else and finally. The official tutorial walks through the same ideas in the Python documentation on errors and exceptions, and it is worth keeping that page open while you learn.

The Basic try and except Block

The simplest form needs only two parts. Put the risky code inside try, and put your rescue plan inside except:

try:
    number = int(input("Enter a number: "))
    print("You entered:", number)
except ValueError:
    print("That was not a valid number. Please try again.")

If the user types 42, everything works and the except block is skipped completely. If the user types hello, int() raises a ValueError, Python jumps straight into the except block, and the friendly message appears instead of a crash. The programme keeps running afterwards, which is the whole point.

Notice that we named the exact error, ValueError. Python has many built-in exception types, and the full list of built-in exceptions in the documentation shows what each one means. Catching a specific error is almost always better than catching everything, because it stops you from hiding real bugs by accident.

Catching Different Errors in Different Ways

Real code can fail in more than one way, and each failure may need a different response. You can stack several except blocks under one try, and Python uses the first one that matches:

try:
    numerator = int(input("Enter the top number: "))
    denominator = int(input("Enter the bottom number: "))
    result = numerator / denominator
    print("Result:", result)
except ValueError:
    print("Please enter whole numbers only.")
except ZeroDivisionError:
    print("You cannot divide by zero. Even Python has limits.")

Here, typing letters triggers the first block, while typing 0 as the denominator triggers the second. Each problem gets a message that actually describes it, which makes your programme far easier to use — and far easier to debug later.

You can also catch several errors with one block by grouping them in brackets, and you can read the error message itself with as:

try:
    age = int(input("Enter your age: "))
    print("Next year you will be", age + 1)
except (ValueError, TypeError) as error:
    print("Something went wrong:", error)

The variable error holds Python's own description of the problem. Printing it during development is a great habit, because it tells you exactly which line complained and why.

The official Python tutorial — reading and writing files is where most beginners meet their first exceptions.

The else Block: Code That Runs Only on Success

The optional else block runs only when the try block finishes with no error at all. Beginners often ask why it exists, when they could simply put the code at the end of try. The answer is clarity and safety: code inside try is protected by your except blocks, so an error there could be caught and hidden by mistake. Code in else is not protected, so any error it raises will still surface properly.

try:
    file = open("scores.txt", "r")
    content = file.read()
except FileNotFoundError:
    print("The scores file could not be found.")
else:
    print("File loaded successfully.")
    print(content)
    file.close()

If the file opens and reads cleanly, the else block runs. If the file is missing, only the except message runs. This pattern pairs naturally with our guide on how to read and write files in Python, where the same open, read and close steps are explained in full.

The finally Block: Code That Always Runs

The finally block is the tidy-up crew. Its code runs whether the try block succeeded, failed, or even returned early. That makes it perfect for releasing resources: closing files, closing network connections, or unlocking something you locked.

try:
    file = open("notes.txt", "r")
    print(file.read())
except FileNotFoundError:
    print("notes.txt does not exist yet.")
finally:
    print("Finished — cleaning up now.")

Whatever happens above, that final message prints. In real projects the finally block usually closes the file instead of printing, so the file is never left open by accident. An open file that never closes can lock the file for other programmes and quietly waste memory, which is nobody's idea of fun.

try, except, else and finally Compared

Here is the whole flow in one table:

Block When it runs Typical job
try Always, first Holds the risky code you want to protect
except Only when a matching error happens Handles the problem with a message or a fallback
else Only when no error happens Runs follow-up code that depends on success
finally Always, last Cleans up: closes files and connections

A useful way to remember it: try is the attempt, except is the rescue, else is the celebration, and finally is switching the lights off when you leave — it happens every single time.

Raising Your Own Exceptions

Sometimes your own code needs to report a problem. Use the raise keyword to trigger an exception on purpose, usually when input breaks a rule your programme depends on:

def set_age(age):
    if age < 0:
        raise ValueError("Age cannot be negative.")
    print("Age set to", age)

try:
    set_age(-5)
except ValueError as error:
    print("Error:", error)

Writing small helper functions like this is much easier once functions feel natural, so if they still feel new, work through our beginner-friendly guide to Python functions explained with examples first. Raising clear errors early stops bad data from travelling deep into your programme, where it becomes much harder to trace.

Common Mistakes Beginners Make

Catching everything with a bare except. Writing except: with no error type catches every possible problem, including typos and real bugs, and then hides them. Your programme looks calm while quietly doing the wrong thing. Name the error you expect instead.

Leaving the except block empty. An except block that does nothing is like a smoke alarm with the batteries removed. At minimum, print or log what went wrong.

Putting too much code in try. Keep the try block small, covering only the lines that can actually fail. A huge try block makes it hard to know which line caused the error.

Forgetting finally for cleanup. If you open something inside try, close it in finally (or use a with statement for files), so it closes even when an error interrupts you.

Frequently Asked Questions

What is the difference between try and finally in Python?

The try block holds code that might raise an error. The finally block holds cleanup code that runs after everything else, whether an error happened or not.

Can I use try without except in Python?

Yes, if you pair it with finally. A try and finally combination is valid and is used purely for guaranteed cleanup. A try block must have at least one except or a finally after it.

What happens if an error is not caught?

Python stops the programme and prints a traceback showing where the error happened. Nothing after that line runs, which is why catching expected errors makes your programme feel much more polished.

Should I catch all exceptions with except Exception?

Only as a last-resort safety net, for example at the very top of a programme, and always log the error when you do. For normal code, catch the specific exception you expect, such as ValueError or FileNotFoundError.

Conclusion

Error handling is what separates a script that works on a good day from a programme you can trust every day. Use try for risky code, except to handle specific problems with clear messages, else for code that should only run on success, and finally for cleanup that must always happen. Start small — wrap your user input and file reading first — and your Python programmes will instantly feel calmer, kinder and far more professional.

title: gRPC vs REST in Java: 7 Things Every Microservices Developer Should Know
description:
gRPC vs REST in Java: 7 Things Every Microservices Developer Should Know

When building microservices in Java, one important architectural decision is choosing how services communicate.

For years, REST has been the default choice. But gRPC is becoming an increasingly interesting alternative, especially when performance, strongly typed contracts, and efficient service-to-service communication matter.

So, what's the difference? And when should you choose one over the other?

Let's explore seven things every Java microservices developer should know.

  1. REST uses JSON, while gRPC uses Protocol Buffers

REST APIs commonly exchange data using JSON.

JSON is human-readable, easy to debug, and supported by almost every programming language.

gRPC uses Protocol Buffers (Protobuf), a compact binary serialization format.

Instead of defining your API through JSON examples or separate documentation, you describe your service in a ".proto" file.

For example:

syntax = "proto3";

service Greeter {
rpc SayHello (HelloRequest) returns (HelloReply);
}

message HelloRequest {
string name = 1;
}

message HelloReply {
string message = 1;
}

From this definition, gRPC can generate client and server code.

Why does this matter?

  • Strongly typed service contracts.
  • Less repetitive boilerplate.
  • Compact message serialization.
  • Code generation for multiple programming languages.
  1. gRPC is built around HTTP/2

REST commonly uses HTTP/1.1, although it can also run over HTTP/2.

gRPC is designed around HTTP/2 and takes advantage of several of its capabilities:

  • Multiplexing: multiple requests can share a single connection.
  • Header compression: reduces repeated header overhead.
  • Binary framing: provides an efficient transport format.
  • Streaming: supports continuous data exchange.

These features make gRPC particularly interesting for communication between backend services.

  1. gRPC supports four communication patterns

Traditional REST APIs typically follow a request-response model.

gRPC supports four communication patterns:

Pattern| How it works
Unary RPC| One request, one response
Server streaming| One request, multiple responses
Client streaming| Multiple requests, one response
Bidirectional streaming| Client and server exchange multiple messages

This flexibility makes gRPC useful for real-time applications, monitoring systems, event-driven architectures, and services that need continuous data exchange.

  1. gRPC provides strongly typed service contracts

With REST, API contracts are often documented separately using tools such as OpenAPI.

With gRPC, the ".proto" file defines:

  • Service names.
  • RPC methods.
  • Request messages.
  • Response messages.
  • Field types.

The same contract can be shared between teams and used to generate client and server code.

This helps reduce inconsistencies between services and makes API evolution more structured.

  1. When should you choose REST?

REST is still an excellent choice.

Consider REST when:

  • You're building public APIs for web or mobile applications.
  • Browser compatibility is important.
  • Human-readable JSON is useful.
  • You need straightforward integration with third-party services.
  • Your application mainly exposes conventional CRUD operations.

REST has a mature ecosystem and remains a practical choice for many applications.

  1. When should you choose gRPC?

gRPC is particularly useful when:

  • Java microservices communicate internally.
  • Efficient serialization and transport matter.
  • You need client-side or server-side streaming.
  • Multiple services share strongly typed contracts.
  • Your architecture includes services written in different programming languages.

For internal service-to-service communication, gRPC can be a very effective alternative to REST.

  1. Building gRPC microservices with Java and Micronaut

Micronaut provides a lightweight framework for building Java microservices.

Combined with gRPC and Protocol Buffers, it offers a practical foundation for implementing strongly typed service-to-service communication.

If you want to experiment with this approach without starting from scratch, I've created a project:

gRPC Micronaut Starter Kit

The starter kit provides a foundation for building Java gRPC microservices with Micronaut.

Explore the project:

  • "GitHub repository" (https://github.com/frekost/grpc-micronaut-starter-kit)
  • "Extended version on Gumroad" (https://frekost.gumroad.com/l/grpc2micronaut)

If you'd like to start with a practical introduction, you can also read my previous tutorial:

"Master Java gRPC with Micronaut: Your First Microservice in Minutes" (https://dev.to/frekost/master-java-grpc-with-micronaut-your-first-microservice-in-minutes-6l2)

Final thoughts

REST and gRPC are not technologies where one must always replace the other.

They solve different problems.

REST remains an excellent option for public APIs and browser-facing applications.

gRPC is a strong choice for efficient communication between backend services, especially when strongly typed contracts and streaming are important.

In many microservice architectures, both technologies can coexist.

What do you use for communication between Java microservices?

Do you prefer REST, gRPC, or a combination of both?

Share your experience in the comments. I'd love to hear your thoughts!

title: Stop Modeling State With Booleans: Make Impossible States Impossible in TypeScript
description:
Here is a type you have probably written:

type UserState = {
  isLoading: boolean;
  error?: string;
  data?: User;
};

It looks reasonable. Then one day your UI shows a spinner on top of an error message, and a user stares at a screen that says both "Loading..." and "Something went wrong".

The bug is not in your rendering code. It is in the type, which allows states that should never exist.

Count the States You Actually Allow

That type has three fields. How many combinations can it represent?

  • isLoading can be true or false: 2
  • error can be a string or missing: 2
  • data can be a user or missing: 2

That is 8 combinations, and your app has 4 real states: not started, loading, failed, succeeded. Four of the eight are nonsense:

{ isLoading: true,  error: 'Failed', data: user }   // loading AND failed AND loaded?
{ isLoading: false, error: undefined, data: undefined } // finished, but with nothing?

Every one of those is a bug waiting for a code path that forgets to reset a flag. Your components have to guess which flag wins, and different components guess differently.

The Fix: One Field That Decides Everything

A discriminated union is a type where one shared field, the discriminant, tells you which shape you have.

type UserState =
  | { status: 'idle' }
  | { status: 'loading' }
  | { status: 'error'; error: string }
  | { status: 'success'; data: User };

Now there are exactly four states, and each carries only the data that makes sense for it. A loading state has no data field to forget. A success state always has data, with no ? and no undefined to check.

TypeScript Narrows It for You 

function UserCard({ state }: { state: UserState }) {
  switch (state.status) {
    case 'idle':
      return null;
    case 'loading':
      return <Spinner />;
    case 'error':
      return <p>{state.error}</p>;       // error exists here
    case 'success':
      return <h2>{state.data.name}</h2>; // data exists here
  }
}

Inside each case, TypeScript knows exactly which variant you are in. Write state.data inside the error branch and you get a compile error, not a runtime crash.

Using It in React 

const [state, setState] = useState<UserState>({ status: 'idle' });

async function load(id: string) {
  setState({ status: 'loading' });
  try {
    const user = await fetchUser(id);
    setState({ status: 'success', data: user });
  } catch (e) {
    setState({
      status: 'error',
      error: e instanceof Error ? e.message : 'Unknown error',
    });
  }
}

Notice what you no longer do: you never reset error before a retry, and you never clear data on failure. Each setState replaces the whole object, so stale fields cannot survive. That is the entire class of bug that booleans create, gone.

Make the Compiler Tell You When You Forgot a Case

Add a new state later, say 'refreshing', and every switch that does not handle it should complain. You can force that with a never check:

function assertNever(value: never): never {
  throw new Error(`Unhandled state: ${JSON.stringify(value)}`);
}

switch (state.status) {
  case 'idle':
    return null;
  case 'loading':
    return <Spinner />;
  case 'error':
    return <p>{state.error}</p>;
  case 'success':
    return <h2>{state.data.name}</h2>;
  default:
    return assertNever(state);
}

If a case is missing, state is no longer never in default, and TypeScript reports an error at that exact line. Adding a state turns into a to-do list generated by the compiler.

The Same Trick for API Responses

Functions that can fail are another place where optional fields hide bugs:

// Allows { data: undefined, error: undefined } and { data: x, error: y }
type Result<T> = { data?: T; error?: string };

Replace it with a union:

type Result<T> =
  | { ok: true; data: T }
  | { ok: false; error: string };

const result = await createOrder(input);

if (!result.ok) {
  showToast(result.error); // error is a string here
  return;
}

redirectTo(`/orders/${result.data.id}`); // data is defined here

The caller cannot touch data without first checking ok. You cannot forget the error path, because the types will not let you reach the success value until you have handled it. This pattern works nicely for Server Actions and API handlers.

Two Gotchas

1. Use a literal for the discriminant. status: string will not work. The field must be a literal type like 'loading' or true, so TypeScript can tell the variants apart.

2. Data from outside still needs checking. A union describes what your code produces. If you receive JSON from a network, TypeScript cannot know it matches. Validate it with a schema library at the boundary, then trust the type inside.

When Not to Bother

Not everything needs a union. A form field with an optional middle name is fine as middleName?: string. Use unions when several fields depend on each other, meaning some combinations are valid and others are not. If you catch yourself writing a comment like "error is only set when status is failed", that comment belongs in the type.

The Rule

If a combination of fields should never happen, make it impossible to write down. Replace booleans and optional fields with one discriminant, let TypeScript narrow it, and add a never check so new states cannot be forgotten.

Quick audit: search your project for isLoading, isError and ?: in state types. Wherever two or more of them appear together, ask which combinations are real. The gap between the number you allow and the number you need is a list of bugs you have not met yet.

If you work with TypeScript and Next.js, you can browse my templates on pixelanas.com for a typed starting point.

Get the templates: https://pixelanas.gumroad.com

What is the strangest impossible state you have ever seen on a screen? Tell me in the comments.

Anas, full-stack Next.js developer building SaaS products and premium templates. X: @ASheikh69751

title: The Best Hyperscaler Alternatives in 2026: AWS, Azure, and Google Cloud Alternatives Compared
description:
The right alternative depends on what you are replacing (raw infrastructure, an app platform, or GPU capacity), and you do not have to leave the hyperscaler entirely. Control Plane runs the same workloads across hyperscalers and alternative providers from one platform.

Control Plane publishes this guide.

TL;DR: What are the best alternatives to AWS, Azure, and Google Cloud?

Start by naming what you want to replace. A hyperscaler bill usually mixes three different things: virtual machines and storage, an application platform for deploying code, and GPU capacity for AI. Each has a different kind of alternative.

  • Raw infrastructure. Developer clouds and VPS or bare-metal providers give you servers and a smaller catalog of services.
  • An app platform. PaaS products take your code or container and run it, so you manage less.
  • GPU capacity. GPU clouds and neoclouds focus on AI hardware.
  • More than one of these at once. A multi-environment platform runs workloads across hyperscalers, infrastructure providers, and GPU clouds from one definition.

Control Plane ranks first because it is the only entry that runs one workload across hyperscalers and the infrastructure and GPU providers listed here. Infrastructure providers follow, then app platforms. The order is editorial, not a benchmark, and each description comes from the vendor’s own page, linked below.

  1. Control Plane: runs one workload across hyperscalers, infrastructure providers, neocloud GPU capacity, and your own servers.
  2. DigitalOcean: a cloud with an AI focus, covering agents, inference, and general cloud services.
  3. Hetzner: cloud servers in shared and dedicated resource plans for developers and teams.
  4. Akamai Cloud (Linode): cloud for applications and AI inference on a globally distributed platform.
  5. Vultr: cloud compute, cloud GPU, and bare-metal servers.
  6. OVHcloud: public cloud with compute, storage, databases, and managed Kubernetes.
  7. Render: an app platform for web services, databases, cron jobs, and workflows.
  8. Fly.io: hardware-virtualized machines and sandboxes for apps and agents.
  9. Heroku: a fully managed application platform built around dynos and add-ons.
  10. Railway: a repo-connected deployment platform with a visual canvas.

What are the three kinds of hyperscaler alternatives?

Type Examples Typical fit What you manage Typical trade-offs
Developer clouds and VPS or bare-metal providers DigitalOcean, Hetzner, Akamai Cloud, Vultr, OVHcloud Replacing virtual machines, storage, and networking Operating systems, deployment, scaling, and often databases and monitoring A smaller service catalog than a hyperscaler, so you assemble more yourself
App platforms (PaaS) Render, Fly.io, Heroku, Railway Deploying code or containers without running servers Application code and configuration Less control over infrastructure, and platform-specific conventions
GPU clouds and neoclouds for AI CoreWeave, Lambda, Nebius Training and inference on GPU hardware Models, data movement, and the surrounding application stack GPU-focused catalogs, so general services and data may live elsewhere
Multi-environment platforms Control Plane Running one workload across hyperscalers, infrastructure providers, GPU clouds, and your own servers The workload definition, with the platform handling placement and routing One platform to adopt, replacing a separate toolchain for each provider

These are general patterns for each type. Check any provider’s specifics against its own documentation and SLA before you commit.

How do the options rank?

1. Control Plane

Control Plane is the platform for running unbreakable apps and agents. It combines any cloud, neocloud, and bare metal into what Control Plane calls a Global Virtual Cloud (GVC).

It runs on Control Plane-managed compute in AWS, GCP, and Azure regions, on neocloud GPU capacity, and on your own servers. It runs serverless, standard, stateful, cron, and VM workloads. You can bring clusters you already run through Control Plane’s Bring Your Own Kubernetes (BYOK), or turn your own machines (bare metal or VMs) into managed locations with Control Plane’s Managed Kubernetes (MK8s). On Control Plane-provided compute, there is no Kubernetes cluster you have to operate. Many teams run it in a single cloud, not only across clouds.

A workload deployed to a GVC runs active-active in every location of that GVC, and a global endpoint routes each request to the nearest healthy location. You get failover without paying for idle standby capacity.

On Control Plane-provided compute, you pay for the CPU and memory a workload reserves, by the millicore and the megabyte, with no contracts or minimums. Control Plane’s Capacity AI right-sizes CPU and memory based on historical usage, within a minimum and maximum you set. Customers typically cut compute costs 30 to 50 percent compared with running directly on AWS, GCP, or Azure.

Workloads can attach NVIDIA GPUs, and the pricing page lists models from T4 to B200. Control Plane’s Universal Cloud Identity gives workloads short-lived, least-privilege access to 600+ AWS, GCP, and Azure services, with no long-lived cloud keys in your code. Control Plane is PCI DSS Level 1, SOC 2 Type II, HIPAA, and GDPR compliant. The CLI, console, Terraform and Pulumi providers, and the Control Plane MCP server all work through the same Control Plane API, and Control Plane ships its own Terraform and Pulumi providers, so it complements the infrastructure as code you already run.

For head-to-head comparisons, see Control Plane vs AWS, vs Render, vs Heroku, vs Fly.io, and vs DigitalOcean App Platform.

2. DigitalOcean

DigitalOcean’s homepage describes an “AI-Native Cloud” and “a unified stack for agents, inference, and cloud.” It lists serverless inference with intelligent routing and “80+ models,” a product called Agent Droplets, and DigitalOcean Managed Agents, which it says is in Public Preview. It also sells CPU and GPU Droplets, Managed Kubernetes, App Platform, managed databases, and storage and backups.

3. Hetzner

Hetzner describes its Cloud as a “cloud-hosting provider for developers & teams.” The page lists server plans with shared resources and with dedicated resources, a price calculator, networks, an API, and one-click apps. It states that the service is made in Germany and GDPR-compliant. Its cloud servers are available in Germany, Finland, Singapore, and the USA. Hetzner also sells S3-compatible Object Storage and Storage Box backup storage.

4. Akamai Cloud (Linode)

Akamai Cloud is presented as “Akamai Cloud for AI, Applications, and Agents.” Akamai says it lets you “run AI with rapid, GPU-powered inference and edge-native compute at global scale,” and that it “runs on one of the world’s most distributed platforms.” Access to NVIDIA GPUs is by request. The page also lists CPU compute, managed Kubernetes, managed MySQL and PostgreSQL databases, object and block storage, and backups.

5. Vultr

Vultr sells cloud compute, cloud GPU, and bare-metal servers. Its documentation also covers object and block storage, managed databases, Kubernetes, load balancers, and a container registry.

6. OVHcloud

OVHcloud’s Public Cloud page describes “over 50 OVHcloud infrastructure services and managed platforms.” It lists compute, storage, databases, and a secure network in 1-AZ or 3-AZ regions, with hourly, monthly, or long-term billing. It also offers managed Kubernetes and container management.

7. Render

Render calls itself “the cloud for builders.” Its page lists web services, Postgres databases, cron jobs, workflows, static sites, background jobs, key value stores, and private services. It describes load-based autoscaling, full-stack previews for each pull request, and managed Postgres with point-in-time recovery, read replicas, and high availability. For a direct comparison, see Control Plane vs Render.

8. Fly.io

Fly.io describes Fly Machines as “hardware-virtualized containers that launch instantly and run only when you need them.” It also offers hardware-isolated sandboxes for running untrusted or AI-generated code, storage options, and managed Postgres. The page says you can deploy from GitHub or its CLI. See Control Plane vs Fly.io for a comparison.

9. Heroku

Heroku describes a “fully managed application platform.” Apps run in dynos, which it calls “smart containers.” The page lists Heroku Postgres, a Key-Value Store, add-ons, buildpacks, team management, and fast rollback. See Control Plane vs Heroku for a comparison. In February 2026, Heroku moved to a sustaining engineering model focused on stability, security, reliability, and support rather than new features.

10. Railway

Railway calls itself “the all-in-one intelligent cloud provider.” You connect a repository, and the page says Railway handles configuration automatically. It offers a visual canvas, built-in networking, scaling, and logs, metrics, and traces. In October 2026, Railway disclosed a security incident, described in its preliminary report and in Control Plane’s guide to rotating keys or migrating.

Which cloud providers are best for full infrastructure control?

Control follows a spectrum, and each step toward more control adds operations work.

Level Example type Control Operations work
Most control Bare metal and VPS providers You choose the operating system, networking, and software Highest. You patch, scale, and recover.
Middle Managed Kubernetes on a cloud You control workloads and configuration Moderate. You run the workloads, the provider runs the control plane.
Least control PaaS You control code and settings Lowest. The platform runs the infrastructure.

Control Plane sits across this spectrum. Bring Your Own Kubernetes (BYOK) lets you keep clusters you already run and add them as locations. Managed Kubernetes (MK8s) turns your own machines (bare metal or VMs) into managed Control Plane locations. You keep your own clusters and servers and manage them under one platform, so you do not give up hardware ownership to get one way of deploying. On Control Plane-provided compute, you can skip operating a cluster.

How do managed hosting platforms compare to hyperscalers for reliability, incident response, and SLAs?

Compare the same four things for every provider, including the hyperscalers.

  1. SLA scope and conditions. Read what the SLA covers. Many apply to specific services or configurations and require a minimum setup, such as more than one instance or location.
  2. Credits versus actual uptime. An SLA usually remedies a miss with service credits. Credits do not replace the revenue lost during an outage, so design for availability yourself.
  3. Multi-region options. Check whether you can run in more than one region or provider, and what that costs.
  4. Status page and incident transparency. Look at how the provider reports incidents, how quickly, and how much detail it gives afterward.

Hyperscalers also have major outages. Control Plane keeps a public record in its cloud outage tracker. Do not assume that size guarantees availability.

Control Plane’s 99.999% availability SLA applies to workloads running at least two replicas in at least two locations. Those locations can be two regions of one cloud or locations on different providers. Take other vendors’ SLA figures from their own SLA pages.

What are common compute, storage, and networking service equivalents when moving off a hyperscaler?

The equivalents below are generic service types, not specific vendors’ products. Confirm that a provider offers a service on its own product page before you plan around it.

Hyperscaler service Generic equivalent elsewhere Migration note
Virtual machines VPS or bare-metal servers Re-create images and configuration, and plan for patching.
Managed Kubernetes Provider-managed or self-managed Kubernetes, or a platform that hides it Check version support and add-ons.
Object storage S3-compatible object storage Check API compatibility for your tools and libraries.
Managed databases Managed PostgreSQL or MySQL, or a self-run database Plan data transfer, backups, and failover testing.
Load balancers Provider load balancer or a reverse proxy Confirm health checks and TLS handling.
DNS Any DNS provider Lower the record lifetime before you cut over.
Secrets Secrets manager or an open-source secrets tool Rotate secrets as part of the move.
Monitoring Open-source monitoring and logging tools Rebuild dashboards and alerts.

You do not have to move everything. With Universal Cloud Identity, workloads running on Control Plane can keep using the hyperscaler services you depend on, such as storage or a managed database, while the compute moves. That lets you separate the move of compute from the move of data. Read how to run the same app on AWS, GCP, and Azure for a walkthrough.

What are good hyperscaler alternatives for small business apps needing databases, backups, and monitoring?

Developer clouds and PaaS platforms are often the simplest fit for small apps. They ship with fewer choices, and several bundle managed databases, backups, and monitoring into one product. Render’s page lists managed Postgres with point-in-time recovery and integrated logs and monitoring. Heroku’s page lists Heroku Postgres and app metrics. Fly.io’s page lists managed Postgres and storage options. Developer clouds such as DigitalOcean, Vultr, and OVHcloud list managed database and storage products on their own pages, and Hetzner lists object storage and backup storage.

Use this checklist for a small app:

  • Does the platform offer a managed database for the engine you use?
  • Are backups included, and can you restore to a point in time?
  • Does it include logs and metrics, or must you add a monitoring tool?
  • What do you pay when the app is idle?
  • How do you move off it if you outgrow it?

What is the simplest cloud platform alternative for small business apps needing predictable monthly pricing?

For most small apps, a PaaS or a developer cloud with plan-based pricing is the simplest fit. Read each vendor’s pricing page for the plan structure.

Control Plane works differently. On Control Plane-provided compute, it bills per millicore and megabyte reserved, with no contracts or minimums. That suits teams that want to pay for what a workload reserves and that expect load to vary. It is not a fixed monthly plan.

How do performance and networking differ between hyperscalers and alternative AI infrastructure providers?

The differences fall into four areas. None of them can be settled with a headline number, so test your own workload.

  • GPU availability. Hyperscalers and GPU clouds both limit capacity at times. A provider that specializes in GPUs may have different hardware and lead times. Check what you can get, for how long, and under what terms.
  • Interconnect options. Training across many GPUs depends on how the GPUs are connected inside the provider. Ask which networking options exist for the cluster size you need.
  • Data transfer between providers. Moving data between a hyperscaler and a GPU provider can add cost and time. Keep data close to compute where you can.
  • Global network reach. Inference serving users in many regions depends on where the provider has locations and how requests are routed.

Control Plane workloads can attach NVIDIA GPUs, and the pricing page lists models from T4 to B200. A GVC can include neocloud GPU capacity next to a hyperscaler region. Control Plane’s GPU Ocean lets you pull GPU capacity from any provider. For a comparison of GPU providers, see best GPU cloud providers in 2026.

Do you have to choose only one provider?

No. Many teams keep a hyperscaler for the services they depend on and add an alternative for cost, control, or GPU capacity. The risk is running a second stack: separate deployment pipelines, separate access control, and separate monitoring for each provider.

Control Plane addresses that risk. You define a workload once, and it runs in every location of a GVC. The locations can be two regions of one cloud or locations on different providers. A global endpoint routes each request to the nearest healthy location. That lets you run a hyperscaler and an alternative together, with one workload definition across both. For the step-by-step version, read how to run the same app on AWS, GCP, and Azure.

FAQ

What are good non hyperscaler options for running containerized web apps as a platform service?

Control Plane runs containerized workloads as a platform service on Control Plane-managed compute, with no Kubernetes cluster for you to operate. App platforms such as Render, Fly.io, Heroku, and Railway also run apps for you.

Which cloud providers are best for full infrastructure control?

Bare metal and VPS providers give the most control and the most operations work. Control Plane lets you keep your own clusters and servers through BYOK and MK8s, under one platform.

How do managed hosting platforms compare to hyperscalers for reliability, incident response, and service level agreements?

Compare SLA scope and conditions, credits versus actual uptime, multi-region options, and status page transparency. Hyperscalers also have major outages, as the cloud outage tracker records. Control Plane’s 99.999% availability SLA applies to workloads running at least two replicas in at least two locations.

What are common compute, storage, and networking service equivalents when moving off a hyperscaler?

Virtual machines map to VPS or bare-metal servers. Object storage maps to S3-compatible storage. Managed databases map to managed PostgreSQL or similar. Load balancers, DNS, secrets, and monitoring each have generic equivalents, listed in the table above. Confirm a specific provider’s offering on its own page.

What are good hyperscaler alternatives for small business apps needing databases, backups, and monitoring?

Developer clouds and PaaS platforms are often the simplest fit. Check each for a managed database, backup and restore options, and built-in monitoring.

What is the simplest cloud platform alternative for small business apps needing predictable monthly pricing?

A PaaS or developer cloud with plan-based pricing is usually the simplest fit. Control Plane bills per millicore and megabyte reserved, with no contracts or minimums, which is a different model from a fixed plan.

How do performance and networking differ between hyperscalers and alternative AI infrastructure providers?

Compare GPU availability, interconnect options, data transfer between providers, and global network reach. Test your own workload rather than relying on a headline figure.

Do I have to leave AWS, Azure, or Google Cloud entirely?

No. You can keep a hyperscaler for the services you depend on and move compute elsewhere. Universal Cloud Identity lets workloads on Control Plane keep using hyperscaler services while compute moves.

Is Control Plane only for multi-cloud?

No. Many teams run it in one cloud. It also runs on your own servers and on premises.

Next steps

Name what you are replacing, shortlist one provider per job, and test one workload before you move more.

  • Sign up free

title: I Built a Haunted Terminal That Scares You Into Taking Breaks
description:
Every break reminder I have ever installed died the same death: a toast slid into the corner of the screen, I thought "in a minute", and that was that. The reminder was polite. Polite is ignorable.

So for Hacktoberfest Week 4, whose theme is Ghost in the Machine, I built the opposite: haunt, a terminal ghost that interrupts you with a horror still, a whisper from a local model, and then refuses to give the screen back until you have stood up and looked at something that is not a monitor.

It is deliberately a little mean. That is the health feature.

What it does

Every few minutes (randomised, so you cannot brace for it), haunt:

  1. asks a local open-weight model to write one unsettling line and one concrete break instruction;
  2. slams a horror image, GIF, or video over your terminal;
  3. replaces it with a calm panel that holds a countdown while you breathe, stretch, and walk away;
  4. logs the break so --stats can tell you how long you actually spent away from the screen. 
$ python3 haunt.py --demo

your last commit message was a whisper too.

[ a 90x28 frame of a haunted house at night, rendered in 24-bit colour ]

╭──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────╮
│ the spirit releases you                                      │
│                                                              │
│ Stand up and roll your shoulders back five times.            │
│ The ghost will wait.                                         │
│                                                              │
│ ███████████████████████████░░░░░░░░░░░░░░░░░░░░░░░░░░░       │
│ 14s away from the screen                                     │
╰──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────╯
  breathe in 4, hold 4, out 6. ctrl+c ends the haunting.

When you quit, it prints the damage: 23 breaks, 46.0 minutes away from the screen.

How it works 

flowchart LR
  T[randomised timer] --> O[local model<br/>llama3.2:3b via Ollama]
  O --> W[whisper + health tip]
  T --> A[Wikimedia Commons asset<br/>still, GIF or video]
  A --> C[local cache + attribution]
  A -. network down .-> P[procedural Pillow art]
  W --> R[ANSI half-block renderer]
  C --> R
  P --> R
  R --> B[calm break panel<br/>countdown + breathing]
  B --> L[break log]

No graphics protocol, no browser, no image library in the terminal. Frames are downsampled with Pillow and printed as half-block cells, two vertical pixels per character, with 24-bit colour escapes:

def ansi_frame(img, cols, rows):
    fitted = ImageOps.fit(img.convert("RGB"), (cols, rows * 2),
                          method=Image.Resampling.LANCZOS)
    data = fitted.tobytes()
    lines = []
    for y in range(rows):
        top = (y * 2) * cols * 3
        bottom = (y * 2 + 1) * cols * 3
        chunks = []
        for x in range(cols):
            i, j = top + x * 3, bottom + x * 3
            chunks.append(
                f"\x1b[38;2;{data[i]};{data[i+1]};{data[i+2]}m"
                f"\x1b[48;2;{data[j]};{data[j+1]};{data[j+2]}m▀"
            )
        lines.append("".join(chunks))
    return "\n".join(lines) + "\x1b[0m"

The ghost itself is a prompt. The model returns JSON with three fields, and the app treats every field defensively, because a small model on a laptop will eventually return something strange:

prompt = (
    "You are the ghost in the machine, haunting a developer's terminal to push them "
    "away from the screen for their health. Reply with JSON keys whisper, health_tip, "
    "theme. whisper: one eerie line under 110 characters, unsettling not gory, lowercase, "
    "second person. health_tip: one concrete ergonomic break instruction under 110 "
    "characters that makes the human leave the screen (eyes, posture, movement, water). "
    "theme: exactly one of ghost, haunted-house, skeleton, cemetery, pumpkin, ofrenda."
)
data = ollama_json(prompt, model)
if len(data.get("health_tip", "")) < 20:
    data["health_tip"] = random.choice(FALLBACK_TIPS)

If Ollama is missing, slow, or returns garbage, curated lines take over. The haunting never fails open into silence; it fails into a break, which is the point.

The break panel is a loop with a progress bar and a countdown, not a notification:

start = time.time()
while True:
    remaining = max(0.0, seconds - (time.time() - start))
    if remaining <= 0:
        break
    bar = "█" * int(bar_width * (1 - remaining / seconds))
    draw_panel(tip, bar, remaining)
    time.sleep(0.12)

The only way past it is time, or Ctrl+C, and Ctrl+C still restores the terminal and prints your stats.

Where the horror comes from

Assets are searched and downloaded from Wikimedia Commons using the public MediaWiki API, filtered to images, animated GIFs, and WebM video, and cached locally in ~/.cache/haunt/assets. Every file keeps its artist and licence, which python3 haunt.py --credits ghost prints:

ghost
  Apparition by Eugeniu Voinescu.jpg — Ruth Tillman (CC BY-SA 4.0)
  Athenodorus - The Greek Stoic Philosopher ... — Henry Justice Ford (Public domain)
  La bimba dal vestitino rosso.webm — Museo Italiano Dell'Immaginario Folklorico (CC BY-SA 4.0)

Commons rate-limits aggressively, so downloads retry with backoff and refuse anything over 12 MB. If the network is gone, the ghost paints its own scene with Pillow: a gradient night, fog, a silhouette house, glowing windows, a moon, scratch marks. --offline never touches the network.

Why open matters here

This tool is supposed to change a habit, and habits fail when the tool fails. Open pieces are what make it keep working:

  • A local model means no key, no cost, and no data leaving the machine. The whisper is generated by llama3.2:3b through Ollama. I can run it on a plane, and nothing about my terminal or my work goes to a provider.
  • Swappable models. The prompt is the contract, not an SDK. --model takes anything Ollama can serve, from a 1B model on a laptop to something larger.
  • Offline is a first-class mode. If Commons is unreachable, procedural art and curated lines still produce a complete haunting. The health habit does not depend on a service that might disappear.
  • The media is genuinely reusable. Public domain and Creative Commons assets, with attribution preserved and printable, instead of scraped images with unclear provenance.
  • You can read all of it. The renderer, the model call, the break loop: nothing is hidden behind a hosted API, so you can change how the ghost behaves or how long it holds you.

A note on safety

A scare tool has to be careful about being a scare tool. --safe disables the audio and the single inverted-frame flash, and audio is off by default whenever you ask for safe mode. The flash is one slow pulse, not a strobe. The health advice is ordinary workplace ergonomics: 20-20-20, standing, movement, water, blinking, posture, wrists. It is not medical advice, and the ghost is not a doctor. It is just rude enough to make you stand up.

Run it 

git clone https://github.com/karan-2004/haunted-terminal
cd haunted-terminal
python3 -m venv .venv && source .venv/bin/activate
pip install -r requirements.txt
ollama pull llama3.2:3b

python3 haunt.py --demo     # one haunting now, short break
python3 haunt.py            # haunt roughly every 5 to 9 minutes
python3 haunt.py --safe     # no sound, no flash
python3 haunt.py --stats    # how long you stayed away

It needs Python 3.10+, Pillow, requests, numpy, and Ollama. paplay/aplay are optional for the sound; ffmpeg is optional for Commons videos. No login, no API keys, nothing to configure.

MIT licensed. Built during the Hacktoberfest Open-Source AI Challenge Week 4 window, with the model running locally and the lights off.

Here is the session where it was built, if you want to see the messy middle:

Building haunt: a haunted terminal that forces screen breaks
You

lets create a script that uses a opensource lightweight model to fetch the horror screens, gifs and videos and render it randomly in the terminal to scare the user randomly and make them move away from the screen. let the horror scenes educate users to take breaks and be considerate about the health

Agent

Plan: a local open-weight model (Ollama llama3.2:3b) writes the whisper and the health tip, assets come from Wikimedia Commons (public domain / CC), Pillow renders frames as 24-bit colour half-blocks, and every scare ends in a forced calm break with a countdown. Check the machine first.

▸ bash python3 -V; which ollama ffmpeg chafa viu; python3 -c 'import PIL, requests'
Input
$ python3 -V; which ollama ffmpeg chafa viu; python3 -c 'import PIL, requests'
Output
Python 3.13.11; /usr/local/bin/ollama; /usr/bin/paplay; PIL 12.3.0; no ffmpeg, no chafa
▸ bash ollama list
Input
$ ollama list
Output
llama3.2:3b 2.0 GB
▸ bash curl Commons API for haunted/halloween media
Input
$ curl Commons API for haunted/halloween media
Output
Commons API returns jpegs, gifs and webm with license metadata; upload.wikimedia.org rate-limits at 429 without backoff
You

can browserbase screens be rendered via cmd through agent or model

Agent

Yes, over CDP: Page.startScreencast or captureScreenshot frames rendered with a terminal image tool, or fed to a vision model. Live View is web-only. For this project the simpler path is local: Pillow half-block rendering, no browser needed, which also keeps it fully offline.

Agent
▸ write haunted-terminal/haunt.py
Input
haunted-terminal/haunt.py
Output
661-line CLI: Commons asset search + cache with retries, procedural Pillow fallback art, ANSI half-block renderer, Ollama oracle with curated fallback lines, WAV scare synth via numpy + paplay, calm break panel with countdown and breathing prompt, break log and stats
▸ write README.md, LICENSE, requirements.txt, .gitignore
Input
README.md, LICENSE, requirements.txt, .gitignore
Output
MIT license, install and usage docs, safety notes, why-open section
▸ bash python3 -m py_compile haunt.py && COLUMNS=80 LINES=24 python3 haunt.py --demo...
Input
$ python3 -m py_compile haunt.py && COLUMNS=80 LINES=24 python3 haunt.py --demo --offline --no-model --safe --calm 2
Output
renders a procedural scene, prints the calm panel, logs the break, restores the terminal; exit 0
▸ bash build_assets('ghost','skeleton','pumpkin')
Input
$ build_assets('ghost','skeleton','pumpkin')
Output
3 assets per theme downloaded from Wikimedia Commons with CC/PD attribution; 429 handled by retry with backoff
▸ bash COLUMNS=100 LINES=30 python3 haunt.py --demo --safe --no-audio --calm 3
Input
$ COLUMNS=100 LINES=30 python3 haunt.py --demo --safe --no-audio --calm 3
Output
model returned whisper 'your code will consume you, if you don't look up soon' and tip 'stand up, stretch, and take a 5-minute walk outside with some water'
You

lets submit this idea

Agent

Checked the HF26 Week 4 challenge, the DEV account link, and GitHub credentials. Wrote the files, published the repo, and staged the submission post with this session embedded.

title: Chi sono e cos'è ZDOS: Il mio viaggio nella programmazione di sistema e nell'architettura sovrana
description:
✦ Chi Sono

Mi chiamo A$apKali, e sono un'architetta di sistemi indipendente e sviluppatrice software. La mia filosofia di sviluppo affonda le radici in un approccio rigorosamente first-principles: credo fermamente che la vera programmazione significhi costruire ecosistemi zero-dependency da zero, padroneggiando l'hardware e il codice a basso livello senza subire passivamente i vincoli dei framework commerciali.

🚀 Cos'è ZDOS?

ZDOS è un ecosistema di calcolo sovrano, modulare e orientato alle massime prestazioni, progettato per uscire dai paradigmi tradizionali dei sistemi operativi commerciali.

L'architettura di ZDOS non è un semplice fork o un wrapper, ma un sistema costruito con una visione radicale di autonomia:

  1. ZLang Core & ZLB2 Runtime: Un linguaggio di programmazione e un motore di esecuzione proprietario progettati per garantire efficienza, gestione diretta della memoria e flessibilità di basso livello (#![no_std] style).
  2. Architettura Modulare: Dalla gestione dei nodi di rete sicuri all'infrastruttura di compilazione autonoma, ogni componente di ZDOS comunica tramite protocolli leggeri e resilienti.
  3. Infrastruttura Distribuita: Un ecosistema che spazia dai kernel micro-customizzati ai server VPS di produzione, pensato per garantire controllo totale sull'hardware e sul software.

🛠️ La Filosofia del Codice

Scrivere ZDOS significa rifiutare la complessità inutile. Significa scrivere codice che parla direttamente all'hardware, ottimizzare ogni singolo ciclo di clock e creare strumenti di sviluppo potenti e indipendenti.

Se anche voi credete nel codice a basso livello, nell'Open Source senza compromessi e nella sovranità digitale, seguite i nostri repository su GitHub (high-cde) e restate sintonizzati per i prossimi rilasci del kernel e del compilatore ZLang.

L'autonomia non si chiede, si ingegnerizza. ⚡

title: Python on Vercel is now generally available
description:
Python is now a first-class language and runtime on Vercel. Build APIs, full-stack applications, and AI agents with native Python SDKs and a shared development and deployment workflow for your Python backend and JavaScript frontend.

Python framework and runtime support

Vercel handles the infrastructure so you can focus on your application:

  • Automatic framework support: FastAPI, Flask, and Django applications are automatically recognized and configured, with framework-specific support for serving static assets through the Vercel CDN.

  • Native Python runtime and tooling: Vercel runs CPython on Linux and supports uv and pyproject.toml for dependency management.

  • Compute for APIs and workers: Scale request-driven applications with Fluid compute and run long-running pull-based workloads with Vercel Daemons.

Native Python SDKs

Within your application, Python SDKs let you build agents, run untrusted code, and orchestrate durable workflows.

  • Sandbox: Give your application or agent an isolated Linux VM on demand.

  • AI SDK for Python (Beta): Generate or stream model responses and call tools. Get started with uv add ai.

  • Workflow SDK for Python (Beta): Persist execution state and retry failed workflow steps.

  • Queues (Beta): Send and receive messages for background work.

  • Connect: Obtain credentials for calling external APIs.

  • Blob: Upload and retrieve files in object storage.

Use the SDKs individually or combine them in the same Python application.

Your frontend and backend, together

For full-stack applications, Vercel Services allows you to deploy your frontend and backends together in one project, with shared previews and atomic deployments and rollbacks. Within that project, you can view logs by service and connect backends privately through service bindings.

For a frontend in frontend/ and a FastAPI app defined in backend/main.py, add this vercel.toml at the repository root.

Requests under /api/ reach matching FastAPI routes with the path unchanged, while other requests reach the frontend. Run both services locally with vercel dev, then deploy them together from the same repository.

Read the Python documentation to get started.

title: StudyLoop: turn your markdown notes into flashcards that can't lie to you
description:
I keep my notes in markdown. Hundreds of files: RFC summaries, postmortems, the bits of HTTP caching I have to re-learn every time a CDN misbehaves. Writing them is easy. Remembering them is not. Two months later I'm searching my own notes and still getting no-cache and no-store mixed up.

Flashcards fix the remembering part, but making them by hand takes so long that I never kept it up. Asking an LLM to make them is fast, but it's risky. Sometimes the model invents an answer that sounds right and isn't in the notes, and then you memorize something false.

So I built StudyLoop, a small terminal tutor that treats your notes as the only source of truth. It is open source (MIT), pure Python stdlib, and has no runtime dependencies: github.com/bayuh85/studyloop.

The real use case: learning HTTP caching from my own notes

The repo ships examples/http-caching/notes.md, a short set of notes on freshness, Cache-Control, validators, conditional requests and Vary. Here is the loop I actually run:

export ATMOROUTER_API_KEY=...        # only card generation needs a key
python3 -m studyloop add examples/http-caching/notes.md --deck caching
python3 -m studyloop study --deck caching --limit 10
python3 -m studyloop ask "what does no-cache mean" --deck caching

On a live run this morning, add cut the file into 14 passages and the model proposed 32 cards. StudyLoop kept 30 and rejected 2:

passages 14  new 14 · moved 0 · unchanged 0 · removed 0
cards 30 accepted · 2 rejected
  rejected  quote not in passage  484e52b3fc7bd77d  What does the `immutable` Cache-Control extension actually do...
  rejected  quote not in passage  484e52b3fc7bd77d  How does `stale-while-revalidate` work...

Those two rejections show the whole idea working. The model wrote reasonable questions about immutable and stale-while-revalidate, but the passage it was given didn't support its answers. So those cards never got into my deck.

How a card is kept or rejected

Each passage is sent on its own, and the model has to return JSON: front, back, and a quote. A card is stored only if:

  • the quote is a contiguous excerpt of that passage (whitespace may differ, words and order may not),
  • at least half of the content words in back appear in the passage, so a real quote attached to an invented answer still fails,
  • any citation the model names matches the passage's own [file:start-end].

Every card carries its line range, so when you review it you can jump straight to the source.

Passages that survive edits

Each passage id is a SHA-256 over the source path plus the exact passage text. If you insert a line near the top of the file, the line ranges shift but the ids stay the same, so your review history stays put. If you edit a passage, it becomes new work. If you delete one, its cards go too. Running add again only sends passages the model hasn't seen yet, so re-syncing a notes folder costs almost nothing.

Review with SM-2, ask with BM25

study is classic SuperMemo SM-2: ease starts at 2.5 and never goes below 1.3, intervals run 1 day, 6 days, then grow by ease, and an again grade puts the card back in the current session.

ask makes no network call. It ranks passages with Okapi BM25 (k1 = 1.5, b = 0.75; hyphenated directives like max-age count as one token) and answers in your notes' own words:

`no-cache` does not mean "do not store this". A cache may store a no-cache
response, but it must revalidate with the origin before every reuse.
[examples/http-caching/notes.md:37-43]

The answer is never made up, because it's your own sentences with a line citation.

Try it without a key

There's an offline demo server that stands in for the model, and the 46-test suite runs against it:

python3 -m studyloop.demo_server --port 8766
python3 -m studyloop add examples/http-caching/notes.md --deck caching \
  --base-url http://127.0.0.1:8766/v1 --api-key demo

Provider

Card generation uses the standard OpenAI chat-completions request, so --base-url works with any compatible server. By default it points at AtmoRouter, a cheap AI API gateway and OpenRouter alternative: 155 models behind one OpenAI-compatible key, pay per token, at up to 89% below official prices. The default model is cc/claude-sonnet-4-6. Turning a whole notes folder into cards costs about as much as a coffee, and asking questions is free because it runs locally.

Repo: github.com/bayuh85/studyloop. Issues and PRs welcome, especially chunking for other heading styles.
