title: Why Modern Android Apps Need Disposable Inboxes for QA & Anti-Spam Testing in 2026
description:
Why Modern Android Apps Need Disposable Inboxes for QA & Anti-Spam Testing in 2026

Testing authentication and user onboarding flows on mobile is notoriously tricky. Every time you run a test on Android emulator or physical device, you need a clean email address to test account creation, magic links, and OTP codes.

Using real personal emails or even standard alias tricks (user+test@example.com) leads to inbox pollution, carrier rate limits, and linked personal data.

The Core Challenge: Mobile QA and Ephemeral Verification

When testing mobile applications, QA engineers face specific hurdles:

  1. App Switching & Memory Management: When an Android test switches from your app to a web browser to check email, low-memory devices often kill background processes.
  2. Delayed OTP Codes: Many disposable email providers have sluggish update cycles, forcing test scripts to timeout.
  3. Domain Blacklists: Generic disposable domains often get rejected by staging firewalls.

Best Practices for Mobile Registration Testing

  • Use Dedicated Clean MX Domains: Ensure your test addresses use clean domains like @mailfo.site or @mailfo.buzz that maintain high sender reputation and pass SPF/DKIM checks.
  • Offline-First Persistence: Use tools that store received messages in a local database (like SQLite/Room DB), so backgrounding the app never wipes active confirmation tokens.
  • Instant Regex Extraction: Automate verification by pulling 4-to-8 digit OTP codes straight out of the incoming payload.

Developer Utility: Mailfo

For Android engineers, developers, and QA teams looking for frictionless ephemeral email:

  • 📲 Google Play App: Download Mailfo on Google Play
  • 🤖 Telegram Bot: @mailfo_official_bot
  • 🌐 Web Portal: https://mailfo.pages.dev/ & mailfo.xyz

title: GBase Database(GBase 8a) Installation: 4 Ways to Troubleshoot SSH Login Failures
description:
When a distributed GBase Database(GBase 8a) installation stops at the file distribution stage with an error like Fail to login xxx errno:-1 Permission denied (publickey...), the message tells you that SSH authentication failed, but not why.

GBase Database multi-node deployment depends on the DBA user being able to connect to every node and distribute installation files. A single broken SSH connection can interrupt the entire installation.

Here are four layers to check, usually enough to pinpoint the problem within ten minutes.

1. Verify SSH Login Manually

Before changing configuration, test the connection manually from the first node to the target node using the DBA user.

su - gbase
ssh -p 22 172.27.237.164
ssh -v -p 22 172.27.237.164

Two situations help narrow down the cause:

  • Manual login works, but the installation script fails: check the installation configuration.
  • Manual login also fails: investigate the SSH service, network, authentication, or system settings.

Use ssh -v to inspect the authentication process. If publickey appears in the authentication methods but is rejected, focus on SSH key configuration.

2. Check the SSH Port

If the cluster uses a non-default SSH port, make sure sshPort in demo.options matches the actual port.

For example:

sshPort = 2222
dbaUser = gbase
dbaPwd = gbase

A port mismatch can produce the same login failure during GBase Database installation.

3. Check Password Configuration

Special characters in passwords may cause parsing problems in some installation scripts.

In a controlled test environment, you can temporarily use simple test passwords to determine whether password parsing is the cause. Restore the required strong passwords before production deployment.

Check both dbaPwd and rootPwd where applicable, and follow the configuration requirements in your GBase Database version-specific manual.

4. Check SSH Key Permissions

For passwordless SSH authentication, verify that the public keys are correctly configured and that file permissions are not too permissive.

Typical permissions are:

  • .ssh directory: 700
  • authorized_keys file: 600

Check them with:

ls -ld ~/.ssh
ls -l ~/.ssh/authorized_keys

Also verify file ownership and confirm that the correct public key has been copied to every target node. In multi-node environments, it is easy to overlook one machine during key distribution.

Check SSH Logs Before Retrying

If all four checks look correct, inspect the target node's SSH service logs and the GBase Database installation logs. They can provide the exact authentication rejection reason.

One important rule: fix SSH login first, then rerun the installation.

Avoid changing passwords or SSH settings while reinstalling. Otherwise, the failure conditions keep changing, making troubleshooting much harder.

Build an SSH Pre-Installation Checklist

Before starting a multi-node GBase Database deployment, verify these items on every node:

  • Node IP address and SSH port
  • Manual login result using the DBA account
  • Password configuration and special characters
  • SSH key availability, ownership, and permissions

SSH connectivity is the foundation of GBase Database distributed installation. Spending ten minutes verifying every node before file distribution can save much more time troubleshooting a failed deployment.

For SSH port settings and parameter syntax, always refer to the manual for your specific GBase Database version.

title: Masked Erosion: How Acceptance Gates Lose Redundant Safeguards in Self-Improving Agents
description:
arXiv:2610.38392v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Self-improving LLM agents edit their own harness, the prompts and rules around a fixed model, and keep an edit only if an acceptance gate scores it higher on a batch of tasks. Such a gate sees what the harness does under the current model, not what it would still prevent if one safeguard failed. When safeguards overlap, deleting one is masked: the others still block the harm, so the gate decides on task success alone and redundancy erodes unseen. We measure harm for every subset of four written safeguards in two agent environments and run 411 improvement loops under ten gate rules, mostly as controlled deletion experiments, plus three runs of the GEPA optimizer. A deletion behind another working safeguard adds almost no observable harm. A paired significance test blocks deletions that pass by chance but not deletions that genuinely raise task success, and a larger evaluation batch lets it delete cheaper safeguards: at the same cost, 20-task batches kept every harness protected while 40-task batches lost all six. Large harm audits prevent exposure but not the loss of depth, which turns into harm when the harness is reused with a weaker model. GEPA kept every safety rule verbatim, yet two of its three final harnesses misused credentials under a weaker model. A statistical model frozen before the runs predicts where each gate's protection breaks as safeguard cost and batch size change, and freezing safety text or auditing one-layer ablations preserves depth.

title: ElevenLabs on AI Gateway
description:
Vercel and ElevenLabs are partnering to bring 14 ElevenLabs models to AI Gateway. To celebrate the launch, all ElevenLabs models are 50% off on AI Gateway for the first 14 days, through November 9th.

AI Gateway supports six different types of ElevenLabs audio models:

  • Speech to text: Transcribe recordings or caption live audio as people speak.

  • Streaming text to speech: Start playing audio while a language model is still writing its reply, so users don't have to wait for the full answer.

  • Realtime voice agents: Let users talk to your app and listen to it respond out loud in a single live session. Useful for support lines, tutors, and in-app assistants.

  • Music: Describe a track in plain text and get back a finished song or instrumental at the length you need.

  • Sound effects: Generate game and interface sounds, or ambience that loops cleanly, from a short description.

  • Multi-voice dialogue: Voice a whole conversation in one call, with a different voice for each speaker.

All of these audio models are accessible through a single gateway API key. Your app or agent can transcribe what a user says, reason over it with your choice of hundreds of models, then answer in an ElevenLabs voice. You can also create soundtracks with generated music and sound effects.

Every request lands in the same usage, cost, and trace views as your other AI Gateway traffic.

Model types

AI Gateway gives you access to 14 ElevenLabs models, spanning speech to text, realtime voice, and music.

Speech and transcription

Scribe v2 Realtime turns a user's speech into text while they are still talking. A language model of your choice then writes the answer. Eleven Flash v2.5, a low-latency ElevenLabs voice model, reads that answer aloud as it streams in, so the user hears the reply begin before the model finishes writing it.

Because each step is its own model, you can swap the transcription, language, or speech model without touching the rest of the pipeline.

In the example below, a user asks whether they’ll make a connecting flight. The text model combines flight status and gate distance to answer, then the speech model delivers the response.

Realtime voice agents

Eleven Realtime v1 Max and Eleven Realtime v1 Mini run the whole spoken conversation in one model, which suits conversations where users expect natural back-and-forth, like a support call or an in-app assistant. Both models take the user's audio in and speak a reply back over a single WebSocket session, so there's no separate transcription or speech step to wire up.

Eleven Realtime hears “Can I change the delivery address for my order?” and responds “I can help with that. What’s your order number?” over one WebSocket session.

In the browser, connect with the useRealtime hook from @ai-sdk/react, which handles the WebSocket connection, microphone capture, and audio playback. In the hook's sessionConfig, set an ElevenLabs voice ID and turnDetection: { type: 'semantic-vad' }. These models support semantic voice activity detection (VAD) to decide when the user has finished speaking, but they don't support server-vad. The realtime guide walks through the full browser setup.

Music and sound effects

Music v2.5 and Music v2 compose original music from a text description. Name a genre, a mood, or the instruments you want, and the model returns a finished track at the length you ask for, with or without vocals. For more control, you can lay out a song section by section and give each section its own style and length.

Sound Effects v2 works the same way for shorter sounds, such as footsteps, a door slamming, or rain that loops under a game level.

All three models use generateSpeech, with text describing the sound you want instead of words to read aloud. This example requests a 30-second track:

Multi-voice dialogue

Eleven v4, Eleven v4 Turbo, and Eleven v3 perform a script with several speakers in a single request. You assign a voice to each line, and each change of voice starts a new turn. A two-host podcast or a scene with a full cast comes back as one continuous recording, so there are no separate clips to stitch together.

About AI Gateway

AI Gateway provides a unified API for calling models, tracking usage and cost, and configuring retries, failover, and performance optimizations for higher-than-provider uptime. It includes built-in custom reporting, Zero Data Retention support, budgets for API keys, routing rules, and more.

AI Gateway reflects provider pricing with no markup and doesn't charge a platform fee on inference, including on Bring Your Own Key (BYOK) requests.

The AI Gateway audio docs have examples across the ElevenLabs models. Browse all audio models on AI Gateway, and try ElevenLabs at 50% off until November 9th.

title: Node doesn't expand ~, and my tests wrote a folder called ~
description:
The demo data in my app has project paths like ~/code/acme-shop. They're fixtures: meant to look like a real person's machine.

Then a test started a run and wrote project settings, and a directory named ~ appeared inside the package, as apps/desktop/~/code/..., in the repo.

The reason is that ~ is a shell feature. Your shell turns it into your home directory before a program sees it. Node's fs doesn't. Hand it ~/code/acme-shop and it treats ~ as an ordinary folder name, relative to the current directory, and creates it.

What I do now:

  • Any test that starts a run or writes project settings points the project at a temp directory first. I wrote it into the project's contributor notes, because the failure shows up as a stray folder and not as a red test.
  • Paths that are stored or passed between processes are absolute. If a path can come from a human, I expand ~ once, at the edge, with os.homedir().
  • git status after a test run is a cheap check. A directory called ~ is hard to miss once you look.

It doesn't apply if all your paths are built with path.join(os.homedir(), ...) from the start. Mine weren't, because fixtures are written for people to read.

title: Python on Vercel is now generally available
description:
Python on Vercel is now generally available. Build and run Python applications with the frameworks, libraries, and tools you already use.

Vercel automatically detects supported frameworks and configures the build and deployment. Your applications run on Fluid compute, which manages concurrent requests and scales with traffic. Idiomatic Python SDKs let you work with storage, queues, durable workflows, and AI models directly from Python. For full-stack projects, the Python backend and frontend share a workflow for local development, preview deployments, and production releases.

Our goals for Python on Vercel

Ten months ago, we set out to make Vercel the best place to build and run Python applications. We wanted the experience to fit how Python developers already work, with three goals guiding our decisions:

  • Idiomatic Python SDKs. Working with Vercel infrastructure should feel familiar to Python developers, with APIs that use type annotations, async/await, and context managers.

  • A shared workflow for both the frontend and backend. Python applications often include a JavaScript frontend, so developers should be able to run both locally, review them in the same preview deployment, and release or roll them back together.

  • Compatibility with the Python ecosystem. The runtime should use CPython, the standard Python interpreter, on Linux to preserve compatibility with the packages and tools Python developers already rely on.

The first test of those goals is what happens when you deploy a Python application on Vercel: its framework, dependencies, and project structure should guide how it’s built and run.

Deploying Python applications on Vercel

We’ve worked to make Python feel native on Vercel. Vercel reads your project’s dependency files, including those managed by uv, and automatically detects frameworks such as FastAPI, Flask, Django, and FastHTML. Framework defined infrastructure configures builds and request routing, with framework-specific support for serving static assets through the CDN.

For applications with a frontend, Vercel Services brings both parts into one project. Running vercel dev starts them together, and shared previews let you test backend changes with the frontend that uses them.

For long-running workers that pull jobs from queues or databases, Vercel Daemons keeps your containers running with your Python code along with any of its packages, and system dependencies.

Python SDKs for Vercel infrastructure

A Python backend might need to store files, send messages, run durable workflows, or call AI models. We’ve built Python SDKs for these tasks, with APIs that follow the conventions of the language:

These SDKs work alongside your framework and libraries, and the example below shows how they connect within a full-stack application.

Start building with Python on Vercel

Whether you’re starting a new project or deploying existing code, the framework guides cover setup and deployment on Vercel. For a guided full-stack project, the Python on Vercel course walks through building a FastAPI backend and Next.js frontend, then deploying them together with Services.

To show how these pieces work together, I built a collaborative web application to create and browse Python notebooks. It lets people create their own notebooks, publish them for others to browse or fork, and work with an AI assistant to write and run Python code.

The application pairs a Vite frontend with a FastAPI backend and uses PostgreSQL for notebook source and chat history. Services keeps the frontend and backend in one deployment, with the frontend served through the CDN.

Here’s how the main parts connect:

  • Editing and running code: When a signed-in user opens their notebook in the editor, FastAPI creates or reuses a Vercel Sandbox running Jupyter, keeping user code isolated from the application backend. The browser connects directly to Jupyter, while mounted Drives provide the Python dependencies and workspace files.

  • Saving and publishing: The browser periodically sends the current notebook to FastAPI. FastAPI saves the source in PostgreSQL, renders changes as HTML, and uploads the result to Blob, so people can read published notebooks through the CDN without starting a Python kernel.

  • Sharing updates: After publishing a change, FastAPI sends a message through Vercel Queues. Each backend instance with connected browsers receives the notification and sends updated notebook listings over WebSockets, so people see changes without reloading.

  • Assisting with code: The agent uses AI SDK for Python and runs inside Vercel Workflows, which saves execution state and retries failed steps. Chat history stays in PostgreSQL, while notebook editing and execution tools work through the connected browser, which sends results back through FastAPI to resume the workflow.

The source code on GitHub includes the complete application and its deployment configuration. You can use it to explore these integrations or as a starting point for your own Python application.

Investing in the Python community

Last December, the Gel Data team, led by me and Elvis Pranskevichus, joined Vercel to build Python support and continue our open-source work.

At the same time, we announced our sponsorship of the Python Software Foundation and committed to funding one year of Serhiy Storchaka’s CPython maintenance through the foundation. Serhiy has authored over 600 commits to CPython’s main branch so far in 2026.

We also sponsored PyCon US and EuroPython this year, where the team and I met Python developers and heard where they were getting stuck. Those conversations help us figure out what to fix next.

We also published PEP 827, which, if accepted, would add type manipulation features that could help frameworks such as FastAPI offer simpler APIs with less boilerplate and more precise type checking.

What’s next for Python on Vercel

We’re continuing to improve Python SDKs, runtime performance, and development workflows for both people and coding agents. If you run into a deployment issue or find something missing in the Python SDKs, share your feedback in Vercel Community so the team can use it to guide that work.

Resources

  • Deploy an eve agent in Python in one click

title: Personal Knowledge Retrieval in Node.js — Private Listings, Citations, Latency Budgets
description:
Node.js Retrieval Contracts for Personal Knowledge Managers — Private Listings and Latency Budgets

Short answer: use a staged retrieval design with explicit collections, bounded queries, and traceable source context. For a privacy-focused personal knowledge manager that aggregates property listings, treat migration and citation policy as part of the retrieval contract, then put a latency budget around each stage.

That contract is the portable unit. A vector store can change; the answer still needs a listing claim, its source, and a freshness rule. I keep those fields in the application-owned record so moving between engines does not silently remove evidence. The practical payoff is boring and valuable: a reranker or provider can be replaced without rewriting the citation layer.

What does a privacy-focused personal knowledge manager need from retrieval architecture and latency budgets?

Start with claim-sized records rather than arbitrary text chunks. Rent, availability date, pet policy, and address can each be retrieved as a claim, with listing_id, source_url, captured_at, expires_at, city, and lease status beside the text. A metadata filter runs before semantic ranking, so an expired listing cannot win on wording alone.

Use three observable stages: eligibility, bounded retrieval, and citation assembly. Give each stage its own timer and count. If eligibility returns zero rows, report “no eligible evidence”; do not widen the search behind the user’s back. A top-k ceiling of eight is a reasonable starting contract for an interactive answer, but it is a policy choice to validate against representative documents and failure cases such as syndicated duplicates and revised rent.

Small rule. A score without provenance is not grounding.

Keep it measurable.

A Node.js migration seam that keeps the answer layer stable

The example below asks the public discovery surface for the current capability manifest, then keeps the retrieval contract local. Discovery is useful during a migration because the surface is self-describing; the actual ranking and citation policy remain yours. The request uses an environment key, an explicit method, status handling, and bounded retry behavior for rate limits.

type ListingClaim = {
  id: string;
  text: string;
  sourceUrl: string;
  capturedAt: string;
  expiresAt: string;
  city: string;
  leaseStatus: "active" | "leased";
};

type StageTrace = { stage: "eligible" | "ranked" | "cited"; elapsedMs: number; count: number };

async function discoveryWithBackoff(baseUrl: string, key: string): Promise<unknown> {
  for (let attempt = 0; attempt < 4; attempt += 1) {
    const response = await fetch(`${baseUrl}/discovery`, {
      method: "GET",
      headers: { Authorization: `Bearer ${key}` },
    });
    if (response.ok) return response.json();
    if (response.status !== 429) throw new Error(`Discovery failed (${response.status}): ${await response.text()}`);
    const retryAfter = Number(response.headers.get("retry-after"));
    const waitMs = Number.isFinite(retryAfter) ? retryAfter * 1000 : 250 * 2 ** attempt;
    await new Promise((resolve) => setTimeout(resolve, waitMs));
  }
  throw new Error("Discovery rate limit did not clear after retries");
}

export async function retrieve(
  claims: ListingClaim[],
  query: string,
  city: string,
  now = new Date(),
): Promise<{ results: Array<ListingClaim & { score: number }>; trace: StageTrace[] }> {
  const key = process.env.INFRAI_API_KEY;
  if (!key) throw new Error("Set INFRAI_API_KEY");
  const baseUrl = process.env.INFRAI_BASE_URL;
  if (!baseUrl) throw new Error("Set INFRAI_BASE_URL");
  await discoveryWithBackoff(baseUrl, key);

  const trace: StageTrace[] = [];
  const start = performance.now();
  const eligible = claims.filter((claim) => claim.city === city && claim.leaseStatus === "active" && new Date(claim.expiresAt) > now);
  trace.push({ stage: "eligible", elapsedMs: performance.now() - start, count: eligible.length });

  const terms = query.toLowerCase().split(/\s+/).filter(Boolean);
  const ranked = eligible
    .map((claim) => ({ ...claim, score: terms.reduce((score, term) => score + (claim.text.toLowerCase().includes(term) ? 1 : 0), 0) }))
    .filter((claim) => claim.score > 0)
    .sort((a, b) => b.score - a.score)
    .slice(0, 8);
  trace.push({ stage: "ranked", elapsedMs: performance.now() - start, count: ranked.length });

  const results = ranked.filter((claim) => claim.sourceUrl.length > 0);
  trace.push({ stage: "cited", elapsedMs: performance.now() - start, count: results.length });
  return { results, trace };
}

The discovery call is deliberately isolated behind one function. During a provider migration, the rest of the application still receives the same ListingClaim shape. For a write path, add an idempotency key and use the documented vector collection or upsert operation; do not let a retry create duplicate claims. Keep the API key on the server, and never pass it to a source URL used for citation. The migration boundary is intentionally narrow: the adapter can switch from one vector implementation to another while the UI, freshness checks, and citation renderer continue to consume the same claims. That is where most privacy-focused projects gain leverage, because a storage change should not force a second audit of every answer template, logging rule, and deletion path.

How should teams compare vector stores when citations and migration risk matter?

The comparison is about control surfaces, not a universal winner. pgvector keeps retrieval beside existing Postgres rows, which can simplify joins and private metadata. Qdrant offers a dedicated vector service with payload filtering. Weaviate provides a managed hybrid-search surface. Each choice changes the work required to preserve the contract above.

Option Migration and governance fit Citation implication Latency budget concern
pgvector Best when Postgres is already the system of record SQL joins keep source fields close to chunks Shared database load must be bounded
Qdrant Clear boundary for a dedicated retrieval service Payload filters can carry listing metadata A network hop becomes explicit
Weaviate Managed hybrid-search workflow More built-in behavior needs review Platform and network layers add variables
Infrai vector surface One REST contract can sit beside other backend capabilities Consistent interfaces help align collection and answer stages Regional network time still belongs in the budget

Infrai’s relevant advantage here is breadth behind a simple surface: one key, one bill, and one REST API span many backend modules. The concrete benefit is pure HTTP with no SDK to install, so any language or runtime can call the same contract as another capability is added. Its public discovery response exposes capability metadata and runnable examples, which gives a migration checklist a machine-readable starting point. That does not decide where private documents live, and it does not replace measuring your own request path.

Infrai offers one REST API.

Infrai uses one key for everything.

What should the release gate measure before changing a retrieval provider?

Freeze a small evaluation corpus from the real workload: duplicate listing feeds, a missing availability date, a revised rent, and a document past its freshness window. For each query, record claim recall, precision of cited chunks, and the fraction of answers whose citations survive the freshness check. Keep those results per stage. An end-to-end score cannot tell you whether a miss came from filtering, ranking, or citation assembly.

The catch is that this design is not suitable for exhaustive cross-document reasoning over an unbounded corpus in one interactive request. Use an asynchronous workflow or a broader search platform when review requires wide evidence. Stick with pgvector when database locality dominates; choose Qdrant when retrieval isolation is the priority; choose Weaviate when managed hybrid features justify their additional control surface.

Before shipping, verify that every claim has a source and freshness timestamp, every query has an explicit metadata filter and top-k ceiling, each stage emits elapsed time and count, and the renderer refuses uncited claims. Replay the failure corpus after each chunking or embedding change. I’m not sure one fixed budget will fit every vault, so keep the stage limits configurable and publish the assumptions with the evaluation set.

Sources

  • https://arxiv.org/abs/2005.11401
  • https://github.com/pgvector/pgvector
  • https://qdrant.tech/documentation/
  • https://weaviate.io/developers/weaviate

title: Detecting Covert Collusion between AI Agents through Partner-Outsider Positive Listening
description:
arXiv:2610.37849v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: AI agents that share a secret convention can coordinate through messages that look innocent, so a monitor that reads only the messages can miss them. We propose a behavioural test: a partner that uses a code reacts to the exact wording of a message, whereas an uninvolved agent placed in its seat does not. Partner--Outsider Positive Listening (PoPLi) is the difference between the two agents in how much their action changes when the message is reworded with its meaning kept, and it is computed after the fact by replaying logged prompts. In a simulated market with five conditions (no collusion, a joint reward with neutral messages, the same with an openly stated intention, a covert first-letter code, and the code with a stated intention), PoPLi is between 0.48 and 0.59 whenever the code is present (95% intervals all above 0.29) and between -0.10 and -0.01 without it. Message-only monitors did not separate the conditions: one reading the speaker's messages answered "no" in all 50 markets, and one reading every seller's messages flagged 9 of 10 markets with no collusion. PoPLi detects the use of a private channel, not collusion as such, and it cannot detect collusion through incentives alone or codes carried by meaning.

title: React List Keys: Keep Edited Text with the Right Record
description:
You type a note in the first row of a list. Then you sort the list. The note stays in the first row, but that row now shows a different record.

This can happen when a React list uses its array index as a key. The rows look correct until someone edits a field and changes the order.

Why the text ends up in the wrong row

Each editor below stores its text with useState. React uses the key to decide which editor instance belongs to which item.

An index key identifies a position: first row, second row. After sorting, a different record can occupy that position while the editor keeps its previous state. A record ID gives React a way to match the editor to the same record after it moves.

Try the example

Paste this component into a React application's App.jsx. Start with the default stable keys, edit a note, and reverse the list. The note should follow its record.

import React, { useState } from 'react';
const initialDrafts = [
  { id: 'incident-42', title: 'Cache invalidation review', body: 'Check the stale key path.' },
  { id: 'incident-57', title: 'Retry policy review', body: 'Check the backoff limits.' },
];
function DraftEditor({ draft, position, stableKeys }) {
  const [body, setBody] = useState(draft.body);
  return (
    <article aria-label={`Draft at position ${position + 1}`}>
      <h2>{draft.title}</h2>
      <label>
        Reviewer notes for {draft.id}
        <textarea value={body} onChange={event => setBody(event.target.value)} />
      </label>
    </article>
  );
}
export default function ReviewQueue({ stableKeys = true }) {
  const [drafts, setDrafts] = useState(initialDrafts);
  const reverseQueue = () => setDrafts(current => [...current].reverse());
  return (
    <main>
      <p>Key strategy: {stableKeys ? 'draft id' : 'array position'}</p>
      <button type="button" onClick={reverseQueue}>Reverse review order</button>
      {drafts.map((draft, position) => (
        <DraftEditor
          key={stableKeys ? draft.id : position}
          draft={draft}
          position={position}
          stableKeys={stableKeys}
        />
      ))}
    </main>
  );
}

To see the bug, render the component with stableKeys={false}. Edit incident-42 before reversing the list. The first row will now display incident-57 while keeping the text you entered for incident-42.

The important line is:

key={stableKeys ? draft.id : position}

In a real editable list, use a stable value that represents the item among its siblings. Avoid generating a new random key during every render: that gives the component a new identity and resets its state.

What keys do not save

If you remove a row from the tree, its local state is discarded. Bringing it back with the same key does not restore the old text. If edits must survive filtering or navigation, store them in a parent or another persistent store, indexed by record ID.

For a single editor, you might deliberately want to clear the local buffer when the selected record changes. Keying that editor by the selected ID makes that reset explicit. Keep the key on the smallest subtree you intend to reset.

Test the interaction that caused the bug

Edit one record, reorder the list, and check that the edited value still belongs to that record. Checking only the displayed row order misses the problem.

Then remove the edited record and bring it back. Decide whether losing the local text matches your product's requirements. That is a persistence decision as well as a rendering decision.

Read more in React's state identity guide and list key guidance.

title: JSX in React – What and Why?
description:
JSX stands for JavaScript XML.

JSX is a syntax extension used in React that allows us to write HTML-like code inside JavaScript.

In simple words, JSX helps us write UI elements using HTML-like syntax inside JavaScript.

  1. What is JSX? Without JSX, we create UI elements using JavaScript's React.createElement() method.

Without JSX:

import React from "react";

function App() {
  return React.createElement(
    "h1",
    null,
    "Hello World"
  );
}

export default App;

With JSX:

function App() {
  return <h1>Hello World</h1>;
}

export default App;

Both produce the same UI.

Easy to understand
JSX makes React code cleaner and easier to read.

  1. Why do we use JSX? Imagine you are developing an e-commerce website.

You need:

  • Navigation bar
  • Product cards
  • Search bar
  • Add to cart button
  • Footer If you use only JavaScript methods like React.createElement(), creating complex UI structures becomes difficult to read.

JSX makes this easier.

Main advantages:

  1. Easy to write HTML-like UI inside JavaScript.
  2. Makes code readable and maintainable.
  3. Supports JavaScript expressions.
  4. Helps create reusable React components.
  5. Makes dynamic UI development easier.

title: Why Big Tech's $828 Billion Infrastructure Bill Will Hit Your API Invoice
description:
Friday's market session wiped out more than one trillion dollars in market value across the Nasdaq 100. The immediate catalyst was the cumulative disclosure from the third-quarter earnings cycle. Five tech operators, Amazon, Alphabet, Microsoft, Meta, and SpaceX with xAI, are set to deploy eight hundred and twenty-eight billion dollars in capital expenditures in 2026 alone. For context, that annual infrastructure check approaches the entire annual defense budget of the United States.

Wall Street spent twenty years bidding up software multiples because the business model was asset-light. A firm wrote code once, deployed it across shared racks, and collected eighty percent gross margins. Operating cash flows compounded internally, funding share buybacks and dividend growth without needing to tap debt capital markets. That corporate cash flywheel broke in the third quarter. Four of the five major compute spenders recorded negative free cash flow. Amazon burned through forty-two billion dollars in negative free cash flow over the trailing twelve months. Meta swung to negative two billion dollars in quarterly free cash flow and filed plans to raise up to ninety-five billion dollars in equity. Even Microsoft, the lone provider maintaining positive operating free cash flow, issued twenty-five billion dollars in corporate bonds, its first debt offering in more than nine years.

Andy Jassy summarized the corporate defense on Amazon's earnings call by noting that while spreading this capital expenditure over twenty-five years might be convenient, the current technological window does not permit that schedule. That logic explains the competitive terror driving the buildout. When every frontier competitor believes that failing to procure gigawatts today forfeits the next platform layer, spending becomes non-discretionary. What the earnings transcripts omit is the asset-liability duration mismatch created when three-year depreciating assets are funded with long-term capital.

A power utility spends tens of billions of dollars on physical infrastructure, but it does so under a regulated rate base. Regulators grant utilities guaranteed returns on equity in exchange for serving captive rate payers. Silicon Valley hyperscalers are building out utility-scale physical grids, substations, and chilled water loops without any regulatory return guarantee. They bear full merchant risk on silicon accelerators that suffer fifty percent economic obsolescence every eighteen to twenty-four months as next-generation clusters deliver higher FLOPs per watt.

That capital intensity shifts the economic burden directly onto downstream software engineering teams and enterprise buyers. When cloud platforms operated on surplus operating cash flow, they could afford to offer loss-leading inference pricing to acquire developer distribution. Token subsidies made sense as customer acquisition cost while the underlying software margins stayed wide. With four out of five providers posting negative free cash flow and servicing new bond coupons, compute infrastructure must generate cash returns.

The eight hundred and twenty-eight billion dollar buildout guarantees that cloud providers cannot keep API token rates artificially depressed beneath their full depreciation load. If a hyperscaler must service twenty-five billion dollars in corporate debt and justify ninety-five billion dollars in prospective equity dilution, the realized carrying cost of those GPU clusters must clear through monthly compute invoices. Engineering teams building autonomous multi-step agent pipelines under the assumption that compute pricing will decline toward zero will find their operating margins squeezed between rising token consumption and cloud providers who need to service hard capital obligations.

title: Why pack_product.py Renders Both a 1280Ã 720 Cover and a 600Ã 600 Thumbnail
description:
Why pack_product.py Renders Both a 1280×720 Cover and a 600×600 Thumbnail

I built 39 products on a 1 vCPU, 2 GB RAM server before I understood why my uploads kept getting rejected. The zip was fine. The files inside were fine. The problem was the packaging layer, and it took me 300+ pages of research across Adobe, Vecteezy, and Dreamstime to figure out that a single cover image was never going to survive every surface it landed on.

Here is what pack_product.py actually does, why it renders two images instead of one, and what that taught me about packaging digital products.

The failure that started it

My first batches looked clean on my laptop. Then the previews rendered. A 1280×720 JPG that read perfectly as a cover got crushed into a square market thumbnail and the text inside the safe area disappeared behind padding I never saw coming. Meanwhile a square thumbnail, when stretched to a banner slot, looked like a placeholder someone forgot to replace.

I was treating "a cover" as one job. It is two jobs with two different aspect ratios, and no amount of careful composition in a single file solves both at once. So pack_product.py renders both, every pack, with no flag to turn either off.

Why 1280×720 for the cover

The cover is the hero image. It is what the buyer sees first on a product page or a marketplace listing, and it is the one they judge in roughly two seconds. 1280×720 gives you a wide 16:9 canvas where a title, a subtitle, and a hint of the contents can all breathe without fighting for room. That is the surface where a product looks like a product, not a file dump.

The cover is also where most of your text lives, and text is the fragile part. A wide canvas keeps the text comfortably inside the frame, so a title that reads fine at full size does not get clipped when the page compresses the image into a card.

Why 600×600 for the thumbnail

The thumbnail is the survival test. It shows up in grids, search results, category rows, and recommendation strips, often at 100px or less, often cropped to a square. If your cover is your only image, the square crop eats your text or your centered art.

600×600 forces you to design for the grid. You get a square canvas, you place the one element that must read at small size in the middle, and you accept that everything else is decoration. When someone scrolls a wall of thumbnails, your square needs to be legible in a glance. That is a different design problem from the hero cover.

The same bundle, two files, one pass

pack_product.py takes the product name, a subtitle, and a count, zips the files, and writes three files in one run: my-product.zip, my-product-cover.jpg, and my-product-thumb.jpg, into a _system folder next to where you run it. Point it elsewhere with --dir or the PACK_ROOT environment variable. No editing the script, no second pass.

python pack_product.py my-product "My Product" "A short subtitle" 9

That command is the whole packaging step. Pillow renders both images. Nothing else is needed, because this is the only script in the kit that touches a third-party image library. The other heavy lifting in the pipeline runs on the standard library.

The rule I now follow

A zip with a real cover sells; a bare file does not. That one line is why pack_product.py exists and why it refuses to render just one image. The cover earns the click, the thumbnail survives the grid, and they are never the same picture.

If you take one thing from this, make it the two-canvas habit. Build the wide hero and the square grid image as separate deliverables in the same pass, and stop trying to make one file do work it was never designed for.

Where this came from

pack_product.py is one of four standalone scripts in the Pipeline Starter Kit: make_metadata.py builds the exact Adobe 5-column, Vecteezy 4-column, and Dreamstime 15-column CSVs; upload_tracker.py is the ledger that stops re-runs from double-posting; md2pdf.py turns Markdown into a clean PDF for selling docs. The whole kit ran on one process at a time, freed memory between assets with gc.collect(), and measured real peak RSS rather than guessing, all on a single-core 2 GB box with no GPU. Those habits are not optional when the server is that small. They are the reason the pipeline ever finished.

That kit is the packaging layer of the full system: 39 finished products, 856 MB of output, and the research notes behind every header rule. The product is called digital asset factory, and the kit in it is the set of tools that actually packaged the catalogue.

Get digital asset factory

title: Corevia V3: Building a Multi-Runtime, AI-Ready Framework for Modern Applications
description:
Corevia is evolving beyond a traditional PHP framework.

It is being designed as a multi-runtime application framework where PHP can remain the core application layer while Python, JavaScript, React, Dart and Flutter can participate through defined contracts, SDKs and services.

The goal is not to replace every technology with PHP.

The goal is to let different technologies do what they are best at — without turning the application into an integration mess.

What Corevia already focuses on

• Modular Actions, Flows and Events

• Durable workflows with retries, pause/resume and compensation

• Runtime idempotency and failure isolation

• Realtime communication through WebSockets

• PHP ↔ Python interoperability

• Cross-runtime application architecture

• HTTP routing and API development

• Database adapters

• CLI tooling and runtime inspection

• Lightweight PHP 8.2+ core

• Architecture designed for custom web applications, APIs, workers and business systems

Multi-platform direction

Corevia is also being expanded to make frontend and application clients easier to integrate.

The direction includes support and SDK patterns for:

• React — web applications and dashboards

• JavaScript / TypeScript — browser and application clients

• Dart — cross-platform application integrations

• Flutter — mobile, desktop and cross-platform clients

• Python — workers, automation, AI services and specialized processing

Instead of tightly coupling these runtimes, Corevia is moving toward explicit contracts that define how applications communicate with the framework.

AI is also becoming an important part of Corevia

AI support in Corevia is not intended to mean simply adding a chatbot endpoint.

The framework architecture is being designed so AI can participate as another application capability.

That opens the door for things such as:

• Local and hosted LLM integrations

• Python-based AI workers

• AI-powered automation flows

• Background inference jobs

• AI agents operating through controlled application actions

• Retrieval and knowledge systems

• Structured tool execution

• AI-assisted CRM and business workflows

• Chatbots and auto-repliers

• Classification, extraction and summarization services

• Local/private AI deployments

• Multi-model provider adapters

The important part is control.

AI services should interact with the application through defined actions, permissions and contracts rather than receiving unrestricted access to the system.

Corevia V3 — Under Development

V3 has not been publicly released yet.

A significant portion of the roadmap has already been implemented internally, while development is continuing on the remaining architectural pieces.

Current V3 work includes stronger framework/application separation, safer upgrades, starter kits, application foundations, background processing, improved SDKs, AI-oriented capabilities and better developer tooling.

Six major architectural areas remain under active development:

1. Deterministic Module Composition

Making module registration, dependency resolution and boot order predictable and reproducible across environments.

2. Runtime Profiles / Capability Presets

Applications should be able to load only what they need.

For example:

Web

API

CLI

Worker

Realtime

AI

Hybrid

instead of booting every framework capability for every process.

3. Explicit Request & Worker Lifecycle

Clear lifecycle boundaries for:

• HTTP requests

• CLI commands

• background workers

• realtime processes

• long-running services

• AI workers

This becomes especially important when PHP and Python services operate together.

4. Machine-Enforced Architecture Boundaries

Architectural rules should not exist only in documentation.

Corevia should be able to detect and prevent invalid dependencies, module violations and incorrect application structure automatically.

5. Reproducible Build & Configuration Fingerprints

A Corevia application should be able to identify exactly which framework configuration, modules and runtime capabilities produced a particular deployment.

This should make development, staging and production environments easier to compare and reproduce.

6. Cross-Runtime Contract Manifest

One of the most important V3 pieces.

A formal contract layer for:

PHP

Python

JavaScript

React

Dart

Flutter

and future runtimes

The manifest will define things such as:

• available actions

• payload contracts

• capabilities

• runtime requirements

• validation rules

• version compatibility

• remote-service discovery

The objective is to make cross-runtime development predictable rather than relying on loosely documented API agreements.

Corevia V3 is not about adding features just to make the framework larger.

It is about making the framework:

More deterministic.

More modular.

More portable.

More AI-ready.

More cross-platform.

And safer to scale across multiple runtimes.

The underlying philosophy remains simple:

Keep simple applications simple — while giving complex systems room to grow.

PHP #Python #Flutter #React #Dart #ArtificialIntelligence #SoftwareEngineering #OpenSource #Framework

title: How often are spot GPU instances interrupted in practice?
description:
Spot GPU interruptions depend more on the GPU and region than on the cloud: in AWS's own data, 85% of H100 pools lost under 5% of instances in the past month, while roughly half of T4, A10G, L4 and L40S pools lost over 20%. Nodus shows an hourly interruption rate for every interruptible GPU offering and restores a reclaimed run from its last checkpoint, so an interruption costs minutes of work instead of the whole run.

We pulled the numbers below from AWS's public advisor data file on October 30, 2026 and tallied every Linux listing (one instance size in one Region) for each GPU family. The rates move every month; the method to check them yourself does not.

What do the published interruption rates actually measure?

Each cloud publishes a different number, so a "5%" on one is not a "5%" on another. Read the unit before you compare.

Cloud What it publishes Unit and window
Amazon EC2 Spot Instance Advisor band per instance type and Region: under 5%, 5-10%, 10-15%, 15-20%, over 20% Share of capacity reclaimed over the trailing month
Google Compute Engine Historical preemption rate per machine type and zone Daily: preempted Spot VMs divided by all Spot VMs that stopped that day, last 30 days
Azure Virtual Machines Eviction rate per VM size and region, shown in the portal and Resource Graph Chance of eviction within the next hour, based on the last 7 days

Sources: the linked AWS, Google Cloud and Microsoft pages; the AWS trailing-month definition comes from the EC2 Spot team's public AMA. Checked October 30, 2026.

The Google number is the easiest to misread. A rate of 0.50 means half of the Spot VMs that stopped that day were preempted rather than stopped by their owners, not that your VM has a 50% chance of dying. Google's Spot VM docs only say the probability of preemption "is generally low, but might vary from day to day and from zone to zone". Azure's hourly figure is the only one you can plug straight into a run-length calculation.

AWS states that the average interruption frequency across all Regions and instance types "has historically been <5%". Across all 19,353 Linux listings in the data file, 35% sat in the under-5% band and 25% in the over-20% band. GPU instances do not follow the average.

Which spot GPUs get interrupted most on AWS?

The big 8-GPU training instances were the calmest and the small inference GPUs were the busiest. Here is our tally from the advisor data, Linux, all 34 Regions in the file.

Family (GPU) Listings <5% 5-10% 10-15% 15-20% >20% Share <5% Share >20%
p5 (H100) 20 17 1 1 0 1 85% 5%
p5en (H200) 10 8 2 0 0 0 80% 0%
p6-b200 (B200) 3 0 1 2 0 0 0% 0%
p4d (A100 40GB) 13 6 1 1 1 4 46% 31%
p4de (A100 80GB) 6 2 0 1 1 2 33% 33%
g6e (L40S) 72 8 6 9 8 41 11% 57%
g6 (L4) 136 27 15 24 13 57 20% 42%
g5 (A10G) 136 44 6 7 9 70 32% 51%
g4dn (T4) 147 23 13 15 20 76 16% 52%
p3 (V100) 33 0 0 0 0 33 0% 100%

Source: AWS Spot Instance Advisor data file, fetched and tallied by us on October 30, 2026. A listing is one instance size in one Region.


On AWS, the 8-GPU H100 and H200 pools were mostly calm; the single-GPU inference families were mostly in the worst band.

Two cautions keep this honest. First, a band is a monthly share across everyone's instances, so a calm pool can still reclaim yours tomorrow; AWS says the actual rate "will depend on point-in-time available capacity". Second, the B200 pool shows how small samples mislead: three listings, none in the calmest band, which says little about next month. The useful rule is narrower: check the band for the exact instance and Region you plan to use, on the day you launch.

What does an hourly rate mean for a 10-hour run?

Turn the hourly rate into the chance your run sees at least one interruption. If each hour has an independent chance p of eviction, a run of h hours survives untouched with probability (1 - p) to the power h.

For a 10-hour run on Azure-style hourly rates:

  • At 5% per hour, 0.95^10 = 0.60, so a 40% chance of at least one eviction.
  • At 10% per hour, 0.90^10 = 0.35, so a 65% chance.
  • At 20% per hour, 0.80^10 = 0.11, so an 89% chance.

Real evictions cluster when demand spikes, so treat these as rough. The takeaway still holds: on a long run, "low" hourly rates still make an interruption likely. Plan for it rather than hope against it. This is also why a monthly AWS band cannot be converted into an hourly chance; it tells you which pools are calmer, not when your instance will go.

What does an interruption actually cost you?

An interruption costs the work since your last checkpoint plus the time to start again, and nothing else. Whether spot still pays off depends on the discount and on how much work you redo.

Take a 10-hour job on 8 x H100 at the 57% spot saving the advisor listed for p5.48xlarge in us-east-1 on October 30, 2026. Call the on-demand cost 100, so spot hours cost 43% of on-demand. Assume two reclaims and 10 minutes of billed restart time each (pulling the image and loading state). These assumptions are ours, picked to make the math easy to follow.

  • On demand: 10 hours, cost 100.
  • Spot with checkpoints every 30 minutes: each reclaim loses about 20 minutes of work plus the 10-minute restart, so 11 paid hours. Cost 11 x 4.3 = 47.3.
  • Spot with no checkpoints: the first attempt dies after 4 hours, the second after 8, the third finishes in 10, plus two restarts. That is 22.33 paid hours. Cost 22.33 x 4.3 = 96.0.


With two reclaims, checkpoints keep spot at about half the on-demand cost; without them the saving nearly disappears.

The decision rule: spot stays cheaper as long as the redone work is less than d / (1 - d) of the job, where d is the discount. At a 57% discount that is 0.57 / 0.43 = 133% of the job. At a 30% discount it falls to 43%, and a run without checkpoints can blow through that with a single late reclaim.

How do you get interrupted less on spot GPUs?

Pick calm pools on purpose and keep your options wide. These steps come straight from what each cloud publishes.

  1. Check the number for the exact instance and location before you launch: AWS's advisor band, Google's capacityHistory preemption history, or Azure's eviction rate in the portal or Resource Graph (28 trailing days).
  2. Accept several GPU types and Regions. AWS recommends being "as diverse as possible" in instance type and Availability Zone, and Google's managed instance groups pick the machine types with the lowest observed preemption rates when you allow several.
  3. Match checkpoint frequency to the pool. In an over-20% pool, save often enough that a reclaim costs minutes. In a calm pool you can save less often and spend less time writing state.
  4. Use the full notice window. Google lets you set a 120-second preemption notice instead of the default 30 seconds; Azure delivers its eviction event up to 30 seconds ahead on a best-effort basis.

Our spot vs on-demand guide covers each cloud's notice window in detail, and how to resume training after spot preemption shows the save-and-restore code.

How does Nodus handle spot interruptions?

Nodus treats interruption as a number to plan with and a failure to recover from automatically. You see the rate before launch, and a reclaimed run continues on another machine from its last checkpoint.

The rate first. nodus get gpus lists offerings, and the wide view adds startup time and, for interruptible offerings, how often that capacity is taken back per hour. These commands are copied from the GPU guide:

$ nodus get gpus --interruptible
$ nodus get gpus --gpu L4 -o wide        # typical and list rates, startup time and interruption rate

Then the choice. You can leave the spot decision to the scheduler, which uses interruptible capacity only when it is cheaper to finish:

spec:
  resources:
    gpu: {type: [H100, H200], count: 8}
  placement:
    interruptible: Allow          # use interruptible capacity only when it is cheaper to finish
    maxRateUSDPerHour: "30.00"

Then the recovery. Per the attempts and recovery docs, on a reclaim notice Nodus asks your run for an urgent checkpoint and prepares a replacement machine at the same time. The replacement starts only once the old machine is provably gone, and a Checkpointed run restores its latest committed checkpoint, so it loses at most the work since that save. A run gets up to 8 recoveries by default (3 for distributed Jobs), and a preemption after progress never counts toward the no-progress limit.

FAQ

Why can't I see Google's preemption rate for my GPU VM?

Google's capacityHistory data does not cover N1 machine types with attached GPUs, custom machine types or TPUs. For those, you have to measure your own preemptions or test the zone.

Does a "<5%" band mean my AWS spot GPU won't be interrupted?

No. It means a small share of that pool was reclaimed over the last month. Your instance can still be reclaimed at any time, so a long run still needs checkpoints.

Does Nodus account for interruptions when it picks capacity?

Yes. Nodus picks among the GPU types and regions you allow by expected cost to finish. A run whose checkpoints are all empty is planned and priced as if it restarts from scratch. Save real state so interruptible capacity can count as the cheaper way to finish.

Do I pay twice when a machine comes back after a reclaim?

Not on Nodus. If the old machine returns before its replacement starts, the replacement is released, your run continues, and you are not charged for the replacement.

Originally published on the Nodus blog.

title: 5 Trending Open-Source GitHub Repos Worth Bookmarking (October 2026)
description:
October 2026 produced a burst of new open-source projects that climbed GitHub quickly. This is a short, practical tour of five of them. For each repo you get what it does, a realistic use case, the primary language and the star count as of 2026-10-30. These projects are weeks old, so treat them as promising rather than battle-tested.

Gathin23/cleanyourtv

Primary language: Python. Stars: ⭐ 46.5k (as of 2026-10-30).

CleanYourTV strips bloatware from an Android TV or Google TV over Wi-Fi and replaces the ad-heavy home screen with a clean, Apple TV-style launcher. The repo ships a pure-Python ADB client, scripts to apply and undo a debloat list, and a prompt you can hand to a coding assistant. Its README says it can't run on Samsung, LG or Roku sets, and that on Fire TV only the debloat half works.

Practical use case: clean up a relative's TV in an afternoon. Keep the restore script handy, because debloating can break features and restoring is the safety net.

Link: https://github.com/Gathin23/cleanyourtv

deepseek-ai/DeepInfer

Primary language: Python. Stars: ⭐ 24.5k (as of 2026-10-30).

DeepInfer is the inference framework DeepSeek says powers its large-scale production services, released under Apache 2.0. The open release currently supports DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash and focuses on offline inference. It includes batch-invariant inference, which keeps results identical across different batch compositions. Pieces such as a cache system and load balancing across machines are not included, so it isn't a complete serving stack yet.

Practical use case: read the code and docs to learn how a production inference engine is structured, or benchmark it against the stack you run today.

Link: https://github.com/deepseek-ai/DeepInfer

wheresryan22/anatomy

Primary language: JavaScript. Stars: ⭐ 23.0k (as of 2026-10-30).

Anatomy is an MIT-licensed agent skill. You describe a technical idea and your coding agent builds an interactive isometric SVG figure of an invented machine that explains it. It can add WebGL effects, and it installs with a single skills CLI command for agents including Claude Code, Codex and OpenCode.

Practical use case: produce explainer visuals for documentation, a launch post or a teaching session without hand-drawing every part.

Link: https://github.com/wheresryan22/anatomy

storytold/wordcraft

Primary language: Rust. Stars: ⭐ 16.7k (as of 2026-10-30).

WordCraft is a clean-room word processor written in pure Rust with a familiar ribbon workflow, tables, track changes and mail merge. It works with DOCX as well as ODT, RTF, HTML and Markdown, and runs on desktop platforms and in the browser. The project describes itself as alpha, and it exposes a command-line tool and an MCP server for headless document work.

Practical use case: edit documents offline without a cloud account, or script document generation from an agent. Keep backups while it matures.

Link: https://github.com/storytold/wordcraft

tangency-labs/solidcraft

Primary language: Rust. Stars: ⭐ 12.3k (as of 2026-10-30).

SolidCraft is a parametric 3D CAD application in pure Rust. You sketch, constrain and extrude, and the feature timeline rebuilds when you change a parameter. It runs on the desktop and in the browser, reads and writes STEP, IGES and STL among other formats, and includes an MCP server so AI agents can model with it. It is dual-licensed under MIT or Apache-2.0.

Practical use case: design a parametric enclosure for a 3D print, then change a dimension and let the model rebuild.

Link: https://github.com/tangency-labs/solidcraft

How we picked these

Criteria: repositories created in October 2026 that are open source, have a clear purpose, and showed up in verified GitHub data with strong star growth. Each was checked against its own GitHub page. The list is ordered by GitHub stars, using exact counts from the GitHub API as of 2026-10-30. Stars measure attention, not quality or security, so review the code and licence before relying on any of these. I skipped repos with no description or unclear purpose, and others whose purpose raised licensing or legal questions.

title: Industrial VAPT for SCADA: A Practical Security Testing Approach for OT Environments
description:
Industrial networks are becoming more connected to enterprise IT infrastructure, remote maintenance services, and external platforms. This improves visibility and operational efficiency, but it also changes the security assumptions around industrial control systems.

For security engineers working with manufacturing, mining, energy, utilities, and other industrial environments, testing OT infrastructure requires a different approach from testing conventional enterprise networks.

The main challenge is balancing vulnerability discovery with operational continuity.

1. Start With Asset Discovery

Before testing an industrial environment, understand what is connected and how the assets communicate.

Depending on the environment, the scope may include:

  • SCADA servers
  • PLCs and RTUs
  • HMIs
  • Engineering workstations
  • Industrial switches and gateways
  • Supporting databases and services
  • Remote access infrastructure

Asset discovery is especially important when network documentation is incomplete or systems have been introduced over several years.

An accurate inventory helps identify assets that may be exposed through unnecessary connections or undocumented communication paths.

2. Understand the OT and IT Boundary

One of the important areas to review is communication between corporate IT and industrial OT networks.

Look at network segmentation, permitted communication paths, firewall rules, remote administration, vendor connectivity, and access restrictions.

The objective is to determine whether each connection is necessary and appropriately controlled.

Insufficient segmentation can increase the possibility that a compromise in one environment creates additional exposure in another.

3. Separate Vulnerability Assessment From Penetration Testing

These activities are related but have different objectives.

A vulnerability assessment identifies known or observable weaknesses such as:

  • Outdated software and firmware
  • Exposed services
  • Weak authentication
  • Insecure configurations
  • Insufficient segmentation
  • Vulnerable communication services

Penetration testing validates selected weaknesses through controlled testing.

In an OT environment, validation must account for the possibility that certain activities could affect sensitive equipment or physical processes.

4. Review Remote Access and Authentication

Remote access is often necessary for industrial maintenance and troubleshooting. However, external connections require clear boundaries.

Security reviews should examine authentication, authorization, user privileges, monitoring, and restrictions on third-party connectivity.

Shared accounts and excessive privileges can make it harder to establish accountability and control access to sensitive assets.

5. Account for Legacy Technology

Industrial assets may remain in operation for many years. Unlike conventional IT endpoints, they may not support frequent patching or replacement.

Compatibility testing, vendor support, maintenance schedules, and downtime requirements can all affect remediation decisions.

Where immediate patching is not practical, organizations can consider segmentation, access restrictions, monitoring, compensating controls, or planned upgrades.

6. Establish Safe Testing Rules

An industrial VAPT engagement should have clearly documented rules of engagement.

These should cover:

  • Authorized systems and networks
  • Excluded assets
  • Permitted testing techniques
  • Approved testing windows
  • Communication procedures
  • Emergency contacts
  • Conditions that require testing to stop

Operational teams should participate in planning because they understand the behavior and sensitivity of industrial systems.

Where direct testing presents unacceptable risk, passive discovery, configuration reviews, controlled laboratory testing, or representative systems may be appropriate.

7. Prioritize Findings Using Operational Context

Technical severity alone is not enough to determine the priority of an industrial vulnerability.

A useful assessment considers the affected asset, its role in the process, network exposure, exploitability, existing safeguards, and potential operational impact.

A weakness on an isolated supporting system may require a different response from one affecting a highly important industrial asset.

Reports should clearly distinguish confirmed vulnerabilities, potential weaknesses, informational observations, and validated exploitation results.

8. Close the Loop With Remediation and Retesting

The assessment should produce actionable recommendations rather than simply a list of technical findings.

Corrective actions may include patching, configuration changes, stronger authentication, network segmentation, access restrictions, removal of unnecessary services, and compensating controls.

Retesting can help verify whether selected vulnerabilities have been addressed.

Industrial VAPT cannot promise zero vulnerabilities, but it can provide useful evidence for improving security posture and reducing exposure.

Final Thoughts

Industrial cybersecurity is an ongoing engineering responsibility. Asset inventories, network documentation, remote access reviews, change management, and regular security assessments all contribute to a stronger OT security program.

For additional information about structured security assessments, see these VAPT and cybersecurity resources.

title: I Rebuilt a Redis GUI on Tauri. The Installer Is 7.9 MB. Here's What It Cost Me.
description:
I keep three Redis GUIs installed: Another Redis Desktop Manager, TinyRDM, and the official RedisInsight. Two of the three are Electron, and those are the heavy ones: ARDM's Windows installer is 59 MB and it sits at 230 MB RSS on my machine once connected; the official RedisInsight is Electron too — its Windows installer is 110 MB. TinyRDM, which uses the system WebView just like Tauri does (Wails and Go), needs only 13 MB. The gap between those lines is what this post is about: not WebView versus no WebView, but bundling Chromium versus not.

You do not have to take my word for any of it. Installer sizes are straight from each project's GitHub Releases asset list (Windows x64, latest version at the time of writing):

Client Framework Installer (Windows x64) Version
RedisME Tauri (system WebView) 7.9 MB v5.6.0, 2026-10
TinyRDM Wails (system WebView) 13 MB v1.2.7, 2026-03
Another Redis Desktop Manager Electron 59 MB v1.7.4, 2026-08
RedisInsight Electron 110 MB 3.8.0, 2026-07

On a 32 GB machine where Docker and an IDE already claim their share, that is a bill I got tired of paying.

So I wrote RedisME on Tauri instead. This is the honest version of that decision: what I gained, what it cost, and which numbers you should not trust.

First: Electron's bill is not waste

Electron is large because it bundles an entire Chromium and a Node runtime. That is also its best feature:

  • Rendering is identical everywhere. Windows, Ubuntu 18.04, CentOS 7 — same pixels. You never think about the host's WebView version.
  • The ecosystem is mature. Any frontend library, any Node module, works.
  • Debugging is familiar. DevTools is right there.

For commercial software that must look identical on every customer machine, those guarantees are worth 200 MB.

But a Redis GUI does not need them. It runs on your workstation, next to Docker and an IDE — not on a fleet of customer machines that must render identically. Its interface complexity is a fraction of an IDE's.

When consistency is not your core constraint, the size and memory you pay for it is pure cost.

What Tauri actually changes

Tauri inverts the model: do not bundle a browser, use the one the OS already has.

Electron Tauri
Renderer bundled Chromium system WebView (WebView2 / WKWebView / WebKitGTK)
Backend Node.js Rust
Installer (Windows x64) 59 MB (ARDM v1.7.4) · 110 MB (RedisInsight 3.8.0) 7.9 MB (v5.6.0)
Idle RSS 200 MB+ ~100 MB (my machine, one connection)

The installer size is the honest, reproducible win: you are not shipping Chromium, so you do not ship its tens of megabytes. Download the release and check the file size yourself — it is the easiest claim in this article to verify. For the record: the macOS dmg is ~11 MB and the Linux deb ~13 MB. (The Linux AppImage is bigger — it bundles the WebKit libraries so it runs anywhere, which is a different tradeoff.)

I am going to hedge on the memory number, because everyone overstates it. 100 MB is what I measured on Windows, one connection, empty key view. Different OS, different WebView build, larger datasets — all of it moves the number. Do not treat it as a spec sheet.

The difference you feel is cold start. On my machine, double-click to usable is under two seconds — there is no Chromium bootstrap in the way.

What it cost me

This is the part most "Tauri vs Electron" posts skip.

1. Three rendering engines, not one

WebView2 is Chromium. WKWebView is Safari's engine. WebKitGTK is a third thing. The same CSS can behave differently on all three.

Bugs I have personally shipped and fixed because of this: fake-bold and blurry font rendering on Linux (WebKitGTK synthesizes font weights; the fix is a dedicated html[data-platform='linux'] patch with font-synthesis: none and antialiased smoothing — the same workaround Yaak and JetPilot ship), macOS titlebar padding that differs across system versions (new macOS releases have bigger corner radii), and a macOS terminal right-click paste permission error that ended with switching to the Tauri clipboard plugin. None of these are Tauri's fault — they are the direct consequence of "use the system WebView."

If your UI depends on pixel-precise layout and animation, Tauri will eat your schedule in platform adaptation.

2. The build chain is longer

Vue + Element Plus on the front, Rust on the back. Change a line of Rust and you wait for a recompile. Shipping requires the Rust toolchain plus per-platform signing and notarization — macOS notarization in particular is its own afternoon.

For a solo maintainer, the release cadence is partly set by the build pipeline, not just by how fast you code.

3. Linux users must install dependencies

WebKitGTK is not present on every distro. A first run on Linux may mean installing libwebkit2gtk and friends. On Windows, WebView2 is effectively a system component now (bundled on 11, mostly delivered via Edge updates on 10), so it is a non-issue there.

4. Fewer ready-made wheels

In Electron, "show a native file dialog" is one line. In Tauri it is a plugin, and version mismatches are a real failure mode. Small frictions, but they accumulate.

Two UI decisions, and what they cost

Read-only mode deletes the buttons

The alternative is to keep every button and pop a "you are in read-only mode" confirmation. More complete, functionally.

I chose the aggressive version: in read-only mode, every mutating control disappears from the UI. Unlock with the padlock in the top bar.

The reasoning: when you are debugging production, every clickable element is a decision you have to make. "Will clicking this change data?" Removing the buttons removes the question.

The cost is real too: new users take a while to find delete. It is documented, but the muscle memory of "buttons are always there" works against it.

Multiple connections in windows, not tabs

Tabs are more popular and tidier in the taskbar.

I use windows because of one workflow: comparing the same key across two clusters. Two windows sit side by side on two monitors, or split half-and-half. With tabs you switch back and forth and have to remember what the other one showed.

Cost: a messy taskbar. Neither choice is correct — it depends on whether your day is "many operations on one database" or "the same operation across several."

Where this thing is actually differentiated

Three features I would point at, rather than a feature list:

1. Runtime config diff against version defaults. Pull CONFIG GET *, compare against Redis 6/7/8 defaults, highlight the differences. When you are asking "why does this node behave differently from the others," this is the only entry point that works. Cluster config drift is a genuinely nasty failure mode: CONFIG SET applies to one node, a failover happens a year later, and behavior changes.

2. Codecs for non-UTF-8 values, taken past "it decodes". RedisInsight and ARDM both read Java serialization (same library I use), so the difference is the layer after: java.time / records / collections rendered as JSON, per-field codec selection on Hash/List/Set/ZSet, and an external script hook (Python/Node/Java) exposing decode and encode for in-house formats. Your codec logic stays in your repo.

3. Cluster command broadcast and node targeting. In the terminal, CONFIG SET can broadcast to every node or run on one specific node. Cluster operations need both; most clients implement one.

Who should use it, who should not

Good fit: memory-constrained machines, multiple simultaneous connections, internal/production clusters behind SSH tunnels, Java services storing serialized objects, people who care about cold start.

Bad fit: software that must render identically on old customer machines; complex custom UI with heavy animation; single-database CRUD where tabs beat windows; anything needing a Redis module I have not implemented.

That last point deserves emphasis. RedisME has 129 stars. Another Redis Desktop Manager has 34.8K, TinyRDM has 13.1K. On ecosystem maturity, edge-case coverage, and community responsiveness, they are better. That is not modesty, it is a fact you should factor into your choice.

Links

GPL-3.0, fully open source, Windows / macOS / Linux, x64 and arm64.

  • Site: https://www.hepengju.com/en/
  • GitHub: https://github.com/hepengju/redis-me?utm_source=devto&utm_medium=article&utm_campaign=tauri
  • Docs: https://www.hepengju.com/en/guide/intro/about.html

I am not asking anyone to switch. I am pointing out that if "three GUI windows ate my RAM" is a problem you have, a 7.9 MB option now exists.

title: SQL EXISTS vs JOIN: Find Customers Who Have Placed an Order
description:
SQL EXISTS vs JOIN: Find Customers Who Have Placed an Order


Imagine your manager asks you to find all customers who have placed at least one order.

You have two tables. Some customers have placed multiple orders, while others haven't placed any.

How would you write this query?

Let's look at the data.

  1. Sample Tables

customers

cust_id| name| city
101| Amit| Pune
102| Neha| Mumbai
103| Rahul| Pune
104| Priya| Delhi

orders

order_id| cust_id| amount
501| 101| 5000
502| 101| 3000
503| 103| 7000
504| 103| 2000

Notice that Amit and Rahul have placed two orders each. Neha and Priya haven't placed any orders.

  1. Find Customers Who Have Placed an Order

One way to solve this problem is by using the "EXISTS" operator.

SELECT c.cust_id, c.name
FROM customers c
WHERE EXISTS (
SELECT 1
FROM orders o
WHERE o.cust_id = c.cust_id
);

  1. Output

cust_id| name
101| Amit
103| Rahul

Only Amit and Rahul are returned.

  1. How Does EXISTS Work?

The database checks each customer against the orders table.

  • Amit: A matching order exists, so he is included.
  • Neha: No matching order exists, so she is excluded.
  • Rahul: A matching order exists, so he is included.
  • Priya: No matching order exists, so she is excluded.

Even though Amit and Rahul have multiple orders, each customer appears only once.

That's because "EXISTS" checks whether at least one matching record is available. It doesn't return the matching order records.

  1. What Happens If We Use JOIN?

We can also write the query using an INNER JOIN.

SELECT c.cust_id, c.name
FROM customers c
JOIN orders o
ON c.cust_id = o.cust_id;

The result will be:

cust_id| name
101| Amit
101| Amit
103| Rahul
103| Rahul

Why do we get four rows?

Because each matching order produces a row in the JOIN result.

If a customer has 10 orders, that customer can appear 10 times.

We could use "DISTINCT" to remove duplicate customers:

SELECT DISTINCT c.cust_id, c.name
FROM customers c
JOIN orders o
ON c.cust_id = o.cust_id;

This returns the same two customers as the EXISTS query.

  1. EXISTS vs JOIN: Which One Should You Use?

Use "EXISTS" when you only need to check whether a matching record is available.

Use "JOIN" when you need columns from both tables or want to combine related records.

Both approaches are useful. The right choice depends on what information you need from the query.

  1. Want to Learn More About SQL Subqueries?

If you want to understand SQL subqueries better, including "EXISTS", "NOT EXISTS", and "IN", have a look at this practical guide:

"SQL Subqueries Explained with Examples – Sankalan Data Tech" (https://www.sankalandtech.com/Tutorials/sql-plsql-faq-interview/subqueries-solve-queries-sql-faq.html)

It covers useful subquery concepts with practical SQL examples.

You can also explore more SQL and PL/SQL tutorials at "Sankalan Data Tech" (https://www.sankalandtech.com/).

  1. One Question for You

What would happen if Amit placed 10 more orders?

Would he appear 11 times in the output when using "EXISTS"?

Think about it before checking your answer.

Answer: No. Amit would still appear only once.

Follow Sankalan Data Tech for more practical SQL examples, database concepts, and interview challenges.
