title: Backends on Vercel: Python, containers, and Daemons
description:
Last year, we expanded zero-config support for Python and TypeScript backend frameworks. By this summer, developers could deploy their frontend and backend together with Vercel Services and coordinate background work with queues and durable workflows.

Today at Vercel Ship in San Francisco, we are expanding the backend workloads you can run on Vercel. Python on Vercel is now generally available, container support in Vercel Functions enables custom runtimes and system libraries, and we are introducing Vercel Daemons in Public Beta for background workers that pull work and stay running between jobs.

Python is now generally available

You can build your backend in Python with the Vercel infrastructure and development experience you know from your frontend, including local development, previews, and production deployments. Frameworks such as FastAPI, Flask, and Django run on standard CPython with your PyPI dependencies, while Vercel handles framework detection, builds, and scaling.

Already, 150,000 teams run Python backends on Vercel, including engineers at OpenAI, Polymarket, and Exa.

SDKs for Python let you use Vercel products from your application, whether you’re storing files in Vercel Blob, sending background jobs to Vercel Queues, coordinating durable steps with Vercel Workflows, running untrusted code in Vercel Sandbox, or streaming model responses and handling tool calls with the AI SDK for Python.

Delphi, which builds AI digital minds from books and talks, moved its Python backend from AWS ECS to Vercel. With ten engineers and no dedicated infrastructure role, the team ships to production more than 100 times a day and uses Queues to handle background jobs.

Visit the Python knowledge base for framework details and examples.

Applications in any language with containers

The Vercel container runtime lets you deploy applications written in any language, packaged with the OS libraries and executables they need. Since container support entered Public Beta, 5,000 teams have shipped 150,000 container deployments on Vercel.

Containers deploy as Vercel Functions on Fluid compute, scaling with traffic and using Active CPU pricing, which doesn’t charge for idle time spent waiting for API responses, database queries, or LLM inferencing. Vercel Services lets you develop and deploy your backend alongside your frontend, while Vercel CDN serves traffic on your domains, Vercel WAF protects it, logs help you investigate issues, and rollbacks restore earlier deployments.

For example, take a video app that uses a container for background processing, preparing a playback copy and thumbnail for each uploaded clip. This Dockerfile packages the Python processor, its dependencies, and ffmpeg to run with Daemons:

When you deploy through Git or the Vercel CLI, Vercel builds the image and stores it in your Vercel Container Registry. Read our containerized Functions deployment guide to get started.

Background workers with Vercel Daemons

Vercel Daemons lets you deploy containers as continuously running background workers on Fluid compute. You choose the number of instances in each region, and Vercel maintains that capacity by restarting processes when they exit or crash.

Daemons launches with support for pull-based workloads, where your code requests work from another system and processes it as it becomes available. That could mean consuming queue messages or fetching pending jobs from a database.

In our example, Daemons runs the video processor continuously as it pulls jobs from Vercel Queues. In vercel.toml, define the Next.js frontend, route requests to it, and add the processor using Dockerfile:

Follow the Daemons deployment guide to add a background worker to your Vercel project.

Run your backends on Vercel

We’re continuing to invest in backend support so more of your existing application can run on Vercel, using the languages, dependencies, and execution patterns it needs.

title: Too Hard, Too Easy, Just Right: Performance-Driven Challenge Adaptation in Virtual Reality Firefighter Training
description:
arXiv:2610.38117v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Effective firefighter training requires practice under dynamic and stressful emergency conditions, yet real-world live-fire exercises are costly, risky, and difficult to scale. Virtual Reality (VR) offers a safe and controllable alternative, but many existing VR firefighter training systems rely on fixed scenarios or provide limited difficulty adaptation, making it difficult to maintain an appropriate level of challenge for skill development as trainees' performance changes over time. To address this limitation, we present ProACT, a performance-driven adaptive training system that regulates scenario difficulty through closed-loop interactions between trainee performance and simulated fire dynamics. Specifically, ProACT combines a global module that continuously adjusts scene-level fire spread dynamics in real time based on trainee performance with a local module that periodically updates object-level flammability across the environment. Our evaluation shows that ProACT improves both objective training performance and subjective user experience compared with existing adaptive and non-adaptive baselines. We further discuss how adaptive immersive environments can extend beyond firefighting to broader training domains.

title: Implementing 2026 Email Event Notifications in Node.js with Reversible Code
description:
A media notification service should treat delivery as a replaceable boundary: accept an event, send the message, poll delivery events, and suppress recipients after a confirmed bounce. The useful implementation detail is the small contract around the provider, because that is what lets an on-call engineer move from one delivery system to another without rewriting the publication pipeline.

Short answer: put one adapter in front of the email API, make every send idempotent, persist the provider message ID and recipient state, and poll /v1/email/event/list for status changes. Send with an HTTP POST to /v1/email/send using fields such as to, subject, and body. For a media team, DNS record setup and mail delivery can use the same base URL and API key, which reduces integration plumbing; the application still owns bounce policy, suppression decisions, and migration tests.

For this workflow, Infrai fits the shared DNS-to-email boundary when the team wants one key and one REST API rather than another SDK surface. Its public discovery endpoint exposes request schemas without a key, and documented capabilities include runnable examples in 10 languages; that makes an adapter easier to inspect before a migration. The limitation is important: it does not provide webhook event push, hosted email OTP, or SMTP relay, so a mail specialist remains the better boundary for those requirements.

The page that fires too late

The page arrives after the damage: a daily digest worker reports an exhausted retry budget, while delivery logs show repeated attempts to an address that has already bounced. The on-call view is usually a message ID, a recipient, and a provider status. It is not a safe suppression decision yet.

Work backward. The earlier signal is a delivery event, and the useful state transition is active -> suppressed for that recipient. Store the event ID or a stable fingerprint, the recipient, the provider message ID, the event kind, and the time observed. A polling worker can fetch events, apply the transition idempotently, and leave an audit record. Two workers may see the same event. That is normal.

The instrumentation change is small: count email_events_polled, email_bounce_candidates, recipient_suppression_writes, and notification_retries; alert on the age of the oldest unprocessed event, not a single failed send. A threshold that is too low pages the team during a provider delay. A threshold that is too high sends another issue to a bad address. On the 2026-10-31 capability snapshot, the platform convention documents a 24-hour default deduplication window, which is a useful boundary for deciding how long to retain retry keys.

The retry policy is measurable.

The trap is treating a provider event as an instruction instead of evidence. A bounce event can be polled twice, arrive after a retry was queued, or be observed by two workers during a deploy. The durable inbox needs a uniqueness rule before the worker starts changing recipient state. I would key it by provider message ID plus event fingerprint, then make the suppression write conditional on the current recipient version. That gives a late event a defined result: it can record an audit fact without silently undoing a newer operator decision. The same boundary also makes a migration test possible. Feed a captured normalized event into the old and new adapters, compare the state transition, and keep the provider-specific payload out of the application fixture. This is slower than wiring a callback directly to a mailing library, but it is the part that protects a publication schedule when the provider changes.

How should Node.js implement email event notifications with replaceable code?

Keep the application interface narrower than any vendor API. Mine would expose SendDigest, PollEvents, and SuppressRecipient. The first accepts a recipient, subject, body, and application idempotency key. It returns an internal delivery ID, not a provider-specific response object. The second normalizes provider events into delivered, bounced, or unknown. The third is a state transition with an audit reason.

Polling is less immediate than a webhook, but it keeps the worker model uniform and makes replay straightforward. This service has no webhook event push, so a design promising real-time multi-channel orchestration would overstate the boundary. Email scheduled sends also have no cancel route. Do not expose cancellation unless your own system can define what cancellation means.

A retry must carry the same client-supplied idempotency key. I keep that key with the notification record and reuse it after a timeout. Otherwise a network failure between the provider and the worker can turn one editorial alert into two emails. That defect looks intermittent in a dashboard and becomes obvious to recipients.

Can DNS setup and mail delivery share one migration seam?

Yes, if the team accepts one provider boundary for both capabilities. The DNS record operation and email send can use https://api.infrai.cc/v1 and the same Authorization: Bearer $INFRAI_API_KEY header. SPF and DKIM setup then is not a copy-paste exercise between two credential stores that nobody re-checks after a key rotation. The shared boundary is useful; it is not a guarantee that DNS propagation or sender policy is correct. Verify the records separately.

This Go example keeps the handoff visible. It creates a DNS record, then places the returned response bytes into an internal notification body and sends that notice through the email route. The adapter checks statuses, honors Retry-After for 429 responses, and sends an idempotency key on both writes. In production, persist the DNS response and send record rather than relying on an in-memory chain.

package main

import (
    "bytes"
    "context"
    "fmt"
    "io"
    "net/http"
    "os"
    "strconv"
    "strings"
    "time"
)

const baseURL = "https://api.infrai.cc/v1"

func postJSON(ctx context.Context, key, path, idem, payload string) ([]byte, error) {
    for attempt := 0; attempt < 4; attempt++ {
        req, err := http.NewRequestWithContext(ctx, http.MethodPost, "https://api.infrai.cc/v1"+path, bytes.NewBufferString(payload))
        if err != nil { return nil, err }
        req.Header.Set("Authorization", "Bearer "+key)
        req.Header.Set("Content-Type", "application/json")
        req.Header.Set("Idempotency-Key", idem)
        resp, err := http.DefaultClient.Do(req)
        if err != nil { return nil, err }
        body, readErr := io.ReadAll(resp.Body)
        resp.Body.Close()
        if readErr != nil { return nil, readErr }
        if resp.StatusCode == http.StatusTooManyRequests {
            delay := time.Duration(1<<attempt) * time.Second
            if seconds, e := strconv.Atoi(resp.Header.Get("Retry-After")); e == nil && seconds > 0 { delay = time.Duration(seconds) * time.Second }
            time.Sleep(delay)
            continue
        }
        if resp.StatusCode < 200 || resp.StatusCode >= 300 { return nil, fmt.Errorf("%s returned %s: %s", path, resp.Status, strings.TrimSpace(string(body))) }
        return body, nil
    }
    return nil, fmt.Errorf("%s remained rate limited after retries", path)
}

func main() {
    key := os.Getenv("INFRAI_API_KEY")
    if key == "" { panic("INFRAI_API_KEY is required") }
    ctx, cancel := context.WithTimeout(context.Background(), 30*time.Second)
    defer cancel()
    dnsResponse, err := postJSON(ctx, key, "/v1/dns/record/create", "media-dns-2026-10-31", `{"domain":"news.example","name":"news.example","type":"TXT","value":"v=spf1 include:sender.example ~all"}`)
    if err != nil { panic(err) }
    body := "DNS record operation response for audit: " + string(dnsResponse)
    payload := `{"to":"deliverability@example.net","subject":"Media mail DNS change","body":` + strconv.Quote(body) + `}`
    if _, err := postJSON(ctx, key, "/v1/email/send", "media-dns-notice-2026-10-31", payload); err != nil { panic(err) }
}

The example is operational rather than a full sending library. Validate the record payload against the discovered DNS schema before production use, and map provider response fields into the internal delivery ID. The invariant is the point: one key, one base URL, two capabilities, and no provider response leaking into the rest of the application.

How do real alternatives change the integration work?

AWS SES is a strong choice when the organization already operates heavily in AWS and wants mail controls near its existing identity and regional setup. It still leaves DNS ownership, event ingestion, suppression storage, and the adapter contract to the application. Resend has a focused developer surface and suits a product team wanting a mail-only integration with a compact API. SendGrid is a mature specialist option with broad email tooling, but its account model and event lifecycle become another provider-specific boundary to normalize.

Option Integration shape Best fit Main limitation
Infrai REST for DNS and email, one key A small adapter spanning backend capabilities No webhook push, SMTP relay, or hosted email OTP
AWS SES AWS mail service plus application-owned event handling Teams already standardized on AWS identity and operations DNS, suppression policy, and normalization remain application work
Resend Mail-focused API A focused product mail integration Separate DNS and provider boundary when the stack grows
SendGrid Specialist email platform and event tooling Teams needing deeper mail-specific controls Another provider-specific lifecycle to normalize

The separate-stack comparison is concrete: Route 53 plus SES or Cloudflare plus Resend means two signups, two credential sets, two audit locations, and glue code passing a verified domain from one system into the other. With one REST boundary, DNS and email use one key and one billing surface. The cost is also concrete: one provider becomes a shared trust and outage surface for both functions.

Infrai is worth trying for a media team that wants the DNS-to-email handoff behind one key and will keep its own normalized delivery adapter. Its public discovery surface describes request schemas and runnable examples, and its idempotency convention gives write retries a defined place to live. Those facts reduce integration and migration work, but they do not remove bounce policy ownership. A mail specialist is better when you need webhook delivery, hosted email OTP, SMTP relay, or deeper email-specific controls; those are outside this boundary.

I would make the decision with three tests before moving a production digest: can the adapter replay a send without a duplicate, can a polled bounce suppress the next send exactly once, and can the stored internal record be replayed against a second provider? If any answer is no, the vendor choice is not reversible yet.

A small migration runbook

Store the application event independently of the provider message ID. Record the request hash and idempotency key. Poll events into a durable inbox and acknowledge them only after the suppression transition commits. Run a shadow comparison for a representative publication window: compare normalized statuses, not raw vendor names. Switch new sends behind a feature flag while preserving the old event reader until its pending window is empty.

Do not use a domestic compliance conclusion merely because a DNS record verified. The listed domestic email vendor remains pending, and SPF is a policy mechanism, not a compliance certification. If this service later adds SMS, geographical spend controls still belong in the business layer.

If this boundary fits the system, start with the Infrai discovery and API documentation and pin discovered schemas in adapter tests.

Further reading

  • RFC 7208: Sender Policy Framework
  • RFC 6376: DomainKeys Identified Mail
  • AWS SES event publishing
  • Resend documentation
  • Twilio SendGrid Event Webhook
  • Cloudflare DNS API
  • Infrai discovery is linked above; use the live API documentation for current schemas.

title: SCOPE: Selective Critical-Step On-Policy Self-Distillation for Agentic Reinforcement Learning
description:
arXiv:2610.38391v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Outcome-based reinforcement learning provides coarse supervision for long-horizon LLM agents: failed trajectories may contain correct steps, while successful trajectories can contain errors. Trajectory-level skills can also shift teacher preferences at unrelated steps, introducing off-target distillation signals. We introduce SCOPE, a framework for Selective Critical-Step On-Policy Self-Distillation. After a supervised warm-up, the policy analyzes its own trajectories, generates step-specific hindsight skills, and distills their guidance only at selected error steps. A bounded signed teacher-student coefficient stabilizes auxiliary updates while preserving positive reinforcement and negative correction. A success-relative pairwise length reward further encourages efficient task completion. Experiments on ALFWorld and WebShop demonstrate consistent improvements across multiple model backbones. With Qwen2.5-3B, SCOPE achieves 97.7% success on ALFWorld and 85.2% on WebShop, outperforming SEED by 5.9 and 6.3 percentage points, respectively. On unseen ALFWorld tasks, SCOPE reaches 89.6% success, improving over GRPO by 23.2 percentage points with 46.7% fewer interactions. Scaling to Qwen3-32B, SCOPE achieves 99.2% success on seen ALFWorld tasks and 94.0% on unseen tasks.

title: Understanding Large Language Models as Numerical Optimizers
description:
arXiv:2610.37932v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have emerged as potential tools for numerical optimization. Despite promising results, their intrinsic optimization capabilities and limitations remain poorly understood, particularly in high dimensions. This paper investigates the ability of LLMs to exploit mathematical problem structures and generate feasible, near-optimal solutions. We develop an evaluation framework that distinguishes solution quality from execution failures, including numerical inaccuracies, constraint violations, and output-format errors. Using representative problems from convex optimization, fractional programming, and constrained projection, we assess LLM performance against deterministic reference solvers across different dimensions. Our results reveal that LLMs can capture useful optimization structures and produce near-optimal solutions, even when their outputs fail to satisfy numerical or formatting requirements. However, reliability deteriorates with increasing problem dimension and depends strongly on the underlying optimization structure. To further investigate the limitations, we deploy an iterative refinement mechanism that provides targeted feedback on feasibility and solution quality. The results demonstrate that iterative refinement substantially improves reliability and extends the range of problem dimensions over which LLMs produce valid solutions. Nevertheless, persistent numerical and structural errors limit their applicability as standalone optimizers. These findings provide insights into the capacity and limits of LLM-based optimization and motivate hybrid approaches that combine LLM reasoning with deterministic numerical verification.

title: Why Scaling Kafka Consumers Is Harder Than Just Adding Pods
description:
Picture this: Traffic to your order processing service suddenly spikes 10x during a flash sale. Unprocessed events pile up, and your Kafka consumer lag metrics shoot through the roof.

The instinctual reaction?
“Scale up the Kubernetes pods!” or “Bump concurrency in the Spring config!”

Ten minutes later, the lag is still climbing, half your pods are sitting completely idle, and a subtle thread starvation bug is quietly preventing several partitions from being read at all.

Scaling Kafka consumers isn’t like scaling a stateless REST API. Because Kafka decouples producers and consumers using partitioned commit logs, scaling requires aligning topic topology, JVM thread pools, batch error isolation, and event-driven autoscaling.

Here are the 4 common traps engineers run into when scaling Kafka consumers, and how to fix them.

1. The 1:1 Partition Rule (Your Hard Concurrency Ceiling)

In standard message queues like RabbitMQ or SQS, 50 workers can pull from a single queue simultaneously. Kafka doesn't work that way.

The Golden Law: Within a single consumer group, a partition can be consumed by at most one consumer thread at any given time.

Maximum Active Consumers = Total Topic Partitions

If your topic has 30 partitions and you spin up 40 consumer instances:

  • 30 consumers actively read from 1 partition each.
  • 10 consumers sit completely idle as expensive hot standbys—burning memory and sending network heartbeats without processing a single message. 
Topic: orders-topic (30 Partitions)
  [Partition 00] ──> Worker 0 (Active)
  [Partition 01] ──> Worker 1 (Active)
   ...
  [Partition 29] ──> Worker 29 (Active)
                     Worker 30 (IDLE STANDBY)
                     Worker 39 (IDLE STANDBY)

The Lesson: You cannot scale past your partition count. If normal traffic requires 4 threads but holiday spikes require 32, provision the topic with 32+ partitions on day one.

Adding partitions to a live keyed topic breaks order hashing (MurmurHash2(key) % numPartitions), causing related customer events to route to different partitions and corrupting chronological order.

2. The Spring Kafka Concurrency Trap: One Thread = One Client

The native Java KafkaConsumer is strictly single-threaded. If two threads call methods on the same consumer instance concurrently, it throws an immediate ConcurrentModificationException.

To give you multi-threaded concurrency, frameworks like Spring for Kafka use an explicit model:

@KafkaListener(
    topics = "orders-topic", 
    groupId = "fulfillment-group", 
    concurrency = "4"
)
public void handleOrder(String message) {
    // Process message...
}

When you set concurrency = "4", Spring doesn’t share a consumer across 4 threads. It:

  1. Instantiates 4 completely separate KafkaConsumer instances.
  2. Assigns each instance its own dedicated thread running an infinite poll() loop.

The Executor Sizing Formula

Because every single unit of concurrency permanently consumes a thread for its blocking poll() loop, your thread pool’s corePoolSize must be greater than or equal to the sum of concurrency across all active listeners:

corePoolSize >= Sum of concurrency across all active listeners

What happens if you violate this?

If you set concurrency = "8" on your listener but leave your ThreadPoolTaskExecutor at corePoolSize = 4, only the first 4 consumer instances acquire a thread. The remaining 4 instances block forever waiting for a thread that will never be released. Half your topic's partitions will silently sit unconsumed!

3. High-Throughput Batching: The Poison-Pill Problem

Processing records one by one wastes throughput on individual database round-trips. Batch listeners solve this by pulling lists of messages (e.g. 500 records per poll cycle) for bulk persistence (like Spring Data's repository.saveAll()).

The catch: What happens when record #147 fails?

If you catch and log the error, you risk data loss. If you fail the whole batch, records 0–146 are reprocessed on retry (risking duplicate writes), or the loop crashes repeatedly on the same poison pill.

Spring provides a clean pattern using BatchListenerFailedException:

@Component
public class BatchOrderListener {

    @KafkaListener(
        topics = "orders-topic", 
        containerFactory = "batchKafkaListenerContainerFactory",
        concurrency = "4"
    )
    public void consumeBatch(List<ConsumerRecord<String, String>> records) {
        for (int i = 0; i < records.size(); i++) {
            ConsumerRecord<String, String> record = records.get(i);
            try {
                processSingleOrder(record.value());
            } catch (Exception e) {
                // Pinpoints the exact index of the failure!
                throw new BatchListenerFailedException("Failed at index " + i, e, i);
            }
        }
    }
}

By passing the loop index i, Spring:

  1. Commits offsets for records 0 through i - 1 (safely acknowledging what succeeded).
  2. Retries record i with backoff.
  3. Routes record i to a Dead Letter Topic (DLT) if retries expire.
  4. Resumes processing the remaining records i + 1 through 499 in the partition.

4. Don’t Scale on CPU — Scale on Lag with KEDA

Standard Kubernetes Horizontal Pod Autoscalers (HPA) scale pods based on CPU or memory utilization.

For Kafka consumers, CPU is an ineffective scaling metric. A consumer waiting on downstream database socket responses or network I/O might sit at 15% CPU while its consumer lag climbs into the hundreds of thousands.

The production standard is KEDA (Kubernetes Event-driven Autoscaling), which queries Kafka broker metrics directly:

apiVersion: keda.sh/v1alpha1
kind: ScaledObject
metadata:
  name: kafka-consumer-autoscaler
spec:
  scaleTargetRef:
    name: order-consumer-deployment
  minReplicaCount: 2
  maxReplicaCount: 8 # Constraint: (maxReplicaCount × concurrency) <= partitions
  triggers:
  - type: kafka
    metadata:
      bootstrapServers: broker1.company.com:9092
      consumerGroup: fulfillment-group
      topic: orders-topic
      lagThreshold: "1000" # Adds pods when lag exceeds 1,000 records

⚠️ The Autoscaling Guardrail: Always ensure that maxReplicaCount × container.concurrency ≤ topic.partitions. Any pod provisioned beyond this boundary will join the group, receive 0 partitions, and consume cloud spend without doing any work.

Quick Production Checklist

  • [x] Size partitions for peak load, not average traffic (Pods × Concurrency).
  • [x] Match thread pools to total concurrency: corePoolSize ≥ sum(concurrency).
  • [x] Use batching with index-aware error handling (BatchListenerFailedException) to isolate bad payloads without blocking partitions.
  • [x] Separate mission-critical consumers into dedicated microservices so an out-of-memory error in analytics doesn’t take down payment processing.
  • [x] Scale Kubernetes workloads using KEDA lag metrics, not raw CPU.

Read the Full Deep Dive

This article is a condensed walkthrough. If you want the full, in-depth architectural breakdown—including:

  • Monolithic vs. dedicated microservice worker deployment topologies
  • Complete Spring Boot @Configuration beans for batch listeners and dead letter publishers
  • Cooperative Sticky Rebalance protocol internals and memory bounds

Check out the full guide on Thelp:

👉 Mastering Kafka Consumer Architecture: Scaling, Concurrency & Deployment Topologies

title: WordPress vs Laravel vs React for a Lahore business site: pick by the job, not the trend
description:
Developers argue about stacks. Business owners pay for the wrong one. Here is the practical split for a Lahore SME site. WordPress with a builder like Elementor gets a brochure, blog or WooCommerce store live fast, and a non-technical team can edit it. Its cost is maintenance: plugins, updates and page speed need discipline, or the site slows down exactly when ads send it traffic. Laravel is the right call when the site is really an application — custom booking, a customer dashboard, inventory, or a checkout that has to sync with Daraz. You pay more up front and you need a developer to maintain it, but you stop fighting a CMS to do things it was never built for. React fits when the interface itself is the product: live filtering, search-as-you-type, or a real-time dashboard. For a plain marketing site it is usually overkill, and it adds SEO work if server rendering is not handled.

Whichever stack you pick, build the SEO groundwork in from day one — site architecture, on-page structure and ad landing pages aligned, rather than bolted on after launch. That is the part a specialist seo company in lahore should be able to explain in plain terms: technical SEO, on-page work, content, and local visibility, before a single rupee goes to ads. Choose the stack that your team can maintain in six months, not the one that looks most impressive in a demo.

title: The best workflow engine is a programming language
description:
The idea of orchestrating long-running, stateful logic on top of unreliable, stateless infrastructure isn't new. We've had message queues, job runners, microservice choreographies, and full-blown workflow engines for a long time. What we never had was a version of it that felt good to write.

I'd spent about six months working on a fork of Temporal, mostly on weekends, trying to turn it into a serverless answer with DX that felt more Vercel-native. Eventually it dawned on me that to ship that experience, I'd need to own the execution environment too. So I dropped the fork, joined Vercel, and started hacking on a new framework from scratch alongside Nathan Rajlich.

Code is already a DAG

A workflow is a DAG, a directed acyclic graph. Before Temporal (and Cadence before it), nearly every workflow framework made you draw that DAG by hand. Apache Airflow is the canonical example. You describe your pipeline as an explicit graph of tasks and dependencies, and your actual logic gets buried inside the nodes."

That always felt backwards to me. We already have a tool for expressing "do this, then that, and these in parallel, and branch here." It's called a programming language. An abstract syntax tree is a DAG. Software itself is a DAG.

I knew that in the abstract, but it didn't truly hit me until I saw Temporal, where you write what looks like normal sequential code and the engine makes it durable underneath. It was the dream all along.

What running Temporal taught me

Temporal is great once your infrastructure exists. I was starting from scratch, and setting it up meant:

  • Standing up Temporal Cloud (or self-hosting the server: Frontend, History, Matching, and Worker services, plus a Cassandra/Postgres/MySQL backend and sharding).

  • Running your own worker fleet: Temporal never executes your code. Your workers poll the server and run your workflows and activities. In practice that's a Kubernetes cluster you own.

  • Wiring it all together: task queues, activity registration, client config.

  • Managing the workers yourself: scaling, uptime, restarts, and the build-and-deploy pipeline for the worker processes.

  • Setting up encryption: workers talk to the control plane over the internet, so you're configuring mutual TLS and a data converter to encrypt payloads before they leave your environment.

Once all of that was in place, the workflow dream mostly became real. But I wanted something easy to start that could still scale as my project grew into production.

Versioning in-flight workflows

Beyond owning the worker build-and-deploy process myself, there was a harder problem. If I changed my workflow code while runs were still in flight, I was kind of stuck. There were no longer any workers running the old, correct version of that code. Replay would hit my new code with an old event history and break on a non-determinism error.

The official answer is the patching API (patched() / GetVersion). You branch your code on a change ID and march it through a multi-stage deprecate-then-remove lifecycle as old runs age out of retention. It works, but it means evolving workflow code very carefully. Over enough changes, the workflow code rots into a thicket of version flags.

I couldn't explain Temporal signals

Whenever I tried to show running Temporal demos to friends, signals / queries / updates turned into the single most confusing part. They're three separate primitives for getting data in and out of a running workflow, each with its own rules. Queries can't block, signals are fire-and-forget and get buffered, and you have to know when to reach for which. The concepts did land but it wasn't very intuitive. To me, that was a DX smell. If I can't explain the human-in-the-loop primitive without a whiteboard, it's too complicated. That's why Workflow SDK replaces all three with a single primitive, the hook.

What Workflow SDK looks like today

With Workflow SDK, you write one file of normal code. "use workflow" marks an orchestrator; "use step" marks a unit of side-effecting work. In between it's just await, try/catch, Promise.all, loops, and conditionals.

A few things fall out of that one file:

  • No DAG file: The compiler reads the directives and splits the code into workflow and client/step bundles. The graph is your control flow.

  • Retries: Uncaught errors retry by default. Throw new FatalError(...) to stop. Throw new RetryableError(..., { retryAfter }) for custom backoff. Set fn.maxRetries = n to tune.

  • Ad-hoc webhooks: const webhook = createWebhook() creates a real, callable URL inside a running workflow, in a single line. The run parks until someone hits it, with no route or handler.

  • Hooks: Webhooks are sugar over a more general primitive. Create a hook with createHook<T>(), await it, and the data someone sends is what comes back. This one concept replaces signals, queries and updates

Here's an ad-hoc webhook end to end. An approval that can pause for seconds or for weeks, with nothing extra to deploy.

A library, not a platform

Traditional engines make you bring infrastructure to the framework. Workflow SDK brings the framework to infrastructure you already have.

DBOS had the right idea

While I was working out how to actually build this, I studied every workflow engine I could find. The one that stood out was DBOS, an open-source durable execution library that runs almost entirely client-side. The only thing its server needs is Postgres.

Workflow SDK adopts that shape. There's no bespoke orchestrator to self-host or pay for, and no new stateful system to operate. The only infrastructure it needs is infrastructure you already run: your app, a database, a queue. All the heavy lifting happens in the library.

The backend is swappable

Workflow SDK pushes the idea past one database. The whole thing is a spec, a way of writing workflows, steps, and hooks that any infrastructure can back. You mix and match the substrate to fit your stack:

  • Redis / Kafka / etc. for your streams

  • Postgres / Cassandra / the file system / Turso / Durable Objects / etc. for durability

  • Vercel Queues / SQS / Cloudflare Queues / etc. for your queue

The runtime only ever talks to a single interface, the World, which covers storage, queuing, auth, and streaming. Swapping any layer never touches your workflow code.

In fact, we maintain a first-party Postgres world inspired by DBOS, using Postgres for durability, queueing, and streaming. And in every world, there's no worker fleet and no control plane. A framework integration exposes two plain HTTP endpoints that deploy like the rest of your app.

Even the Vercel backend is "just" a CRUD API

The Vercel Workflow Server, the thing that backs workflows on Vercel, is stateless and does no compute or orchestration at all. It's just like the Postgres world, but extended with Vercel's authentication and multi-tenancy. A CRUD API, nothing more. It even runs as a regular Vercel deployment. All the heavy lifting, all the actual workflow logic, lives in the open-source, Apache-licensed client-side library, which can be extended freely.

So the "managed" offering isn't a black box you're locked into. It's just another World, one implementation of a spec you can read, fork, and extend. The data format isn't bespoke either. You can swap out any piece of the stack.

Some patterns lean on the platform

I should be upfront. A few of Workflow SDK's design choices are shaped by how Vercel executes code. The clearest example is versioning, the same code-evolution problem that makes traditional engines so painful.

Our answer is to pin each run to the specific deployment that started it. The run keeps executing against the exact copy of the code it began on, so changing your workflow never breaks in-flight runs. It's a clean solution, but it was only easy to build because Vercel already keeps immutable deployments around for long periods. The official Postgres world doesn't track and route versions this way yet. Encouragingly, community worlds have already implemented the spec as intended. Platformatic's version-safe durable workflows on Kubernetes is a great example.

And I think that's exactly the right trade. Pinning moves the complexity of versioning off the developer writing workflows and onto the infrastructure. That burden lands on the world author, the infra provider, and us as the framework authors. If everyone using a framework hits the same hard problem and has to solve it themselves in the same painful ways, the framework has failed them. A good framework moves that complexity upstream.

Steps should be free

Performance is the next big problem for us to solve. Invoking a step isn't cheap. Each step involves networking and a trip over a queue to durably commit its result correctly. For correctness, that's the right thing to do. But it works against the pitch that distributed computing should feel like function calls.

When you write ordinary code, you don't think twice about the overhead of a function call. It's so fast it's effectively free. But if every step carried a heavy overhead, the abstraction leaks. You start rationing steps, reasoning about granularity, declining to turn a small function into a checkpoint because it's "not worth a step."

So the goal is blunt: steps should be free.

In the ideal version of this, you could take any function in an existing codebase, add "use step", and everything would just work, with no serialization constraints and no performance penalty.

That dream drives us.

What if any developer could turn a plain function into something with the performance, networking, observability, and availability of a standalone microservice, but using just two words: "use step"? That would change how we write code.

Workflow v5 (in beta at the time of writing) already delivers up to a 5x performance improvement with no change to the user-facing API, and v6 will push it further while making third-party worlds just as fast. We're sharing details as we go in this GitHub discussion, and you can start testing today with npm install workflow@beta.

I set out to build a durable framework that feels like writing ordinary code, runs on the infrastructure you already have, and is fast enough that you never think twice about reaching for a step. It's real today, and we're building the rest of it in the open.

Come build Workflow SDK with us

If designing durable systems under real-world constraints sounds like fun, the Workflow team at Vercel is hiring.

See open roles.

title: Algorithmic Bias from the Perspectives of Healthcare Professionals
description:
arXiv:2610.38006v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: This paper focuses on algorithmic bias of machine learning and artificial intelligence applications in healthcare information systems. Based on the quantitative data and qualitative comments from a survey and interviews with healthcare professionals, who have different job roles (e.g., clinical vs. administrative), this study provides findings about the relationships between algorithmic bias, perceived fairness, and the intended acceptance and adoption of ML algorithms and algorithm generated outcomes. The results suggest that the opinions of healthcare professionals toward the causes of algorithmic bias, the criteria of algorithm assessment, the perceived fairness, and bias mitigation approaches may vary depending on their job roles, perspectives, tasks, and the algorithm characteristics. More research is needed to investigate algorithmic bias to ensure fairness and equality in healthcare.

title: Disparity Laundering: Consensus Without Fairness in Clinical Multi-Agent Systems
description:
arXiv:2610.38215v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Clinical large language models are increasingly fielded as multi-agent teams, on the assumption that deliberation averages out individual error. It does not average out bias. Across a full factorial of five model families and four aggregation topologies on 120 real MIMIC-IV emergency cases under counterfactual demographic swaps, no configuration neutralizes the disparity: all 20 cells commit the direction of their agents' independent answers, giving Black patients more acute triage. Every model has a topology that amplifies its baseline gap, but which one varies by model, so no design is reliably safe or reliably amplifying: the disparity is relocated, never removed. Late-stage fixes fail: fairness instructions and demographic masking leave the gap untouched, and per-agent self-debiasing widens it, because the bias is already encoded in the agents' ordinary clinical numbers. We call this disparity laundering; the audits now applied to clinical AI, per model, per output, per version, can certify the parts but never the committed decision. Interventions close the gap exactly when they make counterfactual versions visible inside the system and pool them, through deliberation, into the committed decision. A diverse-perspective ensemble does both while keeping the team, with no retraining or architectural change: the disparity falls by 67 to 94% where all five perspectives pool at every round, and the one topology that never pools them is the one it cannot reliably repair. Medical multi-agent systems do not filter demographic bias; they launder it into plausible decisions no single-version audit can catch, and the only defense is to make the bias visible.

title: DecompGym: Benchmarking LLM Agents on Designing Decomposition Algorithms
description:
arXiv:2610.38175v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Benders decomposition and column generation solve large optimization problems by passing cuts, columns, and dual values between a master problem and subproblems, and are hard to implement correctly. Large language models now automate parts of algorithm design, which points toward agents that build decomposition solvers for new problems. As a first step toward such agents, we study how well current coding agents design and implement these two algorithms, and how they fail. We introduce DecompGym, 81 instances from nine problem families (five Benders, four column generation), in which an agent writes a solver for a prescribed method. Each solver must meet three criteria: execution within a 60-second time limit; numerical feasibility together with a method audit, in which an LLM judge reads the solver's code; and an objective within 1% of the stored optimal objective. We evaluate 12 GPT, Claude, and Gemini models running in coding-agent tools. Over up to ten attempts, we compare independent regeneration with reflection, which first diagnoses the failure. On the first attempt, two models solve every instance and seven solve more than 90%. Most Benders failures (48 of 62) are missing or suboptimal solutions. The most common column-generation failure is a method-audit rejection. Output checks alone would accept 93 of the 108 attempts that fail the method audit. The most common rejection, an optimalif, occurs 96 times, 92 of them in one model.Reflection turns 66% of retries into successes, compared with 39% for regeneration, and it repairs method-audit failures, for which the judge names the defecective gaps. Agents for decomposition therefore need checks on how a solver reaches its answer and feedback that locates the error. The benchmark is available at https://github.com/SIKAI-C/DecompGym.

title: Three kinds of empty, and why my game's empty states were lying
description:
Development covered 22 Sep 2026 to 23 Sep 2026 (commit dates).

Every list in a game has an empty state, and it is the least designed screen in most of them. You write "Nothing here yet" once, it looks fine in the editor, and you move on. This window I found that four of mine were telling players something false, and that each false sentence led them to do the wrong thing.

The underlying mistake was identical in all four. A panel showed "there is nothing here" without having established that there was nothing here.

One sentence, three situations

When a panel has no rows to draw, there are at least three reasons. The data has not arrived yet. It arrived and there genuinely is nothing. Or it never arrived, because the connection dropped. Those want three different responses: wait quietly, invite the first action, or say plainly that the information is out of reach right now.

My panels treated all three as the second one. The results:

The bag printed "Your bag is empty. Explore the world to find items!" under a header that said 1 / 8 slots. It said it on every category tab with no matching items and every search that found nothing. So a player who mistyped the name of a pill they owned was told their inventory was gone, and a player looking at the Recipes tab was sent out into the wilderness for something the General Store sells.

The guild list said "No guild is recruiting yet. Found the first one" when the list simply had not loaded. That invites a player to spend a founding cooldown, and possibly collide with an existing guild's name, over a list nobody could read. The discussion hall said "No one has spoken here yet. Say the first thing", so the first post went into a forum that was merely unreachable. The paid store said the catalogue was empty, which on a store reads as "this shop is broken".

The fix is an order, not a message

Each panel now distinguishes the three states in a fixed order: still loading, then failed, then empty. Only when the first two are ruled out does it say there is nothing. A failed read gets its own line, for instance "The catalogue could not be reached. Nothing you own is affected", which answers the question the player is actually asking. The bag now says which kind of empty it is and, for an empty category, where that category of item comes from. Bag space grows with storage treasures, and the Spirit Storage Pouch entry shows the first of them.

A small stele board on the map had the same disease in its purest form. When it had nothing to show, it drew nothing at all, which on a flaky connection told the player that not one person in the whole game had ever left a word in that spot.

An empty state should name the way out

The second half of the work was empty states that were true but useless. The Recycle Counter said "Nothing sellable in your bag right now." Correct, and a dead end, on one of the first market screens a new player opens. It now says where sellable stacks come from and offers a button to go there. The Pawnbroker got the same treatment, plus a line saying what it accepts, because a player opening it for the first time has no idea. The pawnbroker guide covers how those loans work.

The dispatch board answered an empty roster with "All disciples are busy or none recruited." That is two different states in one sentence, and a sect with zero disciples was being told its disciples were busy. It now splits them and tells the empty case where disciples come from.

One I deliberately left alone: the weekly auction says "No lots this week." There is no next step to offer, and inventing a door would be worse than an honest full stop.

A number that looked like a probability

The same reading pass found a cousin of the empty-state lie. The dispatch card showed a chip reading "45% success". The number was not a probability. It was the share of combined power that your side held, and the actual mission outcome depends on that share in a much steeper way. At the values the chip displays, "40%" meant about a four percent chance, "45%" about ten, and "58%" about ninety-five. A player who trusted it lost nine times in ten at 45, and one who skipped a 55 passed up a near certainty.

For now it says "power share", which is what it is. Computing the real odds is a separate change I would rather do carefully than guess at in the label.

What I check now

For any panel that can be empty, I ask three questions. What does it show while it is waiting? What does it show when the information could not be fetched? And when it really is empty, does it tell the player where to go next? If any answer is "the same line as the others", it is lying to someone.

The bag knows the difference now: fill yours, free in the browser.

title: GBase Database(GBase 8a): How to Fix GCware Add-Node Failures
description:
A GBase Database(GBase 8a) cluster installation reaches the final stage but fails with the message fail to add new datanodes to gcware. Network and configuration issues are common suspects, but a missing dependency library can be the actual cause: the service never starts.

Adding nodes to a GBase Database cluster depends on two key services: GCware and GCluster (gclusterd). GCware manages cluster membership and coordination. If it cannot start, the node addition process will fail.

The troubleshooting sequence is important: check GCware first, then GCluster, and finally verify node status. Reversing this order can leave you with multiple nodes showing CLOSE without revealing the root cause.

1. Load the Environment and Check GCware

First, load the DBA user's environment variables before running any diagnostic commands.

source ~/.gbase_profile
gcware_services all start
ldd gcware | grep "not found"
gcluster_services all start
ldd gclusterd | grep "not found"
gcadmin

If gcware_services all start fails, immediately check the GCware binary dependencies:

ldd gcware | grep "not found"

Any library marked not found indicates a missing runtime dependency.

One frequent issue is:

libcrypto.so.10 => not found

This often occurs on operating systems that provide newer OpenSSL versions but do not include the required OpenSSL 1.0 compatibility library.

2. Resolve Missing Shared Libraries

There are two approaches to resolving missing shared library dependencies.

Option 1: Install the matching compatibility package

Install the appropriate dependency package for your operating system and version. This is generally the preferred long-term solution.

Option 2: Create a symbolic link

As a temporary workaround, an existing compatible shared library can sometimes be linked to the missing library name.

However, do not blindly link different major library versions. Binary and ABI compatibility must be verified first. A symbolic link cannot guarantee compatibility between different OpenSSL versions.

For example, after resolving the GCware dependency, check GCluster separately:

ldd gclusterd | grep "not found"

A common missing dependency on the GCluster side is:

libidn.so.11 => not found

Install the appropriate compatibility package for the target operating system.

Important: Check every node individually. Dependencies are installed locally on each machine. One node passing the check does not mean the entire GBase Database cluster is ready.

3. Verify Services and Node Status

After resolving all missing dependencies, start both services:

gcware_services all start
gcluster_services all start
gcadmin

Use gcadmin to check the cluster node status. Confirm that the relevant nodes have successfully joined and show OPEN before proceeding.

Do not run the add-node operation until the underlying services are running correctly.

4. Retry the Add-Node Operation

Once GCware and GCluster are running, return to the GBase Database installation directory and execute:

cd /opt/gcinstall
gcadmin addnodes gcChangeInfo.xml

The gcChangeInfo.xml file is generated during the installation process and describes the nodes involved in the current cluster expansion.

Before executing addnodes, verify that its node list matches the machines you actually intend to add.

Previously installed and uninstalled environments may leave outdated configuration files behind. Using a stale gcChangeInfo.xml can cause node-matching problems and prevent the operation from completing.

Use the generated file as the starting point rather than manually recreating the node list.

5. A Real GBase Database Deployment Case

In a provincial government project deployed on openEuler, the installation encountered the same fail to add new datanodes to gcware error.

Following the troubleshooting sequence revealed two missing dependencies:

  1. GCware failed to start because libcrypto.so.10 was missing.
  2. After resolving that dependency, GCluster startup revealed another missing library: libidn.so.11.

After installing the corresponding compatibility packages, both services started successfully. The gcadmin command then showed all nodes as OPEN.

Finally, rerunning gcadmin addnodes gcChangeInfo.xml successfully added the previously failed nodes.

The entire diagnosis and recovery took less than an hour.

6. Build a Dependency Checklist for Future Deployments

When troubleshooting GBase Database(GBase 8a) add-node failures, avoid jumping straight to reinstallation.

Reinstalling the cluster does not automatically resolve missing operating system libraries. If the dependencies remain unchanged, the same failure can happen again.

For future deployments, record:

  • Node IP address and operating system version
  • GCware startup result
  • GCluster startup result
  • Missing libraries reported by ldd
  • Dependency packages installed on each node
  • Final node status reported by gcadmin

Keep the installation logs and service startup output together. They help identify which library was missing and which machine was affected.

The key takeaway: When GBase Database add-node operations fail, check GCware dependencies first, then GCluster, and only afterward investigate node status and configuration.

Service names and dependency package names may vary across operating system versions. Always verify the required packages against the documentation for your specific GBase Database release and operating system.

title: Event-Driven Architecture on the Cloud
description:
⚡ TL;DR: Replace brittle synchronous calls with events, and learn to pick the right building block: queues, pub/sub, or streams. Because delivery is at-least-once, idempotency is the non-negotiable price of admission.

Contents

  • When one slow call takes down everything
  • The mental model: a newsroom, not a phone tree
  • The picture: one event, many reactions
  • Queues vs pub/sub vs streams
  • Publishing and consuming an event
  • Delivery guarantees: why idempotency is non-negotiable
  • Common mistakes that cost hours
  • When event-driven beats a synchronous call
  • Where to go next

When one slow call takes down everything

You ship an order service. It takes a payment, then calls the email service, then the analytics service, then the warehouse service, one after another, in the same request. It works great in the demo. Then the email provider has a bad afternoon, its API hangs for 30 seconds, and suddenly customers can't place orders at all. Nobody is buying email. They're buying products. But because checkout calls email synchronously, a hiccup in a non-critical service became an outage in your most critical one.

The fix isn't a faster email service. It's changing the shape of the conversation. Instead of checkout calling everyone and waiting, checkout announces "an order was placed" and walks away. Whoever cares, email, analytics, the warehouse, reacts on their own time. That announcement is an event, and designing around it is event-driven architecture.

📌 Who this is for: Developers and junior cloud engineers who can already build a service that calls another service over HTTP, and are starting to feel the pain, cascading failures, slow requests, services that have to know too much about each other. No prior messaging experience needed. We use AWS, GCP, and Azure names, but the ideas are identical everywhere.

The mental model: a newsroom, not a phone tree

Event-driven architecture means services communicate by emitting and reacting to events, facts about what happened, instead of directly commanding each other.

The one-sentence version

Synchronous calls are a phone tree. To tell five teams something, you phone each one, wait for them to pick up, and you're stuck on the line until the last call ends. If one person doesn't answer, you're frozen mid-tree.

Event-driven is a newsroom. A reporter publishes a story. They don't know, or care, who reads it. Subscribers (the sports desk, the weather team, an archive bot) each pick it up and do their own thing, at their own pace. The reporter's job is done the moment the story is filed. Add a tenth subscriber tomorrow and the reporter's code never changes.

In the real world In tech
A reporter files a story A producer publishes an event
The story itself (a fact that happened) The event / message payload
The newswire everyone reads from The topic / queue / stream
The sports & weather desks Independent consumers / subscribers
Anyone can start reading the wire tomorrow Add a consumer without touching the producer

The newsroom maps cleanly onto the building blocks.

The picture: one event, many reactions

Here's the order flow rebuilt around an event. Checkout publishes once to a topic; the topic fans the event out to every interested consumer. Checkout finishes in milliseconds and is completely unaffected if a downstream consumer is slow or down.

A producer publishes once; the topic fans the event out to independent consumers (fan-out).

  1. Customer clicks Buy: Checkout charges the card and persists the order. That part is still synchronous, it must succeed before we promise anything.
  2. Checkout publishes one event: It sends a single OrderPlaced message to the topic with the order id and details, then returns 200 to the customer. Total added latency: a few milliseconds.
  3. The topic fans out: The messaging service delivers a copy to every subscriber, email, warehouse, analytics. Checkout has no idea who they are.
  4. Consumers react independently: Email sends a receipt. The warehouse reserves stock. Analytics records the sale. If email is down, the warehouse and analytics are unaffected, and email retries later.

Queues vs pub/sub vs streams

"Messaging" is three different patterns wearing the same coat. Picking the wrong one is the most common early mistake, so anchor on these distinctions before you reach for a service.

  • Queue, one message, one worker. The message is consumed and gone. Use it to distribute work: ten workers pull from one queue and each grabs different items.
  • Pub/Sub, one message, every subscriber gets a copy. Use it to broadcast a fact so multiple systems can react (this is fan-out).
  • Stream, an append-only log you can replay. Messages aren't deleted on read; consumers track their own position. Use it for ordered history, replay, and analytics.
Queue Pub/Sub Stream
Delivery 1 message → 1 consumer 1 message → all subscribers 1 log → many readers, each at own offset
Ordering Best-effort (FIFO variants exist) Usually unordered Strong, per-partition order
Fan-out No (work is split, not copied) Yes, the whole point Yes (each consumer reads the full log)
Replay No, read = gone No, miss it, miss it Yes, rewind to any offset
Best for Background jobs, task distribution Broadcasting events, decoupling Event sourcing, metrics, audit trails
Managed examples SQS, Pub/Sub (pull), Service Bus queues SNS, EventBridge, Pub/Sub, Service Bus topics Kinesis, Kafka / MSK, Event Hubs

The same event needs different plumbing depending on what you want from it.

💡 Queue + pub/sub is the classic combo: On AWS the textbook fan-out is SNS → SQS: SNS broadcasts the event, and each consumer has its own SQS queue subscribed to the topic. You get broadcast AND a durable buffer per consumer, so a slow consumer never blocks the others. EventBridge plays the same role with richer routing rules.

Publishing and consuming an event

Concretely, publishing is a one-liner and consuming is a small loop. Here's the SNS → SQS fan-out from the diagram, in Python with boto3. First, checkout publishes the event:

publish_order.py

import json
import boto3

sns = boto3.client("sns")
TOPIC_ARN = "arn:aws:sns:eu-west-1:123456789012:OrderPlaced"

def publish_order_placed(order_id: str, total: float, email: str) -> None:
    event = {
        "type": "OrderPlaced",
        "order_id": order_id,
        "total": total,
        "customer_email": email,
    }
    sns.publish(
        TopicArn=TOPIC_ARN,
        Message=json.dumps(event),
        # idempotency: a stable id lets consumers dedupe
        MessageAttributes={
            "event_id": {"DataType": "String", "StringValue": order_id},
        },
    )
    # checkout returns to the customer right here, no waiting on consumers

Each consumer owns an SQS queue subscribed to that topic. The email worker just polls its queue, does its job, and deletes the message to acknowledge it:

email_consumer.py

import json
import boto3

sqs = boto3.client("sqs")
QUEUE_URL = "https://sqs.eu-west-1.amazonaws.com/123456789012/email-queue"

while True:
    resp = sqs.receive_message(
        QueueUrl=QUEUE_URL,
        MaxNumberOfMessages=10,
        WaitTimeSeconds=20,  # long polling, cheaper, less spin
    )
    for msg in resp.get("Messages", []):
        envelope = json.loads(msg["Body"])        # SNS wraps the payload
        event = json.loads(envelope["Message"])   # our actual event

        if not already_processed(event["order_id"]):
            send_receipt(event["customer_email"], event["order_id"])
            mark_processed(event["order_id"])

        # delete = acknowledge. Only do this AFTER the work succeeded.
        sqs.delete_message(QueueUrl=QUEUE_URL, ReceiptHandle=msg["ReceiptHandle"])

Notice the already_processed / mark_processed guard, and that we delete the message only after the work succeeds. That's not optional decoration, it's the heart of running this safely. Here's why.

Delivery guarantees: why idempotency is non-negotiable

Almost every managed messaging service gives you at-least-once delivery. Read that carefully: at least once. Not exactly once. The same event can, and eventually will, be delivered to your consumer more than once. This isn't a bug; it's the honest trade-off that makes the system reliable.

It happens for boring, unavoidable reasons. A consumer processes a message, but its acknowledgement gets lost on the network. The broker never hears "done," so after a visibility timeout it redelivers, and now you've sent two receipt emails for one order. The number of guarantees in plain terms:

  • At-most-once, fire and forget. Fast, but you can silently lose messages. Rarely what you want.
  • At-least-once, never lost, sometimes duplicated. The realistic default for SQS, SNS, Pub/Sub, and Kinesis.
  • Exactly-once, the dream. A few services offer it in narrow conditions (Kafka transactions, SQS FIFO dedup windows), but it's limited and costs throughput. Don't architect around assuming it.

⚠️ Design for duplicates, not against them: Since you'll get duplicates, make your consumers idempotent: processing the same event twice has the same effect as processing it once. Use the event's stable id as a dedup key, record "I've handled order_id X," and skip it if it shows up again. Idempotency turns at-least-once from a liability into a non-issue.

The same instinct covers the other failure: a message your consumer can never process (bad data, a permanent bug). Without a backstop it gets redelivered forever, a "poison pill." Configure a dead-letter queue (DLQ) so a message that fails N times moves aside for inspection instead of blocking the line.

Common mistakes that cost hours

  1. Treating at-least-once as exactly-once. No dedup guard means double-charged cards and duplicate emails the first time a network blip causes a redelivery. Make consumers idempotent from day one.
  2. Acknowledging before the work is done. Delete or ack the message only after processing succeeds. Ack first and crash, and the event is gone forever.
  3. No dead-letter queue. A single malformed message retries endlessly, drowns your logs, and can stall the whole queue. Always wire a DLQ with a sane retry count.
  4. Putting commands in events. An event states a fact (OrderPlaced), not an instruction (SendEmail). If the producer is telling a specific consumer what to do, you've just rebuilt a synchronous call with extra steps and lost the decoupling.
  5. Reaching for a stream when you needed a queue. Kafka/Kinesis are powerful and operationally heavy. If you just need background jobs, a plain queue (SQS) is simpler, cheaper, and enough.
  6. Forgetting ordering isn't free. Standard queues and pub/sub don't guarantee order. If OrderShipped can arrive before OrderPlaced, either use a FIFO/partitioned option or make consumers tolerant of out-of-order events.

When event-driven beats a synchronous call

Event-driven isn't free, you trade the simplicity of a function call for eventual consistency, harder debugging, and new infrastructure. So don't make everything an event. Reach for it when the trade pays off:

  • Multiple consumers care about the same thing, fan-out beats calling each one yourself.
  • The reaction can happen later, receipts, analytics, and indexing don't need to finish before you answer the user.
  • You want failure isolation, a down consumer shouldn't take down the producer.
  • Load is spiky, a queue absorbs bursts and lets workers drain at their own pace.

Keep it synchronous when the caller genuinely needs the answer now to continue, reading a user's profile to render a page, or checking inventory before confirming a price. A request that can't proceed without the response shouldn't be fire-and-forget.

The whole article in seven lines

  • Event-driven = services emit and react to facts, instead of commanding each other directly.
  • Think newsroom (publish, anyone subscribes), not phone tree (call everyone, wait).
  • Queue = work split across workers. Pub/Sub = broadcast a copy to all. Stream = replayable ordered log.
  • Fan-out (one event, many consumers) is the superpower, add consumers without touching the producer.
  • Delivery is at-least-once, so duplicates are guaranteed, make every consumer idempotent.
  • Always add a dead-letter queue so a poison message can't block the line.
  • Use events for fan-out, deferrable work, and failure isolation; stay synchronous when the caller needs the answer to continue.

Where to go next

You now have the vocabulary and the mental model. The fastest way to make it stick is to wire a real producer and consumer, then design a system where events change how it scales.

  • Go deeper on the worker side: Async Processing: Queues & Workers covers retries, visibility timeouts, and worker pools in detail.
  • See how decoupling shapes growth: Scalability Principles shows why queues and fan-out are the backbone of systems that scale.
  • Ready to build the rest of the stack? The Cloud Engineer path walks you from networking to compute to event-driven systems, level by level.

Originally published on TheSimplifiedTech, where this guide is interactive, with in-browser terminal labs and diagrams. Learn cloud and DevOps by doing, no videos.

title: A Birthday Planner Should Help Before the Reminder Is Needed
description:
A birthday reminder is useful when it tells you that a date is coming.

A birthday planner is useful when it helps you do something about it.

That distinction sounds small, but it changes the entire product.

A date is not a plan

Knowing that someone has a birthday next week does not automatically tell you what needs to happen.

You may still need to:

  • buy a gift
  • order something online
  • make a reservation
  • organize a visit
  • coordinate with family
  • write a card
  • prepare a message

The date is only the anchor.

The actual work happens before it.

Good planning starts with visibility

One thing I think matters a lot is seeing upcoming birthdays early.

A useful planner should make it easy to answer:

  • Who has a birthday this week?
  • Who is coming up next month?
  • Which birthdays need preparation?
  • Which ones only need a simple reminder?

This turns the app into a planning tool instead of just a notification system.

Different people need different preparation

Not every birthday deserves the same workflow.

For one person, a reminder on the same day may be enough.

For another, you may need several weeks.

That is why flexible reminders are more useful than one fixed notification.

The app should adapt to the relationship, not force the same timing for everyone.

Notes make the date more useful

A birthday entry becomes much more helpful when it can carry context.

For example:

  • gift ideas
  • previous gifts
  • favorite things
  • travel plans
  • personal notes
  • ideas for future celebrations

The goal is not to turn the app into a database.

It is to keep useful context close to the date.

A planner should reduce mental load

People often remember that a birthday is approaching but still feel unprepared.

That is a product problem.

A good birthday planner should reduce the need to keep everything in your head.

Instead of remembering:

“Sarah’s birthday is soon, I need to think of something.”

the app should help turn that into:

“Sarah’s birthday is in 12 days, and I already have a gift idea saved.”

That feels much more useful.

How this shaped Annum

Annum was designed around the idea that birthdays are easier to manage when they are treated as upcoming plans rather than isolated dates.

The app focuses on:

  • upcoming birthdays
  • early reminders
  • personal notes
  • clear organization
  • preparation before the day arrives

The goal is to help users feel ready instead of surprised.

Final thought

A reminder tells you that something is happening.

A planner helps you prepare for it.

For birthdays, that preparation is often the part that matters most.
