title: How to Containerize a Full-Stack App (Part 1)-Setting Up the Local Development Environment.
description:
Series Navigation:

  • 📍 Part 1: Setting up locally (You are here)
  • ➡️ Part 2: Frontend Multi-Stage Docker Builds
  • ➡️ Part 3: Containerizing the Backend & MySQL

Video

In modern web development, Docker has become the standard for ensuring your application runs consistently across dev, test, and production environments. In this post, we are going to focus specifically on how to containerize a full-stack application built with React, Express.js, and MySQL.

In this tutorial, I will guide you through the end-to-end process of containerizing this stack. This is Part 1, so here we will just set up our full-stack app locally. In the upcoming blog post, I will explain the remaining details.

Here is what we will cover:

  1. Prerequisites: Who is this for? (Frontend, Backend, and DevOps developers).
  2. Setup: Installing Docker Desktop on our machine.
  3. Setting up the Database: Setting up the Mysql Database.
  4. The Baseline: Running our full-stack app locally before containerizing.
  5. Conclusion: Summary and final thoughts.

Let’s get started.

1. Prerequisites

Before we dive in, let’s make sure this guide is right for you. This tutorial is designed to be flexible: whether you want to master the entire full-stack containerization process or need a solution for a specific part, you can leverage the sections that matter to you.

Who is this for?

  • Frontend Developers: You will learn how to serve your React app efficiently without relying on npm start in production.

  • Backend Developers: You will learn how to containerize your backend for production, ensuring your API and database run reliably together on any server.

  • DevOps Enthusiasts: You will gain hands-on experience packaging web applications and using Docker Compose to run them locally—the essential first step before managing them in a cloud environment.

⚠️ Important Note:
This guide is not for absolute beginners. We assume you already have a working knowledge of React and Node.js. I'm not covering how to write the application code itself, but rather how to package and ship it effectively.

What you need:

  • A basic understanding of React and Express.js.
  • Familiarity with the command line.
  • A code editor (VS Code recommended).

2. Setup: Installing Docker Desktop on our machine

To work with containers, we need the Docker engine running on our computer. The easiest and most standard way to do this is via Docker Desktop.

  1. Download: Go to the official Docker website for Mac, for Windows, for Linux and download the installer for your OS (Windows, Mac, or Linux).
  2. Install: Run the installer and follow the on-screen instructions.
  3. Start the App: Once installed, open the "Docker Desktop" application. (Important: Docker commands won't work unless this app is running in the background!)
  4. Verify: Open your terminal (or command prompt) and run the following command to make sure everything is connected: 
docker --version
# Output Example: Docker version 29.0.1, build eedd969

If you see a version number, you are ready to go!

3.Setting up the Database

To run our backend, we need a MySQL database. Instead of installing the heavy MySQL server software directly on your OS, we will use Docker to spin up a MySQL container.

Run this command in your terminal:

docker run --name mysql-container \
  -e MYSQL_ROOT_PASSWORD=myrootpassword \
  -e MYSQL_DATABASE=my_testing_db \
  -p 3306:3306 \
  -d mysql:8.0

Now, go to Docker Desktop and verify that your MySQL container is running successfully

⚠️ Note:
Please save this password and db name as well because we need them later.
Also, if the above command failed. Then try with a different port number. For example, 3307.

docker run --name mysql-container \
-e MYSQL_ROOT_PASSWORD=myrootpassword \
-e MYSQL_DATABASE=my_testing_db \
-p 3306:3306 \
-d mysql:8.0

What Happens When You Run This Command

  1. Docker downloads the mysql:8.0 image (if not present).
  2. Creates a new container named mysql-container.
  3. Starts the MySQL server inside it.
  4. Initialises the database my_testing_db (first run only).
  5. Sets the root user password to whatever you provided.
  6. Exposes MySQL on your machine's port 3306.
  • docker run: Tells Docker to create and start a new container from a specified image.
  • --name mysql-container: Gives the container a custom name: mysql-container. So we can find it easily. If omitted, Docker assigns a random name.
  • -e MYSQL_ROOT_PASSWORD=myrootpassword: Sets the root password (we'll need this for our backend). The official MySQL image requires the MYSQL_ROOT_PASSWORD environment variable to be set.
  • -e MYSQL_DATABASE=my_testing_db: This will set the database with name my_testing_db. This env variable is optional. It creates a database on container creation.
  • -p 3306:3306: Exposes the database port so our local Node.js app can connect to it.
  • -d mysql:8.0: Image name.

4. The Baseline: Running our full-stack app locally before containerizing

Before we start writing Dockerfiles, we need to understand what we are actually containerizing. In this section, we will get the application running on our machine "the old-fashioned way" (mostly) to ensure the code works.

In this section, we will:

  • Fork and Clone the starter repository.
  • Set up the Database.
  • Run the Application to confirm that everything talks to each other.

4.1 Fork and Clone the Repository

I have prepared a starter repository that contains a basic React frontend and an Express backend.

  1. Fork the repository to your own GitHub account.

Go to repo: Repo Link

Click on Fork

Once forked, clone it.

  1. Clone it to your local machine: 
# Clone the repository
git clone https://github.com/YOUR_GITHUB_USERNAME/devops-todo-starter-app.git

# Move into the project directory
cd devops-todo-starter-app

Once you cloned it, open it in VS Code or any IDE.

Note: There are three branches present for each blog post. Make sure you are in the main branch.

You will be able to see two folders: backend, frontend and a README.md file.

4.2 Running the Application

Now that our database is running, let's start the application. Go to your IDE where you open the project.

Go to the backend directory and create a file .env.

Copy content from .env-example. And paste it in .env.

Now replace DB_PASSWORD='<DB_PASSWORD>' with DB_PASSWORD=myrootpassword. And ALLOWED_ORIGIN=http://localhost:4501 with ALLOWED_ORIGIN=http://localhost:8080.

Before proceeding, make sure you are using Node.js version ">=20.0.0". Currently I'm using the LTS version, which is v24.13.0.

Open the terminal and run

node -v

Once you have a compatible node version, start the backend server.

Open a terminal and go to the **backend **directory

Install dependencies

cd backend
npm install

Run the migration

npm run migrate

Once migrated, you will see below the O/P

Run dev server

npm run dev

If everything goes fine, you will see below the O/P

Now, in the browser, open URL http://localhost:5500/api/todos

You will be able to see dummy todos in the browser

Open a new terminal and go to the frontend directory

Install dependencies

cd frontend
npm install

Setup Env Variable:

Go to the frontend directory and create a file .env.

Copy content from .env-example. And paste it in .env.

Start dev server

npm run dev

Open your browser to http://localhost:8080.

If you see data loading from the API, congratulations!🎉. Your baseline environment is set up perfectly.

5. Conclusion

I hope you successfully set up the app locally and enjoyed the process. In the next part, we will learn how to containerize our frontend. Stay tune. Please post your queries if you faced any issues.

title: Retry Budgets in Go: Preventing Retries from Becoming an Outage
description:
Retries are one of the most common ways to make distributed systems more resilient.

A request fails because of a temporary network issue. The client waits briefly and tries again. The second attempt succeeds, and the failure never reaches the user.

That sounds reasonable.

But what happens when the dependency is already overloaded?

Requests start failing. Every caller retries. Those retries create additional traffic, which causes more failures, which trigger even more retries.

A temporary slowdown can turn into a retry storm.

Retries are not free. Every attempt consumes resources, occupies connections, increases queue pressure, and adds work to an already struggling dependency.

This is where retry budgets become useful.

A retry budget places a limit on how much additional traffic a service can generate through retries. Instead of allowing every failed request to retry independently, it establishes a shared budget across requests.

In this article, we'll explore:

  • Why per-request retry limits are not enough
  • How retry amplification creates cascading failures
  • The difference between retry limits and retry budgets
  • How to implement a concurrency-safe retry budget in Go
  • How to combine budgets with exponential backoff and jitter
  • How retries interact with timeouts, bulkheads, and circuit breakers
  • What to measure and test before using retries in production

1. The Problem: Retries Can Amplify Failures

Imagine a service that sends requests to an external market data provider.

Under normal conditions:

  • The service receives 1,000 requests per second.
  • Each request makes one provider call.
  • The provider responds successfully.

Now the provider starts experiencing problems. Its error rate increases, and requests become slower.

The service retries failed requests up to three times.

If every original request fails, the provider may receive:

Attempt Requests
Original requests 1,000
First retries 1,000
Second retries 1,000
Third retries 1,000
Total 4,000

The service has turned 1,000 incoming requests into as many as 4,000 downstream attempts.

This is retry amplification.

The actual situation can be worse. Retries may overlap with new incoming traffic, other services may retry independently, and clients may have their own retry policies.

The dependency is already struggling, but the system keeps sending it more work.

The important distinction is that retries can improve the success rate of individual requests while making the overall system less stable.

A retry policy should not only ask:

How many times should this request retry?

It should also ask:

How much additional traffic can this service afford to generate?

2. Why Max Retries Is Not Enough

A typical retry implementation has a maximum attempt count:

for attempt := 1; attempt <= 3; attempt++ {
    err := callDependency()
    if err == nil {
        return nil
    }
}

This limits retries for an individual request.

But it does not limit retries across the entire service.

Consider a service receiving 10,000 requests per second. Even with only one retry per request, it can generate another 10,000 downstream attempts per second during an outage.

A per-request retry limit provides a local constraint, not a global traffic constraint.

There are two separate controls:

Control What it limits
Maximum attempts Retries for one request
Retry budget Retries across a service or dependency

You generally want both.

A maximum attempt count prevents one request from retrying indefinitely. A shared retry budget prevents thousands of requests from independently exhausting a dependency.

3. What Is a Retry Budget?

A retry budget is a shared allowance for additional attempts.

Instead of allowing every failed request to retry automatically, the service must acquire permission from the budget before performing another attempt.

One practical approach is a token bucket.

The model is simple:

  1. Successful initial requests add tokens to the budget.
  2. Each retry consumes one token.
  3. The budget has a maximum capacity.
  4. When no tokens are available, additional retries are rejected.

For example, suppose a service uses these settings:

  • Maximum budget: 20 tokens
  • Credit per successful initial request: 0.1 tokens
  • Cost per retry: 1 token

Every ten successful initial requests generate one retry token.

If the service experiences a sudden failure, it can spend its accumulated tokens on retries. Once the budget is exhausted, it stops generating additional retry traffic until successful initial requests replenish it.

This creates an important feedback mechanism:

  • Healthy service: successful requests replenish the budget.
  • Unhealthy service: fewer successful requests mean less budget replenishment.
  • Outage: retries consume the remaining budget and eventually stop.

The budget is not a guarantee that a dependency can handle a particular amount of traffic. It is a mechanism for limiting retry amplification.

4. Implementing a Retry Budget in Go

Let's start with the shared budget.

We need a structure that is safe to access concurrently because multiple requests may attempt to consume or replenish tokens at the same time.

package retry

import "sync"

type RetryBudget struct {
    mu sync.Mutex

    tokens          float64
    capacity        float64
    creditPerSuccess float64
}

func NewRetryBudget(
    capacity float64,
    creditPerSuccess float64,
) *RetryBudget {
    return &RetryBudget{
        capacity:         capacity,
        creditPerSuccess: creditPerSuccess,
    }
}

func (b *RetryBudget) RecordSuccess() {
    b.mu.Lock()
    defer b.mu.Unlock()

    b.tokens += b.creditPerSuccess

    if b.tokens > b.capacity {
        b.tokens = b.capacity
    }
}

func (b *RetryBudget) TryTake() bool {
    b.mu.Lock()
    defer b.mu.Unlock()

    if b.tokens < 1 {
        return false
    }

    b.tokens--
    return true
}

The implementation deliberately keeps the budget small and predictable.

RecordSuccess adds credits without exceeding the configured capacity.

TryTake atomically checks and consumes a token. This prevents concurrent requests from spending the same token.

For example:

budget := NewRetryBudget(
    20,   // Maximum tokens
    0.1,  // Credit per successful initial request
)

A successful initial request adds 0.1 tokens. A retry requires one complete token.

The budget starts empty. This is intentional: a newly started instance does not immediately receive permission to generate retries. If a service needs an initial retry allowance, that can be configured explicitly.

5. Building a Retry Executor

A retry budget is only one part of a retry policy.

A useful retry executor should also support:

  • A maximum number of attempts
  • Exponential backoff
  • Jitter
  • Context cancellation
  • Retryable error classification
  • A shared retry budget

First, define the policy:

package retry

import (
    "context"
    "errors"
    "math/rand"
    "time"
)

var ErrInvalidPolicy = errors.New("invalid retry policy")

type Policy struct {
    MaxAttempts  int
    InitialDelay time.Duration
    MaxDelay     time.Duration

    Budget      *RetryBudget
    ShouldRetry func(error) bool
}

MaxAttempts includes the original attempt.

For example, MaxAttempts: 3 means one original attempt and at most two retries.

Next, calculate the exponential backoff.

func backoff(
    attempt int,
    initial time.Duration,
    maximum time.Duration,
) time.Duration {
    delay := initial

    for i := 1; i < attempt; i++ {
        if delay >= maximum/2 {
            return maximum
        }

        delay *= 2
    }

    if delay > maximum {
        return maximum
    }

    return delay
}

The delay grows exponentially until it reaches the configured maximum.

For example:

Retry Maximum delay
1 100ms
2 200ms
3 400ms
4 800ms
5 1.6s

The next step is jitter.

Without jitter, clients that fail at approximately the same time may retry at approximately the same time. This creates synchronized traffic spikes.

Full jitter chooses a random delay between zero and the calculated maximum:

func fullJitter(maxDelay time.Duration) time.Duration {
    if maxDelay <= 0 {
        return 0
    }

    return time.Duration(
        rand.Float64() * float64(maxDelay),
    )
}

The package-level math/rand functions are safe for concurrent use. If you need reproducible tests, inject a random source rather than depending on global randomness.

Now we can implement the retry executor.

func Do(
    ctx context.Context,
    policy Policy,
    operation func(context.Context) error,
) error {
    if policy.MaxAttempts < 1 ||
        policy.InitialDelay <= 0 ||
        policy.MaxDelay < policy.InitialDelay ||
        operation == nil {
        return ErrInvalidPolicy
    }

    if policy.ShouldRetry == nil {
        return ErrInvalidPolicy
    }

    for attempt := 1; attempt <= policy.MaxAttempts; attempt++ {
        if err := ctx.Err(); err != nil {
            return err
        }

        err := operation(ctx)
        if err == nil {
            // Only successful initial attempts replenish the budget.
            if attempt == 1 && policy.Budget != nil {
                policy.Budget.RecordSuccess()
            }

            return nil
        }

        if attempt == policy.MaxAttempts {
            return err
        }

        if !policy.ShouldRetry(err) {
            return err
        }

        // Do not generate more traffic when the shared
        // retry budget has been exhausted.
        if policy.Budget != nil && !policy.Budget.TryTake() {
            return err
        }

        maxDelay := backoff(
            attempt,
            policy.InitialDelay,
            policy.MaxDelay,
        )

        delay := fullJitter(maxDelay)

        timer := time.NewTimer(delay)

        select {
        case <-ctx.Done():
            if !timer.Stop() {
                <-timer.C
            }

            return ctx.Err()

        case <-timer.C:
        }
    }

    return nil
}

A few design decisions are worth highlighting.

First, the budget is consumed before the retry.

Once the service decides to schedule another attempt, it spends a token. If the context is canceled during the backoff period, that token is not refunded.

This is a conservative choice. The budget controls permission to generate retry work, not only completed downstream calls.

Second, only successful initial attempts replenish the budget.

A successful retry does not replenish it. Otherwise, a service could keep generating retries and effectively fund its own retry traffic during a degraded period.

Third, the context is checked before each attempt and during backoff.

A canceled request should not continue generating work.

The executor returns the last operation error when the retry budget is exhausted. This preserves the underlying failure for callers, although production implementations may also expose a separate retry-denied metric or callback.

6. Choosing Which Errors Are Retryable

Not every failure should trigger a retry.

A retry policy should distinguish between transient failures and permanent failures.

Examples of potentially retryable failures:

  • Temporary network errors
  • Connection resets
  • Selected HTTP 5xx responses
  • HTTP 429 responses, subject to server guidance
  • Temporary resource unavailability

Examples of failures that generally should not be retried:

  • Invalid input
  • Authentication or authorization failures
  • Unsupported operations
  • Validation errors
  • Requests that have already exceeded their deadline

A simple classifier might look like this:

func shouldRetry(err error) bool {
    var netErr net.Error

    if errors.As(err, &netErr) {
        return netErr.Timeout() || netErr.Temporary()
    }

    return false
}

This is only an illustration. net.Error.Temporary() is deprecated, and real applications should classify errors according to their HTTP client, database driver, RPC framework, and dependency-specific semantics.

For HTTP clients, for example, a 429 response may include Retry-After. A robust policy should respect that server-provided delay where applicable, while still enforcing the request deadline and retry budget.

Also remember that retrying a request is not always safe.

A GET request is generally easier to retry than a payment or order-creation request. For operations with side effects, use idempotency keys or another deduplication mechanism.

A retry budget controls traffic. It does not make an operation safe to execute twice.

7. Putting It Together

Let's use the retry executor with a market data provider.

budget := retry.NewRetryBudget(
    20,
    0.1,
)

policy := retry.Policy{
    MaxAttempts:  3,
    InitialDelay: 100 * time.Millisecond,
    MaxDelay:     2 * time.Second,
    Budget:       budget,
    ShouldRetry:  shouldRetry,
}

ctx, cancel := context.WithTimeout(
    context.Background(),
    3*time.Second,
)
defer cancel()

err := retry.Do(
    ctx,
    policy,
    func(ctx context.Context) error {
        return marketDataClient.Fetch(ctx, "AAPL")
    },
)

if err != nil {
    // Handle the final operation error.
}

The behavior is now bounded by multiple independent controls:

  • The request can make at most three attempts.
  • The request cannot exceed its context deadline.
  • Each retry uses exponential backoff with jitter.
  • The service must have an available retry token.
  • Only successful initial attempts replenish the shared budget.

This is much safer than allowing every request to retry independently.

8. Retry Budgets and Other Resilience Patterns

Retry budgets do not replace other resilience mechanisms. They complement them.

Mechanism Primary responsibility
Timeout Limits how long an operation can run
Backpressure Controls how much work enters a system
Load shedding Rejects work when capacity is insufficient
Bulkhead Isolates resource consumption
Circuit breaker Stops calls to an unhealthy dependency
Retry budget Limits additional traffic generated by retries

Consider how these mechanisms work together.

A request enters the service. Backpressure controls admission. A bulkhead limits concurrent calls to the provider. The request has a deadline. If the provider fails, the retry policy classifies the error and checks the retry budget. If the dependency is persistently unhealthy, the circuit breaker can stop further calls.

Each mechanism addresses a different failure mode.

A subtle interaction: Bulkheads and retries

Retry placement matters.

Suppose a bulkhead permit is acquired once around the entire retry loop. The permit remains occupied during backoff.

That may be desirable if the goal is to limit the number of complete operations, but it can also waste scarce concurrency capacity while requests are sleeping.

Alternatively, acquiring a permit for each individual attempt releases capacity during backoff. However, this allows more logical requests to remain in progress simultaneously.

Neither approach is universally correct. The choice depends on what the bulkhead is protecting:

  • If it protects active downstream calls, acquire a permit per attempt.
  • If it protects the number of in-flight logical operations, hold the permit across the complete retry operation.

The important thing is to define the resource boundary explicitly.

9. Is a Local Retry Budget Enough?

A mutex-protected retry budget is local to one process.

If you run ten replicas, each replica has its own budget.

For example:

  • 10 replicas
  • 20 tokens per replica
  • 200 tokens of aggregate retry capacity

This may be perfectly acceptable. Local budgets are simple, fast, and do not introduce another distributed dependency.

But if the external provider enforces a strict global quota, local budgets alone may not be sufficient.

Possible approaches include:

  1. Local budgets: Simple and independent, but aggregate capacity grows with replica count.
  2. Centralized budget: Coordinates retry allowance across instances, but introduces network calls and another failure boundary.
  3. Provider-aware limits: Use the provider's documented quota and response headers to coordinate traffic.
  4. Centralized dispatch: Route downstream work through a shared queue or dispatcher that controls the total attempt rate.

Do not introduce a distributed retry-budget service automatically. The coordination mechanism can become more expensive and less reliable than the problem it is trying to solve.

Start with local budgets when they provide sufficient protection. Move to centralized coordination only when the actual quota or failure model requires it.

10. Observability: Measure Retry Behavior

A retry policy that cannot be observed is difficult to operate.

At minimum, expose metrics that help answer:

  • How often are requests retried?
  • How many retries are denied by the budget?
  • Which dependencies consume the most retry capacity?
  • How often do requests exhaust their attempt limit?
  • How much time is spent waiting between attempts?

Useful metrics include:

Metric Type Purpose
retry_attempts_total Counter Total retry attempts
retry_budget_denied_total Counter Retries rejected by the budget
retry_budget_tokens Gauge Current available tokens
retry_exhausted_total Counter Requests reaching the attempt limit
retry_delay_seconds Histogram Time spent in retry backoff

Avoid using raw URLs, request IDs, user IDs, or other high-cardinality values as metric labels.

Prefer bounded dimensions such as dependency name, operation, and outcome.

A particularly useful signal is the ratio of retries to original requests.

If the retry rate starts increasing while the initial success rate drops, the system may be entering a retry-amplification cycle.

The retry budget should make that cycle bounded, but the metrics help you understand why it happened.

11. Testing Retry Budgets

Concurrency behavior should be tested explicitly.

The first test verifies that successful initial requests replenish the budget and that retries consume tokens.

func TestRetryBudget(t *testing.T) {
    budget := NewRetryBudget(2, 1)

    budget.RecordSuccess()
    budget.RecordSuccess()

    if !budget.TryTake() {
        t.Fatal("expected first token")
    }

    if !budget.TryTake() {
        t.Fatal("expected second token")
    }

    if budget.TryTake() {
        t.Fatal("expected budget to be exhausted")
    }
}

The next test checks that concurrent callers cannot consume more tokens than are available.

func TestRetryBudgetConcurrent(t *testing.T) {
    const (
        tokens   = 100
        workers  = 1000
    )

    budget := NewRetryBudget(tokens, 1)

    for i := 0; i < tokens; i++ {
        budget.RecordSuccess()
    }

    var (
        wg       sync.WaitGroup
        accepted atomic.Int64
    )

    wg.Add(workers)

    for i := 0; i < workers; i++ {
        go func() {
            defer wg.Done()

            if budget.TryTake() {
                accepted.Add(1)
            }
        }()
    }

    wg.Wait()

    if got := accepted.Load(); got != tokens {
        t.Fatalf(
            "expected %d successful acquisitions, got %d",
            tokens,
            got,
        )
    }
}

Run the tests with the race detector:

go test -race ./...

You should also test the retry executor itself:

  • A successful first attempt should not retry.
  • A transient failure should retry when budget is available.
  • A permanent failure should return immediately.
  • An exhausted budget should prevent another attempt.
  • Context cancellation should interrupt backoff.
  • The maximum attempt count should be respected.
  • A successful retry should not replenish the budget.
  • A failed initial request should not replenish the budget.

Finally, test behavior under load. A retry policy that passes unit tests can still create unexpected traffic patterns when thousands of requests fail together.

12. Production Checklist

Before enabling retries in a production service, verify the following:

  • [ ] Maximum attempts include the original request.
  • [ ] Retryable errors are explicitly classified.
  • [ ] Every request has a deadline or timeout.
  • [ ] Backoff is exponential and bounded.
  • [ ] Jitter prevents synchronized retries.
  • [ ] A shared budget limits aggregate retry traffic.
  • [ ] Non-idempotent operations have appropriate protection.
  • [ ] Provider-specific rate limits and Retry-After are respected.
  • [ ] Retry behavior is observable.
  • [ ] Bulkhead permit ownership is clearly defined.
  • [ ] Tests cover cancellation, concurrency, and exhaustion.
  • [ ] Replica count and aggregate retry capacity are understood.

Conclusion

Retries are useful, but unlimited retry behavior can turn a temporary dependency failure into a system-wide incident.

A maximum attempt count protects individual requests. A retry budget protects the service from the combined effect of those requests.

The key idea is simple: successful traffic can fund a limited amount of additional work, but retries should not be allowed to generate unlimited traffic when the system is already unhealthy.

In Go, a concurrency-safe token bucket provides a straightforward way to implement this policy. Combined with deadlines, exponential backoff, jitter, bulkheads, and circuit breakers, retry budgets help make failure behavior more predictable.

Resilience is not about trying again forever. It's about knowing when another attempt is worth the cost.

title: Encode Once, Answer Many: Internalizing Context via Parametric Flow
description:
arXiv:2610.38356v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Large language models are typically adapted to a task either by placing knowledge in the input context, which keeps it external and re-encodes it on every call, or by fine-tuning, which internalizes it but demands a costly round of optimization per task. We aim to internalize the knowledge carried by a context directly into model parameters, without per-task optimization and without keeping the context in the input at inference time. To this end, we propose CLIK, a context-conditioned parameter generator that maps a given context to LoRA parameters for internalizing knowledge in a single forward pass through a Transformer encoder with cross-attention, requiring no test-time gradient updates. Once the generated LoRA is inserted into a frozen base model, the model answers downstream queries from the query alone, having internalized the context into its weights rather than re-reading it. Because the adapter depends only on the context, it is generated once and reused for every query on the same document, so the cost of reading that document is amortized across queries. On document question answering, CLIK substantially improves over the no-context base model and outperforms existing hypernetwork-based generators, while remaining behind a base model that reads the context directly, and it carries over to multi-turn dialogue without any multi-turn-specific training. Analysis further shows that the context-dependent part of the generated adapter concentrates in a compact and specific substructure.

title: Designing Smart Home Apps That Handle Failure Well
description:
You tap a button to turn on a lamp. The button changes colour, a loading circle disappears, and the app says everything worked.

But the lamp is still off.

This small failure reveals a bigger design problem. The app has confused a request with a result. It knows someone pressed a button, but it does not know whether the device completed the action.

I run Techsslaash, a website covering everyday technology. Smart home products offer an interesting meeting point between consumer expectations and software design: people want simple controls, while developers must deal with devices, networks, delayed messages, and missing information.

This article uses a fictional smart lamp app to explore those decisions. It is a design walkthrough, not a report of hardware testing.

Disclosure: I run the website linked in this article. This article was prepared with AI assistance.

Start With One Device and One Clear Task

A useful first version does not need to control an entire house.

Start with one lamp. The user should be able to find it, understand its reported state, and request that it turn on or off.

That sounds simple, but it raises several questions:

  • Is the lamp connected?
  • How recently did it report its state?
  • Has the app sent a command?
  • Has the device acknowledged the command?
  • Has the lamp reported the requested state?
  • What should happen if no reply arrives?

Answering these questions is more useful than adding a dashboard full of controls.

For this example, the main task is:

Let someone control a lamp while clearly showing what the system knows.

That last part matters. When information is missing, the interface should make the gap visible.

Separate the Requested State From the Reported State

Suppose the lamp last reported that it was off.

The user taps “Turn on.” At that moment, the requested state becomes “On.” The reported state is still “Off” until fresh information arrives.

Treating these as separate values helps prevent misleading screens.

A simple design might track:

Information Example Purpose
Requested state On Records what the user wants
Reported state Off Records the latest device report
Request status Waiting for confirmation Explains the current operation
Last update 20 seconds ago Shows how fresh the information is
Connection status Unavailable Explains whether the device can be reached

The interface can then show:

Turning on. Waiting for the lamp to respond.

If the device reports that it is on, the app can update the display.

If no confirmation arrives within the chosen timeout, the message should reflect that uncertainty:

We could not confirm the change. Check the lamp before trying again.

A missing reply does not always mean the action failed. The device may have completed the action while its response was lost.

Even a device report has limits. A reported “On” state does not necessarily prove that a bulb is physically producing light. The wording should match what the system can actually observe.

Give Old Information a Visible Age

A device card that says “Off” looks definite.

But what if that information came from yesterday?

The app should distinguish a recent report from an old one. Otherwise, users may make decisions based on a state that is no longer accurate.

A more honest display could say:

Last reported: Off

Updated 15 minutes ago

Device currently unavailable

The developer must decide when information becomes stale. That threshold should reflect how the device communicates and how the information will be used.

A battery-powered sensor that reports occasionally may need different handling from a lamp expected to respond immediately.

Avoid choosing one freshness rule for every device simply because it makes the interface easier to build.

Also avoid presenting a cached reading as a live measurement. Saved information can be helpful during an outage, provided its age is clear.

Explain What “Offline” Means in Your App

“Offline” can describe several different problems.

The phone may have lost its connection. The home may have lost internet access. A cloud service may be unavailable. The device itself may have no power.

These situations can affect different features.

Local control may still work during an internet outage when the device, controller, and local network support it. That does not mean remote access, cloud notifications, or every automation will also continue working.

Instead of displaying one vague warning, explain the limitation you can confirm:

Remote access is unavailable. Local controls may still work when you are connected to the home network.

Only show that message if it accurately describes the product.

The same care applies to compatibility. A shared brand name or connection type does not guarantee that every feature will work together.

Consumer guides to smart home gadgets introduce the devices people may want to connect. For an actual integration, developers still need to check the specific model, supported controls, and manufacturer documentation.

Design Retries Around the Action

When a request times out, retrying it can seem like the obvious solution.

However, not all commands behave the same way.

“Set the lamp to on” describes a target state. “Toggle the lamp” means change whatever state it currently has.

If a toggle succeeds but its response is lost, sending the same toggle again could reverse the first action.

For a simple lamp controller, explicit requests such as “Turn on” and “Turn off” are often easier to reason about than repeated toggle commands.

Where the integration supports them, request identifiers can also help the receiving system recognise duplicate operations.

The interface should discourage repeated accidental taps while a request is pending. It should also provide a clear way forward if confirmation never arrives.

Most importantly, do not silently replay old commands after a long outage. A request made earlier may no longer match what the person wants.

Consider expiry rules, fresh state checks, and explicit user confirmation where appropriate.

Keep Manual Control Useful

A connected lamp still needs to work in a real home.

Someone may use a physical switch. Another household member may control it through a different app. An automation may change it while the current screen remains open.

The app should be prepared for changes it did not initiate.

Where the integration supports state updates, refresh the display when those updates arrive. If updates are delayed or unavailable, explain that the displayed state may be old.

Manual control also deserves thought during product selection and setup. If switching off power makes a smart bulb unreachable, the app should not imply that it can turn the bulb back on remotely.

For a beginner project, keep the scope limited to a non-critical device such as a lamp. Door locks, heating equipment, and other consequential systems need requirements and safeguards beyond this example.

Make Automation Easy to Understand and Pause

A routine that works correctly can still frustrate someone if they cannot understand why it ran.

Imagine a lamp turning off while a person is reading. Was it a schedule, a sensor, another user, or an error?

A useful automation history should explain the cause in ordinary language:

Reading lamp turned off at 10:00 PM because the evening schedule ran.

For each routine, make the basic parts visible:

  • What starts it.
  • Which conditions must be true.
  • What action it requests.
  • When it last ran.
  • Whether the result was confirmed.
  • How to pause it.

Manual overrides should also have a defined duration. If someone changes the lamp themselves, does the routine remain paused until the next schedule, for an hour, or until they resume it?

There is no single answer for every product. The important point is to choose a behaviour and make it understandable.

The same principle applies to technology intended to improve productivity: an automation should reduce repeated work without creating a new cycle of checking and correcting it.

Keep AI Suggestions Separate From Device Actions

An AI assistant might help explain an automation, summarise logs, or draft a routine.

Those tasks are different from allowing it to control physical devices without review.

A useful starting point is to let the assistant propose a change and show exactly what it would affect. The user can then inspect and approve it.

For a related first-person example, Christian Anderson’s DEV article explains how he set boundaries for an AI agent in his Home Assistant setup.

For the fictional lamp app, the AI feature is optional. The core controls should continue to work if that feature becomes unavailable.

Adding an assistant should not make a simple action harder to understand.

Write Error Messages That Offer a Next Step

“Error 504” may help someone investigating logs. It tells an ordinary user very little about the lamp.

A useful message should explain what is known and what the person can do next.

For example:

The lamp did not respond. Check that it has power, then try again.

However, do not claim to know the cause when the system has only detected a timeout.

“The lamp has no power” would be misleading unless there is evidence for that conclusion.

Technical information can remain available under a details section. This gives developers something useful to investigate without forcing every user to interpret service errors.

Also avoid repeated alerts for the same continuing outage. A persistent status message is often clearer than a fresh notification every few seconds.

Keep Household Data Out of Unnecessary Logs

Smart home activity can reveal personal routines.

Device names may contain room names or people’s names. Activity records may suggest when someone leaves home or goes to bed.

Collect the information needed to diagnose problems, and decide how long to keep it.

For a failed lamp request, useful diagnostic fields might include a request identifier, timestamp, response status, and integration name.

Access tokens, passwords, and unnecessary personal details should not appear in logs.

If the app supports several users, permissions should be enforced by the system handling the request. Hiding an administrator button in the interface is not enough.

Removing someone’s access should also affect their active credentials or sessions as appropriate, rather than only removing their name from a screen.

Test the Situations That Break a Good Demo

A successful demonstration proves that one path worked once.

A more useful test plan includes delays, missing replies, changing state, and recovery.

Test situation Behaviour to check
The lamp responds normally The display updates from the device report
The reply is delayed The app shows a pending state
The action succeeds but confirmation is lost The app shows uncertainty instead of claiming failure or success
The user taps repeatedly Duplicate requests are handled predictably
The device loses power Old state remains clearly labelled as old
Another user changes the lamp The display refreshes when new information arrives
The app restarts during a request It checks current state instead of blindly replaying the action
The connection returns Expired requests are not unexpectedly executed
A routine is paused Its status and later behaviour match the explanation
The user operates with a keyboard Controls remain reachable and clearly labelled

Mocks and simulated responses can help test interface behaviour before hardware is available.

They do not replace testing the real integration. A mock only behaves in the ways its author has anticipated.

Record which tests used simulated devices and which used actual hardware. This keeps the evidence behind the project clear.

Build Trust Through Clear Behaviour

A smart home app does not need dozens of features to be useful.

It needs to explain what it knows, what it has requested, and what remains uncertain.

For a first project, one lamp is enough to practise these decisions. Separate requested and reported states. Show the age of information. Handle retries carefully. Preserve manual control. Make routines easy to pause.

A polished screen is welcome, but predictable behaviour is what makes the app comfortable to live with.

When the connection fails, the user should still understand what happened and what to do next.

title: A 9.8 Linux TCP Bug Gave Remote Root in 53 Minutes. Patch Your Servers
description:
Most security bugs we write about need something from you first: a malicious extension you installed, a key you pasted into a dashboard, a library you forgot to update. This one needs nothing. CVE-2026-98432 is a race condition in the Linux kernel's IPv4 TCP code, and the only requirement for reaching the vulnerable path is that your server accepts TCP connections.

The bug was fixed upstream weeks ago. It became urgent this week, because three things landed on top of each other: Anthropic published a working remote root exploit, the Go team warned that Go services quietly opt into the exact feature that exploit uses, and Red Hat issued a Critical bulletin while several distributions still had no patched kernel to install.

This post sticks to what the kernel CVE team, Anthropic, the Go security team, Red Hat, Ubuntu, CIQ and Akamai/Linode have published. Then it turns that into a short, practical triage you can run today.

What happened, in order

  • Early October: the fix (commit e3f33b0a) landed in Linux 7.3-rc7 and was backported to the stable branches: 5.10.272, 5.15.223, 6.1.190, 6.6.159, 6.12.113, 6.18.56 and 7.2.10.
  • October 15: The Linux kernel CVE team published CVE-2026-98432 and scored it 9.8 (CVSS 3.1, network, no privileges, no user interaction). The bug goes back to kernel 4.4.
  • October 27: Anthropic's Frontier Red Team published a post on vulnerabilities found and exploited with Claude. One section describes a zero-click exploit for this CVE, written by an unreleased internal research model "after initial prompting".
  • October 29: The Go security team posted "Protecting against CVE-2026-98432" to golang-announce, pointing out that Go programs enable Multipath TCP (MPTCP) by default on Linux since Go 1.24.
  • October 30: Red Hat published bulletin RHSB-2026-016 with a Critical impact rating for RHEL 8, 9 and 10 and OpenShift, plus an interim firewall rule. CIQ published a mitigation guide for Rocky Linux, noting that no patched CIQ kernel had shipped yet. Akamai posted a customer advisory for Linode.
  • October 31 (01:55 UTC): Akamai's update says it is deploying mitigations for the known attack vector, has "no evidence of this vulnerability being exploited" on its compute platform, and strongly advises customers to apply OS updates from their upstream provider.

When I checked on October 31, CISA's Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog (version 2026.10.30) had no entry for this CVE. That means no confirmed in-the-wild exploitation has been listed, not that none is happening.

The bug, in plain terms

When a server receives a TCP SYN that carries IPv4 options (things like Record Route or Timestamp in the IP header), the kernel stores those options on the pending connection request. When the handshake completes, ownership of that options buffer moves to the new child socket without copying it.

The kernel advisory explains the race: another CPU can be processing a retransmitted SYN for the same request at the same moment and building a SYN-ACK from those same options. If the child socket gets freed first, the options memory is released with a plain kfree() while the other CPU is still reading it. That's a use-after-free. A similar problem exists when request sockets are migrated (net.ipv4.tcp_migrate_req=1 or a BPF_SK_REUSEPORT_SELECT_OR_MIGRATE program).

The fix is small: free those buffers with kfree_rcu() so they survive until concurrent readers are done. Small fixes for old race conditions are exactly the ones that sit unpatched in fleets, because nobody notices them until someone shows an exploit.

IPv6 is not affected by the first issue, according to the commit message, because the IPv6 path copies the options.

What Anthropic actually demonstrated

The Anthropic post is specific about the scope, and it's worth reading carefully rather than via headlines:

  • The exploit targets Linux servers with a multipath TCP listener. An attacker sends packets and ends up running an arbitrary command as root, with no credentials and no user interaction.
  • Stage one defeats KASLR remotely: the race makes the kernel copy extra bytes and send them back, and eventually one reply contains a kernel pointer.
  • Stage two uses the same bug to overwrite a callback pointer and run a chain of existing kernel functions that ends in a shell command.
  • The detail that matters most for defenders: a lost race only fails the handshake. It doesn't crash the box. An attacker can just keep retrying.
  • In their proof of concept, leaking a kernel pointer took 48 minutes, and reaching command execution took about five more.

Anthropic hasn't published the exploit code. The fact that a model built this chain is the reason the story spread so fast, but for your servers the practical point is simpler: a remote root exploit for this bug exists, and the technique is now publicly described.

The MPTCP detail, and why Go teams should read twice

MPTCP is an extension that lets one connection use several network paths. On Linux, applications opt in per socket, and the net.mptcp.enabled sysctl controls whether the kernel allows it at all. CIQ found it off by default on the RHEL-family kernels it tested; other distributions may differ, so check.

Here's the catch the Go team flagged: since Go 1.24, Go programs enable MPTCP by default for listening sockets on Linux. If your API gateway, a sidecar, a metrics exporter or an internal tool is written in Go and built with 1.24 or newer, it may be exposing exactly the kind of listener Anthropic's exploit targets, without anyone on your team having chosen that.

The Go team's guidance:

# Runtime: disable the MPTCP default for one program
GODEBUG=multipathtcp=0 ./your-service

// Build time: add to the main module's go.mod
godebug multipathtcp=0

But they are just as clear that this is a fragile mitigation. One forgotten MPTCP listener leaves the host exposed, and it assumes every viable exploit needs MPTCP. Their words: "the underlying bug is not specific to MPTCP." CIQ backed that up in testing: with net.mptcp.enabled=0, a plain TCP listener on every kernel they tested still answered a SYN carrying a Record Route option, which means the vulnerable code path was still reachable.

So: turning off MPTCP reduces exposure to the demonstrated exploit. It doesn't fix the bug.

Who is exposed

Red Hat's bulletin puts it plainly: the bug affects any system running a vulnerable kernel with IPv4 TCP enabled, and "systems accepting inbound TCP connections are most directly exposed." In practice:

  • VMs and bare-metal servers running RHEL 8/9/10 and rebuilds (Rocky, Alma), Ubuntu, Debian and others on affected kernels. Upstream lists RHEL 6 and 7 kernels as not affected.
  • Kubernetes nodes. Containers share the host kernel. Rebuilding your container images does nothing here. The node OS is what needs the patch.
  • Managed platforms. Akamai told Linode customers to apply OS updates to their workloads themselves. If you run your own VMs on any cloud, assume the kernel is your job unless your provider says otherwise.

When I checked Ubuntu's CVE tracker (last updated October 30), the main kernel packages for supported releases were still marked "Vulnerable" with fixes "work in progress", and CIQ had no patched kernels for the variants it checked. So for a lot of teams, "just patch" isn't available yet. That's why the next section has an interim step.

A triage you can run today

1. Inventory kernels. On every host that accepts inbound connections:

uname -r

Compare against your vendor's advisory, not just the upstream version list. Distro kernels backport fixes under their own version numbers.

2. Check whether MPTCP is on, and who is listening with it.

sysctl net.mptcp.enabled
ss -Mltn

CIQ notes that on newer kernels ss -Mltn shows mptcp rows for MPTCP listeners, while on some older ones it doesn't, so trust the sysctl there.

3. Find your Go binaries. For each service binary:

go version -m /path/to/binary | head -1

Anything built with Go 1.24 or newer listens with MPTCP by default (unless you've overridden it). Add GODEBUG=multipathtcp=0 to its environment as a stopgap, but don't stop there.

4. Apply the interim filter where no patched kernel exists. Red Hat's bulletin gives an nftables table that drops incoming IPv4 TCP packets that carry IP options (a header longer than 20 bytes):

table inet cve_2026_98432 {
    chain input {
        type filter hook input priority -310; policy accept;
        ip protocol tcp ip hdrlength > 5 counter drop
    }
}

sudo nft --check --file cve-2026-98432.nft
sudo nft --file cve-2026-98432.nft
sudo nft list table inet cve_2026_98432

Red Hat says normal application traffic should be fine, because ordinary TCP options live in the TCP header, not the IP header. They also say clearly that this reduces exposure but cannot fully prevent exploitation, and that you should test it before production. CIQ adds a gotcha worth knowing: stopping the stock nftables.service flushes the whole ruleset, including this table.

5. Patch and reboot as soon as your vendor ships. A kernel fix isn't live until the host runs the new kernel. Then remove the interim rule (sudo nft delete table inet cve_2026_98432) and record the running version.

6. Put the boring stuff first. Hosts that face the internet directly (load balancers, bastions, anything with a public IP) go first. Internal hosts behind a load balancer that terminates TCP are less exposed, but not immune to anything that can reach them from inside.

What we do on our projects

Most of what we build for clients is Django (plus some .NET) running on Linux servers, with Flutter and React front ends. For a kernel bug like this, our routine is the same every time: inventory first (which hosts accept inbound TCP, which kernel each runs), internet-facing hosts first, interim mitigation only where the vendor has no fix yet, and a scheduled reboot window instead of an ad-hoc one. The step this bug adds to our checklist is asking which processes on each host are Go binaries (proxies, exporters and CLI-installed agents count) and how they were built, because a language default is not something we used to think about during kernel triage. The slowest part is never the patch. It's finding every host that needs it.

What's still unclear

  • Whether hosts without an MPTCP listener can be exploited the same way. Anthropic only demonstrated the MPTCP case. The Go team says "it is possible that systems with no MPTCP listeners are vulnerable to similar attacks." Treat every vulnerable kernel as exposed.
  • Severity scores differ by source. The kernel CNA gives 9.8 (CVSS 3.1). Ubuntu's page also shows a CVSS 4.0 score of 8.3. Red Hat rates the impact Critical. The ranking doesn't change what you should do.
  • Patch timelines. These vary by distribution and are moving daily. Check your vendor's tracker rather than any blog post, including this one.

I'll update this post if exploitation in the wild is confirmed or major distributions ship fixes.

How many of your servers would you have to log into to answer "are we patched?"

Honestly, for most teams the answer is "all of them". Do you have a single place that shows the running kernel version of every host you own? And did anyone on your team know Go turned on MPTCP by default? Tell me in the comments.

title: Why My IQ Test Has a 15-Minute Timer (and Why That's Harder Than It Sounds)
description:
Why My IQ Test Has a 15-Minute Timer (and Why That's Harder Than It Sounds)

When I published my first post here about how the scoring on IQCognify works, a few people asked about the other design decision that shapes every result: the timer. The test gives you 15 minutes for the full run. That number wasn't picked to create pressure. It exists because of what the test is trying to measure — and enforcing it fairly in a browser turned out to be one of the harder engineering problems in the whole project.

Timing is part of the measurement

Working memory and processing speed are real components of cognitive ability, and every standardized test accounts for them. An untimed puzzle test mostly measures how long you're willing to sit there. A timed one measures something closer to how you actually think: pattern recognition under mild constraint, decisions made without infinite deliberation.

But the moment you add a timer, you take on an obligation: the clock has to be fair. A fair timer never punishes someone for a slow network, a background tab, or a laptop that decided to run a virus scan mid-test.

The three ways a browser timer lies

1. Tab switches. Browsers throttle JavaScript timers in inactive tabs — a setInterval that fires every second in the foreground may fire once a minute in the background. Count ticks and your clock drifts. The fix is to never count ticks at all: record a start timestamp, and compute elapsed time from Date.now() differences every time the UI updates. Throttling then affects how often the display refreshes, never how much time has actually passed.

2. Slow asset loading. If question images load lazily, a user on a slow connection spends their 15 minutes watching spinners. Every question asset in the test is tiny and preloaded before the clock starts, so the measured time is thinking time, not download time.

3. Server round-trips. If the timer lives on the server, latency becomes part of the test. The whole run — questions, timing, scoring — happens client-side. The server never gets a vote on how long you took.

The edge case nobody warns you about

Sleep. A laptop closing mid-test can produce a four-hour "elapsed time" on wake. The honest handling is to detect a discontinuous jump in elapsed time and end the session rather than score it — an unscored attempt is a better outcome than a garbage score presented as real. Silent data corruption is worse than a lost session, in testing and everywhere else.

Why 15 minutes

Long enough that the constraint is mild for most people, short enough that speed still differentiates. It's a calibration choice, and like the scoring model, it should be a deliberate one — if you build anything similar, decide what your timer is for before you decide how long it is.

The test itself is live at IQCognify if you want to see the timer behave — 27 questions, no signup, and your time is measured by timestamps, not ticks.

title: Surviving Zone Capacity Is the Failover Test Most Teams Never Run
description:
Surviving zone capacity decides whether a zone failover works, and Google's europe-west2 incident on October 19 is a documented case of a failover that had somewhere to go and not enough room when it got there. According to Google's incident report, a power failure took one zone offline, and the load redirected to the other zones saturated their compute slots and processing capacity. Customers saw elevated admission queues, delayed database failover completions and intermittent HTTP 500 and 503 errors.

The zone loss was the trigger. Surviving zone capacity was the second failure, and it is the one architecture reviews rarely measure. This Field Note covers what the report says, what a zone-loss capacity test has to record, and what the test deliberately leaves out. The incident details below are attributed to Google's incident page as it currently stands. Its expanded report includes root-cause and remediation details, while an older preliminary-report notice remains on the page.

What Google's Incident Report Says Happened

Google's incident page records the incident from October 19 at 23:00 to October 20 at 05:08 US/Pacific, a duration of 6 hours 8 minutes, which is 06:00 to 12:08 UTC on October 20. The page's older preliminary section gives 05:10 instead, so the timestamps are not fully consistent across the report. It attributes the zone loss to an underground utility cable fault that cut primary feed A while feed B was locked out for repairs. The facility PLCs sensed voltage upstream of the isolated feed B breaker, concluded a healthy utility source was available and never commanded a generator start, which Google’s root cause section calls a misconfiguration of the PLC logic. When the UPS batteries ran down, servers, network equipment and local storage in europe-west2-b lost power.

The report then describes the part that matters here. Redirected query executions, high-availability database failovers and compute workloads saturated the available compute slots and processing capacity in the other zones. Google reports the symptoms as elevated admission queues, delayed database failover completions and intermittent HTTP 500 and 503 errors.

For mitigation, the report lists traffic isolation, scheduler and capacity adjustments to prioritize active customer reservations, restoration and testing of the generator automation, progressive infrastructure reactivation and controlled traffic readmission. Those are accounts of what Google did during this incident. I treat them as history, not as a property to design against and not as guidance on what a customer should configure.

That is a cloud strategy assumption hiding inside a resilience diagram: that the capacity you fail over to exists, unclaimed, at the moment you need it.

Surviving Zone Capacity Is a Separate Failure From the Zone Loss

A three-zone design draws an arrow from the failed zone to the two that remain. The arrow is a routing statement. It says traffic can go there. It says nothing about whether the compute, the admission path and the database replicas in those zones can take it. Surviving zone capacity answers that, and in europe-west2 the report describes the gap where the answer should have been.

Your failover is also not the only one running. In a regional event, every affected tenant's load is redirected into the same surviving zones at the same moment, and the retries from clients that lost connections arrive with it. This is reasoning from how shared capacity works, not a claim from the report, but the report's description of saturation across the other zones is consistent with it.

Two earlier posts frame the neighboring questions. Two Nodes Can Preserve Availability. They Can't Preserve N+1 Capacity. covers capacity after a failure when the operator owns the nodes. In a public cloud region you cannot add a node to a surviving zone. You hold a claim on capacity the provider holds, and the question is what that claim is worth during the event. The HA strategy playbook states the pattern in one row of a table: retries storm the surviving zones and capacity limits reject failover. The europe-west2 report is documented evidence for that row, and it adds what the row lacks, which is a way to measure it.

A Second Mechanism, Kept Separate: Cross-Zone Control-Plane Validation

Google’s preliminary report describes synchronous control-plane validation dependencies across zonal boundaries; the expanded report shortens this to control-plane dependencies across zonal boundaries. Calls to metadata and catalog components in the offline zone timed out, causing initial job-submission stalls and API latency spikes. This is a separate mechanism from compute-capacity exhaustion in the surviving zones, and I am keeping it out of the capacity argument on purpose.

Capacity saturation shows up as queues and slow failovers because the surviving zones have no room. A validation dependency is about operations that depend on a check spanning zones, and it can delay or block them whether or not room exists. A post-incident review that files both under "the other zones were overloaded" will fix one mechanism and miss the other. The test below covers the first. The second needs its own test.

The Zone-Loss Capacity Test

The artifact is a table that measures surviving zone capacity for each workload tier, from a calculation first and a constrained rehearsal second. A real region cannot be told to lose a zone, so the first pass is arithmetic against your own peak numbers. Its job is to put a number where the diagram has an arrow.

Record The question it answers Where the number comes from
Displaced demand How much compute, memory and database failover load does the lost zone carry at peak, including client retries? Your metrics at peak, not the daily average
Surviving capacity What can the remaining zones serve right now, split into capacity you have reserved and capacity you would have to obtain on demand? Quotas, reservations and what autoscaling can actually acquire under contention
Admission queue How long between a scale-up request and a running instance when every tenant is asking at once? Observed provisioning latency under constraint, not the documented happy path
Database failover completion How long until the promoted replica accepts writes while the displaced load is arriving? A failover run under load, not at idle
Per-workload outcome For each service: served, degraded, queued, rejected or failed over late? One row per workload tier, signed by the service owner

The last row is the point. The test does not output a headroom percentage. It outputs a decision for each service about what happens when the load does not fit. A workload that tolerates a queue and a workload that returns a 503 to a customer are different business decisions, and the table forces someone to make them before the event.

A reservation is a zone-scoped claim, as Compute Engine's About reservations page describes it: capacity set aside in a specific zone. That makes the split in the second row a real input. It is a question about which of your claims on the surviving zones are held and which are hoped for.

The headroom this test justifies will appear on a cost dashboard as idle capacity. The test does not prescribe how much to hold. It makes the decision visible, and that is all it is for.

What the Test Leaves Out

The zone-loss capacity test assumes failover runs and asks only whether it has room. Whether failover is configured and exercised at all is the subject of Multi-Cloud Failover Is Mostly Theater, and this test does not repeat that argument.

It does not test whether state is recoverable after a zone loss, which is the boundary drawn in Multi-AZ Is Not a Recoverability Boundary. It does not test shared network capacity inside a region, the failure domain mapped in GCP's us-west1 Outage Mapped a Failure Domain Your Service List Couldn't. Those are different failure domains with their own tests. It does not cover the cross-zone validation dependency described above, and it says nothing about storage recovery after power returned.

Within those limits, it measures surviving zone capacity and answers one question a three-zone diagram cannot: when one zone is gone, which of your workloads fit in the other two.

Architect's Verdict

Zone redundancy is a claim about where load can go. Surviving zone capacity is a claim about whether it fits. The europe-west2 report documents the distance between the two, and most architectures are drawn as if that distance were zero.

The real problem is that nobody owns the number. The capacity lives in the provider's pool, your claim on it lives in a reservation or an assumption, and the gap between them is visible for the first time during the outage. Until someone writes the per-workload outcome down, the failover plan is a routing diagram with a hope attached.

The arrow was drawn. The number on it was never measured.

Originally published at rack2cloud.com

title: How Delphi ships 100 times a day with its Python backend on Vercel
description:
Delphi on Vercel

  • 10 engineers with no dedicated infrastructure role

  • Everyone ships code, including product and design

  • 100+ production deploys a day behind feature flags

Delphi builds digital minds. They capture what someone has written, recorded, and taught, so anyone can tap that expertise on demand. Delphi is “a destination where you can find and interact with interesting minds,” says founding engineer Spencer Schoeben.

Nobody has built a digital mind network before, so Delphi figures out what to build by shipping features and watching how people use them. That only works if the product is fast to change. "If we are going to win, we need to have an excellent developer and agentic experience," Spencer says. "Otherwise, we could not adapt to how fast our user’s demands change."

Delphi's frontend had run on Vercel since day one. "The frontend has always been easy," Spencer says, "but the backend was a nightmare." Six months ago, the team rebuilt its Python backend on Vercel as well. Today the whole team ships to production 100+ times a day.

Building a Python backend that's easy to work on

The backend slowed every change

Delphi's backend previously ran on AWS, with ECS, Docker Desktop, and local databases. In the earliest days, the setup worked because the team was small and much of the context lived in people’s heads. As Delphi grew, that made onboarding slower than the team wanted: getting a new engineer to their first deploy took a full day of environment setup. 

Delphi could have fixed that without leaving AWS. But fixing it properly would have meant designing and owning the infrastructure themselves, and the team didn't want to own infrastructure at all. "That is not our current goal as a company," Spencer says. After moving the backend to Vercel, new engineers could get to production much faster, with the same deploy workflow the rest of the team used every day.

Workflows and Queues made the move possible

When Delphi was founded, Vercel Workflows and Vercel Queues didn't exist. Without them, Spencer says, the move would have been much harder, if possible at all.

Delphi's backend depends on long-running work and queued background jobs. Digital minds need durable agents that generate content ahead of time, plus ingestion that turns a person's books and talks into a knowledge graph.

Workflows handles the long-running work and Queues handle the background jobs. Neither requires setup. A developer writes the workflow or the queue handler as a function in the codebase, and Vercel provisions what's needed to run it on deploy.

100+ deploys a day, straight to production

Moving the backend to Vercel let Delphi stop treating backend changes as heavyweight releases and ship them as everyday product work. The team used to deploy to staging, then production. Now it skips the middle step, shipping 100+ times a day behind feature flags and running A/B tests instead of batching changes into a release.

Vercel Agent's anomaly detection watches production at that pace, flagging when something is misbehaving and why. Before, Spencer says, they often would not have known.

Moving fast has helped clear a backlog of small experiments that never used to make the priority list. Many of those experiments test how to turn a visitor into an owner, someone who arrives to talk to a mind and leaves having started their own.

Shipping isn't limited to engineers, either. Delphi's CPO and its growth teams build and deploy dashboards, prototypes, and experiments themselves, which Spencer says wouldn't have happened on the old setup.

Infrastructure built for agents and engineers

Preview deployments are how agents check their work

Delphi's engineers hand problems to cloud agents, with very little development happening locally. The preview deployment is where they first see what the agent built. Vercel preview deployments give every push its own live URL, so anyone can check the result from a phone or a Slack thread without pulling the branch.

When an agent fails, it's usually because it couldn't get at the information it needed. Vercel exposes the data and controls agents need through the SDK, MCP, and CLI, so an agent can read logs, inspect a deployment, or change an environment variable through whichever it's using. For Delphi, agents are now the main users of those tools, so the platform has to be as easy for them as it is for people.

An internal agent on Sandbox for customer success

Delphi's own agents run on Vercel as well. One of them, an internal agent on Vercel Sandbox, simplifies working with the company's codebase. The customer success team uses Slack to ask it about reported issues, find the problem, and hand an engineer a root cause and a proposed fix.

Edge cases used to fall through the cracks. "Before, we either couldn't get to everything, or we had to spend way more time than we had available," Spencer says. "Now we have an agent they can just ask in Slack."

Vercel Sandbox gives the agent an isolated environment with a file system, where it can check out the codebase, run it, and pull in whatever data a question needs. The agent itself is built with eve, Vercel's agent framework. Delphi's first version ran on a hosted agent platform and could only use the integrations that platform offered. In eve, tools are code Delphi writes, so when a question needs one that doesn't exist, the team adds it.

AI Gateway picks the model for each mind

Delphi's chat traffic runs through AI Gateway. Every digital mind is different, and some come out better on one model than another, so Delphi picks the model for each customer and adjusts as its own evals change. When a new model ships, open-source or otherwise, Delphi can route to it the same day.

Gateway also handles failover. Before, Delphi worked directly with a model provider to line up fallback capacity on other clouds, and it was hard. "With AI Gateway, we always know that we're going to get the fallbacks if they exist," Spencer says.

What's next

Delphi's first chapter was training digital minds and letting people chat with them. Now it is building the interface beyond chat. Spencer describes a search page where you bring a question, get perspectives from several minds at once, and have the page adapt to who you are.

That work runs as long-running agents on Workflows, with AI Gateway supplying whichever model each experiment calls for.

About Delphi: Delphi is a platform that turns a person's knowledge, thinking, and voice into a digital mind others can talk to. Anyone can create their own Delphi to make their expertise discoverable and accessible, part of a network of minds people can seek out, learn from, and converse with.

title: Your API returns 200. Your agent still gets garbage.
description:
Here is a failure no dashboard will show you.

An API your agent calls every morning answers 200 OK. The JSON schema has not changed. Every field is still there. But 42 of the 50 products now have "price": null, and updated_at has not moved in months.

Your uptime check is green. Your schema diff is green. A person looking at this data would notice the empty column in two seconds. Your agent does not stop: it writes a confident report from what it received, and nobody finds out until a customer does.

Status codes say the server answered. Schemas say the shape is valid. Neither says the data your agent depends on is still there.

Test the data, from the consumer's side

So I built a small tool that treats this as a testing problem. A contract says what your agent needs from a source, and a check tells you when the source stops delivering it:

  • Coverage: at least 90% of items carry a usable price. null, "", [] and {} do not count.
  • Freshness: the newest updated_at is less than 3 days old.
  • Volume: the list has at least 25 items, so an empty array is a failure and not a success.
  • Distinct values: the column is not stuck on one value, like a price of 0 everywhere.

You do not have to write that by hand, and you do not need the provider's cooperation. You put a local proxy between your agent and the source, and it learns the contract from the real calls. It stores shapes, never values.

Try it in a minute 

git clone https://github.com/driftprobe/driftprobe && cd driftprobe && npm install

# A demo API, and the proxy in front of it
node examples/demo-api.mjs &
node bin/driftprobe.mjs record --upstream http://127.0.0.1:4010 --port 8787 &

# Your agent calls the proxy instead of the API
curl -s http://127.0.0.1:8787/products > /dev/null
curl -s http://127.0.0.1:8787/products > /dev/null

# Learn a contract from those calls
node bin/driftprobe.mjs learn --observed .driftprobe/observed.jsonl --out-dir contracts

# The source degrades, and still answers 200 OK
curl -s -X POST http://127.0.0.1:4010/__break
curl -s -o /dev/null -w "HTTP %{http_code}\n" http://127.0.0.1:8787/products

Then the check:

$ node bin/driftprobe.mjs check contracts/*.yaml
GET /products
  x price: only 16% of 50 items carry a value (contract: at least 90%)
  x updated_at: newest value is 289 days old (contract: 3d)

1 contract(s): 0 ok, 1 broken, 0 could not be checked

Exit code 1, so it fails your CI. It also works on MCP tools, including over server-sent events.

How often does this really happen?

I do not know yet, and I could not find anyone who has measured it. So I am measuring it.

The official MCP registry listed 53,434 servers on 31 October 2026. I took a sample of 2,000 remote endpoints that do not declare a required credential, in a stable random order, at most 5 per domain:

  • 655 asked for credentials anyway
  • 1,115 answered with their tool list
  • 770 declared at least one read only tool
  • 415 returned data from a read only call with neutral arguments

From those, I picked 100 that return real lists, across 98 domains. I call one read only tool on each, twice a day, for 30 days, and record shapes only. I will publish the results whatever they show, including if almost nothing breaks.

To avoid crying wolf, the analysis only counts a break when the same rule fails on consecutive observations, and I tested the method on simulated servers where nothing changes: at most 2% get flagged.

What it does not do

It does not know if a value is true, only if it is there, fresh and varied. It learns what your agent receives: narrowing that to what your agent actually reads is manual for now (--fields name,price).

If you run LangGraph, quietfail watches behaviour from inside the agent, which is complementary. ToolBench grades how well MCP tools are defined, and FlareCanary watches tool schemas. This one sits outside the agent and looks at the data that comes back.

The code is MIT: github.com/driftprobe/driftprobe. If one of your sources has failed this way, I would like to hear how you found out.
