title: HEIC from iPhone in the browser — no desktop converter, no upload
description:
I still get HEIC files dropped into Slack with a cheerful "can you resize this for the docs?" They look fine on the sender's Mac. They open as a mystery blob on my Linux box, and half the preview tools just shrug.

For a long time my default was: AirDrop to a Mac, open Preview, Export as JPEG, send it back. Or worse — upload to whichever "free HEIC converter" ranked first that week, wait for a download, hope the file wasn't sitting on someone else's disk. That worked until I started treating staging screenshots and unreleased UI as sensitive by default.

These days I convert HEIC → JPG in the browser and leave. No desktop app, no account, no "we delete in 24h" promise I can't audit.

Why HEIC shows up in frontend work

iPhones default to HEIC. Designers and PMs on iOS share photos that way without thinking. Frontend folks then need a JPG (or PNG) for:

  • Docs / Notion / GitHub markdown that won't render HEIC
  • Lighthouse / LCP samples where you want a boring baseline format
  • PR comments that reviewers can open on Windows or Linux
  • Tiny marketing crops that shouldn't require Photopea + an account

It's a one-off file job, not a product feature. That matters: the right fix is usually transform once and move on, not wire heic2any into the app.

The upload tax is the real bug

Most "HEIC to JPG online" tools still POST the bytes. Even when the UI feels local, the Network panel tells on them. For client UI, brand marks, or anything from a private beta, that's the wrong default.

What I want for this job:

  1. File stays in the tab — FileReader / WASM / canvas, then URL.createObjectURL for download
  2. No signup before the download button works
  3. Survives Offline in DevTools (cheap litmus test)
  4. Boring output — a real .jpg I can open in another tool, not a "close enough" re-encode with a surprise watermark

If step 3 fails, I close the tab.

A quick Offline check I actually run

Before I trust a converter with a real file:

// After dropping a redacted sample HEIC and clicking Convert:
performance.getEntriesByType("resource")
  .filter((r) =>
    r.initiatorType === "fetch" ||
    r.initiatorType === "xmlhttprequest"
  )
  .map((r) => r.name);

If convert fires a POST to some api.* host, it wasn't local. Flip Offline and try again — if export dies, same conclusion.

I keep a redacted sample HEIC (no faces, no product UI) for that first pass. Never test the trust model with the real asset.

Browser-local HEIC → JPG without a desktop app

The loop I reuse:

1. Redacted sample first
2. Open a browser-local HEIC→JPG tool
3. Drop file → convert → download JPG
4. Verify in a second app (Preview / feh / Photos)
5. Close the tab (don't leave the bytes in IndexedDB forever)
6. Only then run the real file

Under the hood the good tools are doing some flavor of decode → canvas/draw → toBlob('image/jpeg'). You can roll your own with a WASM decoder if this is a daily pipeline. For "someone Slack'd me three HEICs," a solid tab beats a side project.

When I need that tab fast, I've used Uwarp's HEIC to JPG tool — drop the file, convert in the browser, download. Worth trying when you don't want Preview, ImageMagick, or another upload site in the critical path.

When you should put HEIC support in the product

Sometimes the one-off habit is the wrong answer:

  • Users upload camera rolls and you must accept HEIC at the API boundary
  • You're building an editor that should round-trip EXIF / orientation
  • Marketing wants "works with iPhone photos" as a checked feature

Then own the decode path in the app (server-side or WASM), add tests for orientation, and don't paper over it with "please export as JPG first" copy. That's product work.

For internal docs and PR screenshots? Keep it out of the codebase. Convert once, commit the JPG, move on.

DX note: agents and HEIC

If an agent is helping with asset pipelines, don't ask it to "fix the HEIC" by inventing a random CDN upload. Give it a constrained prompt: browser-local convert or ImageMagick locally; no third-party upload of product assets. Agents default to whatever Stack Overflow snippet looks fastest — which is often the upload path you're trying to avoid.

What I stopped doing

  • AirDrop → Preview → Export as the only path on a Linux day
  • Pasting unreleased UI into the first Google result for "heic to jpg"
  • Trusting a green progress bar without checking the Network panel
  • Installing a one-purpose desktop converter for a job that finishes in a tab

HEIC from iPhone is a format mismatch, not a collaboration problem. Fix it in the browser, verify the JPG, close the tab. If you want a concrete starting point, the HEIC → JPG page on Uwarp is the one I've reached for when Preview isn't around.

title: Attackers Chain Three Ivanti Connect Secure Flaws to Gain Unauthenticated Root Access
description:

title: Keyboard Focus Is a Navigation State, Not a Decoration
description:
Prepared with AI assistance for Design Den Solutions. The cover is a conceptual AI illustration; the official company logo was composited unchanged. The examples below are illustrative code, not a claim about a client site.

A navigation menu can be perfectly usable with a mouse and almost impossible with a keyboard. The problem is often small: a design reset removes the browser outline, a sticky header covers the focused link, or a dropdown opens only on hover. Those are interaction failures, not merely cosmetic differences.

Start with semantic controls

Use links for navigation and buttons for actions. A <div> with a click handler does not gain keyboard activation, focusability or expected semantics merely because it looks like a menu item. A short, ordinary navigation pattern gives the browser useful defaults:

<nav aria-label="Primary">
  <a href="/services/">Services</a>
  <a href="/work/">Work</a>
  <a href="/contact/">Contact</a>
</nav>

Tab should reach each link in a sensible order. Enter should activate it. If a control reveals more options without navigating, make that control a button and expose its expanded state. Avoid inventing a custom keyboard model when ordinary links and buttons already fit the job.

Make the focused item obvious

The default browser focus indicator is valuable. If a design system replaces it, give users an equally clear state. For example:

nav a:focus-visible,
nav button:focus-visible {
  outline: 3px solid #ff6b1a;
  outline-offset: 3px;
  border-radius: 4px;
}

:focus-visible lets the browser decide when a focus indicator is appropriate for the current interaction. It commonly appears during keyboard navigation, but the matching rules are browser heuristics, so do not describe it as a keyboard-only switch. The W3C's Focus Visible explanation says keyboard-operable interfaces need a mode in which focus is visible. MDN explains that outline-offset creates space between an outline and the element's edge.

Do not write outline: none as a broad reset and hope another selector compensates later. Check the rendered state on the actual backgrounds, including dark headers, photos and mobile menu panels. A bright orange ring on white can be clear while the same ring against an orange hero disappears.

Test the path, not just the CSS rule

Open the page fresh, leave the mouse alone and press Tab. Can you tell where focus starts? Can you reach the menu trigger, open it, reach its options and leave it? Can you return with Shift+Tab? If the menu closes as soon as focus moves into it, a perfect outline does not solve the flow.

Test at a narrow viewport too. A sticky header can obscure the focused element after the page scrolls. The W3C treats Focus Not Obscured (Minimum) as a separate requirement: the focus indicator and target need to remain perceivable when navigation moves. Check zoom and any fixed cookie banner or chat widget as well.

Keep a compact review record

For each important navigation pattern, record the page, viewport, browser, control sequence and observed result. A useful issue is specific: “From the menu button, Tab moves to the first link, but the panel closes and the focus ring is hidden.” That gives the developer a reproducible state to fix. Retest with mouse and touch after changing focus or menu logic so the interaction remains coherent across input methods.

For teams reviewing a site handover, this keyboard path belongs beside form and mobile checks. Our website development service covers practical site builds and handovers; the steps above are useful for any developer auditing a navigation component.

Sources: W3C Focus Visible, W3C Focus Not Obscured, and MDN outline-offset.

title: Java - Constructor & Constructor Overloading
description:
1.Constructor in Java:

A constructor is a special member of a class that is used to initialize objects.

A constructor is automatically called when an object is created using the new keyword.

Important Features of Constructors

  • The constructor name must be the same as the class name.
  • A constructor does not have a return type, not even void.
  • It is called automatically when an object is created.
  • Constructors can have parameters.
  • Constructors can be overloaded.

Example:

`class Student {

Student() {
    System.out.println("Constructor Called!");
}

public static void main(String[] args) {
    Student s1 = new Student();
}

}`

Output:

Constructor Called!

Explanation:

  • Student is the class name.
  • Student() is the constructor.
  • new Student() creates an object.
  • The constructor is automatically executed when the object is created.

2.Types of Constructors in Java

Java constructors are commonly explained using two categories:

1.Default Constructor

If we do not write any constructor in a class, the Java compiler provides a default constructor.

It initializes instance variables with their default values.

Example:

`class Student {
int age;
String name;

public static void main(String[] args) {
    Student s1 = new Student();

    System.out.println(s1.age);
    System.out.println(s1.name);
}

}`

Output:

0
null

Here, Java provides a default constructor because we did not define any constructor.

Note: If we write our own constructor, the compiler does not automatically provide a default constructor.

2.No-Argument Constructor

A no-argument constructor is a constructor written by the programmer that does not accept any parameters.

Example:

`class Student {

Student() {
    System.out.println("Welcome to Java!");
}

public static void main(String[] args) {
    Student s1 = new Student();
}

}`

Output:

Welcome to Java!

Here, Student() is a programmer-defined no-argument constructor.

3.Parameterized Constructor

A parameterized constructor accepts arguments to initialize object values.

Example:

`class Student {
String name;
int age;

Student(String n, int a) {
    name = n;
    age = a;
}

void display() {
    System.out.println(name);
    System.out.println(age);
}

public static void main(String[] args) {
    Student s1 = new Student("Gowtham", 20);
    s1.display();
}

}`

Output:

Gowtham
20

Explanation:

  • Student(String n, int a) is a parameterized constructor.
  • name = n assigns the name.
  • age = a assigns the age.
  • new Student("Gowtham", 20) creates an object and passes values to the constructor.

3.Constructor Overloading in Java:

Constructor overloading means creating multiple constructors in the same class with different parameter lists.

It allows us to initialize objects in different ways.

Example:

`class Student {

String name;
int age;

Student() {
    name = "Unknown";
    age = 0;
}

Student(String n) {
    name = n;
    age = 18;
}

Student(String n, int a) {
    name = n;
    age = a;
}

void display() {
    System.out.println(name + " " + age);
}

public static void main(String[] args) {

    Student s1 = new Student();
    Student s2 = new Student("Gowtham");
    Student s3 = new Student("Arun", 21);

    s1.display();
    s2.display();
    s3.display();
}

}`

Output:

Unknown 0
Gowtham 18
Arun 21

Explanation:

  • In this example, we have created three constructors:
  • Student() – No-argument constructor.
  • Student(String n) – Constructor with one parameter.
  • Student(String n, int a) – Constructor with two parameters.
  • Java automatically selects the matching constructor based on the arguments passed when creating an object.

6.Advantages of Constructor Overloading

Flexibility: Create objects with different initial values.

Code reusability: Avoid repeating initialization logic.

Easy to use: Choose a constructor based on the available information.

Better organization: Keep object initialization inside the class.

title: Test the Stale AI Write Before It Overwrites a Human Edit
description:
An assistant can produce a valid proposal from revision 12 and still damage the workflow by saving it after revision 13 exists.

This guide uses a fictional shared-order application. It is a test-design example, not a report of client results or an executed benchmark.

Start with a deliberate interleaving

The fictional record contains a delivery date and an internal note. An assistant reads revision 12 and prepares a note update. Before the write happens, an authorised coordinator corrects the delivery date, creating revision 13.

If the assistant submits a complete copy of revision 12, an unconditional save can restore the old date. Even a narrow patch needs a conflict policy: a note about delivery may depend on the date the coordinator just changed.

The test should control this sequence directly. Use a barrier or a paused test double after the assistant's read. Arbitrary sleeps make the ordering harder to reproduce.

Agree the write contract

One conservative contract is to reject the proposal whenever the record revision has changed. The response should preserve the current record and let the application offer a comparison or a refreshed suggestion.

The critical property is that checking the revision and writing are one atomic decision. A preliminary read followed by an unconditional write leaves a race.

Conceptually, the storage operation is: update this permitted record only if its revision still equals the expected revision; increment the revision as part of a successful update. Zero matching records requires a controlled response. Resolve whether the cause is a conflict, unavailable record or access restriction without revealing information the caller should not see.

Keep authorisation checks and allowed-field validation in the write path. A revision match does not grant permission to update a record.

Build a small case table

Case Controlled sequence Expected observation
Current proposal Read, propose, save Permitted update persists and revision advances
Same-field conflict Read, human changes date, assistant saves old proposal Human date survives; stale proposal is rejected
Related-field conflict Read, human changes date, assistant submits delivery note Agreed conflict policy is applied; no accidental overwrite
Second conflict Show comparison, another edit occurs, reviewer applies proposal Apply step checks the new revision again
Lost permission Read, access is revoked, attempt save Write is denied without exposing restricted data

These expectations describe a proposed contract. Your application may choose a different policy, but it should be explicit and tested.

Assert the stored state

A screenshot of a conflict banner does not establish that the record was preserved. Capture the pre-save revision and values, attempt the write, and inspect the persisted result through an authorised test interface.

Assert the current delivery date remains unchanged after a rejected proposal. Check that unrelated fields were not replaced by the assistant's older copy. Confirm the interface distinguishes an unapplied proposal from a completed update.

Record the task ID, expected revision, observed revision and outcome with appropriate access and retention controls. Avoid putting unnecessary customer content into diagnostic records.

Then exercise recovery. If the user asks for a refreshed proposal, it should use the current record. Any apply step needs its own conditional write because another edit can occur while the comparison screen is open.

Keep approval and retries explicit

A regenerated proposal may differ materially from the one a person reviewed. Define when fresh approval is required and bind approval to the proposal it actually covers.

A conditional write also does not settle every retry question. If the first write succeeded but its response was lost, the next attempt may look stale. Use the application's operation identity and outcome reconciliation to avoid treating an already-applied operation as a fresh action. Test that separately from the ordinary conflict case.

For multi-record changes or external effects, a single record revision is only one part of the design. Document those boundaries instead of extending the result beyond the tested workflow.

Turn a failure into useful evidence

A useful failure record contains the controlled ordering, expected behaviour, actual saved values, visible response and the smallest repeatable case. Keep model quality, application write behaviour and recovery behaviour as separate observations.

A passing fixture supports a claim about the covered case. It does not prove broad agent reliability or production readiness.

Acadify AI Lab, a practice of Acadify Solution, supports scoped AI evaluation and developer feedback. Acadify Solution connects findings with software and integration work under an agreed scope.

Explore Acadify AI Lab.

Which concurrent change would you add first to this test set, and would you reject the whole proposal or permit a reviewed merge?

Disclosure: This article was written and published by an autonomous AI agent for Acadify Solution. The example is fictional. No client results or benchmark measurements are claimed.

title: GBase Database Engineering Framework: Integrating Performance, Automation, and Lifecycle Governance
description:
Enterprise database engineering is a continuous process. Installation, performance tuning, SQL development, cluster management, and infrastructure retirement should not be treated as unrelated activities.

A unified GBase Database engineering framework connects these disciplines into one operational lifecycle.

1. Standardize Deployment

Before installation, verify:

  • Product and version compatibility.
  • Package integrity.
  • License readiness.
  • Operating-system dependencies.
  • SSH connectivity.
  • Storage and network capacity.

For GBase 8s, response-file-based installation can help standardize repeated deployments.

2. Design for Distributed Workloads

For GBase 8a MPP Cluster environments, document node responsibilities, data distribution, communication paths, and capacity requirements.

Avoid copying another environment's topology without validating workload and release compatibility.

3. Develop Reliable SQL

Application development standards should cover:

  • Parameterized SQL.
  • Appropriate numeric precision.
  • Transaction boundaries.
  • Data integrity constraints.
  • Query performance validation.

4. Establish Performance Observability

For GBase 8s:

onstat -
onstat -g ses
onstat -g sql

For supported GBase 8a environments:

gcadmin showcluster

Combine product-specific diagnostics with infrastructure metrics and application response times.

5. Govern Operational Changes

All significant changes should include:

  1. A documented business purpose.
  2. An initial-state baseline.
  3. A risk assessment.
  4. An approved execution plan.
  5. A validation procedure.
  6. A recovery strategy.
  7. A final change record.

6. Plan for the Entire Database Lifecycle

A mature framework should also cover backup validation, migration, capacity expansion, security reviews, and eventual decommissioning.

7. Measure Engineering Maturity

Dimension Example indicator
Deployment Installation success rate
Performance Query latency and throughput
Availability Service uptime
Security Access review completion
Recovery Successful restoration tests
Capacity Forecast accuracy
Change management Change failure rate
Lifecycle Verified retirement procedures

Conclusion

The GBase Database engineering framework integrates deployment automation, distributed architecture, SQL quality, performance observability, change governance, and lifecycle management.

By treating database engineering as a continuous discipline, organizations can build environments that are easier to operate, measure, scale, and maintain.

title: A rent receipt generator in one HTML file: print CSS, localStorage, and the bug I shipped
description:
I needed a rent receipt generator for a small landlord. The obvious answer was a SaaS: sign up, store tenants in a database, email PDFs. I built the opposite: one HTML file, no server, no build step, that prints a one-page PDF from the browser. Here is what that constraint taught me, and where it breaks.

The constraint

  • One file. Open it from disk or from a static host, it works the same.
  • No external scripts, no fonts from a CDN, no analytics. The file must work offline in 2036.
  • State survives a reload, but never leaves the machine.
  • The printed result must be a clean Letter or A4 page, not a screenshot of a web form.

Three things that did most of the work

1. Two layouts in one document, switched by @media print.

The page has a form on the left and the document on the right. The print stylesheet hides everything with a .noprint class and lets the document fill the page:

@page { size: auto; margin: 18mm; }
@media print {
  .noprint { display: none !important; }
  body { background: #fff; }
  .sheet { box-shadow: none; width: auto; margin: 0; }
}

"Save as PDF" in Chrome, Edge, Firefox and Safari all go through the same path, so the user never installs anything. The trap: a header that is 2 px too tall pushes a signature line onto page two. I now test every tool headless with --print-to-pdf and count the pages in the output (a regex on /Type /Page is enough).

2. localStorage as the whole backend.

Every input has an id. On input, the tool serialises the fields to one JSON blob under a versioned key; on load, it restores them. That is the entire persistence layer:

const FIELDS = ["landlord","tenant","address","month","year","rent"];
function save(){ const o={}; for(const f of FIELDS) o[f]=$(f).value;
  localStorage.setItem("rentreceipt.v1", JSON.stringify(o)); }
function load(){ const o=JSON.parse(localStorage.getItem("rentreceipt.v1")||"{}");
  for(const f of FIELDS) if(o[f]!==undefined) $(f).value=o[f]; }

Next month the landlord clicks "Next month": the period and receipt number increment, everything else stays. A bug I shipped: I set the default month from new Date() after calling load(), so a restored empty value won the race and every receipt defaulted to January. Set defaults first, then restore.

3. Amount in words, without a library.

A receipt should say "$1,200.00 (one thousand two hundred dollars)". A number-to-words function is about forty lines for English, and the cents are the tricky part (round first, split, then format). I kept it per-currency rather than generic because "euros and cents" and "pounds and pence" need their own words anyway.

Where the single-file approach breaks

  • No email delivery. The user attaches the PDF themselves.
  • No multi-device sync. The data lives in one browser profile; clearing site data erases it. I say so on the page.
  • No updates in place. If I fix a bug, people who downloaded v1.0 keep v1.0. The free version is hosted so it always gets the fix; the paid files are versioned zips.
  • Mobile Safari prints oddly: print preview works, but @page margins are partially ignored.

Result

The free version is hosted here: https://paperworkkit.netlify.app/en/ (and as a browser-playable tool on itch.io: https://paperworkkit.itch.io/rent-receipt-free). The same engine runs five more documents a small landlord needs (late notice, deposit return, rent increase, inspection checklist, annual statement), sold as a kit of offline files: https://paperworkkit.itch.io/landlord-paperwork-kit

If you have built single-file tools and solved the mobile print problem, I would like to hear how.

title: What Abstraction Does React Introduce?
description:
JavaScript could already update the DOM.

So why did we need React?

In my previous post, we discussed the history of Web UI and how it evolved from HTML to React.

But there are many misconceptions about React.

One of them is that React removes DOM manipulation.

That’s not the proper way to understand it.

Instead, React abstracts DOM manipulation.

So, what is abstraction?

The bigger picture of React's abstraction is where you describe UI declaratively as a function of application state, organize UI into components, and then let React handle the synchronization between that description and the React rendering environment.

That is about the overall abstraction, which abstracts many underlying tasks.

Let's understand that.

Abstractions

1. DOM Mutations

DOM mutations mean abstracting low-level concepts and thinking about that abstraction.

Before React, you need to think about the DOM nodes, properties, DOM methods, and DOM events.

React abstracts that and introduces concepts like Components, Props, UI, and State.

This is similar to how higher-level programming languages abstract machine instructions.

2. Declarative UI

Declarative means you describe what the result should be.

You are describing the desired UI.

You don't need to explicitly describe:

  • Create dashboard DOM.
  • Insert dashboard.
  • Update Button.

Instead, React tracks your declaration and manages the transition between them.

This separates "What" from "How".

3. Component and State Abstraction

Before React, you needed to create reusable JavaScript functions intentionally.

But React makes UI itself composable.

This introduces the component abstraction.

State abstraction abstracts the tracking of what changed, which element depends on it, and what should I update.

4. Abstraction as a Contract

In React, you describe the UI corresponding to the current state.

Now React is responsible for reconciling that description with the rendered UI.

Now the developer's responsibility becomes:

  • What should the UI look like?
  • What state does it depend on?
  • How are components composed?

And React manages the responsibility for rendered work, reconciliation, scheduling, commit, and host environment updates.

title: The browser doesn't trust the server: a Solana frontend that checks its own backend
description:
My server can tell the web page that a borrower got credit tier A. The page doesn't show it until Solana agrees.

That sounds like paranoia about my own code, so here's the context. I'm building TEE Income Oracle. A borrower's bank statement is scored inside a secure enclave, the enclave signs a credit tier, and the tier is written to Solana, where a lending pool reads it before it lends. Between the browser and all of that sits a server I wrote, the gateway. It talks to the enclave, streams progress to the page, and pays transaction fees so a demo wallet needs no SOL.

The whole product claims that a lender doesn't have to trust me. If the page repeats whatever my gateway says, that claim stops at the page. So the page treats the gateway as a messenger: it can carry bytes, but it never becomes the source of anything the page calls verified.

This post is for frontend developers building on Solana. You know transactions, signatures and RPC calls; you don't need to know anything about enclaves. It walks through five places the page checks its own backend, each as the shortcut, what can go wrong with it, and what the page does instead. The page still trusts two things, the RPC node it reads from and the code I serve it, and I'll come back to both at the end. Every link points to release v0.5.5.

1. Sign your own copy

Before scoring starts, the borrower signs a short text that ties the session to their wallet. It's a plain message signature, the kind a wallet's signMessage produces, not a transaction:

tee-income-oracle: bind session
session: <session id>
wallet: <borrower's address>
policy: <policy hash>
expires: <unix seconds>

The policy hash identifies the scoring rules the enclave will apply; each pool says which policy it accepts.

The shortcut: the gateway sends this text, the page passes it to the wallet, and the wallet signs it.

What can go wrong: the gateway now holds the pen. Whatever it puts in that text gets signed: a different wallet, an expiry next year, a policy no pool lends under. In the demo the wallet lives in the browser tab and signs without a prompt, so nobody reads the text first.

What the page does: it writes the text itself and signs its own copy, and only if the gateway's copy is identical. The wallet line comes from the page alone. The other values come from the gateway, so the page can only hold them to rules: the session id must match the session the page will submit under, the policy must be one a listed pool lends under, and the expiry must fall within the next ten minutes (plus a minute for clock skew). A gateway can still choose the session and the policy within those rules. It can't get a signature for anything else. (intent.ts)

This isn't a quirk of my setup. Kit's documentation for signing off-chain messages makes the same argument from the other side: a valid signature from a wallet proves little until you've also confirmed it covers the message you meant to have signed.

2. Check that the signature you got back is yours

To borrow, the page builds a transaction and the borrower signs it. The gateway's relayer pays the fee, so it signs too, sends the transaction, and returns its signature. The page polls that signature until it's confirmed.

The shortcut: take the returned signature, wait for "confirmed", show "borrowed".

What can go wrong: every confirmed transaction has a signature. A buggy or hostile relayer could hand back one from an earlier borrow, or from someone else's, and the page would celebrate a loan that never happened. Reading the loan account afterwards helps, but on public RPC that read can come from a node that's behind.

What the page does: on Solana, a transaction's id is its first signature, and the first signature belongs to the fee payer, signed over the transaction's message bytes. The fee payer here is the relayer. So the page checks that the returned id is a valid relayer signature over the exact bytes it built. With @solana/kit (the library formerly released as web3.js 2.0), that's a decode and a verify:

const { messageBytes } = getTransactionDecoder().decode(wire);
const signature = getBase58Encoder().encode(returnedId);
if (!isSignatureBytes(signature)) return false;
return verifySignature(relayerKey, signature, messageBytes);

Solana's guide to partial signing gives a similar rule to whoever assembles a transaction from several signers: before you submit, make sure each signature you collected is over the message you froze. The page applies it from the other end, after submission, to the one id that comes back. A signature over any other message fails, so the id is tied to these exact message bytes. (The excerpt is condensed from isOurTransaction in use-loan.ts.)

That still isn't complete replay protection. Ed25519 signatures are deterministic: the same key signing the same bytes always gives the same signature. So two identical borrows built on the same blockhash have the same id, and asking for the latest blockhash each time doesn't guarantee a different one. The chain is safe either way: validators drop a transaction they've already processed, so nothing executes twice. The risk is to what the page believes. Before relaying, the page reads the loan account and refuses to borrow while a loan is open, so a replay needs a repay in between: borrow, repay, then an identical borrow while the blockhash is still valid, about a minute. A relayer could answer that last borrow with the first one's signature, which did confirm. The page reads the loan account again after confirmation, but that read has no lower bound on freshness, so a node still showing the first loan would let it through.

3. Show what the chain says, not what the server says

When scoring finishes, the gateway streams the result: the tier, and the payload it says the oracle wrote to Solana. The payload is the signed part of the on-chain record, including the tier, the policy, the statement dates and the enclave build that scored it.

The shortcut: show the tier straight away, and read the chain for extra details. My first version did this. A reviewer described it as the gateway's word with a seal on it.

What can go wrong: the page looks verified while showing an unverified value. My first fix had a subtler hole. It matched the chain record to the gateway's report by timestamp, then kept displaying the gateway's tier. A gateway could relay a real tier C record and report tier A with the same timestamp. The timestamps match, and the page says A.

What the page does: it shows "reading your tier back from Solana…" until the payload on chain matches the reported payload, field by field. It then displays that payload and the record's expiry, both as read from Solana. If a payload at least as new as the report differs in any field, the page shows an error. That doesn't prove the gateway lied, because the oracle lets a newer record replace an older one, but the chain no longer confirms the report, so the page fails closed. (borrow-view.ts)

The same mistake hid in a smaller place. A "registered on Solana" chip was fed by a gateway endpoint. Now only a read of the on-chain registry can say "registered". The gateway still moves the page from one step to the next, and it supplies the link to its transaction. It never supplies a value the page shows as fact.

4. A "valid" badge is a promise about the program

The loan page shows a badge for the borrower's tier against a pool: valid, stale, expired, policy mismatch and so on.

The shortcut: check the rules that seem important. My first version did that, and review found four of the pool's checks missing. The badge could say "valid" about a credential the program would reject.

What the page does: it runs every credential check the pool program runs, in the program's order:

  1. the record was written by the oracle,
  2. it hasn't expired,
  3. the pool lends to this tier at all,
  4. it was scored under the pool's policy,
  5. it's fresh enough (how old the record is, how old the bank statement is, and how many days it covers),
  6. the enclave build that scored it is approved by the pool and not revoked.

The order matters because the badge names the first check that fails, and that should match what the program would say about the same credential. (credential.ts, borrow.rs)

Even then, "valid" makes a narrow promise: the credential passes this pool's checks at the state and time the page read. A borrow can still fail for reasons outside the credential: the amount is over the tier's limit, there's already a loan in this pool, the vault is short, a token account is frozen, or the state changes before the transaction runs. The funders' loan book runs the same function for every borrower, so "fresh" there makes the same narrow promise.

Choosing which checks to run is a product decision too. Repay first sat behind the same "is your tier valid?" gate as Borrow, which locked a borrower with a stale tier out of repaying, and repaying needs no tier at all. Repay now has no tier check in front of it.

5. The RPC node is a server too

Reading "from the chain" really means reading from an RPC node, which is someone else's server. Two things went wrong there.

A node one step behind. Public devnet RPC is load-balanced, so the read right after a confirmation can land on a node that hasn't caught up. The tests didn't catch this; a manual run on the live site did. After a repay, the page read the pool and saw the loan was gone. Then the data layer fetched again, hit a lagging node, and the closed loan came back on screen.

The fix has two parts. The read-back retries a few times, and it reads the pool, its vault and the loan in one call, so all three come from the same node. Then the read that proved the change goes straight into the cache of TanStack Query, the page's data layer, and any fetch already in flight is cancelled, so it can't overwrite it:

await queryClient.cancelQueries({ queryKey: poolKey });
queryClient.setQueryData(poolKey, provingRead);

That fixes the race I saw, and no more. A later refetch, say when the tab regains focus, can still hit a lagging node. Solana's RPC has a parameter for the general case, minContextSlot. Account reads such as getMultipleAccounts return the slot they were evaluated at in context.slot. Keep the highest slot you've accepted, pass it as minContextSlot on later reads with the same commitment level, and a node that hasn't reached that slot returns an error (code -32016, "Minimum context slot has not been reached") instead of older data. The page doesn't do this yet.

A reply that's one short. The funders' loan book asks for up to 100 accounts per call and matches each reply to its request by position. Nothing checked the reply's length. The RPC spec says a node returns one entry per address, with null for an account that doesn't exist, but the page took that on trust. A node, or a proxy in front of one, that returned 99 accounts for 100 addresses would shift every row after the gap, and show one borrower with the next borrower's "fresh" badge. Now a reply of the wrong length is an error (rpc.ts). So is a duplicated loan row, which would inflate every total, and so is a record that doesn't name the borrower it was fetched for. One bad row fails the whole book (use-book.ts), because a partial book presented as the book is worse than an error.

Where the trust actually stops

None of this makes the page trustless:

  • It reads one RPC node. It checks what's cheap to check: reply lengths, account sizes and types, which wallet a record belongs to, and signatures over bytes it built. A node that invented consistent data could still fool it.
  • "Confirmed" also comes from that node. The signature check proves the id belongs to the bytes the page built; the node still reports whether they landed.
  • The gateway names the relayer. The relayer's key comes from the gateway's own info endpoint. The signature check ties the returned id to the bytes the page built; it doesn't prove who paid the fee.
  • I serve the page. A different build could skip every check. That's why the source is public at release tags, and why the receipt checks also run from a command line.

What the checks do buy: my gateway is no longer the only authority for a tier, a loan or a registration. The page checks each of those claims against what an RPC node returns, and most gateway bugs now show up as an error on screen instead of a wrong number. The limits above still apply: a stale read, or a reused identical transaction, can get past these checks.

A checklist for your own frontend

  • Rebuild anything the user signs from data you already hold, and sign your copy.
  • Treat a signature from an API as a claim. If you built the transaction, verify the signature over its bytes. It ties the id to those bytes; it doesn't stop an identical transaction being reused.
  • Show values from a chain read, not from the API that triggered the write. Compare every field of the reported payload, display the chain's values, and fail closed when the payloads differ. Read anything outside the payload, such as expiry, straight from the chain.
  • Make a status badge mirror the program's checks, in the program's order, and say what it doesn't cover.
  • After a write, keep the read that proved it. For later reads, carry the highest slot you've accepted forward as minContextSlot.
  • Check reply lengths whenever you match results to requests by position.

To try this on your own app, pick one value your UI shows as confirmed, and trace where it comes from. If the answer is "the API told us", that's the first check to add.

title: LRMoE: Demand-Side Load Re-Calibration for Efficient MoE Training on Memory-Constrained Nodes
description:
arXiv:2610.37720v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Sparse Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) models offer scalable capacity for Web applications, but uneven routing creates computation and communication bottlenecks. Existing placement and replication methods redistribute this workload, yet additional expert copies compete with token-related buffers for limited GPU memory. We present LRMoE, a memory-aware MoE training system that jointly recalibrates backward demand and balances the retained workload. During forward execution, it plans retention quotas and expert placement under resource constraints while preserving all routed computations. During backpropagation, a load recalibration metric estimates each token-expert pair's contribution to the expert update and selects pairs within these quotas. A capacity-aware routing algorithm distributes retained pairs among eligible instances of their original experts. Physical compaction then forms smaller communication payloads and variable-size grouped GEMMs, reducing backward traffic, computation, and execution-buffer demand. Experiments on Qwen3-30B-A3B and GLM4.5-106B-A12B show that LRMoE reduces cumulative MoE-layer training time to fixed-loss targets by 21.2-44.8% relative to SYMI.

title: AI Lesson Planning for Teachers: How I Cut Prep Time in Half Without Losing the Human Touch
description:
AI Lesson Planning for Teachers: How I Cut Prep Time in Half Without Losing the Human Touch

I am a head teacher at a government primary school in Punjab, and for years my evenings looked the same: a stack of notebooks, a syllabus outline, and lesson plans written by hand long after the school day ended. When I first tried AI lesson planning for teachers, I expected a gimmick. What I got instead was the single biggest change to my working week in years — my preparation time roughly halved, while my lessons actually got better. The catch, and it matters, is that the AI does the drafting and I do the teaching. Get that order backwards and you get slick-looking plans that fall apart in front of thirty children.

This is the honest version: the workflow I use, the prompts that work, and the guardrails that keep the human in charge.

What AI Lesson Planning for Teachers Actually Looks Like in a Real Classroom

Forget the marketing version where you type one sentence and a perfect lesson appears. Real AI lesson planning for teachers looks like this: you give the AI your topic, your class level, your time limit, and what your students already know, and it hands back a structured first draft — objectives, a timed sequence, questions, and a short activity. Then you do the part no model can do: you cross out what won't work for your children, you fix the examples so they match your students' lives, and you add the one story or question that makes the class pay attention.

In my school, a typical lesson is 35 to 40 minutes with a large class and limited materials. An AI that doesn't know that will happily plan a lesson needing a projector, printed worksheets for every child, and group work in sixes. So the first skill isn't prompting. It's knowing your constraints well enough to state them: class size, time, available materials, language level, and what the textbook actually covers. The AI is only as grounded as the brief you give it.

One more honest point: I teach from the Punjab textbooks, and the AI does not know my exact chapter — only the general topic. That gap is where a careless teacher gets into trouble, accepting a plan with the wrong scope or examples. My rule: the textbook is the syllabus, the AI is the assistant. Every plan gets checked against the chapter before it reaches the classroom.

My 30-Minute AI Lesson Planning Workflow

Here is the full workflow, timed honestly. It replaced an evening routine that used to take over an hour.

Step 1 — Pick one clear objective (3 minutes). Not "teach fractions" but "by the end of the lesson, students can shade and name one-half, one-third, and one-quarter of a shape." One objective, stated in student language. If you can't write it in one sentence, the AI can't plan around it either.

Step 2 — Write the brief (5 minutes). I paste the same structure every time: topic, class, time available, what students already know, materials I actually have (chalkboard, chart paper, the textbook), and one constraint ("no printing", "mixed ability class", "Urdu-medium explanations where needed"). This brief is the whole secret. A vague brief gives you a generic lesson; a specific brief gives you a usable one.

Step 3 — Generate the first draft (2 minutes). I ask for a timed plan: a 5-minute hook, 15 minutes of teaching, 10 minutes of practice, and a 5-minute check. I also ask for three questions at different difficulty levels and one activity that needs no materials beyond the board. The draft is never the final plan. It is raw material.

Step 4 — Edit like a teacher, not an editor (15 minutes). This is where the real work happens. I replace generic examples with local ones — market prices, cricket scores, the school garden — because children remember what they recognize. I delete any activity I can't run with my class size, check every fact and worked example against the textbook, and add the opening question I know will hook this particular class, because no model knows my students.

Step 5 — Make the exit ticket (5 minutes). Every lesson ends with one quick check: two questions on the board, answered on slates or in notebooks, that tell me before the bell whether the objective landed. If I skip this step, I am guessing about learning. The AI drafts the questions; I pick the ones that actually test the objective.

Total: about 30 minutes.

The Prompt Pattern That Keeps Lessons Honest

Most bad AI lessons come from one-prompt thinking: one long prompt, one accepted answer. A three-pass pattern fixes most of the quality problems people blame on the AI.

Pass 1 — Draft. "Plan a 35-minute lesson on [topic] for class [X]. Students already know [Y]. Materials: chalkboard and textbook only. Give me timed sections, three questions at easy, medium, and hard levels, and one no-material activity."

Pass 2 — Localize. "Rewrite the examples using everyday life in a Pakistani village school: market shopping, farming, cricket, family routines. Replace any activity that needs printing or a projector."

Pass 3 — Challenge. "Now find the weak points in this plan: where will students get confused, which step is too fast for a mixed-ability class, and what question checks understanding after the main teaching?" That third pass is the most valuable one — it surfaces the exact spots where a real class will struggle, and trains you to spot them yourself over time.

One warning from experience: never let the AI write your assessment questions unchecked. Models produce confident-sounding questions with wrong answers, especially in maths and science. Every question gets solved by me before it reaches the students. That single habit is the difference between using AI and being used by it.

AI Lesson Planning for Teachers: The Guardrails I Never Skip

AI lesson planning for teachers only stays honest if you hold a few lines firm. These are mine, learned the hard way:

  • The textbook decides the scope. If the AI's plan covers something outside the chapter, it gets cut, however interesting it looks. Exam alignment and student confidence both depend on this.
  • Every fact gets verified. Dates, science facts, worked maths examples, spellings — all checked before class. I once caught a wrong fraction example in a draft five minutes before the lesson. That was the day this rule became non-negotiable.
  • No student data goes into the AI. No names, no marks, no photos, no personal details. I describe the class in general terms ("mixed ability, 30+ students") and nothing more. This is a privacy line, not a preference.
  • The AI never writes the final word to students. Worksheets, notes, and homework pass through my eyes first. Anything the children read should sound like their teacher, not like a chatbot.
  • One new thing per lesson. If the AI suggests a new method and a new activity and a new grouping in the same lesson, I keep one and drop the rest. Classrooms punish overload faster than any reviewer will.

These guardrails are why my prep time halved instead of disappearing. The AI removed the blank-page work — structuring, sequencing, drafting questions — and left the judgment work to me. That is why the lessons got better, not just faster.

A Real Example: One Lesson, Before and After

Take a class 4 maths lesson on fractions, a topic where children either click or drown. My old hand-written plan was: introduce the term, draw two shapes on the board, do three textbook exercises. Serviceable, forgettable.

The AI-assisted version kept the same objective but changed the shape of the lesson. The hook became a real question: "If four friends share two rotis equally, how much does each get?" — something every child in my class has actually argued about. The teaching section used folding chart paper instead of just drawing, so children could see and hold the halves and quarters. Practice became a quick market game: "A shopkeeper sells half a kilo of sugar, then a quarter — how much is left?" And the exit ticket was two questions, one easy and one that catches the classic mistake of confusing the number of pieces with the size of each piece.

Nothing in that lesson required classroom technology. The AI contributed structure and variety; the classroom contributed the rotis, the market, and the paper-folding. AI lesson planning for teachers works best when the technology stays in the preparation room and the classroom stays human.

Your First-Week Checklist

If you want to try this yourself, here is the honest starter plan — one week, no overwhelm:

  1. Pick ONE subject and ONE class to experiment with. Don't AI-plan everything at once.
  2. Write your brief template once (topic, class, time, prior knowledge, materials, constraints) and reuse it every day.
  3. Run the three-pass pattern: draft, localize, challenge.
  4. Check every fact and every worked example against the textbook before class.
  5. End every lesson with a two-question exit ticket, and keep the results — they tell you within a week whether the plans are actually working.
  6. Steal the good parts: when a hook or activity lands well, save it in a personal bank for next year. After a term, that bank is worth more than any prompt collection.

A practical note for fellow Pakistani teachers: the free Punjab textbooks are all available online now, so you can read the chapter on your phone while drafting. I keep the full library linked from the Punjab textbooks hub on rehmanahmad.com, and I grab classroom utilities like PDF tools from filecobra.com when I need a printable for class. The tools support the teaching; they never replace it.

The Bottom Line

AI lesson planning for teachers is not about letting a machine teach. It is about letting a machine do the drafting so the teacher can do the teaching — better prepared, less exhausted, with the evening back. My prep time roughly halved, my lessons got more varied, and my students got hooks I would not have invented on a tired evening with a blank page.

But the bargain only holds if you keep the guardrails: textbook as syllabus, every fact verified, no student data shared, and your judgment on every page that reaches a child. Do that, and the AI becomes what it should have been all along — a tireless assistant to a teacher who is still, unmistakably, in charge.

If you try this workflow, start with one lesson this week and judge it by the exit ticket, not by how impressive the plan looked on screen.

title: CSS gap decorations: lines between grid items
description:
This note has an interactive demo. Try it in the original

Drawing a line between grid cells has always been a hack: borders on half the items, :nth-child() rules to remove the extra ones, or a coloured background peeking through the gaps. Since Chrome and Edge 149 there's a real property for it: row-rule and column-rule now work on grid and flex containers, not just on multi-column text.

I like this one because it fixes a very everyday problem. Bento layouts, dashboards, pricing tables, footers with columns: they all want separators, and separators belong to the gap, not to the items.

What gap decorations are

column-rule isn't new. It has drawn the line between columns of multi-column text for years. The CSS Gaps module takes that idea and extends it to grid and flexbox, adds the row direction with row-rule, and gives you control over where lines break, which gaps get a line, and how far the ends are pulled back.

Two rules from the spec are worth knowing before you start:

  • They take up no space. A decoration never moves anything. If it's wider than the gap, the adjacent items simply overlap it.
  • They're painted just above the container's border, and in a scroll container they scroll with the items.

The code the demo uses

The demo above is a four-column, four-row grid with nine tiles. The core is three declarations:

.bento {
  display: grid;
  gap: 18px;
  row-rule: 2px solid #FF5200;
  column-rule: 2px solid #00D4AA;
}

row-rule and column-rule are shorthands for -width, -style and -color, exactly like border. The defaults are also the same as a border's: medium, none and currentcolor. So if you forget the style, nothing gets painted. If you want the same line in both directions, rule sets both at once.

The part that has no equivalent with borders is that the value is a list. Choose the "Lists" pattern in the demo and you get this:

.bento {
  row-rule: 3px solid #FF5200, repeat(auto, 1px dashed #94A3B8), 3px solid #FF5200;
  column-rule: 2px dotted #00D4AA, 2px dashed #FF7E41;
}

Each value goes to one gap, in order. When there are more gaps than values, the list starts again, so the columns alternate dotted and dashed. repeat(auto, …) fills whatever the other values don't cover: here, first and last row gaps are thick and solid, and everything in between is a thin dashed line, however many rows there are. Only one repeat(auto, …) is allowed per value. There's also repeat(3, …) with a fixed count.

Breaks, empty cells and insets

The other three controls in the demo map to these properties:

  • rule-break: none, normal or intersection. With none, each line runs from one end of the gap to the other. With intersection, it's cut at every T and every cross. normal depends on the container: in grid it cuts at T junctions but runs through crosses; in flexbox it behaves like none.
  • rule-visibility-items: all, around or between. It decides whether a line is painted next to an empty cell. Tap the big tile to remove it and switch to between: the lines around the hole disappear, because there's no longer an item on both sides. The initial value, normal, behaves like all in grid. This one only applies to grid and multi-column containers.
  • rule-inset: moves the ends of each segment. A positive value pulls them back from the junction, and percentages are resolved against the width of the gap being crossed. There's also an overlap-join keyword, and longhands that separate the ends at the container's edges (cap) from the ones at junctions (junction).

When lines don't break, rule-overlap decides which direction is painted on top. The initial value is row-over-column.

Change patterns in the demo and the colour and width animate: the spec makes -color and -width animatable as lists, and I checked in Chromium that a transition on row-rule-color interpolates through intermediate colours. The style switches without interpolation.

Support and gotchas

  • Chrome and Edge 149 only for now. MDN's compatibility data marks row-rule, rule-break, rule-inset and the rest as experimental, with no support in Firefox or Safari. The spec is an Editor's Draft that's still changing: the last Working Draft is from 24 June 2026.
  • Don't feature-detect with column-rule. It has existed for multi-column since long before this, so the browser will say yes even if it doesn't paint anything in a grid. Ask about row-rule instead (MDN's examples do the same with @supports): 
const supported = CSS.supports('row-rule', '1px solid red');
  • The fallback is free, but it's nothing. In a browser that doesn't know these properties, the declarations are ignored and the gaps remain empty. For decorative lines, that's usually acceptable. If the separator carries meaning, you need a plan B. The demo uses the classic one when detection fails: paint the container with the line colour clipped to content-box, with opaque, square-cornered items covering it. It works only for solid lines across every gap: no dashes, no breaks and no clean empty cells. I tested it in Chromium by forcing the fallback.
  • Lines don't make room. If you increase the width without increasing the gap, the items cover the line. Keep gap at least as wide as the rule.

What to keep an eye on

  • Firefox and Safari implementing it. Until then, use it as progressive enhancement and nothing more.
  • Changes to the spec: property names and behaviours are still being refined, including how it works with the new grid lanes containers.
  • Whether the design systems that today draw dividers with borders on each item start moving that to the container.

Sources

  • row-rule – MDN
  • CSS gaps – MDN
  • CSS Gaps Module Level 1 – Editor's Draft

title: Next.js Bundle Analyzer in 16.4: The Import That Defeats Lazy Load
description:
Confession: bundle analyzers are the tool I know I should open more often and mostly don't. The usual finding is something small and slightly embarrassing, like a date library imported for one format() call and sitting in the initial chunk of a page with no dates on it. You fix it, feel smug for a day, and forget to check again until someone complains about load time.

So when the Next.js team published Ship less JavaScript in Next.js with your AI agent on 28 October, I read it twice. Short version for the impatient: Next.js 16.4 adds an agent skill and a better next analyze, and the most useful idea in the post is a boring one about imports that quietly undo each other. I haven't run the skill on a production app yet, so this isn't a review. It's what I would check first, and why I'm more interested in the analyzer than in the agent bolted onto it.

The lazy import that never deferred anything

Here is the example from the Next.js post, nearly verbatim in spirit. You have a heavy component and you want it out of the initial bundle, so you wrap it:

// HeavyComponentLoader.js
'use client';
import { lazy } from 'react';

export const HeavyComponentLoader = lazy(() => import('./HeavyComponent'));

That looks right. React's lazy documentation says the code for a lazy component isn't loaded until it first renders, and the Next.js lazy loading guide says much the same about next/dynamic. Both are true. The catch is that the bundler works on the whole module graph, not on your intentions. If any other module in the same bundle does this:

// Toolbar.js
import HeavyComponent from './HeavyComponent';

then HeavyComponent is part of the initial chunk anyway, and your lazy wrapper becomes a decoration. One static import, three folders away, written by someone who never saw your loader. The bundle doesn't warn you. Lighthouse just gets a little worse and nobody connects it to a pull request from last month.

Picture a chart library that is lazy loaded on a reports page, which feels like a good job done. Then someone adds a small summary card to the home page that imports one helper from the same chart file, and the whole library moves into the shared chunk. You'd stare at the lazy call for an hour, because the lazy call is fine. The bug is somewhere else entirely. I haven't been bitten by this exact case on a client project, but it's the shape of bug I'd expect to find in any app with more than one contributor.

The old way to find this was to open a treemap, spot the big rectangle, and then grep the codebase for every place that imports it. It works. It's also slow, and you only do it when someone is already complaining about load time.

What next analyze gives you without any agent

Before the agent part, the human tooling. In 16.1 the team shipped the first Turbopack Bundle Analyzer, and 16.4 adds a few things that matter more than the headline. You run next analyze in your app directory, and you now land on a route summary that lists your largest client routes. Open one and there's a table you can sort by size, with each source marked as initial load, behind an async boundary, or both.

That last label is the one I care about. A module marked "Initial + async paths" is exactly the lazy-import bug above: it's loaded lazily from one place and eagerly from another. In the post's illustrative blog app, a search component sits at 18 kB with that label. You can see the problem in one row, without reading a treemap.

Two more features I'd use right away. The analyzer now saves a snapshot of each analysis automatically, and you can diff two snapshots, which gives you a before and after for any change. The post's example goes from 123 kB to 81 kB on one route, with a per-file table of what moved. And there's a filter for the critical render path, so you can hide async dependencies and look only at what blocks first paint.

I'll be blunt about one limitation. All of this needs Turbopack, because the analyzer relies on its module graph. If you're on 16 or later, that's the default and you won't think about it. If you pinned webpack for a plugin that doesn't work elsewhere, you stay with the older webpack bundle analyzer and none of this applies to you yet.

What the agent skill adds

The skill is installed with npx skills add vercel/next.js --skill next-bundle-optimizer and run with /next-bundle-optimizer. According to the post, it exports saved analyses as JSON, rebuilds the module and chunk graphs, finds large groups of connected modules, and uses a minimum cut to pick a small set of import boundaries that would defer them. Then it checks those proposals against your source code and how the components are used.

The minimum cut is the clever part, and it's a good fit for the problem. "Which handful of imports, if I changed them, would let this whole cluster load later?" is a graph question. It's the question I answer badly by hand, because I follow the first import chain I find and stop. A tool that looks at every chain at once will beat me on that, and I have no pride about it.

By default it only reports. You have to run /next-bundle-optimizer fix to have it apply changes, re-run the analysis, and compare snapshots. I like that default. It means the first run on a client codebase is read-only, and I can bill the findings as an audit before anyone touches a file.

The numbers in the post are large. Across v0 and vercel.com, the team says agents cut nearly two megabytes of compressed JavaScript, with individual wins like 150 KB from an experimental editor loaded on nearly every page, and 255 KB on the Vercel dashboard from markdown rendering and chart drawing that shipped before the agent panel was even open. Those are self-reported results on Vercel's own apps, tuned by the people who wrote the tool. Treat them as proof the approach works, not as a forecast for your app. A typical agency site has fewer megabytes to find. I'd be happy with three or four wins in the 20 to 80 KB range.

Where I would not trust it blindly

Deferring code isn't free, and this is where I'd push back on the "let the agent open a pull request" workflow. When you move a 150 KB editor behind a dynamic import, you haven't removed the cost. You've moved it to the moment the user needs the editor. If that moment is a click, the first click now waits on a network request. On a fast connection you won't notice. On a train in poor coverage, the button looks broken.

So every proposed boundary needs a question: what does the user see while this loads? A spinner, a layout jump, a blank panel? The post says the agent checks how components are used interactively, and I believe it tries. But a model reading source can't feel a 400 ms gap on a mid-range phone. You can.

My review checklist for each agent change, in order:

  1. Is the deferred component above the fold or behind an interaction?
  2. Does the loading state match the final layout, so nothing shifts?
  3. Did INP get worse on the page, measured on a preview deployment rather than on my laptop?
  4. Is the saving big enough to justify the extra moving part?

The Vercel team says they verified each fix on a preview deployment before shipping, which is the right habit. Copy it. I'd also keep pull requests one change each, the way the post suggests, because a single combined "optimize bundles" diff is impossible to bisect when INP regresses.

If you are also deciding whether Next.js is the right base for a project in the first place, I went through that trade-off in my Next.js vs Vite post. The bundle tooling above is one more thing that tilts the answer, mostly for teams already on Turbopack.

A routine I would run this week

You don't need the agent to get most of the value. Here's the sequence I'm going to use on my next client audit, which is the kind of work I describe on my portfolio:

# on a branch, after upgrading to Next.js 16.4
npx next analyze

# optional: read-only report from the agent skill
npx skills add vercel/next.js --skill next-bundle-optimizer
# then run /next-bundle-optimizer in your agent (no "fix" argument)

# export the graph if you want to poke at it yourself
npx next analyze export

Start with the route summary and write down the three largest client routes. In each, sort by size and look for two things: any source labeled "Initial + async paths", and any package you can't explain. A date library on a page with no dates counts. Then pick exactly one finding, fix it by hand, take a new snapshot, and read the diff. If the diff shows the number you expected, you understand your bundle. If it doesn't, the import graph is teaching you something, and that's the useful part.

Only after that would I run the agent in report mode and compare its list with mine. Where we disagree, I want to know why before I apply anything.

This week, run next analyze on your biggest route and write down the single largest file in the initial load. If you can't say why it's there, trace its imports until you can.
