title: Online Consultation Booking For Service Businesses
description:
Online Consultation Booking For Service Businesses

As a principal frontend engineer and conversion architect, I have encountered numerous service businesses struggling to implement effective online consultation booking systems. Standard off-the-shelf templates and generic forms often fail to meet the unique requirements of these businesses, resulting in missed opportunities and frustrated customers.

The primary reason for this failure is the lack of customization and flexibility in these templates. Service businesses have distinct needs, such as varying consultation durations, multiple service providers, and specific scheduling requirements. Generic forms and templates are unable to accommodate these nuances, leading to a poor user experience and decreased conversion rates.

Furthermore, standard templates often neglect the importance of user experience and interface design. A well-designed online consultation booking system should guide the user through a seamless and intuitive process, minimizing friction and maximizing the chances of a successful booking. However, generic templates frequently prioritize functionality over user experience, resulting in a clunky and confusing interface.

From an engineering perspective, there are several key takeaways for building an effective online consultation booking system:

  1. Customization is key: A bespoke solution that takes into account the unique requirements of the service business is essential for success. This includes flexible scheduling, multiple service providers, and customizable consultation durations.
  2. User experience is paramount: A well-designed interface that prioritizes user experience can significantly increase conversion rates and reduce friction. This includes clear and concise language, intuitive navigation, and a seamless booking process.
  3. Integration with existing systems is crucial: Online consultation booking systems should be integrated with existing customer relationship management (CRM) systems, payment gateways, and scheduling software to ensure a streamlined and efficient process.

By prioritizing customization, user experience, and integration, service businesses can create online consultation booking systems that meet their unique needs and drive business growth.

Vareli breaks this down in the complete analysis:
https://vareli.info/blog/online-consultation-booking-for-service-businesses

title: Trust But Verify: My Solo Developer AI Agent Workflow for Shipping Without Regrets
description:
Trust But Verify: My Solo Developer AI Agent Workflow for Shipping Without Regrets

I am a head teacher by day and a solo developer by night, and my solo developer AI agent workflow runs almost entirely while I am asleep or at school. AI agents draft my articles, patch my websites, and queue my content — and that sentence should terrify any solo builder, because when you are the only human in the loop, there is nobody else to catch the mistake. I learned that the hard way, more than once. The workflow below is the one I use now: agents do the building, and I do the verifying. That split is the whole system.

This is not a theory post. Every rule here exists because I broke the opposite rule and paid for it in public, in broken deploys, or in hours of quiet repair work at midnight.

Why I Stopped Trusting the Word "Done"

The first lesson came from a deploy tool that told me everything was fine. A push helper reported "OK pushed," and I believed it. Days later, a routine check showed the remote repository did not contain the files at all — the helper had written to a wrong path, reported success, and moved on. Nothing had failed loudly. Nothing had failed at all, according to the tool. The work simply was not there.

That is the central danger of a solo developer AI agent workflow: agents report completion, not truth. A green checkmark means the step ran, not that the result landed where it should. A test command that passes can mean the tests ran, or it can mean only a comfortable subset ran. An agent that says "verified" may have verified its own output against its own assumptions, which is not verification at all.

So I changed one thing, and it changed everything: no agent verifies its own work. Verification is always a second, independent step — a different command, a different check, against the live system, not against the agent's memory of what it did. If the agent pushed a file, I check the remote tree. If the agent ran tests, I run the full suite. If the agent says a page is live, I open the live URL.

The Solo Developer AI Agent Workflow, in Five Steps

Here is the workflow, exactly as I run it on a normal night.

Step 1 — Write a brief a stranger could follow

Before any agent touches a task, I write a short brief: the outcome in one sentence, the constraints (budget, scope, what not to touch), and the check that will prove it worked. The check matters most. "Publish the app page" is not a brief. "Publish the app page, then confirm the live URL returns the new content" is. If I cannot state the check, I am not ready to delegate the task — I am just hoping.

A good brief also names the boundaries. Mine include a hard zero-spend rule on automation: no paid service gets switched on by an agent, ever. I batch small pushes to save automation minutes, and I never let an agent start a new task to fix a failed one without me seeing the failure first.

Step 2 — Build small, in one direction

Agents are brilliant at producing a lot of output quickly, and that is exactly the risk. A 500-line change at midnight is not progress; it is a haystack I will have to search at 1 a.m. when something breaks. So every task is scoped to the smallest change that is still useful: one page, one feature, one batch of related fixes. Big work gets cut into small, separately verifiable pieces, each with its own check.

I also keep one direction of travel per task. An agent fixing a bug does not also "improve" three nearby files. Scope creep from an agent looks like helpfulness, and it is how a clean fix turns into a broken deploy. Anything else it spots goes in the log for tomorrow, not into tonight's change.

Step 3 — Verify against the live system, never the report

This is the step most solo builders skip, and it is the entire article in one sentence. After the work, I verify against the real thing:

  • After a push, I fetch the remote tree and confirm the exact paths are present. A helper's success message is not evidence; the remote tree is.
  • After a test run, I run the full suite — library tests and integration tests — because I once watched a builder report a green suite that had only run the easy half while dozens of integration tests were failing quietly underneath.
  • After a content publish, I open the live URL and read the page, including the parts I did not write. A page that renders is not a page that is correct.

Each check takes minutes. Each skipped check has cost me hours. That arithmetic is why this step is non-negotiable, even on tired nights.

Step 4 — Ship in batches, on a schedule I control

Solo shipping is a pacing problem as much as a technical one. I batch related changes into single deploys instead of firing off a deploy per fix, and I keep publishing on a schedule — a few posts a week, not a flood. Flooding helps nobody: readers cannot keep up, platforms get suspicious of bursts, and every extra publish is another chance for an unverified mistake to go live.

Scheduling also protects the human gate: work built at night gets reviewed in daylight before it goes public. Nothing in my system publishes itself straight from an agent's hands to the public internet.

Step 5 — Log it, or it never happened

Every completed task gets one line in a log: date, what shipped, where it lives. That log is how I avoid repeating topics, re-fixing fixed bugs, and re-approving work I already approved — and how I answer the only question that matters at month's end: what actually shipped? Agents forget. Logs do not.

The Green Test Suite That Wasn't

Let me make the testing lesson concrete, because it is the one I see other solo builders repeat most. A builder on one of my projects reported a green test run and moved on. When I ran the suite independently, the picture was different: the builder had run only the library tests, while the integration tests — the ones that exercise the real user flows — were failing in large numbers. The report was honest as far as it went. It just did not go far enough.

The fix became a rule I now apply to every project: the definition of "tests pass" is written in the brief, and it means the full suite, every time, run by someone — or some step — other than the one that wrote the code. A partial run is reported as a partial run, never as a pass. If your agent tells you tests pass, ask one question: which tests? If the answer is vague, the suite has not passed yet.

The same logic applies to content. A draft that reads well is not a draft that is accurate. Links get clicked, facts get checked against the source, and every element the brief specified gets ticked off before anything is presented as finished.

Solo Developer AI Agent Workflow: The Verification Checklist

Here is the checklist I run before anything ships, whether it is code, a page, or a post. Steal it wholesale — it is short on purpose:

  1. Remote truth: is the change actually present in the live system (remote tree, live URL, published page), confirmed by fetching it fresh?
  2. Full suite: did the complete test set run, including integration tests, not just the convenient subset?
  3. Scope check: did the change touch only what the brief asked for, with nothing extra smuggled in?
  4. Human read: have I personally read the final version — the page, the post, the diff — at least once, end to end?
  5. Reversibility: if this is wrong, can I undo it in minutes? If not, it ships smaller or not at all.
  6. Log entry: is it written down, with the date and the link, so future me can find it?

Six checks, a few minutes each. I have never regretted running them. I have regretted skipping every single one at least once.

What the Human Gate Is Actually For

People hear "human in the loop" and picture a manager approving every line, which sounds like the opposite of automation. In a solo developer AI agent workflow, the human gate is narrower and more valuable than that. Agents handle volume: drafting, formatting, repetitive fixes, research, scheduling. I handle judgment: is this true, is this safe, is this mine to publish, does this match what I actually want to say?

That division is why I keep drafts as drafts until I have read them, why no post goes live on an agent's word alone, and why my publishing rule is simple: the agent proposes, I dispose. A one-word approval from me is enough to move — I do not want bureaucracy either — but that one word comes after I have looked, not before. Automation without a gate is not leverage; it is just faster mistakes.

There is a second, quieter benefit. Verifying a change teaches me what my agents did, so I can brief the next task better. Builders who fully hand off stop understanding their own systems, and then they cannot fix them when — not if — something goes wrong. The gate is how I stay the developer of my own projects instead of a bystander to them.

The Bottom Line

A solo developer AI agent workflow does not fail because the agents are bad. Mine are good — they let a teacher with a full-time job run a textbooks library, a software site, and a publishing schedule that would have been impossible alone a few years ago. You can see the results in the free Punjab textbooks library I keep at rehmanahmad.com/textbooks, and in the free, verified Windows software I publish at filecobra.com. The workflow fails when "done" stops meaning "verified."

So here is my bargain, and I recommend it to any solo builder: let agents do the building, keep the verifying for yourself, write the check into the brief before the work starts, and never accept a success message as evidence. Ship small, ship on a schedule, log everything, and keep one human gate between your agents and the public.

title: The Measurement I Kept Skipping
description:
For months my test notes had a gap I could not see: I always measured the device at the moment it looked most interesting. Right after a heavy scene, right after a long export, right after the thing that made me want to write something down.

That instinct is exactly backwards. A reading taken at the peak tells you what the cooling system does under a spike. A reading taken ten minutes after the peak tells you what the device is actually like to hold.

I switched to a fixed mark — twelve minutes after each scene ends, no exceptions — and the notes stopped being dramatic. They also stopped contradicting each other. Two sessions that used to read as "hot" and "fine" now read as 41 and 38, which is a difference I can explain rather than a mood I have to describe.

The same move fixed battery notes. Instead of "drains fast", I write the percentage at the same two marks every session. One percent every eight minutes is ordinary. One percent every four minutes in the second half is a pattern, and in my case it was never the chip: it was the screen staying at full brightness on a page that never idled.

None of this is clever. It is the least clever thing in my notebook. But it is the only part that survived contact with a second week of testing.

If you are starting a log like this, pick the fixed mark before you start. Any mark will do. The discipline of the mark is the whole instrument.

title: Rubricon: Automated Rubric Generation and Refinement for LLM Evaluation and Training
description:
arXiv:2610.38220v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Rubrics enable reward assignment on tasks without verifiable answers, but are expensive to manually produce from scratch. We present Rubricon, a pipeline that generates discriminative rubrics without requiring human preference labels, rubric annotation, or generator-model training. Using any LLM, Rubricon samples multiple rubrics, selects the most discriminative candidate, adds criteria to capture overlooked requirements or response flaws, and prunes criteria that are misaligned or shallow. Alongside LLM self-critique and test-time scaling, Rubricon uses observed criterion pass rates on example model responses to guide refinement. Across five professional, consumer, clinical, and general-use LLM benchmarks, Rubricon produces rubrics whose scores of frontier LLM responses exhibit 9% greater alignment with labor-intensive expert-authored rubrics, compared to the best alternative synthetic rubric generation method among RRD, QSRG, OpenRubrics, and agentic generation via harnesses like Codex. On HealthBench, post-training a Qwen3.5-9B model with Rubricon rubrics yields 4.5% better performance than training with rubrics from the strongest alternative synthetic rubric generator, RRD.

title: Stop Losing Days to Time Zones: How to Hire an Offshore Development Team That Delivers While You Sleep
description:
Same budget range, same technology, opposite outcomes. The difference was never the time zone itself; it was how the team was organized around it — which is why the strongest offshore operations, like the four-delivery-center model at https://elgrith.com/, sell structure before they sell hours. This guide covers the decision honestly: what offshore really costs, the overlap models that work, the vetting questions that filter properly, and the ownership terms that keep you safe.

The Real Math: What Offshore Actually Costs (and What the Rate Never Tells You)
The rate card is where everyone starts, so start there — but read the whole column before deciding anything:

Factor Onshore (US/UK) Nearshore Offshore (South Asia)
Typical senior developer day rate $600–$1,200 $300–$600 $150–$400
Talent pool depth Tight; hiring takes months Moderate Deep — the world's largest engineering workforce
Time-zone overlap with US/UK Total Good (Americas) / moderate (Europe) Depends entirely on the team's structure — see below
Where the savings go if managed well — Mid-range More scope per dollar, faster builds, or genuine runway extension
Where the savings go if managed badly — Re-work Re-work, delays, and a rebuild with a local team
Notice the honest framing: offshore does not save money automatically. It converts money into optionality — the same budget buys more engineering, or the same scope buys back months of runway. That conversion only happens when communication, process, and ownership are handled properly, which is what the rest of this article is about.

The Time-Zone Myth: Overlap Hours Beat Hourly Rates
Here is the detail that separates professional offshore delivery from the horror stories: great offshore teams do not sell you hours in their time zone — they structure their day around yours. The mature models look like this:

Dedicated overlap model. The team shifts core hours to overlap with yours — say, 2 p.m. to 9 p.m. India time for a London client, or overnight-evening hours for a New York one. Questions get answered the same working day. Standups happen live. This is the baseline standard; accept nothing less.
Follow-the-sun model. Delivery centers in multiple regions hand work to each other across time zones. Your feedback in New York gets picked up in London or New Delhi the same calendar day. Done well, your project effectively gains a second working day per week — which is where the real offshore advantage lives, far beyond the rate card.
The dark model (avoid). The team works "when they work," answers when they answer, and every miscommunication marinates for eighteen hours before anyone can correct it. This model is not a time-zone problem; it is a management problem wearing a geography costume.
The practical test is embarrassingly simple: before signing, ask a candidate team what time their developers will be online relative to your calendar, and how questions raised at 4 p.m. your time get resolved. Teams with real global operations — the New Delhi, New York, London, and Shanghai structure used at https://elgrith.com/ — answer instantly, because the answer is their org chart. Teams without one will improvise an answer, and improvisation is the product you will actually receive.

The 8 Questions That Separate Real Offshore Teams From Resumes With a Logo
Who exactly is on my team, and can I meet them before signing? Rotating "resources" mean the people you evaluated are not the people you hired.
What hours will the team overlap with mine, and where do you have delivery centers? The follow-the-sun answer is the strongest one.
Where does the code live, and on day one, whose is it? Correct answer: your repository, from the first commit. Anything else is the lock-in mechanism.
How does the pricing work — fixed written quote or hourly? Fixed quotes after discovery, with scope and timeline in writing, are how professional teams keep your budget a decision instead of a slow leak.
What do the weekly demos look like? Working software every week, on your screen, or the engagement is running on faith.
What exactly happens at handover — accounts, credentials, documentation? You should own the cloud, the domain, the store accounts, and the repository from day one regardless.
What is your English communication culture — written summaries, recorded demos, live calls? Asynchronous clarity is a skill; ask for evidence of it.
Can I speak to a client in a similar time zone and industry who shipped in the last year? References that match your situation, not their best-case portfolio.
The Ownership Terms: How to Never Get Held Hostage From 8,000 Miles Away
Offshore relationships concentrate power in one place — the party that holds the code, the accounts, and the knowledge. Structured correctly, that party should be you, from the first hour of the engagement. The non-negotiables are short enough to memorize: the code is committed to your repository from day one; every cloud, domain, and third-party account is registered in your company's name; documentation is a deliverable, not a favor; and the contract contains a no-lock-in exit — meaning if the relationship ends tomorrow, any competent new team picks up where the last one left off within days. Teams that deliver this way treat it as standard operating procedure rather than a special concession, and it is the single most reliable signal of maturity in the entire offshore market. Confident firms with a decade of cross-border delivery and a thousand-plus projects behind them volunteer these terms unprompted, because their retention strategy is being good, not being essential — and time zones have never once been a substitute for that.

The Red Flags of Offshore Engagements (Learn to See Them Early)
The rate that is too good. A day rate dramatically below the market band above is not a bargain; it is a preview of the rework invoice.
Generic portfolios. No client names, no live links, no launch dates. Screenshots are free; shipping history is evidence.
Vague team composition. "We have a large team" is not an answer. Names, roles, and a video call with your actual developers.
No overlap commitment in writing. "We're flexible about timing" means you are not. Get the hours specified in the contract.
Hourly billing with wide ranges. "400–800 hours" is an open invoice. Fixed quotes with defined scope are the professional alternative.
Slow first responses. If pre-sales takes two days to answer a simple question, imagine the engineering queue after you have paid.
Resistance to your repository. Any excuse for keeping the code on their infrastructure is disqualifying. There are no good versions of this answer.
How to Run the Engagement: A 5-Step Operating Rhythm
Start with discovery, not development. An audit of requirements, a defined scope, and a fixed written quote with timeline — in your currency — before the first commit. This is also where you discover whether the team asks sharp questions or just agrees with everything.
Set the overlap schedule in week one. Standing live standups inside your shared hours, plus an asynchronous written summary for everything outside them.
Demand weekly demos of working software. Judge progress by what you can click, not by what you are told. Drift caught in days costs conversations; drift caught in months costs budgets.
Keep every asset yours from day one. Repository, cloud, accounts, credentials, documentation — audited monthly, not discovered at handover.
Close each sprint with a written record. What shipped, what changed, what is next. Six months in, this record is the difference between a team that runs itself and a project that depends on memory.
Final Thoughts: Buy Structure, Not Hours
The offshore decision is not really about geography — it is about structure. A team organized around your time zone, on a fixed written quote, shipping working software into your repository every week, with every account and credential in your name, will outperform an expensive local hire who is 60 percent available. A cheap team in the dark model will lose to both. So ask the eight questions, check the ownership terms before the price, demand the overlap schedule in writing, and weight everything by one criterion: does this team's structure make distance irrelevant, or does their pitch merely assume you will not notice it? Firms that run true multi-time-zone delivery — New Delhi to New York to London, the way https://elgrith.com/ does — have already made distance their product. The founders who win with offshore teams are the ones who learned to hire structure first and geography second.

title: 6 Best API Gateways for Developers Breaking Their Routing Logic
description:
Six API gateways compared through the lens of routing: path matching, rewrites, header-based rules, and traffic splitting. Here is what each one does well, where it falls short, and which one I would choose for different projects.

Last reviewed: October 2026. Pricing, licensing, and features change often in this category, so check each vendor's current docs before you commit.

TL;DR

  • AWS-native and fully managed: Amazon API Gateway.
  • Enterprise API programs with governance and policies: Apigee.
  • Microsoft and Azure shops: Azure API Management.
  • Fine-grained route matching and a big plugin ecosystem: Kong Gateway (read the licensing note first).
  • Stateless, declarative, and good at aggregation: KrakenD.
  • Open-source core with an optional dashboard: Tyk.

Most gateway bugs are routing bugs. A trailing slash that returns a 404. A rewrite that doubles a path segment. A canary that sends everything to the new version. A header rule that never fires because the casing is different.

Every gateway here can route a request. They differ in how you express rules, split traffic, ship config changes, and what happens when a rule is wrong.

I compared 6 gateways across two groups: cloud-managed and self-hosted. This is an editorial comparison based on each product's documented capabilities, not a benchmark in which every gateway handled identical traffic.

My biggest takeaway: the best gateway is the one whose routing rules you can read, test, and change safely when something breaks at 2 a.m.

What is an API gateway?

An API gateway is the single entry point between clients and your services. It receives every request, decides which upstream should handle it, and applies cross-cutting rules on the way: authentication, rate limits, transformations, and logging.

For example, a client calls /v1/orders/42, and the gateway authenticates it, rewrites the path to /orders/42, and forwards it to the orders service without the client knowing where that service lives.

That routing step is where gateways differ most. Some express rules as declarative config, some as XML policies, some as code-like expressions. That distinction should drive your choice.

How gateway routing works

Every gateway in this guide runs roughly the same pipeline for each request:

Stage What happens Typical failure
1. Match Find the route by host, path, method, and headers Wrong route wins, or no route matches
2. Authenticate and limit Check keys, tokens, and quotas Rule applied to the wrong route
3. Transform Rewrite the path, add or strip headers Doubled or missing path segments
4. Select upstream Pick a backend: static, weighted, or conditional Split ratios that don't match the config
5. Proxy Forward with timeouts, retries, and health checks Retries on non-idempotent calls
6. Respond Return, transform, or aggregate the response Leaked internal headers or errors

Here is how each gateway expresses the routing-specific parts:

Gateway Match on Rewrite with Split traffic with
Amazon API Gateway Resource path and method Integration request mapping Canary release settings on a REST API stage
Apigee Base path, plus conditions on request variables Policies and the target Path Weighted load balancer across target servers
Azure API Management Operation URL template and method, plus policy expressions The rewrite-uri policy A choose policy with a random expression, or backend pools
Kong Gateway Paths (including regex), methods, hosts, and headers strip_path and the service path Weighted targets in an upstream
KrakenD Endpoint and method; header conditions in Enterprise url_pattern on each backend Repeated hosts for weights, or DNS SRV weights
Tyk listen_path, API versions, and rewrite rules strip_listen_path and target_url Load balancing with weights set in the Dashboard

One routing problem, six configs

To compare gateways fairly, I use the same problem throughout:

  • Rewrite: GET /v1/orders/{id} must reach the upstream as /orders/{id}.
  • Split: 90 percent of traffic goes to orders v1, and 10 percent goes to orders v2.
  • Override: a request with the header X-Canary: true always goes to v2.

Each tool section shows the config for this problem. Where a gateway can't do a part natively, I say so. The testing section at the end includes a small harness you can run against any of them.

How the tools are compared

A gateway that routes a demo request tells you little about production. So the tools are judged on five criteria that matter once real traffic and real teams arrive:

  1. Routing expressiveness: how precisely you can match requests and rewrite them.
  2. Traffic splitting and releases: how well it supports canary, blue/green, and header-based overrides.
  3. Config model and GitOps: whether rules live in reviewable files you can test and deploy from CI.
  4. Operations: how much infrastructure you run, and how it scales and fails.
  5. Cost and licensing clarity: how predictable the pricing and license terms are.

The better gateway is the one that lets you change a routing rule safely, review it in a pull request, and roll it back quickly.

The 6 tools at a glance

Tool Category Best for Config style
Amazon API Gateway Cloud-managed AWS-native APIs, Lambda, and private VPC integrations OpenAPI and infrastructure as code
Apigee Cloud-managed Large API programs with governance XML proxy bundles and policies
Azure API Management Cloud-managed Azure-based teams and hybrid deployments XML policies and Bicep or ARM
Kong Gateway Self-hosted Rich route matching and plugins Declarative YAML, decK, or Admin API
KrakenD Self-hosted Stateless gateways and API aggregation A single JSON file
Tyk Self-hosted Open-source core with optional dashboard API definitions in JSON or YAML

Scorecard against the five criteria

These ratings reflect my editorial judgment based on documented capabilities, not measured test results.

Tool Routing expressiveness Traffic splitting and releases Config model and GitOps Operations Cost and licensing clarity
Amazon API Gateway Medium High Medium High High
Apigee High Medium Medium High Low
Azure API Management High Medium Medium High Medium
Kong Gateway High High High Medium Low
KrakenD Medium Low High High High
Tyk Medium Medium High Medium Medium

The trade-off is clear. Cloud-managed gateways remove the operations work but tie your routing logic to one vendor's model. Self-hosted gateways give you declarative config and portability, and you run them yourself.

Who should pick what

You are... Start with Why
An AWS-native team using Lambda or private services Amazon API Gateway Fully managed, with native canary releases on REST APIs
A large organization with an API governance program Apigee Policy-driven proxies and API product management
A team standardized on Azure Azure API Management Policy expressions and deep Azure integration
A team that needs flexible route matching and plugins Kong Gateway Routes by path, host, header, and regex, plus weighted upstreams
A team that wants a stateless gateway in one JSON file KrakenD Simple deployment and built-in aggregation
A team that wants an open-source core and a dashboard Tyk Open-source gateway with a commercial dashboard option

My default picks: Amazon API Gateway if you're on AWS, Azure API Management if you're on Azure, KrakenD for a simple self-hosted gateway, and Kong when you need the richest route matching and can accept its licensing terms. Replace any of these if the specifics below fit your project better.

Category 1: Cloud-Managed Gateways

These run as a service, so you don't patch or scale gateway nodes. They are the best place to start if your backends already live in that cloud.

1. Amazon API Gateway


Amazon API Gateway is AWS's managed gateway. It offers REST, HTTP, and WebSocket APIs, and it integrates directly with Lambda, HTTP backends, and private services inside a VPC. Its canary release documentation describes how to send a percentage of traffic to a new deployment.

What makes it useful

  • Fully managed, with no gateway servers to run or scale.
  • Stage variables let one API definition point to different backends per stage.
  • Canary release deployments on REST API stages, with a percentTraffic setting and stage variable overrides.
  • Native integrations with Lambda, authorizers, usage plans, and AWS services.
  • Configuration through OpenAPI, the AWS CLI, and infrastructure-as-code tools.

Here is the rewrite part of the running problem for a REST API. The integration URI uses a stage variable for the host, and the path parameter is mapped from the method request to the integration request.

openapi: "3.0.1"
info:
  title: orders-gateway
  version: "1.0"
paths:
  /v1/orders/{id}:
    get:
      parameters:
        - name: id
          in: path
          required: true
          schema:
            type: string
      x-amazon-apigateway-integration:
        type: http_proxy
        httpMethod: GET
        uri: http://${stageVariables.ordersHost}/orders/{id}
        requestParameters:
          integration.request.path.id: method.request.path.id
        passthroughBehavior: when_no_match

The 90/10 split comes from a canary release. First deploy to the stage with the production host in a stage variable, then deploy again with canary settings that override that variable for 10 percent of traffic:

# 1. Deploy v1 to the stage, with the host in a stage variable
aws apigateway create-deployment \
  --rest-api-id abcd1234 \
  --stage-name prod \
  --variables ordersHost=orders-v1.internal.example.com

# 2. Deploy again as a canary that overrides the variable for 10% of requests
aws apigateway create-deployment \
  --rest-api-id abcd1234 \
  --stage-name prod \
  --canary-settings percentTraffic=10,stageVariableOverrides={ordersHost=orders-v2.internal.example.com}

The important part is that the split is percentage-based and applies to the whole stage. I didn't find a native way to force a header such as X-Canary: true to v2 in the documentation I reviewed, so a header override needs a separate stage or a layer in front.

Where it falls short: A canary deployment covers the whole API stage, so you can't canary a single route. The documented canary workflow is for REST APIs, so check the current feature matrix if you plan to use the lighter HTTP API type. Routing rules also live partly in OpenAPI extensions and partly in stage settings, which makes them harder to review in one place.

My verdict: Amazon API Gateway is my default for AWS-native teams that want a managed gateway and simple percentage-based canaries.

2. Apigee


Apigee is Google Cloud's API management platform. You build an API proxy from a bundle of XML: a ProxyEndpoint that receives requests, a TargetEndpoint that calls your backend, and policies in between. Its load balancing documentation covers target servers and the available algorithms.

What makes it useful

  • RouteRules with conditions let one proxy send requests to different TargetEndpoints.
  • Target servers separate backend hosts from proxy config so that you can change them per environment.
  • A built-in load balancer with RoundRobin, Weighted, and LeastConnections algorithms.
  • A large policy library for transformation, security, and traffic management.
  • Managed and hybrid deployment options.

This proxy covers the whole routing problem: the BasePath handles /v1/orders, a header-based RouteRule overrides to v2, and a weighted load balancer splits everything else.

<ProxyEndpoint name="default">
  <HTTPProxyConnection>
    <BasePath>/v1/orders</BasePath>
  </HTTPProxyConnection>

  <!-- Header override: always v2 -->
  <RouteRule name="canary-header">
    <Condition>request.header.x-canary = "true"</Condition>
    <TargetEndpoint>orders-v2</TargetEndpoint>
  </RouteRule>

  <!-- Default rule goes last -->
  <RouteRule name="default">
    <TargetEndpoint>orders-split</TargetEndpoint>
  </RouteRule>
</ProxyEndpoint>

<TargetEndpoint name="orders-split">
  <HTTPTargetConnection>
    <LoadBalancer>
      <Algorithm>Weighted</Algorithm>
      <Server name="orders-v1"><Weight>9</Weight></Server>
      <Server name="orders-v2"><Weight>1</Weight></Server>
    </LoadBalancer>
    <Path>/orders</Path>
  </HTTPTargetConnection>
</TargetEndpoint>

<TargetEndpoint name="orders-v2">
  <HTTPTargetConnection>
    <LoadBalancer>
      <Server name="orders-v2" />
    </LoadBalancer>
    <Path>/orders</Path>
  </HTTPTargetConnection>
</TargetEndpoint>

The request path after the BasePath is appended to the target Path, so /v1/orders/42 reaches the backend as /orders/42. The orders-v1 and orders-v2 names refer to target servers that you define in the environment.

The important part is that every server in one load balancer shares the same Path. If v2 lived at a different path, a weighted balancer can't express that, and you would need conditional routes or a separate proxy in front.

Where it falls short: The XML bundle model is verbose, and routing logic spreads across proxy endpoints, target endpoints, and target servers. Enterprise-grade pricing and platform breadth make it heavy for a small team that only needs routing. Check the current pricing model before you commit.

My verdict: Apigee is the strongest option when routing is one part of a larger API governance program, and a poor fit when it is the whole job.

3. Azure API Management


Azure API Management, or APIM, is Microsoft's managed gateway. Its routing logic lives in policies, XML snippets that run in the inbound, backend, outbound, and on-error sections of a request. Policies can be set at global, product, API, or operation scope. See the set-backend-service policy reference.

What makes it useful

  • Policy expressions use C# syntax so that conditions can inspect headers, query strings, and variables.
  • set-backend-service switches the backend by base URL or by a named backend entity.
  • Backend entities can form a load-balanced pool with circuit breaker rules.
  • Gateway options include classic, v2, consumption, and self-hosted gateways for hybrid setups.
  • You can configure this through the portal, Bicep, ARM, and the management API.

Here is an operation-level policy for the running problem. It rewrites the path, then picks a backend with a header override or a 10 percent random split.

<policies>
  <inbound>
    <base />
    <rewrite-uri template="/orders/{id}" />
    <choose>
      <when condition="@(context.Request.Headers.GetValueOrDefault("x-canary", "") == "true" || new System.Random().Next(1, 101) > 90)">
        <set-backend-service base-url="https://orders-v2.internal.example.com" />
      </when>
      <otherwise>
        <set-backend-service base-url="https://orders-v1.internal.example.com" />
      </otherwise>
    </choose>
  </inbound>
  <backend>
    <base />
  </backend>
  <outbound>
    <base />
  </outbound>
  <on-error>
    <base />
  </on-error>
</policies>

The operation's URL template would be /v1/orders/{id}. Published examples of this pattern note that APIM has no dedicated traffic-splitting policy, so you build it from a random expression, and each request is decided independently.

The important part is to keep the split values in named values, not hard-coded in the expression, so you can change the percentage without editing policy code.

Where it falls short: XML plus C# expressions is hard to unit test, and a quoting mistake is a runtime error. The random split is not sticky, so the same user can bounce between versions. Tier choice affects features and cost, so check the tier comparison before you design around a capability.

My verdict: Azure API Management is the natural choice for Azure-centric teams, and its policy expressions make header-based routing easy. Plan to build and test the traffic split yourself.

Category 2: Self-Hosted Gateways

These run on your infrastructure, in containers or on Kubernetes. You get portable, declarative config and full control, and you take on the operations and the licensing questions.

4. Kong Gateway


Kong Gateway models routing with services, routes, upstreams, and plugins. Routes match requests by path (including regex), method, host, and headers, and upstreams hold weighted targets. Its documentation covers the entities and the declarative config format.

A licensing note before you adopt it. Starting with Gateway 3.10, released in March 2025, Kong stopped publishing prebuilt open-source Docker images and removed free mode, so running 3.10 or later without a license behaves like an expired Enterprise license. The last open-source line is 3.9, which Kong's community discussions describe as frozen. Confirm Kong's current licensing and downloads before you choose it.

What makes it useful

  • Precise route matching on paths, regex, methods, hosts, and headers.
  • Upstreams with weighted targets and health checks, so a 90/10 split is a config value.
  • A large plugin ecosystem for authentication, rate limiting, and transformation.
  • Declarative config you can validate and sync from CI with decK, or run without a database.
  • Kubernetes support through its ingress controller.

This declarative file covers the running problem. The main route sends traffic to a weighted upstream, and a second, more specific route sends the canary header straight to v2.

_format_version: "3.0"

upstreams:
  - name: orders-upstream
    targets:
      - target: orders-v1.internal:8080
        weight: 90
      - target: orders-v2.internal:8080
        weight: 10

services:
  - name: orders
    host: orders-upstream
    path: /orders
    routes:
      - name: orders-route
        paths:
          - /v1/orders
        methods:
          - GET
        strip_path: true

  - name: orders-v2
    host: orders-v2.internal
    port: 8080
    path: /orders
    routes:
      - name: orders-canary-header
        paths:
          - /v1/orders
        methods:
          - GET
        headers:
          x-canary:
            - "true"
        strip_path: true

# Preview, then apply (older decK versions use `deck diff` and `deck sync`)
deck gateway diff kong.yaml
deck gateway sync kong.yaml

The important part is how the rewrite works. With strip_path set to true, Kong removes the matched route path, /v1/orders, and prepends the service path, /orders, so /v1/orders/42 reaches the backend as /orders/42.

Where it falls short: The licensing change is the biggest risk, because the free path now ends at an older release and current builds need a license. Route precedence between a plain route and a header route is easy to get wrong, so confirm the winner with a test request. Plugin availability also varies by tier, so check that the plugins you need are in the plan you choose.

My verdict: Kong has the most expressive routing in this list. Weigh the licensing terms first, and pick it when you will use that expressiveness.

5. KrakenD


KrakenD is a stateless gateway driven by one JSON file, with no database. You declare endpoints, and each endpoint lists the backends it calls. Its backend documentation explains how host, url_pattern, and aggregation work. The Community Edition is open source under Apache 2.0, and an Enterprise Edition adds features.

What makes it useful

  • Stateless and database-free, so deployment is a container and a config file.
  • An endpoint can call several backends in parallel and merge the results, which suits backend-for-frontend designs.
  • The url_pattern on each backend rewrites the path, using variables from the endpoint.
  • Egress load balancing across a host list, with DNS SRV records for weighted balancing.
  • Enterprise adds API key authentication and conditional routing, and the configuration is compatible with the Community Edition.

Here is the Community Edition config for the running problem. KrakenD's documentation describes a simple way to weight a host list: repeat the host. Nine entries for v1 and one for v2 give a 90/10 split.

{
  "$schema": "https://www.krakend.io/schema/krakend.json",
  "version": 3,
  "endpoints": [
    {
      "endpoint": "/v1/orders/{id}",
      "method": "GET",
      "output_encoding": "no-op",
      "backend": [
        {
          "encoding": "no-op",
          "url_pattern": "/orders/{id}",
          "host": [
            "http://orders-v1:8080", "http://orders-v1:8080", "http://orders-v1:8080",
            "http://orders-v1:8080", "http://orders-v1:8080", "http://orders-v1:8080",
            "http://orders-v1:8080", "http://orders-v1:8080", "http://orders-v1:8080",
            "http://orders-v2:8080"
          ]
        }
      ]
    }
  ]
}

The header override needs Enterprise conditional routing. In that edition, you split v1 and v2 into separate backends and let a header rule choose between them, with a fallback for everything else:

"backend": [
  {
    "url_pattern": "/orders/{id}",
    "host": ["http://orders-v2:8080"],
    "extra_config": {
      "backend/conditional": {
        "strategy": "header",
        "name": "X-Canary",
        "value": "true"
      }
    }
  },
  {
    "url_pattern": "/orders/{id}",
    "host": ["http://orders-v1:8080"],
    "extra_config": {
      "backend/conditional": {
        "strategy": "fallback"
      }
    }
  }
]

The important part is KrakenD's design rule that one endpoint can't have several write backends, which keeps the gateway from acting as a transaction coordinator.

Where it falls short: Weighted splitting in the Community Edition is a workaround, not a feature, and header-based routing and API keys are Enterprise-only. By default, url_pattern must be RESTful, which you can relax with disable_rest. KrakenD has also announced that it is dropping plugin support in the open-source edition, so check the current status if you depend on custom plugins.

My verdict: KrakenD is my default for a simple self-hosted gateway, especially when you want aggregation and a config file you can review in one place. It is the weakest option here for fine-grained traffic splitting.

6. Tyk


Tyk is a gateway whose routing lives in API definitions. Each definition sets a listen_path, a target_url, and options such as strip_listen_path and load balancing. The gateway is open source, and the Dashboard and other management features are offered commercially. Its load balancing documentation covers target lists and weighting.

What makes it useful

  • Simple API definitions, expressed as JSON or as Kubernetes resources through Tyk Operator.
  • Native round-robin load balancing with a target_list.
  • Weighting in the Dashboard so that you can send, for example, 10 percent of traffic to a beta backend.
  • Service discovery integrations, such as Consul and etcd, for dynamic target lists.
  • Rewrite rules that can act on request details, plus gRPC load balancing.

Here is a Tyk Operator definition for the running problem. Without weights, the two targets share traffic evenly.

apiVersion: tyk.tyk.io/v1alpha1
kind: ApiDefinition
metadata:
  name: orders
spec:
  name: orders
  use_keyless: true
  protocol: http
  active: true
  proxy:
    listen_path: /v1/orders
    strip_listen_path: true
    target_url: http://orders-v1.internal:8080/orders
    enable_load_balancing: true
    target_list:
      - http://orders-v1.internal:8080/orders
      - http://orders-v2.internal:8080/orders

The rewrite follows the documented rule: Tyk strips the listen path and appends what remains to the target URL, so /v1/orders/42 reaches the backend as /orders/42. For the 90/10 ratio, set weights of 9 and 1 in the Dashboard's load balancing settings. A header override can use a URL rewrite rule that matches the header, and the exact syntax depends on your Tyk version, so check its rewrite documentation.

The important part is how Tyk treats versions. Its documentation recommends a separate, non-versioned API definition for each URL-based version (e.g., /v1 and /v2), because versions in an API definition assume the same URL structure.

Where it falls short: Weighted routing is documented through the Dashboard, so confirm how you will express weights in your deployment model, whether files, the Operator, or the Dashboard. Without strip_listen_path, proxied requests are literal, so the listen path leaks into the upstream URL. Check which management features your use case needs a commercial license for.

My verdict: Tyk is a solid choice if you want an open-source gateway with a Kubernetes-friendly definition format and the option of a dashboard.

Kong, KrakenD, or Tyk?

Kong has the richest route matching and plugin ecosystem, but it carries the licensing risk described above. KrakenD is the simplest to run and the best at aggregation, but it has the weakest traffic splitting in its Community Edition. Tyk sits between them, with an open-source gateway, simple definitions, and weighting that lives in its Dashboard. Test each on the same routing problem, using the harness below, before you decide.

Pricing, licensing, and lock-in

Prices change too often to list, but the models differ in ways that matter:

  • Cloud-managed gateways charge by usage, tier, or subscription. Amazon API Gateway bills per request, Azure API Management sells tiers with different features, and Apigee uses enterprise-style pricing, so model your expected traffic before you compare.
  • Kong changed its terms in 2025: the free path ends at the 3.9 open-source line, and later releases need a license.
  • KrakenD has a free Community Edition under Apache 2.0 and a commercial Enterprise Edition that is quoted on request.
  • Tyk offers an open-source gateway, with commercial management features such as the Dashboard.

Lock-in lives in your rules. XML policies and C# expressions don't port between vendors, while declarative route definitions are easier to translate. Keep business logic out of the gateway, so switching is a routing migration, not a rewrite.

In general, the more routing logic you put into vendor-specific policy, the more you should check export options and exit costs before you commit.

Test your routing logic before production

Routing rules fail quietly, so test them like code. The setup below works against any gateway in this guide. First, a tiny upstream that reports its path and version, so you can see exactly what the gateway sent.

# echo.py  (pip install flask)
import os
from flask import Flask, jsonify, request

app = Flask(__name__)
VERSION = os.environ.get("VERSION", "v1")

@app.get("/orders/<order_id>")
def get_order(order_id):
    response = jsonify({"id": order_id, "path": request.path, "version": VERSION})
    response.headers["X-Served-By"] = VERSION
    return response

if __name__ == "__main__":
    app.run(host="0.0.0.0", port=8080)

Run one copy as v1 and another as v2, point the gateway at them, then assert the three requirements from the running problem:

import collections
import requests

GATEWAY = "http://localhost:8000"

def test_path_is_rewritten():
    r = requests.get(f"{GATEWAY}/v1/orders/42", timeout=5)
    assert r.status_code == 200
    assert r.json()["path"] == "/orders/42"

def test_header_forces_v2():
    for _ in range(50):
        r = requests.get(
            f"{GATEWAY}/v1/orders/42",
            headers={"X-Canary": "true"},
            timeout=5,
        )
        assert r.headers["X-Served-By"] == "v2"

def test_split_is_close_to_90_10():
    counts = collections.Counter()
    n = 2000
    for _ in range(n):
        r = requests.get(f"{GATEWAY}/v1/orders/42", timeout=5)
        counts[r.headers["X-Served-By"]] += 1
    v2_share = counts["v2"] / n
    assert 0.06 <= v2_share <= 0.14, counts

The tolerance on the split matters. With 2,000 requests, a true 10 percent split will vary by well under a percentage point, so a band of 6 to 14 percent catches a wrong ratio without flaking. Run these in CI against a staging gateway whenever routing config changes.

Common routing bugs

Symptom Likely cause What to check
404 only when the URL ends in a slash Trailing-slash handling differs between gateways Test the path with and without a trailing slash
The backend receives /v1/orders/42 The route prefix wasn't stripped strip_path, strip_listen_path, or a rewrite rule
The backend receives /orders/orders/42 A stripped prefix plus a service path that repeats the segment Compare the route path with the service or target path
The canary header is ignored Route precedence, or the rule never matches Send the header through a test and confirm which route wins
The split is off at low volume Random selection needs a large sample Measure with at least 1,000 requests
Users bounce between versions The split is random per request, not sticky Route by header, cookie, or a hash of the user ID
Duplicate writes appear The gateway retried a non-idempotent call Limit retries to idempotent methods

Roll out a canary with a rollback

A percentage split is only safe if something watches it. This sketch shows the loop: raise the weight in steps, compare the error rate with the baseline, and roll back when it worsens. Wire set_weight and error_rate to your gateway's API and your metrics.

STEPS = [1, 5, 25, 50, 100]

def promote(set_weight, error_rate, baseline, tolerance=0.005):
    for percent in STEPS:
        set_weight(percent)
        # Let traffic soak here, then compare against the baseline
        if error_rate() > baseline + tolerance:
            set_weight(0)
            raise RuntimeError(f"Rolled back at {percent}%")

Also set explicit upstream timeouts, add health checks or circuit breakers where the gateway supports them, and tag every response with the version that served it so that you can compare error rates and latency per version.

What gateways can't replace

A gateway centralizes routing, but it doesn't remove the need for good design.

  • Business logic belongs in services: Complex orchestration in gateway policy is hard to test, version, and debug. Keep the gateway to routing, security, and cross-cutting rules.
  • Authentication isn't authorization: A gateway can verify a token, but your services still decide what each caller may do.
  • Config drift is a real risk: Rules edited in a console and not in version control will diverge from what you reviewed. Treat gateway config as code.
  • Observability is your job: Without per-route metrics, logs, and traces, a bad rule looks like a flaky backend.

Gateways work best when they handle routing and policy, and you stay responsible for testing the rules, watching the traffic, and keeping the logic simple.

Final verdict

No single gateway suits every team. If you're on AWS, start with Amazon API Gateway for managed canaries. If you're on Azure, use Azure API Management and plan to build your own traffic split. If you run a large API program with governance needs, consider Apigee. If you want a simple self-hosted gateway, use KrakenD. If you need the richest route matching and can accept its licensing terms, use Kong. If you want an open-source gateway with an optional dashboard, consider Tyk.

A gateway shortens the path between a client request and the right service, but the first working route is only the beginning. Choose the gateway whose rules you can read, test in CI, and change safely when traffic and teams grow.

Frequently asked questions

What is the best API gateway for microservices?

It depends on where you run. Amazon API Gateway suits AWS, Azure API Management suits Azure, Apigee suits large governed API programs, and Kong, KrakenD, and Tyk suit self-hosted setups on Kubernetes or containers.

What is the difference between an API gateway, a reverse proxy, and an ingress controller?

A reverse proxy forwards requests to backends. An ingress controller routes external traffic into a Kubernetes cluster. An API gateway adds API-level features, such as authentication, rate limiting, transformation, and developer management. The lines blur, and several products play multiple roles.

How do I run a canary release at the gateway?

Send a small percentage of traffic to the new version and watch error rates and latency before raising it. Amazon API Gateway has canary settings on REST API stages, Kong uses weighted upstream targets, Apigee uses a weighted load balancer, and Azure API Management needs a policy expression. Use a header or cookie rule if users must stay on one version.

Is Kong still open source?

Kong's source repository is open, but the open-source distribution stopped at the 3.9 line. Starting with 3.10, Kong stopped publishing prebuilt open-source images and removed free mode, so current builds need a license. Check Kong's current terms before you adopt it.

Should I put business logic in my API gateway?

Generally no. Keep the gateway to routing, authentication, rate limiting, and transformation. Business rules in gateway policy are hard to test and tie your system to one vendor.

title: 8 Agent UI Patterns
description:
A chatbot answers. An agent acts: it searches, calls APIs, edits files, sends emails. That changes what the interface has to do. The user is no longer reading a reply; they are supervising a worker they can't see.

After building a lot of agent interfaces, I keep coming back to the same eight patterns. None of them are about looking clever. They are about one thing: letting the user trust what the agent is doing.

1. A thinking state that isn't a spinner

The gap between "send" and the first token is where users decide whether the app is broken. A generic spinner says "loading". A thinking state says "working on your thing".

Keep it calm: slow motion, a short label that can change ("Searching the web…", "Reading 3 files…"), and respect prefers-reduced-motion.


Example: Thinking wave

2. Streaming text without layout shift

Streaming is table stakes, but jumping layouts are not. Reserve space for the message, render markdown incrementally, and don't re-flow code blocks on every token.

3. Tool calls the user can read

When the agent calls a tool, show it: the tool name, the arguments as they stream in, a running state, then the result. Collapse finished calls so a long turn doesn't become a wall.

This is the single biggest trust win. Users stop wondering "what is it doing?" because they can see it.

Example: Tool call. It takes a Vercel AI SDK tool part directly:

{message.parts.map((part, i) =>
  part.type.startsWith("tool-") ? <ToolCall key={i} part={part} /> : null
)}

4. Approval before side effects

Anything hard to undo (sending, paying, deleting, publishing) should stop and ask. Show the exact arguments, not a summary: who gets the email, what the subject is, which file is attached. Two buttons, clear outcome.

Example: Tool approval

5. A plan with live progress

For multi-step work, show the plan first, then tick steps off as they finish. It sets expectations ("4 steps") and makes long runs feel shorter.

Example: Task checklist

6. Sources and inline citations

If the agent read something, show where. Inline citation chips next to the claim, and a sources list the user can open. Uncited answers from an agent that clearly browsed feel like it is hiding something.

7. An artifact panel

When the output is a thing (a document, a chart, code), put it in its own panel next to the chat, with versions. Chat is for talking about the artifact, not for scrolling through it.

8. Voice that shows it's listening

Voice agents need a visible state machine: idle, listening, thinking, speaking. One orb or ring that changes motion per state beats four different icons.

Example: Voice agent

The pattern behind the patterns

Every one of these answers a question the user would otherwise ask out loud: Is it working? What is it doing? Is it about to do something I didn't want? Where did that come from? Answer those in the UI and the agent feels trustworthy, even when it is wrong sometimes.

I'm collecting these as copy-paste React + Tailwind components at nextui.dev. The code lands in your repo, no runtime package. I'd love to hear which agent UI pattern you find hardest to get right. Tell me in the comments.

title: Finding ZMODEM in a Terminal Byte Stream: How `rz`/`sz` Works Inside an SSH Client
description:
Originally published on MistLab. Part 5 of Building an SSH Terminal.

Part 5 of "Building an SSH Terminal". Code excerpts are from MistTerm v1.2.26, an open-source (AGPL) SSH terminal client by MistLab; they are trimmed, and source comments are translated from Chinese.

TL;DR

ZMODEM, implemented by the lrzsz tools rz and sz, is a file-transfer protocol that runs inside the terminal session itself, so it works over SSH without a second connection. The client has to find ZMODEM frame headers in ordinary output, then route the PTY stream to the protocol instead of the emulator. MistTerm only starts a transfer when it sees a valid header and the user has just run sz or rz.

On many production servers the quickest way to move a file is still sz file.tar.gz to download it, or rz to upload one. These are the lrzsz tools, implementing ZMODEM, a file-transfer protocol from 1986 designed for modems and serial lines. It works over SSH because it never needs a separate connection. It runs inside the terminal session, over the same PTY bytes as everything else.

That is also what makes it hard for a terminal. The client has to spot the start of a transfer inside a stream that is otherwise text for the screen. It then has to take the stream away from the emulator, run a protocol over it, and hand it back cleanly.

How does ZMODEM work? Just enough of the protocol

The protocol is described in Chuck Forsberg's ZMODEM specification. The parts that matter here:

  • Frames start with a header. Header bytes include ZPAD (*) and ZDLE (0x18, the same value as ASCII CAN), followed by a format byte. B is a hex header, encoded entirely in printable hex digits and ended by CR LF. A is binary with CRC-16, C is binary with CRC-32. A hex header looks like ** ZDLE B + two hex digits for the frame type + eight for flags + four for the CRC. Binary headers formally use a single ZPAD.
  • Frame types relevant to startup: ZRQINIT (type 0), sent by the sender to ask for a receiver; and ZRINIT (type 1), sent by the receiver to say it is ready and to state its capabilities.
  • ZDLE escaping. In binary data, ZDLE and certain control characters are escaped, so a frame survives links that interpret XON/XOFF.
  • Cancellation. Five or more consecutive CAN (0x18) bytes abort a session.

The roles follow from the command. sz on the server is the sender: it starts by printing rz\r (a hint to terminals that auto-start a receiver) and a hex ZRQINIT. The client must become the receiver and answer with ZRINIT. rz on the server is the receiver: it announces itself with ZRINIT (lrzsz also prints the text "rz waiting to receive."). The client must become the sender and start with a file header (ZFILE).

ZMODEM over a PTY: detection, then the protocol takes over the stream

How does a terminal detect rz/sz? Not mistaking text for a frame

A terminal that turns into a file receiver whenever **\x18B00 scrolls past would misfire on cat-ing a binary file, on log output, or on someone viewing this article over SSH. MistTerm combines three signals.

Scan a bounded tail, not just the latest read. A header can be split across reads (Part 2). Output from the session is appended to a detection tail, capped at the last 512 bytes, and the scanner runs over that window:

fn push_zmodem_detect_tail(&mut self, data: &[u8]) {
    const TAIL_CAP: usize = 512;
    self.zmodem_pty_detect_tail.extend_from_slice(data);
    if self.zmodem_pty_detect_tail.len() > TAIL_CAP {
        let drop = self.zmodem_pty_detect_tail.len() - TAIL_CAP;
        self.zmodem_pty_detect_tail.drain(..drop);
    }
}

Parse headers structurally. The scanners check the full prefix (ZPAD ZPAD ZDLE + format byte) and decode the type digits. They accept the variants found in the wild, such as a parity-stripped ZPAD (0x80), the single- and double-ZPAD binary forms, and an ASCII **B… form without ZDLE, which the code's comments attribute to the Windows build of lrzsz:

fn hex_scan_for_type(data: &[u8], want: u8) -> bool {
    // at least 6 bytes: `** ZDLE 'B' HH` (HH = frame type as a hex pair)
    for i in 0..data.len().saturating_sub(5) {
        if !is_zpad(data[i]) || !is_zpad(data[i + 1]) || data[i + 2] != zmodem::ZDLE {
            continue;
        }
        let hb = data[i + 3];
        if hb != zmodem::ZHEX && hb != b'B' && hb != b'b' { continue; }
        if let Some(t) = hex_pair(data[i + 4], data[i + 5]) {
            if t == want { return true; }
        }
    }
    false
}

Require intent. A header alone does not start a download. The client also tracks the command line the user submits. If its first word is sz/lsz (any path, .exe allowed), download detection is armed for 30 seconds. Uploads work the same way with rz/lrz, armed for 45 seconds:

pub fn is_sz_shell_command(line: &str) -> bool {
    let base = shell_word_basename(first_shell_word(line));
    let lower = base.to_ascii_lowercase();
    matches!(lower.as_str(), "sz" | "lsz" | "sz.exe" | "lsz.exe")
}

A download starts only when a ZRQINIT is seen and that window is open. echo sz and where rz do not arm it. An upload starts on any of: rz's own prompt text ("rz waiting to receive.", "Awaiting rz", "rz rz rz"), the Windows ASCII **B01 form, or a header seen while an upload is expected. The text check is deliberately specific to lrzsz's messages. The header check is gated by intent.

A naming note for readers of the source: some comments in this code path say that rz "sends ZRQINIT". By the specification, the receiver sends ZRINIT, and ZRQINIT comes from the sender. We list this in the review notes for the series.

Taking over the stream

Once a transfer starts, PTY output belongs to the protocol. Feeding ZMODEM frames to the terminal emulator would put binary garbage on screen and, worse, could be read as control sequences. The handover has a few constraints:

  • One reader. The shell pump thread owns the SSH channel (Part 2). A transfer must not open a second reader, which would race for bytes. Instead the pump forwards PTY output to the ZMODEM engine through a bypass:

Uploads (local sz → remote rz): ZMODEM frames on the PTY can only reach this point through the SSH pump thread; they must be bypassed to the transfer engine, and the Channel must not be read again from another thread.

  • Capture before the file dialog. For an upload, the remote rz is already talking when the user is still choosing a file. MistTerm starts capturing the handshake (begin_rz_handshake_capture) as soon as it is detected, before opening the file picker. Otherwise the receiver's ZRINIT is consumed by the emulator, and the sender waits for a header that already went by.
  • Bounded buffering. While waiting for the first header, or while frames are being reassembled, incoming bytes are buffered up to 512 KiB (RX_INCOMING_CAP). Past that the receive is aborted rather than growing without bound.

The protocol work itself (frame encoding, CRCs, ZDLE escaping, the ZRPOS/ZACK exchange) is done by the zmodem2 crate, vendored in the repository. For comparison testing, setting MISTTERM_ZMODEM_USE_EXTERNAL_SZ=1 makes MistTerm drive a local sz binary instead of the built-in sender.

Two safety details

The remote picks the file name, so treat it as untrusted. The file name arrives in the data subpacket that follows the sender's ZFILE header. A hostile or buggy server could send ../../.bashrc or an absolute path. MistTerm keeps only the final path component and never overwrites:

fn disambiguate_download_path(download_dir: &Path, raw_name: &[u8]) -> Result<PathBuf, String> {
    let base = String::from_utf8_lossy(raw_name);
    let only = Path::new(base.trim())
        .file_name()
        .and_then(|s| s.to_str())
        .filter(|s| !s.is_empty())
        .unwrap_or("zmodem.bin");
    let mut file_path = download_dir.join(only);
    let mut counter = 1u32;
    while file_path.exists() {
        // name_1.ext, name_2.ext, …
    }
    Ok(file_path)
}

Path::file_name returns None for names ending in .., which then fall back to zmodem.bin.

Cancel must jump the queue. When the user cancels an upload, the session queue may still hold file data. A single Ctrl+C is not guaranteed to stop rz/sz, because while they run the PTY is in raw mode. The cancel goes through the priority queue described in Part 2:

// In ZMODEM protocol state a single Ctrl+C may not be recognized by the remote
// rz/sz; send the CAN sequence at high priority, then ETX.
let cancel = vec![
    0x18, 0x18, 0x18, 0x18, 0x18, 0x18, 0x18, 0x18, // CAN x8
    0x08, 0x08, 0x08, 0x08, 0x08, 0x08, 0x08, 0x08, // erase noise
    0x03, // ETX
];
handle.send_priority_interrupt(cancel)

Eight CANs exceed the spec's five-CAN abort threshold. The backspaces mirror lrzsz's own cancel string (CANs followed by backspaces), erasing the CANs if the line ends up back at a shell. The final ETX covers the case where the remote program has already exited.

Summary

  • ZMODEM runs inside the terminal stream. The client has to find frame headers within ordinary output.
  • Detection needs a bounded scan window, a real header parse, and proof the user just submitted sz/rz.
  • During a transfer, the PTY stream must bypass the emulator through the single channel owner, with bounded buffers.
  • Treat the sender's file name as untrusted, and send cancellation ahead of queued data.

FAQ

How does rz/sz work over SSH?

ZMODEM runs inside the terminal session over the same PTY bytes as normal output, so no separate connection is needed. The terminal must detect the start of a transfer and take the stream over.

What do ZRQINIT and ZRINIT mean?

ZRQINIT (frame type 0) is sent by the sender to ask for a receiver. ZRINIT (frame type 1) is sent by the receiver to say it is ready and to state its capabilities.

Why doesn't MistTerm start a download whenever it sees a ZMODEM header?

Headers can appear in ordinary output, such as a binary file printed with cat. MistTerm also requires that the user has just submitted an sz or rz command.

How do you cancel a ZMODEM transfer?

Five or more consecutive CAN (0x18) bytes abort a session. MistTerm sends eight, ahead of any queued file data.
Related in this series

  • SSH Flow Control, and Why an SSH Client Must Keep Reading While It Writes
  • Command Auditing in an SSH Terminal: What the Client Can See, and What Only the Server Can Enforce

title: Building a Zero-Trust API Gateway with Certificate-Based Auth
description:
Most API gateways authenticate callers with API keys or JWTs — shared secrets that get stolen, rotated lazily, or leaked into logs. Certificate-based mutual TLS (mTLS) eliminates that class of risk entirely: every client proves cryptographic identity on every request, and there is no bearer token to exfiltrate. Here is how to build a minimal zero-trust gateway in Go that enforces it.

Why API Keys Keep Failing

API keys work until they don't. They're long-lived, embedded in environment variables, accidentally committed to repos, passed through logging middleware, and shared across services. The OWASP API Security Top 10 consistently ranks broken authentication as the top risk, and API key misuse is a major contributor.

A client certificate solves these problems at the transport layer:

  • Certificates can't be replicated without the private key
  • Revocation is built in (via CRL or OCSP)
  • Identity is tied to a cryptographic keypair, not a string that can be copied with Ctrl+C

The tradeoff: you need a PKI. For an internal API gateway, a self-signed CA is entirely appropriate.

Setting Up a Minimal CA

Before writing Go code, we need certificates. OpenSSL gives us a CA, a server cert, and a client cert:

# Generate the CA key and self-signed certificate
openssl genrsa -out ca.key 4096
openssl req -x509 -new -nodes -key ca.key -sha256 -days 3650 \
  -subj "/CN=Internal CA" -out ca.crt

# Server certificate
openssl genrsa -out server.key 2048
openssl req -new -key server.key -subj "/CN=api.internal" -out server.csr
openssl x509 -req -in server.csr -CA ca.crt -CAkey ca.key \
  -CAcreateserial -out server.crt -days 365 -sha256

# Client certificate (one per service or team)
openssl genrsa -out client-service-a.key 2048
openssl req -new -key client-service-a.key \
  -subj "/CN=service-a/O=backend-team" -out client-service-a.csr
openssl x509 -req -in client-service-a.csr -CA ca.crt -CAkey ca.key \
  -CAcreateserial -out client-service-a.crt -days 365 -sha256

The /CN and /O fields in the client cert are your identity claims — we'll extract them in the gateway to make routing decisions.

Building the Gateway in Go

The core of a zero-trust gateway is tls.Config with ClientAuth: tls.RequireAndVerifyClientCert. Go's standard library handles the certificate verification chain; we extract the identity and pass it downstream.

package main

import (
    "crypto/tls"
    "crypto/x509"
    "fmt"
    "log"
    "net/http"
    "net/http/httputil"
    "net/url"
    "os"
    "strings"
)

func loadCA(path string) *x509.CertPool {
    pool := x509.NewCertPool()
    pem, err := os.ReadFile(path)
    if err != nil {
        log.Fatalf("reading CA: %v", err)
    }
    if !pool.AppendCertsFromPEM(pem) {
        log.Fatal("failed to parse CA cert")
    }
    return pool
}

func identityMiddleware(next http.Handler) http.Handler {
    return http.HandlerFunc(func(w http.ResponseWriter, r *http.Request) {
        if r.TLS == nil || len(r.TLS.PeerCertificates) == 0 {
            http.Error(w, "client certificate required", http.StatusUnauthorized)
            return
        }
        cert := r.TLS.PeerCertificates[0]
        cn := cert.Subject.CommonName
        org := ""
        if len(cert.Subject.Organization) > 0 {
            org = cert.Subject.Organization[0]
        }
        r.Header.Set("X-Client-CN", cn)
        r.Header.Set("X-Client-Org", org)
        next.ServeHTTP(w, r)
    })
}

var routePolicy = map[string]string{
    "/admin/":    "ops-team",
    "/internal/": "backend-team",
}

func authzMiddleware(next http.Handler) http.Handler {
    return http.HandlerFunc(func(w http.ResponseWriter, r *http.Request) {
        org := r.Header.Get("X-Client-Org")
        for prefix, required := range routePolicy {
            if strings.HasPrefix(r.URL.Path, prefix) && org != required {
                http.Error(w, "forbidden", http.StatusForbidden)
                return
            }
        }
        next.ServeHTTP(w, r)
    })
}

func main() {
    upstream, _ := url.Parse("http://127.0.0.1:8080")
    proxy := httputil.NewSingleHostReverseProxy(upstream)

    mux := http.NewServeMux()
    mux.Handle("/", identityMiddleware(authzMiddleware(proxy)))

    cert, err := tls.LoadX509KeyPair("server.crt", "server.key")
    if err != nil {
        log.Fatalf("loading server cert: %v", err)
    }

    srv := &http.Server{
        Addr:    ":8443",
        Handler: mux,
        TLSConfig: &tls.Config{
            Certificates: []tls.Certificate{cert},
            ClientCAs:    loadCA("ca.crt"),
            ClientAuth:   tls.RequireAndVerifyClientCert,
            MinVersion:   tls.VersionTLS13,
        },
    }

    fmt.Println("Gateway listening on :8443 (mTLS enforced)")
    log.Fatal(srv.ListenAndServeTLS("", ""))
}

This gateway:

  1. Terminates TLS and verifies the client certificate against your CA
  2. Rejects any request without a valid cert with 401 Unauthorized
  3. Injects X-Client-CN and X-Client-Org headers before proxying upstream
  4. Enforces TLS 1.3 minimum — no downgrade possible
  5. Checks route-level authorization based on the client organization field

Testing the Gateway

With the certs generated, you can test immediately with curl:

# Should succeed — valid client cert
curl --cert client-service-a.crt --key client-service-a.key \
     --cacert ca.crt https://localhost:8443/internal/status

# Should fail — no cert
curl --cacert ca.crt https://localhost:8443/internal/status
# curl: (56) OpenSSL SSL_read: error:... alert handshake failure

# Should fail — wrong org for /admin/
curl --cert client-service-a.crt --key client-service-a.key \
     --cacert ca.crt https://localhost:8443/admin/users
# HTTP/2 403 forbidden

The TLS handshake failure for the no-cert case happens before any HTTP code runs — the connection is dropped at the transport layer, not the application layer. That is exactly what zero-trust means in practice.

Revocation and Certificate Rotation

Revocation is where cert-based auth gets operationally expensive if you're not deliberate about it.

Short-lived certs are the simplest approach: issue certs valid for 24-72 hours and automate renewal. A compromised cert expires before most incident response workflows could react. Tools like SPIFFE/SPIRE handle this in Kubernetes environments; for simpler setups, a cron job plus a renewal endpoint works fine.

CRL approach: if you need immediate revocation, host a certificate revocation list and embed the CRL distribution point URL at issuance time. Go's x509 package checks CRLs if you configure a custom VerifyPeerCertificate callback.

Serial blocklist: the simplest fast-revocation mechanism is a Redis set of revoked serial numbers checked in identityMiddleware. Not cryptographically rigorous, but operational within minutes of detecting a compromise.

We maintain free security hardening checklists covering PKI hygiene in depth — OCSP stapling, CRL caching, rotation timelines, and cert pinning tradeoffs.

The Takeaway

mTLS-based API gateways eliminate the entire API key leakage risk category. The Go implementation is compact — standard library tls.Config does the verification work. The hard part is operational: issuing certs, rotating them before expiry, and handling revocation when something goes wrong.

Start with long-lived certs and a manual blocklist. Automate rotation only after you've validated the issuance pipeline end-to-end. The zero-trust claim here is precise: every request carries cryptographic proof of identity, verified on every connection, with no session state to steal.
