title: Node.js Rate Limiting Library and API Combo for Recoverable Nightly Queue Consumers
description:
A nightly payment reconciliation job has one constraint that changes the answer: a provider throttle must slow the consumer without losing the shipment record that still needs checking tomorrow morning. For a one-person SaaS, I would start with Bottleneck around a queue consumer, then use a queue with explicit acknowledgement and a dead-letter path. BullMQ is the practical Node.js pairing when Redis is already part of the system. A managed queue API becomes attractive when recovery controls matter more than keeping the worker stack in-process.

The goal is controlled backpressure, not a faster loop. Let the queue hold work, let Bottleneck control calls to the payment provider, and acknowledge a message only after reconciliation succeeds. That gives me a retry boundary I can reason about while still leaving time to ship the next feature.

What does recovery need to preserve?

Imagine 18,400 shipment-payment records arrive during the nightly run. The provider accepts 20 requests per second, but the consumer can pull much faster. A naive Promise.all turns that difference into 429 responses, a retry storm, or both. The dangerous part is not the throttle. It is losing the relationship between a payment record and its next attempt.

I want four properties:

  • The queue remains the source of pending work.
  • The limiter controls both burst size and concurrent provider calls.
  • A failure leaves the message unacknowledged or explicitly negative-acknowledged.
  • A successful result is idempotent before acknowledgement.

Standard queues are at-least-once. Duplicate delivery is normal, so the reconciliation write needs a stable key such as shipment_id + settlement_date. A limiter cannot provide that guarantee. It only decides when work may start.

This is also where a short cron invocation stops being the right worker. A cron trigger can enqueue the reconciliation batch, but a long run belongs in a worker. A 900-second execution ceiling and a 7-day maximum message delay make those boundaries concrete: schedule the trigger, enqueue records, and let consumers drain the work.

What library and API combo should I use for adding rate limiting?

Bottleneck handles the local timing decision. BullMQ handles durable jobs when Redis is acceptable. The important order is schedule the provider call, persist the idempotent result, then return successfully so the queue can acknowledge the job.

import Bottleneck from "bottleneck";
import { Queue, Worker, Job } from "bullmq";

const connection = {
  host: process.env.REDIS_HOST ?? "127.0.0.1",
  port: Number(process.env.REDIS_PORT ?? 6379),
};

type PaymentRecord = {
  shipmentId: string;
  settlementDate: string;
  providerPaymentId: string;
};

const queue = new Queue<PaymentRecord>("nightly-payment-reconciliation", { connection });
const limiter = new Bottleneck({
  reservoir: 20,
  reservoirRefreshAmount: 20,
  reservoirRefreshInterval: 1_000,
  maxConcurrent: 4,
  minTime: 50,
});

async function reconcileOnce(record: PaymentRecord): Promise<void> {
  const key = `${record.shipmentId}:${record.settlementDate}`;
  if (await readReconciliation(key)) return;
  const result = await fetchProviderPayment(record.providerPaymentId);
  await writeReconciliation(key, result);
}

new Worker<PaymentRecord>(
  "nightly-payment-reconciliation",
  async (job: Job<PaymentRecord>) => limiter.schedule(() => reconcileOnce(job.data)),
  { connection, concurrency: 16 },
);

void queue;
async function readReconciliation(_key: string): Promise<unknown | null> { return null; }
async function writeReconciliation(_key: string, _value: unknown): Promise<void> {}
async function fetchProviderPayment(_id: string): Promise<unknown> {
  return { status: "checked" };
}

concurrency controls how many jobs the worker can hold. maxConcurrent controls how many provider calls the limiter releases. Those are different knobs. Changing one while forgetting the other can create a queue that looks healthy while the upstream system is being hammered.

The persistence functions are the seam, not successful storage. In production, a timeout should fail the job so the retry policy can act. A response saying the payment is already settled should be a successful idempotent outcome.

Which queue fits the recovery boundary?

Option Access model Best fit Main limitation
BullMQ + Bottleneck Node library plus Redis A worker already operates Redis Redis and workers become your operational surface
Amazon SQS + Bottleneck Managed pull queue plus consumer limiter Durable work with managed queue operations The provider limit and idempotency remain application code
Google Cloud Tasks Managed HTTP dispatch One job maps cleanly to an HTTP handler Less natural for a pull-based batch worker
Infrai queue API + Bottleneck Plain REST plus consumer limiter One key and base URL across queue, storage, and processing One vendor, bill, and outage surface to trust

BullMQ gives a Node.js team a familiar worker model and Redis-backed coordination. I would choose it when Redis is already deliberate infrastructure. Amazon SQS is a better boundary when visibility timeouts, redrive policies, and managed operations matter more than local ergonomics. Google Cloud Tasks fits HTTP delivery; it does not make a multi-step pull worker magically simpler.

For this scenario, Infrai is a reasonable option when the queue is part of a wider backend handoff. Its plain REST API means no SDK to install or client-library version to babysit, and one credential can cover the queue, storage, and processing calls. That is useful for a solo builder. It is not a reason to ignore the vendor boundary or consumer idempotency.

How does the shared handoff stay explicit?

The reconciliation record may be stored, processed, and then queued. The same key and base URL can cross those calls. The request schemas should come from the platform's discovery document rather than guesses about response fields, so the example passes each JSON response on as an opaque value.

const baseUrl = process.env.INFRAI_BASE_URL;
const apiKey = process.env.INFRAI_API_KEY;
if (!baseUrl || !apiKey) throw new Error("INFRAI_BASE_URL and INFRAI_API_KEY are required");

async function post(path: string, body: unknown, idempotencyKey: string): Promise<unknown> {
  for (let attempt = 0; attempt < 5; attempt += 1) {
    const response = await fetch(`${baseUrl}${path}`, {
      method: "POST",
      headers: {
        Authorization: `Bearer ${apiKey}`,
        "Content-Type": "application/json",
        "Idempotency-Key": idempotencyKey,
      },
      body: JSON.stringify(body),
    });
    if (response.status !== 429) {
      if (!response.ok) throw new Error(`POST ${path} failed: ${response.status}`);
      return response.json();
    }
    const retryAfter = Number(response.headers.get("retry-after") ?? 0);
    const delay = retryAfter > 0 ? retryAfter * 1_000 : 250 * 2 ** attempt;
    await new Promise((resolve) => setTimeout(resolve, delay));
  }
  throw new Error(`POST ${path} exceeded retry limit`);
}

async function enqueueReconciliation(input: unknown): Promise<unknown> {
  const stored = await post("/storage/bucket/create", input, "reconcile-storage-2026-10-29");
  const processed = await post("/pdf/parse", stored, "reconcile-parse-2026-10-29");
  return post("/queue/publish", processed, "reconcile-queue-2026-10-29");
}

The alternative S3 + sharp worker + BullMQ stack means separate system choices, storage and queue credentials, a processing dependency to package, and glue for object handoff, retries, and observability. The combined approach has a cost too: one vendor to trust, one bill, and one outage surface. I would accept that trade when reducing integration work increases revenue per hour and keeps weekly shipping realistic.

The queue still needs consumer idempotency. A shared key does not change at-least-once delivery, and it does not create a Kafka-style replay log. Message bodies have a 256 KB limit, retention tops out at 30 days, and delayed delivery tops out at 7 days. Keep the durable reconciliation record in storage or a database; keep the queue message small.

That is the boundary.

I initially wanted the worker to own every retry because the code looked easier to follow. Then the recovery question became harder: which records were still pending, which provider calls had succeeded, and which retry belonged to the same settlement? Keeping the queue as the durable work list makes those answers visible, even though it adds explicit acknowledgement and idempotency work.

What changes at scale?

At higher volume, move rate state out of process. An in-memory limiter is sufficient for one worker, but two replicas with independent reservoirs can double the effective provider rate. A distributed store is needed when the limit applies to the whole consumer fleet.

I would also separate retryable provider failures from malformed records, route poison messages to a dead-letter queue, and add an operator action for redrive. I would not add workflow orchestration just because the pipeline has three calls. If the business later needs joins, fan-out aggregation, or long-running stateful workflows, this queue shape has reached its boundary and Airflow or Temporal becomes a more honest comparison.

Start with Bottleneck and a compatible queue API. Make the provider limit, concurrency, idempotency key, retry policy, and recovery path visible in code. Then choose the queue whose failure controls match the number of hours I can spend operating infrastructure each week.

References

  • Bottleneck documentation: https://github.com/SGrondin/bottleneck
  • BullMQ documentation: https://docs.bullmq.io/
  • Amazon SQS developer guide: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AWSSimpleQueueService/latest/SQSDeveloperGuide/welcome.html
  • Google Cloud Tasks documentation: https://cloud.google.com/tasks/docs
  • RFC 2104, HMAC keyed-hashing for message authentication: https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc2104

Sources

  • RFC 2104: https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc2104

Anthropic ships Fable 5.1 with cybersecurity and biology safety classifiers enabled. Finding vulnerabilities in source code is allowed, but some routine coding and debugging may still be refused. To ensure requests are still serviced when the safety classifiers are triggered, use model fallbacks.

title: Implement SMS OTP-Based 2FA in Node.js: 2026 API Integration for Property Support
description:
A property-management contact form should not decide support ownership by guessing from a phone number, and an SMS OTP should not become a second, unrelated login flow. The practical trade-off is to keep identity verification in the authentication boundary while keeping queue selection in a versioned template owned by the support team. That separation makes it possible to implement SMS OTP-based 2FA in a Node.js API without letting authentication logic choose a business queue: the OTP proves control of a phone number for a short transaction, while the verified form payload selects maintenance, leasing, or resident-account support.

The implementation below uses the same backend shape I use for communication systems: a short-lived challenge record, a single-use verification transition, and an explicit routing policy. The example uses Python only to keep the protocol mechanics visible; the HTTP calls map directly to a Node.js client. No provider-specific SDK is required.

The five-minute expiry and five-attempt ceiling are policy inputs, not magic security constants.

How can I implement SMS OTP-based 2FA in a Node.js API?

An SMS OTP proves possession of a destination at one point in time. It does not prove that the sender is a tenant, that the unit number is valid, or that the message belongs in a particular queue. Those claims need separate checks. Treating the code as a general identity token is the first design mistake.

For a contact form, I would persist a challenge with a random identifier, a hash of the code, an expiry, an attempt counter, and the normalized destination. The plaintext code belongs in neither logs nor the form record. The form submission references the challenge ID and receives a server-side status such as verified; it does not send the code through the queueing path again.

The challenge lifecycle is deliberately boring:

  1. Normalize the phone number to an accepted international representation and apply a per-destination and per-IP rate limit.
  2. Generate a cryptographically random code and store only its hash, with a narrow expiry such as 5 minutes chosen by policy.
  3. Send the message through the communication API, but do not treat an accepted request as proof of delivery.
  4. Compare a submitted code against the stored hash, atomically consume the challenge, and record the result.
  5. Route the contact form using the verified state and a template revision.

The atomically consumed transition matters. A correct code accepted twice can produce duplicate tickets, duplicate callbacks, or a second privileged action.

Keep the state transition one-time.

Here is the core shape, with provider calls represented by an interface rather than a product SDK.

from dataclasses import dataclass
from datetime import datetime, timedelta, timezone
import hashlib
import hmac
import secrets


@dataclass
class Challenge:
    id: str
    destination: str
    code_digest: str
    expires_at: datetime
    attempts: int = 0
    consumed: bool = False


def create_challenge(destination: str, now: datetime) -> tuple[Challenge, str]:
    code = f"{secrets.randbelow(1_000_000):06d}"
    digest = hashlib.sha256(code.encode("ascii")).hexdigest()
    challenge = Challenge(
        id=secrets.token_urlsafe(18),
        destination=destination,
        code_digest=digest,
        expires_at=now + timedelta(minutes=5),
    )
    return challenge, code


def verify_challenge(challenge: Challenge, submitted: str, now: datetime) -> bool:
    if challenge.consumed or now >= challenge.expires_at or challenge.attempts >= 5:
        return False
    challenge.attempts += 1
    digest = hashlib.sha256(submitted.encode("ascii")).hexdigest()
    if not hmac.compare_digest(digest, challenge.code_digest):
        return False
    challenge.consumed = True
    return True

In production, the read, attempt increment, expiry check, and consume operation need one transactional boundary. An in-memory object demonstrates the state machine; it is not a multi-instance store. The send operation should also carry an idempotency key derived from the challenge ID when the communication API supports one. That key protects retries at the application boundary, while the consumed flag protects the verification boundary. They solve different duplicate problems.

How does template ownership change the routing design?

The support queue should be selected from a small, reviewable template rather than from free-form model output or a pile of controller conditionals. A template owner can change the wording, required fields, and destination mapping without changing OTP security rules. The backend still validates the result against an allowlist.

For example, a property-management form might have these stable intents: maintenance, leasing, and resident_account. The template revision can require a unit reference for the first and third intents, while a prospective renter may have no unit yet. That is a business rule, not an SMS rule. Keep both in the record so a later audit can answer which policy made the decision.

ROUTES = {
    "maintenance": "queue-maintenance",
    "leasing": "queue-leasing",
    "resident_account": "queue-resident-account",
}


def route_verified_form(form: dict, template_revision: str) -> dict:
    if form.get("otp_status") != "verified":
        raise ValueError("phone verification is required")
    intent = form.get("intent")
    queue = ROUTES.get(intent)
    if queue is None:
        raise ValueError("unsupported support intent")
    if intent in {"maintenance", "resident_account"} and not form.get("unit_reference"):
        raise ValueError("unit reference is required")
    return {
        "queue": queue,
        "template_revision": template_revision,
        "challenge_id": form["challenge_id"],
    }

This is where ownership pays off operationally. The communication team owns message templates and their approvals; the support team owns queue mappings; the identity boundary owns challenge semantics. One team can revise a template while the other two retain their invariants. I would reject a change that silently combines those responsibilities, even if the first demo is faster.

That boundary is easy to lose.

Which failure modes deserve a test before launch?

Start with the edges that create confusing resident experiences or noisy queues. A valid code after expiry must fail. A wrong code must consume an attempt but reveal no information about the stored destination. Two simultaneous verification requests must not both win. A timeout from the SMS API must leave the challenge in a retryable state without claiming delivery. A form replay must not create a second ticket.

Rate limits need more than one key. Use destination, source address, account context where available, and a global send budget. Do not make the error response distinguish “number unknown” from “code wrong”; that distinction is useful to an attacker and rarely useful to a resident. Store structured events such as challenge.created, message.accepted, challenge.failed, and form.routed, with redacted destinations and correlation IDs.

I initially treated delivery status as the decisive signal. That was too narrow. An API can accept a message request while the handset remains unreachable, and a delivery receipt can arrive after the user has already abandoned the form. The useful product decision is therefore a bounded retry and an honest state shown to the caller, not a promise that the code will arrive. The long tail is where the implementation earns its keep: if the first request times out after the remote service accepted it, a blind retry can send two codes; if the callback arrives after the challenge expired, accepting it can reopen a transaction the user no longer controls. Correlation IDs, an idempotency key, and an explicit expiry check make those cases observable without pretending the network is synchronous.

The login path also needs a recovery policy. SMS is exposed to number reassignment, SIM-swap risk, filtering, and unavailable coverage. For higher-risk changes, require an additional factor or an out-of-band support process; do not stretch one SMS code into proof of every account attribute. NIST SP 800-63B is a useful reference for treating authentication factors and verifier controls as separate design concerns.

What should be compared in an API integration?

Compare boundaries, not logo checklists. A hosted messaging API can reduce carrier integration work, while a self-hosted gateway can provide more control over deployment and routing but shifts delivery operations to your team. A queue-oriented messaging service may make asynchronous status handling natural; a transactional email or notification service may expose a broader channel abstraction. None of those choices removes the need for local challenge storage, rate limiting, template ownership, or audit events.

The decision record should cover five concrete questions: can the integration authenticate requests without embedding long-lived secrets in application logs; can it expose request and delivery states distinctly; can the application retry without multiplying messages; can templates be versioned and approved; and can the team export enough events for incident review? Run a fake transport in tests and a contract test against the selected API in staging. Keep the provider adapter narrow so changing that boundary does not rewrite the verifier.

For Node.js, that usually means one module owns the API client and timeout policy, another owns challenge persistence, and the route handler composes them. Validate incoming JSON before calling either module. Use a monotonic request deadline, redact authorization headers, and make the final queue write idempotent. Those details are less exciting than the SMS call, but they are what keep a contact form from becoming an operational inbox full of duplicates.

A compact rollout for a property-management form

Ship the policy in stages. First, add the challenge table, metrics, redacted event schema, and a template revision field while keeping the existing form route observable. Next, enable verification for a small set of intents and test expired, replayed, throttled, and provider-timeout paths. Then require verified status for the queues that expose resident information, with a support-desk fallback that records why verification was unavailable.

Watch send attempts, accepted requests, verified completions, expiry rate, retry rate, and duplicate form suppression. Break those numbers down by destination region and intent; one aggregate success rate can hide a carrier or template problem. A rollback should disable the requirement or restore the previous routing revision without deleting challenge history.

The durable rule is simple: OTP is a narrowly scoped possession check, and the contact-form template is a separately owned routing policy. Keep those contracts explicit, versioned, and observable. The result is easier to secure and easier for a property-management team to change without asking an authentication change to carry business meaning.

Sources

  • https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/rfc6238
  • https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/rfc7489
  • https://pages.nist.gov/800-63-4/sp800-63b.html
  • https://cheatsheetseries.owasp.org/cheatsheets/Authentication_Cheat_Sheet.html
  • https://nodejs.org/api/crypto.html

title: Why We Rebuilt the Hosting Control Panel from Scratch (Go, NestJS, React & Native AI)
description:
For over two decades, the traditional web hosting industry has relied on legacy architectures designed in the early 2000s.

If you've ever tried to manage modern web infrastructure using legacy panels, you know the pain points:

  • The Squeeze: You pay one heavy license fee for server control, and another separate license fee for client management and billing.
  • Modern App Friction: Hosting a PHP script is straightforward, but deploying a Node.js, Python, or Go app with auto-SSL requires jump-roping through complex server configurations or setting up custom reverse proxies manually.
  • Architectural Bloat: Managing multi-server setups on legacy Perl/PHP-heavy background services often feels sluggish and resource-intensive.

We set out to change that by building OrbixPanel—a unified, high-performance platform that combines server control, Vercel-style Git deployments, reseller storefronts, and automated billing into a single ecosystem.

Here is a look under the hood at how it works and why we built it.

The Tech Stack: Designed for Speed & Modularity
We chose a modern, decoupled stack to ensure low memory consumption, instant UI rendering, and scalable backend orchestration:

  • Backend Orchestration: Go (Golang) handles high-concurrency low-level sysadmin operations, process management, and daemon tasks with minimal memory footprint.
  • Application API Layer: NestJS manages modular business logic, authentication, reseller workflows, and API integrations.
  • Frontend Experience: React powers an ultra-responsive, single-page interface with real-time metric updates.

Key Architectural Innovations

1. Vercel-Style Git Deployments

Instead of manually creating web roots and setting up reverse proxies, OrbixPanel lets you point directly to a GitHub repository URL. The panel automatically detects application environments (Node.js, Python, Go, PHP, etc.), provisions environment variables, builds the app, and assigns Let's Encrypt SSL certificates automatically.

2. Unified Infrastructure + Automated Billing

Instead of running two separate pieces of software (and paying two separate recurring license fees), OrbixPanel natively integrates:

  • Server resource monitoring & process management
  • Client management, automated suspension, and domain controls
  • Out-of-the-box reseller storefront with native payment gateway integrations (Stripe, PayPal)

3. Native AI Copilot & Open API System

OrbixPanel includes a built-in AI Copilot layer. System administrators and reseller tenants can connect 3rd-party AI APIs or run local LLMs directly on the server to handle automated sysadmin tasks, diagnostic scripts, and smart deployment pipelines via secure internal APIs.

1-Command Installation 

Bash

curl -fsSL https://orbixpanel.com/install.sh | bash

No credit card is required to install or use it.

Community Edition & Open Feedback

We believe foundational hosting tools should be accessible to everyone. The Community Edition of OrbixPanel is FREE forever, and we are currently providing free platform credits for developers to test out our advanced paid features.

We built this panel to give control back to developers, sysadmins, and hosters. I’d love to hear your thoughts, feedback, or any features you'd like to see added next!

Check it out at orbixpanel.com and let me know your thoughts in the comments below.

title: Where to Find robots.txt and What the File Reveals About Crawling
description:
You find robots.txt at the root of a site's host, which means you append the filename to the bare domain: example.com/robots.txt, never to a subfolder path. Google for Developers states the rule plainly, and everything confusing about this file follows from it. Most people who go looking for robots.txt are chasing a symptom, not a file. A page stopped ranking, a Search Console report threw an error, an /inurl:robots.txt search returned a wall of unrelated results. They find the file within a minute. Then they stare at four lines of text and have no idea which one is costing them traffic.

That gap is the whole point. Locating the file is a two-minute mechanical task that never needed a consultant, and the file itself is the least interesting part of a crawl audit. What matters is what the rules are doing to your URLs, and whether the assumptions you made when you wrote them survive contact with how search engines actually behave. If you already know what a disallow line is, you still may not know that it does far less than its name suggests. This piece is about the second half of the job.

Type the bare host into the address bar and add the filename. That is the entire procedure for the common case, and it works on your own site and on anyone else's. A robots.txt lookup is a read operation on a public file, so no credentials, no tool, and no plugin are involved in retrieving it.

Three quirks trip people up. The first is that most frameworks serve the file from a route rather than from disk, so the content you see may be generated. The second is that a Content Delivery Network can intercept the request and return a cached copy that no longer matches what the origin serves. The third is that a redirect chain can quietly send you to a different host, and the rules you are reading then belong to a site you do not own. If the URL resolves through two hops, verify the final destination before you conclude anything about your own crawl rules.

You should also read what you found instead of scanning for the word disallow. The rules that hurt are usually the ones you wrote years ago and never revisited.

  • What the File at the Root Actually Does
  • How Crawlers Read What You Wrote
  • Checking Any Site in Under Two Minutes
  • Six Dimensions That Separate a Working File From a Decorative One
  • Where Site Owners Fool Themselves
  • Reading the Signals Before You Rewrite Anything
  • Frequently Asked Questions

What the File at the Root Actually Does

Robots.txt is a plain-text set of instructions addressed to automated crawlers, published at a fixed location so that any robot can find it without being told. It is a convention, not a gate, and that distinction decides how much weight to give it. The file tells well-behaved crawlers which paths they may request. It cannot enforce anything, and it never controls what a page does once a crawler has it. The robots.txt collection rules exist to make the location predictable, which is the only reason a file with this little syntax works at all.

The adjacent concept people confuse it with is the meta robots tag. That tag lives inside a page, and it governs indexing rather than fetching. A noindex directive removes a URL from results. A disallow rule removes your ability to crawl it. They solve different problems, and mixing them up is how a site ends up with thousands of pages that Google can see in the index but has never actually read. We have written elsewhere about robots.txt disallow rules do far less than most site owners assume, and that page digs into the indexing consequences in detail.

The file serves two audiences with opposite needs. Search engines read it to know where not to go. Everyone else reads it to learn what a site considers off-limits: staging environments, internal search, cart funnels, admin panels. The second audience is why a robots.txt is semi-public by design, and why writing confidential paths into it is a mistake rather than a security measure.

How Crawlers Read What You Wrote

A crawler requests the file before it requests anything else on a host, caches it, and then applies the rules to every subsequent fetch. A single file per host, protocol, and port covers the whole site, so there is no reason to look anywhere else once you have the root copy in front of you. That combination rule matters because http and https versions of the same site can each carry their own file, and so can a non-standard port. If your site moved to HTTPS and the old file was never cleaned up, the http copy still exists and still applies to the http host.

Directives are grouped by user-agent, and the specificity logic is not a priority ranking. A crawler picks the most specific group that names it, and ignores more general groups entirely when a specific match exists. An asterisk group is the fallback for every crawler without a named group. If you wrote a wildcard block and later added a Googlebot block, crawlers matching Googlebot read only the Googlebot block. Everything in the wildcard group stopped applying to them the moment you saved that change.

Path matching is prefix-based and case-sensitive. Disallowing a directory blocks every URL that starts with that string, which is usually what you want and occasionally a disaster. Disallowing a single dynamic parameter string can catch thousands of filter combinations you never intended to block. Query strings complicate this further: a rule that blocks a URL with parameters does not automatically block the parameter-free version, and vice versa.

The file is also parsed leniently. A malformed line is skipped rather than crashing the parse, which is forgiving until it means a rule you depended on simply stopped existing. There is no rewrite, no validation warning, and no error surfaced anywhere unless you go looking for the report.

Checking Any Site in Under Two Minutes

The sequence below is the one worth running on your own domain every quarter, and on any domain you are about to compete against.

  1. Open the bare host in a browser and append the filename to the root, so you are requesting the file from the host itself rather than through a search result. If the address bar shows a path segment before the filename, the request is wrong and the file you get back is meaningless.
  2. Hard-refresh the page. Browser caches and CDN caches both serve stale copies, and a file that shows yesterday's rules while tomorrow's live ruleset is already deployed will send you chasing the wrong problem.
  3. Confirm which host, protocol, and port you actually landed on, since a redirect can move you off the origin you meant to inspect.
  4. Read the file top to bottom and note where each user-agent group begins and ends. A line that looks global may be sitting under a named group that only applies to one crawler.
  5. Cross-check the file against Search Console's robots.txt report, which shows the version Google last fetched and flags syntax errors the file itself will never tell you about. Search Console's robots.txt report is the fastest way to see what a crawler actually received rather than what you intended to send.

Two minutes is honest. Ten seconds gets you the file. The rest is checking whether the version you are reading is the version that is live.

Six Dimensions That Separate a Working File From a Decorative One

A robots.txt that exists is not a robots.txt that works. These are the dimensions worth scoring any file against, whether it is yours or a competitor's.

Dimension What to look for
Placement The file resolves at the host root, not at a subfolder, and not only behind a redirect
Coverage Named user-agent groups exist for the crawlers that matter, and no stale wildcard block silently overrides them
Path specificity Disallow patterns block exactly the paths intended, with no accidental prefix collisions on shared directory names
Indexing alignment Pages that must not appear in results carry a noindex directive, not just a disallow rule
Freshness The live file matches what Search Console last fetched, and there is a process for updating it when the site changes
Error visibility Syntax is clean enough that the Search Console report shows no warnings, and someone actually reads that report

Most audits fail on two of these at once. Coverage and indexing alignment are the usual pair: a team adds a Googlebot block to protect a staging path, then forgets that the same path is linked from production and still indexed. Placement failures are rarer but more expensive, because a file at the wrong address has no effect at all while giving the team a false sense of protection.

The freshness dimension is the one that decays fastest. Sites get restructured, content moves under new directories, and the disallow list keeps pointing at paths that no longer exist while the new ones go unprotected. A robots.txt is not a set-and-forget artifact. It is a configuration file, and it drifts.

Where Site Owners Fool Themselves

The belief that hurts most is the one about secrecy. Teams treat robots.txt as a way to hide internal paths from competitors, then list staging subdomains, admin routes, and API endpoints by name. A file intended to reduce crawl load becomes a directory of everything worth probing. If a path needs protection, it needs authentication, not a line in a text file that is deliberately public.

A subtler mistake is assuming that a disallow rule prevents indexing. It does not. Crawlers cannot read a page they are told not to fetch, but the URL itself can still be indexed if other pages link to it with anchor text. The result is a search result with no snippet, which looks like a penalty and is not one. The disallow did exactly what it said it would do, and the indexing happened anyway through signals the page never controlled.

Teams also write rules against the wrong host. An old robots.txt sitting on the plain-http version of a site looks harmless until you realise the crawler fetches it for that host. Configuration templates make this worse: a starter file copied from a framework's documentation can reference directory structures that exist in the template and nowhere in your actual site.

Then there is the caching blind spot. A CDN configured to cache aggressively can keep serving an old robots.txt for hours after a deploy, so a rule change appears not to have taken effect. Teams respond by editing the file again, layering a second set of contradictory rules on top of the first, and now two versions of the same directive are in circulation.

The final one is quieter. Some teams disallow a path to reduce crawl budget, check that rankings held steady, and conclude the rule was harmless. Nothing was measured, nothing was verified, and the rule stays because no one wants to be the person who unblocked something that seems to be working.

Reading the Signals Before You Rewrite Anything

You face a specific decision once you have the file open: leave it alone, edit it, or rebuild your crawl rules from scratch. The signals tell you which.

Leave it alone when the file is clean, the paths it blocks are genuinely private, Search Console shows no fetch errors, and your indexed pages are the ones you want indexed. A working configuration does not need attention just because you looked at it.

Edit it when you find a specific, nameable problem. A disallow rule catching a directory of content pages. A stale wildcard block shadowing a newer named group. A path that moved six months ago while the rule stayed pointed at the old one. These are surgical fixes, and they take minutes.

Rebuild when the file has become a museum of decisions no one remembers. If nobody on the team can explain why a group exists, what it was protecting, or when it was last relevant, the ruleset is not a configuration, it is an archaeology site. Start from a short list of paths that genuinely must not be crawled, write groups only for the crawlers you care about, and check each one against a live URL before you publish.

The trigger worth acting on immediately is a mismatch between what you intend and what Search Console reports. If the live file shows rules you did not write, or the fetched version is weeks old while your deploy was this morning, stop editing and diagnose the caching layer first. Changing rules against a stale copy is how a small problem becomes two.

There is a version of this job that scales past one domain. When you are running multiple sites, the manual quarterly check turns into a crawl-health process, and that is a different kind of work: watching for coverage drops, tracking which URLs stopped getting fetched, and reacting before a blocked path has been blocked long enough to lose its rankings. That is what GrowGanic is for, and it treats crawl visibility as one input among many rather than a one-off checklist item. On paid plans, a rank drop triggers a fresh read of the search results and a refresh of the page that slipped, which is a faster loop than a quarterly reminder in a calendar.

The routine inspection is still yours, and it should be. Finding the file takes two minutes and tells you something no dashboard can: whether the rules you set years ago still describe the site you run today.

Free gets you an article. Pro publishes thirty a month. Business publishes a hundred and fifty. Current pricing: growganic.io/pricing. Stop writing articles. Start shipping them.

Frequently Asked Questions

Where do I find the robots.txt file?

Append the filename directly to a site's root domain, so the request goes to the host itself rather than to any path beneath it. Google's documentation on creating the file specifies that it must sit at the host root to apply. If a subfolder version exists, it controls nothing beyond that folder's own host context, and the root copy is the one crawlers actually read.

Does robots.txt still work?

It works for its stated purpose: telling compliant crawlers which paths not to request. It does not enforce anything, block a determined scraper, or prevent indexing on its own. A disallowed URL can still appear in results when other pages link to it, because the rule governs fetching rather than indexing. Treat it as a load-management convention with indexing side effects, not as access control.

How to get robots.txt from a website?

Request it from the bare host in a browser and hard-refresh to bypass any cached copy. If you want to know what a search engine actually received, the Search Console robots.txt report shows the last fetched version along with any syntax warnings. For a domain you do not own, the browser request is the whole method and needs no tooling at all.

How to fix blocked by robots.txt error?

Read the file first and find the user-agent group that matches the crawler reporting the error. Look for a disallow pattern that prefixes the blocked URL, then check whether the live file still matches what Search Console shows as fetched. If no rule explains it, the cause usually sits outside the file: password protection, a firewall rule, or a hosting-level restriction. Remove the specific rule, redeploy, and request a re-fetch rather than deleting the file wholesale.

OmniPost DEV.to integration check

This is an account-owner-approved test article created to verify the connection between OmniPost and DEV.to. It is clearly marked as a test and contains no personal information or credentials.

What this test checks

Expected result

A successful connection should preserve the article title and Markdown content, return a working link, and display the observed statistics in OmniPost. A count of zero should be shown as zero when the platform reports it; missing data should remain unavailable.

This post does not claim that comment replies, every media format, or all historical data have been verified. Those are separate checks.

title: Vercel Ship 2026 recap
description:
For a decade, Vercel has shaped how the web is built. Now, we’re doing the same for agents. The companies that win the next decade will build on infrastructure designed for agents from the start, and thousands of people gathered across London, Berlin, New York, Sydney, and San Francisco to do just that at Vercel Ship 2026.

Agentic infrastructure

Guillermo Rauch (CEO, Vercel) opened Ship SF with a vision for the next era of software and agentic infrastructure: interfaces generated for any task in front of you, agents that reproduce and fix bugs autonomously, and software that takes production context and continuously improves itself.

Agentic infrastructure has three parts:

  • Vercel is where you build and deploy your own apps and agents. We give you every tool you need to build and run apps and agents in production, securely, at scale.

  • Vercel is where coding agents deploy that software. When you ask your harness where to deploy, you get Vercel, because Vercel is built for the way agents work. We have over 200 CLI commands that your agent can use to operate our entire platform.

  • Vercel itself is automated by agents. Vercel runs your apps in production, handling traffic, traces, observability, and anomalies. That data gives our agents the context they need to investigate autonomously, and then surface pull requests, not just alerts.

Agentic Infrastructure is for developers

In his opening keynote, Guillermo pointed to claims that AI would replace developers, then used Vercel's own data to prove them wrong. In the last 12 months:

  • The number of developers on Vercel has grown 3x

  • The number of new projects developers ship has doubled

  • The number of their agent-triggered deployments has increased 28x

"We built Vercel for developers," he said, "because they are the difference between a world full of slop and a world full of software worth using."

Backends on Vercel

In the next keynote, Malte Ubl (CTO, Vercel) showed how frontends, APIs, backend services, containers, MCP servers, and background workers can all run on Vercel, with support for custom runtimes and system dependencies.

He then announced that Python is now generally available on Vercel. Run FastAPI, Flask, or Django with standard CPython, PyPI dependencies, uv, and pyproject.toml. With Vercel Services, your frontend and backend deploy together, with previews of the full app.

Malte also introduced Vercel Daemons, now in public beta, for continuously running background workers. Deploy your code or container image, set the number of instances, and Vercel keeps them running and replaces them if they fail. Bring Celery, Dramatiq, Temporal workers, or your existing worker processes.

Vercel is for shipping agents

Tomo Occhino (CPO, Vercel) walked through the Agent Stack and its latest updates. The Agent Stack gives you everything you need to build, run, and scale agents in production.

  • Vercel Drives, now generally available for Sandbox, gives agents persistent workspaces. Code, data, and saved memory survive across runs, so you can change runtimes or compute without rebuilding the workspace.

  • eve, our open-source framework for building agents, now has persistent memory across sessions, extensions for installing tools and skills, and agent creation and deployment from the Vercel dashboard.

  • Vercel Connect is generally available, with more than 1,000 connectors. And MCP Events, now in public beta, lets agents respond to events from MCP servers. Connect handles subscriptions, renewals, and secure delivery.

  • AI Gateway now lets you set budgets for API keys, projects, individuals, and teams. You can also choose US-only inference to keep model processing in the United States, or enable Zero Data Retention so providers don’t retain your prompts or responses. He also introduced Vercel Token Pass, now in early access for Pro teams. Get $80 in GLM 5.3 and Kimi K3 token credit for $30/month, with more models coming soon.

Vercel for enterprise

Jeanne Grosser (COO, Vercel) focused on what happens when everyone in a company can build. Engineers, marketers, analysts, and sellers need a common place to deploy, with controls over who can ship, who can access an app, which systems agents can use, and how much they can spend. Company building is now agent building.

Vercel for Enterprise brings those controls together, with two additions announced:

  • Bring Your Own Cloud on AWS is now generally available. Your application functions run in your own AWS account, within your security and network boundaries.

  • Enterprise-Managed Authorization for Vercel Connect launched in public beta. With supported services and your identity provider configured, agents can act on employees’ behalf without asking each person to authorize every connection separately.

Watch the full day of programming

Ship week in San Francisco

The rest of Ship SF brought more than 2,700 developers, founders, and technical leaders to the Palace of Fine Arts for talks, workshops, startup studio sessions, and agent labs.

Ship day sessions

  • Assaf Elovic from Ora showed how his team tests whether websites work for agents by sending real agents to sign up, integrate, and pay, then tracing every step. Ora built that fleet on eve and used Is-Agentic to score a live site.

  • Katelyn Lesse from Anthropic covered the work that starts after an agent is running: keeping it fast and improving its performance across thousands of production sessions with Claude Managed Agents on Vercel.

  • Prashant Ratanchandani from Meta Superintelligence Labs joined Tomo to discuss building products including Muse on Vercel.

  • Matt Lewis from Vercel and Mala Neti from Slack explained how we built v, our internal agent, around Vercel’s own data and working practices. Connect and Passport secure its access, and Slack gives employees a place to use it where their work already happens.

  • Max Peters from Adapta broke down the router behind Brazil’s largest generative AI platform. Built on AI Gateway, it serves 168 models through one integration, selects a model in under 200 milliseconds, and handles more than three million requests a day with automatic failover and per-user budgets.

  • Sarah Sachs from Notion and Malte Ubl discussed how AI is changing the software teams build and the context agents need to do useful work.

  • Olawale Oladehin from AWS walked through production patterns for agents on AWS and Vercel, from self-correcting agents to multi-agent orchestration, and how BYOC lets teams run application functions within their own AWS environment.

  • Philip Miseldine and Sophia Levens from SAP showed how SAP is using v0, eve, and json-render to build generative interfaces, with a focus on consistent design and government requirements.

  • Aaron Brown and Arty Vohmincevs from Mercor explained how hundreds of employees build internal tools without losing control of access or spending. Apps inherit a managed identity layer, while AI Gateway gives the team visibility into model usage and budgets.

  • Yury Izrailevsky from ClickHouse traced the company’s path from an open-source analytics database to a platform spanning observability, AI engineering, and managed Postgres. His focus was how open source earns developer trust and helps infrastructure expand into new workloads.

Panel: Fast AI

Diogo Almeida, co-founder and CEO of TypeSafe AI, the company behind Jev, and Andrew Feldman, founder and CEO of Cerebras, joined Vercel for a discussion on model reliability, latency, and cost. The panel brought together the model and hardware sides of fast inference, from specialized models to wafer-scale chips.

Closing fireside with Tobi Lütke

Guillermo sat down with Tobi Lütke, CEO of Shopify, for "The Third Customer," a conversation about building for a world where agents research, compare, and buy products on people’s behalf.

Guillermo Rauch: What excites you about agentic commerce?

Tobi Lütke: It’s early, but the opportunity goes beyond handling purchases people already make. Think about project-based commerce: planning Halloween decorations for your house, or a 3D-printing project with your kids, then ordering everything to arrive before the weekend. Agents can help people follow through on things they otherwise wouldn’t have had time to do.

Guillermo Rauch: Where does that leave traditional storefronts?

Tobi Lütke: There’s still room for exceptional shopping experiences. A distinctive, thoughtful storefront can grow, just as a well-executed boutique can. The businesses that will struggle are the ones offering an undifferentiated experience. Quality and originality still matter.

Guillermo Rauch: How is AI changing engineering at Shopify?

Tobi Lütke: We now think of ourselves as verification engineers, building harnesses and acceptance tests that make changes verifiable. We’re rewriting our storefront renderer from Ruby to Rust, where we can compare the output byte for byte before switching over. We also celebrate simplification and code deletion. At a company hackathon, our internal Slack agent, River, topped the code-deletion leaderboard by a wide margin.

Guillermo Rauch: What should developers in this room go build?

Tobi Lütke: Explore the catalog APIs. They give you access to products from Shopify merchants, so you can build new commerce experiences without first recruiting both sides of a marketplace. Product discovery, recommendations, and curation are real business opportunities. People will pay for tools that help them find what they need.

Ship week San Francisco

Fast Forward hackathon

The day before Ship, Vercel and Meta hosted Fast Forward, with support from Shopify and Neon Postgres. Builders worked across three tracks: agents that keep working after you step away, multimodal apps, and immersive VR experiences.

Founder dinners, executive conversations, and Partner Day

Founders, partners, and enterprise leaders gathered throughout the week for dinners, Partner Day, and conversations on building with AI. The executive program focused on what happens when anyone with an idea can build, and how do you govern what ships.

Ship 2026 in London

Ship day keynotes

  • Tomo introduced the Agent Stack, bringing model access, durable execution, sandboxed compute, and messaging together for production agents.

  • Hedi launched Vercel Connect in public preview, giving agents scoped access to external tools and data without storing long-lived provider credentials in environment variables.

  • Shar demoed eve, our open-source agent framework. Each agent lives in a directory, with instructions in Markdown and tools in TypeScript. Durable execution, approvals, subagents, and evals are already wired in.

  • Jeanne introduced Vercel for Enterprise Apps and Agents, including Vercel Passport in public beta for protecting internal apps with your identity provider, and Bring Your Own Cloud on AWS in private beta.

Ship week London

Our first Ship outside the U.S. ran five days of events leading into the keynote, and an ice cream truck spent the week working its way across the city.

Built in London hackathon

Two hundred builders shipped agents on Codex and Vercel in a hackathon with OpenAI. Three projects stood out. Stella hunts down unclaimed grants for London SMBs, Oscar is a co-pilot that sharpens your prompts before you send them to a model, and Phone Jail blocks distractions and roasts you when you reach for your phone anyway.

Media, Founder, VC, and CTO dinners

Reporters traded story ideas over a media dinner. Twelve founders talked through the future of AI in EMEA at a VC dinner. And a dozen CTOs from teams including Marks & Spencer and Currys went off the record on what it takes to build and scale agents in the enterprise.

Day Zero builder night

Day Zero, the day before the keynote, turned into a 400-person builder night. Enterprise teams Mentimeter, Okta, and MongoDB joined Vercel in a packed room alongside partners DeepMind, ElevenLabs, and Cursor.

AI Social Club

A 160-deep waitlist formed for Malte's talk A New Stack for a New Era of Software, followed by Guillermo and Deliveroo's Will Shu's chat on building the agentic enterprise.

Ship day sessions

  • André Balleyguier from Anthropic showed Claude Managed Agents on Vercel, where Anthropic hosts the agent loop while every command the agent runs executes inside a Vercel Sandbox you own, keeping its filesystem, processes, and network egress in your environment.

  • Tomas Jansson from Currys/Elkjøp showed how his team evolved a Nordic retailer's ecommerce stack from storefronts toward shopping agents in three phases, anchored by a Next.js migration that cut time to first byte by 40%. The end state is one where customer intent replaces navigation.

  • Matan Kushner from Vercel broke down how Vertex, Vercel's support agent, now automates 91% of support tickets and saves 5,000 engineer-hours a month without degrading as its context grows.

  • Jas Sagoo and Sam Bellen from Auth0 made the case that getting an agent into production depends more on identity than on model quality. They demoed four standards-based identity patterns on the Vercel AI SDK, Token Vault, CIBA approvals, agents as first-class principals, and on-behalf-of delegation, so every action is scoped and traces back to a human decision instead of a shared API key.

  • Abhi Sivasailam from Vercel went deep into d0, Vercel's internal data agent built on eve, which runs analyses in a sandbox and now gets 45% of its questions from other agents, rather than people.

  • Romain Huet from OpenAI showed developers how to ship faster by delegating whole tasks to Codex Cloud Agents on Vercel, and made the case that as agents become users of your product, you design for agent experience with scoped API keys, markdown docs, and plugins.

  • Michał Pierzchała from Callstack demoed a QA agent that runs mobile apps on real devices, explores user flows on its own, and posts screenshots, recordings, and logs to pull requests on every PR.

  • Alex Holt from ElevenLabs paired the ElevenLabs Speech Engine with the AI SDK to build a voice agent that can reply in under a second, take interruptions mid-sentence, and switch language mid-conversation.

  • Malavika Balachandran Tadeusz from Vercel showed the mechanics of how software can ship itself, extending the agent loop past development into testing, observability, and experimentation with primitives like Vercel Flags and Skills.

Panel: Agents in production

Jeanne Grosser, COO of Vercel, moderated a panel on taking agentic workloads from prototype to production with some of the EU's top CTOs and AI leaders from frontier labs. A few highlights:

Arthur Viegers (Cursor): Autonomy should track risk, and the better an agent can assess the risk of a change, the more you can let it run on its own. Shopify and Amplitude already auto-review and merge 60-70% of low-risk PRs with no developer time, while a two-line change to authentication still goes to a human.

André Balleyguier (Anthropic): To decide what an agent can do on its own, judge each action by how reversible it is and how large its blast radius is, then contain it accordingly, for example inside a self-hosted sandbox. As you grant more autonomy, observability and evals become the things that keep it safe.

Ryan den Rooijen (Currys): The predicted death of stores never arrived, and Currys leads its markets by betting on humans. The open question for agentic commerce is which shopping journeys customers want an agent to handle and which they still want a person for.

Nicolas Le Pallec (AKQA): AI-native customer experience replaces navigation with intent. Reaching it takes three layers: a way to capture true customer intent, a brand brain that stores brand and product data for AI systems to retrieve, and generative UI that composes pages on the fly instead of serving static ones.

Fireside chat with Harry Stebbings

The day ended with a fireside chat between Guillermo and Harry Stebbings from 20VC. Below are excerpts from the lightning round at the end of the discussion.

Guillermo Rauch: What are the attributes of a founder you want to back?

Harry Stebbings: The profile has changed completely. It used to be a sales-led CEO who could fundraise and grow customers, where personality and sales carried the company. Now I want an engineering- and product-led founder.

Guillermo Rauch: Can you teach someone to become a voice for their industry?

Harry Stebbings: You can, but it's hard. You have to do it for six months straight. It's a muscle you build, and you have to commit to it every day and every hour.

Guillermo Rauch: When anyone can produce content and software, how do you stand out?

Harry Stebbings: You come up with a new format, a new intro, a new way to tell the story and shape the work. The content itself has shifted too. We used to do shows about leadership and hiring, and nobody cares about that anymore. What lands now is a founder and AI. Those are the two things.

Ship 2026 in Berlin

The Berlin event opened at the Old Mint, “Alte Münze”, where coins were once hammered by hand, before machine automation took over. It is also where the JavaScript logo was born, and where Guillermo Rauch (CEO) met Malte Ubl (CTO) for the first time at JSConf EU.

Software is moving the same way, from hand to machine, and Vercel is paving the way for building in the agentic era. Over 500 people gathered from across Germany to do just that at Ship 2026 in Berlin.

Ship day sessions

  • Suyog Rao from Vercel announced AI SDK 7. The AI SDK is now downloaded over 16 million times a week. Version 7 turns it into a toolkit for building and running agents that reason, call tools, run across many turns, and work across files and sandboxes, all behind one provider-agnostic interface with no lock-in.

  • Philip Miseldine from SAP showed how the company rebuilt its design system to be composable, so people and agents assemble interfaces from the same parts, with v0 running across its build, deliver, and decide stages.

  • Building with AI SDK 7 brought three speakers on stage. Lars Grammel, the primary engineer behind the update, went deep on the release, with the new harness layer and generation beyond text as the headline additions. Carsten Høyer from AKQA demoed the Starbucks ChatGPT app as a "generative store" that composes branded results from Starbucks' own products and visual identity, flipping the funnel so customers pull the brand into their conversation instead of visiting its site. Stephen Batifol from Black Forest Labs showed where the Flux image models fit in an agentic stack: sub-second generation and editing today, heading toward real-time generation and world models.

  • Arthur Viegers from Cursor showed how coding agents move from autocomplete to working across an entire codebase on their own.

Panel: CTOs on AI and growth

Chris Williams (Head of Forward Deployed Engineering, Vercel) moderated a CTO panel on building and scaling as the cost of creation trends toward zero. A few highlights:

Sven Rosemann (Flaconi): AI won't fix a broken business model, so the work is still operational excellence. He compares ecommerce to a decathlon, you win by being top-tier across every discipline at once. What's changing is discovery, which is moving into chat, so Flaconi is investing in the data foundation that makes its catalog retrievable by agents, betting that buying and checkout eventually happen there too.

Tjaž Silovsek (Astra AI): venture funding is no longer a prerequisite. For many ideas, you ship, find distribution, and iterate instead. Astra reached 10 million users and $25M ARR fully bootstrapped, with a small team kept fast by a stable foundation and agents given a lot of autonomy while kept as safe as possible.

DACH Partner Award

Vercel presented its first-ever DACH Partner Award to Valtech, for the exceptional impact and delivery, strategic thinking and team enablement it brought to clients. The presentation also thanked the event's sponsors: Auth0, Storyblok, Cursor, SAP, Accenture Song, Blazity, and JVM.

Ship 2026 in New York

Ship week New York

Ship NYC was the most in-demand of any stop yet with over 3,000 people registered. Founders, partners, leaders, and builders gathered for five days of hackathons, executive receptions, workshops, and more, with Ship day at the center.

Built in NYC

The week opened with Built in NYC, a hackathon co-hosted by Vercel and Anthropic alongside Sentry, Auth0, Resend, and Supabase. More than one hundred people joined us for an afternoon of building and demoing agents on Vercel.

VC, CTO, and VIP dinners

Jeanne DeWitt Grosser and Nick Bogaty gathered the leaders shaping AI-native development at a VIP reception. Founders traded notes on the future of agents over a VC dinner. At Per Se, Guillermo, Jeanne, Tom, and Malte took CTOs and CIOs for a closed-door conversation on where traditional architectures start to break in the agent era.

AI Social Club

AI executives and senior leaders assembled at Moss for a fireside chat led by Tom Occhino with William Anderson (CTO, Bloomberg Media), Jeremy Bunting (VP Engineering, Serhant), and Ali Patterson (Staff Design Program Manager, DoorDash). They discussed what's working, what's not, and where agentic infrastructure is driving meaningful outcomes for enterprises.

Ship day sessions

  • Ryan Coyne from SERHANT. walked through S.MPLE, a real estate agent built on Vercel that drove a 144% increase in commission income in its first full year.

  • Brandon Bloom from Brex gave its expense-audit agent a bash-only shell so it manages its own context instead of drowning in tool responses, cutting tool calls and token usage by 75%.

  • Ari Schapiro and Chris Sev from Auth0 demoed how to give an agent scoped, revocable power instead of a master key, with standards-based identity patterns like Token Vault and out-of-band human approval, live on the Vercel AI SDK.

  • Jenny Wang from Alta and Maxwell Osborne from PUBLIC SCHOOL NYC showed how Alta's AI styling app runs on Vercel, generating an avatar a second and 250M+ outfits so far. Together they built a custom version for PUBLIC SCHOOL's New York Fashion Week relaunch.

  • Charlton Roberts from FLORA showed three creative-production workflows running on Vercel Sandboxes. They collapsed 18 bespoke tools into two by letting the agent run and write its own code against the AI SDK.

  • Prasad Wangikar from Stripe broke down how to give agents spending power and capture agent-driven revenue using emerging protocols like MCP, UCP, and x402 for the machine-to-machine economy.

  • Shaown Nandi from AWS discussed how Vercel and AWS work together, with native AWS databases and OpenSearch available in the Marketplace and models through the AI Gateway, proven out by The Weather Company's 350M+ users.

Panel: Internal apps and agents in production

Jeanne moderated a panel on building and deploying internal agents with technical leaders on who should build, what governance looks like, and how teams can move from experiment to production. A few highlights:

Andy Martin (MJH Life Sciences): The way to win the shadow-IT battle is to constrain the stack and stay permissive inside it. His AI Accelerator trains non-engineers, marketers, and early-career staff to build internal apps on a deliberately tight stack of Claude Code, Vercel, and GitHub, with ephemeral preview deployments as the guardrail. As he put it, "If it becomes the Department of No, you will have people working around you."

Greg Chan (SERHANT): The cleanest way to structure agents is to mirror a human software team. Product-manager agents write requirements in Linear, engineering agents generate specs, and build-and-QA agents take it from there, so engineers become leads running multiple streams. To keep output safe, SERHANT runs evals for hallucination and compliance, including a custom model for Fair Housing Act rules.

Victor Oliveros (ZoomInfo): Embedding v0 inside your own product lets your customers build their own workflows. At ZoomInfo, 40,000+ of them do, turning the voice of the customer into a pull request. Agents analyze recorded calls and open PRs, so the product team decides what ships instead of synthesizing feedback. They pair Vercel's deployment guardrails with ZoomInfo's context-graph permissions, so each agent only touches data its user can see.

Fireside chat: Building agentic storefronts

Tom sat down with Vanessa Lee (VP of Product, Shopify) to discuss where commerce and software go next. Below are highlights:

Tom Occhino: Vercel and Shopify have shipped something new together. What is it?

Vanessa Lee: We boiled Hydrogen down to the parts of commerce that are genuinely hard (analytics, optimistic cart UI, variants) and made them work with any framework. So if you're on Next.js on Vercel, Shopify's commerce primitives now drop in, with an integration in the Vercel Marketplace. Read more here.

Tom Occhino: You also opened the Catalog API. What does it unlock?

Vanessa Lee: There's never been a good open product-search API. We have billions of products and millions of merchants, so we built one, the only widespread shopping API, made for commerce. It lets anyone embed shopping anywhere. Someone in my Toronto running group used v0 to build a site with a leaderboard and the weather, and the Catalog API surfaced products from nearby stores. Commerce stops being a destination and becomes part of what you build.

Tom Occhino: Shopify and Vercel both obsess over reducing friction. Why does that matter so much?

Vanessa Lee: Early on, Tobi's insight was that tools shape the market. The TAM was never limited by demand, it was limited by how hard the tools were to use. Make building easier and more people build. There's resourcefulness in the general population that's just untapped, and lowering the friction is what releases it.

Closing keynote with Ivan Zhao

We closed out Ship in New York with a conversation between Guillermo Rauch and Ivan Zhao (CEO, Notion). A few highlights:

Guillermo Rauch: You've started telling designers to design for the API first and the UI last. Why?

Ivan Zhao: Because your next customer isn't only a human, it's a human and an agent, and agents are blind. They don't see your interface, they read your semantics and your API. The most enduring software has always been a data structure anyway, the spreadsheet, or our block, a data structure that happens to have a UI. So design the structure and the meaning first, the interface last. A great tool for developers turns out to be a great tool for agents.

Guillermo Rauch: Vercel and Notion are both aggressively model-agnostic, Switzerland in the model wars. Why?

Ivan Zhao: The models leapfrog each other every few weeks, so picking a side is a losing game. We route automatically by the intelligence a task needs, frontier models for coding, smaller and faster ones for support and summarization. What excites me most is that as more use cases stop needing frontier intelligence, you can shape smaller models to your product and win back speed and cost. And speed creates discontinuities, a model five times faster can change the kind of interface you'd even design.

Guillermo Rauch: When a billion knowledge workers are agents, how does that reshape us?

Ivan Zhao: We can't fully see it, and that's the point. First-order effects are easy, the iPhone was an iPod plus a phone plus a browser. The second-order effects are the ones that surprise you, like what social media did to teenagers. We shape our tools, and then our tools shape us. With software that can think, the second-order effects are the ones we won't predict.

Guillermo Rauch: Taste or velocity, keep one.

Ivan Zhao: Taste. It's the distillation of wisdom from a lot of shots on goal.

Ship 2026 in Sydney

The Sydney event opened at Machine Hall, a 1930s electrical substation that ran the city's trams and wharves for half a century. Over 200 people gathered there to build for the agentic era at Ship Sydney.

Ship week Sydney

The week kicked off with the AI SYD meetup, where developers, AI engineers, and the Sydney technical community joined for an evening of lightning talks and networking. At the AI Social Club, senior leaders gathered at Shell House for a talk from Malte Ubl and a fireside with Suyog Rao and David Hyman (Founder, monō ai) on how agentic infrastructure is driving meaningful outcomes for enterprises.

Ship day sessions

  • Belen Garcia Fava and Vivek Katial from Heidi Health showed how their team ships fast in a regulated space with agents and Vercel, and made the case that trust is engineered, not granted.

  • Robin Yoong from Cursor created an eve agent by voice alone. Three models coded in parallel, and a spoken approval shipped it to Vercel.

  • Nonny Bell (Startup Manager APAC, Vercel) moderated a panel with Matthew Blode (AI Engineer, Linktree), Aarush Issar (GM AI Engineering, Auto & General Australia), and Leonardo Borges (Chief Engineer Gen AI, CommBank) on how their teams are adopting AI agents in production.

  • JJ Lecocq (Sales Director AUNZ, Vercel) led a discussion on how organizations are reshaping people, culture, and structure for AI.

Ship what's next

Thanks for joining us for Ship 2026 in London, Berlin, New York, Sydney, and San Francisco. We'll see you in May for Ship 2027.

title: The fx adapter now runs the harness on the host
description:
The fx adapter for the AI SDK’s HarnessAgent now uses libfx, the TypeScript library for fx. The harness and model requests run in your application’s process, while built-in filesystem and shell operations remain isolated in the sandbox.

This simplifies sandbox setup: you no longer need to install fx inside the sandbox, run a sandbox bridge, or expose a sandbox port. Model credentials stay on the host, outside the environment where the agent runs commands.

The rewrite also adds:

  • Built-in tool filtering: choose which built-in tools the agent can use

  • Mid-turn steering: send new instructions while a turn is running

  • Structured output: generate responses that match a schema

  • Image tool results: return images to the model through toModelOutput()

Sessions can be saved and resumed in a new host process.

Update @ai-sdk/harness-fx to the latest version to use the new adapter. Learn more in the fx harness documentation.

title: A Free Google Scholar Alternative API: Search 250M Papers With OpenAlex in Python
description:
Google Scholar has no API, and its terms don't allow scraping. If you need research papers in a script (for a literature review, a reading list, or a RAG pipeline), use OpenAlex instead. It's a free, open catalog of over 250 million scholarly works (the successor to Microsoft Academic), and its data is CC0, so you can reuse it however you like.

The script

Search titles and abstracts, keep papers from 2015 on, and sort by citations:

"""Search scholarly papers with the free OpenAlex API. Usage: python3 paper_search.py '"growth mindset"'"""
import json
import sys
import urllib.parse
import urllib.request

query = sys.argv[1]
params = {
    "filter": f"title_and_abstract.search:{query},publication_year:2015-",
    "sort": "cited_by_count:desc",
    "per-page": 10,
    # "api_key": "YOUR_KEY",  # free at openalex.org/settings/api ($1/day of usage)
}
url = "https://api.openalex.org/works?" + urllib.parse.urlencode(params)
data = json.load(urllib.request.urlopen(url, timeout=30))

print(f"{data['meta']['count']:,} papers match {query}. Most cited since 2015:\n")
for w in data["results"]:
    venue = ((w.get("primary_location") or {}).get("source") or {}).get("display_name", "")
    pdf = (w.get("best_oa_location") or {}).get("pdf_url") or ""
    print(f"{w['cited_by_count']:>6}  {w['publication_year']}  {w['title']}")
    print(f"        {venue}  {pdf}")

Real output (October 2026):

$ python3 paper_search.py '"growth mindset"'
9,092 papers match "growth mindset". Most cited since 2015:

  1694  2019  PISA 2018 Results (Volume I)
        Programme for international student assessment/Internationale Schulleistungsstudie
  1511  2019  A national experiment reveals where a growth mindset improves achievement
        Nature  https://www.nature.com/articles/s41586-019-1466-y.pdf
  1259  2019  Mindsets: A View From Two Eras
        Perspectives on Psychological Science
  1054  2016  Motivation to learn: an overview of contemporary theories
        Medical Education  https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/pdfdirect/10.1111/medu.13074

Quotes around the phrase matter. Without them, OpenAlex matches the words anywhere, and "most cited" fills up with unrelated famous papers.

Useful details

  • Abstracts come as an "inverted index" ({"word": [positions]}). Rebuild the text by sorting positions: " ".join(w for _, w in sorted((i, w) for w, idx in inv.items() for i in idx)).
  • Free PDFs: best_oa_location.pdf_url links to a legal open-access copy when one exists. Add is_oa:true to the filter to keep only those.
  • Filters chain with commas: type:review, cited_by_count:>100, publication_year:2020-2024.
  • DOI lookups: filter=doi:10.1038/s41586-019-1466-y|10.1177/1529100612453266 fetches up to 50 at once.
  • Limits: without a key, you share a small free daily budget with everyone on your IP. A free key (openalex.org/settings/api) gives you $1/day of usage, where a search costs $0.001 for up to 100 results. That's plenty for most projects.

No-code version

If you'd rather get a spreadsheet, I wrapped this as Research Paper Search on Apify. Type queries or paste DOIs, set filters (year, citations, type, open access), and export CSV or Excel with authors, institutions, journal, citations, the full abstract, topic, and PDF link. It costs $2 per 1,000 papers, and no key is needed.

The script is yours either way. Happy reading.

title: Production-Ready FastAPI Async JWT Authentication & Session Flow with Redis
description:
Implementing secure authentication in modern async Python APIs is often fraught with subtle pitfalls: stateless tokens that cannot be revoked on logout, refresh token reuse, and missing brute-force protection.

fastapi-redis-auth-flow is a production-ready template and library providing bulletproof JWT authentication for FastAPI backed by high-speed Redis session tracking.

seotarek / fastapi-redis-auth-flow

Production-ready async JWT authentication & session management using FastAPI, Redis token blacklisting, and rate limiting.

FastAPI Redis Auth Flow 🔐⚡

A production-ready asynchronous authentication service using FastAPI, dual JWT access/refresh token rotation, and instant Redis session blacklisting.

Developed by Tarek Mohamed (@seotarek)

📌 Features

  • 🔑 Dual Token Lifecycle: Short-lived access tokens (15m) and persistent refresh tokens (7d).
  • 🚫 Instant Session Revocation: Immediate logout invalidation via Redis token blacklisting.
  • ⚡ Asynchronous Redis Driver: Ultra-fast sub-millisecond session state checks with redis.asyncio.

🚀 Quickstart

docker-compose up -d

Test login:

curl -X POST http://localhost:8000/login \
     -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
     -d '{"username": "admin", "password": "admin123"}'

📜 License

Licensed under the MIT License.


View on GitHub


🔒 Security Best Practices Implemented

  • Refresh Token Rotation: Every token refresh invalidates the previous refresh token; if a token is reused, all sessions are immediately revoked.
  • Instant Revocation (Blacklisting): Immediate session termination across devices using Redis TTL keys.
  • Async & Non-Blocking: 100% async Python powered by redis-py and pydantic v2.

Check out the full repository and Docker Compose setup:
👉 https://github.com/seotarek/fastapi-redis-auth-flow

title: Speed Insights now has a free tier
description:
Speed Insights now has a free tier that gives you a high-level performance overview from your real users. The new free tier:

  • Is available on every plan, for any number of projects

  • Includes 10,000 events per team, every 30 days

Install Speed Insights:

Previously, free Speed Insights was limited to a single project on Hobby, and upgrading to Pro meant losing access unless you paid for the add-on. Now your free tier carries over, and you only pay if you upgrade.

The paid product, now called Speed Insights Plus, includes deeper diagnostics and historical data. If you were already paying for Speed Insights, only the name has changed, and your capabilities and price are the same.

Install @vercel/speed-insights in your project to start reporting real-user data, or open the Speed Insights dashboard to view your results.

Learn more in the Speed Insights documentation.

Speed Insights reports how real visitors experience your pages, using live traffic rather than lab conditions. Speed Insights Plus adds slow-route diagnosis and detailed breakdowns for finding where pages get slow, and historical data to track performance over time. It also provides access to Drains and the Vercel CLI for working with performance data outside the dashboard.
