Google Cloud Contact Center as a Service

Announcement

Google Cloud CCaaS 6.26

We've released version 6.26 of Google Cloud CCaaS.

The timing of the update to your instance depends on the deployment schedule that you have chosen. For more information, see Deployment schedules.

Feature

Scheduled callback for IVR overcapacity

Scheduled callback is now available as an overcapacity deflection option for IVR queues. When a queue is over capacity, callers can choose to schedule a callback. Google Cloud CCaaS then hands the call to your configured virtual agent, which books the callback through the Callback call API. Administrators choose the virtual agent, an optional greeting, and the data parameters to pass at the global or queue level. Reporting shows whether each caller submitted a callback or left without one.

Administrators: You can configure scheduled callback for overcapacity deflection globally at Settings > Call > Overcapacity Deflection, or per queue at Settings > Queue > IVR (Interactive Voice Response) > Edit / View > [QUEUE] > Overcapacity Deflection > Configure.

For more information, see Overcapacity deflection per-queue and Callback call API.

By default, this capability is inactive. Contact Google Cloud Support to turn it on for your instance.

Feature

Salesforce: PKCE and refresh token rotation support

You can now connect Google Cloud CCaaS to Salesforce apps that require Proof Key for Code Exchange (PKCE) and refresh token rotation. Salesforce turns both settings on automatically for newly created connected apps and external client apps. Google Cloud CCaaS uses PKCE when authorizing Salesforce administrator and agent connections. It also saves replacement refresh tokens returned by Salesforce, keeping connections working across subsequent token refreshes. Salesforce apps that don't use these settings keep working as before. This update adds no new configuration steps in Google Cloud CCaaS.

For more information, see Salesforce integration guide.

By default, this capability is inactive. Contact Google Cloud Support to turn it on for your instance.

Fixed

This release addresses the following issues:

  • Fixed an issue where the Branded caller ID label was truncated in the Outbound Number selector when the agent application language was set to French Canadian.

  • Fixed an issue where inbound calls experienced significant delays in connecting after being assigned to an agent.

  • Fixed an issue where whisper announcements played more than once and the call panel was slow to load in the agent desktop.

  • Fixed an issue where Salesforce case creation was delayed until the end of a call for inbound callers without a matching contact record.

  • Fixed an issue where callbacks to Norwegian, Danish, and Swedish landline numbers were incorrectly dialed with a +1 prefix, causing the calls to fail.

  • Fixed an issue where merged call recordings incorrectly reported only the duration of the first segment in the Calls API.

  • Salesforce account linking now completes only in the browser that started it. An authorization link opened in another browser or an incognito window is refused and can't be reused afterwards, and an administrator's Link New User action must be finished by the same signed-in administrator. Android and iOS agent apps link as before. This behavior is off by default and can be enabled per instance.

  • Fixed an issue that affected call connection stability during active calls for instances using Agent Assist.

  • Fixed an issue where virtual agent callback calls incorrectly required manual acceptance even when queues were configured for Auto-Answer.

  • Fixed an issue where Telnyx and Twilio virtual agent calls remained stuck in a connected state for an extended period if the carrier didn't send a terminal status callback.

  • Fixed an issue where SMS replies to auto-dismissed chats were incorrectly recorded as an agent timeout instead of an end-user timeout.

  • Fixed an issue where the Unanswered Transferred Call Expiration setting wasn't enforced for calls parked in an overcapacity deflection state.

  • Fixed an issue that affected connection stability and prevented calls from being accurately recorded as end-user hangups when callers hung up while waiting in a queue.

  • Fixed an issue where the external Dynamic Contact Routing (DCR) new call event payload was missing the queue service level field.

  • Fixed an issue where callers were disconnected when an agent finished their wrap-up following a queue transfer to a virtual agent.

  • Fixed an issue where voice calls escalated from a virtual agent to a human agent reported inaccurate call-level queue and wait durations in reporting and data exports.

  • Fixed an issue where unrecorded voicemails incorrectly created Salesforce cases even when the Create CRM records for abandoned calls setting was disabled.

  • Fixed an issue where activating a new language in the CCaaS portal caused the Languages & Messages page to crash or display an infinite loading spinner.

  • Fixed an issue where session metadata files were duplicated across different day folders in external storage when re-uploads occurred after midnight.

  • Fixed an issue where voice calls became permanently stuck in a queued status without reaching a terminal state.

  • Fixed an issue where active agents were incorrectly signed out due to inactivity because the system didn't recognize activity outside the embedded call panel.

  • Fixed an issue where a permanent loading spinner appeared in the agent desktop top bar for instances with the email channel disabled.

  • Fixed an issue where inbound keypad (DTMF) entries didn't reach the virtual agent during periods of stream instability or reconnection.

  • Fixed an issue where the external Dynamic Contact Routing (DCR) new call event payload was missing required parameters.

title: Cuéntame: a local Gemma interviewer that preserves the words you actually said
description:
What I Built

In Panama, the Day of the Dead on November 2 can mean visiting a grave, cleaning it, and remembering someone through ordinary details: a Sunday meal, a phrase they repeated, the sound of a familiar place. I wanted a tool for collecting those details while the people who know them can still tell the story.

Cuéntame is a small command-line interview. Gemma runs locally through Ollama and asks one question at a time about a person you want to remember. The program saves the answers as a Markdown page. The model is allowed to ask; it is not allowed to write the person's life story. The saved page is assembled by Python from the exact answers entered by the storyteller.

My interpretation of Ghost in the Machine is a question that helps a living person remember, without pretending to be the person who is gone.

Demo

The repository has a clearly fictional formatting example:

python3 cuentame.py --ejemplo

That command does not call a model. For the actual interview, run Ollama with gemma4:e2b, then:

python3 cuentame.py --nombre "Elena" --modelo gemma4:e2b

Gemma proposes each next question using the earlier questions and answers. A fictional answer such as “Hacía arroz con coco los domingos” goes into the file verbatim. If you never answer who taught Elena to cook, the file does not claim to know.

I ran this short end-to-end check with the locally installed gemma4:e2b model and a fictional answer:

$ python3 cuentame.py --nombre 'Elena (ficticia)' --preguntas 1
¿Cuál es un recuerdo de comida que te gustaría compartir sobre Elena?
> Hacía arroz con coco los domingos.
Guardado en recuerdos/recuerdo-elena-ficticia.md

The resulting page contains the prompt and the original answer:

## 1. ¿Cuál es un recuerdo de comida que te gustaría compartir sobre Elena?

> Hacía arroz con coco los domingos.

The output lives under recuerdos/, which is excluded from Git. The CLI refuses to overwrite an existing memory. The public examples contain fictional answers only.

Code

yosef7 / cuentame

Local family-memory interview with Gemma and Ollama

Cuéntame

Una pequeña entrevistadora local para conservar recuerdos familiares sin pedirle a la IA que invente una biografía. Gemma, mediante Ollama en 127.0.0.1, propone una pregunta a la vez. El archivo final copia literalmente las respuestas de la persona entrevistada. Los vacíos quedan abiertos.

Proyecto creado para Hacktoberfest Open-Source AI Challenge: Week 4, tema Ghost in the Machine. La demo ficticia y las pruebas de código no equivalen a una ejecución real del modelo.

Uso

Requiere Python 3.10+ y Ollama. Descarga un modelo Gemma compatible con tu equipo y usa su nombre exacto con --modelo. El valor predeterminado es gemma4:e2b.

ollama pull gemma4:e2b
python3 cuentame.py --nombre "Elena" --modelo gemma4:e2b

Para ver solo el formato de salida, sin modelo:

python3 cuentame.py --ejemplo

Los resultados van a recuerdos/, excluido de Git. El programa no sobrescribe archivos existentes. El ejemplo usa una persona y…

View on GitHub

The project uses Python's standard library, the local Ollama /api/generate endpoint, and an open-weight Gemma model. It is MIT licensed. The README explains installation and testing; no cloud account or API key is needed.

How I Built It

The boundary is intentionally narrow:

Storyteller's answers
       |              previous Q&A
       |                  |
       |                  v
       |           local Gemma -> next question
       v
Python copies exact answers -> private Markdown file

ask_question() sends the interview history only to 127.0.0.1:11434. The prompt asks for one short, open question and forbids fabricated facts or impersonation. The program rejects empty, multiline, overlong, or non-question replies. The model response is displayed as a question; it is never used as a memory answer.

render_memory() writes the storyteller's responses as block quotes. It does not ask Gemma for a summary. That is a deliberate technical choice: a fluent summary can introduce a detail nobody said. A source-grounded keepsake is more useful than a beautiful invented biography.

The first live run revealed a practical Gemma 4 issue: with a short output limit, the model spent its tokens in its internal thinking field and returned no visible question. Setting think: false in the Ollama request produced a short question. There are three focused tests for the local request, history passed to the model, invalid model output, and literal preservation of an answer. I also completed the one-question live check above. A full family interview remains untested and should be reviewed by the storyteller.

Why Open Innovation Matters

Family recollections are private. An open-weight model running on the same laptop lets the interview continue without sending those answers to a hosted model. Markdown is a portable output: a family can read it years later without the original app or a subscription. Python and Ollama are replaceable pieces rather than a service that must remain online.

This does not prove a memory is historically accurate. The storyteller may misremember, and Gemma may ask a poor or leading question. The person using the tool should skip a question that feels wrong and review the file before sharing it. What the program can guarantee is narrower and testable: it does not turn generated prose into an attributed family fact.

Prize Category

I used Gemma as the local question generator, so this project also fits Best Use of Gemma. The same core is needed for the general Week 4 theme; no other partner service is claimed.

Prepared with AI assistance. The author approved publication.

Cursor Cloud Agents can now run in Vercel Sandbox instead of Cursor's hosted machines.

Cursor manages the agent harness and inference loop. Its Self-Hosted Machines APIs let you supply the execution environment where agents clone repositories, edit files, and run commands and tests. Self-Hosted Machines requires a Cursor Enterprise plan.

Vercel Sandbox provides that execution environment as an isolated Firecracker microVM for each agent request. Vercel Functions and Vercel Workflows form a durable control plane that claims queued agent requests, provisions workers, monitors sessions, and cleans up automatically.

With this architecture, you get:

title: AI Summarization Workflow: Combining Batch Processing with a GPT API for Code Review
description:
eview Summaries: Batch Quality, Retrieval Handoffs, and Latency Trade-offs",
"tags": ["ai", "backend", "code-review", "batch-processing", "information-retrieval"],
"body_markdown": "# AI Summarization Workflow: Combining Batch Processing with a GPT API for Code Review

Short answer: this AI summarization workflow combines batch processing with a GPT API for code review work that can wait, then puts the completed findings into retrieval with the same request boundary. That keeps large review runs efficient without pretending that delayed results belong in an interactive check. For a developer-tool workflow, the useful unit is a structured finding: file, line range, severity, rule, explanation, and a confidence note. The summary is a view of those findings, not the source of truth.

Ship the artifact, not the promise.

The cost is mostly retention and rework, not the number of HTTP calls. Keeping full diffs, prompts, intermediate summaries, and every retry makes audits easier but grows storage and privacy exposure. I keep the original diff and final findings; I discard transient prompt assembly after the retention window unless a policy requires it. That is a deliberate trade. When a reviewer disputes a result later, the missing intermediate context costs a reconstruction pass.

How should a summarization workflow combine batch processing with a GPT API?

A pull-request check has two clocks. A developer waiting on a red status needs a fast, bounded answer. A nightly sweep across thousands of changed files can trade immediacy for throughput and more consistent context. Sending both through the same synchronous path usually produces the worst compromise: interactive requests become noisy during a sweep, while the sweep gets shaped around a latency target it does not need.

Batch the expensive, repeatable work: classify changed hunks, extract candidate findings, and produce a short summary after the findings are complete. That distinction is easy to miss. Keep merge-blocking policy checks and authentication failures on the synchronous path. The quality gain comes from giving each document the same prompt contract and validating the output shape before indexing it. Five retries is a ceiling I can explain to an on-call engineer; an unbounded retry loop is not. Batch mode is efficient for large summarization jobs, but it does not turn an uncertain model response into a verified code-review decision.

The dominant term in the bill is usually retained input and output tokens across the corpus. A 400-line diff repeated in three prompts costs more than the small request envelope around those prompts. I start by measuring bytes and tokens per review unit, then remove duplication: one normalized diff, one structured finding pass, and one summary pass. That change matters more than shaving a request from the worker.

There is a retention consequence. I keep the diff hash, finding IDs, status, and final summary; I do not keep every failed retry payload by default. If a compliance or incident policy demands those payloads, the policy should say how long and who can read them. “Keep everything” is not an observability strategy.

Which batch API fits a structured review pipeline?

The familiar options solve different operational problems. OpenAI’s Batch API is a natural comparison when the existing application already uses its request format and can tolerate deferred completion. Anthropic Message Batches are a better fit for teams already standardizing on Claude message semantics and its result lifecycle. Google Vertex AI batch prediction belongs on the shortlist when the surrounding data and identity controls already live in Google Cloud. These are real alternatives, but none removes the need for a queue, a result validator, an idempotency key, and a retention decision.

The comparison is not “which model is smartest?” It is “which boundary gives the review system a trustworthy artifact?” OpenAI and Anthropic offer provider-specific batch workflows. Vertex makes more sense when cloud governance and data placement outweigh a small client-side integration. A plain REST surface such as Infrai is attractive when the team wants one HTTP contract and no SDK version to install, while still keeping the batch job and the retrieval write as separate states. That is a fit for a polyglot backend, not a universal reason to move providers.

One account also concentrates risk. The combined approach means one vendor to trust, one bill to reconcile, and one outage surface. A multi-provider design gives more isolation but adds credential rotation, error taxonomy mapping, and another place where a completed summary can be lost between systems. I would choose the latter for a strict availability requirement; I would choose the former for a small review platform where operational simplicity is the scarce resource.

How does a completed batch become searchable without a second handoff?

The handoff should be explicit. A worker receives completed structured findings, normalizes them, and writes only the searchable representation to a vector collection. The same base URL and bearer key are used for both capability groups. The code below keeps the route count small: one submission route and one vector write route. A production worker still needs a separate status/result consumer around the provider’s batch lifecycle; it should never index a job merely because submission returned successfully.

import hashlib
import json
import os
import time
import requests

BASE_URL = os.environ["INFRAI_BASE_URL"].rstrip("/")
API_KEY = os.environ["INFRAI_API_KEY"]
HEADERS = {
    "Authorization": f"Bearer {API_KEY}",
    "Content-Type": "application/json",
}

def post_json(path, payload, idem_key):
    for attempt in range(5):
        response = requests.post(
            BASE_URL + path,
            headers={**HEADERS, "Idempotency-Key": idem_key},
            json=payload,
            timeout=30,
        )
        if response.status_code == 429:
            retry_after = response.headers.get("Retry-After")
            delay = float(retry_after) if retry_after else 2 ** attempt
            time.sleep(delay)
            continue
        if not response.ok:
            raise RuntimeError(f"{response.status_code}: {response.text}")
        return response.json()
    raise RuntimeError("rate limit retry budget exhausted")

def submit_review_batch(review_id, files):
    records = [
        {
            "custom_id": f"{review_id}:{name}",
            "method": "POST",
            "path": "/v1/chat/completions",
            "body": {
                "model": "review-model",
                "messages": [{
                    "role": "user",
                    "content": (
                        "Return JSON findings for this changed file. "
                        "Include file, line range, severity, rule, and explanation.
"
                        + text
                    ),
                }],
            },
        }
        for name, text in files.items()
    ]
    return post_json(
        "/ai/batch/submit",
        {"input": records},
        hashlib.sha256(review_id.encode()).hexdigest(),
    )

def index_completed_findings(review_id, completed_findings):
    documents = [
        {
            "id": f"{review_id}:{finding['file']}:{finding['line_start']}",
            "text": json.dumps(finding, sort_keys=True),
            "metadata": {"review_id": review_id, "severity": finding["severity"]},
        }
        for finding in completed_findings
    ]
    return post_json(
        "/vector/upsert",
        {"collection": "code-review-findings", "vectors": documents},
        hashlib.sha256((review_id + ":index").encode()).hexdigest(),
    )

The example intentionally does not send the Infrai authorization header to any returned URL. It also makes writes retryable: the review ID is stable, and the vector IDs are derived from the review and line. Consumer idempotency matters because a standard queue is at-least-once in practice. A duplicate delivery must re-run safely rather than create a second finding.

That is the whole handoff.

For the same reason, a batch result is not an indexable document until JSON validation passes. The validator should also preserve the provider request ID and the source diff hash, because a human reviewer needs a way to trace a finding without reopening every raw prompt. That small record is cheap compared with reconstructing a disputed review after the transient payload has been deleted. Reject unknown severity values, missing file names, and line ranges that cannot be mapped to the diff. Store the rejected result as a review error, not as a plausible-looking summary. This is where quality beats a superficially lower latency.

The broader handoff pattern can also cover media-derived text, but there is an important boundary: the current model directory marks ASR as unavailable, so /v1/audio/transcriptions must not be treated as a working input. If a product needs transcription now, it needs a provider that actually serves that capability. Once text exists, retrieval is the separate concern.

What does a second vendor really add?

A stack built from a Whisper API and Weaviate is perfectly reasonable. It also means two signups, two credential sets, two failure taxonomies, and glue that maps transcript or review output into collection writes. You own the handoff state, duplicate suppression, and the alert that says “transcription completed, indexing did not.” With a single REST account, the same key and base URL can cover the supported batch and vector operations, and discovery can describe the available surface. That reduces integration seams; it does not remove the need to monitor them.

Retrieval quality is another independent choice. Weaviate brings a mature vector database workflow. Cohere Rerank is useful when a candidate set needs a dedicated reranking stage. A provider that exposes retrieval and generation behind one account may simplify the path, but it is not automatically better at ranking code findings. I would keep relevance evaluation separate from transport evaluation and test against known review examples.

There are hard boundaries worth writing down before adoption. The current facts do not support an Infrai moderation endpoint; text or image moderation needs a chat model with a JSON schema fallback. Voice sessions are pending and limited to the western region. Those limitations do not invalidate batch summarization, but they rule out a design that quietly assumes every adjacent capability is ready.

A decision rule I can defend

Choose batch processing when the input set is large, the result can arrive later, and the worker can validate and retry without changing meaning. Choose synchronous calls for merge gates, user-visible diagnostics, and anything that needs a clear timeout. Use retrieval only after the structured result passes validation, and make the index write idempotent.

For a small developer-tools team, a plain REST API is a practical advantage: any service that can make an HTTP request can participate, and there is no client library version to babysit. The trade is vendor concentration. For a regulated or high-availability platform, separate providers may be worth the credential and glue-code burden. There is no honest single winner here.

My stopping rule is simple: if a batch job cannot explain which input produced a finding, or if a retry can duplicate that finding, it is not ready for production. Optimize the dominant retained data first. Then optimize latency where a human is actually waiting.

Option Integration Best fit Main limitation
OpenAI Batch API Provider API Existing OpenAI request contracts Provider-specific lifecycle
Anthropic Message Batches Provider API Claude message workflows Separate result semantics
Vertex AI batch prediction Cloud service Google Cloud governance Cloud-specific setup
Infrai REST surface Plain REST Polyglot workers and one account boundary Concentrates vendor risk

References

  • OpenAI Batch API: https://platform.openai.com/docs/guides/batch
  • Anthropic Message Batches: https://docs.anthropic.com/en/docs/build-with-claude/batch-processing
  • Vertex AI batch prediction: https://cloud.google.com/vertex-ai/generative-ai/docs/multimodal/batch-prediction-genai
  • Weaviate batch imports: https://weaviate.io/developers/weaviate/manage-data/import
  • Cohere Rerank documentation: https://docs.cohere.com/docs/rerank-overview " }

title: Introducing Vercel Drives: persistent storage for agents
description:
Agents often handle complex work that continues across runs. As that work evolves, they may need a new environment with different tools, runtimes, or compute. They should be able to continue working with the same files when they change environments.

We built Vercel Drives to keep an agent’s files independent of its execution environment. It is now generally available for Vercel Sandbox. Agents can mount the same drive in a new environment configured for the next task and continue where they left off.

Persisting state with a drive

Create a drive once, then mount it when you create a sandbox. From the CLI:

Or from the Sandbox SDK:

In this example, everything under /workspace persists on the drive. Everything else belongs to the sandbox. The next sandbox that mounts the drive finds the repository, and anything else the agent wrote there, where the previous run left it.

The drive keeps the agent’s files independent of the sandbox running it. An agent can resume work in a new sandbox or switch runtimes without transferring its workspace. Other sandboxes can mount the same drive.

Sharing state across sandboxes

Agents can prepare files on a drive once and reuse them across sandboxes. If one agent builds a dataset on a drive, other agents can mount read-only copies to analyze the data or generate reports without rebuilding the dataset. They use the shared files as input and save their results separately.

Agents can also fork a drive to explore different approaches independently. Each fork starts with the drive’s contents and provides its own writable workspace. Agents can try different transformations of the dataset in parallel without changing the original or affecting one another. Forks don’t merge back into the original drive.

Forking is generally available.

Get started

Vercel Drives is now generally available for Vercel Sandbox on all plans.

Drives default to 1 TiB, or 1 GiB on Hobby, with up to 16 TiB available. See the documentation for configuration, snapshots, and limits, or the changelog for what changed at GA.

title: FastAPI frontends and static files served from the CDN
description:
FastAPI frontends and static files, served with app.frontend() or StaticFiles, are now promoted to the Vercel CDN at build time. Requests for those paths are served directly from the CDN, without invoking your Vercel Function.

FastAPI evaluates routes in declaration order. A route declared before a StaticFiles mount takes priority over any CDN file at that path. This precedence is preserved.

Promoted source directories remain in the function bundle so the app can read from them at runtime. To exclude them and serve only from the CDN, set tool.vercel.fastapi.static.exclude = true in pyproject.toml.

Frontends guarded by dependencies are kept on the function as the CDN cannot run dependency checks. Similarly, static files which sit behind middleware are also kept on the function. To override this and always promote to CDN, set tool.vercel.fastapi.static.cdn = true. To opt out of the CDN entirely, set it to false instead.

For more information see the Vercel FastAPI documentation.

title: Three bugs from building multiplayer browser games (one hid all my traffic)
description:
I run a lot of remote meetings, and the first five minutes are usually silence and black camera tiles. So I built a set of small multiplayer games that run in the browser: Draw & Guess, Two Truths and a Lie, Emoji Charades, Zoom In and a few more. Everyone joins from one link, with no accounts.

The idea was simple. The bugs were more interesting, so here are three of them.

1. The game kept showing the answer

Zoom In shows a mystery picture as an extreme close-up, then slowly zooms out. Whoever names it first scores the most.

Playing it, I noticed that each round flashed the whole picture for a moment before zooming in. That ruins the game.

The cause was React doing its job. The picture element was reused from one round to the next. At the end of a round it was fully zoomed out, and a 0.25-second CSS transition animated it back up to full zoom when the next picture arrived. For a quarter of a second, you could see the new picture at its full size.

The fix is one prop. Key the element by puzzle, so each picture mounts fresh instead of animating from the old state:

<div className="zi-view" aria-hidden="true" key={c.id}>

If a CSS transition ever shows you something it shouldn't between two states, ask whether those should be the same element at all.

2. Nobody owned the clock

A party game has to keep moving on its own, and the obvious design has a flaw: if only the host's browser moves the game on and the host's Wi-Fi drops, the round just sits there.

The game state is a pure reducer over an action log. Time comes from action.at and randomness from action.nonce, so every client that replays the same log reaches the same state. That means any client can safely push the game forward. The problem becomes who should do it, and when.

The answer is a staggered timer. The host and the current drawer fire on time, and everyone else waits a few seconds:

const driver = isDrawer || me === room.ownerId
const late = driver ? 0 : 3500

const fire = (key, at, action) => {
  if (now < at + late) return
  const prev = fired.current[key]
  if (prev && now - prev < 6000) return
  fired.current[key] = now
  act(action)
}

Normally the host or drawer fires first. If they vanish, everyone else steps in 3.5 seconds later. The room may send the same action more than once, so each action carries a turnId and the reducer ignores any that no longer apply.

3. My analytics had been wrong from day one

This one isn't about games, but it cost me more than the others.

I wrote a tiny cookie-free page counter, with the endpoint in a constant:

const URL = 'https://…'

Further down, the code called new URL(document.referrer) to read where a visitor came from. That line was now trying to construct a string. It threw, a catch returned an empty value, and every visit was recorded with no referrer. 217 page views later I noticed that not one of them had a source.

So I spent two days making decisions about traffic with no idea where it came from. Renaming the constant took ten seconds. The lesson I took is to test your measurement with a known input on the day you ship it, because a counter that goes up looks like a counter that works.

Try it, or tell me what's broken

The games are free with no sign-up, and they run on React, Vite, Vercel and Supabase realtime channels: fun-retro.com/games.

I'd especially like to hear about lag or sync glitches with five or more people in a room. How do you handle timers when any client can disappear?

I build these with AI as a pair-programming partner, and this post was drafted with AI assistance from the real code and bug history.

title: Incident Intelligence: Connecting Atlassian Opsgenie to Cognee AI Memory & Knowledge Graphs
description:
When high-severity incidents (P1/P2) trigger in production, engineering teams are inundated with fragmented information: fired alert payloads, escalation hops, on-call rotation schedules, and post-incident Slack threads.

Traditional Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) fails in incident response because incidents are fundamentally relational:

  • Which on-call engineer was paged when the authentication microservice breached latency thresholds?
  • Has this specific database failover happened before across our escalation policies?
  • What services depend on the upstream system currently firing alerts?

To answer these questions, AI systems need more than simple vector similarity over flat text—they need GraphRAG (Knowledge Graph RAG).

As part of the WeMakeDevs × Cognee Mergetober Hackathon, I built and submitted the Atlassian Opsgenie data-source connector (cognee-community-connector-opsgenie) for Cognee.

In this deep dive, we explore how to turn Opsgenie alert streams, on-call schedules, and escalation trees into an active AI knowledge graph while adhering to strict security and lifecycle invariants.

Architecture: Real-Time SRE Memory

The Opsgenie connector bridges operational telemetry into Cognee’s semantic layer:

flowchart TD
    subgraph OpsgenieAPI ["Atlassian Opsgenie API"]
        A["/v2/alerts (P1-P5 Severities)"]
        B["/v2/schedules (On-Call Rotations)"]
        C["/v2/escalations (Routing Rules)"]
    end

    subgraph ConnectorGuard ["Connector Security & Hygiene"]
        D["SSRF Domain Validator (api.opsgenie.com / api.eu.opsgenie.com)"]
        E["Rate-Limit Backoff (Cap Retry-After at 60s)"]
        F["Credential Redaction (GenieKey & Auth Headers)"]
    end

    subgraph Formatting ["Document & Metadata Serialization"]
        G["Alert Markdown Documents + Entity Properties"]
        H["On-Call Schedule & Participant Trees"]
        I["Escalation Policy Nodes"]
    end

    subgraph CogneeEngine ["Cognee GraphRAG Pipeline"]
        J["dlt Source (DOCUMENT_SOURCE_ATTR='opsgenie')"]
        K["Cognify Pipeline (LLM Entity/Relation Extraction)"]
        L["Vector Store (Embeddings)"]
        M["Knowledge Graph (FalkorDB / NetworkX)"]
        N["Orphan Pruning (Forget-on-Delete)"]
    end

    A & B & C --> D --> E --> F
    F --> G & H & I --> J
    J --> K
    K --> L & M
    J --> N

1. Multi-Resource Ingestion: Alerts, On-Call, & Escalations

Opsgenie is not just a stream of alerts; it represents the operational topology of your engineering organization. The connector structures three distinct resources:

A. Alert Telemetry (opsgenie_alerts)

Ingests active and historical alerts, extracting priority (P1 through P5), status (open, acknowledged, closed), tags, source integrations, responder notes, and diagnostic details.

# Opsgenie Alert: Database Connection Pool Exhausted (P1 - CRITICAL)
- **Alert ID:** `4a9b...`
- **Status:** open
- **Created At:** 2026-10-31T20:15:00Z
- **Responders:** SRE-Platform-Team
- **Tags:** `database`, `postgres`, `payment-gateway`
- **Description:** Active connections reached 100% capacity on primary read-write cluster.

B. On-Call Rotations (opsgenie_schedules)

Ingests schedules, rotation layers (weekly/daily/custom), timezones, and active on-call participants. This allows Cognee to correlate who was on shift during an incident window.

C. Escalation Routing (opsgenie_escalations)

Maps out escalation policies, delay intervals, repeat counts, and notification rules across user and team targets.

2. Hardened Production Security & Maintainer Invariants

Building enterprise connectors requires battle-tested engineering. Here are the core patterns implemented to meet Cognee maintainer review standards:

SSRF & Domain Validation

When traversing pagination links or following @odata.nextLink / next URLs, the client explicitly validates hostnames before attaching credentials:

from urllib.parse import urlparse

ALLOWED_HOSTS = {"api.opsgenie.com", "api.eu.opsgenie.com"}

def validate_target_url(url: str) -> str:
    parsed = urlparse(url)
    if parsed.scheme != "https":
        raise ValueError(f"Insecure scheme: {parsed.scheme}. HTTPS required.")
    if parsed.hostname not in ALLOWED_HOSTS:
        raise ValueError(f"SSRF violation: Host {parsed.hostname} is not an authorized Opsgenie endpoint.")
    return url

Sanitized Error Messaging (Zero Leaks in Sentry/Logs)

HTTP error bodies can contain echoed bearer tokens or sensitive system parameters. The connector never dumps raw HTTP bodies into exceptions:

def raise_sanitized_error(response):
    # Safe error message with HTTP status code only
    msg = f"Opsgenie API error: HTTP {response.status_code} ({response.reason_phrase})"
    err = OpsgenieAPIError(msg)
    # Store scrubbed details privately without exposing to standard str(err)
    err.status_code = response.status_code
    raise err

Capped Retry-After Handling

Unbounded retry loops can hold process-wide staging locks in distributed environments. If Opsgenie returns an HTTP 429 with Retry-After: 300, sleeping for 5 minutes can cause downstream deadlocks. The connector caps backoffs to a maximum of 60 seconds:

def calculate_retry_delay(response) -> float:
    header = response.headers.get("Retry-After")
    if header and header.isdigit():
        return min(float(header), 60.0)
    return 2.0

3. The "Forget-on-Delete" Invariant in Action

Incident management data is ephemeral: alerts close, schedules rotate, and temporary escalations expire. If an AI memory system retains resolved or deleted alerts forever, retrieval precision degrades.

By configuring:

setattr(source, DOCUMENT_SOURCE_ATTR, "opsgenie")

and tagging resources with:

write_disposition="replace"

Cognee's ingestion engine recognizes when an alert is resolved or deleted upstream. During synchronization, Cognee computes the snapshot delta and triggers automatic orphan cleanup, pruning stale entities and edges from FalkorDB/NetworkX and Qdrant without corrupting existing historical relationships.

Quickstart: SRE Knowledge Graph in 40 Lines of Python

Here is how you can index your active Opsgenie alerts and on-call schedules into Cognee:

import asyncio
import os
import cognee
from cognee_community_connector_opsgenie import opsgenie_source

async def main():
    # 1. Configure the Opsgenie source
    # Filters to open high-priority alerts while syncing active schedules
    source = opsgenie_source(
        api_key=os.environ["OPSGENIE_API_KEY"],
        base_url="https://api.opsgenie.com",
        query="status: open AND priority: P1",
        include_schedules=True,
        include_escalations=True,
    )

    # 2. Add to Cognee memory and build the Knowledge Graph
    print("Ingesting Opsgenie telemetry...")
    await cognee.add(source)

    print("Running Cognify: Extracting SRE entities and building relationships...")
    await cognee.cognify()

    # 3. Query the SRE Memory
    query = "Who is currently on-call for critical P1 database alerts, and what is the escalation path?"
    print(f"\nQuerying Cognee: '{query}'")

    results = await cognee.search(query)
    for result in results:
        print(f"\n[Insight]: {result}")

if __name__ == "__main__":
    asyncio.run(main())

What Happens Behind the Scenes?

During cognee.cognify(), Cognee extracts entity nodes like:

  • Alert("Database Connection Pool Exhausted")
  • Team("SRE-Platform-Team")
  • Person("Jane Doe", role="Primary On-Call")
  • EscalationRule("Step 1 -> Page Jane Doe; Step 2 (5 min) -> Page Platform Lead")

It establishes graph edges (ASSIGNED_TO, ESCALATES_TO, AFFECTS_SERVICE), enabling the LLM to give grounded, deterministic operational answers.

Verification & Code Quality

The connector is verified with a comprehensive offline test harness:

  • 14/14 Unit Tests Passing: Zero live network calls using respx HTTP mocking (tests/test_opsgenie.py).
  • CodeQL CLI Security Audit: 100% clean across 174 rules (python-security-and-quality.qls) with 0 CWE findings.
  • DCO Certified: Verified Developer Certificate of Origin (git commit -s).

Check Out the Code

The Atlassian Opsgenie connector is open for review in the Cognee Community ecosystem:

  • Pull Request: topoteretes/cognee-community#478
  • Upstream Discussion: topoteretes/cognee#5682

Building SRE agents or interested in GraphRAG for operations? Let me know your thoughts or feedback in the comments!

title: Planning a CMS Closed Beta: Test Scenarios for Web Studios
description:
A useful closed beta is not a race to click every control. It is a chance to learn whether a real team can complete a small task, hand it to someone else, and explain what happened when the result differs from expectations.

Morlix CMS is collecting applications from web studios for a future closed beta. Testing has not started, and participation is subject to review and approval. The public release target is March 11, 2027; it may change and is not a beta start date or an invitation deadline.

The exercises below are a preparation framework for studios. They are not an announced beta test protocol, a list of features guaranteed in a future build, or a report of completed participant tests.

Choose a small scenario

Start with a fictional service website: a home page, one service page, and a short news item. Assign a developer, a designer, and an editor to it, even if one person plays several roles. Write down the job each person needs to complete.

For example, an editor wants to change the opening paragraph of a service page, have a colleague review the result, and understand the next step. A useful test asks whether the allowed workflow is clear and whether the result matches expectations. It does not assume a particular approval feature exists.

Before attempting any scenario, read the terms and instructions for the build you actually receive. Only use actions and environments permitted by the project. If a feature is unavailable, mark the scenario as unavailable rather than trying to bypass a restriction.

Capture the starting conditions

A test result becomes more useful when someone else can repeat it. Record the supplied build version, relevant environment, browser, device, assigned permissions, and any configuration choices. If an instruction is unclear, note the exact step and the information needed to proceed.

Use synthetic content and a separate test environment. Do not place a real client's site, personal data, credentials, or private keys into an experimental setup merely because access is available. Any exception requires the actual test rules and the relevant client's agreement.

The live Morlix website already has published pages and a blog with categories and tags. That is evidence about one installation, not a guarantee that every beta participant will receive the same components or configuration.

Four workflow checks worth preparing

Content and handover

If the provided build allows it, prepare a page with headings, a link, and an image. Save the work and check the rendered result. Ask a colleague unfamiliar with the setup to find the content and explain what they would do next.

Compare what happened with the expected outcome. Was the text preserved? Is the link still correct? Can the colleague identify where help is needed? Treat the availability of drafts, publication rights, and review steps as questions for the actual version, not assumptions.

Design across page sizes

Prepare two sample pages and agree on a few visual rules: heading hierarchy, image proportions, and readable spacing. Where permitted, make a small change and compare the output on a phone and a desktop.

Separate a design preference from an interface that is difficult to understand and from a reproducible defect. They need different follow-up, even when a screenshot shows all three.

Components and changes

If the beta rules allow extension testing, record the components in the starting configuration. Change one component at a time, then rerun the same small set of permitted tasks. This makes it easier to identify when a change affects another part of the project.

A single successful combination does not prove compatibility with every theme, extension, server, or future version. Ask which dependencies and update conditions apply to the actual components.

Access and recovery

Create a simple responsibility matrix: who prepares content, who reviews it, and who manages configuration. If the build provides relevant accounts and the rules permit the test, check that each participant can perform their intended actions without gaining unrelated access. Do not try other people's accounts or bypass permissions.

For backups, first agree on the permitted scope. If a recovery test is available, record the initial state, make a safe test change, and restore to an isolated environment following the supplied instructions. Check content, files, and settings only where they are part of the allowed scenario. Creating a backup file alone does not establish that restoration works.

Write feedback that can be reproduced

A concise report can follow five fields:

  1. Goal: what the person was trying to accomplish.
  2. Conditions: build, environment, account permissions, and device, where available.
  3. Steps: the smallest sequence that demonstrates the issue.
  4. Expected and actual result: what you thought would happen and what you observed.
  5. Impact: whether work is blocked, a workaround is needed, or the issue is a smaller inconvenience.

Include an anonymised sample or screenshot only when the test rules allow it and secrets have been removed. An unexpected result may come from an unsupported scenario or an environment setting, so state the observation before suggesting a cause.

For product feedback, describe the need and context. “An editor needs to know who reviewed a change” is more useful than asserting that a particular button must exist. It does not imply that the feature has been promised.

Interpret a successful test carefully

Passing one scenario on one build says little about untested environments. An issue-free limited beta is not proof that there are no security defects. An invitation is not a guarantee that the system is ready for every client or that a particular support arrangement exists.

Before a production decision, studios still need to confirm licensing, component compatibility, data ownership, backup and recovery responsibilities, and agreements with the customer for the actual product and version.

Web studios can apply through morlix.ru and follow Morlix on Telegram for updates. The public release target remains March 11, 2027 and may change. Read the original Russian article.

title: GBase 8a Cluster Maintenance Engineering: Safe Mode Transitions and Service Verification
description:
Enterprise database maintenance requires more than executing administrative commands. A cluster-mode transition must be planned around application dependencies, current cluster health, and the expected operating state.

For supported GBase 8a environments, cluster management tools can help administrators inspect and manage operational modes.

1. Establish the Maintenance Scope

Before maintenance, document:

  • The target cluster or virtual cluster.
  • The reason for the transition.
  • Application write requirements.
  • Active workloads.
  • Expected maintenance duration.
  • Recovery and escalation procedures.

2. Inspect Cluster Health 

gcadmin showcluster

For a supported virtual-cluster deployment:

gcadmin showcluster vc vc1

Confirm that the current state is consistent with the maintenance plan.

3. Execute an Approved Mode Change

For supported GBase 8a releases, a transition to normal mode may use:

gcadmin switchmode normal

A virtual-cluster-specific command may also be supported:

gcadmin switchmode normal vc vc1

These are release-dependent examples. Check the exact syntax, supported source states, permissions, and prerequisites before running them.

4. Verify the Cluster After the Change 

gcadmin showcluster

Then perform application-level validation:

  • Database connectivity.
  • Representative read operations.
  • Authorized write operations.
  • Application connection-pool health.
  • Database and cluster logs.
  • Monitoring and alert status.

5. Maintain an Auditable Change Record

Record the initial cluster state, approved procedure, commands executed, operator, execution time, and final validation results.

Do not assume that a reverse transition is safe in every cluster state.

Conclusion

GBase 8a cluster maintenance should be handled through controlled state transitions and evidence-based verification. A documented runbook helps database teams minimize operational risk and protect application continuity.

title: Turn Any Docs Site Into Clean Markdown for RAG (Python, No Dependencies)
description:
If you're building a RAG chatbot or giving an AI agent "the docs", the first problem is boring: web pages are 80% navigation, footers, cookie banners, and script tags. Feed that raw HTML to an embedding model and your chunks fill up with "Skip to main content" and menu links.

What you want is the main content as Markdown: headings kept (they make great chunk boundaries), code blocks fenced, lists intact, and everything else gone.

The script

Standard library only. It keeps <main> (or role="main"), drops nav/header/footer/aside/script and ARIA navigation landmarks, and converts headings, paragraphs, lists, inline code, and <pre> blocks:

"""Turn a docs page into clean Markdown for RAG, with the standard library only.
Usage: python3 docs_to_markdown.py https://docs.python.org/3/library/json.html > json.md"""
import re
import sys
import urllib.request
from html.parser import HTMLParser

SKIP = {"script", "style", "nav", "header", "footer", "aside", "form", "noscript", "svg"}
HEADINGS = {"h1": "# ", "h2": "## ", "h3": "### ", "h4": "#### "}


class ToMarkdown(HTMLParser):
    def __init__(self):
        super().__init__()
        self.out, self.skip, self.pre = [], 0, False

    def handle_starttag(self, tag, attrs):
        role = dict(attrs).get("role", "")
        if tag in SKIP or role in ("navigation", "banner", "contentinfo"):
            self.skip += 1
        elif self.skip:
            return
        elif tag in HEADINGS:
            self.out.append("\n\n" + HEADINGS[tag])
        elif tag in ("p", "div", "section"):
            self.out.append("\n\n")
        elif tag == "li":
            self.out.append("\n- ")
        elif tag == "pre":
            self.pre = True
            self.out.append("\n\n```

\n")
        elif tag == "code" and not self.pre:
            self.out.append("`")

    def handle_endtag(self, tag):
        if tag in SKIP:
            self.skip = max(0, self.skip - 1)
        elif self.skip:
            return
        elif tag == "pre":
            self.pre = False
            self.out.append("\n```\n")
        elif tag == "code" and not self.pre:
            self.out.append("`")

    def handle_data(self, data):
        if not self.skip:
            self.out.append(data if self.pre else re.sub(r"\s+", " ", data))


url = sys.argv[1]
req = urllib.request.Request(url, headers={"User-Agent": "docs-to-markdown"})
html = urllib.request.urlopen(req, timeout=30).read().decode("utf-8", "replace")
main = re.search(r"<main\b.*?</main>|<div[^>]+role=\"main\".*", html, re.S | re.I)  # prefer the main content
parser = ToMarkdown()
parser.feed(main.group(0) if main else html)
md = re.sub(r"\n{3,}", "\n\n", "".join(parser.out).replace("¶", "")).strip()
print(md)
print(f"\n<!-- {len(md.split())} words from {url} -->", file=sys.stderr)
``{% endraw %}{% raw %}`

Real run (October 2026):

```shell
$ python3 docs_to_markdown.py https://docs.python.org/3/library/json.html > json.md
<!-- 3810 words from https://docs.python.org/3/library/json.html -->
``{% endraw %}{% raw %}`

The output starts like this, with no menus and no breadcrumbs:

```python
# `json` — JSON encoder and decoder

Source code: Lib/json/__init__.py

JSON (JavaScript Object Notation), specified by RFC 7159 ...
``{% endraw %}{% raw %}`

## Why Markdown and not plain text?

- **Headings become chunk boundaries.** Split on `##` and each chunk is about one topic, which retrieves far better than fixed 500-token windows.
- **Code stays fenced.** Your model can tell code from prose.
- **It's compact.** Markdown is much smaller than the HTML it came from, so you spend fewer tokens per page.

## What this script doesn't do (and what bites at scale)

- **Tables and links.** It flattens them. For docs heavy on parameter tables, convert `<table>` to pipe tables and keep `[text](url)` links.
- **Crawling.** One page is easy. A whole docs site needs the sitemap, link-following that stays in scope (only `/docs/v2/`, not the blog), and deduplication.
- **robots.txt.** Be a good citizen and check it before crawling. Also, Python's `urllib.robotparser` mishandles `*` wildcards and rewrites `Disallow: /?` as `Disallow: /`, so test it against real files.
- **JavaScript-rendered docs.** Plain HTTP sees an empty shell. Those need a headless browser.

## The no-code version

I packaged a fuller version (tables, links, nested lists, sitemap plus in-scope crawling, robots.txt, about 2 seconds for 8 pages) as [Website to Markdown on Apify](https://apify.com/kramer_labs/website-to-markdown). Give it a start URL like `https://docs.python.org/3/library/` and get one Markdown record per page, ready for LangChain, LlamaIndex, or your vector store. It costs $2 per 1,000 pages, and failed pages and pages robots.txt disallows are free.

Either way, the script above is yours to copy.

*More free scripts and tools from [Kramer Labs](https://kramer-labs.netlify.app/).*

title: GPT-Live 1 now available on AI Gateway
description:
GPT-Live 1 from OpenAI is now available on AI Gateway.

GPT-Live 1 is a full-duplex voice model and can listen and speak at the same time. Many voice models use turn detection to respond. Full duplex removes that boundary, so a user can pause, interrupt, or add detail while GPT-Live is speaking.

GPT-Live 1 also supports client delegation. Client delegation lets you choose the background model independently from GPT-Live 1. A basic session runs only the voice model. When deeper work is needed, your application can handle delegation-created with any text model on AI Gateway while the conversation continues.

Install AI SDK 7, @ai-sdk/openai 4.0.67 or later, and a WebSocket client:

Simple example without delegation

This starts openai/gpt-live-1 without calling another model. Wait for session-started before sending audio.

Delegate work and keep talking

You can call a text model for GPT Live to delegate to, then return the result on the commentary channel for it to speak. This example uses openai/gpt-5.6-sol, but you can substitute any text model available on AI Gateway:

Your application controls delegated work and its permissions, confirmations, and cancellation. Delegated model requests are billed separately through AI Gateway; voice-session usage continues while they run. These snippets omit WebSocket connection, event parsing, transcript assembly, audio streaming, and shutdown. See the GPT-Live guide in the AI Gateway docs for connection setup, audio streaming, and complete examples. For all audio models on AI Gateway, go to the model list.

title: My open-source text-to-SQL layer is #1 on BIRD Mini-Dev in all three dialects
description:
BIRD Mini-Dev is 500 text-to-SQL questions over 11 databases, in SQLite, PostgreSQL and MySQL versions, scored by whether the query returns the right rows. BIRD keeps the leaderboard and checks the submissions.

schemagate, the Apache-2.0 library I maintain, is now first in all three columns:

schemagate Next entry
SQLite 81.0 75.6
PostgreSQL 72.6 69.0
MySQL 72.4 49.2

The setup is plain: schemagate picks the tables a question needs, the prompt carries only those plus BIRD's column notes, and Claude Opus 5.5 writes one query. No candidate voting and no agent loop. If the query errors, the model sees the error and tries again.

schemagate's main job is access control. It removes the tables the caller may not read before the model sees the schema. A benchmark doesn't test that part, but it shows the filtering doesn't cost accuracy.

What it isn't: the main BIRD board, which uses a hidden test set. Our first test result there was 72.11, and a rerun is pending.

  • Run files and commands: https://github.com/ashishsinha1602/schemagate/tree/main/benchmarks/results/bird_minidev

title: SkillCT: A Multidimensional Benchmark and Execution-Free Baseline for Agent Skill Assessment
description:
arXiv:2610.38147v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Agent skills package instructions, scripts, and resources for specialized tasks and are increasingly distributed through public Web repositories. However, existing skill benchmarks primarily focus on downstream task execution, insufficiently assessing specification quality, behavioral robustness, semantic alignment, and responsibility boundaries. Their reliance on task-specific tools, environments, and repeated executions limits scalability and pre-deployment assessment. To address these challenges, we introduce SkillCT, a benchmark that broadens skill assessment from downstream utility to a multidimensional characterization of skill quality. SkillCT evaluates skills across nine complementary dimensions spanning three aspects: Static Assessment, which captures intrinsic properties of the skill specification; Dynamic Assessment, which measures whether the induced behavior remains stable across backbone models and request variations; and Human-Assisted Assessment, which examines behavior-chain consistency and task granularity. These dimensions provide a broader view of skill quality than execution success. Applying SkillCT to a public skill corpus establishes a reference benchmark for analyzing quality weaknesses and relationships across dimensions. Building on this benchmark, we propose an execution-free quality evaluation baseline that predicts the multidimensional quality profiles of unseen skills by retrieving and leveraging similar reference skills, without executing the skills under evaluation. This reduces token consumption and evaluation time, while preserving consistency with the full assessment. Furthermore, SkillCT-guided optimization improves downstream task success and execution efficiency, demonstrating its value for skill refinement. These findings highlight the effectiveness of SkillCT in supporting scalable skill assessment, optimization, and repository maintenance.

title: Azure's cross-tenant hole got four fixes. The fourth fix reopened the third hole.
description:
Azure's cross-tenant hole got four fixes. The fourth fix reopened the third hole.

Binary Security's "Azure's Weakest Link" series just landed its third installment (published 2026-10-02, on Hacker News' front page today with 255 points), and it reads less like a vulnerability report than a tragicomedy in five acts. One researcher, one Azure subsystem — API Connections, the part of Logic Apps that lets workflows talk to backends — five critical elevation-of-privilege vulnerabilities, and $200,000 in bounties. That is $40,000 per critical on average, which is either a generous program or a very leaky abstraction. The post suggests it is both.

The architecture that makes it possible

The design is the vulnerability, and the author says so plainly. A Logic App queries a shared Azure API Management instance, which checks the connector's swagger definition, then swaps the caller's token for the token configured on the backend connection, then finishes the call against the backend. The backend can be anything: a Key Vault, an Azure SQL database, Jira, Salesforce.

The catch is the middle step. The APIM instance that performs the token swap is reached through ARM, and ARM, as a resource manager, effectively has access to everything. So if you can trick the calling service into operating on a different connection than your own, you spend the victim's token on the victim's backend. The only thing standing in the way is input validation bolted onto various layers — and, as the post demonstrates five times, bolted-on validation is exactly the kind that misses edge cases.

The five acts

# Primitive What it got the attacker
1 DynamicInvoke path traversal (part 2) Cross-tenant Key Vault secret read. Four ../ segments, percent-encoded as %2e%2e, walked from the attacker's connection to the victim's: path/%2e%2e/.../apim/keyvault/<victim-id>/secrets/victimsecret/value. Response: HTTP 200, secret value dontreadme.
2 Undocumented sibling endpoints After Microsoft restricted DynamicInvoke's paths, the researcher found four more functions sitting next to it in the extracted Logic App host code — DynamicList and friends, reachable by swapping the name in the URI. Same traversal, now a cross-tenant SQL write: Insert INTO MySecrets VALUES ('NewEvilSecrets', 3) against the victim's database.
3 host.api.RuntimeUrl swap Consumption Logic Apps create Version 1 connections, and unlike dedicated-host Standard apps, they have no managed identity to authorize — so every Consumption app implicitly reaches every V1 connection, gated only by validation. The host.api.RuntimeUrl parameter let a workflow keep the validated victim connection reference but execute against a completely different runtime URL, as long as it ended in azure-apihub.net. The victim's secret came back.
4 RuntimeUrl path traversal Microsoft fixed #3 with an exact-match check: the runtime URL must equal the expected endpoint for the referenced connection. Sane — except the check ran before path normalization. A URI that matched the expected prefix string normalized to somewhere else. Same result, again.
5 The regression When Microsoft fixed #4's traversal, the original RuntimeUrl path was no longer validated at all. Attack #3 worked again, with the same screenshots. The fix for the bypass re-opened the original hole.

Four fixes shipped. One of them undid an earlier one. The final state, per the author, is that the dynamic endpoints are simply blocked and no other mitigations seem to be in place — "if these endpoints ever become accessible again, I would assume they would be vulnerable."

I rebuilt the mechanism, not the exploit

I have no Azure account in this story and I did not touch a live tenant. But the core mechanism — validate the raw value, resolve the normalized one — is twenty lines of Python, and it is worth seeing because it is the same bug wearing two costumes:

from urllib.parse import unquote, urlparse
import posixpath

def naive_validator_ok(raw_path: str) -> bool:
    return "../" not in raw_path  # the slap-dash fix

def resolve(base_path: str, raw_path: str) -> str:
    return posixpath.normpath(posixpath.join(base_path, unquote(raw_path)))

case1 passes raw validator: True
case1 traversal segments: 4
case1 resolved: /apim/keyvault/fd8d0f4f4069495991ccb4974f96a1ed/secrets/victimsecret/value
case1 escapes own connection: True
case2 passes prefix validator: True
case2 normalized path: /apim/apim/sql/88d28f5ff7b642cfb91df184938d074c
case2 still under expected endpoint: False
control passes validator: True
control stays inside: True
bounty per critical on average: $40,000

The validator sees %2e%2e and shrugs — there is no literal ../ in the string. The resolver decodes first, then normalizes, and walks out of the connection. Same shape in case 2: a prefix check on the raw URL passes, normalization moves it. The control case stays inside, which is the point: the check is not wrong on honest input. It is wrong exactly on the input an attacker sends, which is the only input a security check exists for.

The lesson that survives all five acts

Every one of these bugs is a check running at the wrong layer of abstraction: on the raw string instead of the decoded one, on the pre-normalization URI instead of the resolved one, on the referenced connection instead of the executed runtime. And the series' real punchline is organizational: the researcher deliberately reported DynamicList alone first, hoping Microsoft would fix the whole family — and got a blocklist. He reported the RuntimeUrl traversal and got a fix that regressed the previous fix.

"Validate what you resolve, not what you receive" is the kind of sentence that sounds obvious until you count how many fixes it took to not implement it. Four. And the fifth vulnerability was the fourth fix.

Sources: Binary Security, "Azure's Weakest Link — Five Full Cross-Tenant Compromises" (2026-10-02), including the DynamicInvoke and DynamicList payloads and the $200,000 total; my own check-vs-resolve model above (2026-10-30). All five vulnerabilities are reported fixed; the mechanism demo uses no live Azure service.

title: FACTS-MAS: A Multi-Agent Architecture for Adaptive Forecasting from Heterogeneous Evidence
description:
arXiv:2610.38225v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Real-world forecasting often requires integrating heterogeneous evidence whose predictive value varies across horizons, operating regimes, and domains. We introduce FACTS-MAS, a domain-agnostic multi-agent forecasting framework that decomposes evidence into specialized channels for temporal dynamics, exogenous context, seasonality, structural information, and discrete events. Each agent generates an independently testable forecast through a common interface, while leakage-safe historical validation measures its predictive skill relative to a naive reference. These skill estimates are used to weight and combine agent forecasts, so that uninformative evidence is either removed or downweighted rather than forced to participate. A calibration procedure selects domain-specific constant means based on historical validation folds. We evaluate FACTS-MAS on weekly for-sale housing inventory from Zillow and weekly unemployment insurance claims from FRED, for 15 U.S. metropolitan areas at 4-, 8-, and 13-week forecasting horizons. Our method outperforms both a naive last-value forecast method and the TimesFM foundation model. However, a factor-adjusted exponential smoothing model performs as well as the fused forecast. The evidence therefore supports FACTS-MAS as a systematic protocol for testing, calibrating, and recomposing evidence channels before assembling them into the strongest single model for a specific application domain. Code, data, and results are available at https://github.com/Madumita24/FACTS-MAS.

title: İnternet yokken kartla ödeme nasıl onaylanır?
description:
İnternet ya da elektrik gidince marketteki POS bankaya ulaşamaz. Bugün çoğu yerde kartla ödeme orada biter ve kasiyer nakit olup olmadığını sorar. Mastercard bunu Avrupa'da değiştiriyor: 8 Ekim'de duyurduğu kurala göre Şubat 2027'den sonra basılan her Mastercard kartı, Mayıs 2027'den sonra takılan her yeni POS da bağlantı yokken ödeme alabilecek (The Paypers).

Çevrimdışı ödeme (offline payment), POS'un o an bankaya soramadığı kart ödemesi. Bu adla iki ayrı şey anılıyor: kartın çipinin ödemeyi kendisi onaylaması ve POS'un işlemi saklayıp bağlantı gelince bankaya sorması. Mastercard'ın kuralı birincisi. Aradaki fark, para yetmediğinde açığın kimde kalacağını belirliyor.

Diyagram: Kesintiden kurala zaman çizelgesi. Nisan 2025'te İspanya ve Portekiz'de elektrik kesintisi. Ekim 2026'da Mastercard çevrimdışı ödeme kuralını duyurdu. Şubat 2027'den itibaren yeni basılan kartlar, Mayıs 2027'den itibaren yeni takılan POS'lar çevrimdışı ödemeyi destekleyecek.

28 Nisan 2025'te İspanya ve Portekiz'de elektrik kesildi. Mastercard kuralı 8 Ekim 2026'da duyurdu. Şubat 2027'den sonra basılan kartlar, Mayıs 2027'den sonra takılan ya da değiştirilen POS'lar bağlantısız ödeme alabilecek.

Kural nereden çıktı?

28 Nisan 2025'te İspanya ve Portekiz'de elektrik kesildi. Mastercard'a göre o gün yaklaşık 55 milyon kişi dijital ödeme yapamadı. Danimarka, İsveç, Estonya ve Letonya'da çevrimdışı ödeme zaten kullanılıyor; Letonya'daki bir fırtınada jeneratörle çalışan dükkânlarda kartla ödeme sürmüş (Electronic Payments International).

Yeni kural bunu Avrupa'nın geneline yayıyor. POS tarafı bir gecede değişmeyecek; dükkânlar cihazlarını yeniledikçe yayılacak.

Kart kendisi onaylayınca

Kartın çipi küçük bir bilgisayar. Ödeme sırasında POS çipe tutarı ve kendi kontrollerinin sonucunu verir, çip de üç cevaptan birini döner: onay (TC), "bankaya sor" (ARQC) ya da ret (AAC). Normal bir günde çip neredeyse her zaman "bankaya sor" der ve kararı banka verir.

Bağlantı yokken bu yol kapalı. Burada devreye giren, çipli kartların ödeme standardı EMV'nin bağlantısız onayı; sektörde adı offline EMV. Karar, bankanın kartı basarken çipe yazdığı kurallara kalıyor: PIN doğru mu, tutar çevrimdışı limitin içinde mi, kart art arda kaç kez bankaya sorulmadan kullanılmış. Hepsi tamamsa çip işlemi imzalayıp onaylıyor. Bu imza, bankanın işlemi sonradan gördüğünde gerçekten o karttan geldiğini doğrulamasını sağlıyor.

Diyagram: Bağlantı yokken onayı çip verir. POS bankaya ulaşamıyor ve tutarı çipe soruyor. Çip, bankanın önceden yazdığı kurallara bakıyor: PIN doğru mu, tutar çevrimdışı limitin içinde mi, art arda kaçıncı bağlantısız işlem. Üç cevaptan birini veriyor: onay (TC, çip işlemi imzalar), bankaya sor (ARQC, bağlantı olmadığı için yapılamaz) ya da ret (AAC).

Normal günde çip neredeyse her zaman "bankaya sor" der. Bağlantı yokken bu yol kapalı; karar, bankanın kartı basarken çipe yazdığı kurallara kalır.

Mastercard'ın kuralında harcama limiti çipte duruyor ve onu kartın bankası belirliyor. Tek işlemde üst sınır 200 euro. Limit çipte olduğu için kart hangi POS'a takılırsa takılsın harcama aynı sayaçtan düşüyor; iki ayrı markette art arda alışveriş yapıp limiti ikiye katlamak mümkün değil.

Çipin bilmediği tek şey hesaptaki para.

Bakiye yetmezse işlem yine onaylanmış olur ve bağlantı gelince takasa gider. Açık bankada kalır. Limiti bankanın koyması da bu yüzden: ne kadar risk alacağına kendisi karar veriyor.

POS saklayıp sonra sorunca

İkinci yolun adı store and forward (sakla ve ilet). Burada çip yine "bankaya sor" der. POS soramayınca işlemi saklar, ekranda kabul gösterir ve bağlantı gelince normal onay isteğini gönderir. Yani o anda kimse onay vermemiştir, karar yalnızca ertelenmiştir (offline EMV ile farkı).

Banka saatler sonra işlemi yetersiz bakiye ya da kapalı hesap yüzünden reddedebilir. Satıcı ürünü çoktan vermiştir. Adyen'in dokümanı bunu açıkça yazıyor: çevrimdışı alınan ödemelerde başarısız tahsilat ve itiraz riski satıcıda (Adyen). Sağlayıcıların bu yolda tutar, adet ve süre sınırı koyması bundan.

Backend'den bakınca bu, idempotency yazısındaki "bankaya iletildi" durumuna benziyor: ödeme alınmış görünüyor ama sonucunu henüz kimse bilmiyor. Farkı, burada ürünün çoktan kapıdan çıkmış olması.

Risk kimde kalıyor?

Diyagram: Çevrimdışı ödemenin iki yolu. Çip onaylar (offline EMV): kararı çip bankanın kurallarıyla verir, banka sonradan reddedemez, para yetmezse açık bankada ve limitle sınırlı kalır. POS saklar (store and forward): o anda kimse onay vermez, POS kabul gösterir; banka saatler sonra reddedebilir ve açık satıcıda kalır.

İkisi de kasada "onaylandı" gösterebilir. Farkı, para yetmediğinde ortaya çıkar.

Çevrimdışı EMV'de risk bankanın çizdiği limitle sınırlı. Çip PIN'i kendisi doğruladığı için PIN'i bilinmeyen çalıntı bir kart da işe yaramıyor. Store and forward'da sınırı ödeme sağlayıcısı koyuyor ama bedeli satıcı ödüyor. Kasadaki ekran iki durumda da "onaylandı" diyebilir.

Türkiye'nin bu kurala dahil olup olmadığını duyurulardan çıkaramadım. Haberler "Avrupa" diyor ve ülke listesi vermiyor.

Bu yazı ilk olarak huseyinbozdemir.com'da yayımlandı.

title: Rust won't save your agent from a double charge
description:
An agent sends a payment request. The provider accepts it, the connection drops before the response arrives, the worker times out, the orchestrator retries. The customer is charged twice, and a Rust rewrite would not have prevented it.

Rust's ownership model removes use-after-free bugs and data races in safe code. It can't know whether a remote API finished an operation before the network failed. That takes durable state, idempotency and a recovery protocol that separates safe retries (a read-only search) from operations that need reconciliation (a payment).

Raw speed is a weak argument too. In an illustrative run of 4 model calls at about 800 ms, 6 tool calls at about 150 ms and 100 ms of orchestration, removing orchestration completely saves about 2.4%.

Where Rust earns its place is concurrency: how many agent sessions one worker sustains in a fixed memory budget at acceptable tail latency. Memory safety, concurrency correctness, distributed execution correctness. Rust covers the first, helps with the second, and leaves the third to your architecture.

Full piece, with the state store, queue, worker and recovery design: Why Rust might be the most important language for the next era of AI
