title: Think, act, ask: one agent run through Cuelark's 29 agent components
description:
The map told you where each piece goes. This one follows a single run, moment by moment, and shows the code that renders each one.

Two days ago we drew the map of an agent interface: seven places every agent app shares, and which component belongs in each. That answered where.

This post answers when, and how. An agent run is a sequence of moments: someone asks, the agent thinks, it acts, it stops to get an approval, it answers, and someone who cares about cost or bugs observes the run afterwards. Cuelark UI's agent kit is 29 React components for shadcn/ui, grouped by exactly those moments.

We'll follow one run through all six, with the real props for every component. The run is fictional (file names, counts and timings are made up for the example), but every API is the one in the registry.

The run: "Invoice totals are a cent off for EU customers. Find out why and fix it."

Setup

One line in components.json:

{
  "registries": {
    "@cuelark": "https://ui.cuelark.com/r/{name}.json"
  }
}

Then install by name, for example npx shadcn@latest add @cuelark/reasoning @cuelark/tool @cuelark/plan. Each component lands in components/ui/ as source you own. The installation guide covers the by-URL route and the shadcn MCP server.

1. Ask

Prompt Input · Queue · Model Selector (and Suggestions)

<PromptInput
  status={running ? "streaming" : "idle"}
  onSubmit={({ text, files }) => send(text, files)}
  onStop={stop}
  toolbar={<ModelSelector models={models} value={model} onValueChange={setModel} />}
/>

status="streaming" is the one prop that matters most: it swaps Send for Stop and binds Esc. The toolbar slot is where Model Selector lives; it's a compact pill that opens a searchable list grouped by provider, with each model's context window.

Thirty seconds in, the user remembers credit notes. The agent is busy, so the follow-up waits:

<Queue items={queued} onItemsChange={setQueued} />

Alt+↑/↓ reorders, × removes, and the agent takes items one at a time.

Which one when: if your agent answers in two seconds, skip Queue. If you only have one model, skip Model Selector. Prompt Input is never optional.

2. Think

Reasoning · Chain of Thought · Task

The model starts thinking. Stream it, then let it get out of the way:

<Reasoning streaming={isThinking}>{reasoningText}</Reasoning>

When streaming flips to false, it folds to "Thought for 6s". Omit duration and it measures itself.

Once there's an approach, named steps read better than raw thought:

<ChainOfThought title="Tracking down the rounding error">
  <ChainOfThoughtStep label="Searched for tax calculation" />
  <ChainOfThoughtStep label="Read src/tax.ts and src/invoice.ts" />
  <ChainOfThoughtStep status="active" label="Checking EU VAT rounding rules" />
  <ChainOfThoughtStep status="pending" label="Propose a fix and run tests" />
</ChainOfThought>

Steps default to "complete", so you only mark the active and pending ones.

Which one when: three components, three shapes of thinking.

  • Reasoning for free text the model produced. You don't control its structure.
  • Chain of Thought for steps your orchestrator names, where order matters.
  • Task for a checklist with a progress bar, where order doesn't: <Task title="Migrate invoices" items={[{ label: "Write helper", status: "done" }]} />.

A common mistake is rendering orchestrator steps inside Reasoning. Then the one thing the user wants to scan is in the faded window they've learned to ignore.

3. Act

Tool · Subagent · Terminal · File Diff · Test Results

The agent searches the code and fetches the VAT guidance:

<Tool name="search_code" status="success" input={{ query: "roundTax" }} output={matches} duration={0.8} />
<Tool name="web_fetch" status="running" input={{ url: vatGuideUrl }} />

status runs "pending" → "running" → "success" or "error". Keep name as the real tool name, not a friendly label. People learn web_fetch in one run, and the real name is what they'll paste into a bug report.

Between calls there's sometimes a beat with nothing to inspect. That's not a Tool; it's a status line:

<TextShimmer>Comparing rounding modes…</TextShimmer>

Text Shimmer is the kit's status line for "doing something right now": CSS-only, and plain muted text under reduced motion.

Then the agent hands the tests to a helper:

<Subagent name="test-runner" task="Run the invoice suite" status="running" activity="Running vitest…">
  <Terminal title="vitest" lines={output} streaming={testsRunning} />
</Subagent>

The sub-agent's own transcript sits on an indented rail inside it. When it's finished, set status="done" and pass duration. Once the run completes, swap the console for structure:

<TestResults
  suites={[{ name: "invoice", tests: [
    { name: "rounds EU totals once", status: "pass" },
    { name: "keeps US line rounding", status: "pass" },
  ] }]}
/>

A suite with a failure opens itself, failing assertion under the test.

And the change itself:

<FileDiff
  filename="src/tax.ts"
  lines={[
    { type: "context", content: "export function roundTax(items: LineItem[]) {" },
    { type: "remove", content: "  return items.map((i) => round(i.tax)).reduce(sum, 0);" },
    { type: "add", content: "  return round(items.map((i) => i.tax).reduce(sum, 0));" },
    { type: "context", content: "}" },
  ]}
  onAccept={apply}
  onReject={discard}
/>

Unchanged runs fold after six lines (foldAfter), and the header records Accept or Reject.

Which one when:

  • Terminal is the live process; Test Results is the verdict. Show Terminal while it runs, Test Results when it's done. Most apps show both, stacked.
  • File Diff is a decision; a plain Code Block is just code. If you want a yes or no, it's a diff.
  • Subagent whenever a different agent did the work, even a short one. Nesting is the only thing that keeps "who did this?" answerable.

4. Approve

Plan · Confirmation · Checkpoint

Before touching code, the agent proposes a plan:

<Plan
  steps={[
    { label: "Round the invoice total once in roundTax" },
    { label: "Call it after summing in invoice.ts" },
    { label: "Run the invoice suite" },
    { label: "Open a draft pull request" },
  ]}
  onApprove={run}
  onReject={cancel}
  autoRun={10}
/>

autoRun={10} drains a ring on Run; the plan starts unless someone cancels. We use it for low-stakes plans in trusted workspaces and leave it off everywhere else. visible (default 4) sets how many steps show before folding; shortcuts={false} frees ⌘Enter and Esc if your app needs them.

Later the agent wants to rewrite stored totals on staging. One action, real side effects:

<Confirmation
  risk="high"
  title="Recalculate 214 staging invoices"
  description="Rewrites stored totals with the new rounding."
  command="pnpm tsx scripts/recalc-invoices.ts --env=staging"
  onApprove={execute}
  onDeny={skip}
/>

risk="high" turns approve into press-and-hold. The command is shown verbatim, so what you approve is what runs.

And before the diff is applied, a way back:

<Checkpoint label="Before rounding fix" time="14:02" onRestore={restore} />

Which one when: Plan approves intent across steps. Confirmation approves one action. Checkpoint isn't an approval at all; it's the undo you place right before anything you might regret. Approving a plan doesn't remove the need for a Checkpoint; they answer different questions. (For reloads, both Plan and Confirmation render past decisions as receipts. We covered that in the map post, so we won't repeat it here.)

5. Answer

Streaming Text · Inline Citation · Sources · Artifact · Branch

The answer streams:

<StreamingText text={answer} streaming={answering} />

New chunks fade up out of a slight blur; text already on screen never moves.

The claim about VAT gets its evidence right next to it:

<p>
  For this invoice type, VAT is rounded on the total, not per line
  <InlineCitation index={1} source={{ title: guideTitle, url: vatGuideUrl, excerpt: quote }} />.
</p>
<Sources sources={[{ title: guideTitle, url: vatGuideUrl }, { title: "src/tax.ts", url: fileUrl }]} />

If the agent also wrote a summary for the finance team, that's too big for a message:

<Artifact kind="Document" title="Rounding fix: summary" onClose={close} onDownload={download}>
  {summary}
</Artifact>

If the user regenerates the answer, keep the old one:

<Branch versions={[firstAnswer, secondAnswer]} onIndexChange={setIndex} />

Which one when:

  • Inline Citation and Sources are a pair, not alternatives. A Sources list on its own makes people guess which source backs which sentence.
  • Artifact for anything people will read full screen or download; the message just points at it.
  • Branch only when there really are versions. Don't show "1 / 1".

6. Observe

Context Meter · Trace Waterfall

This moment isn't for every user. It's for whoever pays the bill or fixes the bug.

<ContextMeter used={84000} max={200000} cost={0.42} breakdown={{ input, output, cached, reasoning }} />

A ring that warms from ink to amber to red as the context fills, with the token breakdown and cost on hover. (Figures above are example values.)

And the whole run on one timeline:

<TraceWaterfall
  spans={[{
    id: "run", name: "fix-eu-rounding", kind: "agent", start: 0, end: 41,
    children: [
      { id: "m1", name: "plan", kind: "llm", start: 0, end: 6, tokens: 1840 },
      { id: "t1", name: "search_code", kind: "tool", start: 6, end: 6.8 },
      { id: "t2", name: "web_fetch", kind: "tool", start: 7, end: 9.5 },
      { id: "sa", name: "test-runner", kind: "agent", start: 22, end: 39,
        children: [{ id: "t3", name: "vitest", kind: "tool", start: 23, end: 38 }] },
    ],
  }]}
/>

kind is "agent", "llm" or "tool". start and end are seconds from the start of the run; leave end off and the span grows live. Set error on a span and it turns red. Hover any bar for duration, tokens and cost. You can see it with real interaction on the Trace Waterfall page.

Which one when: Chain of Thought is the user's view of progress, inside the turn. Trace Waterfall is the developer's view of the whole run, in the run header or a debug panel. If you put a waterfall in a consumer chat thread, you've built a dashboard nobody asked for.

The whole turn, composed

Everything above, as one assistant turn. Data loading is yours; every prop is real.

export function AgentTurn({ run }: { run: Run }) {
  return (
    <Message from="assistant">
      <MessageContent>
        {/* think */}
        <Reasoning streaming={run.thinking}>{run.reasoning}</Reasoning>
        <ChainOfThought title={run.title}>
          {run.steps.map((s) => (
            <ChainOfThoughtStep key={s.label} status={s.status} label={s.label} />
          ))}
        </ChainOfThought>

        {/* act */}
        {run.tools.map((t) => (
          <Tool key={t.id} name={t.name} status={t.status} input={t.input} output={t.output} duration={t.duration} />
        ))}

        {/* approve */}
        <Plan steps={run.plan} onApprove={run.approve} onReject={run.reject} defaultState={run.planDecision} />

        {/* act, delegated */}
        <Subagent name="test-runner" task="Run the invoice suite" status={run.tests.status} duration={run.tests.duration}>
          <TestResults suites={run.tests.suites} />
        </Subagent>

        {/* approve, then act */}
        <Checkpoint label="Before rounding fix" time={run.checkpointAt} onRestore={run.restore} />
        <FileDiff filename="src/tax.ts" lines={run.diff} onAccept={run.apply} onReject={run.discard} />

        {/* answer */}
        <StreamingText text={run.answer} streaming={run.answering} />
        <Sources sources={run.sources} />
      </MessageContent>
    </Message>
  );
}

Outside the thread, the observe moment:

<header className="flex items-center justify-end gap-3">
  <ContextMeter used={run.tokens.used} max={run.tokens.max} cost={run.cost} />
</header>
<TraceWaterfall spans={run.trace} />

Read the comments top to bottom and you get the run: think, act, approve, act, answer. The order of components is the story of the run. If your JSX reads in an order that doesn't match what happened, your users will be confused in the same place.

What this run taught us

  • One moment, one component. The kit has three ways to show thinking because there are three shapes of thinking. Pick by shape, not by looks.
  • Defaults are compact, errors aren't. A failed Tool and a failing test suite open themselves. Everything else waits for a click.
  • Approvals come in three kinds. Intent (Plan), action (Confirmation), and the way back (Checkpoint). Most apps ship only the middle one.
  • Observe lives outside the thread. Context Meter and Trace Waterfall are for the people who pay for or debug the run.

Try it

The fastest way to learn the kit is to take one apart. On the live agent demos, hover any part of the coding, research or data agent and it names itself; click the tag to open its page and copy the code.

Cuelark UI is free and open source (MIT): github.com/cuelark/ui.

FAQ

What are AI agent UI components? Components for the moments of an agent run: asking, thinking, acting, approving, answering and observing. A chat kit covers asking and answering; an agent kit covers the four in between.

How many agent components does Cuelark UI have? 29. By moment: ask (Prompt Input, Queue, Model Selector, Suggestions), think (Reasoning, Chain of Thought, Task, Text Shimmer), act (Tool, Subagent, Terminal, File Diff, Test Results, Stack Trace, Code Block, File Tree, Web Preview), approve (Plan, Confirmation, Checkpoint), answer (Conversation, Message, Streaming Text, Inline Citation, Sources, Artifact, Branch) and observe (Context Meter, Trace Waterfall).

Do they work with the Vercel AI SDK? Yes, or with any stream. They take plain props such as status, input, output, steps and spans.

Are they shadcn/ui components? Yes. They install as source with the shadcn CLI and use your Tailwind CSS v4 theme tokens.

title: GAAC: Lossless KV Compression for Bandwidth-Efficient LLM Inference on Personal Devices
description:
arXiv:2610.38210v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Weight-only, lossy quantization substantially reduces the storage and memory requirements for serving large language models (LLMs), but the growing key-value (KV) cache remains a bottleneck for long-context inference on personal devices. We present Group-Adaptive Additive Codec (GAAC), a lossless KV compression and serving system that exploits exponent redundancy to reduce storage and accelerate attention without introducing KV approximation. GAAC encodes BF16 exponents using calibrated per-channel base-plus-offset codes over contiguous ranges. GAAC adapts code widths across small groups while preserving KV values bit-for-bit. A fused attention kernel reconstructs KV tiles on the fly, avoiding full-cache decompression. Block-wise compression and fixed-capacity slots support incremental cache updates and paged serving. Across five tested models, GAAC achieves 1.405-1.407$\times$ lossless BF16 KV compression. We also study compression performance on low-precision tensors FP8 E4M3 caches ( 1.09-1.14$\times$) and E5M2 caches (1.25-1.30$\times$). On NVIDIA DGX Spark, GAAC accelerates decode attention at a 64K-token context by 1.19-1.27$\times$ and end-to-end W4A16 decode steps by 1.04-1.15$\times$. In serving, it reduces resident KV memory by approximately 26% and increases aggregate throughput by 13-29% under comparable KV-memory budgets. On Apple M4, GAAC achieves 1.02-1.25$\times$ attention speedups, demonstrating portability beyond NVIDIA GPUs.

title: Two sector taxonomies, 20 ids against 4, and the one word they share means the opposite thing in each
description:
CogniPrep asks two questions after signup: which
employer you are applying to, and which role. The role answer comes from a
closed list that lives in one file of 1,001 lines, and the shape of that list
is worth a post on its own, because the same word in it means two different
jobs depending on which module is reading.

Counted by importing the module rather than grepping it:

sectors:                     20
role ids:                    140   (121 hand-written, 19 generated)
sectors that have roles:      19
keyword strings:             725   (626 distinct)
roles with no keywords:        0
largest sector:               12 roles
source file:              32,421 bytes
the same data as JSON:    22,568 bytes

The 19 generated role ids are a catch-all appended per sector by a function
rather than written out nineteen times, so the id convention cannot drift:

function withOtherRole(sector: OnboardingSector): OnboardingSector {
  if (sector.roles.length === 0) return sector;
  return {
    ...sector,
    roles: [...sector.roles, { id: `${sector.id}-other`, label: 'Other / not listed', ... }],
  };
}

That guard in the first line is the thread I want to pull.

The sector is never asked. It is derived

The flow used to be two screens, sector then role inside it. It is now one,
because a candidate knows the title from the job advert and not our category
names. The sectors still exist, to group the roles and to give each search
result its second line, and the stored sector is whatever the picked role
belongs to:

/** The sector a role belongs to, which is how the sector answer is derived. */
export function getSectorIdForRole(roleId: string | null | undefined): string | null {
  return getRoleById(roleId)?.sector.id ?? null;
}

export function isValidSectorRolePair(sectorId: string, roleId: string): boolean {
  return ROLE_BY_ID.get(roleId)?.sector.id === sectorId;
}

The pair is validated together rather than each half independently, because a
client can otherwise post a valid sector and a valid role from a different
sector and produce a row whose two halves disagree. That is the whole reason
the second function exists.

Matching runs in the browser against the in-memory list. There is no search
endpoint, which is the stated trade in the file's own header: 22 KB of JSON is
cheaper to ship once than a round trip per keystroke, and it keeps the search
instant. All three importers are client components, so the list does ship.

The 20th sector has no roles, so the search cannot return it

19 of the 20 sectors carry roles. The last one is this:

{
  id: 'other',
  label: 'Something else / still deciding',
  keywords: ['not sure', 'undecided', 'unsure', 'dont know', 'other', 'open', 'anything'],
  roles: [],
},

It exists for the candidate who has not decided yet. Every result the ranker
emits, though, is emitted from inside a loop over sector.roles, so a sector
with no roles can never produce one. Running the real search function over a
few queries:

not sure     8 results
other        8 results
open         8 results   (Fintech & Payments, Learning & Development, ...)
undecided    0 results
unsure       0 results
dont know    0 results
anything     0 results

Four of its own seven keywords return nothing at all, and a fifth matches
unrelated roles on the substring. The two that behave return this:

Other / not listed (Banking & Finance)
Other / not listed (Accounting & Professional Services)
Other / not listed (Consulting & Strategy)
Other / not listed (Technology & Software)
... (8 of the 19 generated catch-alls, cut off by the result limit)

Eight rows with the same label, differing only in the second line, which is a
worse answer than none. The candidate who types "undecided" into a flow
with no skip button gets an empty list; the one who types "not sure" gets asked
to pick which sector they are not sure about.

The fix is not more keywords. It is that a bucket with no roles has no business
being in a list that is searched by role, so either it gets a single role of
its own or the escape hatch does the job instead. The escape hatch already
exists and is the sentinel id the free-text answer uses, capped at 80
characters, and isValidRoleId deliberately returns false for it.

20 ids in, 4 out

The other taxonomy is lib/sectors.ts, and it has four members:

export type Sector = 'engineering' | 'finance' | 'corporate' | 'public-sector';

These are the practice-content sectors: interview question pools, marking
profiles, exercise tags. One function joins the two taxonomies, and most of it
is a comment explaining what not to do:

 * The two taxonomies share a word but not a meaning, which is the trap here.
 * Practice 'engineering' is the technical *tech* repertoire - software, data,
 * architecture - so the onboarding family that feeds it is 'technology'
 * ("Technology & Software"), NOT the identically named onboarding
 * 'engineering' ("Engineering & Manufacturing": mechanical, civil, aerospace).
 * Matching on the shared word is exactly backwards: it hands a civil engineer
 * the system-design and model-validation content and marks a software
 * engineer against the corporate values/strengths rubric.

So technology maps to engineering, twelve families map to corporate,
finance and accounting map to finance, public-sector and healthcare
map to public-sector, and two of the twenty map to nothing:

    // Listed rather than left to fall through, so the absence of a mapping
    // reads as a decision and not an omission someone should "fix" back to
    // 'engineering' on the strength of the shared name.
    case 'engineering':
    case 'energy':
      return null;

null is a first-class answer here, not a failure: callers treat it as the
"General" session, drawn from the untagged pool with every sector still one tap
away. A confident wrong preselection reads as the product having misunderstood
your answer, which is more expensive than no preselection at all.

The fourth onboarding question used to be study level. It is gone, for the
reason written where it used to be, and the column it wrote is still there:

// Study level ("are you an undergraduate, apprentice, school leaver…?") used to be
// the fourth question. It is gone: it was never used to pick or difficulty-tune a
// test, and every extra screen loses people before the two answers that do matter.
// The `study_level` column stays in the table for rows the earlier flow wrote.

Two writers still set it, both to null.

See it

The four-member taxonomy is on a public page.
cogniprep.app/assessment-centre-practice
renders all four with their blurbs, and the Engineering one is the trap in
plain sight:

curl -s https://cogniprep.app/assessment-centre-practice \
  | grep -o "Technical graduate scheme scenarios[^<]*"
# Technical graduate scheme scenarios for software engineers, architects and data
# scientists - incident triage, design and build-vs-buy trade-offs, ...

Software engineers, architects and data scientists, under a heading that says
Engineering. A mechanical engineer reading that page is being shown the content
the mapping function refuses to give them, and the refusal is the right call.
cogniprep.app/interview names the same four
in prose, and section 8 of
cogniprep.app/privacy is the 20-sector
taxonomy described from the other end: a role from a fixed list, 80 characters
if you type your own, and the sector we work out rather than ask for.

title: Ghostlog: a local séance for dead data pipelines
description:
This is a submission for the Hacktoberfest Open-Source AI Challenge Week 4: Ghost in the Machine

What I Built

Every data team has a graveyard. It holds the nightly job nobody remembers writing, the .sql file in legacy/, and the cron log that just stops one night in March. Someone always asks what that job did, and the person who knew left two reorgs ago.

Ghostlog holds a séance for that job. You point it at the remains, either an old cron or Airflow log or a deprecated SQL file, and it:

  1. reads the remains: the job's name, how many nights it ran, its usual start time, every SQL statement it executed, and the error that ended it;
  2. rebuilds the job's table lineage with sqlglot (raw.orders -> stg.orders -> mart.daily_revenue);
  3. asks Gemma, running locally through Ollama, to let the job speak in the first person;
  4. carves an ofrenda-style tombstone page with the job's years, an epitaph, its testimony, and its lineage.

It fits Día de los Muertos: the job gets remembered properly, and the next person who inherits the warehouse gets the context it took with it.

Demo

Summoning a nightly ETL job that died on 2025-03-14 when an upstream column disappeared. This is real Gemma output (gemma3:4b on a CPU-only Linux machine, about 8 seconds):

The tombstone it wrote:

A 60-second narrated walkthrough of a real run, summoning the job with Gemma and then opening its tombstone:

Live tombstone: nightmoose.github.io/ghostlog/sample/tombstone.html. All the samples are at nightmoose.github.io/ghostlog.

The raw transcripts and generated pages are committed in docs/sample/, including one run against a deprecated SQL file with a CTE and one run with --offline.

Code

nightmoose / ghostlog

A local séance for dead data pipelines: Gemma via Ollama + sqlglot lineage, fully offline.

Ghostlog

A local séance for dead data pipelines.

Point Ghostlog at the remains of a retired job (an old cron or Airflow log, or a deprecated .sql file) and it summons the job's ghost. Ghostlog reads the remains, rebuilds the job's table lineage with sqlglot and asks Gemma, running locally through Ollama, to let the job speak for itself in the first person Then it carves an ofrenda-style tombstone page you can open in any browser.

Everything runs on your own machine. Your logs and SQL stay on your laptop, and it keeps working with the Wi-Fi off.

Built for the DEV Hacktoberfest Open-Source AI Challenge, Week 4: Ghost in the Machine.

Quick start

git clone https://github.com/nightmoose/ghostlog
cd ghostlog
python -m venv .venv && . .venv/bin/activate
pip install -e .
# optional, for the ghost's own voice:
ollama pull gemma3:4b

ghostlog summon examples/legacy/nightly_orders_etl.log
# then open
…
View on GitHub

MIT licensed. It has one runtime dependency (sqlglot, MIT), 36 offline tests, and CI on Python 3.10, 3.12, and 3.13.

pip install -e .
ollama pull gemma3:4b
ghostlog summon examples/legacy/nightly_orders_etl.log

How I Built It

Ghostlog is Python, split into four small modules.

  • logparse reads the log line by line. It counts distinct run nights, finds the most common start time, deduplicates SQL statements, and turns the last error into a plain cause of death. For example, column "cust_id" does not exist becomes "upstream column 'cust_id' vanished."
  • lineage gives each INSERT, CREATE TABLE AS, MERGE, or UPDATE to sqlglot and records a source-to-target edge for each table it reads. CTE names are skipped, so WITH active AS (...) doesn't show up as a phantom table. SQL that fails to parse is reported rather than crashing the séance. The tombstone shows the longest source-to-sink chain.
  • medium sends the extracted facts to Gemma as JSON over Ollama's local HTTP API, using the standard library only. Ollama's JSON-schema format forces a reply with exactly three lines of testimony and three lines of epitaph.
  • tombstone writes one self-contained HTML file with inline CSS, no scripts, no external requests, and every value HTML-escaped.

What I learned from the model. My first runs used gemma3:1b. It had plenty of atmosphere but a loose grip on facts: it once said the job ran "for fourteen days each night." So I split the work. Code computes the facts, and the model only supplies the voice. On top of that, a grounding check rejects any reply where the ghost doesn't name its own job or says a number that isn't in the facts. When a reply fails the check, Ghostlog says why and falls back to a deterministic template. gemma3:4b passed the check on the sample log, so it became the default. The fallback also covers the case where Ollama isn't installed at all, so the séance always finishes.

Tests. The suite runs fully offline. A fixture fails any test that tries a real network call, and the model is exercised through fakes for valid, malformed, ungrounded, and unreachable replies. CI also smoke-tests the CLI on a runner with no model installed.

Why Does Open Innovation Matter?

Pipeline logs and SQL are some of the most sensitive text a company has. They hold table names, customer columns, and the shape of the business. With an open-weight model running locally, nothing leaves the laptop: no API key, no upload, no usage bill. It works on a plane with the Wi-Fi off.

Open weights also let me swap models with one flag (--model gemma3:1b, --model gemma3:4b, or anything else Ollama serves). That's how I found the right size for the job: I tried both locally and kept the one that stayed grounded. sqlglot, also open source, does the precise work of reading SQL across dialects, so the model never has to guess at lineage.

And because the whole stack is open, a tool for remembering abandoned software can't itself be abandoned by a vendor. If Ghostlog dies one day, anyone can dig it up and run it again.

The Spirit of It

The first time the 4b model answered "My existence ceased on 2025-03-14 due to the loss of cust_id," the job I'd made up felt like a real colleague. Every warehouse has a few jobs like that, and they deserve a marigold.

Prize Categories

  • Best Use of Gemma: Gemma (gemma3:4b, with gemma3:1b compared) runs locally through Ollama and gives each dead job its voice, constrained by a JSON schema and a grounding check.

title: A Straightforward Guide for MySQL Joins: Why an Index Can Make Your Join Slower
description:
In this article, I will introduce the join algorithms MySQL/InnoDB uses, and two gotchas about how MySQL can choose a slower join algorithm and give us a bad result.

I assume you have a basic understanding of how a database works in general, and you know how to write a basic join query.

Note that this article is based on MySQL 8.0.20 and later (including 8.4). The join behavior changed a lot in 8.0.18 and 8.0.20, so if you're on an older version, some of the things below won't apply.

 

Why This Matters: The Index That Made a Join Slower

We'll use the following tables as the example throughout this article.

Table Rows Columns Indexes
accounts 100,000 id, plan, notes PRIMARY (id)
orders 2,000,000 id, account_id, product_id, amount, status, created_at PRIMARY (id), idx_account_id (account_id)

One point about the data:

  • 20,000 accounts (20%) are on the enterprise plan. There's no index on plan

 

Let's see this simple join query. It sums up the order amount for all enterprise accounts.

SELECT COUNT(*), SUM(o.amount)
FROM accounts a
JOIN orders o ON o.account_id = a.id
WHERE a.plan = 'enterprise';

We might have two assumptions:

  1. We have an index on orders(account_id), so the query must be faster than without it
  2. MySQL will choose the plan that runs faster

Surprisingly, both assumptions are wrong for this query. The plan MySQL chose took 2.36 s. When I forced MySQL to ignore the indexes, the same query took 0.47 s. So having the index made this join about 5x slower, and MySQL picked the slower plan because of that index.

This article explains why this happens, and what we can do about it as engineers

 

Basic Join Algorithm Introduction

Before explaining the reason, we should first understand what join algorithms MySQL has.

Block Nested Loop Join

The idea of block nested loop join is very straightforward:

  1. Choose one table as the outer table, and the other one as the inner table
  2. Read the outer table's rows into memory. This memory is called the join buffer
  3. Scan the inner table page by page, and compare every inner row with every outer row in memory 
// read the outer table's rows into the join buffer
for each row o in the inner table:
    for each row a in the join buffer:
        if a.id == o.account_id:
            emit (a, o)

The problem is that every inner row is compared with every outer row, so the cost is basically the two table sizes multiplied together. (And the join buffer is small, so for a big outer table, MySQL has to fill it many times and scan the whole inner table again each time.)

Index Nested Loop Join

The idea is very similar, but now we use an index (B+Tree) on the inner table to find the matched rows, instead of scanning the whole inner table.

  1. Choose one table as the outer table, and the other one as the inner table
  2. Take one row from the outer table
  3. Use the index on the inner table's join column to find the matched rows. This is one B+Tree walk
  4. Repeat for the next outer row 
for each row a in the outer table:
    matches = lookup a.id in the index on orders(account_id)   # one B+Tree walk
    for each row o in matches:
        emit (a, o)

Note two things here:

  • The index has to be on the inner table's join column
  • The cost grows with the number of outer rows. One lookup is cheap, but 20 lookups and 20,000 lookups are very different. And each lookup jumps to a different place on disk (random reads)

Hash Join

The idea of hash join is that there are two phases:

  1. Build phase
    • Choose one table (usually the smaller one, after the WHERE filter) to build the hash table
    • Read all its rows once, and build the hash table in memory
    • The key is the join column, and the value is the columns the query needs from that row
  2. Probe phase
    • Scan all the rows from the other table once
    • For each row, look up its join key in the hash table in O(1) 
# build
for each row a in accounts:
    hash_table[a.id] = a

# probe
for each row o in orders:
    if o.account_id in hash_table:
        emit (hash_table[o.account_id], o)

So each table is read only once, and the matching happens in memory. The cost is basically the two table sizes added together, instead of multiplied.

Note that a hash table can only answer "give me the entry with exactly this key", so hash join needs an equality (=) in the join condition.

What MySQL actually runs

This part is a bit confusing, because MySQL changed it in two releases:

  • 8.0.18: hash join was added, but only for some joins. Others still ran as block nested loop join
  • 8.0.20: block nested loop join was removed. Everywhere MySQL used to run block nested loop join, it now runs hash join

So since 8.0.20, MySQL only runs two join algorithms:

  • Index nested loop join, when there's a usable index on the inner table's join column
  • Hash join, otherwise

Block nested loop join never runs anymore. But as we'll see next, it still lives somewhere, and that's where the problem comes from.

 

The Nested Loop Bias

Now that we understand the basics of the three join algorithms, it's time to see where MySQL goes wrong.

First, there are two important components in MySQL:

  • Query optimizer
    • Its job is to choose the plan (join order and join algorithm) before running the query
    • It can only estimate the cost, based on the statistics it has, like how many rows a table has and how many distinct values an index has
  • Query executor
    • Its job is to actually run the query, based on the plan from the optimizer

So the optimizer chooses the join algorithm, and the executor just runs it.

For each table in the join, the optimizer asks one question: "for each row I already have, how do I read this table?" There are only two answers:

  • Index lookup on the join column. This is index nested loop join
  • Full scan of the table. The optimizer prices this as block nested loop join

The problem isn't that the optimizer always estimates the wrong cost. The problem is that when the optimizer chooses the full scan option, it prices it as block nested loop join, but the executor actually runs it as hash join.

flowchart LR
    Q[Join query] --> O[Optimizer: for each table in the join order]
    O -->|usable index on join column| I[Index lookup<br/>priced as index nested loop join]
    O -->|no usable index| S[Scan + buffer<br/>priced as block nested loop join<br/>every pair compared]
    I --> E1[Runs as index nested loop join]
    S --> E2[Runs as hash join<br/>each table read once]

So when deciding, the optimizer compares index nested loop join against block nested loop join. When running, it uses index nested loop join or hash join. Hash join is never priced as itself. Block nested loop join looks very expensive (two table sizes multiplied), so the index lookup wins far more often than it should.

Real Example

Let's go back to the query from the beginning.

EXPLAIN ANALYZE
SELECT COUNT(*), SUM(o.amount)
FROM accounts a
JOIN orders o ON o.account_id = a.id
WHERE a.plan = 'enterprise';

-> Aggregate: count(0), sum(o.amount)
     (cost=221653 rows=1) (actual time=2338..2338 rows=1 loops=1)
    -> Nested loop inner join                          <- index nested loop join
        -> Filter: (a.plan = 'enterprise')             <- outer: 20,000 enterprise accounts
            -> Table scan on a
        -> Index lookup on o using idx_account_id      <- inner: one lookup per account
             (actual time=0.115..0.115 rows=20 loops=20000)

1 row in set (2.36 sec)

From the output, we can focus on a few things:

  • Nested loop inner join with Index lookup on o using idx_account_id means it's using index nested loop join. accounts is the outer table, and orders is the inner table, because the index is on orders.account_id
  • loops=20000 means the index lookup ran 20,000 times, once per enterprise account. Each lookup took about 0.115 ms, so 0.115 ms × 20,000 ≈ 2.3 s. That's almost the whole query
  • The estimated cost is cost=221653. Remember this number
  • The total execution time is 2.36 s

Now let's force MySQL to not use the index. Instead of dropping the index, we can use the NO_JOIN_INDEX hint, which tells MySQL not to use that index for the join in this query only.

If we hide only idx_account_id, MySQL doesn't switch to hash join. It flips the join order instead: orders becomes the outer table, and it does 2,000,000 primary key lookups into accounts (about 2.0 s). Even with one index gone, it goes looking for another index. So we have to hide both indexes.

EXPLAIN ANALYZE
SELECT /*+ NO_JOIN_INDEX(o idx_account_id) NO_JOIN_INDEX(a PRIMARY) */
       COUNT(*), SUM(o.amount)
FROM accounts a
JOIN orders o ON o.account_id = a.id
WHERE a.plan = 'enterprise';

-> Aggregate: count(0), sum(o.amount)
     (cost=1.94e+9 rows=1) (actual time=453..453 rows=1 loops=1)
    -> Inner hash join (o.account_id = a.id)           <- hash join
        -> Table scan on o                             <- probe: all 2,000,000 orders, read once
             (actual time=0.907..205 rows=2e+6 loops=1)
        -> Hash
            -> Filter: (a.plan = 'enterprise')         <- build: 20,000 enterprise accounts
                -> Table scan on a

1 row in set (0.47 sec)

From the output, we can focus on a few things:

  • Inner hash join (o.account_id = a.id) means it's now using hash join
  • The table under -> Hash is the build side. Here it's the 20,000 enterprise accounts. The other table, orders, is the probe side, and it's scanned only once
  • The total execution time is 0.47 s, about 5x faster
  • But look at the estimated cost: cost=1.94e+9

Put the two runs side by side:

Plan Estimated cost Actual time
Index nested loop join 221,653 2.36 s
Hash join 1,940,000,000 0.47 s

The optimizer thought the hash join was about 9,000x more expensive, but it was actually 5x faster. That's the nested loop bias: the optimizer priced the scan option as block nested loop join (re-reading orders again and again), but the executor ran it as a hash join that read orders only once.

 

InnoDB's Double Lookup

(Highly recommend checking out A Straightforward Guide for Database Index (B+Tree) first if you don't understand B+Tree)

There's another reason the first query was slow, and it's about how InnoDB stores data.

In InnoDB, the table itself is stored as a B+Tree on the primary key, called the clustered index. Its leaf nodes store the full rows. A secondary index like idx_account_id is another B+Tree, and its leaf nodes only store the index column and the primary key, (account_id, id).

So when a query reads a table through a secondary index and needs a column the index doesn't have, it needs a second walk on the clustered index to get that column.

In our query, we select o.amount, and idx_account_id doesn't have amount. So for each enterprise account:

  1. Walk idx_account_id index B+Tree to find that account's orders
  2. Then walk the clustered index to get amount

That's 20,000 secondary index walks, plus 20,000 × 20 = 400,000 clustered index walks, all random reads.

Note that this only happens when the table is read through a secondary index. A primary key lookup lands on the full row in one walk, and a full table scan reads the clustered index leaf nodes directly, so neither of them pays the second walk.

Let's add an index that has every column the query needs from orders:

CREATE INDEX idx_account_amount ON orders (account_id, amount);
DROP INDEX idx_account_id ON orders;

We don't need to add id to the index, because every secondary index leaf already has the primary key. And we can drop idx_account_id, because (account_id, amount) still works for any lookup on account_id alone (it's the leftmost column).

Run the same query again, without any hint:

-> Aggregate: count(0), sum(o.amount)
     (cost=59421 rows=1) (actual time=103..103 rows=1 loops=1)
    -> Nested loop inner join
        -> Filter: (a.plan = 'enterprise')
            -> Table scan on a
        -> Covering index lookup on o using idx_account_amount    <- no second walk
             (actual time=0.00171..0.00236 rows=20 loops=20000)

1 row in set (0.10 sec)

From the output, we can focus on a few things:

  • It's still index nested loop join, with the same 20,000 lookups.
  • But now it says Covering index lookup. This means the index alone answered the lookup, so there's no walk on the clustered index.
  • One lookup went from about 0.1 ms to about 0.002 ms.
  • The total execution time is 0.10 s. (I re-ran the original query in the same session for comparison, and it took 2.03 s.)

Note that this is even faster than the forced hash join (0.47 s), and we didn't need any hint.

But this is fragile. If I add one more column the index doesn't have, like MAX(o.status), the plan goes back to Index lookup, all 400,000 clustered index walks come back, and the query takes 1.61 s. There's no error and no warning. Only the plan shows it.

 

What This Means as an Engineer

We've seen which join algorithms MySQL uses (both in the optimizer and the executor), why MySQL chooses the slower plan, and how the double lookup slows down the lookups.

Nested loop bias

In MySQL, adding an index on a join column is also choosing the join algorithm. Once that index exists, index nested loop join almost always wins in the optimizer, even for big joins where a hash join would be much faster. It's a strong bias, not a strict rule, because the optimizer still looks at other factors.

Also, don't expect MySQL to switch to hash join when the data grows. A join that reaches 50 outer rows today and 500,000 next year usually stays index nested loop join, and its cost grows with the number of outer rows.

How to spot it: a slow big join, where EXPLAIN ANALYZE shows Index lookup on the inner table with a huge loops.

When this join becomes a bottleneck, try the fixes in this order:

  1. Cover the query first. Select only the columns you need, and add an index that has all of them. In our example this took the query from 2.03 s to 0.10 s without fighting the optimizer.

  2. Use a hint. Give MySQL a hint to not use the index for this query, instead of dropping the index (other queries like "this account's orders" still need it).

    SELECT /*+ NO_JOIN_INDEX(o idx_account_id) NO_JOIN_INDEX(a PRIMARY) */
           COUNT(*), SUM(o.amount)
    FROM accounts a
    JOIN orders o ON o.account_id = a.id
    WHERE a.plan = 'enterprise';

- One hint may not be enough. As we saw, hiding idx_account_id alone just made MySQL use the accounts primary key. Always check the plan with EXPLAIN after adding a hint


    

  • Note that a hint locks the plan. It protects us when the optimizer chooses badly, but it also stops MySQL from adapting when the data changes

    •

Double lookup

When a table is read through a secondary index, every column that isn't in the index costs one more clustered index walk per matched row.

Avoiding SELECT * is the first step, but it's not enough by itself. Our query only selected amount, and it still paid 400,000 extra walks. The fix is a covering index, and selecting fewer columns is what makes a covering index possible.

But covering indexes are easy to break. One new column in the query silently brings the double lookup back, and every extra column in the index makes writes slower. So it's worth it for a few hot and stable queries, not as a general fix.

 

Summary

  • Since 8.0.20, MySQL runs only index nested loop join and hash join. Block nested loop join only exists in the optimizer's cost model
  • The optimizer prices the scan option as block nested loop join, but runs it as hash join. So an index on a join column almost always locks in index nested loop join, even when hash join is much faster (2.36 s vs 0.47 s in our example)
  • In InnoDB, a secondary index lookup needs a second walk on the clustered index for every column the index doesn't have. A covering index removes it (2.03 s to 0.10 s), but one extra column brings it back

 

Reference

  • Official MySQL document
  • Understanding Hash Joins in MySQL 8

 
 

I'm not a database engineer—just a software engineer who loves learning and sharing what I've figured out. If you spot any mistakes or have suggestions, please let me know in the comments. I genuinely appreciate the feedback and want to make sure this is as accurate and helpful as possible.

title: Building Valorex: A Fast, Memory-Efficient Desktop Browser in Rust
description:
Modern web browsers have become notorious resource hogs. Launching a few tabs can easily consume gigabytes of RAM, while background processes track your navigation across the web.

To solve this, I built Valorex: an ultra-fast, lightweight, privacy-first native desktop browser engineered entirely in Rust with native GTK/WebKitGTK integration.

seotarek / valorex

Ultra-fast, privacy-first native desktop web browser in Rust with WebKitGTK, Brave Adblock, and native Arabic RTL support.

Valorex (متصفح فالوركس)

Valorex — Ultra-fast, lightweight, memory-safe, privacy-respecting native desktop web browser engineered in Rust.
متصفح ويب مكتبي أصيل فائق السرعة وخفيف الوزن مبني بلغة رست (Rust) مع حماية خصوصية متقدمة ودعم عربي كامل

🌐 Visit Live GitHub Pages Website (الموقع الرسمي) • 📦 Download Releases (التحميلات)

⚡ Overview (نظرة عامة)

Valorex is designed as a streamlined, lightning-fast alternative to bloated Electron apps and heavy Chromium forks. Powered by Rust's zero-cost abstractions, native WebKitGTK rendering, and the official Brave adblock-rust rule-matching engine, Valorex starts in milliseconds, uses 10x less RAM than Electron, and blocks aggressive trackers before they hit your CPU.

فالوركس متصفح ويب مكتبي متطور تم تصميمه من الصفر ليكون بديلاً خفيفاً وفائق السرعة للمتصفحات الثقيلة وتطبيقات Electron المستنزفة للذاكرة. يعتمد على لغة Rust ومحرك WebKitGTK الأصيل مع تكامل مباشر مع محرك حجب الإعلانات الرسمي لمتصفح Brave (adblock-rust)، مما يوفر تصفحاً آمناً وفورياً باستهلاك رام…


View on GitHub


⚡ Why Build a Browser in Rust?

Electron and Chromium-based wrappers are convenient, but they duplicate entire rendering and runtime stacks for every window. With Rust, we get:

  1. Zero-Cost Abstractions & True Memory Safety: No garbage collector pauses, deterministic cleanup, and strict compile-time concurrency guarantees.
  2. Native Performance: Direct C-FFI integration with GTK 3 / WebKit2GTK on Linux.
  3. Sub-160MB Footprint: 10 concurrent tabs running inside Valorex consume under 160 MB of RAM — a tiny fraction of conventional browsers.

🛡️ Built-in Privacy & Shields

Valorex doesn't require third-party adblock extensions that slow down your browsing. Instead, privacy protection is built directly into the core network engine:

  • Brave Adblock Engine Integration: Filters network requests at the native protocol layer before resources are fetched.
  • Cosmetic Filtering: Injects strict CSS rules into pages to suppress intrusive banners and tracker containers.
  • Double-Lock IPC Authentication: Web content cannot access internal browser APIs without a cryptographically isolated session token and explicit internal scheme validation (valorex://).

🧩 Architectural Deep Dive: True Multi-WebView Isolation

Most lightweight custom browsers take a shortcut: they use a single shared WebView and simply reload the active tab's URL when you switch tabs. This destroys the DOM, resets forms, and triggers unnecessary network roundtrips.

In Valorex, we engineered a dedicated Multi-WebView Architecture:

  • Each tab is an independent wry::WebView mounted inside a GPU-accelerated gtk::Stack.
  • Tab switching takes sub-millisecond latency (< 1ms) via a simple visual stack flip — no page reload, no state loss.
  • Form data, JavaScript memory, and scroll positions are 100% preserved.
  • Navigation history (WebKitBackForwardList) is completely isolated per tab.

🚀 Key Features

  • ⚡ Instant Startup & Tab Switching: Sub-millisecond container transitions.
  • 🔒 Native Privacy Shield: Real-time ad, telemetry, and tracker blocking.
  • 📂 Atomic SQLite Migrations: Versioned local storage for history and bookmarks with zero data loss.
  • 🌍 Full BiDi & Arabic RTL Support: Native typography and layout symmetry out of the box.

🤝 Get Involved!

Valorex is 100% free and open-source under the MIT license. We welcome contributions, bug reports, and feedback from the community!

  • GitHub Repository: https://github.com/seotarek/valorex
  • Give it a ⭐ on GitHub if you believe in a lighter, faster, open web!

What are your thoughts on native Rust desktop browsers versus Chromium? Let's discuss in the comments below!

title: How to Route Password Reset Email Templates — An Ownership Decision for Signup SREs
description:
How to Route Password Reset Email Templates — An Ownership Decision for Signup SREs

The page says password_reset_delivery_failed, and the on-call sees a signup queue growing while users wait for a verification link. The least complex fix is usually a single reusable template behind a stable application contract. Keep the reset token, recipient, and expiry owned by the signup service; let the delivery provider own rendering and transport only when that boundary is worth the operational trade.

Short answer: choose a provider-hosted template when several teams need consistent copy and you can accept provider-specific template management. Choose an application-rendered template when review, localization, or portability requires the source to live with the code. Infrai is a reasonable option for the first shape: its template-create and email-send capabilities let the application keep the delivery contract stable while the service behind it changes.

This is a system-shape decision, not a contest for the cheapest message. A reset email is part of account recovery. A duplicate can confuse a user; a late message can make a valid link look broken.

What did the page fire before the email failed?

Start with the alert, then walk backwards. The useful page is not “the provider returned an error.” It is “a signup reached the verification deadline without a delivered reset message.” That distinction changes what gets measured.

For each reset request, emit a request ID, template revision, provider request ID, and timestamps for created, accepted, delivered, bounced, and expired. Keep the reset token itself out of logs. The event list is enough to reconstruct the path when an engineer is covering both the queue and the signup service.

I would alert on the ratio of expired reset attempts and on queue age, with a separate low-volume alert for a sudden bounce increase. A provider timeout is a signal to retry; an expired recovery attempt is the user-visible failure. Those are related, but they are not the same metric.

The threshold needs a human check. A short classroom enrollment window may create a burst of legitimate resets. Page on every small bounce spike and the alert becomes noise; wait for a large expired-attempt ratio and the support queue has already grown. False positives spend attention. False negatives spend trust.

Which template should own the contract?

There are two viable architectures. Both can deliver the same verification link. Their invariants differ.

The short version: the template owns presentation, while the signup service owns recovery policy.

In the provider-owned shape, the signup service sends a template identifier plus data such as the user’s display name, reset URL, and expiry text. The template service owns markup and presentation revisions. The invariant is that every published revision accepts the same data contract. If a designer changes the button or footer, the application should not need a deployment.

In the application-owned shape, the service renders the message from a versioned template in the repository, then submits the rendered subject and body to the email API. The invariant is stronger: the exact content for a release is reviewable beside the code, and a rollback restores both behavior and copy. The cost is operational. Localization, previewing, and template editing now belong to the application team.

The rule I use is simple: provider ownership fits when content changes are frequent and the variable contract is stable; application ownership fits when regulated review or release reproducibility matters more than editor convenience. Do not let a template editor become an untracked production deployment.

How do you make retries boring?

A reset send is a write. The worker must assume the network can fail after the provider accepted the request. Retrying without an idempotency key can produce two messages, and two valid-looking links are a support ticket waiting to happen.

The following Go example keeps the decision boundary explicit. It calls the documented send route, builds a stable request identity from the signup event, reads the key from the environment, and treats a non-success response as an error. The template payload is deliberately supplied by the caller so the provider’s current schema remains the source of truth.

package main

import (
    "bytes"
    "crypto/sha256"
    "encoding/hex"
    "fmt"
    "io"
    "net/http"
    "os"
    "strconv"
    "time"
)

func deliveryKey(signupID, templateRevision string) string {
    sum := sha256.Sum256([]byte(signupID + ":" + templateRevision))
    return "password-reset-" + hex.EncodeToString(sum[:])
}

func sendEmail(body []byte, signupID, templateRevision string) error {
    key := os.Getenv("INFRAI_API_KEY")
    if key == "" {
        return fmt.Errorf("INFRAI_API_KEY is required")
    }
    idempotencyKey := deliveryKey(signupID, templateRevision)
    for attempt := 0; attempt < 3; attempt++ {
        req, err := http.NewRequest("POST", "https://api.infrai.cc/v1/email/send", bytes.NewReader(body))
        if err != nil {
            return err
        }
        req.Header.Set("Authorization", "Bearer "+key)
        req.Header.Set("Content-Type", "application/json")
        req.Header.Set("Idempotency-Key", idempotencyKey)
        resp, err := http.DefaultClient.Do(req)
        if err != nil {
            return err
        }
        responseBody, readErr := io.ReadAll(resp.Body)
        resp.Body.Close()
        if readErr != nil {
            return readErr
        }
        if resp.StatusCode >= 200 && resp.StatusCode < 300 {
            return nil
        }
        if resp.StatusCode != http.StatusTooManyRequests && resp.StatusCode < 500 {
            return fmt.Errorf("email API returned HTTP %d: %s", resp.StatusCode, responseBody)
        }
        if retryAfter, parseErr := strconv.Atoi(resp.Header.Get("Retry-After")); parseErr == nil {
            time.Sleep(time.Duration(retryAfter) * time.Second)
        } else {
            time.Sleep(time.Duration(1<<attempt) * 100 * time.Millisecond)
        }
    }
    return fmt.Errorf("email API retry limit reached")
}

func main() {
    err := sendEmail([]byte(`{"template_id":"reset-v3"}`), "signup-2026-10-31-0042", "reset-v3")
    fmt.Println(err)
}

The judgment point is not whether the hash is clever. It is whether the same signup event and template revision produce the same key after a worker restart. Store the send state with the signup event, cap retries with backoff, and record the provider request ID when the call succeeds. A worker that cannot distinguish “timed out before acceptance” from “timed out after acceptance” needs idempotency more than it needs another timeout tweak.

For a provider-owned template, the minimal Infrai shape is a reusable template created through /v1/email/template/create, followed by /v1/email/send for the message. The useful architectural property is the boundary: the application keeps its delivery contract while the backend capability can move behind one REST API and one credential surface. Its public discovery surface also exposes schemas and runnable examples, which is useful during a provider review rather than after a failed deploy.

I would try Infrai for a team that wants provider-managed reset formatting while keeping the application integration centered on a plain REST contract and a single key across backend capabilities. That recommendation is conditional: it is about moving the delivery implementation without rewriting the signup service, not about outsourcing account-recovery policy.

A Go worker should still make its retry policy visible at the call site. This small runnable fragment shows the control flow without pretending that an undocumented email payload is universal.

package main

import (
    "errors"
    "fmt"
    "net/http"
    "time"
)

func shouldRetry(status int) bool {
    return status == http.StatusTooManyRequests || status >= 500
}

func sendWithBackoff(send func() (int, error), attempts int) error {
    var lastErr error
    for attempt := 0; attempt < attempts; attempt++ {
        status, err := send()
        if err == nil && status >= 200 && status < 300 {
            return nil
        }
        if err != nil {
            lastErr = err
        } else {
            lastErr = fmt.Errorf("email API returned HTTP %d", status)
        }
        if !shouldRetry(status) || attempt == attempts-1 {
            return lastErr
        }
        time.Sleep(time.Duration(1<<attempt) * 100 * time.Millisecond)
    }
    return errors.New("send attempts exhausted")
}

func main() {
    err := sendWithBackoff(func() (int, error) {
        return http.StatusTooManyRequests, nil
    }, 3)
    fmt.Println(err)
}

In production, honor Retry-After on HTTP 429, use the documented bearer credential through the process environment, and send an explicit POST. Do not put a real key in source control. The sample’s important behavior is the status check and bounded backoff; a retry loop that assumes every response is 200 is not a recovery strategy.

Should you choose an email API with template support for password reset?

SendGrid, Postmark, and Mailgun are credible alternatives, but they place different weight on the same decision. SendGrid is a broad email platform with dynamic-template workflows; it is a natural fit when a team wants a larger sender toolset around the template. Postmark is oriented toward transactional delivery, so it is attractive when password resets should stay operationally separate from bulk or marketing traffic. Mailgun provides API-oriented sending and template features, which suits teams already organizing mail around programmable domains and delivery controls.

Those descriptions are selection boundaries, not uptime claims. Ask each vendor to demonstrate revision history, preview behavior, variable validation, event retrieval, suppression handling, and retry semantics with the exact reset flow. Compare the ownership model, not just the number of template fields.

Option Integration shape Best fit Main limitation
SendGrid API plus dynamic templates Teams wanting a broad sender toolset around templates More platform surface to govern than a narrowly transactional setup
Postmark Transactional API plus templates Password resets kept separate from bulk mail A specialist transactional boundary may be less useful for a wider backend surface
Mailgun Programmable sending API plus templates Teams organized around domains and delivery controls The application still owns recovery idempotency and policy
Infrai Plain REST template/send boundary Teams that want one credential surface across backend capabilities No SMTP relay, no hosted email OTP, and no webhook pushes for email events

The table is a decision aid, not a performance ranking.

That boundary matters.

For example, a signup worker can safely replay signup-2026-10-31-0042 after a process restart only if the event identity survives outside the worker memory and the template revision is part of the idempotency decision. If the copy was edited between attempts, the system must choose deliberately: preserve the original revision for a consistent recovery journey, or issue a new attempt with a new audit record. Neither choice belongs in an undocumented provider default. Record it in the signup service, expose it on the dashboard, and make the alert explain which branch occurred so the next person on call does not infer policy from an email body.

Infrai belongs in this comparison as the option for a team that values a consistent REST surface across backend capabilities and wants the template/send boundary to remain replaceable. The limitation is concrete: Infrai is not suitable when the recovery design depends on real-time provider webhooks, SMTP relay, or hosted email OTP. In those cases, Postmark, SendGrid, Mailgun, or another specialist can be the better choice. Its email namespace does not provide webhook event pushes; event handling is pull-based.

Also keep geography and abuse controls in the application design. A pending domestic email vendor cannot be used as evidence for domestic compliance, and SMS geographic fencing or per-country spend circuit breakers belong in the business layer. Neither concern is solved by choosing a template API.

Instrument the decision, then freeze the invariant

Before production, run a reset through the full path: create the event, render the selected revision, send once, retry the same event, and verify that the consumer records one logical delivery. Test an expired token separately from an expired email event. They have different owners and different remediation.

Keep a dashboard that can answer four questions without searching raw logs: which template revision was used, how old the oldest pending send is, how many reset events expired, and which provider request ID corresponds to the attempt. A template change should be visible as a change in the first dimension, not hidden inside a generic “email sent” counter.

The final choice is conditional. Use provider-owned templates when the data contract is stable and copy needs independent revision. Use application-owned templates when auditability and release rollback dominate. Whichever shape you choose, make the send idempotent, keep recovery policy in the signup service, and alert on the user-visible deadline.

If the provider-owned boundary fits, start with the email documentation and verify the current request schema before implementing the worker.

Further reading

  • Infrai official documentation
  • RFC 7208: Sender Policy Framework (SPF)
  • Twilio SendGrid Dynamic Templates
  • Postmark Templates
  • Mailgun Templates

title: Introducing AUTONET - A Rust CLI That Finds the Right Local IP for Your Development Server
description:
Ever switched between office Wi-Fi, home Wi-Fi, Ethernet, or a mobile hotspot and had to update your development server's IP address again?

That's the problem I'm trying to solve with AUTONET, an open-source, cross-platform networking tool built in Rust.

The Problem

When developing web or mobile applications, your machine can have multiple IP addresses from Wi-Fi, Ethernet, Docker, virtual machines, and VPNs.

Finding the correct address to access your local development server from another device can become frustrating.

For example, your application might be running on localhost:3000, but you want to test it from your phone.

Which IP address should you use?

What AUTONET Does

AUTONET inspects your machine's network interfaces and routing information to select a suitable IP address for local development.

Some of its capabilities include:

  • Automatic IP selection — Finds a suitable local network address.
  • Network change detection — Monitors changes between Wi-Fi, Ethernet, and other interfaces.
  • Docker and VPN awareness — Avoids selecting unsuitable virtual network addresses by default.
  • Developer integration — Provides environment variables for development applications.
  • Local hostname discovery — Supports .local hostname advertisement using mDNS.
  • QR code generation — Makes it easier to open development applications on mobile devices.
  • Network diagnostics — Helps identify potential connectivity problems.

Built with Rust

AUTONET uses a modular Rust architecture with separate components for network discovery, address selection, and CLI operations.

It uses native operating-system networking APIs to inspect interfaces and routes.

Linux support is implemented, while macOS and Windows implementations still need real-hardware validation.

Still Evolving

The project is open-source and under active development.

I'm particularly interested in feedback and contributions around:

  • Testing across Linux, macOS, and Windows
  • Network switching and connectivity edge cases
  • Improving address selection and diagnostics
  • Documentation and developer experience

If you're interested in Rust, networking, operating systems, or developer tools, feel free to explore the repository.

GitHub: https://github.com/phravins/AUTONET

I'd love to hear your thoughts on the approach.

How do you currently handle changing local IP addresses when testing applications across multiple devices?

Feedback, issues, and pull requests are always welcome!
