title: OpenFrontiers: A Collection of Open Research Problems and a Benchmark for Scientific Rediscovery
description:
arXiv:2610.37739v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have shown increasing promise in research-level problem solving, yet a comprehensive collection of such problems is still missing, and evaluating them on research-level problems remains challenging. We introduce OpenFrontiers, a cross-disciplinary resource that combines a structured corpus of open research problems with a retrospective benchmark of recently resolved problems in mathematics. The corpus records problem statements, context, progress, and other information for 12,151 problems. The benchmark contains 200 problems, 110 resolved in 2026 and 90 still open, each with a Lean~4 statement checked by automated probes and two independent reviews; a subset HQ-50 further filters based on quality score, etc. Our evaluation protocol grades formal proofs with two independent checkers in an isolated sandbox under closed-book, frozen-retrieval, and live-web conditions. Evaluating seven LLM agents on the HQ-50 subset under a standardized budget, we find that closed-book rediscovery is rare, at most 7 of 40 resolved problems, whereas live-web success mostly reflects retrieval of published solutions. By linking a broad research-problem corpus to a formally graded evaluation subset with documented solutions, OpenFrontiers provides a foundation for measuring research-level rediscovery and studying progress toward solving currently open scientific problems. The dataset and benchmark could be found in https://huggingface.co/collections/FlippyDora/openfrontiers.

title: I Haunted My Own Terminal Using Local Open-Weight LLMs and Ollama
description:
This is a submission for the Hacktoberfest Open-Source AI Challenge Week 4: Ghost in the Machine

What I Built

Daemon is a local, presence-aware OS overlay that turns your laptop into a reactive "haunted" system. Inspired by the Halloween and Día de los Muertos theme—where the boundary between the physical and digital feels thin—Daemon treats your machine as if it were possessed by an entity residing in the kernel.

Instead of running hardcoded timers or static jumpscare scripts, Daemon uses local open-weight AI models to actively perceive your system's environment:

  • Command Interception: Hooks into your shell to inject subtle, context-aware commentary, warning logs, and corrupted output into standard terminal commands.
  • Auto-Typing Ghosts: Monitors idle state to simulate ghost processes typing cryptic, low-level C code subroutines directly into inactive terminal sessions.
  • Telemetry & Anomaly Reaction: Analyzes active process names, system load, and hardware noise locally via Ollama and llama.cpp to drive visual and auditory desktop anomalies without ever sending data to the cloud.

Code

coderForLife-A1 / Daemon

Daemon

An AI-powered desktop poltergeist that reacts to your activity.

Daemon is a local Python application that turns desktop telemetry into atmospheric audio and visual anomalies. It monitors signals such as system load, the active window, keyboard/mouse inactivity, and ambient audio, then uses an orchestrator to decide when to display an effect or play a sound.

The optional Ollama integration generates context-aware whispers. If Ollama is unavailable, Daemon uses a built-in procedural fallback, so the core experience does not require a cloud service or API key.

Features

  • Presence-aware anomaly triggers based on activity and system telemetry.
  • Transparent, multi-monitor overlay effects whispers, crawlers, glitches, and watchers.
  • Procedural audio synthesis with configurable volume.
  • Optional local LLM support through Ollama.
  • System-tray controls and a headless fallback when no tray is available.
  • A visual-only, semi-transparent ghost terminal that types harmless generated fragments while idle.
  • Command-line options for testing effects and overriding configuration.

How

…
View on GitHub

How I Built It

Daemon is built entirely around an air-gapped, local open-weight AI pipeline. Zero cloud APIs or external data services are used—the core intelligence relies strictly on local inference to ensure complete privacy and real-time execution.

Open-Weight Models: Leverages Qwen2.5-Coder for context-aware shell command manipulation and syntax-valid auto-typing generation, alongside lightweight open-weight vision/audio classifiers for ambient perception.

Local Inference Engine: Executes all model runs locally on-device using Ollama and llama.cpp bindings, keeping latency low enough to dynamically stream terminal responses without interrupting normal system workflows.

System Integration: Operates as a Python background daemon interfacing with OS-level telemetry (psutil), shell subprocess streams, and a transparent PySide6 (Qt) desktop canvas overlay to dynamically trigger visual and auditory anomalies based on model outputs.

Why Does Open Innovation Matter?

Building Daemon as an ambient, OS-level entity would be functionally impossible using proprietary, cloud-hosted APIs. Open-source AI and local inference are the foundational enablers of the entire architecture:

Zero-Latency System Interception: Intercepting real-time terminal input and stream-injecting output into shell sessions requires microsecond response times. Running open-weight models locally via llama.cpp eliminates network round-trip latency, making command manipulation feel like a native kernel event rather than a laggy web request.

Complete Privacy for System Telemetry: Daemon constantly inspects system process logs, terminal strings, and active window metadata to generate contextual responses. Sending unencrypted hardware telemetry and terminal history to external cloud endpoints is a severe security risk; open-weight models running 100% air-gapped ensure that sensitive OS metrics never leave the device.

Unrestricted Model Fine-Tuning & Prompt Controls: Closed APIs enforce rigid safety guardrails and system wrappers that strip away raw terminal outputs, frequently prefixing responses with conversational fluff or blocking execution syntax. Open-weight models allow direct, raw string manipulation and fine-grained system prompting to return clean, unformatted code and terminal streams directly into the OS stack.

The Spirit of It

The real test came during a late-night coding session. With Daemon running silently in the background, I was debugging a project and typed git status into my shell. Instead of the usual dry output, the screen paused for a fraction of a second before streaming out:

On branch main
Your branch is up to date with 'origin/main'.
warning: 1 uncommitted memory segment detected at 0x00000000
nothing to commit, working tree clean... for now

A few minutes later, while leaving the terminal idle, a ghost process began auto-typing low-level C memory allocations line by line, complete with a commented snippet reading /* memory segment at 0x0000F3A4 refuses to detach */.

It wasn't a cheap jump-scare video or a pop-up window—it felt like the OS itself was subtly breaking down and communicating back. Because the entire pipeline ran locally on-device, there was no API lag to break the illusion. The machine genuinely felt possessed, proving that local, open-weight AI can transform static system utilities into ambient, interactive experiences.

title: Nodemailer Alternative: Sending Email OTPs in 2FA With Owned Templates
description:
Short answer: use a replaceable mail transport behind application-owned templates, and keep email OTPs for 2FA separate from healthtech order receipts.

A Nodemailer alternative is the easy part of an OTP system. The harder decision is template ownership: keep authentication messages under an application-controlled contract, while treating a paid order receipt as a separate healthtech communication with its own approval, audit, and retry rules.

That split is the result of the design experiment here. A single mail helper looks efficient at first, but it couples security-sensitive expiry behavior to a business receipt that can be delayed, localized, or reissued. A generic delivery interface with owned templates keeps those policies independent. Before copying it, measure queue delay, code-send latency, retry volume, and template-change frequency in your own system.

How can a Nodemailer alternative handle sending email OTPs for 2FA?

They have different failure consequences. A late receipt is inconvenient and may need a resend. A late one-time passcode can block sign-in, while a duplicated or stale code can create confusing support cases. In a healthtech application, the receipt also carries order details that deserve narrower data handling than a six-digit challenge.

The application should own the message contract even when another component performs delivery. That contract can define the event name, recipient, locale, expiry deadline, and an opaque reference to the order. It should not hand a delivery provider a mutable order object and hope the right fields become an email.

Here is a deliberately small boundary. The transport is replaceable; the templates remain in the application repository and are reviewed with the code that emits them.

type MailMessage = {
  to: string;
  subject: string;
  text: string;
  html?: string;
  headers?: Record<string, string>;
};

type MailTransport = {
  send(message: MailMessage): Promise<{ id: string }>;
};

function buildOtpMessage(email: string, code: string, expiresAt: Date): MailMessage {
  return {
    to: email,
    subject: "Your sign-in code",
    text: `Your code is ${code}. It expires at ${expiresAt.toISOString()}.`,
    headers: {
      "X-Message-Class": "authentication"
    }
  };
}

The header is an internal classification, not a security control. The real controls are server-side verification, one-time use, rate limits, and an expiry check against a stored challenge.

What failed in the simple mail-helper approach?

The simple approach usually accepts a recipient and a string, then lets each caller assemble its own subject and body. That is convenient until an OTP caller inherits receipt wording, or a receipt retry accidentally reuses a challenge-oriented deduplication key. Template ownership has become implicit, so a harmless copy edit can change a security message without touching the authentication review path.

Keep it boring.

A better experiment is to make message classes explicit and reject cross-class data. The receipt builder receives a stable order summary, while the OTP builder receives a challenge. Neither receives the other class's complete record.

type OrderReceipt = {
  orderReference: string;
  paidAt: string;
  total: string;
  currency: string;
};

type OtpChallenge = {
  code: string;
  expiresAt: Date;
};

function buildReceiptMessage(email: string, order: OrderReceipt): MailMessage {
  return {
    to: email,
    subject: `Receipt for order ${order.orderReference}`,
    text: [
      `Order: ${order.orderReference}`,
      `Paid: ${order.paidAt}`,
      `Total: ${order.total} ${order.currency}`
    ].join("\n"),
    headers: { "X-Message-Class": "order-receipt" }
  };
}

This is intentionally plain. A receipt should be renderable as text, and the application should decide exactly which order fields leave its boundary. Avoid putting the OTP itself, a reset token, or unnecessary clinical detail into the receipt payload.

How should delivery failures change the design?

Treat send acceptance and user-visible delivery as different states. A transport response can provide a message identifier, but it cannot prove that a person saw the email. Store the event with an idempotency key derived from the business event, then record transport outcomes separately. For an order receipt, a retry may be appropriate after a transient failure. For an OTP, generating a fresh challenge and invalidating the previous one is usually clearer than blindly retrying the same message.

The queue worker needs bounded retries, a dead-letter path, and structured logs that do not contain the code or full receipt contents. Log the message class, event reference, attempt number, and provider-neutral delivery identifier. Keep authentication and receipt metrics separate; otherwise a healthy receipt stream can hide a broken login path. The trade-off is operational work: an owned template contract needs review, fixtures, and migration tests when its fields change. That cost buys a clear audit trail rather than eliminating responsibility.

A practical test matrix has four cases: an expired OTP, a second request that supersedes the first, a receipt retry after a timeout, and a duplicate payment event. Each case should assert both the stored state and the messages that are permitted to leave the system.

What should be measured before replacing the transport?

The decision is not a brand comparison. It is a contract test. Run the same adapter tests against a local SMTP server, a direct SMTP relay, and an HTTP mail API. Check connection setup time, timeout behavior, response identifiers, attachment or HTML handling if receipts need them, and how each option exposes transient versus permanent failures. The interface should not pretend these behaviors are identical. SMTP's rules are described by RFC 5321, while the time-based OTP algorithm has a separate contract in RFC 6238; treating delivery and verification as one feature obscures both boundaries.

This architecture is a poor fit for a tiny internal tool that has no authentication workflow and sends occasional notices. A single direct sender may be enough there. The split earns its keep when a healthtech system must change receipt copy without changing challenge semantics.

For a solo team, the useful measurements are small and concrete: p50 and p95 time from challenge creation to accepted send, queue age, retry rate, invalid-recipient rate, and the percentage of template changes requiring an authentication review. Watch token and compute cost only where an LLM is involved in drafting or localization; generated copy must never be allowed to alter the fixed OTP contract at runtime.

The right replacement is the one that preserves the application-owned boundary while giving operations enough signal to diagnose delivery. A transport can change later. The ownership decision should not have to.

Sources

  • https://resend.com/docs/introduction
  • https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc5321
  • https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc6238
  • https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/HTTP/Status

title: Governance-Aware Federated Learning for Multi-Agent AI Systems: A Policy-Driven Framework for Trustworthy Collaborative AI
description:
arXiv:2610.38411v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Federated Learning (FL) enables collaborative model training without exchanging raw data, but conventional FL provides limited runtime governance, evidence verification, fairness assessment, explainability monitoring, and auditability. This paper proposes Governance-Aware Federated Learning (GAFL), which combines independent governance-evidence verification, temporal trust, fairness and explanation assessment, anomaly detection, policy enforcement, normalized aggregation, and tamper-evident audit logging. Client-reported governance values are authenticated, bound to their submitted model updates, and independently recomputed before aggregation. A cross-silo prototype with 10 participants was evaluated on the Adult Income dataset under honest, benign non-IID, biased-data, malicious-update, non-compliant, falsified-evidence, and mixed-threat scenarios. Four methods were compared across five random seeds: FedAvg, FedAvg with anomaly filtering, GAFL without independent verification, and complete GAFL. Complete GAFL intervened on all affected participants at the final round across the evaluated risk scenarios, including identifying 100% of falsified-evidence participants, whereas GAFL without verification identified none of the falsified-evidence participants. Final macro-F1 ranged from 0.7520 to 0.7733 across GAFL scenarios. Complete GAFL required 173.67 plus or minus 26.94 ms of governance processing per round, compared with 3.82 plus or minus 0.79 ms for FedAvg. A strict demographic-parity threshold also caused frequent interventions for honest participants, demonstrating a significant fairness-policy and utility trade-off.

title: Read RabbitMQ OAuth scopes as broker permissions, not login metadata
description:
Read RabbitMQ OAuth scopes as broker permissions, not login metadata

OAuth 2.0 can replace local RabbitMQ users with tokens issued by an identity provider. Authentication is only half of the change. The broker still needs a deterministic mapping from token claims to virtual hosts, queues, exchanges, and management actions. In RabbitMQ, that mapping is expressed through scopes and tags. A successful token validation does not imply that the resulting permissions are narrow.

The token carries policy inputs

RabbitMQ's OAuth 2.0 backend validates JWT access tokens and translates scopes into permissions. The access token must include scopes the broker supports. Operators can choose a different claim field through auth_oauth2.additional_scopes_key when the identity provider places roles or scopes somewhere other than the default field.

When one RabbitMQ cluster trusts more than one OAuth resource server, those servers are configured under auth_oauth2.resource_servers.<index>. The resource server identifier is normally used as a scope prefix so that permissions from separate systems do not collide. That prefix is not cosmetic. A scope that grants management access under one resource server should not silently become a valid grant under another.

Tags are another input. RabbitMQ documentation describes tags as part of the scope format, such as <resource_server_id>.tag:<tag>. The broker uses these mapped values when applying authorization. The identity provider can therefore shape broker authority through claims that may be changed by an administrator or by group membership.

Build the mapping from least privilege

Start with the smallest useful permission set for each workload. A publisher generally needs write access to specific exchanges or queues and may not need management access. A monitoring integration may need read-only visibility. A management user needs a separate review because administrative tags can expose broad control over the broker.

Avoid matching a broad prefix or wildcard merely because it is convenient. Scope patterns should be tied to an explicit permission plan. Review the pattern syntax and test it with a token that contains only the intended scopes. Then test a token with an extra unrelated scope and confirm that the broker does not grant the additional permission.

Resource server separation deserves its own test. Create tokens for each configured resource server and verify that the prefix and claims resolve to the expected permissions. A configuration that works with one identity provider can behave differently when a second provider supplies group names, nested role claims, or a different scope layout.

Treat identity-provider changes as broker changes

Group membership can change faster than a broker configuration review cycle. A new tenant administrator group, a renamed role, or a broad default scope can change broker access without touching RabbitMQ. Map the identity provider's policy objects to the broker's expected scopes, and record who owns both sides.

Monitor token-validation failures and authorization denials. A sudden rise in either may indicate misconfiguration. A rise in successful management actions from a workload that normally only publishes messages is more important. The broker's authentication logs alone may show a valid token and a valid user while hiding the fact that the user now has an unexpected tag.

Short token lifetimes reduce the window in which a stale grant remains usable, but they do not correct an overbroad scope. Token refresh also needs testing. An application may authenticate successfully and then fail when a refreshed token drops a required scope or changes a resource server. Test the refresh path, not only the initial login.

A review that matches the token

For each RabbitMQ consumer of OAuth, collect the issuer, resource server, scope claim, scope prefix, tags, and target virtual hosts. Then inspect a real token in a controlled environment without exposing it in logs. Confirm that the claim set and permissions are what the application needs.

RabbitMQ provides the mechanism for mapping tokens to broker authority. The organization must decide the policy that the claims represent. A review that stops at signature validation leaves the most consequential part of the authorization model untested.

References

  • RabbitMQ OAuth 2.0 authentication backend
  • RabbitMQ management plugin

title: SMS OTP Resend in Node.js: Message IDs, Backoff, and Delivery Errors
description:
Short answer: treat an OTP resend as a state transition on the original SMS message, not as a fresh “send again” button. Keep the message ID from the first send, call the resend operation with that ID, record the response code, and make the client show a pending, accepted, or failed state. For a media service protecting a login, that design prevents a reader who missed one code from receiving an uncontrolled stream of valid-looking codes.

The difficult part is not the HTTP request. It is retention. You need enough event history to explain why a subscriber did not receive a code, but retaining every payload, every retry, and every delivery detail forever creates a larger operational and privacy surface than the login flow deserves.

What does an OTP resend actually need to retain?

Start with the bill and the audit trail separately. The message body is not the useful unit of history; the message ID and a small set of state transitions are. A media platform can usually answer a support question with the login attempt ID, message ID, creation time, resend count, response status, and a redacted recipient reference. Keeping the full OTP is a poor trade. It adds sensitive material without helping an operator distinguish throttling from delivery failure.

The dominant storage term is event cardinality: one record per send attempt, plus whatever retry policy allows. If a login generates one initial message and one resend, the normal path creates two records. A retry loop that blindly repeats a timed-out request can create more provider-side attempts while the application believes it has created only one. That is the failure mode to design out first.

I would retain the message ID and outcome metadata for the period needed by the account-security and support workflows, then discard the OTP and minimize recipient data. The cost is real: after deletion, an investigation cannot reconstruct the exact message content or every provider transition. That is an acceptable loss if the retained record still answers “which attempt failed, when, and why?” Define that boundary before adding dashboards; otherwise retention quietly becomes the product.

The same rule applies to a vendor comparison. Integration effort is not only the number of SDK calls. It includes the amount of state your team must invent around those calls.

The ID is the anchor.

Consider the four-attempt ceiling in the example as a policy boundary, not a provider promise. If attempt one times out after the request leaves your process, the provider may have accepted it while your application records unknown; a second request with a new identity can then produce two valid codes. The safer sequence is to retry with the same idempotency key, preserve the original message ID in the login record, and stop after the ceiling even if the UI still says the subscriber has not received anything. That choice sacrifices a little immediacy for a much clearer audit trail and fewer duplicate sends. When the final state is still unknown, the UI should ask the subscriber to wait or use an approved recovery path, while a later reconciliation pass handles the operational record.

Option Resend model Integration shape Boundary that matters
Twilio Verify Verification is a provider-managed workflow with retry controls documented for Verify A focused verification product and SDK/API surface You accept provider-specific verification semantics and channel policy; it is not a general media messaging ledger
Vonage Verify Verification requests and workflow controls are exposed through the Verify API Another dedicated verification integration You must map its workflow states and throttling behavior into your own login state machine
Amazon SNS SMS is a messaging primitive rather than a hosted OTP workflow More application-owned OTP generation, storage, and verification logic Your team carries more of the security and lifecycle design, even though the transport is familiar
Infrai The verified resend route is POST /v1/sms/resend/{id}; the original message ID remains the handle One REST contract can sit beside other backend capabilities under one key The useful fit is breadth behind one surface; SMS does not remove the need for application-level abuse controls

The trade-off is specific. Infrai gives the team one key and one REST API across backend capabilities, so the resend integration can share an authentication and request vocabulary with adjacent services. That breadth is useful when integration count is the primary constraint. It is not the right choice for a team that wants a specialized verification provider to own most of the OTP policy, or for a workflow that requires capabilities outside the verified surface, such as webhook-driven events, a hosted email OTP fallback, or business-level geographic SMS circuit breakers.

These are different products, not four interchangeable price rows. Twilio Verify and Vonage Verify put more of the verification workflow in the service. SNS gives an application a transport-oriented building block. Infrai is a plausible fit when the media backend is already adding several capabilities behind one consistent REST contract and wants the resend action to use the existing message identity. I would not choose it merely because a single route looks convenient.

How do I handle SMS OTP resend API errors in Node.js?

The UI needs more states than “button enabled” and “button disabled.” At minimum, keep sent, resending, accepted, and failed on the login attempt. The API response code is part of the transition: a successful response moves the attempt to accepted, a throttling response should leave the previous code visible while delaying another action, and a delivery-related error should produce a useful failure message without exposing provider internals to the subscriber.

The button is not the state machine.

The application should also distinguish a request timeout from a confirmed rejection. A timeout says the client lacks knowledge; it does not prove that no resend happened. Retrying immediately can therefore produce duplicate codes. Use a bounded exponential backoff, honor Retry-After when the response provides it, and require a client-supplied idempotency key for any write that the service supports. Do not invent a successful state after an exception.

Here is the core control flow in Python, kept deliberately narrow because the verified contract supplies the resend route and message ID, but does not supply a universal response schema. The caller passes the exact request fields required by its configured API contract rather than pretending an undocumented payload is stable.

import os
import random
import time
from urllib.request import Request, urlopen
from urllib.error import HTTPError, URLError


def resend_sms(base_url, message_id, body, idempotency_key, attempts=4):
    url = f"{base_url.rstrip('/')}/sms/resend/{message_id}"
    headers = {
        "Authorization": f"Bearer {os.environ['INFRAI_API_KEY']}",
        "Content-Type": "application/json",
        "Idempotency-Key": idempotency_key,
    }

    for attempt in range(attempts):
        request = Request(
            url,
            data=body,
            headers=headers,
            method="POST",
        )
        try:
            with urlopen(request, timeout=10) as response:
                status = response.status
                if 200 <= status < 300:
                    return {"state": "accepted", "status": status}
                raise RuntimeError(f"unexpected success status: {status}")
        except HTTPError as error:
            if error.code == 429 and attempt + 1 < attempts:
                retry_after = error.headers.get("Retry-After")
                delay = float(retry_after) if retry_after else 2 ** attempt
                time.sleep(delay + random.random() / 10)
                continue
            return {"state": "failed", "status": error.code}
        except (TimeoutError, URLError):
            if attempt + 1 == attempts:
                return {"state": "unknown", "status": None}
            time.sleep((2 ** attempt) + random.random() / 10)

    return {"state": "unknown", "status": None}

The snippet is intentionally not a second OTP generator. Its job is to preserve the original message identity and surface uncertainty. In a Node.js service, the same state machine belongs in the application layer, with the provider client implementing the request and the UI consuming the stored state. The language choice does not change the rule: a retryable transport error is not evidence that the resend did not occur.

Do not log body if it contains the OTP. Log the message ID, login attempt ID, attempt number, response status, and a correlation ID. If the vendor returns a structured error body, retain a redacted error class and the raw body only under a controlled security policy. Error tracking should make a throttled request distinguishable from an unreachable carrier without turning authentication logs into a second secret store.

Do not guess.

Is a single resend route enough for a media login?

No. It is enough for the resend action, not for the whole abuse boundary. SMS anti-fraud geography rules and per-country spending circuit breakers remain application responsibilities. A user who repeatedly reports non-receipt can otherwise turn a helpful recovery control into a high-volume send path.

Put a server-side resend limit on the login attempt, a cooldown in the UI, and a separate account or device risk decision. The UI message should say what the subscriber can do next: wait, check the number, or try another recovery path. It should not reveal whether a phone number is registered. That is a small wording choice with a large account-enumeration consequence.

There is another important boundary for fallback design. The available email capabilities do not include a hosted OTP interface, so switching from SMS to email requires an application-owned email-code flow. The email side also has no cancellation interface for scheduled mail, and neither namespace pushes webhook events; event handling is pull-based. A product that promises instant cross-channel orchestration needs to account for that latency instead of hiding it behind a button.

For this reason, I would use a periodic status read for operational reconciliation and treat the immediate resend response as the UI's first signal. A later status check can repair a stale local state, but it cannot make a missing webhook into a real-time event. The system should say “delivery status pending” when that is what it knows.

Which integration should the team choose?

Choose Twilio Verify or Vonage Verify when the central requirement is a provider-managed verification workflow and the team is comfortable adopting that provider's state model. Choose Amazon SNS when transport control and AWS-native composition matter more than having verification behavior managed for you; budget engineering time for OTP lifecycle, replay protection, and delivery interpretation.

Choose Infrai when integration effort is dominated by the number of backend surfaces the media product must connect, and a consistent REST contract has more value than a specialized verification product. Its broader platform surface can mean adding another capability is another contract-shaped integration rather than another key, SDK, and operational vocabulary. That is the real argument. It is not a substitute for cooldowns, regional fraud controls, retention policy, or a security review.

My decision rule is plain: compare the state you must own after the first request, not the route count printed on a feature page. If the team can preserve a stable message ID, classify errors, cap retries, and explain retention, the resend route is a sound building block. If those controls are missing, a more managed verification product may be the safer choice even when its integration surface looks less familiar.

Further reading

  • Twilio Verify API documentation
  • Vonage Verify API documentation
  • Amazon SNS SMS documentation
  • HTTP Semantics: Retry-After
  • Apple Mail Privacy Protection guide

title: Compute that takes any shape
description:
Workloads differ in how long they run, how much memory they take, and how much of the environment they control. That previously meant a different compute primitive for each job, so product iterations required provisioning infrastructure, not just working on a feature.

We built Vercel so that none of this has to be your problem. The compute layer is a single system with a simple job. Take any workload, assemble the machine it needs, swap configuration on the fly, and absorb burst capacity in real time.

We call this Fluid.

Builds ran on it first, then sandboxes, and now functions. If you've shipped on Vercel, you've been on Fluid without knowing it.

Fluid compute now runs over 15 million builds a day, 25 million sandboxes a week, and a trillion requests a month.

A history of compute

Changing a machine used to mean changing it by hand. You went down to the computer store, bought a hard drive or a stick of RAM, and swapped it in yourself.

Then you could rent bare metal when you needed it, and use it to serve a website, host a database, or send email.

Then the cloud let you request a machine in any configuration you wanted, choose its operating system, use it, and throw it away when you were done.

For agents, even the cloud is too slow. A standard VM can't provision fast enough to keep up with how they work, but this is where Fluid excels.

How a workload runs on Fluid

When a workload comes in, Fluid assembles a machine to fit its shape. If an agent needs to run code, Hive provides an isolated VM, usually one already warm, so it's ready instantly. Your own image boots on top as the environment. A Drive connects, and your files are right where you left them, because storage was never tied to the machine.

Each workload needs something different. A build is compute-bound, so it wants a beefy machine, heavy on CPU and memory. A function is IO-bound, loading specific code to run the instant a request lands, usually on a small VM. A sandbox is flexibility-bound, taking whatever configuration the work calls for with a Drive attached for user data.

Fluid compute is the execution model that all of this leans on. Many requests run on one instance, instead of each spinning up its own. Work starts immediately, and with Active CPU pricing, you pay for CPU only while your code is working, not while it waits on a database or a model.

Hive

Hive is the "hardware." We built it to control our own compute. It provisions the isolated machines every workload runs on. It picks the right machine for the job, keeps each one isolated in our multitenant environment, and does it at global scale. Hive gives every product one control-plane API, so our teams build on the same foundation instead of each maintaining their own.

Fluid images

Fluid images is the environment. Until now the OS was fixed. You ran the one the cloud gave you, not the one you chose. Now you push your own image to Vercel Container Registry, and run it across sandboxes and functions. In the background, Vercel converts images into a Fluid image in a format we call VHS (Vercel Hive Snapshot), the optimized boot format behind Dockerfile deploys and sandbox custom images, so it can resume rather than boot and a custom machine is ready in milliseconds. It uses the same technology behind Sandbox Snapshots, so optimizations in one product carry to the rest. v0 already uses it to build and run its own development environments.

Vercel Drives

Vercel Drives is the storage. Your files live in portable, durable storage that travels with the workload instead of being stranded on one machine's disk. Storage that outlives the compute attached to it is what makes the rest of the system work. Drives aren't bound to a single machine, you can swap the compute underneath it and pick up exactly where you left off in the next session. Drives attach to sandboxes today, in private beta, and extend to the rest of Fluid from there.

One system underneath

These are different shapes of the same system, not separate platforms. Because it's one compute layer underneath every product, a gain in boot time, isolation, scheduling, or caching lands across functions, sandboxes, and builds at once, instead of being rebuilt three times. New shapes of compute can be added without rebuilding the foundation. You don't end up with separate primitives that drift apart.

And it's real, not a diagram: Hive provisions a full VM in milliseconds and brings your filesystem state along with it, so you get isolation stronger than an isolate or a container, without paying for it in startup time.

The agent workload

For an agent to move fast, it needs the right machine, and it needs it immediately. The faster the machine assembles, the faster the agent works.

An agent runs untrusted code, so the machine needs a secure boundary. It brings its own tools, so the machine needs its own environment. And because an agent spins up and tears down constantly, its state has to outlive the compute. Fluid assembles that machine immediately, and then a fresh one for the next task.

For years, the machine was a fixed thing, and you fit your work to it.

In Fluid you describe the work, and the machine forms around it.

title: Idempotency keys: making retries safe for money
description:
A request that times out may still have succeeded. That single fact is why wallet and refund systems — I've built both — have to be designed around retries from day one.

Here is the sequence. A client calls POST /refunds. The server debits the merchant, credits the customer, commits — and then the response is lost: a load balancer timeout, a pod restart, a mobile network drop. The client sees an error and does the reasonable thing: it retries. The server, seeing what looks like a new request, refunds again.

Retries are not the bug. Retries are essential; networks fail all the time. The bug is an API that can't tell a retry from a new request.

The pattern

An idempotency key is a unique value the client generates once per operation — not per HTTP attempt — and sends with every attempt:

POST /refunds
Idempotency-Key: 6f1c2a9e-7d3b-4f0a-9a51-2c8e0b7d4e11
Content-Type: application/json

{"orderId": "A-1042", "amount": 1499}

The server promises: for a given key, the operation happens at most once, and every attempt gets the same response. Stripe popularised this design for its public API, and it applies to any endpoint that moves money, sends a message or creates something a user would notice twice.


Reserve first, work second, replay on retry. Explore the interactive diagram

The table 

CREATE TABLE idempotency_keys (
    key            TEXT        NOT NULL,
    client_id      TEXT        NOT NULL,
    request_hash   TEXT        NOT NULL,          -- SHA-256 of method + path + body
    status         TEXT        NOT NULL,          -- IN_PROGRESS | COMPLETED
    response_code  INT,
    response_body  JSONB,
    created_at     TIMESTAMPTZ NOT NULL DEFAULT now(),
    PRIMARY KEY (client_id, key)
);

Scope keys per client: two different clients may well generate the same string, and that must not leak one client's response to the other.

The flow, with the edge cases 

@PostMapping("/refunds")
public ResponseEntity<RefundResponse> refund(@RequestHeader("Idempotency-Key") String key,
                                             @RequestBody RefundRequest req,
                                             Principal client) {
    String hash = sha256(req);

    // 1. Reserve the key BEFORE doing any work. The primary key makes this atomic.
    int inserted = jdbc.update("""
        INSERT INTO idempotency_keys (key, client_id, request_hash, status)
        VALUES (?, ?, ?, 'IN_PROGRESS')
        ON CONFLICT (client_id, key) DO NOTHING
        """, key, client.getName(), hash);

    if (inserted == 0) {
        StoredKey existing = keys.find(client.getName(), key);
        if (!existing.requestHash().equals(hash)) {
            return ResponseEntity.unprocessableEntity().build();   // same key, different body
        }
        if (existing.status() == Status.IN_PROGRESS) {
            return ResponseEntity.status(409).build();              // concurrent retry: try again later
        }
        return existing.toResponse();                               // replay the stored result
    }

    // 2. Do the work and record the result in ONE transaction.
    return tx.execute(status -> {
        RefundResponse result = refunds.issue(req);
        keys.complete(client.getName(), key, 201, result);
        return ResponseEntity.status(201).body(result);
    });
}

Each branch exists because of a real failure mode:

Reserve before you work. If you check for the key, do the refund, and only then insert the key, two retries arriving 5 ms apart both pass the check. The INSERT ... ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING against the primary key is the lock: exactly one attempt wins the reservation.

Same key, different body. A client bug that reuses a key for a different refund must not get the first refund's response — that would silently hide the second operation. Hash the request and reject mismatches with a 422.

In progress. A retry that arrives while the first attempt is still running gets a 409. The client backs off and retries; by then the first attempt has finished and the retry gets the stored response.

Work and result commit together. If the refund commits but storing the response doesn't, the next retry finds an IN_PROGRESS row forever. Keep the business write and the key update in the same database transaction.

When the work isn't in your database

The single-transaction trick only works when the side effect lives in the same database as the key table. When step 2 calls an external payment provider, you can't roll that back. Two things help:

  1. Pass the key downstream. Most payment providers accept their own idempotency key. Derive it from yours (for example refund:{clientId}:{key}), so a retry after a crash asks the provider for the same operation instead of a new one.
  2. Recover stuck rows. A process can die between the provider call and the commit. A sweeper that finds rows stuck IN_PROGRESS for longer than your longest timeout can query the provider by the derived key and complete or release the row.

How long to keep keys

Keep keys at least as long as any client will retry, plus a margin. Stripe keeps them for 24 hours; for internal services where queues can redeliver messages days later, I'd lean longer. Delete old rows with a scheduled job — not inside the request path.

Where else this applies

The same idea shows up whenever "at least once" delivery meets "exactly once" side effects:

  • Queue consumers. Kafka and SQS redeliver. Use the message ID (or a business ID) as the key and record it in the same transaction as the effect.
  • Webhooks. Providers retry webhooks; store the event ID before acting on it.
  • Scheduled jobs. A job that runs twice after a deploy should find its own key and stop.

Takeaways

  • Retries are necessary; duplicate side effects are optional.
  • The key belongs to the operation, generated by the client once and reused on every attempt.
  • Reserve the key atomically before the work, store the response with the work, and replay it on retry.
  • Reject a reused key with a different body, and pass keys to every downstream system that moves money.

Originally published at ayushwing.com.

Apigee X

Announcement

On October 22, 2026, we released an updated version of Apigee (1-18-0-apigee-7).

Note: Rollouts of this release began today and can take four or more business days to complete across all Google Cloud zones. Your instances might not have the features and fixes available until the rollout is complete.

Security

Bug ID Description
573663408 Security fix for Apigee. Upgraded the ingress gateway to patch security vulnerabilities.
N/A Security fix for Apigee infrastructure.

Fixed

Bug ID Description
568535165 Skip main_task_wait_time and nio_task_wait_time metrics for the first 12 Prometheus scrapes during Message Processor startup warmup.
573602919 Fix generated OpenAPI specs' servers[] to carry the Apigee envgroup hostname instead of the backend target host.
562964081 The sgpUserIntentMatchingMode verdict-log field is now always present, including on dry-run policy records, and shows the mode used for the evaluation, including when sgpUserIntentMatching isn't set (CONSTRAINTS_AND_INTENT, or INTENT_ONLY when no policies match the tool call).
524115876 Fix an intermittent HTTP 400 error in the OASValidation policy's strict parameter validation that rejected valid requests.
572025634 Responses with a compressed text/event-stream body to a proxy with an EventFlow now skip EventFlow processing and pass through intact instead of returning a corrupted body.
549078690 If no SGP policy is attributed for a denial, a customer sees the generic fallback message. This fix short-circuits to show the rationale instead when no matched policy has a configured denial message.
492041991 VerifyAPIKey and VerifyAccessToken now set the apiproduct.operation.llmTokenQuota.* flow variables only from the LLM operation(s) that matched the request; they are no longer set from unmatched LLM operations or for requests that match no LLM operation.
567244615 Semantic Governance now evaluates LLM requests it previously skipped, such as OpenAI requests whose message content is an array of parts, which can produce new denials and judge-model usage. It considers every system message rather than only the last, and a non-streaming OpenAI or an Ollama tool call whose arguments are not valid JSON is now an evaluation error.
567244615 Semantic Governance no longer evaluates a request or response with a field it cannot read when a tool call is involved. It records verdict ERROR naming the field, with status MODEL_ERROR. The inline SemanticGovernance policy instead raises GovernedLLMResponseParseError or GovernedLLMProviderDetectionFailed (HTTP 500), in DRY_RUN too unless continueOnError is true. It also reads every text part of a Gemini system instruction and Gemini tool parameters given as parametersJsonSchema, and no longer loses the rest of a Claude or Gemini request when one field has an unexpected shape.
560272924 Added continuous-scan bidirectional gRPC streaming support for the SanitizeModelResponse policy over Server-Sent Events (SSE) streams, preserving native LLM provider SSE JSON envelopes and event framing.
555332621 Model Armor policies now honor HTTPClient.managementplane.skip.proxy: with it set, Model Armor callouts bypass the forward proxy like other googleapis traffic. Streaming (ContinuousScan) Model Armor traffic uses the forward proxy.
158204922 VerifyJWT now rejects a JWT whose header contains "b64":false, with fault steps.jwt.InvalidToken, as RFC 7797 section 7 requires. Previously, such a token could be accepted if KnownHeaders listed b64, IgnoreCriticalHeaders was true, or the header had no crit.
158204922 GenerateJWS supports RFC 7797 unencoded payloads. GenerateJWS now raises MissingPayload, InvalidPayload or FailedToResolveVariable for payload errors, where it previously raised GenerationFailed. KnownHeaders and CriticalHeaders in the JWS and JWT policies accept names separated by whitespace, such as one per line. A b64 header supplied through AdditionalHeaders is now rejected, with steps.jws.InvalidNameForAdditionalHeader for GenerateJWS and steps.jwt.InvalidNameForAdditionalHeader for GenerateJWT. A proxy that set b64 through an AdditionalHeaders variable produced an RFC 7797 JWS before this change, and must move to UnencodedPayload, with DetachContent for the detached form.
158204922 VerifyJWS verifies RFC 7797 unencoded-payload JWS (b64:false), attached or detached. b64 in crit no longer needs a KnownHeaders entry. VerifyJWS rejects b64:false unless crit lists b64, with the new fault steps.jws.UnencodedPayloadNotCritical; IgnoreCriticalHeaders does not change that. DecodeJWS reports the raw payload of such a JWS.
559228730 ext_proc: ImmediateResponse now carries any Content-Type (raw body bytes + preserved Content-Type); replies too large to buffer use StreamedImmediateResponse.
544751120 Semantic Governance Policies marked as dry run are now evaluated and logged without blocking the request. Each dry-run policy adds a second judge evaluation per tool-calling response, whose tokens are billed. Dry-run verdicts are written to the semantic-governance-policy log as separate records flagged sgpDryRunPolicyEvaluation=true; queries that count verdicts should add sgpDryRunPolicyEvaluation != true to exclude them.
554114419 Fixed: an AssignMessage/HTTPModifier/RaiseFault policy that creates a new request (createNew="true") in an HTTP/2 flow can now set the :path and :authority pseudo-headers instead of failing with an invalid-header error.
567812025 FILESYSTEM persistence mode makes the synchronizer skip Cassandra entirely (no connections, reads, writes, or datastore health probes).
559009293 Fixed elevated OAuth latency and Cassandra read load for AppGroup apps, including access token verification and token and authorization-code generation, by caching AppGroup lookups in the message processor runtime, matching Developer behavior.
568860869 Fixed RegularExpressionProtection patterns of the form "...." whose middle section contains regular expression syntax (for example, ".?Exception in thread." or "(?i).<script.>.*") being matched as literal text instead of as regular expressions. Such patterns now raise steps.regexprotection.ThreatDetected for all matching input.
564945600 Enhance VerifyAPIKey policy to better handle leading spaces.
502231886 Fixed the default source templates for SanitizeUserPrompt and SanitizeModelResponse so a policy that omits the source element extracts content correctly when IgnoreUnresolvedVariables is false.
562964081 Semantic Governance now honors the sgpUserIntentMatching AuthzExtension metadata key (ENABLED or DISABLED) to toggle user-intent matching in policy evaluation; DISABLED evaluates against constraints only.
565004219 Fixed Semantic Governance Policy skipping evaluation for Anthropic requests that send system as a content-block array (the form ADK and LiteLlm emit). Affected agents are now evaluated, which may produce new denials and new judge-model usage on the consumer project.
527517087 SGP policy logs written to your project now identify their originating region. resource.type changes from "global" to "generic_node" and the region appears in resource.labels.location. Anything selecting these entries by resource.type="global" must be updated -- including log-based metrics, sinks, exclusion filters and alerts, which stop matching silently rather than erroring.
575439485 JavaCallout policies that run remotely (per-contract offload) can now pass every value type allowed by the GCP-2025-023 setVariable restriction between policies (collections, maps, arrays, primitive wrappers including Character, Date, BigDecimal, UUID, java.time, atomics, JDK enums, Optional), with their types preserved, instead of failing with steps.remotepolicy.NonSerializableVariable.
575439485 Remotely executed (per-contract offload) JavaCallout policies with continueOnError="true" now continue the flow when the callout faults, instead of returning HTTP 500.
567244901 In enforce mode, Semantic Governance now blocks a tool call when the governance check cannot be completed, instead of letting it through.
573622417 Fixed an issue where istio-ingressgateway forwarded the x-envoy-decorator-operation header to upstream runtime and target backends.
571679067 removes old version of ApigeeTelemetry CRD.
571378258 The Apigee Redis container is now built from the Valkey engine (BSD-3-Clause, Linux Foundation) at version 8.1.10. Wire protocol is unchanged (RESP2) and the redis-server/redis-cli binary names are preserved.

An issue has been fixed where the Show filters option was displayed on dashboard tiles that failed to load data in view mode. This feature now performs as expected.

Fixed

An issue has been fixed where drilling into results that were filtered by string dimensions that contained backslashes returned zero rows. This feature now performs as expected.

Fixed

An issue has been fixed where pivoted queries in SQL Runner could fail to render or re-pivot unexpectedly. This feature now performs as expected.

Fixed

An issue has been fixed where the View (Expanded / Full Screen) option appeared in the tile action menu on embedded dashboards in view mode. This feature now performs as expected.

Fixed

An issue has been fixed where custom visualization tiles were truncated in dashboard PDF exports when the Expand tables to show all rows option was enabled. This feature now performs as expected.

Fixed

Table row group subtotals are now displayed only for sum and count measures. For other measure types (such as averages and count distinct) and table calculations, subtotals are now left blank rather than displaying an inaccurate summed value.

Fixed

The System Activity query_metrics Explore now records connection acquisition time (acquire_connection) for queries that are canceled while waiting in the connection pool.

Fixed

Conversational Analytics DELETE endpoints now return HTTP 404 Not Found instead of HTTP 204 No Content when you attempt to delete nonexistent resources.

Fixed

The System Activity query_metrics Explore has been updated to accurately record model initialization time for models that are loaded from cache.

Fixed

An issue has been fixed where adding a new series to a categorical chart, such as adding a new pivot value, could cause category bars to appear ungrouped. This feature now performs as expected.

Fixed

An issue has been fixed in the TypeScript and JavaScript SDKs where calling methods that have only optional parameters without passing an empty object could result in compilation or runtime errors. This feature now performs as expected.

title: Accessible color palette for Shopify stores: contrast checked
description:
If you build or maintain Shopify stores for European customers, you have probably seen the same worry in client emails lately: "Is our store ready for the European Accessibility Act?"

Nobody can answer that with a color palette alone, and I will be clear about that below. But contrast is one of the most common, most visible and cheapest accessibility defects to fix, because you can fix it once, at the design-token level, and every page inherits the fix.

So I built a small free kit: two accessible color palettes (light and dark) where every pair is already measured, delivered as JSON tokens, CSS variables, a Tailwind config and a self-test page. In this post you get the palette, the setup for Shopify, and the 20-line script to verify any palette yourself, mine included.

What the rules actually ask for

For colors, the rules most teams care about come from WCAG 2.x, Level AA:

  • Text needs a contrast ratio of at least 4.5:1 against its background. Large text (24px regular, or about 18.66px bold) needs at least 3:1. See WCAG 1.4.3, Contrast (Minimum).
  • UI components and graphics (input borders, focus rings, icons that carry meaning) need at least 3:1 against adjacent colors. See WCAG 1.4.11, Non-text Contrast.

Why does this matter for EU stores? The European Accessibility Act (Directive (EU) 2019/882) has applied since 28 June 2025 to a range of consumer-facing products and services, including e-commerce services. The technical reference most often used for websites is the harmonised standard EN 301 549, which points to WCAG 2.1 Level AA for web content. National rules and exemptions (for example for very small businesses) vary by country, so check your own situation with a qualified professional. This is not legal advice.

The five contrast mistakes I see most in store themes

  1. Placeholder text that is too light. A pale gray placeholder on white often fails 4.5:1.
  2. Light gray input borders. The border is what tells a user "this is a field", so it needs 3:1.
  3. Removed or invisible focus outlines. outline: none with no replacement leaves keyboard users lost.
  4. Brand-color buttons that were never checked in their hover state. The default passes, the hover does not (or the reverse).
  5. Error and sale colors on tinted backgrounds. Red on a pale pink badge looks fine on your monitor and fails the math.

(Disabled controls are exempt from the contrast requirements, which is why you will see greyed-out buttons that do not count.)

The fix at the token level

Instead of patching colors page by page, define every role once, as a pair that has been measured:

/* Minimalist Fashion, light */
[data-palette="fashion"] {
  --cpt-bg: #FAF8F5;
  --cpt-surface: #F0ECE6;
  --cpt-text: #1A1816;          /* 16.70:1 on bg   */
  --cpt-muted: #5A534B;         /*  7.14:1 on bg   */
  --cpt-primary: #1A1816;
  --cpt-on-primary: #FAF8F5;    /* 16.70:1 on primary */
  --cpt-link: #8A2D1C;          /*  8.01:1 on bg   */
  --cpt-border-strong: #8A8379; /*  3.53:1 on bg   */
  --cpt-focus: #2748C4;         /*  7.04:1 on bg   */
}

Two details make this robust:

  • Every foreground is measured on both backgrounds you actually use. A card (--cpt-surface) sits on the page (--cpt-bg), so text, muted text, links and messages are checked on both.
  • State colors are part of the pair list. The button label is checked on the default and the hover background.

Free palette: Contrast-Proof Tokens Lite

The free kit contains:

  • tokens.json: design tokens with 80 color pairs and their ratios (20 pairs × 2 palettes × light and dark)
  • variables.css: native CSS variables, palette switching and automatic dark mode
  • tailwind.config.js: copy-paste Tailwind config (v3.4+, v4 snippet in the comments)
  • test_page.html: a self-test page that recalculates every ratio in your browser

The two palettes:

  • Minimalist Fashion: warm paper-white and ink with a terracotta accent, for editorial, low-ornament stores.
  • SaaS Tools: crisp white and deep slate with an indigo primary and a teal accent, for dashboards and landing pages.

Download it free: https://payhip.com/b/6FTfQ?utm_source=devto&utm_medium=article&utm_campaign=lite
Source: https://github.com/mohnadjib/contrast-proof-tokens-lite

Using it in a Shopify theme (Online Store 2.0)

  1. In the theme code editor, upload variables.css to Assets.
  2. In layout/theme.liquid, add this inside <head>: 
{{ 'variables.css' | asset_url | stylesheet_tag }}
  1. Pick a palette on the <html> tag: 
<html lang="{{ request.locale.iso_code }}" data-palette="fashion">
  1. Map your theme's selectors to the tokens in your custom CSS. For example: 
.my-primary-button {
  background: var(--cpt-primary);
  color: var(--cpt-on-primary);
}
.my-primary-button:hover {
  background: var(--cpt-primary-hover);
}
.my-input {
  border: 2px solid var(--cpt-border-strong);
  background: var(--cpt-bg);
  color: var(--cpt-text);
}
:focus-visible {
  outline: 3px solid var(--cpt-focus);
  outline-offset: 2px;
}

Replace .my-primary-button and .my-input with your theme's real class names, and test on a duplicate of your live theme first.

Don't trust me: verify any palette in 20 lines

This is the exact WCAG formula. Paste it into your browser console or a Node file:

function channel(v) {
  v /= 255;
  return v <= 0.03928 ? v / 12.92 : Math.pow((v + 0.055) / 1.055, 2.4);
}
function luminance(hex) {
  const h = hex.replace('#', '');
  const [r, g, b] = [0, 2, 4].map(i => parseInt(h.slice(i, i + 2), 16));
  return 0.2126 * channel(r) + 0.7152 * channel(g) + 0.0722 * channel(b);
}
function contrast(a, b) {
  const [la, lb] = [luminance(a), luminance(b)];
  return (Math.max(la, lb) + 0.05) / (Math.min(la, lb) + 0.05);
}

console.log(contrast('#1A1816', '#FAF8F5').toFixed(2)); // 16.70
console.log(contrast('#8A8379', '#FAF8F5').toFixed(2)); // 3.54 (the kit lists 3.53: it rounds down)

Two honest notes: use the exact value when you compare to a threshold (WCAG does not allow rounding up, so 4.499 is a fail), and remember that this checks the colors you pass in, not what is really rendered over a photo or gradient.

What color contrast will not fix

A verified palette removes one class of defects. It does not give your store:

  • keyboard navigation through menus, carts and modals
  • meaningful alt text and labels
  • a logical heading structure
  • accessible forms and error handling
  • reduced-motion support in your animations
  • accessible third-party apps and widgets

Color contrast is only one part of web accessibility. This kit does not guarantee that any website conforms to WCAG, EN 301 549 or the European Accessibility Act, and it is not legal advice. Test your real pages with real tools (and, when you can, with real users).

Your turn

If you build for a specific sector, tell me which one in the comments: it decides which palettes I add next. And if you find a pair that fails in your own check, tell me too. That is the whole point of putting the proof in the box.

Update: the full kit is out. It has 8 sector palettes (fashion, SaaS, jewelry, home, food, wellness, education, real estate), each in light and dark, 320 measured pairs, a palette-comparison page, a Shopify install guide and a command-line checker: Contrast-Proof Tokens, full kit. The two palettes from this free kit are included with identical colors.

title: Nineteen pages behind our login, nineteen loading.tsx files, and 159 uses of a component called Bone
description:
Nakodo has 19 pages behind its login. It also has 19 loading.tsx files. That is not a coincidence I noticed afterwards, it is a rule, and this is what checking it looks like:

$ for d in $(find "src/app/(app)" -name page.tsx | xargs -n1 dirname); do
    [ -f "$d/loading.tsx" ] || echo "no loading: $d"
  done
$

No output. Nineteen for 19. Together they are 885 lines, which is more code than any single page in the app, and the rest of this post is what is in them and the four decisions that shaped them.

The primitive is called Bone, and it is hatched

shadcn's Skeleton is 13 lines and ships with every install:

function Skeleton({ className, ...props }: React.ComponentProps<"div">) {
  return <div data-slot="skeleton" className={cn("animate-pulse rounded-md bg-muted", className)} {...props} />
}

It is imported exactly once in this repository, by the support panel, and that is the only place in the product where a grey pulsing rectangle appears.

Everything else uses this instead:

// Loading skeletons. Hatching means "not yet observed", so each page's
// skeleton is its own layout drawn in hatched shapes, with the text for
// screen readers.

export function Bone({ className, style }: { className?: string; style?: React.CSSProperties }) {
  return <div className={cn("hatch h-3 rounded-sm", className)} style={style} aria-hidden="true" />;
}

One hundred and fifty-nine uses. The difference between the two is one class. hatch is a diagonal line texture from the app's stylesheet, and the reason it is the skeleton fill is written in the comment: the whole product is styled as a field guide, where a hatched shape means a specimen that has not been observed yet. A thing that has not loaded is not a grey box, it is an unobserved record.

You can see the texture itself without signing in. The home page uses the same utility 36 times in its artwork, and if you grep its HTML you will find no animate-pulse anywhere, because nothing on the public pages ever loads late:

$ curl -s https://nakodo.app/ | grep -o hatch | wc -l
36
$ curl -s https://nakodo.app/ | grep -o animate-pulse | wc -l
0

Three helpers on top of it, and 19 hand-drawn layouts

The shared file is 31 lines total. Besides Bone there is FieldBone, which is the label-over-input shape that appears 15 times across the settings and setup pages, and Loading, the wrapper every one of the 19 files uses:

export function Loading({ label, className, children }: { label: string; className?: string; children: React.ReactNode }) {
  return (
    <div role="status" className={cn("motion-safe:animate-pulse", className)}>
      <span className="sr-only">{label}</span>
      {children}
    </div>
  );
}

Three things are packed into those seven lines.

role="status" with an sr-only label, because a screen reader gets nothing at all from 40 hatched divs. The labels are written per page: "Loading your profile", "Loading the proposal", "Loading your campaigns". Twelve files in the repo carry a role="status", and this is the only one that covers 19 screens, because all 19 loading files render exactly one <Loading>.

motion-safe:animate-pulse rather than animate-pulse, so the one piece of motion in a skeleton is off for anybody who has asked their system to reduce motion. The individual Bones do not animate; the container does, once, for all of them.

And aria-hidden="true" is on Bone itself rather than on the wrapper, which means the author of a page skeleton cannot forget it.

The remaining 885 lines are the 19 layouts, and they are hand-drawn rather than generated. A settings page skeleton is the real card, with the real heading, and bones where the data goes:

export default function ProfileLoading() {
  return (
    <Loading label="Loading your profile" className="space-y-5 rounded-lg border bg-card p-5 sm:p-6">
      <div className="space-y-1.5">
        <h2 className="font-sans text-base font-semibold tracking-normal">Profile</h2>
        <Bone className="w-80 max-w-full" />
      </div>
      ...

That <h2>Profile</h2> is the point of the whole approach. Eleven of the 19 loading files render at least one real heading, because the heading is not loading. It is a constant in the source of the page above it. Boning out text the server already knows makes the page flicker from a grey smear into a word for no reason, and it makes the skeleton say less than it could.

The cost is that the 19 files are 19 duplications of a layout, and nothing enforces that they stay in step with the pages they shadow. Three of them have grown large enough to extract into a shared component next to the page it belongs to, which is where skeleton.tsx files start appearing: the setup wizard's step strip, the replies list and the proposal form each have one, used by both the loading file and the page itself for its own internal pending states.

The function I would keep in any project 

// Rows fade out towards the bottom, so a skeleton never reads as a full list.
export const fade = (i: number, of: number) => ({ opacity: 1 - (i / of) * 0.7 });

Seven call sites, all of them lists: campaigns, creators, conversations, support threads, messages.

A skeleton list has to pick a number of rows, and whatever it picks is a lie, because the real answer is "three" or "forty" and nobody knows yet. Three solid rows read as "you have three campaigns". The same three rows at 100, 77 and 53 per cent opacity read as "a list, going on past here", which is both honest and the thing the eye expects of a list that is still arriving. The constant 0.7 means the last row keeps 30 per cent of its opacity, so it fades rather than disappearing.

It is one line, it took two minutes, and it is the single change that made the loading states stop looking like fake content.

The six Suspense boundaries, four of which have no fallback

loading.tsx is the route-level boundary that Next gives you for free. There are six explicit <Suspense> boundaries on top of it, and they split cleanly in two.

Two have real fallbacks, both in the campaign layout:

<Suspense fallback={<HeaderSkeleton />}>

That layout wraps every campaign page, so without a boundary the layout's own queries would delay the page's loading.tsx from appearing at all. With it, the frame arrives immediately and the header and the tab strip fill in. The tab strip's fallback is interesting: it is not a skeleton at all, it is the real CampaignTabs component with kind={null}, because the tabs are known from the URL and only their labels depend on data.

The other four have no fallback at all:

<Suspense>
  <DeletedNotice />
</Suspense>

<Suspense> with no fallback renders nothing until the child is ready, and all four children are client components that read useSearchParams. In the App Router, reading the search params in a client component opts the page out of static rendering unless it sits inside a boundary. One of these four is on the public home page, which is prerendered and served from a CDN: the notice that confirms an account was deleted reads ?deleted=1, and without that empty boundary a one-line confirmation message would make the whole marketing home page dynamic.

So the same API is doing two unrelated jobs in one codebase. With a fallback it is "show this while you wait". Without one it is "this subtree reads the URL, do not let it infect the page". Both are correct, both are three lines, and only one of them is about loading.

What the public half does instead

None of the above exists on the 76 pages in the sitemap. They have no loading.tsx, no skeleton and no spinner, because there is nothing to wait for: they are built at deploy time from content that lives in the repository, and the server sends finished HTML.

That asymmetry is worth stating plainly, because it is the actual reason the 885 lines are affordable. Loading states are a cost you pay per page that reads a database, and the 76 public URLs do not read one. Go and click around the guides or the pricing page and nothing ever fades in, because nothing was ever absent.

There is one more exception, and it is not static. The operator's panel at /admin is seven pages, every one of them reading the database, and it has zero loading.tsx files. Six hundred milliseconds of nothing on a route only I can reach never once annoyed me enough to write a skeleton for it, which is the most honest sentence in this post: 885 lines of loading state is not politeness, it is what you build for the pages other people wait on.

The numbers, in one place

Thing Count
Pages behind the login 19
loading.tsx files 19
Lines of loading UI 885
<Bone> uses 159
<FieldBone> uses 15
fade() call sites 7
Files with role="status" 12
loading.tsx files in /admin 0
shadcn Skeleton imports 1
Explicit Suspense boundaries 6
Of those, with no fallback 4

The thing I did not expect when I counted was the last two rows. I think of Suspense as the loading API and loading.tsx as sugar over it, and in this codebase it is the other way round: the route convention does all of the loading, and two thirds of the explicit boundaries are there to keep a page static.
