title: Bulk Domain Expiry & WHOIS Lookup in Python with RDAP (and the .io Trap)
description:
WHOIS is on its way out. The registries now publish the same data through RDAP, a JSON API that's free, needs no key, and returns registrar, creation and expiry dates, and status in a consistent format. If you track client domains, buy expiring names, or audit a portfolio, a few lines of Python replace a paid WHOIS API.

The script

rdap.org is a public bootstrap service: request rdap.org/domain/<name> and it redirects you to the right registry. Standard library only:

"""Bulk domain lookup with RDAP (the official successor to WHOIS): registrar, created, expires, status.
Usage: python3 domain_expiry.py apify.com python.org some-free-name-123.com"""
import json
import socket
import sys
import urllib.error
import urllib.request
from concurrent.futures import ThreadPoolExecutor


def rdap(domain):
    url = f"https://rdap.org/domain/{domain}"  # redirects to the right registry's RDAP server
    try:
        with urllib.request.urlopen(urllib.request.Request(url, headers={"Accept": "application/rdap+json", "User-Agent": "domain-expiry-script"}), timeout=20) as r:
            data = json.load(r)
    except urllib.error.HTTPError as e:
        if e.code != 404:
            return {"domain": domain, "status": f"HTTP {e.code}"}
        # 404 means "no RDAP record", which is NOT proof it's free: some registries (.io, .co…) have no RDAP at all
        try:
            socket.getaddrinfo(domain, None)
            return {"domain": domain, "status": "registered (no RDAP)"}
        except socket.gaierror:
            return {"domain": domain, "status": "maybe free"}
    events = {e["eventAction"]: e["eventDate"][:10] for e in data.get("events", [])}
    registrar = next((v[3] for ent in data.get("entities", []) if "registrar" in ent.get("roles", [])
                      for v in ent.get("vcardArray", [None, []])[1] if v[0] == "fn"), "")
    return {"domain": domain, "status": "registered", "registrar": registrar,
            "created": events.get("registration", ""), "expires": events.get("expiration", "")}


with ThreadPoolExecutor(5) as pool:
    for row in pool.map(rdap, sys.argv[1:]):
        print(f"{row['domain']:28} {row['status']:20} {row.get('expires', ''):11} {row.get('registrar', '')}")

Real run (October 2026):

$ python3 domain_expiry.py apify.com python.org openalex.org github.io zzqxv-free-name-12345.com
apify.com                    registered           2035-06-02  Amazon Registrar, Inc.
python.org                   registered           2033-03-28  Gandi SAS
openalex.org                 registered           2028-03-14  GoDaddy.com, LLC
github.io                    registered (no RDAP)
zzqxv-free-name-12345.com    maybe free

Three traps I hit writing this

  1. The .io trap. My first version printed github.io → available?, which is obviously wrong. Some registries (.io, .co, and others) don't run RDAP at all, so a 404 means "no RDAP record", not "free". The fix: on 404, check DNS. If the name resolves, it's registered.
  2. 403s from .org. The .org registry rejected requests with no User-Agent. Always send one.
  3. "Maybe free" really means maybe. No RDAP record and no DNS still isn't proof: names can be reserved, premium, or registered with no DNS. Confirm at a registrar before you get excited.

Also: RDAP servers rate-limit. Keep concurrency low (5 here) for big lists.

Thousands of domains, scheduled

For portfolio checks or weekly expiry monitoring, I put a fuller version on Apify: WHOIS Domain Lookup. It covers RDAP across 1,200+ endings, DNS records (A, MX, NS, TXT), deduplication, and graceful handling of registries without RDAP. It costs $2 per 1,000 domains, and endings without RDAP are DNS-only and free. It never returns registrant contact details.

Either way, the script above is yours.

More free scripts and tools from Kramer Labs.

title: NuPrint: printing without the phone app
description:
I have a little ZEITEL SC03h thermal printer. It's handy for labels, to-do lists and small notes, but using it meant going through the phone app. Even when whatever I wanted to print was already on my laptop, I had to send it to my phone first.

I wanted to get rid of that extra step. That was how NuPrint started.

It wasn't something I built in one stretch. I work full time and have other things going on, so I'd pick it up when I had time, make some progress, then leave it for a while. There were a few attempts before this one that didn't get very far.

Getting it to print

There wasn't any public documentation for the printer, so I started looking through the Android app with JADX. The app already knew how to talk to it; I needed to work out what it was sending.

A lot of that was digging through commands, checksums and the way images were converted into something the printer could understand. There were also a few things that weren't obvious at all. The Bluetooth service it advertised wasn't the one it used for printing, which explained why looking for the printing service wasn't finding it. Even the capitalisation of the model name mattered. Two names that looked almost identical needed different settings.

I did most of that initial digging myself. Eventually I gave what I had to Codex, and it got the remaining pieces working in about an hour. I had a small Python app that could actually print.

That was the point where it started moving again. I'd spent all this time figuring out the printer, and now there was something working to build on. From there, I planned the Rust app with Claude Code, and I've spent roughly the last month building it around my day job.

The Python version was basic. A little window, some text and image handling, and Bluetooth. The first test was a strip with a border and some text. It came out properly, and I kept that version around as a reference for the rewrite rather than trying to turn it into the finished app.

The Rust version

NuPrint is now a Rust app with a Tauri and React UI, plus a command-line tool. I kept the printing logic separate from the UI so both could use the same code, without tying the whole thing to one operating system.

The working Python version helped here. I could compare what the Rust code produced against output I already knew printed correctly. There are tests for that now, along with plenty of other checks that don't need the printer connected.

Getting a clean print was only part of it, though. I also had to think about what happens when Bluetooth disconnects or the app closes halfway through a job. I didn't want it automatically trying again when it had no way of knowing how much paper had already come out. Interrupted jobs are left for the user to check instead.

That also affected the wording in the app. Sending everything successfully isn't quite the same as knowing the print came out correctly, so I avoided simply calling that "printed".

There was some cleanup around saved jobs and logs too. A review caught text and PDF passwords being retained with jobs, which I fixed. Exported logs leave out identifying details by default.

A detour into Slint

Somewhere along the way I started wondering whether I could make the UI in Rust as well, without the web view.

I asked Opus about egui and Slint. The advice was to stay with Tauri for what I wanted, especially with the possibility of mobile later. But I still wanted to try Slint, and the shared core meant I didn't have to rewrite the printing side to do it.

So I had Opus build a Slint version of the UI. It got surprisingly far: printer discovery, previews, the queue, settings. It was usable enough that I kept working on it.

The fonts were the first thing that bothered me. Small text looked blurry and different from the other apps on my machine. Switching to Skia sorted that out, but then I got a different problem on Windows: the NVIDIA overlay decided this little printer app was a game. The window was also flickering on my HDR monitor.

Using Skia's software rendering fixed that. I looked at Qt as another option, but didn't take that further.

The oddest problem was moving the window between my monitors. They use different scaling settings, and the window kept getting bigger as I dragged it back and forth. Eventually it was wider than the screen. I traced that back to how Slint handled the scaling change and added a workaround to keep the size consistent.

I spent more time on fonts and window behaviour than I'd expected to spend on a printer app.

The Slint version ended up staying. Releases now include both versions, although Tauri is still the main app and the Slint one is less tested. They use the same printing core, so I don't have two separate implementations of the protocol to maintain.

Making it something other people could use

Once it was working on my machines, I started sorting out the repository, installers and releases. I put it under the MIT licence and set up pull requests and CI across Windows, macOS and Linux. Releases build installers for both apps, and everything has to pass before the release is published.

There were a few things to learn there too. I put a version override in an empty commit for release-please, only for GitHub to drop the commit during the rebase merge. The release came out with a different version than I'd intended. That override now goes on a commit that actually changes something.

I also had Opus review the code and help plan some cleanup. For performance work, the rule was to measure first and keep a change only if it made a useful difference.

Some changes were worth doing. Keeping the log file open instead of reopening it for every line helped, and limiting how many previews were being rendered at once brought memory use down quite a bit. Other ideas would have saved a few milliseconds on a print that spent far longer being sent over Bluetooth, so I left those alone.

I managed to confuse myself with the benchmarks as well. One change initially looked like it did nothing. It turned out that two copies of the repo were sharing a build directory, and I was testing the same old binary twice. Separate build directories gave me the comparison I'd meant to run.

Testing cancellation also turned up a Windows Bluetooth issue. Cancelling a scan could leave the next scan apparently finding nothing. That needed some recovery handling rather than just assuming another scan would work.

Signing, updates, and what's left

The installers still have the usual unsigned-app warnings. I haven't done Apple notarization, and I've applied to the SignPath Foundation for Windows signing but am still waiting on that.

The release builds do have GitHub attestations, so there's a way to verify where a download came from. The update files are signed too, although that's separate from getting rid of the operating system's installer warnings.

I've added in-app updates, with checking turned off unless you enable it or check manually. I didn't want a printer app going online without being asked. Updates also wait while something is printing, rather than restarting in the middle of a job.

A review caught a problem in the Slint updater's version checks, which is fixed. Adding updates also broke the Mac packaging on the first attempt because the app bundle wasn't being kept for the update step. That held up the release until I fixed the build.

I haven't watched an update install end to end yet. This is the first release with the updater in it, so that test comes with the next one.

As for printer support, I've used NuPrint with my SC03h on Windows and macOS. There's a Linux build, but I haven't tested it with the printer yet. The phone app listed other models with matching settings, so I've exposed those as experimental. I only own the one printer, and I don't want to imply I've tested hardware I haven't.

It's grown quite a bit from the Python test. AI helped me get past the point where the earlier attempts had stalled, and a lot of the work since then has been testing, reviewing and fixing things I wouldn't have thought about at the start.

NuPrint is open source under the MIT licence, with builds for Windows, macOS and Linux. If you have one of these little printers and try it, I'd be interested to hear how it works for you.

First posted on my blog, Free practice.

title: How to Rate-Limit OTP Requests for SMS-Based 2FA in Node.js: Delivery Reliability
description:
Short answer: to rate-limit OTP requests for SMS-based 2FA in Node.js, put the limit in your backend before you ask an SMS provider to send anything. Count requests by normalized phone number and login session, enforce a fixed window, then add progressive backoff for repeated denials. The provider route is the delivery boundary; it should never be your abuse-control system.

For a password-reset message with a short expiry, delivery reliability is the decision axis. A fast SMS that can be requested 40 times in a minute is not reliable for the account, the carrier, or the bill. In a Node.js service, I model the workflow as two separate decisions: may this identity request another code, and did the delivery service accept the permitted request? Keeping those decisions separate makes provider changes much less disruptive.

Infrai belongs at that second boundary, not in the security policy. Its POST /v1/sms/otp capability can be the delivery adapter while the application keeps the same counters and verification state; the public discovery surface gives the adapter a contract to inspect before it sends. That separation is useful when the backend service changes but the reset flow should not.

Small limits matter.

So does a clear boundary.

How should Node.js rate-limit OTP requests for SMS-based 2FA?

Use two counters, not one. The phone key protects a destination from an attacker who can replay a reset form. The session key protects a single account flow when the user changes devices or enters the wrong number repeatedly. Store each request timestamp in Redis or a database, with a short expiry longer than the request window. A useful starting policy is one request per phone in 60 seconds, with a small session allowance and a longer backoff after denials. Tune those values with delivery and support data; they are policy, not a universal constant.

The counter operation must be atomic. A read followed by a write has a race: two application workers can both observe a free slot and send two messages. Redis transactions, a Lua script, or a database row protected by a lock can make the check-and-increment one decision. Keep the response deliberately vague. “Try again later” tells a real user what to do without confirming whether a phone number has an account. That detail is easy to miss in a notebook and painful to discover after adding a second Node.js worker, because the in-process map then becomes two independent rate limiters.

Here is a complete in-memory version of the policy. It is useful as an evaluation harness and as a notebook-to-prod reference; replace the dictionary with an atomic Redis operation before using it across workers.

from dataclasses import dataclass, field
from time import monotonic
from typing import Dict, List, Tuple


@dataclass
class OtpLimiter:
    window_seconds: int = 60
    phone_limit: int = 1
    session_limit: int = 3
    base_backoff_seconds: int = 30
    requests: Dict[str, List[float]] = field(default_factory=dict)
    denials: Dict[str, int] = field(default_factory=dict)

    def allow(self, phone: str, session_id: str) -> Tuple[bool, int]:
        now = monotonic()
        phone_key = f"phone:{phone}"
        session_key = f"session:{session_id}"

        for key in (phone_key, session_key):
            recent = self.requests.get(key, [])
            self.requests[key] = [stamp for stamp in recent
                                  if now - stamp < self.window_seconds]

        if len(self.requests[phone_key]) >= self.phone_limit:
            return self._deny(phone_key, now)
        if len(self.requests[session_key]) >= self.session_limit:
            return self._deny(session_key, now)

        self.requests[phone_key].append(now)
        self.requests[session_key].append(now)
        self.denials.pop(phone_key, None)
        return True, 0

    def _deny(self, key: str, now: float) -> Tuple[bool, int]:
        count = self.denials.get(key, 0) + 1
        self.denials[key] = count
        wait = self.base_backoff_seconds * (2 ** min(count - 1, 4))
        return False, wait


limiter = OtpLimiter()
print(limiter.allow("+15551234567", "reset-session-1"))
print(limiter.allow("+15551234567", "reset-session-1"))

Before wiring the send adapter, this small client checks the live public contract. It uses the same error discipline I want around the OTP call: an explicit method, bounded 429 backoff, and a useful exception for other failures. The discovery response is the input to the adapter, so the example does not invent an OTP field.

import os
import time

import requests


def load_infrai_discovery():
    url = "https://api.infrai.cc/v1/discovery"
    headers = {"Authorization": f"Bearer {os.environ['INFRAI_API_KEY']}"}

    for attempt in range(5):
        response = requests.request(method="GET", url=url, headers=headers, timeout=10)
        if response.status_code == 429:
            retry_after = int(response.headers.get("Retry-After", "1"))
            time.sleep(min(retry_after, 32))
            continue
        if not response.ok:
            raise RuntimeError(f"Infrai discovery failed: {response.status_code} {response.text}")
        return response.json()

    raise RuntimeError("Infrai discovery remained rate-limited after 5 attempts")


discovery = load_infrai_discovery()
print(discovery["version"])

The first result should be allowed and the second should return a denial with a wait value. In production, return HTTP 429 with a Retry-After value derived from the policy, and log the reason without logging the OTP itself. The application should not retry a 429 immediately.

The adapter still needs the live OTP schema. Do not turn a guessed request body into a production integration.

Why does a short expiry change the design?

A five-minute code and a one-minute request window are different clocks. The code record needs a single-use state, an expiry, and an attempt counter. A request limiter needs a rolling history. Reusing one field for both creates odd behavior: a user can be locked out after one expired code, or an attacker can keep requesting fresh codes while never verifying one.

I also make the send boundary idempotent. Generate a request identifier from the reset session and code generation event, pass it through the provider adapter, and persist the accepted result before returning success. A retry after a network timeout must not create a second SMS. If the delivery surface does not accept an idempotency key, deduplicate in the application and treat an ambiguous response as pending rather than blindly sending again.

For an Infrai-backed adapter, the relevant SMS capability is POST /v1/sms/otp. Its public discovery surface describes the contract, so the adapter can keep the rest of the reset flow independent of the service behind it. That is the practical advantage of a stable boundary: changing the delivery implementation does not require rewriting counters, expiry, or verification state. The request schema should be loaded from discovery at integration time rather than guessed in an article.

Which provider fits the operating bill?

The cheapest-looking send call is rarely the whole workload. Count the application state, retry behavior, delivery status handling, abuse controls, and the time spent reconciling a second integration. Then compare that total with the traffic pattern you actually have: normal resets, resend bursts, carrier delays, and attack traffic.

Option Where it fits Boundary to keep visible
Twilio Verify A managed verification flow with established messaging integrations Your product still needs account-specific throttling, reset-session state, and its own recovery policy
Vonage Verify A verification product for teams already aligned with Vonage's communications stack Confirm regional sender, carrier, and fallback behavior before making it the only path
AWS End User Messaging SMS Teams that want SMS delivery close to an existing AWS control plane More of the OTP lifecycle and abuse policy belongs in your application
Infrai A plain REST boundary when one key and a consistent backend surface reduce integration overhead It does not remove your rate limiter, geography-based spend guard, or delivery-event polling work

Twilio and Vonage are reasonable choices when a managed verification product is the primary requirement. AWS is a natural candidate when operational ownership already sits in AWS. Infrai is worth trying for the delivery portion of this workflow when keeping the application contract stable while the service behind it changes matters more than buying a specialist verification product. Its public discovery endpoint is self-describing, and documented capabilities include runnable examples across ten languages; that reduces adapter and maintenance work without moving security policy into the provider.

The trade-off is important. Infrai has no hosted email OTP interface, no webhook event push in these namespaces, and no voice, WhatsApp, or RCS channel. SMS geography fences and country-based spend breakers remain application work. If your recovery design requires a managed multi-channel verification journey or real-time push events, Twilio Verify or Vonage may be the better fit.

My recommendation is narrow: try Infrai for the SMS delivery adapter when your team already owns the OTP state machine and wants a stable REST contract across backend capabilities. Keep the limiter, expiry, idempotency, and regional policy in your service. That is where reliability is decided.

What should you measure before switching?

Start with a replayable test set rather than a vendor leaderboard. Include one normal request, two concurrent requests for the same phone, repeated requests after a denial, a delayed provider response, and a retry after a timeout. Assert that only one code is active, the second concurrent request is rejected, a rejected request does not call the provider, and the user-facing response does not reveal account existence.

Track accepted requests, 429 responses, delivery status, verification success, expiry rate, and duplicate-send rate. Keep provider cost and latency metadata beside the reset-session identifier, not beside the phone number in logs. This gives you an effective workload bill and a way to spot a policy that is too strict for real users or too permissive for bots.

If this boundary fits your system, start with the SMS OTP guidance and validate the live request schema before wiring the adapter.

References

  • Twilio Verify documentation
  • Vonage Verify overview
  • AWS End User Messaging SMS
  • Google email sender guidelines
  • Infrai public capability discovery

title: Webhook-only 'paid': wiring Google sign-in and Razorpay for a one-time Rs 3,999 product
description:
Content365 sells one thing: a year of branded social media posts for one business, for Rs 3,999 including GST, paid once. I built it, and the payment path is small enough to describe in one post. The design goal was boring on purpose: exactly one way for an order to become paid, and nothing the browser says can change that.

Here is the flow and the reasoning behind each piece. No keys and no secrets, just the shape.

Sign-in stores as little as possible. Customers sign in with Google. We keep four things: Google's stable account id, the email, the name and the profile picture. We do not keep Google access or refresh tokens, because we never call Google on the user's behalf. The session is an HttpOnly cookie that lasts 30 days. Fewer stored credentials means fewer things to leak and fewer things to rotate.

The order comes first, payment second. After sign-in, the customer creates a brand. The only required field is the business name; the logo and details can come later. Creating the brand creates an order, and that order starts on the free plan: every account gets 2 free posts for its brand every 48 hours. If the customer later pays, the same order continues to the full 365 days and keeps the free posts already made. A customer who clicks 'Buy now' gets an order marked as a purchase, which skips the free previews and goes straight to checkout.

The point of one order for both paths is that nothing has to be migrated at the moment of payment. Paying only changes the order's state.

The server sets the price. The browser never sends an amount. When checkout opens, the server creates the Razorpay order for 399900 paise. Money is stored as integer paise, which avoids floating-point drift, and the GST split is fixed in code: Rs 3,388.98 plus Rs 610.02 at 18%. If someone edits the page's JavaScript, the worst they can do is break their own checkout.

Only the signed webhook means 'paid'. Razorpay Checkout runs in the browser and calls a success handler when the customer completes payment. It is tempting to mark the order paid right there. We don't. The browser callback only updates the screen to say the payment is being confirmed. The order is marked paid when Razorpay's server calls our webhook endpoint with a signed payload and the signature checks out. Then, and only then, the order is queued for its full year.

Why be this strict? Because the browser is the one party in the transaction we cannot trust. It can be closed mid-flow, replayed or edited. The webhook comes from Razorpay, signed, server to server. A single source of truth also keeps support simple. If a customer says they paid and the order is not paid, the question is always 'did the webhook arrive?', never 'which of three code paths ran?'.

Two practical notes if you build this yourself. Webhooks can arrive more than once and out of order, so make the transition to paid idempotent. And keep checkout behind a server-side switch, as we do, so you can turn buying off without a deploy if something upstream misbehaves.

Analytics follow the same rule. Our Meta Conversions API events are built on the server, and the Meta pixel never loads on signed-in pages. The server reports a Purchase only for a real Razorpay payment reference. Demo orders and orders our team marks as paid by hand never count as purchases, and those server events carry only a hashed email and a user id. A test can't inflate the purchase numbers.

On refunds and changes, we keep it simple and honest while the written policy is finalised: they are agreed case by case before work begins, and we ask buyers to ask us before paying what can be changed.

What I would tell anyone building a one-time product in India: keep the price on the server, store paise rather than rupees, let exactly one signed message decide 'paid', and tie purchase events to real payment references. None of it is clever. All of it saves you a bad day.

If you want to see the flow from the customer side, https://content365.si lets you make 2 free posts every 48 hours with no payment, and https://content365.si/offer is the full year at Rs 3,999 including GST per brand, one time. We don't post for you, and Reels are not included yet. Questions about the wiring are welcome in the comments.

title: Northflank is the ninth AI platform breached in October. I read its status page like a timeline.
description:
Northflank is the ninth AI platform breached in October. I read its status page like a timeline.

Northflank's status page has one sentence every platform dreads writing, and it wrote it in plain language: "Assume all environment variables have been decrypted." No hedging, no "out of an abundance of caution." If you stored secrets in Northflank, the company told you on October 30 to act as if they were all gone — workloads, secret groups, global secrets — and to rotate everything. I read the whole status page as a timeline, because the gaps between updates tell you what the incident actually cost in time.

The timeline, with the gaps counted

All times UTC, from Northflank's own status page (October 30–31):

Oct 30 11:43  Wiz sends a threat alert
Oct 30 11:44  Northflank engineers review the alert            (+1 min)
Oct 30 12:02  initial network policy patch                     (+18 min)
Oct 30 12:50  additional patching deployed                     (+48 min)
Oct 30 13:00  Wiz incident-response (CIRT) support requested   (+10 min)
Oct 30 13:05  additional patching deployed                     (+5 min)
Oct 30 13:40  first customer warning: rotate env vars          (+35 min)
Oct 30 13:58  "Assume all environment variables have been
             decrypted. Disable/rotate all keys."            (+18 min)
Oct 30 15:12  secret rotation enabled for Postgres and MongoDB;
             "multiple users are confirming that their AI
             keys have been used"                             (+1h 14min)
Oct 30 19:28  "investigation is ongoing... no further
             confirmed findings"                              (+4h 16min)
Oct 30 23:38  users report unauthorized use of AI API keys;
             rotate at the issuing provider, check provider
             usage and billing logs                           (+4h 10min)
Oct 31 01:04  audit logs enabled for all customers,
             including free users                             (+1h 26min)
Oct 31 13:34  secret rotation for MySQL and Redis now
             available to all customers                       (+12h 30min)

Two numbers stand out. First: 1 hour 57 minutes from the Wiz alert to the first customer-facing warning, and 2 hours 15 minutes to the blunt "assume everything is decrypted" version. That is fast for an incident response, and it still wasn't fast enough — by 15:12, barely three and a half hours after the alert, users were already confirming their AI keys had been used. Second: 12 hours 30 minutes between audit logs for everyone and rotation tooling for MySQL and Redis. Rotation tooling rolls out database by database, which means the remediation itself was a queue, and the last customers in that queue waited more than a day from the alert (25 hours 51 minutes, alert to MySQL/Redis rotation).

Why "assume all decrypted" is the honest sentence

The status page never says what was taken, how the attacker got in, or how many customers are affected. As of the latest update I read, there is no published root cause and no statement about whether bring-your-own-cloud customers are affected. In that vacuum, "assume all decrypted" is the only instruction that doesn't depend on facts the company doesn't have yet. The alternative — "rotate the keys we think were touched" — would have been a guess dressed as precision.

It also matches the pattern of the whole month. Wiz's "Black October" research, published October 30, counts nine AI developer platforms disclosing incidents in October alone:

Oct  6  Fireworks AI
Oct  9  Andromeda
Oct 14  Zeabur
Oct 15  Lightning AI
Oct 16-17  OpenCode
Oct 20  Railway
Oct 23  Warp
Oct 28  CommandCode
Oct 30  Northflank

Wiz says there is no single vulnerability or dependency linking them. What links them is the target: stored environment variables, with AI keys first in line. And Wiz traced what happened to two enterprise Bedrock keys stolen in this wave: tested within 30 minutes of the reported credential access — a single model call from a residential IP, part of a one-minute sweep across many organizations — then left nearly silent for four and seven days, then roughly 2.5 million calls and over $100,000 at list price. The quiet days are the part that should scare you: a stolen key that passes a spot check on day one can still detonate on day seven. Northflank's advice to check provider billing logs, not just rotate, is aimed exactly at that window.

Two things to keep straight. Wiz does not say the two traced Bedrock keys came from Northflank — only from "one of these vendor breaches." And nobody has shown the nine incidents share one attacker. The shared fact is narrower and worse: a platform that stores its customers' secrets in one place only needs one break-in to pay off many times over, and this month it happened nine times.

What to actually do, in order

If you have anything in Northflank, the status page's own ordering is right: revoke at the issuing provider first (rotating inside Northflank alone leaves the old key valid wherever it was copied to), then AI keys and payment keys, then database and cloud credentials, then everything else — and check provider usage logs for the quiet window, not just the loud one. If you don't use Northflank, the month still applies to you: any AI key sitting in a third-party platform should be treated as a credential with a resale market, because this month proved there is one, with same-day liquidity and a one-minute test sweep.

The uncomfortable question Northflank's timeline leaves open is the one no status page can answer yet: how does a platform decrypt — or lose control of — its customers' environment variables at all? Until that answer exists, "assume all decrypted" is not just Northflank's incident response. It's the threat model for every platform that holds your secrets.

Sources: Northflank status page, "Security incident" (updates October 30–31, 2026), read October 31, 2026; Wiz "Black October" research (October 30, 2026) as reported in contemporaneous coverage, including the nine-platform list and the two traced Bedrock keys (tested within 30 minutes, quiet 4 and 7 days, ~2.5M calls, >$100k at list price). Northflank has not published a root cause or an affected-customer count as of the updates I read; the Bedrock keys are not attributed to Northflank specifically.

title: What is the Frappe framework?
description:
When you think about building a web application, you probably think about several technologies working together: a backend framework, a frontend library, a database, authentication, APIs, and a user interface. Traditionally, developers have to select, configure, and integrate these different components before they can even begin building the actual application.

_But what if you had a framework that brought most of these essential building blocks together?

That's where Frappe Framework comes in._

Frappe is an open-source, full-stack web application framework built primarily with Python 🐍 and JavaScript. It provides developers with the tools needed to build database-driven applications without having to reinvent common functionality every time they start a new project.

Whether you're building an enterprise resource planning (ERP) system or a custom business application, Frappe provides a foundation to get you started. Let me know what you think, would you explore the Frappeverse? 😀

title: How to Build a Reusable Modal Component in React with Tailwind CSS
description:
A few months ago, I ran into some frustrating challenges when trying to build a reusable modal component using ReactJS. Of course, there are many good modal libraries out there. But, what if you don't want to overengineer your project and keep the dependencies minimal?

If you’ve ever found yourself in the same boat, let me walk you through how I solved it.

📦 Source Code: You can find the complete source code for this project in this GitHub Repository.

Prerequisites

Before following this tutorial, make sure you have:

  • Node.js (v22.0 or later) installed on your machine.
  • A code editor installed (e.g., VS Code).
  • Basic knowledge of React (Hooks, State, and Props) and JavaScript (ES6+).
  • Familiarity with running basic commands in your terminal or VS Code integrated terminal.

What We'll Cover

In this guide, we will walk through the entire process step-by-step:

  1. Setting up a New React Project with Vite
  2. Installing and Configuring Tailwind CSS
  3. Configuring vite.config.js
  4. Importing Tailwind CSS Directives
  5. Organizing the Project Folder Structure
  6. Building the Reusable Modal Component
  7. Implementing the Modal in the Main App
  8. Conclusion

📌 Environment & Versions Used in This Tutorial:

  • Vite: v8.x
  • React: v19.x
  • Tailwind CSS: v4.3.x (using @tailwindcss/vite plugin for Vite)

Note: Tailwind CSS syntax and plugin setups often change between major versions (e.g., v3 vs v4). Make sure you are using the corresponding version or refer to the official Tailwind documentation if you encounter setup issues.

Setting up a New React Project with Vite

First create a new project using this command:

npm create vite@latest tailwind-react-modal -- --template react

During the setup, the CLI will prompt you with a few interactive options:

  1. Which linter to use? Choose ESLint for code quality standards.
  2. Install with npm and start now? Choose Yes to let the CLI automatically install dependencies and launch the development server for you.

Note: If you choose Yes on Install with npm and start now? question, make sure you're in the root project when restarting the server again

Once the process finishes, your terminal will display the local development URL, typically at http://localhost:5173/.

Installing and Configuring Tailwind CSS

Run this command in your terminal to install official tailwind v4 and its vite plugin:

npm install tailwindcss @tailwindcss/vite

Configuring vite.config.js

Add @tailwindcss/vite plugin in your vite.config.js. So, your file will look like this:

/* vite.config.js */

import react from '@vitejs/plugin-react';
import { defineConfig } from 'vite';
import tailwindcss from '@tailwindcss/vite';

// https://vite.dev/config/
export default defineConfig({
  plugins: [react(), tailwindcss()],
});

Importing Tailwind CSS Directives

Open your main css file of the project in src/index.css. Then, delete everything there.

After that import tailwindcss there:

/* src/index.css */

@import 'tailwindcss';

Different from tailwindcss v3, in tailwindcss v4, we no longer need to import @tailwind base, @tailwind components, and @tailwind utilities.

The last step for this setup is to make sure src/index.css css is being called in src/main.jsx. The file should look like this:

/* src/main.jsx */

import { StrictMode } from 'react';
import { createRoot } from 'react-dom/client';
import './index.css';
import App from './App.jsx';

createRoot(document.getElementById('root')).render(
  <StrictMode>
    <App />
  </StrictMode>,
);

Organizing the Project Folder Structure

To organize this project, we'll use this folder structure:

src
├── App.jsx
├── assets
│   ├── confirmationModal.jpg
│   ├── editProfileModal.jpg
│   ├── hero.png
│   ├── infoModal.jpg
│   ├── modalTriggers.jpg
│   ├── react.svg
│   └── vite.svg
├── components
│   ├── common
│   │   └── Modal.jsx
│   └── modals
│       ├── DeleteModal.jsx
│       ├── EditProfileModal.jsx
│       └── InfoModal.jsx
├── hooks
│   └── useModal.js
├── index.css
└── main.jsx

I'll delete the App.css, but you can keep it if you want.

We'll create three modals for this sample project: info modal, delete modal and edit profile modal. So, we can see how our reusable modal being used in three different scenarios.

Everything we need to build the project is in place. Now, it's time for the main course.

Building the Reusable Modal Component

Modal Custom Hook

We'll start our modal wiring by creating a custom hook. You might wonder: Do we really need a custom hook for something as simple as a modal? Isn't that overkill?

The hook will keep our main modal component stay clean. It also makes our modal modular and easier to manage.

Create hooks folder inside src and create a new file called useModal.js. This is how our custom hook will look like:

/* src/hooks/useModal.js */

import { useState, useCallback } from 'react';

// Simple hook to toggle modal state without repeating useState everywhere
export const useModal = (initialState = false) => {
  const [isOpen, setIsOpen] = useState(initialState);

  const openModal = useCallback(() => setIsOpen(true), []);
  const closeModal = useCallback(() => setIsOpen(false), []);
  const toggleModal = useCallback(() => setIsOpen((prev) => !prev), []);

  return { isOpen, openModal, closeModal, toggleModal };
};

We use useState to check whether our modal is open or closed, defaulting to false.

Then, we use useCallback to set the modal state. This prevents unnecessary re-renders every time a component calls the hook.

Our hook will return the modal state and our functions.

By wrapping the state inside our useCallback, we can manage multiple modals on a single page. Avoiding state collisions in each different modal.

Reusable Modal Base Component

After our hook is ready, the next thing we should take care of is the reusable modal component.

Create a new folder inside src, name it components. Inside the components folder, create a new folder called common. This is where our reusable modal component, Modal.jsx, lives.

/* src/components/common/Modal.jsx */

import { useEffect } from 'react';

export const Modal = ({
  isOpen,
  onClose,
  title,
  children,
  footer,
  maxWidth = 'max-w-lg', // flexible width so we can reuse it for different sizes
}) => {
  // Close on ESC and lock body scroll when the modal is up
  useEffect(() => {
    const handleKeyDown = (event) => {
      if (event.key === 'Escape' && isOpen) {
        onClose();
      }
    };

    if (isOpen) {
      document.body.style.overflow = 'hidden';
      window.addEventListener('keydown', handleKeyDown);
    }

    return () => {
      document.body.style.overflow = 'unset';
      window.removeEventListener('keydown', handleKeyDown);
    };
  }, [isOpen, onClose]);

  if (!isOpen) return null;

  return (
    <div
      className='fixed inset-0 z-50 flex items-center justify-center p-4 bg-slate-900/50 backdrop-blur-sm transition-opacity'
      aria-hidden='true'>
      {/* Click outside to dismiss */}
      <div
        className='absolute inset-0'
        onClick={onClose}
        aria-label='Close modal backdrop'
      />

      {/* Main dialog box */}
      <div
        role='dialog'
        aria-modal='true'
        aria-labelledby='modal-title'
        className={`relative w-full ${maxWidth} bg-white rounded-2xl shadow-2xl border border-slate-100 overflow-hidden transform transition-all z-10`}>
        {/* Header section */}
        <div className='flex items-center justify-between px-6 py-4 border-b border-slate-100'>
          <h3 id='modal-title' className='text-lg font-semibold text-slate-800'>
            {title}
          </h3>
          <button
            onClick={onClose}
            className='p-1.5 text-slate-400 hover:text-slate-600 hover:bg-slate-100 rounded-lg transition-colors cursor-pointer'
            aria-label='Close modal'>
            <svg
              className='w-5 h-5'
              fill='none'
              viewBox='0 0 24 24'
              stroke='currentColor'>
              <path
                strokeLinecap='round'
                strokeLinejoin='round'
                strokeWidth={2}
                d='M6 18L18 6M6 6l12 12'
              />
            </svg>
          </button>
        </div>

        {/* Content area */}
        <div className='px-6 py-4 text-slate-600 text-sm leading-relaxed'>
          {children}
        </div>

        {/* Optional footer for actions */}
        {footer && (
          <div className='flex items-center justify-end gap-3 px-6 py-4 bg-slate-50 border-t border-slate-100'>
            {footer}
          </div>
        )}
      </div>
    </div>
  );
};

Our reusable modal will be able to receive the following props:

  • isOpen: To check the modal state.
  • onClose: To trigger the close modal function. It'll be handled by the useModal hook.
  • title: To set the modal title displayed in the title bar.
  • footer: This is optional. If the modal is just for notice and information display, we might not need it. If the modal needs action buttons for cancellation or acceptance, we can place those buttons here.
  • maxWidth: To set the max-width of the modal, in case we need it.

We use !isOpen to return null early, so the modal stays hidden when the app first loads. Once a user triggers an action, the state flips to open and the modal pops up.

To handle side effects like managing the keydown event listener and locking background scrolling (document.body), we’ll lean on useEffect with isOpen and onClose as dependencies.

Another important thing to note is we employ role="dialog", aria-modal="true", using esc keyboard key to close modal, and lock body scroll when one of the modals is visible. What we do here is to improve user accessibility.

Use Cases

To prove that our reusable modal works, we'll use it in three different scenarios: info modal, delete modal and edit profile modal.

We'll wire each individual modal from our reusable modal component. Later, we'll call it in our App.jsx.

All individual modals will reside in src/components/modals/.

All individual modals will import Modal from ../common/Modal. Then, we'll use and fill the reusable modal properties based on our needs.

Info Modal

Our first type of modal is an info modal. Here, we'll use it for informational purposes only. Therefore, we don't need to add action buttons in the footer.

This is how InfoModal.jsx will look like:

/* src/components/modals/InfoModal.jsx */

import { Modal } from '../common/Modal';

export const InfoModal = ({ isOpen, onClose }) => {
  return (
    <Modal
      isOpen={isOpen}
      onClose={onClose}
      title='System Maintenance Notice'
      maxWidth='max-w-md'>
      <p>
        Our platform will undergo scheduled maintenance this Sunday from 2:00 AM
        to 4:00 AM UTC. Some services may be temporarily unavailable during this
        window.
      </p>
    </Modal>
  );
};

Delete Modal

Different from the info modal, in the delete modal, we'll use footer to display action buttons for the deletion process which asks for the user permission, namely: Cancel and Confirm Delete.

/* src/components/modals/DeleteModal.jsx */

import { Modal } from '../common/Modal';

export const DeleteModal = ({ isOpen, onClose, onConfirm }) => {
  return (
    <Modal
      isOpen={isOpen}
      onClose={onClose}
      title='Delete Account'
      maxWidth='max-w-md'
      footer={
        <>
          <button
            onClick={onClose}
            className='px-4 py-2 text-sm font-medium text-slate-600 hover:text-slate-800 transition-colors cursor-pointer'>
            Cancel
          </button>
          <button
            onClick={onConfirm}
            className='px-4 py-2 text-sm font-medium bg-rose-600 text-white rounded-lg hover:bg-rose-700 transition-colors cursor-pointer'>
            Confirm Delete
          </button>
        </>
      }>
      <p>
        Are you sure you want to delete your account? All of your data will be
        permanently removed. This action cannot be undone.
      </p>
    </Modal>
  );
};

Edit Profile Modal

The last modal is the edit profile modal. It'll also use the footer to display different action buttons: Cancel and Save Changes.

/* src/components/modals/EditProfileModal.jsx */

import { Modal } from '../common/Modal';

export const EditProfileModal = ({ isOpen, onClose, onSubmit }) => {
  return (
    <Modal
      isOpen={isOpen}
      onClose={onClose}
      title='Edit Profile Information'
      footer={
        <>
          <button
            onClick={onClose}
            className='px-4 py-2 text-sm font-medium text-slate-600 hover:bg-slate-100 rounded-lg transition-colors cursor-pointer'>
            Cancel
          </button>
          <button
            onClick={onSubmit}
            className='px-4 py-2 text-sm font-medium bg-indigo-600 text-white rounded-lg hover:bg-indigo-700 transition-colors cursor-pointer'>
            Save Changes
          </button>
        </>
      }>
      <div className='space-y-4'>
        <div>
          <label className='block text-xs font-semibold uppercase tracking-wider text-slate-500 mb-1'>
            Full Name
          </label>
          <input
            type='text'
            defaultValue='John Doe'
            className='w-full px-3 py-2 border border-slate-300 rounded-lg text-sm focus:outline-none focus:ring-2 focus:ring-indigo-500'
          />
        </div>
        <div>
          <label className='block text-xs font-semibold uppercase tracking-wider text-slate-500 mb-1'>
            Email Address
          </label>
          <input
            type='email'
            defaultValue='john@example.com'
            className='w-full px-3 py-2 border border-slate-300 rounded-lg text-sm focus:outline-none focus:ring-2 focus:ring-indigo-500'
          />
        </div>
      </div>
    </Modal>
  );
};

Implementing the Modal in the Main App

We've created everything we need. Now, it's time to see our reusable modal in action.

Edit src/App.jsx and delete everything in the App.jsx boilerplate. Then, make it to look like this:

/* src/App.jsx */

import { useModal } from './hooks/useModal';
import { InfoModal } from './components/modals/InfoModal';
import { DeleteModal } from './components/modals/DeleteModal';
import { EditProfileModal } from './components/modals/EditProfileModal';

export const App = () => {
  // Hook up states for each modal we need on this page
  const infoModal = useModal(false);
  const deleteModal = useModal(false);
  const formModal = useModal(false);

  const handleDeleteConfirm = () => {
    alert('Account deleted successfully!');
    deleteModal.closeModal();
  };

  const handleFormSubmit = () => {
    alert('Profile changes saved successfully!');
    formModal.closeModal();
  };

  return (
    <div className='min-h-screen bg-slate-50 flex flex-col items-center justify-center p-6 gap-4'>
      <h1 className='text-2xl font-bold text-slate-800 mb-2'>
        Reusable Tailwind Modal
      </h1>

      <div className='flex gap-4'>
        <button
          onClick={infoModal.openModal}
          className='px-4 py-2 bg-emerald-600 text-white font-medium rounded-lg shadow-sm hover:bg-emerald-700 transition-colors cursor-pointer'>
          Open Info Modal
        </button>

        <button
          onClick={deleteModal.openModal}
          className='px-4 py-2 bg-indigo-600 text-white font-medium rounded-lg shadow-sm hover:bg-indigo-700 transition-colors cursor-pointer'>
          Open Confirmation Modal
        </button>

        <button
          onClick={formModal.openModal}
          className='px-4 py-2 bg-white text-slate-700 border border-slate-300 font-medium rounded-lg shadow-sm hover:bg-slate-50 transition-colors cursor-pointer'>
          Open Form Modal
        </button>
      </div>

      {/* Render modals cleanly outside the main layout flow */}
      <InfoModal isOpen={infoModal.isOpen} onClose={infoModal.closeModal} />

      <DeleteModal
        isOpen={deleteModal.isOpen}
        onClose={deleteModal.closeModal}
        onConfirm={handleDeleteConfirm}
      />

      <EditProfileModal
        isOpen={formModal.isOpen}
        onClose={formModal.closeModal}
        onSubmit={handleFormSubmit}
      />
    </div>
  );
};

export default App;

The first step we import our useModal hook and every single modal we've created: InfoModal, DeleteModal and EditProfileModal.

Since we'll use three different modals, we'll create three different variables to call our useModal hook.

Some of you might be wondering why we need three. It's because each variable will hold the state for one of the three different modals we're demonstrating here.

Notice how we call the isOpen and closeModal methods from each variable.

For the DeleteModal, we will create handleDeleteConfirm where we trigger an alert to confirm our delete modal is executed successfully.

We also create handleFormSubmit function for the EditProfileModal to handle profile changes.

The handleDeleteConfirm and handleFormSubmit will go to their respective modals.

For the last step, we need to make something to trigger the modals. Here, we'll use three different buttons with their own label.

Here is the layout we've got:

Test it to see our reusable modal in action by clicking each trigger button.

Congratulations! All of our reusable modals will work seamlessly. This reusable modal component can be used anywhere in our application.

Conclusion

Many good modal libraries exist, and we can pick whatever we want from that list.

However, for those who prefer minimal project dependencies or want to avoid overengineering, a simple and modular approach like what we just did is a solid alternative.

Using just a custom hook, useModal.js, and basic react knowledge, we can easily create a reusable modal component that works seamlessly anywhere in our application.

title: From Inertia::render() to a page type
description:
You type your Inertia props by hand. Then a controller changes, and the types drift.

Inertia Typegen generates TypeScript types and route helpers for Inertia pages. It reads them from Scramble's OpenAPI document. You write no types by hand.

This post walks from the PHP input to the TypeScript output.

Install 

composer require vagebond/inertia-typegen
composer require --dev dedoc/scramble

Scramble is a development dependency. Inertia Typegen requires PHP 8.3+, Laravel 12 or 13, and Scramble 0.13.49+. It also needs inertia-laravel 2 or 3, Node 22.18+ and Vite 6+.

The PHP input

Here is a controller with an enum and a paginated resource collection.

enum PostStatus: string
{
    case Draft = 'draft';
    case Published = 'published';
}

class PostController
{
    public function index()
    {
        return Inertia::render('Posts/Index', [
            'posts' => PostResource::collection(Post::paginate()),
            'status' => PostStatus::Draft,
        ]);
    }
}

The page type

Each Inertia::render() call becomes a page type. The output below is simplified for this post.

type PostStatus = 'draft' | 'published'

type PostsIndexProps = SharedData & {
  // the paginator keeps its real shape
  posts: PostCollection
  status: PostStatus
}

Three things happen here.

  • PHP enums become a union of their values.
  • JSON resources, collections and paginators keep their real shape.
  • Shared data from the Inertia middleware becomes one type that each page type includes.

Form data

Form request rules become the type of the form data.

class StorePostRequest extends FormRequest
{
    public function rules(): array
    {
        return [
            'title' => ['required', 'string'],
            'status' => ['required', Rule::enum(PostStatus::class)],
        ];
    }
}

type StorePostData = {
  title: string
  status: PostStatus
}

You change a rule in PHP. The form type follows.

Route helpers

You also get typed route helpers for each named route.

Keeping files fresh

The Vite dev server regenerates files after a PHP change. A CI check fails when committed files are stale. You commit the generated files, so a production build needs no PHP.

No HTTP endpoint is added by default. Plugins with hooks can change the document, routes and output.

The limit

The release status is 0.x. Minor releases can contain breaking changes until 1.0. So pin the minor version and check each upgrade.

Inertia Typegen is MIT licensed. The docs cover setup, route helpers and plugins:

https://baken.vagebond.nl/r/dpRMA9Ze

title: AI SDK harness layer now supports native subscription authentication
description:
The AI SDK harness layer now supports authenticating harnesses through their native subscriptions, where the underlying harness supports them. The harness layer runs different coding agents through the same HarnessAgent interface, so you can switch agents without changing your application code.

No code changes or new settings are required. The direct authentication mode uses explicit provider environment credentials when they are present, and otherwise a native subscription found on the host. The default auto mode does the same when no AI Gateway credentials are set. The ai-gateway mode never reads native subscriptions.

Native subscription credentials stay on the host. Just like with API keys, credentials are resolved at the host boundary. OAuth access tokens are refreshed there as needed. Where the sandbox supports it, the harness receives placeholder credentials and the real token is injected into outbound requests on the host.

Native subscriptions work across harness adapters wherever the harness itself supports subscription login. These include Claude Code, Cline, Codex, Cursor, fx, GitHub Copilot, Grok Build, OpenCode, and Pi.

Read the harness documentation to learn more.

title: Vercel Security Dashboard is now generally available
description:
The Vercel Security Dashboard is now generally available on all plans, giving you one place to see your security posture across every account and project.

You can access the Security Dashboard in the UI or run vercel security check in the Vercel CLI.

As teams grow and coding agents make it faster to spin up projects, small misconfigurations add up quietly. The Security Dashboard automatically flags issues like:

  • Team members without 2FA

  • Long-lived credentials that can be replaced with OIDC

  • Public preview deployments

  • Non-sensitive and stale environment variables

The Security Dashboard UI

Misconfigurations are ordered by risk with the most severe first, and each finding links to the settings that fix them.

Findings that are just noise for your team can also be muted, and all results can be exported to a CSV file for triage or reporting.

The Security Dashboard CLI

You can also run the same checks in your terminal through the new Vercel CLI vercel security check command, allowing your agents to work through the findings for you.

An agent using vercel security check --findings can read what failed, apply the fix and re-check to confirm. Fixes an agent can apply include:

  • Turning on Git fork protection

  • Marking an environment variable as sensitive

  • Replacing a static credential with OIDC federation

You can also scope the check to one project with --project when you want a narrow change set.

In CI or any other non-interactive environment, the command writes the report to stdout as JSON automatically, giving agents structured output without extra flags.

Get started by running your first scan from the Security Dashboard, and learn more in the Security Dashboard documentation.

title: Cookie Security Flags: Auditing Secure, HttpOnly, SameSite
description:
Most session hijacking bugs I find in audits are not exotic. They are a session cookie missing one attribute: HttpOnly left off so an XSS payload can read it, Secure missing so it rides over a plain HTTP request, SameSite=None set "to fix a login bug" and never reverted, or a Domain=.example.com scope that hands the cookie to every forgotten subdomain. Each takes one line to fix and about two minutes to audit, if you know what to look for in the Set-Cookie header.

I build PixelValut, a set of browser-side developer and security tools, and I run this exact audit on every Laravel and Node app I ship. Below is the workflow with real header output, the attack each flag stops, and a checklist you can paste into a pull request template.

Which cookie security flags should a session cookie have?

Direct answer: A session cookie should be set with Secure, HttpOnly, SameSite=Lax (or Strict), Path=/ and no Domain attribute, ideally using the __Host- name prefix, which the browser only accepts when those conditions hold. Add a short Max-Age or session lifetime, and regenerate the session ID on login to prevent fixation.

What each attribute does and what it stops

Attribute What the browser does Attack it limits Common mistake
Secure Sends the cookie only over HTTPS Interception on HTTP requests Missing on apps that "redirect to HTTPS anyway"
HttpOnly Hides the cookie from document.cookie Session theft through XSS Turned off so a front-end can read a token
SameSite=Lax Withholds the cookie on most cross-site subrequests and POSTs CSRF on state-changing requests Set to None globally to fix one embed
SameSite=Strict Withholds it on all cross-site requests, including top-level links CSRF, cross-site leaks Users appear logged out after clicking an email link
Domain= Shares the cookie with all subdomains Nothing; it widens scope .example.com exposes it to every subdomain
Max-Age / Expires Persists beyond the browser session Limits the replay window when short Sessions valid for a year
__Host- prefix Rejected unless Secure, Path=/ and no Domain Subdomain cookie injection and overwrite Not used because the framework default name is fixed
__Secure- prefix Rejected unless Secure Overwrite from HTTP pages Assumed to imply HttpOnly (it does not)

Without a SameSite attribute, Chromium treats a cookie as Lax, but other browsers have differed; set it explicitly.

Step 1: Read the raw Set-Cookie headers with curl

Start with a header-only request against the login page or home page. These are real responses from this morning, with values redacted:

$ curl -sI https://github.com/ | grep -i '^set-cookie'
set-cookie: _gh_sess=<redacted>; path=/; HttpOnly; secure; SameSite=Lax
set-cookie: _octo=<redacted>; expires=Sun, 31 Oct 2027 05:23:32 GMT; domain=.github.com; path=/; secure; SameSite=Lax
set-cookie: logged_in=no; expires=Sun, 31 Oct 2027 05:23:32 GMT; domain=.github.com; path=/; HttpOnly; secure; SameSite=Lax

$ curl -sI https://pixelvalut.com/ | grep -i '^set-cookie'
Set-Cookie: XSRF-TOKEN=<redacted>; expires=Sat, 31 Oct 2026 07:23:36 GMT; Max-Age=7200; path=/; secure; samesite=lax
Set-Cookie: pixelvalut_session=<redacted>; expires=Sat, 31 Oct 2026 07:23:36 GMT; Max-Age=7200; path=/; secure; httponly; samesite=lax

How I read them:

  • _gh_sess is a textbook session cookie: host-only (no Domain), HttpOnly, Secure, Lax, and no Expires, so it dies with the browser session.
  • _octo and logged_in are scoped to .github.com on purpose: non-secret state shared across subdomains, fine for a flag, never for a session ID.
  • XSRF-TOKEN on PixelValut, a Laravel app, is deliberately not HttpOnly. It is the CSRF token that the JavaScript client reads and echoes back in the X-XSRF-TOKEN header. That is by design; the secret is the session cookie next to it.
  • pixelvalut_session has Secure, HttpOnly, Lax and a two-hour Max-Age. What it lacks is the __Host- prefix, which is the next hardening step I cover below.

If you prefer the browser, the Security Headers Checker shows the response headers alongside CSP and HSTS, and my guide on auditing HTTP security headers covers the rest of that response.

Step 2: Confirm what the browser actually stored in DevTools

In Chrome or Edge, open DevTools, go to Application > Storage > Cookies and select the origin. In Firefox it is Storage > Cookies. Check four columns:

  1. HttpOnly and Secure ticked for every session or auth cookie.
  2. SameSite shows Lax or Strict, not blank or None.
  3. Domain shows the exact host (no leading dot) for session cookies.
  4. Expires / Max-Age shows "Session" or a short lifetime.

Then open the Network tab, click the login request and look at the response's Cookies sub-tab. A yellow warning icon next to a cookie means the browser blocked or modified it, and hovering shows why, for example "This Set-Cookie was blocked because it had the SameSite=None attribute but did not have the Secure attribute". That message explains most "works in Postman, not in the browser" login tickets.

Step 3: Test the scenarios that actually get exploited

Session fixation

If the session ID stays the same before and after login, an attacker who can plant a known ID in the victim's browser inherits the authenticated session. Test it:

# 1. Get an anonymous session cookie
curl -s -c jar.txt -o /dev/null https://app.example.test/login
grep session jar.txt | awk '{print $7}'   # note the value
# 2. Log in with the same jar
curl -s -b jar.txt -c jar.txt -o /dev/null -X POST https://app.example.test/login \
  -d 'email=test@example.test&password=...&_token=...'
grep session jar.txt | awk '{print $7}'   # must be different

The fix is to regenerate the ID on every privilege change. In Laravel, $request->session()->regenerate() after Auth::attempt() (the starter kits already do this); in Express with express-session, call req.session.regenerate() before setting the user.

CSRF through a permissive SameSite

SameSite=Lax blocks the cookie on cross-site POST form submissions and on cross-site fetches, which neutralizes most classic CSRF. It still sends the cookie on top-level GET navigations, so any state-changing GET endpoint (/logout, /delete?id=, /approve?invoice=) remains exposed. Audit routes for that, and keep a CSRF token on forms anyway; SameSite is a second layer, not a replacement.

If you genuinely need SameSite=None (a cross-site iframe), set it only on that cookie, always with Secure.

Subdomain cookie injection

A cookie set with Domain=.example.com from blog.example.com, or from a compromised marketing subdomain, can shadow or overwrite the session cookie of app.example.com. The __Host- prefix closes this: the browser refuses a __Host- cookie that has a Domain attribute, a path other than /, or no Secure flag, so no subdomain can plant one.

Set-Cookie: __Host-session=<value>; Path=/; Secure; HttpOnly; SameSite=Lax; Max-Age=7200

In Laravel that is a config change, SESSION_COOKIE=__Host-app_session, SESSION_DOMAIN=null, SESSION_SECURE_COOKIE=true in .env. In Express:

app.use(session({
  name: '__Host-sid',
  secret: process.env.SESSION_SECRET,
  resave: false,
  saveUninitialized: false,
  cookie: { httpOnly: true, secure: true, sameSite: 'lax', path: '/', maxAge: 2 * 60 * 60 * 1000 }
}));
app.set('trust proxy', 1); // behind a TLS-terminating proxy, or secure cookies are never sent

The trust proxy line is the failure I see most in Node deployments: behind Nginx or a load balancer, Express thinks the request is HTTP and silently refuses to set the Secure cookie.

Tokens in readable cookies

If your SPA stores a JWT in a non-HttpOnly cookie or in localStorage, any XSS can exfiltrate it. Decode one with the JWT Decoder and check its lifetime; my article on JWT security pitfalls explains why I prefer an HttpOnly session cookie for first-party apps.

Severity framework for findings

Finding Severity I assign Why
Session cookie without HttpOnly High Any XSS becomes account takeover
Session cookie without Secure on an HTTPS site High One HTTP request leaks it
Session ID not regenerated on login High Enables session fixation
SameSite=None on the session cookie Medium to high CSRF depends entirely on tokens
Domain=.example.com on the session cookie Medium Every subdomain receives it
No __Host- prefix Low Hardening against subdomain injection
Session lifetime of weeks or more Low to medium Larger replay window

The 10-point cookie audit checklist

  1. Run curl -sI on the login page, the post-login redirect and one API route.
  2. List every cookie and mark which ones are secret (session, refresh, remember-me).
  3. Secret cookies: Secure and HttpOnly present.
  4. Secret cookies: SameSite=Lax or Strict, set explicitly.
  5. Secret cookies: no Domain attribute; consider the __Host- prefix.
  6. Lifetime matches policy; remember-me tokens are separate and rotate.
  7. Session ID changes after login and after privilege changes.
  8. No state-changing GET routes; CSRF tokens on forms.
  9. DevTools Network tab shows no blocked-cookie warnings.
  10. Behind a proxy, the app trusts X-Forwarded-Proto so Secure cookies are actually sent.

Frequently asked questions

Does HttpOnly prevent XSS?

No. It prevents JavaScript from reading the cookie, which stops the most common XSS payoff, session theft. An attacker can still act inside the victim's session while the page is open, so you still need output encoding and a Content Security Policy.

Is SameSite=Lax enough to stop CSRF?

It blocks the cookie on cross-site POSTs and subrequests, which covers most CSRF. It still sends the cookie on top-level GET navigations, so state-changing GET routes stay exposed. Keep CSRF tokens on forms and treat SameSite as a second layer.

Why is my Secure cookie not being set in production?

Usually because a reverse proxy terminates TLS and the app sees plain HTTP. Configure the framework to trust the proxy's X-Forwarded-Proto header, such as Express's trust proxy setting or Laravel's TrustProxies middleware, and the cookie will be issued.

What is the difference between __Host- and __Secure- cookies?

A __Secure- cookie must have the Secure flag. A __Host- cookie must also have Path=/ and no Domain attribute, which locks it to one exact host. Neither implies HttpOnly or SameSite.

Should the CSRF token cookie be HttpOnly?

Not when the pattern requires JavaScript to read it, as with Laravel's XSRF-TOKEN cookie that the client echoes in a request header. The token is not a credential on its own; the session cookie it pairs with must be HttpOnly.

Can I audit cookies without logging in?

Partly. Anonymous responses show the session cookie's attributes, since most frameworks issue one on the first visit. For fixation and post-login cookies, use a test account, never a real user's session.
