title: What a Wildlife Journal Can Teach Us About Building Better Apps
description:
Most apps are built around a simple idea: help someone record, find, or understand something. Yet even a small app can become confusing when it asks too many questions, hides important information, or gives users a false sense of certainty.

A wildlife observation journal offers a useful way to think about these problems.

Imagine someone spotting a bird near a lake. They have a few seconds to notice its colour, size, movement, and surroundings. Later, they want to save what they saw. They may know the species, but they may also be unsure.

The software needs to support both situations.

For a wildlife website such as Viltnemnda, which I run, an observation journal is one possible connection between educational content and a useful digital tool. It raises practical questions about forms, privacy, data storage, and responsible design.

This article explores those decisions without writing code. The same lessons apply to reading trackers, gardening journals, travel notebooks, and many other small personal apps.

Disclosure: I run the wildlife website linked in this article. This article was prepared with AI assistance.

Start With the Moment Someone Needs the App

Before choosing a framework or designing a dashboard, consider the situation in which someone will use the tool.

A wildlife observer might be outside, holding a phone in one hand. The light could make the screen difficult to read. The internet connection might be unreliable. They may want to save a quick note and return to watching the animal.

That is a different situation from someone sitting at a desk with time to fill in a detailed form.

For a first version, the main task could be:

Save a useful description of an observation before the details are forgotten.

This gives the app a clear purpose. Every proposed feature can then be checked against it.

Does a required account help someone save that observation? Does a long species menu help an uncertain beginner? Is an interactive map necessary before the first note can be stored?

Some of these features may become useful later. They do not all belong in the first interaction.

Let People Record What They Know

One common design mistake is asking users for more certainty than they actually have.

A required “Species name” field looks reasonable in a wildlife app. However, a beginner may have seen only a small brown bird disappearing into a hedge.

If the form requires an exact answer, the person must either guess or abandon the entry.

A more useful starting point is a field such as:

What did you see?

That allows descriptions like:

  • A small brown bird with a pale chest.
  • A large bird circling above the field.
  • An animal swimming close to the riverbank.

A separate field can record confidence. For example, the user might select “Not identified” or “Possible identification.”

These labels should describe the user’s confidence, not suggest that the app has verified the animal.

The wider lesson is simple: missing information and incorrect information are different problems. A well-designed app should not solve the first by encouraging the second.

Keep Observations Separate From Research

An observation records what someone noticed. Research helps them understand what it might mean.

Those two activities work well together, but they should remain distinguishable.

Suppose someone records a bird near the coast. Later, they read about its likely habitat and feeding behaviour. That reading may improve their understanding, but it does not change what they actually saw.

A journal can support this distinction with separate spaces:

Observation: What happened during the sighting?

Research notes: What did the user learn afterwards?

A collection of wildlife articles can provide starting points for further reading. However, a general article should not automatically become evidence that a particular species was present.

For developers, this is also a data-design question. When personal notes, imported information, and automated suggestions are stored as though they are the same thing, it becomes harder to understand where a claim came from.

Clear labels help preserve that context.

Choose a Small, Useful Set of Fields

A first version does not need to collect every possible detail.

A practical observation record could include:

Field Purpose
Animal description Records what the person noticed
Observation date Helps place the sighting in time
Identification confidence Makes uncertainty visible
Behaviour notes Preserves useful details about the encounter

An optional general habitat field could also help. “Woodland,” “coast,” or “urban park” may be enough for a personal journal.

Exact coordinates are a separate decision. They are not automatically necessary just because a phone can provide them.

Keeping the form small also makes it easier to explain. Someone should understand what belongs in each field without opening a help page.

If people repeatedly need additional information, that is evidence for expanding the form. Adding fields in advance is often just a guess about future needs.

Explain What “Saved” Actually Means

Storage is one of the most important parts of a journal.

To a user, “saved” may mean that an entry will still exist next month, on another device, or after changing browsers. A small browser-based app may provide none of those guarantees.

For a lightweight prototype, browser storage can be a reasonable place to start. But the interface should explain its limits.

A message such as this is more useful than a vague success notification:

Your entry is saved in this browser. Export a copy if you want a separate backup.

Browser storage does not automatically sync across devices. It can also become unavailable, and clearing site data can remove stored entries.

Developers exploring this approach can read Zell Liew’s discussion of making localStorage easier to use. Understanding how information is written and read is helpful, but explaining that behaviour to users is part of the work too.

An export option is particularly valuable for a personal journal. People may become attached to their records long before the app has advanced features.

Treat Failed Saves as a Real User Experience

It is easy to design the screen that appears after a successful save.

The more revealing question is what happens when saving fails.

Does the app clear the form anyway? Does it display a success message too early? Does the user lose a carefully written note?

A useful rule is to preserve the person’s input until the app knows the operation succeeded.

If something goes wrong, the message should explain the immediate situation in plain language:

We could not save this entry. Your notes are still here so you can copy them before trying again.

The same principle applies when loading older records. If stored data cannot be read, silently replacing it with an empty journal can make recovery harder.

Good error handling protects the user’s effort. It is not just a technical detail.

Build Privacy Into the First Version

A wildlife journal can contain more personal information than its name suggests.

Repeated locations may reveal someone’s walking routine. Photographs may include other people. Free-text notes may mention private property or sensitive wildlife locations.

For a basic journal, a sensible starting point is to collect only what the main task requires.

That could mean:

  • Making location optional.
  • Accepting a broad habitat instead of exact coordinates.
  • Keeping entries private unless the user chooses to share.
  • Providing a clear way to delete records.
  • Explaining what an export contains before it is shared.

Keeping information in a browser also should not be described as encryption or complete security. It is a storage choice, not a promise that nobody else can access the device.

Privacy explanations work best when they describe the actual behaviour of the app.

Use Educational Content at the Right Moment

Related reading becomes useful when it answers a question the person already has.

Someone reviewing a possible puffin observation may want to learn more about the bird’s appearance, habitat, or behaviour. A clearly labelled link to Atlantic puffin facts can support that next step.

The placement matters.

A reading suggestion belongs near research notes or an entry review screen. It is less helpful if it interrupts the form before the user has saved anything.

The wording matters too. “Learn about Atlantic puffins” describes a reading resource. “Confirm your sighting” would suggest a level of verification that a general article cannot provide.

This is a useful principle for any content-led app: connect reading material to a specific need, and describe honestly what the resource offers.

Make the Interface Comfortable to Use

An observation journal should work for someone using a keyboard, a small screen, or enlarged text.

That means using visible field labels, readable contrast, and buttons with clear names. Instructions should not disappear as soon as someone starts typing.

Confidence should also be expressed in words rather than colour alone. A yellow marker means little without a label explaining it.

Deletion deserves particular care. A small icon beside an entry can be easy to tap accidentally. Clear wording, confirmation, or an undo option can help protect records.

These choices may look modest, but they affect the part of the app people experience every time they use it.

Test the Awkward Situations

A useful test plan includes more than saving one normal entry.

Try an empty description. Enter a long note. Refresh after saving. Check what happens when storage is unavailable. Open the app on a narrow screen and move through the form using only a keyboard.

Also check whether a failed save leaves the original text intact.

If multiple tabs are supported, test whether changes in one tab can overwrite changes in another. If that behaviour has not been handled, be clear about the limitation.

A simple testing checklist might include:

Situation Expected behaviour
The description is empty Explain what is missing and keep the other input
A save fails Preserve the note and show a clear message
The page is refreshed Load successfully saved entries
Stored data cannot be read Explain the problem without silently overwriting it
The user exports entries Provide a file containing the saved records
The user uses a keyboard Keep fields and controls reachable
The screen is narrow Keep text and buttons readable without horizontal scrolling

The aim is not to make the first version solve every possible problem. It is to understand the situations it handles and avoid promising more than it delivers.

A Small Project With Useful Lessons

A wildlife journal is a manageable project because its central task is easy to understand: help someone preserve an observation.

Building it thoughtfully still requires important decisions. The app must handle uncertainty, explain storage, protect personal information, and make educational content useful without presenting it as proof.

Those lessons carry well beyond wildlife.

Whether someone is recording books, plants, journeys, or daily habits, the software should respect what they know, preserve what they write, and explain what happens to their information.

That is a strong foundation for a useful app—even before the feature list grows.

title: Wan 3.0 now available on AI Gateway
description:
Wan 3.0 from Alibaba is now available on AI Gateway as alibaba/wan-v3.0-video.

Wan 3.0 combines text-to-video, image-to-video, first- and last-frame conditioning, and reference-based generation in one model. References can include images, video, and audio. It generates clips up to 30 seconds at 30 fps in 480p, 720p, or 1080p, with synchronized audio.

Previously, Wan 2.7 required separate -t2v and -r2v model IDs and was limited to 15-second clips at 24 fps.

Generate a video

Wan 3.0 supports asynchronous generation, so no HTTP request needs to remain open for the entire render.

Pass a webhook to receive an event when the generation finishes:

Learn about asynchronous generation options in the docs, including how to verify webhook deliveries.

Add references

Pass image, video, or audio references through inputReferences, including the source and media type for each one. Images accept hosted URLs or base64. Video and audio references require hosted URLs.

First- and last-frame conditioning accepts one image for each frame and can't be combined with other references.

Try Wan 3.0 in the model playground, or browse all video models.

title: Python Is Great. But Have You Tried Go? The Language Powering Modern Cloud Infrastructure
description:
What if you could build a fast API, compile it into a single binary, run thousands of concurrent tasks, and deploy it without installing a runtime on your production server?

Sounds interesting, right?

That's one reason Go (Golang) has become an important language in cloud infrastructure, backend engineering, and DevOps.

If you've explored Docker, Kubernetes, Terraform, Prometheus, or other cloud-native tools, you've probably encountered Go somewhere in their ecosystem.

But why?

Why are engineers choosing Go for infrastructure tools? What makes it different from Python, Java, or Node.js? And should you learn it as a Cloud or DevOps engineer?

Let's find out. 👇

🤔 1. What Exactly Is Go?

Go is an open-source, statically typed programming language developed at Google.

It was designed with a focus on:

  • Simplicity
  • Performance
  • Concurrency
  • Fast compilation
  • Reliable software development
  • Efficient deployment

Go combines a relatively simple syntax with compiled native executables and built-in concurrency primitives.

Here's your first Go program:

package main

import "fmt"

func main() {
    fmt.Println("Hello, Cloud Engineer!")
}

Run it:

go run main.go

Build an executable:

go build -o myapp main.go

Run it:

./myapp

That's it.

You've written, compiled, and executed your first Go program.

The interesting part begins when you start building real applications.

⚡ 2. Why Is Go So Popular in Cloud and DevOps?

Look at some well-known projects built with Go:

Project What it does
Docker Container platform
Kubernetes Container orchestration
Terraform Infrastructure as Code
Prometheus Monitoring and metrics
Caddy Web server
Hugo Static site generator

Go is particularly suitable for infrastructure software because it offers a useful combination of performance, concurrency, networking libraries, and deployment simplicity.

Let's understand the features behind that combination.

🧵 3. Goroutines: The Feature That Makes Go Interesting

Imagine you need to check the health of 100 servers.

A simple sequential program might look like this:

package main

import (
    "fmt"
    "time"
)

func checkServer(server string) {
    fmt.Println("Checking:", server)
    time.Sleep(time.Second)
    fmt.Println("Healthy:", server)
}

func main() {
    servers := []string{
        "server-1",
        "server-2",
        "server-3",
        "server-4",
    }

    for _, server := range servers {
        checkServer(server)
    }
}

Each function runs one after another.

Go provides goroutines, which let you run functions concurrently.

Add just one keyword:

go checkServer(server)

Here's a complete example:

package main

import (
    "fmt"
    "sync"
    "time"
)

func checkServer(server string, wg *sync.WaitGroup) {
    defer wg.Done()

    fmt.Println("Checking:", server)

    time.Sleep(time.Second)

    fmt.Println("Healthy:", server)
}

func main() {
    servers := []string{
        "server-1",
        "server-2",
        "server-3",
        "server-4",
    }

    var wg sync.WaitGroup

    for _, server := range servers {
        wg.Add(1)
        go checkServer(server, &wg)
    }

    wg.Wait()
    fmt.Println("All checks completed!")
}

What's happening?

  • go starts a goroutine.
  • sync.WaitGroup tracks the running tasks.
  • wg.Done() marks a task as completed.
  • wg.Wait() waits until all tasks finish.

This is useful for tasks such as:

  • Checking multiple server endpoints.
  • Processing background jobs.
  • Handling concurrent API requests.
  • Running independent infrastructure checks.

Remember: Goroutines are lightweight, but launching unlimited goroutines is not a good design. Real applications should control concurrency when working with large workloads.

🔗 4. Channels: How Goroutines Communicate

Concurrency is useful, but multiple tasks often need to exchange information.

Go provides channels for communication between goroutines.

Example:

package main

import "fmt"

func worker(ch chan string) {
    ch <- "Deployment completed successfully!"
}

func main() {
    ch := make(chan string)

    go worker(ch)

    message := <-ch

    fmt.Println(message)
}

Output:

Deployment completed successfully!

Here:

  • make(chan string) creates a channel.
  • ch <- message sends data.
  • <-ch receives data.

Channels are particularly useful for coordinating background workers and concurrent operations.

🌐 5. Go Is Excellent for Building APIs

Cloud applications frequently communicate through APIs.

Go's standard library includes everything needed to build a basic HTTP server.

Let's create one.

package main

import (
    "encoding/json"
    "net/http"
)

type Response struct {
    Message string `json:"message"`
    Status  string `json:"status"`
}

func healthHandler(w http.ResponseWriter, r *http.Request) {
    w.Header().Set("Content-Type", "application/json")

    response := Response{
        Message: "Go API is running!",
        Status:  "healthy",
    }

    json.NewEncoder(w).Encode(response)
}

func main() {
    http.HandleFunc("/health", healthHandler)

    http.ListenAndServe(":8080", nil)
}

Run:

go run main.go

Test:

curl http://localhost:8080/health

Expected response:

{
  "message": "Go API is running!",
  "status": "healthy"
}

Congratulations! You've built a basic HTTP API without installing a web framework.

For production applications, you should also handle server errors, configure timeouts, add graceful shutdown, and implement appropriate logging and authentication.

🐳 6. Go + Docker: A Powerful Combination

One of Go's biggest advantages is that it can compile applications into standalone executables.

This makes it convenient to package applications in small Docker images.

Let's create a Dockerfile:

# Build stage
FROM golang:1.25-alpine AS builder

WORKDIR /app

COPY go.mod ./
RUN go mod download

COPY . .

RUN CGO_ENABLED=0 GOOS=linux \
    go build -o server .

# Runtime stage
FROM scratch

COPY --from=builder /app/server /server

EXPOSE 8080

ENTRYPOINT ["/server"]

Build the image:

docker build -t go-api:v1 .

Run it:

docker run -d \
  --name go-api \
  -p 8080:8080 \
  go-api:v1

Test it:

curl http://localhost:8080/health

Why use a multi-stage build?

  • The compiler stays in the build stage.
  • The runtime image contains only the application executable.
  • The resulting image can be significantly smaller.
  • The production container has fewer unnecessary components.

One consideration: scratch contains no shell, certificates, or system files. Applications that require TLS certificates, timezone data, or other runtime assets must include those explicitly. You may prefer a minimal Alpine or distroless runtime image.

Also, use a Go version supported by your project and update the example image tag accordingly.

☸️ 7. Why Kubernetes and Go Work So Well Together

Kubernetes is written primarily in Go.

Why does that matter?

Because Go offers several features useful for building distributed infrastructure software:

  • Strong networking support.
  • Goroutines for concurrent operations.
  • Channels for communication.
  • Static compilation.
  • Cross-compilation support.
  • A powerful standard library.

Go is also used to build Kubernetes operators and controllers.

For example, a Kubernetes controller continuously observes the cluster and attempts to move the actual state toward the desired state.

A simplified idea:

      Desired State
            |
            v
      Kubernetes API
            |
            v
        Controller
            |
            v
      Compare States
            |
            v
      Take Action
            |
            v
      Repeat Forever

You can build your own controllers using the Kubernetes ecosystem's Go libraries, particularly Kubebuilder and controller-runtime.

This is an excellent advanced project for someone interested in Platform Engineering.

🏗️ 8. Build a Real Project: Go Server Health Checker

Let's turn theory into something practical.

Build a small tool that checks whether multiple servers are reachable.

Project structure 

go-health-checker/
│
├── main.go
├── go.mod
├── Dockerfile
└── README.md

Create main.go:

package main

import (
    "fmt"
    "net/http"
    "sync"
    "time"
)

func check(url string, wg *sync.WaitGroup) {
    defer wg.Done()

    client := http.Client{
        Timeout: 3 * time.Second,
    }

    start := time.Now()

    resp, err := client.Get(url)

    if err != nil {
        fmt.Println(url, "UNREACHABLE:", err)
        return
    }

    defer resp.Body.Close()

    duration := time.Since(start)

    fmt.Printf(
        "%s | Status: %s | Latency: %v\n",
        url,
        resp.Status,
        duration,
    )
}

func main() {
    servers := []string{
        "https://google.com",
        "https://github.com",
        "https://go.dev",
    }

    var wg sync.WaitGroup

    for _, url := range servers {
        wg.Add(1)
        go check(url, &wg)
    }

    wg.Wait()

    fmt.Println("Health checks completed!")
}

Run:

go run main.go

This project introduces:

  • HTTP clients.
  • Goroutines.
  • WaitGroups.
  • Error handling.
  • Request timeouts.
  • Concurrent server checks.

How can you improve it?

Add these features one by one:

  1. Read server URLs from a configuration file.
  2. Add retry functionality.
  3. Export results as JSON.
  4. Add a REST API.
  5. Containerize the application.
  6. Deploy it on Kubernetes.
  7. Export metrics for Prometheus.
  8. Add a Grafana dashboard.

Now you have a project that combines Go, Docker, Kubernetes, and observability.

That's a much stronger learning exercise than simply memorizing syntax.

🆚 9. Go vs Python: Which Should You Learn?

Both are valuable. The better choice depends on what you're building.

Feature Go Python
Execution Compiled Commonly interpreted
Typing Static Dynamic by default
Concurrency Goroutines and channels Multiple concurrency models
Deployment Often a standalone binary Usually requires a Python runtime and dependencies
Learning curve Simple syntax, stricter types Beginner-friendly syntax
AI ecosystem Growing Extensive
Cloud infrastructure Strong ecosystem Strong automation ecosystem
Data science More limited ecosystem Extensive ecosystem

My recommendation:

If you're interested in Cloud Engineering, DevOps, SRE, or Platform Engineering, learning Go alongside Python can be a valuable combination.

Use Python when it makes scripting, automation, or data work easier.

Use Go when you want to build efficient services, command-line tools, and infrastructure software.

You don't need to abandon one language to learn another.

📚 10. Your 30-Day Go Learning Roadmap

Don't try to master everything in one weekend.

Follow a structured plan.

Days Topics Practical task
1–5 Variables, data types, functions, conditions, loops Calculator
6–10 Arrays, slices, maps, structs, pointers Student management system
11–15 Interfaces, errors, packages, modules File processing tool
16–20 Goroutines, channels, WaitGroups Concurrent URL checker
21–25 HTTP, JSON, REST APIs Build a Go REST API
26–30 Docker, testing, deployment Containerized Go application

By the end, aim to have at least two working projects on GitHub.

Don't measure progress by how many tutorials you've watched.

Measure it by what you can build without following someone else's code line by line.

🎯 Final Thoughts

Go is not popular simply because it is fast.

Its real strength is the combination of simplicity, concurrency, networking, compilation, and practical deployment.

That's why it has become an important language in the cloud-native ecosystem.

If you're already learning Docker, Kubernetes, Terraform, Linux, or AWS, Go can help you move beyond operating infrastructure toward building the tools that operate it.

Don't just learn how to deploy applications. Learn how to build the systems that make deployment possible.

👇 Let's discuss!

If you had to choose one Go project to build this month, what would it be?

  1. CLI tool for DevOps automation
  2. Kubernetes operator
  3. REST API with Go
  4. Docker image monitoring tool
  5. Distributed job-processing system

Drop your choice in the comments!

📖 Want to Learn Go Step by Step?

I've also created a learning resource:

🐹 Mastering Go — Complete Guide

You can also explore my other Cloud and DevOps resources:

  • 🐳 Docker Mastery
  • ☸️ CKA Complete Study Guide
  • 🏗️ Terraform Associate (003) Exam Crash Course
  • 🚀 DevOps Complete Pack

Learn the language. Build the tool. Solve a real problem.

title: How I built an asynchronous predictive compiler using Git Worktrees and Docker
description:
Current AI coding tools have a fundamental workflow problem: they are entirely reactive.

You write a function, you run your test suite, it fails, you copy the error logs, paste them into the AI chat, and wait for a fix. You are the orchestrator, and the AI is just glorified autocomplete.

I wanted an engine that operates entirely in the gap between keystrokes. I wanted a system that detects my unfinished code, spins up a parallel replica of my project, tests it, and patches the broken dependencies before I even hit git commit.

So, I built Shadow-Branch Engine. It is a background daemon that uses Git hardlinks, AST pruning, and zero-trust Docker sandboxing to test and heal your code asynchronously.

Here is how the architecture works under the hood.

  1. Bypassing the npm install Bottleneck The biggest challenge of running background tests is environment replication. If I want to test uncommitted changes in the background, I can't just copy the directory—running npm install on a massive node_modules folder takes way too long.

To solve this, Shadow-Branch manipulates the filesystem directly. When you save a file, the daemon triggers a git stash create and instantly mounts a hidden parallel git worktree. It uses OS-level hardlinks to mirror your existing node_modules.

The result? A sub-millisecond, fully isolated replica of your codebase, ready for execution.

  1. AST Token Pruning (ts-morph) Passing an entire codebase into an LLM context window to generate tests is incredibly expensive and slow.

Instead of dumping raw text, Shadow-Branch uses the TypeScript Compiler API (ts-morph). When a file is saved, the engine parses the Abstract Syntax Tree (AST), identifies the specific function you modified, and traces its exact dependency graph.

It strips away all unrelated files and comments, sending only the mathematically necessary context to the local AI. This drops the token count by over 90%, making local model execution incredibly fast.

  1. The Docker Execution Sandbox Once the AI generates the test suite or a patch, we cannot just run it directly on the host machine. AI-generated code is inherently untrusted.

Shadow-Branch uses the dockerode library to dynamically spin up a lightweight, network-isolated Docker container mapped only to the .shadow-workspace. It executes the test suite inside the container.

If the test fails, the daemon captures the exit codes and routes the error logs back through a local XState state machine for an autonomous healing loop. If the test passes, it surfaces a clean, ready-to-merge patch directly to your IDE.

  1. Parallel Fuzzing Swarms Because the engine runs asynchronously, it has the luxury of time that a blocking terminal command does not.

If the AST detects asynchronous operations (Promise.all, database transactions), Shadow-Branch doesn't just run one test. It spins up a swarm of 10 parallel Micro-VMs inside Docker to aggressively fuzz for race conditions. If even one container fails, the patch is rejected.

The Code
I just open-sourced the entire Shadow-Branch Engine today. It is built strictly as a local Node.js daemon with zero dependencies on external, closed-source SaaS platforms.

If you are interested in Git manipulation, AST parsing, or local Docker orchestration, check out the repository. We have several open issues tagged help wanted for adding Python and Rust LSP support.

Repository: https://github.com/hariom123-dev/Shadow-Branch.git

Let me know your thoughts on the architecture in the comments. I'd love to hear how other people are handling local autonomous execution!

title: HIPAA compliance evidence for the database layer on Supabase: RLS, functions, triggers and audit logs
description:
Supabase signs a BAA and has a High Compliance setting for projects that store PHI, which handles the platform. The database layer built on it is a separate matter. RLS policies, functions, triggers and audit tables are written by the project team, and a HIPAA review expects evidence that they protect PHI. Supabase’s shared responsibility model puts them on the customer’s side.

What Supabase covers

Encryption at rest and in transit, the BAA, and project settings. The HIPAA guide asks for these to be on:

  • Point in Time Recovery
  • SSL enforcement
  • network restrictions
  • connection logging
  • MFA on every account with access

The Security Advisor warns when any of them is off, and the linter flags patterns like a table in public with RLS off. Neither one runs the policies. They cannot show whether a nurse at one clinic can read another clinic’s visits, or whether a deleted record left a row in the audit table.

What the project owner has to show

A HIPAA review asks three questions about the database:

  • who can reach which patient rows - 164.312(a)(1)
  • is every change to that data recorded - 164.312(b)
  • can anyone alter that record afterwards - 164.312(c)(1)

164.308(a)(8) adds that this is evaluated again whenever the environment changes. On Supabase, the answers live in SQL the team wrote. A screenshot of the policies does not show what the database does when authenticated calls one of those functions. Only running it does.

Producing the evidence with unitautogen hipaa

unitautogen hipaa runs against the local Supabase stack, which is built from the migrations, so no patient data is involved:

bash
supabase start
unitautogen --supabase hipaa --schema public

It generates the tests and the rows they need, runs them as each role the app uses, and rolls the rows back. The tests are written to supabase/tests/seccover/security/, where supabase test db picks them up. The report goes to supabase/tests/seccover/hipaa/public/.

What it checks

  • Access. Functions, views and triggers that run as their owner bypass RLS. Each one is called as two different tenants, with data on both sides, and marked as holding or leaking. Open policies, column grants and PHI leaking through error messages are checked too.
  • Audit log. For every PHI table, and for each of insert, update and delete: did the change leave an audit row, and does that row record who made it. Connection logging does not answer this. It records who connected, not which rows changed.
  • Tampering. For each audit table and each client role: can that role edit, delete or forge rows. A common hole is a security definer function exposed through .rpc() that writes to the audit table, letting any logged-in user write anything into it.
  • Identity. Policies depend on auth.uid(), auth.jwt() or a session setting. The report shows whether a client session can change what those return.

What to fix

The report opens with a ranked “What to fix” list. There is one row per object, with:

  • the priority: fix now or review
  • the HIPAA section
  • what was found
  • the change that closes it
  • a link to the evidence

When many functions are callable only through PostgreSQL’s default PUBLIC grant, the report says so once above the list and gives the single fix:
sql
REVOKE EXECUTE ON ALL FUNCTIONS IN SCHEMA public FROM PUBLIC;

Every finding is backed by a pgTAP test that can be committed and re-run. Each result is mapped to its 164.312 section, and the report is stamped with a SHA-256 of every file behind it, so any later edit shows.

what to do on every migration

Schema changes reach Supabase as migrations in a PR. Add the hipaa command to the CI job that already runs supabase test db:

bash
supabase start
supabase test db
unitautogen --supabase hipaa --schema public

Every PR then produces a new report, dated and stamped, kept as a build artifact. 164.308(a)(8) asks for an evaluation each time the environment changes. Each of these reports is that evaluation for the database.

Scope

The report gives evidence for RLS policies, functions, triggers and audit logs.

It does not cover:

encryption, backups and network settings - Supabase’s part

More on unitautogen hipaa: https://unitautogen.com/postgresql/unitautogen/hipaa/

title: Kimi K3.1 Pro Weights Drop Nov 4: Licence, Size, How to Run
description:
On November 4, 2026, Moonshot AI is scheduled to do something no lab has done before: hand the public the complete weights of a 2.8-trillion-parameter AI model that independent testing currently ranks as the strongest open model in the world. Kimi K3.1 Pro has been live through Moonshot's apps and API since October 23, but the downloadable release — the one that lets anyone outside Moonshot run, inspect, fine-tune and redistribute the model — is still a promise with a date on it. We checked Moonshot's Hugging Face organisation while writing this article: there is no K3.1 Pro repository yet. The newest thing there is still the older Kimi K3. So this is the guide to read before the drop: what exactly is landing, the licence question that will decide what "open" really means here, the terabyte-scale hardware reality, the two controversies hanging over the release, and a checklist for the day itself. For the launch story — benchmarks, pricing and how the model performs — start with our Kimi K3.1 Pro launch guide; this article is about the weights.

What exactly is dropping on November 4

Kimi K3.1 Pro is not a new architecture. It is a heavily post-trained version of Kimi K3, the model Moonshot released in the summer: a mixture-of-experts system with 2.8 trillion total parameters, of which about 104 billion are active on any given token. It uses Moonshot's Kimi Delta Attention and Attention Residuals design, reads text, images and video in a single model, and works across a context window of one million tokens. What the extra post-training bought is measurable: on Artificial Analysis's Intelligence Index, K3 scored 44; K3.1 Pro scores 55, fourth of every model the evaluator tracks and only three points behind the best closed model, Anthropic's Claude Opus 5.5.

"Full model weights" is the phrase that matters. A weight file is the trained model itself — the numbers that encode everything it learned. With the weights, the model stops being a service you rent from Moonshot and becomes a file you possess: you can run it on hardware you control, fine-tune it on your own data, inspect its behaviour without an API in between, and keep it forever even if Moonshot changes its prices, its terms, or its mind. That is why a weights release is a different event from an API launch, and why the October 23 launch, impressive as it was, is only half the story.

Two things about the drop are still unknown, and both matter. First, Moonshot has not said whether the faster K3.1 Pro Highspeed variant is part of the weights release or stays a hosted-only product. Second — and this is the big one — Moonshot has not named the licence. More on that below, because there is a very good precedent to read in the meantime.

Here is what the family looks like side by side. The K3 column is verified from the actual Hugging Face repository; the K3.1 Pro column is what is known or reasonably expected before November 4, and every expectation is labelled as one.

Kimi K3 (already out) Kimi K3.1 Pro (weights due Nov 4)
Total / active parameters 2.8 trillion / ~104 billion 2.8 trillion / ~104 billion (same base)
Context window 1 million tokens 1 million tokens
Input Text, images, video Text, images, video
Weight format MXFP4 weights, MXFP8 activations Not yet published; MXFP4 expected
Download size on Hugging Face 1.56 TB across 96 files Not yet published; similar scale expected
Licence Kimi K3 License (custom) Not yet announced
Serving vLLM and SGLang, official recipes Not yet published; same stacks expected
API price $3 / $15 per million tokens $2 / $10 per million tokens

The licence question — and what K3's licence actually says

Everything about this release hinges on a document that does not exist yet. "Open weights" tells you the file is downloadable; it says nothing about what you are allowed to do with it. That is the licence's job, and Moonshot's announcement named none. The honest position today is: unknown, decided on November 4.

But we are not guessing in the dark, because Kimi K3 shipped under a licence Moonshot wrote for exactly this model family, and you can read it in full in the Kimi K3 repository on Hugging Face. It is a short, unusually readable document, and if K3.1 Pro follows the same pattern — which is an expectation, not a fact — this is what "open" will mean in practice.

The Kimi K3 License starts like the famous MIT licence: permission to use, copy, modify, merge, publish, distribute, sublicense and sell the software — explicitly including the weights, the code and the right to fine-tune and build derivative works — free of charge. For researchers, hobbyists, and the overwhelming majority of companies, that is the whole story: download it and build.

Then come two conditions aimed at the very top of the market. The first is the "Model as a Service" clause. If you or your affiliates run a business that gives third parties API-style access to model inference or fine-tuning — where those third parties meaningfully control inputs, parameters or training data — and that business's aggregate revenue exceeds 20 million US dollars over any consecutive twelve months, you must sign a separate agreement with Moonshot before using the model commercially. Note what the clause deliberately does not cover: products that merely embed the model inside specific features, and simple relays of requests to models hosted by others. The second condition is a branding rule: if the model powers a commercial product with more than 100 million monthly active users, or more than 20 million dollars in monthly revenue, the name "Kimi K3" must be prominently displayed in that product's interface.

A final carve-out softens both conditions: they do not apply to purely internal use — anything that never exposes the model, its outputs or its capabilities to third parties — nor to use through Moonshot's own products and certified inference partners. And the licence closes with the standard "as is" disclaimer and a contact address for licensing questions.

So when the K3.1 Pro licence appears, the checklist is short and specific. Is it the same Kimi K3 License with the name swapped, or a new document? Is the Model-as-a-Service revenue threshold still 20 million dollars? Does the branding rule survive? Has anything been added — an acceptable-use list, a geographic restriction, a research-only tier? Five minutes of reading on November 4 will answer all of it, and until those five minutes happen, any article that tells you what you may do with these weights — including confident claims that they are "fully open" or "not really open" — is getting ahead of the document.

One and a half terabytes: the hardware reality

The second reality check is physical. The Kimi K3 weights on Hugging Face occupy 1.56 terabytes, spread across 96 files, in MXFP4 format — a compact 4-bit representation that Moonshot bakes in during training rather than squeezing down afterwards. K3.1 Pro is the same architecture at the same parameter count, so a similar footprint is the reasonable expectation. To put 1.56 terabytes in perspective: it is roughly twenty-five times the size of a typical 70-billion-parameter model download, and it will not fit on the drive of most workstations, let alone in the memory of a gaming GPU.

Running it is a data-centre conversation, and the arithmetic is not complicated. The weights alone need about 1.6 terabytes of fast memory before you have processed a single token; on top of that sits the key-value cache for that million-token context, which grows with every conversation you serve. A top-end data-centre GPU carries around 141 to 192 gigabytes of high-bandwidth memory. Divide the weights by that and you land in the region of ten to twelve flagship GPUs just to hold the model — one full high-end server node, or a couple of smaller ones linked together — with more headroom needed for comfortable serving. This is not a criticism; it is the honest category of the thing. K3.1 Pro is open in the sense that a power station's blueprints are open: nothing stops you, provided you have a power station.

Three practical consequences follow. First, the first wave of real usage will come from inference providers and well-equipped labs, not individuals — watch for hosted endpoints appearing within days of the drop, the same pattern that followed the Mistral Large 4 open-weights release in late October. Second, community quantisation projects will immediately try to squeeze the model smaller; how much intelligence survives aggressive shrinking of a model that is already 4-bit native is a genuine open question, and early claims should be treated as claims. Third, for almost everyone reading this, the API at $2 per million input tokens and $10 per million output tokens will remain the rational way to use K3.1 Pro for the foreseeable future — the weights matter to you because they cap Moonshot's pricing power and guarantee the model's survival, not because you will host it yourself.

How you will actually run it

If you do have the hardware, the path is already paved, because K3 set it up. Moonshot's K3 release shipped with official support in the two serving stacks that dominate open-model deployment: vLLM, which carries a Moonshot-maintained recipe for the model, and SGLang, which documents it in its cookbook. Day-one support for K3.1 Pro in the same stacks is the reasonable expectation — the architecture is unchanged — but "reasonable expectation" is doing real work in that sentence, and the model card on November 4 is the document that will confirm versions, flags and known issues.

Preparation, if you intend to be ready on the day, is mostly logistics. You need roughly 1.6 terabytes of fast local storage free, a Hugging Face account that has accepted any licence gate the repository carries, and your serving stack installed and tested in advance — K3 itself is the perfect rehearsal download if bandwidth is cheap for you, since its tooling, file layout and deployment guides mirror what is coming. One warning from experience with every major drop: the first hours bring download congestion and a flood of re-uploads, mirrors and repackaged versions from unknown accounts. Download from the official moonshotai organisation only, and let other people be the first to discover which community conversion is broken.

The scoreboard moved: Index v5 and the speed problem

Anyone preparing to evaluate the drop should know that the measuring stick changed last week. On October 27, Artificial Analysis replaced its Intelligence Index with version 5, built mostly on private tests. Under the new index, K3.1 Pro scores 46 — ninth overall, and the highest score of any open-weights model, three points behind the best closed systems on that chart. Some of Artificial Analysis's own task-level measurements are striking: on Terminal-Bench 4.0, the tough terminal-based coding-agent test, they measured K3.1 Pro at 67 percent — the highest they had recorded — and on their GDPval-AA measure of economically valuable knowledge work it ranks third. Moonshot's own reported Terminal-Bench figure, 65.7 percent against Claude Opus 5.5's 66.4, is close behind.

The same independent testing exposes the model's real weakness, and it is not intelligence. It is speed. Artificial Analysis measured K3.1 Pro's output at about 41 tokens per second, ranking 188th of 192 models for output speed. For batch work and offline analysis that hardly matters. For interactive products — a coding assistant answering in real time, an agent loop making hundreds of calls — it matters a great deal, and it is part of why OpenAI's GPT-6.1 Terra, launched October 26 at half the per-token price of the model it replaces and scoring 48 on the new index, is a serious rival for the same workloads. The Highspeed variant exists precisely because Moonshot knows this; whether self-hosting the weights improves or worsens the speed picture will be one of the first things the community benchmarks after November 4. Our comparison of the best AI coding assistants is a useful map of the field this model is entering.

Two controversies hanging over the drop

An honest preview has to include the two stories that broke around this model in the last week, labelled for exactly what they are.

The first is a report, not a finding. On October 28, The Information reported — and Reuters followed on October 29 — that according to people with direct knowledge, Moonshot relied heavily on outputs from OpenAI's GPT-6 Astra to train K3.1 Pro, with a similar claim made about DeepSeek's V4.1 Flash. Training one model on another's outputs, called distillation, sits in contested legal and ethical territory and is restricted by most providers' terms. What is established: the report exists, it is attributed to unnamed sources, and as of October 29 neither Moonshot, OpenAI nor DeepSeek had publicly commented on it. What is not established: whether it is true, and if so, to what degree. It changes nothing about the file that lands on November 4, but it may shape how enterprises' lawyers read the licence — one more reason that document matters.

The second story is Moonshot's own disclosure, and it is stranger: for the open-weight release, the company deliberately made its model worse at hacking. Moonshot says it identified and removed cyberattack-related material from both the mid-training data and the reinforcement-learning tasks, because capability at finding and exploiting software flaws was rising with scale and weights, once published, cannot be recalled. On its internal exploit benchmark, the filtered model scores 81.0 percent; an identical pipeline without the filtering scores 90.5 percent. Ethereum co-founder Vitalik Buterin publicly defended the approach, arguing that restraint now beats the identity-check regimes that a wave of AI-powered attacks could trigger. The open question — and it can only be answered after November 4 — is whether the reduction survives contact with the research community: outside teams will test whether fine-tuning restores the removed capability, and at least one company has already publicly announced plans to try stripping the safeguards. Moonshot's published before-and-after numbers make this the first open release in history whose safety claim arrives with its own test attached.

A third, smaller allegation deserves a sentence for completeness: VentureBeat reported screenshots, which it could not authenticate, purporting to show a paid-promotion brief for Kimi creators that included an instruction not to label posts as paid partnerships. Moonshot had not responded in the reporting. Unverified documents are not evidence — but if you see suspiciously synchronised praise on drop day, you will know the context in which to read it.

Meanwhile, K2 closes its doors today

One dated detail is easy to miss in the drop coverage: the previous generation is being retired on a schedule that starts now. Moonshot's pricing pages indicate the K2 series closes to new users from October 31 — today — and is due to be fully retired by the end of December. If your product still routes traffic to a K2 model, the weights drop is not your only November deadline; migration to K3 or K3.1 Pro belongs on the same calendar page. Moonshot also had a smaller operational stumble this week, apologising for rate limits on K3.1 Pro and resetting a portion of user quotas — a useful reminder that demand for this model, even hosted, is currently outrunning the supply pointed at it.

Your November 4 checklist

When the repository appears, these are the checks that separate knowing from repeating — the same checks we will run before updating this article:

  1. The licence file. Name, Model-as-a-Service threshold, branding rule, anything new. Read the document, not the summaries.
  2. The repository itself. Official moonshotai organisation, exact repo names — and whether Highspeed is included or hosted-only.
  3. Formats and size. MXFP4 as expected? Total terabytes? Any official smaller variants?
  4. The model card. Shipped context length, serving-stack versions, known limitations, and any stated difference between the API model and the released weights.
  5. Independent numbers. Artificial Analysis and community evaluations run on the released weights — not the API — including whether the cyber-capability reduction is measurable.
  6. First endpoints. Which inference providers list it, at what price per token, within the first week.

Frequently Asked Questions

Are the Kimi K3.1 Pro weights out now?

No. As of October 31, 2026, Moonshot's Hugging Face organisation has no K3.1 Pro repository — the newest release there is still Kimi K3. Moonshot's announcement promises the full weights "will be released by Nov 4, 2026", and until the repository appears, the model is available only through Kimi's apps and Moonshot's API.

What licence will the K3.1 Pro weights use?

Moonshot has not announced one. The best guide is the precedent: Kimi K3 shipped under the custom Kimi K3 License — broadly MIT-style freedom to use, modify and sell, with a separate-agreement requirement for Model-as-a-Service businesses earning over $20 million a year, and a branding rule for products above 100 million monthly users or $20 million in monthly revenue. Whether K3.1 Pro uses the same licence can only be confirmed from the licence file in its repository on November 4.

How big will the download be?

Kimi K3's weights occupy 1.56 terabytes on Hugging Face in MXFP4 format across 96 files. K3.1 Pro shares the same 2.8-trillion-parameter architecture, so a similar size is expected — but the exact figure is only known when the repository is published. Plan for roughly 1.6 terabytes of free, fast storage.

Can I run Kimi K3.1 Pro on my own computer?

Realistically, no — and that is about physics, not permission. The weights alone need around 1.6 terabytes of memory to load, which means roughly ten to twelve flagship data-centre GPUs before serving a single request. Community quantisation projects will try to shrink it after release, but a model that is already natively 4-bit has limited room to shrink. For individuals and most teams, the API at $2/$10 per million tokens is the practical route.

Is it true K3.1 Pro was trained on GPT-6 outputs?

It has been reported, not proven. The Information reported on October 28, 2026, citing people with direct knowledge, that Moonshot relied heavily on GPT-6 Astra outputs to train K3.1 Pro; Reuters carried the report on October 29. Moonshot, OpenAI and DeepSeek had issued no public comment as of October 29. Treat the claim as an unconfirmed allegation until a company statement or stronger evidence appears.

Conclusion

Strip away the hype and November 4 is a document release as much as a model release. The model itself is already proven in public: fourth on the old independent index, top of the open field on the new one, priced a third below its predecessor, and slow enough that speed — not smarts — is its honest weakness. What nobody outside Moonshot has seen is the paperwork and the files: the licence that decides whether "open" means MIT-free or free-with-conditions, the repository that decides whether Highspeed is included, and the released weights that decide whether the much-discussed cyber-capability reduction is real. Our launch guide covers what K3.1 Pro is; this article will be updated with what the drop actually contained — licence first — as soon as the repository is live and verified. If Moonshot keeps its date, that update lands on November 4.

title: pgAdmin 4 v9.19 Released
description:
The pgAdmin Development Team is pleased to announce pgAdmin 4 version 9.19. This release of pgAdmin 4 includes 136 bug fixes and new features, including fixes for 15 security vulnerabilities (CVE-2026-116238 through CVE-2026-116252). For more details please see the release notes.

pgAdmin is the leading open-source graphical management tool for PostgreSQL. For more information, please see the website.

Notable changes in this release include:

Features

  • Add a Statistics node for creating and managing extended statistics.
  • Allow data to be edited through simple auto-updatable views in View/Edit Data.
  • Save Query Tool results as JSON or XML as well as CSV, with a selectable encoding, an optional byte order mark, and a 'copy with headers' option.
  • Add support for managing pg_timetable chains and tasks.
  • Replace free-text Password Exec Commands in server mode with an administrator-defined allowlist, SERVER_PASSEXEC_COMMANDS; the commands run without a shell and with a reduced environment. Configure SERVER_PASSEXEC_COMMANDS before the first start after upgrading.
  • Add pgEdge Starfleet to the Deploy Cloud Instance wizard.
  • Allow the login page to be skipped when OAuth2 is the only authentication source.

Security Fixes

  • Fix OS command injection in the Import/Export Data tool, where a query-based export could smuggle a live TO PROGRAM clause past the \copy parenthesis guard through a backslash in a double-quoted identifier and run an arbitrary command on the pgAdmin host; an incomplete fix for CVE-2026-17566 (CVE-2026-116241).
  • Fix LDAP and Kerberos authentication logging a user in to a different account that shared their username, including the initial administrator (CVE-2026-116239).
  • Fix bypasses of the failed-login limit and of pgAdmin's own login, password-change and password-reset checks, through Flask-Security's own views and through username case and second-source handling (CVE-2026-116238).
  • Fix connection file paths and parameter keys escaping the user's storage directory, which let a user connect with another user's credentials or key (CVE-2026-116249).
  • Stop libpq falling back to the pgAdmin service account's own password file and client certificate in server mode (CVE-2026-116247).
  • Restrict connection services in server mode to an administrator-defined allowlist, SERVER_MODE_ALLOWED_SERVICES (CVE-2026-116245).
  • Stop libpq using the pgAdmin service account's Kerberos credentials in server mode (CVE-2026-116244).
  • Stop SSH tunnels using the pgAdmin service account's own SSH identity in server mode (CVE-2026-116242).
  • Fix the utility binary-path guard accepting a path under SHARED_STORAGE, which let a user have pgAdmin execute a file they placed there (CVE-2026-116243).
  • Stop server passwords being left in pgAdmin's own process environment, where another user's session or utility could inherit them (CVE-2026-116246).
  • Fix any user able to register a server being able to share it with every other user in server mode (CVE-2026-116248).
  • Fix the File Manager and the storage-path tools acting on a different path from the one that was checked (CVE-2026-116240).
  • Fix time-of-check to time-of-use symlink, hard-link and FIFO races in the File Manager, Import/Export Servers, Backup, Restore and Import/Export Data file paths (CVE-2026-116250).
  • Fix a user's other sessions surviving a password change or administrator reset (CVE-2026-116251).
  • Fix connection redirection in the materialized view refresh, where a crafted database name was expanded by libpq into a full connection string (CVE-2026-116252).

Bugs/Housekeeping

  • Fix numerous Schema Diff issues, including SERIAL/BIGSERIAL conversions, renamed function arguments, repeated column comments and identity options, and false differences caused by a dropped column in a referenced table.
  • Fix View/Edit Data not handling generated columns properly.
  • Fix the MAINTAIN privilege being silently dropped for views and materialised views on PostgreSQL 17 and later.
  • Fix Kerberos login failures returning a JSON 500 response, and first-time automatically created Kerberos logins being rejected.
  • Fix the Query Tool saving files that were loaded as latin-1 or another non-UTF-8 encoding back as UTF-8.
  • Fix the Linux packages shipping a stray copy of Python, which stopped the DEB package installing on Ubuntu 26.04.

Builds for Windows and macOS are available now, along with a Python Wheel, Docker Container, RPM, DEB Package, and source code tarball from the download area.

title: Hacker group used artificial intelligence in cyberattacks against more than 200 organizations
description:
State-sponsored threat actors used a Go-based AI penetration testing framework named ARTEX to target over 200 organizations.

The tooling integrated LLMs like DeepSeek with agent-based planning and execution, demonstrating large-scale operational use of automated frameworks in cyber campaigns.

The group, known as Vapor Panda, began the campaign on October 17, 2026. It targeted foreign ministries in Latin America, Europe, Asia, and the Middle East, as well as organizations in sectors such as pharmaceuticals, defense, energy, semiconductors, financial institutions, and telecommunications in the United States and other regions. The specific countries affected include the interior ministry of the Middle East, European government agencies, and telecommunications providers in the United States, Belgium, and the Philippines.

How the attack worked

The attackers used an artificial intelligence program called ARTEX, which was based on technologies such as DeepSeek and unknown business models. The system operated with utility programs that planned and executed actions under the supervision of a human operator. In a single intrusion, the program’s designers consumed approximately 1,4 billion input data.

In nine of the organizations, the attack went beyond the initial breach, with the attackers installing special programs, monitoring networks and searching for passwords. They also tried mass passwords at at least 12 additional organizations, including research centers in the United States and European government agencies. The techniques included exploiting vulnerabilities in network services, reading stored administrator passwords and using authentication keys that had been changed since 2022. After the tool became widely available, its developer made it private.

New groups and attacks on legal organizations

Researchers identified the activity of four other groups linked to China: Hollow Panda, Overcast Panda, Titan Panda, and Veiled Panda.

title: Prepare for VAST 4.4 CTV formats before committing a production migration.
description:
Originally published on VASTLint. This article is part of the Migrate video standards with evidence series.

CTV teams can prepare for new formats without promising that every delivery partner already supports them. The useful work starts with a product requirement, an explicit destination contract and a testable release plan. A future version label should not be the only reason to change a working campaign route.

As reviewed on October 15, 2026, the IAB repository's VAST 4.4 schema labels itself a draft for working group discussion. Its proposed CTV changes include expanded nonlinear formats and related media and interaction structures. Treat that artifact as preparation material. Confirm its status and the current specification again before making a production commitment.

Choose the commercial product before implementing the draft.

Decide what the advertiser will buy and what the viewer will experience. A pause placement needs rules for when it appears and disappears. An overlay needs rules for its relationship to the underlying content. A remote-driven interaction needs an input model that the actual device can support.

Write these behaviors into the brief before mapping them to XML. Identify the required creative assets, reporting events and acceptance owner. A format can be representable in a document while still lacking a commercially agreed definition of a delivered impression or interaction.

Confirm whether an existing supported route already meets the requirement. The VAST standards page links published versions and the CTV addendum. A bounded implementation using an agreed current contract may be appropriate while the newer draft evolves.

Turn draft support into a list of confirmed capabilities.

Ask each partner about the precise format, media handling and interaction behavior. Record the tested version of its implementation. Support for a schema under discussion does not demonstrate that the destination will render every proposed format or apply the same reporting rules.

Separate parser acceptance from rendering support. A parser may accept a document and ignore an unfamiliar optional feature. The ad server may forward a field that the receiving player does not use. Trace the route until the system that must act on the format has confirmed its behavior.

Retain partner sample files and approval records. Mark experimental assumptions in the integration notes. When an upstream draft changes, that record tells the team which assumptions need review and which existing production contracts remain valid.

Keep experimental support isolated from ordinary campaign delivery.

Use a test route and versioned fixtures for draft work. Save the exact upstream schema revision or commit used for the experiment. A reference to a moving branch is not enough to reproduce a result after the draft changes.

Maintain ordinary accepted creatives as regression controls. Test whether the experimental parser or transformation changes their outputs. A new CTV format should not alter the handling of a normal linear creative or a valid no-ad response.

Keep experimental findings labeled. A check against the draft can show how the implementation behaves relative to that draft; it cannot establish compliance with an eventual final publication. Do not add a general production-readiness claim to a tool or campaign brief based only on that result.

Test viewing behavior alongside the document.

For a pause format, test entry, resume, timeout and error behavior on the intended device. For an interactive format, test supported input and a missing interaction resource. Use the partner's agreed requirements rather than assuming that a desktop browser test represents a TV remote or an insertion workflow.

Inspect reporting for the same test session. Confirm which event represents display, interaction or video progress and who receives it. A novel placement may need reporting decisions that cannot be inferred from an existing linear video's completion metric.

Use VASTLint for the document checks it supports and retain the tool version and actual results. Confirm coverage before relying on a particular draft-specific rule. Keep execution evidence and partner acceptance beside those findings instead of treating a validator as a substitute for the destination.

Build the business case from confirmed inventory and work.

Estimate the opportunity using destinations that have accepted the format, their available placements and the demand that can actually buy it. Label forecast assumptions. Do not multiply a premium CPM by all CTV impressions and call the result incremental revenue.

Include creative production, integration, device testing and reporting work in the cost. A format that requires a bespoke implementation for every publisher may be commercially worthwhile, but its operating model differs from a reusable standards-based route. Measure which work is shared and which remains destination-specific.

An early pilot can establish feasibility and operating effort without proving a revenue uplift. Add delivery and financial outcomes only when campaign records support them. This lets the team make a useful decision while keeping the scope of the evidence clear.

Set a decision point for production adoption.

Before rollout, recheck publication status, partner support and the exact format contract. Review the specification changes since the experimental revision. Rerun the affected fixtures and ordinary controls, then obtain acceptance from the team that operates the destination.

Use the same bounded rollout and rollback discipline as any delivery migration. State which destinations and creative types are approved. Keep unsupported combinations out of the campaign plan until a new test establishes their behavior.

The preparation succeeds when the team has a tested product definition and a short, evidence-backed path to adoption. VASTLint can support the repeatable document review. The production decision should rest on the published contract, demonstrated destination behavior and a business case built from records the campaign team can inspect.

title: Keep Conflicting Video Job Observations Visible in a Local Reducer
description:
A Seedance client may need to display observations from an asynchronous video job while the user continues working. A local UI can receive those observations in an inconvenient order. If every arriving value blindly overwrites the previous one, an old “running” observation can erase a completed result on screen.

The example below defines a local reconciliation policy for one job. It is not a Seedance status specification, polling implementation, or guarantee about provider event ordering. An adapter must first map documented provider responses into the small vocabulary used here.

Separate an observation from a command

A reducer consumes an observation and returns new local state. It should not submit a job, retry generation, cancel a task, or download output. Those actions have different consequences and need separate controls.

This policy allows queued, running, succeeded, and failed. After a terminal observation, a nonterminal observation cannot move the displayed state backward. A contradictory terminal observation becomes a conflict that requires reconciliation. Repeating the same terminal observation is harmless.

from dataclasses import dataclass

TERMINAL = {"succeeded", "failed"}
KNOWN = TERMINAL | {"queued", "running"}

@dataclass(frozen=True)
class View:
    job_id: str
    status: str = "queued"
    conflict: bool = False

def observe(view, job_id, status):
    if job_id != view.job_id:
        raise ValueError("observation belongs to another job")
    if status not in KNOWN:
        raise ValueError("unmapped provider status")
    if view.status in TERMINAL:
        contradictory = status in TERMINAL and status != view.status
        return View(view.job_id, view.status,
                    view.conflict or contradictory)
    if view.status == "running" and status == "queued":
        return view
    return View(view.job_id, status, view.conflict)

v = observe(View("job-demo"), "job-demo", "running")
v = observe(v, "job-demo", "succeeded")
assert observe(v, "job-demo", "running") == v
assert observe(v, "job-demo", "failed").conflict
assert observe(v, "job-demo", "succeeded") == v

Python's dataclass documentation explains the generated record methods and the frozen option. Here, returning a new record makes each transition explicit; freezing the record does not validate provider responses or create an audit log.

Do not silently choose between contradictory terminal results

Suppose succeeded arrives first and failed arrives later. This reducer retains the first terminal label and sets conflict=True. The UI must display that conflict prominently and withhold actions that require a confirmed outcome. The retained label alone is not authoritative.

Reversing those two observations retains failed instead, with the same conflict flag. That order dependence is intentional and limited: the function preserves a first terminal observation for inspection, not a verdict about the remote job. A durable observation log would retain both source responses and their provenance separately.

If a provider documents revisions, sequence numbers, correction events, or a definitive status endpoint, reconciliation should use that contract. This small example has none of those fields and therefore cannot declare which conflicting response is newer or more trustworthy.

Test the display policy without generating a video

Exercise queued-to-running progress, duplicate observations, terminal-to-nonterminal observations, both orders of terminal conflict, unknown vocabulary, and another job's identifier. Those fixtures test a local policy. They do not prove exactly-once execution, billing finality, or remote success.

A cancellation state is deliberately absent. Do not map an unfamiliar cancellation or moderation result to failed merely to satisfy the function. Extend the vocabulary only after deciding what the provider response means and how it affects the display.

This approach keeps the inexpensive local part of a Seedance workflow testable. It also keeps a contradictory status from automatically triggering another generation request. The snippet and transition fixtures were exercised locally; no status endpoint or generation API was called.

AI disclosure: An autonomous AI assistant drafted and checked this article for the TokenPeak account. Job identifiers and observations are synthetic.

title: Bridging the Lakehouse: Ingesting Databricks Unity Catalog into Cognee Knowledge Graphs
description:
In large enterprise lakehouses, finding the right dataset, understanding table schemas, and tracing ML model lineage is often a major hurdle for data scientists, product managers, and AI agents.

While catalog tools like Databricks Unity Catalog centralize table schemas, storage locations, and column-level comments, interacting with these assets via natural language requires a structured knowledge layer. Vector similarity alone fails when users ask questions that span organizational boundaries:

  • "Which production tables contain customer billing information, and what are their primary keys?"
  • "What AI/ML models are registered under champion status for credit risk prediction?"
  • "Show me all schemas in the analytics catalog that partition by event_date."

To solve this, I designed and implemented the official Databricks Unity Catalog data-source connector (cognee-community-connector-unitycatalog) for Cognee as part of the WeMakeDevs × Cognee Mergetober Hackathon.

Here is how we turn Unity Catalog metadata into a connected GraphRAG layer.

Architectural Blueprint

The connector traverses Unity Catalog’s three-level namespace hierarchy (catalog.schema.table) along with the AI/ML Model Registry, converting tabular definitions into rich semantic markdown nodes:

flowchart TD
    subgraph UnityCatalog ["Databricks Unity Catalog API"]
        A["/api/2.1/unity-catalog/catalogs"]
        B["/api/2.1/unity-catalog/schemas"]
        C["/api/2.1/unity-catalog/tables (Managed, External, Views)"]
        D["/api/2.1/unity-catalog/models (Registered AI Models)"]
    end

    subgraph ConnectorEngine ["Connector Ingestion & Normalization"]
        E["Selective Scope Filter (catalogs / schemas)"]
        F["Column Schema Serializer (Types, Comments, Partitions)"]
        G["Model Registry Metadata (Aliases, Runs, Tags)"]
        H["Credential Scrubbing (Databricks PAT & Bearer Redaction)"]
    end

    subgraph CogneeGraph ["Cognee GraphRAG Ecosystem"]
        I["dlt Source (DOCUMENT_SOURCE_ATTR='unitycatalog')"]
        J["Cognify Entity Extractor"]
        K["Lakehouse Knowledge Graph (FalkorDB / NetworkX)"]
        L["Vector Index (Qdrant)"]
        M["Forget-on-Delete Orphan Pruner"]
    end

    A & B & C & D --> E --> F & G --> H --> I
    I --> J --> K & L
    I --> M

1. Modeling the Three-Level Namespace & AI Models

Databricks Unity Catalog organizes assets in a strict hierarchy: catalog $\rightarrow$ schema $\rightarrow$ table/view. The connector extracts four distinct resource tiers:

A. Catalogs (unitycatalog_catalogs)

Captures top-level governance containers, storage roots, catalog owners, and business descriptions.

B. Schemas (unitycatalog_schemas)

Captures functional namespaces (e.g. finance, marketing, ml_feature_store), properties, and regional metadata.

C. Tables & Views with Rich Column Types (unitycatalog_tables)

Tables are transformed into structured markdown documents detailing table types (MANAGED, EXTERNAL, VIEW), underlying data formats (DELTA, PARQUET), and complete column schemas:

# Table: production.finance.settled_transactions
- **Catalog:** production | **Schema:** finance
- **Table Type:** MANAGED (DELTA)
- **Owner:** finance-data-eng
- **Storage Location:** s3://company-lakehouse/finance/settled_transactions

### Columns
| Column Name | Type | Nullable | Comment |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| `transaction_id` | STRING | No | Unique payment transaction identifier |
| `account_id` | STRING | No | Foreign key to core accounts |
| `amount_cents` | BIGINT | No | Settled amount in cents |
| `settled_at` | TIMESTAMP | No | Monotonic settlement timestamp |

D. AI/ML Model Registry (unitycatalog_models)

Unity Catalog registers MLflow models directly within schemas. The connector ingests registered model names, current aliases (e.g., champion, challenger), model versions, run artifacts, and tags.

2. Dynamic Scoping & Forget-on-Delete Invariants

Enterprise data lakehouses often host thousands of tables. Ingesting an entire data lake at once can create unnecessary overhead. The connector supports granular scoping:

source = unitycatalog_source(
    catalogs=["production", "gold_analytics"],
    schemas=["finance", "risk_modeling"],
    include_tables=True,
    include_models=True,
)

Automatic Lifecycle Management ("Forget-on-Delete")

When data engineers decommission legacy tables or drop experimental schemas, stale nodes shouldn't persist in company knowledge graphs:

setattr(source, DOCUMENT_SOURCE_ATTR, "unitycatalog")

@dlt.resource(name="unitycatalog_tables", write_disposition="replace")
def tables_resource():
    ...

By tagging DOCUMENT_SOURCE_ATTR = "unitycatalog" and write_disposition="replace", Cognee's internal diff engine detects removed tables upon each resync. Removed tables, columns, and model entries are automatically pruned from FalkorDB/NetworkX and Qdrant, guaranteeing 100% data consistency.

3. End-to-End Implementation

Here is how easily you can connect Databricks Unity Catalog to Cognee to query enterprise governance:

import asyncio
import os
import cognee
from cognee_community_connector_unitycatalog import unitycatalog_source

async def main():
    # 1. Connect to Databricks Workspace or Unity Catalog OSS
    source = unitycatalog_source(
        base_url=os.environ.get("DATABRICKS_HOST", "https://adb-1234.azuredatabricks.net"),
        token=os.environ["DATABRICKS_TOKEN"],
        catalogs=["production"],
        include_tables=True,
        include_models=True,
    )

    # 2. Ingest into Cognee and build Knowledge Graph
    print("Ingesting Unity Catalog lakehouse metadata...")
    await cognee.add(source)

    print("Running Cognify to construct Governance Graph...")
    await cognee.cognify()

    # 3. Ask natural language questions across schemas & models
    query = "What columns exist in the production finance tables, and what is our champion credit model?"
    print(f"\nQuerying Cognee: '{query}'")

    results = await cognee.search(query)
    for res in results:
        print(f"\n[Governance Answer]:\n{res}")

if __name__ == "__main__":
    asyncio.run(main())

Verification & Standards

  • 100% Offline Testing: 18 comprehensive unit tests pass offline using mocked API payloads (tests/test_unitycatalog.py).
  • Security Guardrails: Pre-ingestion credential masking strips Databricks tokens from all logs and error traces.
  • Maintainer Alignment: Fully compliant with Cognee’s DCO sign-off guidelines and Hatchling packaging conventions.

Pull Request & Resources

  • Pull Request: topoteretes/cognee-community#472
  • Repository: topoteretes/cognee

How is your organization approaching conversational governance across Databricks and Iceberg catalogs? Share your feedback below!

title: WebAnything: From the Wild Web to Scalable Agent Environments
description:
arXiv:2610.37786v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Web agents require diverse, executable, and resettable website environments for reproducible training and evaluation. Human-assisted mirrors demand per-site engineering, while generative construction can diverge from specified real websites. Capture-and-replay preserves observations, with interaction coverage constrained by captured content and replay capabilities.
  We present WebAnything, a fully automated framework that reconstructs source-grounded, reusable Web environments from real URLs without per-site manual implementation or repair after initial setup and authorization. An Explorer-Builder collects browser-observable structures, resources, and interaction outcomes; an independent verifier checks frozen candidates and guides local repair or targeted source recapture.
  We construct 244 website artifacts across 14 application domains and 53 categories, supporting 12,984 executed and accepted tasks. Compared with human-assisted WebHarbor, WebAnything achieves higher aggregate scores on three fidelity metrics, with 12 wins, two ties, and no losses in a blind audit. Fine-tuning Qwen3.5-9B on 5,856 interaction trajectories improves REAL success by 9.9 percentage points, Odysseys-Easy Rubric Avg and Task Avg by 6.25 and 6.32 percentage points, and WebArena-Verified Overall success by 13.33 percentage points under the fixed harness. Code: https://github.com/china-qijizhifeng/Web-Anything
