title: Building a Tech News Aggregator with GraphQL, gRPC and Go Microservices
description:
As an engineer, I read a lot of tech articles every day: Qiita, Zenn and Hatena Bookmark in Japanese, and dev.to and Hashnode in English, plus a long list of company engineering blogs. Opening ten tabs every morning got old, so I built Check Picks, a personal tech news aggregator. It collects articles in one place and lets me bookmark them, sort them into favorite folders, and build my own custom feeds.

It's also a playground for architecture I wanted to try for real: a GraphQL BFF in front of Go gRPC microservices. This post walks through how it's structured, why I made the choices I did, and what I'd change next time.

The whole thing is open source:
👉 https://github.com/YukiOnishi1129/techpicks

The big picture 

%%{init: {"flowchart": {"curve": "basis", "nodeSpacing": 30, "rankSpacing": 55}, "themeVariables": {"fontSize": "16px"}}}%%
flowchart TB
    WEB["Web client<br/>Next.js 15 · Apollo Client · gql.tada"]

    GW["BFF<br/>NestJS · Apollo Server<br/>Supabase auth guard"]

    subgraph Services["Go gRPC microservices · Cloud Run"]
        direction LR
        CONTENT["content-service<br/>articles · feeds · OGP"]
        BOOKMARK["bookmark-service"]
        MYFEED["my-feed-service"]
        FAVORITE["favorite-service"]
    end

    subgraph Batch["batch-service · Cloud Run Jobs"]
        direction LR
        CRAWL["RSS crawlers<br/>company blogs · tech sites"]
        TREND["Trend crawler<br/>Qiita · Zenn · Hatena · dev.to · Hashnode"]
    end

    subgraph Supabase["Supabase"]
        direction LR
        AUTH["Auth"]
        DB[("PostgreSQL")]
    end

    PROTO[["checkpicks-protocol-buffers<br/>Go module + npm package"]]

    WEB == "GraphQL + JWT" ==> GW
    GW == "gRPC" ==> Services
    GW -. "verify token" .-> AUTH
    Services --> DB
    Batch --> DB
    PROTO -. "shared contract" .-> GW
    PROTO -. "shared contract" .-> Services

    classDef client fill:#e0f2fe,stroke:#0284c7,color:#0c4a6e
    classDef bff fill:#ede9fe,stroke:#7c3aed,color:#3b0764
    classDef svc fill:#dcfce7,stroke:#16a34a,color:#14532d
    classDef job fill:#fef3c7,stroke:#d97706,color:#78350f
    classDef data fill:#f8fafc,stroke:#475569,color:#0f172a
    class WEB client
    class GW bff
    class CONTENT,BOOKMARK,MYFEED,FAVORITE svc
    class CRAWL,TREND job
    class AUTH,DB,PROTO data
    style Services fill:#f0fdf4,stroke:#16a34a
    style Batch fill:#fffbeb,stroke:#d97706
    style Supabase fill:#f8fafc,stroke:#475569

The request path is simple: Next.js → GraphQL → NestJS BFF → gRPC → Go services → PostgreSQL. Separately, batch jobs fill the database with articles. All the gRPC contracts come from one shared Protocol Buffers repo.

Everything lives in one monorepo:

Layer Tech Hosting
Web client TypeScript, Next.js 15, Apollo Client, gql.tada, shadcn/ui, Tailwind Cloud Run
Admin panel Next.js, supabase-js, shadcn/ui Cloud Run
BFF NestJS, Apollo Server, @grpc/grpc-js Cloud Run
Microservices Go, gRPC, sqlboiler Cloud Run
Batch Go, sqlboiler Cloud Run Jobs
DB & Auth Supabase (PostgreSQL + Auth) Supabase

The domain is split into content (articles, feeds, OGP, comments), bookmark, my-feed (user-defined feed folders), favorite (favorite article folders), and user.

Why GraphQL and gRPC?

The two protocols do different jobs, and that's the whole point of the setup.

  • GraphQL at the edge. The frontend has screens that need very different slices of the same data. An article card needs the platform, feeds, bookmark state, which favorite folders it's in, and my comment. GraphQL lets each screen ask for exactly that, and the schema is a great contract for frontend work.
  • gRPC between services. Inside the backend I wanted strict, versioned contracts, generated clients in both Go and TypeScript, and cheap service-to-service calls. Protocol Buffers give me all three.

The BFF is the translator between the two worlds: it takes a GraphQL request, fans out to one or more gRPC services, and shapes the result back into the GraphQL types.

One repo for all the contracts

The .proto files live in their own repository, checkpicks-protocol-buffers, which publishes generated code for both languages:

  • a Go module: checkpicks-protocol-buffers/checkpicks-rpc-go
  • an npm package: @checkpicks/checkpicks-rpc-ts

So the Go services and the NestJS BFF import the same contract at a pinned version (currently v1.5.5 on both sides):

import (
    bpb "github.com/YukiOnishi1129/checkpicks-protocol-buffers/checkpicks-rpc-go/grpc/bookmark"
    cpb "github.com/YukiOnishi1129/checkpicks-protocol-buffers/checkpicks-rpc-go/grpc/content"
)

import { ContentServiceClient } from '@checkpicks/checkpicks-rpc-ts/src/grpc/content/content_grpc_pb';

Changing an API means: edit the proto, release a new version, bump it in each consumer. It's a little ceremony, but the compiler tells me every place that broke, and nothing goes out of sync by accident.

The BFF: NestJS + Apollo Server

The GraphQL schema is written schema-first in .graphql files, grouped by domain (article, bookmark, feed, favorite, myFeed, …). NestJS generates TypeScript classes from them, so resolvers stay type-safe:

type Query {
  articles(articlesInput: ArticlesInput!): ArticleConnection!
  articleOpg(articleUrl: String!): ArticleOGP!
}

type Article implements Node {
  id: ID!
  platform: Platform
  feeds: [Feed!]
  favoriteArticleFolderIds: [String!]!
  title: String!
  articleUrl: String!
  isBookmarked: Boolean!
  comment: ArticleComment
  # ...
}

Lists use Relay-style connections (edges, node, cursor, pageInfo), which pair nicely with infinite scroll on the client.

Authentication at the edge

Auth is handled by Supabase. The client sends the Supabase access token, and a NestJS guard verifies it once, at the BFF:

@Injectable()
export class SupabaseAuthGuard implements CanActivate {
  private supabase = createClient(process.env.SUPABASE_URL, process.env.SUPABASE_ANON_KEY);

  async canActivate(context: ExecutionContext): Promise<boolean> {
    const ctx = GqlExecutionContext.create(context).getContext();
    const req = ctx.req || context.switchToHttp().getRequest();
    const token = req.headers.authorization?.split(' ')[1];
    if (!token) throw new UnauthorizedException('Authorization token not found');

    const { data: { user }, error } = await this.supabase.auth.getUser(token);
    if (error || !user) throw new UnauthorizedException('Invalid or expired token');

    req.user = user;
    return true;
  }
}

After that, the resolver passes user.id down to the gRPC services as an explicit request field. The Go services never deal with JWTs; they trust the BFF and focus on business logic.

@Query(() => ArticleConnection)
@UseGuards(SupabaseAuthGuard)
async articles(@Args('articlesInput') input: ArticlesInput, @Context() context: GraphQLContext) {
  return this.articleService.getArticles(context.req.user.id, input);
}

Calling gRPC from NestJS

Each downstream service gets a small injectable wrapper around its generated client. It uses plaintext locally and TLS in staging/production (Cloud Run gives every service an HTTPS endpoint), with a 10-second deadline:

const grpcCredentials =
  process.env.NODE_ENV !== 'production' && process.env.NODE_ENV !== 'staging'
    ? grpc.credentials.createInsecure()
    : grpc.credentials.createSsl();

@Injectable()
export class GrpcContentClientService implements OnModuleInit {
  private grpcContentService: ContentServiceClient;

  onModuleInit() {
    this.grpcContentService = new ContentServiceClient(grpcUrl, grpcCredentials, { deadline: 10000 });
  }

  getGrpcContentService() {
    return this.grpcContentService;
  }
}

The domain services (ArticleService, BookmarkService, …) build the protobuf request, call the client, and map the response to GraphQL types. Proto3 has no "optional" for scalars by default, so I use the well-known wrapper types (StringValue, Int64Value) to tell "not set" apart from "empty":

const req = new ListArticleRequest();
if (input?.first) req.setLimit(input.first);
if (input?.after) req.setCursor(input.after);
if (input?.languageStatus) req.setLanguageStatus(new Int64Value().setValue(input.languageStatus));
req.setUserId(new StringValue().setValue(userId));

The Go microservices

Every service follows the same layered structure, so jumping between them feels the same:

content-service/
├── cmd/main.go                     # wiring (manual DI)
└── internal/
    ├── interfacess/handler/        # gRPC handlers
    ├── application/usecase/        # business logic
    ├── domain/                     # domain types + repository interfaces
    ├── adapter/
    │   ├── persistence_adapter/    # builds queries for the use cases
    │   └── external_adapter/       # wraps calls to other services
    └── infrastructure/
        ├── persistence/            # sqlboiler-backed repositories
        └── external/               # gRPC clients to other services

There's no DI framework. main.go wires everything by hand, layer by layer, which is wordy but very easy to follow:

// infrastructure layer
aps := persistence.NewArticlePersistence(db)
bex := external.NewBookmarkExternal(bClient)

// adapter layer
apa := persistenceadapter.NewArticlePersistenceAdapter(aps)
bea := externaladapter.NewBookmarkExternalAdapter(bex)

// ...then use cases, then handlers, then grpc.NewServer()

Handlers are deliberately thin: they just delegate to the use case.

func (ch *contentHandler) ListArticle(ctx context.Context, req *cpb.ListArticleRequest) (*cpb.ListArticleResponse, error) {
    return ch.contentUseCase.ListArticle(ctx, req)
}

sqlboiler for data access

I chose sqlboiler because it's database-first: the schema is managed by Supabase migrations, and sqlboiler generates type-safe Go models straight from the real tables. Queries are built with query mods, which stay readable even when they get big:

q := []qm.QueryMod{
    qm.InnerJoin("platforms ON articles.platform_id = platforms.id"),
    qm.LeftOuterJoin("feed_article_relations ON articles.id = feed_article_relations.article_id"),
    qm.Load("FeedArticleRelations.Feed.Category"),
    qm.Where("articles.is_private = ?", false),
    qm.Limit(limit),
}

// cursor-based pagination
if req.GetCursor() != "" {
    q = append(q, qm.Where(
        "articles.published_at < (SELECT published_at FROM articles WHERE id = ?)",
        req.GetCursor(),
    ))
}

Service-to-service calls

Some services call each other over gRPC too. For example, content-service asks bookmark-service and favorite-service about the articles it returns. These calls go through the external / external_adapter layers, so the use cases only depend on an interface and are easy to mock in tests.

Real-database tests with Testcontainers

For repository and use-case tests I didn't want to mock SQL. Each test starts a throwaway PostgreSQL 16 container with testcontainers-go, loads the schema, and runs against a real database:

pgContainer, err := postgres.Run(ctx, "docker.io/postgres:16-alpine",
    postgres.WithInitScripts(scripts...),
    postgres.WithDatabase("postgres"),
    postgres.WithUsername("root"),
    postgres.WithPassword("password"),
    testcontainers.WithWaitStrategy(
        wait.ForLog("database system is ready to accept connections").
            WithOccurrence(2).
            WithStartupTimeout(5*time.Second)),
)

It's slower than mocks, but it catches the bugs that actually happen with SQL, like a wrong join or a missing deleted_at IS NULL.

Batch: where the articles come from

The batch-service is a set of Go commands deployed as Cloud Run Jobs and run on a schedule:

  • article-company-crawler: pulls RSS feeds from company engineering blogs
  • article-site-and-summary-crawler: pulls from tech sites and summary/curation sites
  • trend-article-crawler: collects trending articles and their like/bookmark counts from Qiita, Zenn, Hatena Bookmark, dev.to and Hashnode
  • migrate-seed: seeds platforms and feeds

Each source has its own repository (qiita_repository.go, zenn_repository.go, devCommunity_repository.go, …) behind a common interface, so adding a new platform mostly means writing one more repository. The crawlers also fetch OGP metadata so every card gets a proper thumbnail.

Jobs fit this much better than an always-on service: they start, crawl, write to Postgres, and exit, and I pay only for the time they run.

The frontend: Next.js + Apollo + gql.tada

The web client uses the Next.js App Router with @apollo/experimental-nextjs-app-support, so the same Apollo setup works in Server Components and Client Components.

For type safety I point GraphQL Code Generator directly at the BFF's schema files in the monorepo:

const config: CodegenConfig = {
  schema: "../../bff/apollo-gateway/src/schema/**/*.graphql",
  documents: ["./src/**/*.tsx", "./src/**/*.ts", "!node_modules/"],
  generates: {
    "src/graphql/type.ts": {
      plugins: ["typescript", "typescript-operations", "typescript-react-apollo"],
    },
  },
};

On top of that, gql.tada infers result types from the query string itself and supports fragment colocation, so each component declares the fields it needs right next to the JSX that uses them. If someone changes the schema in the BFF, the frontend fails to type-check in the same PR. That's one of the nicest benefits of a monorepo.

The code is organized by feature (features/articles, features/bookmarks, features/favorites, features/myFeeds, features/trends, …) rather than by technical layer.

Local development & CI/CD

Locally, Supabase CLI runs Postgres and Auth, and Docker Compose starts the BFF and all Go services on the same Docker network. Go services use Air for hot reload. A Makefile wraps the common commands:

make supabase-start   # local Postgres + Auth
make dcb && make dcu  # build & start BFF + services
make migrate          # apply migrations

CI is one GitHub Actions workflow per app, filtered by path, so a change to bookmark-service only runs bookmark checks. Go workflows run golangci-lint, go test (with Testcontainers), and go build.

CD uses a cloudbuild.yaml per service: build the image, push to Artifact Registry, gcloud run deploy. Same pattern for every service, which keeps the pipeline boring in a good way.

What I'd do differently

This was a learning project, and some trade-offs are worth sharing honestly.

1. It's microservices, but with a shared database. All services connect to the same Supabase Postgres. That kept things simple (joins still work, one migration history), but it means the services aren't truly independent: a schema change can affect several of them. For a solo project it was the right call. For a team, I'd move toward a schema per service, or at least strict table ownership.

2. Mapping protobuf ↔ GraphQL by hand is a lot of code. The BFF has plenty of toObject() and field-by-field mapping. Next time I'd look at ts-proto for plain TypeScript interfaces, or Connect for a nicer client API, or generate the mapping code.

3. Watch out for N+1 across services. GraphQL makes it easy to ask for nested data, and every nested field could become another gRPC call. I mostly avoided this by making the gRPC responses "fat" (the content service already returns bookmark and favorite info). In a bigger system I'd add DataLoader-style batching in the BFF.

4. Is this overkill for a personal app? Honestly, yes. A single Next.js app with Supabase would have shipped faster. But the goal was to learn how these pieces fit together in production, with Cloud Run, real auth, real CI/CD and real data, and it did that very well.

Wrapping up

The pattern I'd keep is GraphQL at the edge, gRPC inside, one shared proto repo for contracts, and a monorepo that ties types together end to end. Each part does one job, and the type safety flows from the .proto files and the .graphql schema all the way to the React components.

If you're curious, the full source is here:
👉 https://github.com/YukiOnishi1129/techpicks

Questions or ideas? Leave a comment. I'd especially like to hear how others handle the proto ↔ GraphQL mapping layer. And if you found this useful, a ⭐ on the repo would make my day!

title: Vercel for Enterprise
description:
AI adoption in the enterprise is growing rapidly, and expanding beyond engineering users.

In the last three months, token usage by enterprise companies on AI Gateway has quadrupled, and OpenAI recently reported that from August 2025 to June 2026, non-developer Codex users grew 189x.

Our customers call these builders citizen developers. They know their part of the business better than anyone else, and with AI they can create the software they need to ship work faster and deliver better customer experiences.

Building has never been easier, but that also means that control and governance have never been harder. Employees are using AI tools whether they are approved or not, and if a citizen developer vibe codes a login page incorrectly, private data can reach the public internet.

Enterprise leaders have to figure out how to let everyone build, without giving up security or control.

Enterprise Apps and Agents

We built Enterprise Apps and Agents to solve these challenges at Vercel, and in June, we made it available to our customers. Enterprise Apps and Agents is a central control plane for governing every builder, app, agent, token, and dollar.

Today, we are expanding the platform:

  • Bring Your Own Cloud (BYOC) on AWS is generally available, giving you the full Vercel developer experience, while keeping compute and data inside your AWS boundary.

  • Enterprise-Managed Authorization through Vercel Connect is launching in public beta, giving agents the ability to access connected services on behalf of employees through your IdP.

A single control plane for governing enterprise AI

Enterprise Apps and Agents gives you a single deployment destination for both engineers and citizen developers, with central governance over access, providers, models, data retention, token budgets, integrations, and policies, managed through your existing IdP.

Vercel centralizes AI governance so that company policies can be applied consistently across control domains.

Control domain

Vercel controls

Deployment governance

Enterprise Managed Users and RBAC

Access governance

Vercel Passport, Deployment Protection, and Vercel Firewall

Integration and data governance

Vercel Connect and Enterprise-Managed Authorization

Model and token governance

AI Gateway, including US-only inference and budget controls

Apps and agents run on the same infrastructure that powers billions of production deployments, and Vercel gives you a single place for observability and security monitoring across every project, through analytics, audit logs, and the Security Dashboard.

Secure Compute provides private connectivity to enterprise systems, while BYOC on AWS lets your application functions run in your own AWS account under your permissions and network controls.

Deployment governance

Citizen developers and engineers use different tools. A marketer might use ChatGPT to build a landing page, an analyst might use Claude Code to run queries and build a report, and an engineer might use Codex, OpenCode, or fx.

No matter the harness, Vercel gives you a single deployment target, and connects to your existing IdP, so you can control who creates deployments.

How Klaviyo's built a secure internal app platform

Before Vercel, shipping a simple internal app at Klaviyo took two weeks of chasing IT, opening tickets for engineering, and following up with the platform team. They built an internal app-building platform on top of Enterprise Apps and Agents, and now anyone in the company can deploy an idea in three minutes. In their first two weeks on Vercel, 512 employees deployed 356 apps.

Access governance

Controlling who can deploy doesn't protect the apps, agents, and data that make it into production.

On Vercel, you can configure every deployment to be private by default, and with Vercel Passport, you can require employees to authenticate through your IdP before they can access internal apps.

Integration and data governance

Agents are only useful when they can access your systems and data, but that often means using long-standing environment varibles with wide-ranging permissions to your CRM, databases, Slack, and other systems.

Vercel Connect implements connectors with scoped access, and mints tokens for each agent task, meaning agents only access the specific context they need for the job. And now, with Enterprise-Managed Authorization, when employees sign into Vercel through your IdP, agents can use connected services automatically, without a separate authorization prompt.

Connect also integrates with Passport, so individual employee permissions also apply at the integration and data layer. If someone can't see data in a source system, they can't access it through an app or agent either.

Model and token governance

The average enterprise company using Vercel AI Gateway routes across 17 different models. Without a model router, that would require integrating with multiple separate providers, spreading API keys and budget management across platforms.

AI Gateway gives you access to hundreds of models through a single API, with no markup on cost, and Zero Data Retention keeps your data from being stored or trained on. You can also elect to route through US-only providers to maintain compliance.

How Mercor manages model governance at scale

Mercor connects AI labs with subject-matter experts who help train and evaluate models. Their engineers need access to hundreds of models to enable that work, but before migrating to Vercel, access was spread across direct integrations and third-party routers, making stolen credentials a huge risk, and token spend impossible to manage.

They moved their model routing to AI Gateway, and now engineers can access hundreds of models with a single, expiring secret, and they can set budgets per person or project.

In their first 10 days on AI Gateway, they processed 63 billion tokens without hitting any rate limits.

Centralized visibility and security

Vercel Observability gives you a single view for app and agent telemetry across every project, so you can easily manage performance and troubleshoot problems for both internal tools and customer-facing products.

The Security Dashboard flags risks across your team and apps, including missing MFA, unprotected preview deployments, long-lived credentials, and framework vulnerabilities. Each finding links to the settings needed to fix it.

Bring Your Own Cloud on AWS

BYOC on AWS is generally available. With BYOC, application functions execute in your AWS account, within your security and network boundaries.

Meta Superintelligence Labs runs on Vercel via BYOC, giving its AI teams the ability to test and deploy ideas quickly, inside their own AWS environment. Leaders at Meta said that in their first week on Vercel, they shipped a month worth of work.

From idea to global scale on one platform

Vercel let's everyone in your company build safely, and makes it easy for engineers to ship the best ideas at global scale, all on a single platform.

That is how we built Vertex, our customer support agent. We were previously using a vendor, but it couldn't answer all of our customers questions. When our support team built agents and skills to cover the gaps and increase our responses times, and we realized they had laid the foundation for the experience we wanted to deliver directly to our customers.

Our GTM engineering team took that foundation and made it production ready with evals and model failover.

Today, Vertex handles 91% of our customer support cases autonomously, processing thousands of tickets a week, and it runs on the same platform where the idea started.

Ship your best ideas, securely

Contact sales to learn more about enterprise governance on Vercel and get a custom demo of the platform.

title: How to Find Broken Links on Any Website (Free Python Script + No-Code Option)
description:
Broken links quietly hurt a site. Readers hit dead ends, and search engines waste crawl time on pages that don't exist. Most broken-link checkers are browser extensions that check one page, or SEO suites that cost $100+ a month.

Here's a free Python script that checks every link on a page, using only the standard library, no installs. After that, a no-code option for checking a whole site.

The script

It does three things:

  1. Downloads the page and pulls out every <a href>.
  2. Checks each link with a HEAD request, falling back to GET because some servers refuse HEAD.
  3. Prints anything that returns 4xx/5xx or doesn't connect at all. 
"""Find broken links on one web page. Usage: python3 find_broken_links.py https://example.com"""
import sys
import urllib.error
import urllib.parse
import urllib.request
from concurrent.futures import ThreadPoolExecutor
from html.parser import HTMLParser

UA = {"User-Agent": "Mozilla/5.0 (link checker)"}


class Links(HTMLParser):
    def __init__(self):
        super().__init__()
        self.hrefs = []

    def handle_starttag(self, tag, attrs):
        href = dict(attrs).get("href")
        if tag == "a" and href:
            self.hrefs.append(href)


def status(url):
    for method in ("HEAD", "GET"):  # some servers refuse HEAD
        try:
            req = urllib.request.Request(url, method=method, headers=UA)
            with urllib.request.urlopen(req, timeout=15) as r:
                return r.status
        except urllib.error.HTTPError as e:
            if method == "GET" or e.code not in (403, 405, 501):
                return e.code
        except Exception as e:
            return f"error: {getattr(e, 'reason', e)}"


page = sys.argv[1]
html = urllib.request.urlopen(urllib.request.Request(page, headers=UA), timeout=15).read().decode("utf-8", "replace")
parser = Links()
parser.feed(html)
links = {urllib.parse.urldefrag(urllib.parse.urljoin(page, h))[0] for h in parser.hrefs}
links = sorted(u for u in links if u.startswith("http"))

with ThreadPoolExecutor(10) as pool:
    results = list(zip(links, pool.map(status, links)))

broken = [(u, s) for u, s in results if not isinstance(s, int) or s >= 400]
print(f"Checked {len(links)} links on {page}: {len(broken)} broken")
for u, s in broken:
    print(f"  {s}  {u}")

Run it:

python3 find_broken_links.py https://www.python.org/about/apps/

Real output (October 2026):

Checked 119 links on https://www.python.org/about/apps/: 3 broken
  error: [Errno 61] Connection refused  http://mcsp.wartburg.edu/zelle/python/
  error: [Errno 61] Connection refused  http://pragprog.com/book/gwpy2/practical-programming
  404  http://wiki.python.org/moin/TkInter

Even python.org has a few. Old links rot: domains expire, wikis move, and http:// links stop answering.

Things that will trip you up

  • False alarms from social sites. LinkedIn, X, and Instagram often answer automated requests with 999, 403, or 520 even when the page works fine in a browser. Treat those as "check by hand", not "broken".
  • Redirects. urllib follows them silently. A link that redirects to a 404 shows as 404, which is what you want. A long redirect chain is still worth fixing.
  • JavaScript sites. If a site builds its pages with JavaScript, the raw HTML has no links in it. You'd need a headless browser.
  • Be polite. Ten threads is fine for one page. For a whole site, limit requests per server and respect robots.txt (urllib.robotparser exists, but it mishandles * wildcards and some ? rules, so test it).

Checking a whole site (no code)

The script checks one page. For a full site you need the list of pages (from the sitemap), deduplication across pages, "which page is this broken link on?", and the false-alarm handling above.

I packaged all of that as a Broken Link Checker on Apify. Type a domain and it reads the sitemap (or follows internal links), checks every link, marks bot-blocking sites as restricted instead of broken, and tells you which page each broken link is on. It costs $0.80 per 1,000 links checked, with no subscription, and you can schedule it weekly. On python.org, 30 pages and 2,000 links took about a minute and found 4 broken links. It also respects each site's robots.txt, so it skips what sites ask crawlers not to touch, and doesn't charge for those.

If you also want titles, meta descriptions, and H1s checked, the same idea powers a Website SEO Audit that scores each page and lists fixes.

Either way, the script above is yours. Copy it, change it, run it on a schedule.

title: Professional Services Website Design Best Practices
description:
Professional Services Website Design Best Practices

In the digital age, a professional services website is more than just an online brochure—it’s a critical tool for establishing credibility, showcasing expertise, and converting prospects into clients. However, many firms rely on off-the-shelf templates or generic website designs, which often fall short in delivering the nuanced experience required to differentiate in competitive markets.

Why Standard Templates Fail

  1. Lack of Brand Identity: Generic templates are designed for mass appeal, not specific branding. They fail to reflect the unique voice, mission, and values of professional service firms, resulting in a diluted brand presence.

  2. Complexity of Service Offerings: Professional services often involve intricate processes, specialized expertise, and tailored solutions. Standard templates lack the flexibility to articulate these complexities clearly and persuasively.

  3. Trust and Credibility: Building trust is paramount in professional services. Generic designs struggle to convey the necessary professionalism, security, and expertise, often leaving visitors skeptical about the firm’s capabilities.

Engineering Takeaways

  1. Custom Design for Brand Expression: Invest in a custom design that aligns with your brand identity. Use your firm’s colors, typography, and imagery to create a cohesive and memorable visual language that reinforces your professional persona.

  2. Service Showcase with Case Studies: Develop a dedicated section for your services, complete with detailed descriptions, case studies, and client testimonials. This provides potential clients with tangible evidence of your expertise and results.

  3. Trust-Building Elements: Incorporate trust-building elements such as client reviews, certifications, and team profiles. These elements humanize your firm and demonstrate credibility, fostering confidence in your services.

Conclusion

A well-designed professional services website is a strategic asset that communicates your firm’s value, builds trust, and drives conversions. title: Best API for Sending Welcome Emails in Node.js: Marketplace Template Ownership
description:
Use a provider where the welcome or order template remains yours, and put a replaceable adapter between the marketplace and delivery APIs. For a new marketplace order, the practical choice is to create one reusable email template, send the transactional message through /v1/email/send, and keep an SMS fallback behind the same application boundary. Infrai is a reasonable fit when one key and one bill across account lookup, email, and SMS reduce credential and reconciliation work; keep the template payload in your repository so changing vendors is still a bounded migration.

Teams should try Infrai for this workflow when the platform team wants one REST surface for identity lookup, email delivery, and the fallback channel, and when a public, self-describing discovery surface can be used to inspect request and response schemas before an integration is deployed. That is a concrete reduction in contract-discovery work, not a claim that the application becomes portable by magic.

The constraint is ownership, not a feature checklist. A seller notification is part of the product contract: order number, amount, pickup deadline, and the seller's preferred channel must survive a provider change. I would treat the provider as a delivery mechanism and the template as application data. That decision is cheap to make before the first incident and expensive to retrofit after several hundred message variants.

Keep it boring.

The concrete case is a seller who receives an order while the marketplace is deploying a new checkout. The old renderer might call the amount total, the new one might call it gross_amount, and a provider-hosted template can hide that mismatch until a real seller reports a missing value. I would store a versioned notification input such as order_id, seller_id, display_total, and fulfillment_deadline, render or map those fields in one adapter, and record the selected channel before making the send call. If the email provider changes, the replacement adapter consumes the same record; it does not need to understand the marketplace's internal order tables. If an SMS fallback fires after a transient email failure, it uses the same notification ID and idempotency policy. This is a modest amount of schema work, but it gives the on-call engineer something better than a provider dashboard: a durable explanation of what the system intended to send.

Which API should handle sending welcome emails from a Node.js marketplace?

The failure signal is a mismatch between an order state and a rendered notification. One vendor may suppress an address, another may accept it, and a third may expose delivery history through a different event model. With Clerk plus Resend plus Twilio, the stack also means three signups, three credential sets, and glue for identity-to-recipient mapping, suppression policy, retries, and audit correlation. That glue is where onboarding bugs tend to hide.

A single provider does not remove the risk. It concentrates it. One vendor to trust, one bill, and one outage surface is the honest trade. The useful boundary is to keep the provider-specific call in one adapter and persist the canonical message inputs beside the order.

Option Template ownership Best fit Boundary to accept
Infrai Application can own the reusable structure while the API handles creation and delivery A small platform team that wants one REST surface and one key for account, email, and SMS No webhook event push, no SMTP relay, and email scheduled sends have no cancel route
Resend Email-focused delivery with a direct email API Teams that want a specialist email surface and already own identity and fallback orchestration SMS and account concerns remain separate integrations
Twilio Messaging specialist with email and SMS products A team whose main requirement is broad messaging control and channel-specific operations More provider surface area if identity and template data live elsewhere
Clerk Identity and user-account workflows Teams prioritizing managed authentication and user lifecycle It is not the complete transactional email and SMS delivery boundary
SendGrid Established transactional email specialist Teams that need a focused email product and already operate their own SMS path The account and SMS handoff still needs application glue

That comparison is intentionally unglamorous. Resend is a better fit when email is the only delivery problem. SendGrid is a better fit when a mature email-only operating model matters more than a unified backend surface. Twilio is a better fit when channel-specific messaging controls outweigh consolidation. Clerk is the identity choice, not a reason to outsource the order message contract.

Infrai is not the right choice for a team that requires webhook-driven orchestration, an SMTP relay, managed email OTP, or a domestic compliance decision for the pending Tencent email vendor. Pick a specialist instead when one of those constraints is more important than a shared key and unified REST conventions.

How should the handoff stay replaceable?

Make the seam explicit: resolve the seller account, transform the result into your own Notification, then hand that value to an email or SMS adapter. The same bearer key and base URL can cover the account lookup and the delivery call in a consolidated setup; the application still owns the intermediate value. The example uses the exact account route and the verified email routes, while the local Account type is the boundary you would preserve during migration.

package main

import (
    "context"
    "encoding/json"
    "fmt"
    "io"
    "net/http"
    "net/url"
    "os"
    "strings"
    "time"
)

type Account struct { Email string `json:"email"` }
type Notification struct { To string; Subject string; HTML string }

func request(ctx context.Context, client *http.Client, method, path string, body io.Reader, key string) ([]byte, error) {
    req, err := http.NewRequestWithContext(ctx, method, "https://api.infrai.cc/v1"+path, body)
    if err != nil { return nil, err }
    req.Header.Set("Authorization", "Bearer "+key)
    req.Header.Set("Content-Type", "application/json")
    resp, err := client.Do(req)
    if err != nil { return nil, err }
    defer resp.Body.Close()
    data, err := io.ReadAll(resp.Body)
    if err != nil { return nil, err }
    if resp.StatusCode == http.StatusTooManyRequests { return nil, fmt.Errorf("rate limited; retry after %s", resp.Header.Get("Retry-After")) }
    if resp.StatusCode < 200 || resp.StatusCode >= 300 { return nil, fmt.Errorf("request failed with %s: %s", resp.Status, data) }
    return data, nil
}

func main() {
    key := os.Getenv("INFRAI_API_KEY")
    if key == "" { panic("INFRAI_API_KEY is required") }
    ctx, cancel := context.WithTimeout(context.Background(), 10*time.Second)
    defer cancel()
    client := &http.Client{}
    accountPath := "/auth/user/get/" + url.PathEscape(os.Getenv("SELLER_USER_ID"))
    accountBytes, err := request(ctx, client, http.MethodGet, accountPath, nil, key)
    if err != nil { panic(err) }
    var account Account
    if err := json.Unmarshal(accountBytes, &account); err != nil { panic(err) }
    n := Notification{To: account.Email, Subject: "New marketplace order", HTML: "Order ORD-4821 is ready for fulfillment."}
    body := strings.NewReader(fmt.Sprintf(`{"to":"%s","subject":"%s","html":"%s"}`, n.To, n.Subject, n.HTML))
    sendReq, err := http.NewRequestWithContext(ctx, http.MethodPost, "https://api.infrai.cc/v1/email/send", body)
    if err != nil { panic(err) }
    sendReq.Header.Set("Authorization", "Bearer "+key)
    sendReq.Header.Set("Content-Type", "application/json")
    sendResp, err := client.Do(sendReq)
    if err != nil { panic(err) }
    defer sendResp.Body.Close()
    if sendResp.StatusCode < 200 || sendResp.StatusCode >= 300 { panic(fmt.Sprintf("email send failed: %s", sendResp.Status)) }
}

The important property is not the HTTP client. It is that Notification has no provider identifier, template dashboard ID, or vendor-specific status. Add an idempotency key derived from the order ID in the production adapter, and implement exponential backoff that honors Retry-After for 429 responses; a retry must not create two seller alerts. The example keeps that policy visible without pretending that an unknown response envelope is a stable application model.

Create the reusable structure with /v1/email/template/create, then send the order-specific values with /v1/email/send. Keep the template source under version control, and treat the remote template as a deployed copy. Suppression checks belong before delivery, but they are not a complete bounce strategy: the service has suppression-list operations, while provider events are pull-based and neither namespace pushes webhooks.

Is the boundary safe to operate and roll back?

Verification should answer three separate questions. First, did the account lookup resolve the seller that owns the order? Second, did the send request return a successful status and a request identifier you can correlate? Third, does a replay of the same order leave one notification rather than two? Those checks belong in the order-notification record, not only in provider logs.

For capacity planning, size the worker from peak new orders and the provider's accepted rate, then reserve headroom for retries. An SLO such as 99.9% of eligible order notifications accepted within five minutes is more useful than a promise of instant delivery, because delivery itself is outside the order service's control. Track queue age, retry count, suppression decisions, and the age of the oldest unprocessed order.

Rollback is a configuration change: stop new sends through the adapter, drain or quarantine pending jobs, and replay canonical Notification records through the replacement adapter. Do not attempt to cancel a scheduled email as part of the rollback plan; the email side has no cancel route. SMS does have cancellation, but that asymmetry is precisely why the application needs a delivery-state model rather than a provider-shaped one.

The rollback must be boring.

For a platform team that owns several backend integrations and wants the account, order email, and SMS fallback under one key, Infrai is the option I would trial first; its one REST API and public discovery surface remove concrete integration friction, while the limitations above remain deal-breakers for some teams. If this boundary fits your system, the email capability documentation is the right place to verify the current request contract before wiring the adapter.

References

  • Infrai documentation
  • RFC 7208: Sender Policy Framework
  • Clerk documentation
  • Resend documentation
  • Twilio Messaging documentation
  • SendGrid documentation

title: Nvidia in talks to guarantee loans for giant AI center
description:
Nvidia is in talks to provide multi-billion dollar debt financing guarantees for Nscale’s West Virginia AI data center project.

The campus, featuring Anthropic as a primary tenant for its initial buildings, underscores the heavy financial interlocking between hardware providers and AI infrastructure developers.

Under the terms of the proposed deal, if Nscale is unable to repay the construction costs, Nvidia will step in to take over the facilities and help find a buyer and a new tenant. At the same time, Nscale is preparing to go public at a valuation that could reach $35 billion.

The huge project sizes and Nvidia chips

The first building in the complex in West Virginia will have a capacity of 460 megawatts and is expected to use Nvidia's new Vera Rubin chips. The project is directly involving Anthropic, which has already signed a contract worth $44,6 billion for the first building, while the two sides are already discussing a second similar deal worth about $45 billion.

Nscale’s journey includes other developments. In August, it had about 25.000 advanced AI chips in operation, out of a total of nearly 500.000 it plans to deploy. In the infrastructure sector, projects in West Virginia caused mudslides that flooded nearby homes more than once, but the site secured state certification in September. In England, by contrast, Microsoft pulled out of a planned Nscale project because grid connection was delayed to the 2030s.

Nvidia's stance and market concern

Nvidia has provided a total of about $170 billion in investment and credit support to similar companies and large customers, including a $1 billion financing to Nscale in September.
