title: From Natural Language to Real Schematics: An Automated Workflow for Power Electronics Schematic Synthesis
description:
arXiv:2610.38201v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Designing power electronics converters traditionally requires intensive human expertise across topology sizing, commercial component selection, circuit simulation verification, and schematic drafting. While Large Language Models (LLMs) show promise in electronic design automation (EDA), applying standalone LLMs directly to board-level power electronics schematic synthesis suffers from severe engineering hallucinations, including inaccurate analytical sizing, fabricated or mismatched component part numbers, violated voltage derating margins, and broken topological connectivity. In this paper, we propose a Bounded Dual-Loop Automated Schematic Synthesis Framework that translates natural language specifications into verified, editable KiCad schematics and manufacturing deliverables. Our workflow integrates six stages across three functional columns: (1) requirement parsing and knowledge-driven power stage synthesis covering non-isolated (Buck, Boost) and isolated/resonant (Flyback, DAB, half-bridge LLC) topologies; (2) contract- and evidence-coordinated component selection grounded in distributor APIs and OEM datasheets, coupled with closed-loop ngspice transient verification and stress feedback; and (3) modular control hardware integration and multi-format deliverable generation featuring native KiCad netlist round-trip verification. End-to-end case studies on a 24-36V to 12V,2A Buck converter (29 positions, 83 verified terminals) and an isolated 48V to 24V, 0.5A, Dual-Active Bridge (DAB) converter (87 positions, 341 verified terminals), alongside comparative evaluations against a Vanilla LLM baseline, demonstrate that our framework improves component verification coverage from 22.2 to 98.6, nominal value consistency from 0 to 97.7, and SPICE simulation pass rates from 0 to 100.

title: Semantic HTML and Accessibility: What I Learned
description:
When I started building my portfolio, I made every part of the page with <div> tags. A <div> is just a box, and it doesn't tell the browser what is inside it.

Semantic HTML means using tags that describe what the content is, like <header>, <nav>, <main> and <footer>. People who are blind use screen readers, and these tags tell the reader what each part of the page is, so they can jump straight to the menu or the main content. Search engines also understand the page better, and the code is easier to read.

Alt text is another important part. It is a short description inside an image tag. Without it, a screen reader has nothing meaningful to read, so a blind person misses what the image shows.

Before and after 

<div class="header">
  <div class="nav">...</div>
</div>
<div class="main">
  <div class="article">...</div>
</div>

<header>
  <nav>...</nav>
</header>
<main>
  <article>...</article>
</main>

The page looks the same, but now every part has a meaning.

Three problems I fixed

  1. Missing menu. My contact page had no navigation, so a person using a keyboard or screen reader couldn't reach the other pages. I added a <nav> to every page.
  2. A broken email link. My "Get in touch" link pointed to a fake address, your-email@example.com. I changed it to my real email so the link works.
  3. A hidden focus outline. My form CSS removed the outline that shows which field is selected. People who use a keyboard need it, so I deleted that line.

See it live

https://fairyfaiyth.github.io/iyf-s12-week-02-fairyfaiyth/

What I learned

I learned that tags like <nav> and <main> tell screen readers what each part of a page is. I also learned that small fixes, like a working email link and a visible focus outline, make a website easier for everyone to use.

Before this week I did not think much about how a page sounds to someone who cannot see it. Now I check that every page has a menu, working links and a clear structure.

title: Run your own model endpoint on a rented GPU with vLLM: your own API key, an SSH tunnel, and an optional LoRA adapter
description:
Short answer: rent a GPU with SSH access, install vLLM in a fresh Python environment, start it so it listens only on the instance's own localhost, require an API key of your own, and reach it from your machine through an SSH tunnel. If you have a LoRA adapter for the same base model, vLLM can serve it next to the base model under its own name. When you are done, copy out what you need and destroy the instance.

Disclosure: I work on CloudGPU, and the GPU rental in this guide is ours. Each step ends with a "What to check" line, because versions, flags and defaults change.

Which kind of endpoint is this?

CloudGPU's terms (section 6) say that each running instance with a service URL gets a public HTTPS address; these URLs are "hard to guess but they are not authenticated by default", and if you need authentication you configure it inside your instance, for example an API key on your Ollama deployment. The docs say that templates that serve an API, such as Ollama and ComfyUI, get such a URL.

This guide takes a different route on purpose. You rent a raw GPU, run vLLM on it, and do not publish any URL: the server listens only on the instance's own localhost, requires your own API key, and you reach it through an SSH tunnel from your machine. That gives you an endpoint only you can use, as long as you keep the SSH access and the key to yourself.

vLLM's own security guide is clear about the limits of the key: --api-key protects only the endpoints under the /v1, /v2, /inference and /cohere prefixes, other endpoints on the same server are not covered, and it says not to rely on --api-key alone. It also notes that some underlying components may listen on all network interfaces. So treat the key as one layer, keep the tunnel as the way in, and do not send anything to the instance that you would not put on a rented machine.

Read these things first

  1. The license of your base model. An adapter sits on top of a base model, so the base model's license applies to what you serve. The walkthrough uses Mistral 7B Instruct v0.3, whose model card lists the Apache-2.0 license (read 2026-10-27). If you use a small Llama or Gemma model instead, read the Llama 3.2 Community License or the Gemma Terms of Use first, including what they say about derivative models. This guide gives no legal conclusions.
  2. What your adapter was trained on. Use only data you have the right to use; CloudGPU's acceptable use policy (section 1.8) prohibits training on datasets you do not have rights to use. If your adapter was trained on text generated through DeepSeek's API and you publish its outputs, DeepSeek's Terms of Use (Last Update: March 27, 2026) require you to label published outputs as AI-generated (section 3.1).
  3. CloudGPU's terms. Read the terms before you rent. Section 1 says compute comes from third-party data centres and supplier networks, which can change, so this guide does not claim your data stays on any particular machine.

What you need

  • A CloudGPU account with balance. GPU instances are billed per minute, rounded up, with a 1-minute minimum, and billing stops when you destroy the instance (terms). Rates are on the pricing page. Payment is by card or USDT (payments).
  • A terminal with ssh, scp and Python 3 on your own machine.
  • Optional: a LoRA adapter trained on Mistral 7B Instruct v0.3, stored in the usual Hugging Face PEFT layout (a folder with adapter_config.json and adapter_model.safetensors), for example the one from the self-critique guide in this series. Without an adapter, do everything below and skip the adapter parts; you will serve the base model only.

What to check: ssh -V prints a version, and python3 --version prints a version. If you have an adapter, its folder contains the two files above.

Step 1: make your endpoint key and look at your adapter (on your own machine)

The key is a long random string that only you and the server know. Generate one:

python3 -c "import secrets; print(secrets.token_urlsafe(32))"

Keep it in a password manager. Make a new one for every instance; never reuse a key from another service.

If you have an adapter, open adapter_config.json in its folder and note two fields: base_model_name_or_path and r (the LoRA rank).

What to check: the command printed a long random string that you have stored somewhere other than a shell history you share. For an adapter, base_model_name_or_path is mistralai/Mistral-7B-Instruct-v0.3 (if not, the adapter belongs to another base model and this guide's command will not match it), and r is a number you can compare with the rank limit in Step 4.

Step 2: rent a raw GPU

On Deploy, choose Raw GPU and a card. The CloudGPU docs say that every template is a ready-made image with root SSH and that for anything a template does not cover you rent a raw GPU (Deploy â†’ Raw GPU) and install what you need over SSH. The docs' GPU table lists 16 GB as the minimum VRAM for models from 0.5B to 8B parameters; vLLM also needs Linux and an NVIDIA GPU with compute capability 7.5 or higher, according to its installation page. A 7B model in 16-bit needs memory for the weights plus a cache for requests, so a card with more than the minimum is the easy fix if the server reports it cannot fit.

Connect with the SSH details of your running instance. If you have an adapter, upload its folder from your own machine (scp takes the port with a capital -P):

scp -r -P <ssh-port> ./adapter-selfloop <ssh-user>@<ssh-host>:/workspace/

What to check: ssh -p <ssh-port> <ssh-user>@<ssh-host> connects, nvidia-smi lists a GPU, and (with an adapter) ls /workspace/adapter-selfloop shows adapter_config.json and adapter_model.safetensors.

Step 3: install vLLM in a fresh environment

The vLLM installation page recommends uv for the Python environment. uv can be installed from PyPI (see the uv installation page). On the instance:

pip install uv
cd /workspace
uv venv --python 3.12 --seed --managed-python
source .venv/bin/activate
uv pip install vllm --torch-backend=auto

These lines follow the vLLM page as read on 2026-10-27; if the page now shows different commands, use its commands.

What to check: with the environment active, vllm --version prints a version, and python3 -c "import torch; print(torch.cuda.is_available())" prints True. If the install stops with an error, read the error text and the troubleshooting parts of the vLLM page.

Step 4: start the server on localhost, with your key

Use your own key in place of <your-endpoint-key>. With an adapter:

cd /workspace && source .venv/bin/activate
nohup vllm serve mistralai/Mistral-7B-Instruct-v0.3 \
  --host 127.0.0.1 --port 8000 \
  --api-key <your-endpoint-key> \
  --tokenizer-mode hf \
  --enable-lora --max-lora-rank 16 \
  --lora-modules selfloop=/workspace/adapter-selfloop \
  > /workspace/vllm.log 2>&1 &

Without an adapter, remove the --enable-lora, --max-lora-rank and --lora-modules lines.

What the flags do, from the vLLM serve reference and LoRA page: --host 127.0.0.1 keeps the HTTP server on the instance's localhost; --api-key makes requests under /v1 carry that key; --tokenizer-mode hf uses the Hugging Face tokenizer instead of letting auto pick the mistral_common tokenizer for Mistral models; pinning it is meant to match how an adapter was trained with the Hugging Face tokenizer, so drop the flag if your adapter was trained another way; --lora-modules name=path registers the adapter under the name selfloop; --max-lora-rank must be at least the adapter's r and the docs list the allowed values (the default is 16), so if your r from Step 1 is larger than 16, use the next allowed value. The key is visible in the instance's process list while the server runs, which is one more reason to use a fresh key per instance.

Wait until the log says the server is ready before you send a request. If the process exits, read the end of the log with tail -n 50 /workspace/vllm.log. A message about memory for the cache is fixed by adding --max-model-len 8192 or by choosing a card with more memory.

What to check: on the instance, curl -s -i http://127.0.0.1:8000/v1/models | head -n 1 prints an HTTP status line that is not a success (an authentication error is expected, because you sent no key), and curl -s -H "Authorization: Bearer <your-endpoint-key>" http://127.0.0.1:8000/v1/models prints JSON that lists the base model and, with an adapter, selfloop.

Step 5: open the tunnel and call your endpoint (on your own machine)

In one terminal, open the tunnel. Nothing is printed while it runs; leave it open:

ssh -N -L 8000:127.0.0.1:8000 -p <ssh-port> <ssh-user>@<ssh-host>

If local port 8000 is already used, pick another local port (for example -L 8001:127.0.0.1:8000) and use it in the URLs below. In a second terminal:

curl http://127.0.0.1:8000/v1/models -H "Authorization: Bearer <your-endpoint-key>"

Now the same request through the OpenAI SDK (pip install openai on your own machine). Put this in a file named ask.py:

import os
import sys

from openai import OpenAI

client = OpenAI(base_url="http://127.0.0.1:8000/v1", api_key=os.environ["ENDPOINT_KEY"])

BASE = "mistralai/Mistral-7B-Instruct-v0.3"
ADAPTER = "selfloop"  # delete this name from the loop below if you started without an adapter

question = sys.argv[1] if len(sys.argv) > 1 else "Explain what a LoRA adapter is in two sentences."

for name in (BASE, ADAPTER):
    reply = client.chat.completions.create(
        model=name,
        messages=[{"role": "user", "content": question}],
        temperature=0,
        max_tokens=300,
    )
    print("==", name)
    print(reply.choices[0].message.content)
    print()

Run it with the key in an environment variable, not in the file:

export ENDPOINT_KEY="<your-endpoint-key>"
python3 ask.py "Explain what a LoRA adapter is in two sentences."

Any tool that lets you set an OpenAI-compatible base URL and a key can use the same two values (http://127.0.0.1:8000/v1 and your key) while the tunnel is open.

What to check: the curl call lists the model names you expect; ask.py prints one answer per model name; and a call with a wrong or missing key is refused rather than answered. If the tunnel command prints "address already in use", use another local port. Reading two answers is not a test of your adapter; for that, use questions the adapter never saw and compare them yourself, as in the self-critique guide.

Step 6: stop, copy out what you need, destroy

Close the tunnel with Ctrl+C in its terminal. Before you destroy anything, copy what you want to keep. The docs have a section called "What to save before you destroy an instance"; read it in the CloudGPU docs. For example, copy the server log from your own machine:

scp -P <ssh-port> <ssh-user>@<ssh-host>:/workspace/vllm.log ./

Then destroy the instance from your Dashboard (the docs: "You can destroy an instance at any time"). Minutes spent copying are billed like any other minute, and billing stops once the instance is destroyed. The endpoint key was meant for this instance only; do not reuse it.

What to check: the instance no longer appears as running in your Dashboard, and the curl call from Step 5 now fails to connect.

Privacy and access, in plain terms

  • This is your own endpoint, with your own API key, reached through your own SSH tunnel. It is not a public URL.
  • Per CloudGPU's terms (section 5), you keep ownership of any data, models, code or output you create on or upload to an instance, and CloudGPU says it does not access, inspect, copy or back up the contents of your instance except in three listed cases: a credible report of a violation of section 3, valid legal process, or to protect the safety of users or third parties.
  • Per the same terms, destroying an instance permanently deletes its local storage, and you are responsible for backing up what you want to keep.
  • Whatever you send to the endpoint is processed on that rented instance. Do not send secrets or personal data you would not put on a rented machine.
  • If you call a model through CloudGPU's AI API instead of your own instance, the request is forwarded to the model provider and its terms apply; see the privacy policy.

Sources

All read on 2026-10-27 (UTC+8).

  • vLLM: installation (NVIDIA CUDA), serving LoRA adapters, serve command reference, security guide.
  • uv: installation.
  • Licenses: Mistral 7B Instruct v0.3 model card, Llama 3.2 Community License, Gemma Terms of Use.
  • DeepSeek: Terms of Use (Last Update: March 27, 2026).
  • CloudGPU: terms, acceptable use policy, privacy policy, docs, pricing.

title: The Engineering Problem Behind Always-On Consumer AI: Context, Memory and Battery
description:
A smartwatch can track movement throughout the day, a smart ring can monitor sleep overnight and smart glasses can capture information about the world around the wearer. But what happens when these devices are expected to do more than collect data? What if they are also expected to understand what is happening, remember previous interactions and offer useful assistance without requiring the user to open an app every time?

This is where always-on artificial intelligence becomes an engineering challenge. An AI assistant running on a consumer wearable must work within strict limits on battery capacity, memory, processing power and physical space. At the same time, it needs enough context to produce useful responses instead of treating every interaction as an isolated request.

The difficult part is balancing these requirements. A wearable must decide what information matters, what it should remember and when running an AI model is worth the energy it consumes.

Why Always-On AI Is Different From a Regular Chatbot

A conventional chatbot receives an explicit text request, processes it, returns an answer and waits idle for the next interaction. An always-on system has a very different workload: it may need to continuously or periodically observe signals from its environment and decide whether any action is necessary.
This shift introduces three critical differences. First, there is continuous input. Audio, motion, location or camera frames from your smart glasses arrive without an explicit user request. Second, the system requires a persistent state, meaning it needs some representation of previous interactions and relevant daily events. Finally, there are strict limited resources. Wearables have finite battery capacity, restrictive thermal headroom, tight RAM and narrow processing bandwidth.
For a smartwatch or smart glasses, detecting a wake word or recognizing a simple gesture is inexpensive compared to transcribing full sentences and running a language model. As outlined in a Review on TinyML: State of the Art and Prospects, deploying machine learning on resource-limited edge devices requires carefully managing these strict constraints. The important distinction is that being available all day does not mean running the most expensive model all day.

Challenge One: How Much Context Should an AI Keep?

Suppose you tell your smart glasses assistant in the morning that you have a meeting scheduled later in the day. Several hours later, you ask whether you have enough time for a quick walk. A useful assistant needs to connect the current time with the earlier conversation to give an accurate answer.
But how does the wearable preserve that information until it becomes relevant?

More Context Does Not Automatically Mean Better Answers

The context window is the amount of information a model can consider in a particular processing step. Previous messages, retrieved notes and current sensor input can all contribute to this context.
While giving the model a massive transcript of your whole day seems ideal, longer inputs can heavily increase processing requirements and memory use. Crucial details can also get buried among less useful background noise. A larger context window does not guarantee that a model will reliably find or use every relevant detail. Furthermore, the actual energy cost of processing context depends heavily on the model's architecture, sequence length, hardware caching and implementation.

Context Selection Is an Engineering Decision

To manage this, engineers use selective retrieval and context compression. Instead of feeding the model an entire day's worth of information, a system might retrieve only the earlier conversation about the meeting, the current time and the user's preferred walking pace. Google DeepMind's ReadAgent research explores this concept by summarizing long inputs into compact gist memories and retrieving original passages only when more detail is needed.
An always-on assistant needs a deliberate strategy for selecting context, not simply a larger context window.

Challenge Two: Memory Is More Than Saving Chat History

There is a fundamental difference between a model's immediate working context and the persistent information that remains available across interactions. A system can store an entire conversation log in a database and still fail to remember what matters. It needs to decide which details are useful, how long they remain relevant and when they should be retrieved.

Short-Term Context Versus Long-Term Memory

Memory in wearables can be grouped into three practical categories. The working context is the information needed for the current request, like your current location. Episodic memory involves records or summaries of previous events, such as an earlier conversation about dinner plans. Semantic memory includes more stable facts, preferences and relationships extracted from earlier experiences, like knowing you prefer vegan restaurants.
Clarify that these are useful conceptual categories, not a universal architecture used by every AI system. For example, a wearable assistant might need the current activity as working context, a summary of a previous conversation as episodic memory and a user's preferred notification style as semantic memory.

The Hard Part Is Deciding What to Keep

Useful memory introduces complex engineering questions: When should a new detail be saved? When should an old detail expire? How should contradictory information be handled? How can the system avoid retrieving irrelevant or outdated facts? How should sensitive information be protected?
Saving more information is not always beneficial, as persistent memory introduces storage, indexing and retrieval overhead. In fact, as highlighted in a 2026 ICML paper on how to Understand and Accelerate Memory Processing Pipeline for Large Language Model Inference, the computational stages involved in preparing, ranking, retrieving and applying memory during inference carry significant overhead.
Useful AI memory depends entirely on what is carefully retained and precisely retrieved, not merely on how much data is stored.

Challenge Three: Battery Life Changes the Entire AI Architecture

A model can produce a highly accurate, useful answer in a fraction of a second and still be completely unsuitable for a wearable if the system consumes too much energy every time it runs. In an always-on device, the cost of repeated background work matters as much as the cost of an individual response.

The Hidden Cost of Continuous Processing

Several factors drain battery life. These include continuous sensor sampling and data capture, audio processing and speech recognition, model inference and moving data between memory and processors. Wireless communication with a phone or cloud service is another heavy tax. Finally, keeping processors awake rather than allowing them to enter low-power states acts as a massive baseline drain.
These costs vary significantly by device and workload. AI inference is not always the largest source of battery drain. For example, continuous audio monitoring can be handled by a small, low-power detector that recognizes a wake word without invoking a large speech or language model. Only if the detector identifies something relevant does the system activate more expensive processing.

Why Small Models and Quantization Matter

Engineers use specific techniques to fit models onto battery-constrained wearables. Quantization involves representing model weights using lower-precision numbers to reduce memory requirements and potentially improve inference efficiency. Pruning removes selected model components or connections to reduce computation and model size. Specialized accelerators, such as hardware specifically designed to execute machine-learning operations efficiently, can also manage the load.
These techniques involve necessary trade-offs. A smaller model may be less accurate and the actual speed or energy improvement depends on the hardware support and software implementation. The technical research paper Deploying Transformers on the Apple Neural Engine demonstrates how optimizing model execution for memory use and responsiveness directly impacts battery efficiency on specific hardware configurations.
Battery constraints must influence the architecture from the beginning rather than being treated as a final optimization task.

The Engineering Solution: Use Different Levels of Intelligence

An efficient always-on assistant uses a staged processing pipeline rather than sending every incoming signal to the largest available model.

A Practical Tiered Architecture

Consider this illustrative sequence for smart glasses: First, low-power monitoring uses a small detector to check incoming sensor data for potentially relevant events. Next, event filtering determines whether the noise requires further analysis. If it does, context retrieval selects relevant memories and recent information. Then, model inference processes the request using a suitable on-device model. If the task is too complex, an escalation step hands it over to a more capable local or remote model that handles tasks the smaller model cannot reliably complete. Finally, a memory update allows the system to save selected information if it is useful for future interactions.
This is a proposed architectural pattern, not a strict requirement that every product follows.

When Should the Device Use the Cloud?

Routing tasks effectively is crucial. On-device processing reduces network dependence, response latency and the need to transmit sensitive raw data. However, cloud processing provides access to larger models and much greater computing resources. Relying on network communication naturally introduces latency, energy costs, connectivity requirements and additional privacy considerations.
A hybrid architecture routes simple tasks locally and escalates complex requests selectively. The Apple Intelligence Foundation Language Models report illustrates this dynamic well, describing a small on-device model operating alongside a larger server-based model to show how model placement can reflect different computational requirements.
The most efficient design does not use the same amount of computation for every event.

The Trade-Offs Developers Need to Measure

Building this system requires developers to evaluate metrics far beyond a model's isolated reasoning capabilities.
Engineers must measure the energy per task to see how much power a typical inference or interaction consumes. They also monitor idle power, tracking how much energy the system uses while simply waiting for relevant input. End-to-end latency is just as crucial, measuring the time from detecting an event to actually producing a response. Developers also need to monitor peak memory usage to ensure the model and its context fit within available RAM without stalling the device.
Other critical performance metrics include context retrieval quality (whether the system grabs the correct information when needed) and the false activation rate (how often the assistant performs completely unnecessary processing). Finally, developers must observe thermal behavior, as sustained activity can cause a wearable device to overheat or throttle its performance.
A single benchmark cannot capture the full user experience. A model that performs well in an isolated inference test may still perform poorly when combined with continuous sensing, background processes and wireless communication. Engineers must test realistic day-long workloads rather than measuring only short demonstrations. Evaluate the complete system under realistic usage conditions, not just the model in isolation.

Conclusion: Always-On AI Is a Resource Management Problem

Always-on consumer AI requires far more than a model that can intelligently answer questions. It needs a reliable way to interpret incoming signals, retrieve relevant memories, preserve useful context and decide when additional computation is truly justified.
These technical decisions are fundamentally connected. Retaining unnecessary information can complicate retrieval, processing every single event wastes precious energy and relying exclusively on the cloud can introduce frustrating latency and connectivity problems. The real engineering challenge is to build a system that remains constantly useful without treating every moment as a reason to run an expensive model.
The future of always-on AI will depend not only on how intelligently a device can respond, but also on how intelligently it decides when to think.

title: hotellobby (LobbyDuo): UX Notes on Preview-Before-Pay AI Booth Videos
description:
How I shipped a two-photo → Hotel Lobby booth duo on Cloudflare Workers — optimizing framing preview before Stripe, with Seedance via TryAllAPI.

Trend video products usually fail at the same moment: the user pays, then discovers their faces are cropped wrong. For tryhotellobby.app (product name hotellobby / LobbyDuo) I optimized the UX before the charge, not another prompt textarea.

Upload two adult face photos → ~15s orange COLORS-style booth duo (9:16 / 16:9 / 21:9, 480p or 720p) with original/AI booth audio. Independent tool — not affiliated with any artist group. This post is the builder + UX walkthrough. Prices and model ids change; treat live site / console as source of truth.

UX thesis: preview framing, then unlock Create

The homepage copy is blunt: free scene preview before you pay — upload two photos, check framing in the orange booth layout, then unlock Create with a one-time pack.

That sequence matters more than fancy motion poetry:

  1. Photo 1 → left of the booth duo.
  2. Photo 2 → right.
  3. Local/layout preview of how faces sit in the booth.
  4. Only then: Stripe → credits → Seedance render.

Users who can see “my face is too small / off-center” before paying convert better and refund less. Free-form “make a hotel video” prompts do the opposite: ambiguity first, charge second, regret third.

Live packs verified on-site while writing: Single $8.88 (≈ 500 credits / one 720p), 3-pack $16.99, plus larger packs (and occasional cheaper 480p messaging). Guest Stripe — no account for a single video. Always re-check the create CTA before you screenshot a price for a friend.

Why left/right roles beat a single “upload faces” dump

Booth memes are spatial. If the UI does not say who stands where, users invent their own convention and then complain the sample “looks different.” Fixed seats:

  • Remove “who is who?” support tickets.
  • Stabilize the locked template prompt sent upstream.
  • Make demos honest — the sample matches the seats.

Aspect ratio is a first-class control (9:16 default for Reels/TikTok; 16:9 / 21:9 for other cuts). Original/AI booth audio means the download is shareable without hunting a track.

Stack overview

Layer Choice Role
Front / SSR TanStack Start (Vite) Landing, upload panel, generation status
Runtime Cloudflare Workers Edge deploy, secrets, API routes
DB Cloudflare D1 Credits, orders, task rows (table prefixes if DBs are shared)
Payments Stripe Checkout One-time packs + optional larger packs; guest checkout
Video upstream TryAllAPI → Seedance Async create + poll
Analytics GA Funnel sanity check 
two faces → booth layout preview
→ check credits (else Stripe)
→ Worker creates Seedance task via TryAllAPI
→ poll until MP4 URL → store / show
→ on failure: refund credits

Demo clips are self-hosted. Do not hotlink someone else’s sample MP4 for marketing.

Why a video API aggregator

Operational checklist after register / top-up:

  1. Confirm available USD balance in the console (not only the checkout success page).
  2. Create a token in pay-as-you-go style billing.
  3. Enable the video / Seedance-related channel group on that token. Wrong group → “no available channel” even when the model id looks right.
  4. Prefer separate keys per product (hotellobby-prod vs sandbox).
  5. Put the key only in Workers Secrets (for example TRYALLAPI_API_KEY). Never in the frontend bundle or a blog post.

Conceptually the call shape looks like this (field names follow the aggregator’s v3 contents API; always re-check current docs):

POST /api/v3/contents/generations/tasks
Authorization: Bearer <TRYALLAPI_API_KEY>
Content-Type: application/json
Accept-Encoding: identity

GET /api/v3/contents/generations/tasks/{id}

I send Accept-Encoding: identity from the Worker because some gateways behave badly with transparent decompression. Model ids used in production look like Seedance 2.x family strings — treat console ids as source of truth, not this paragraph.

Seedance parameters that matter for booth duos

A few details that bit me across this family of sites:

  • Pass duration as an explicit integer. Some models default to “smart length.” Omitting duration can silently lengthen the clip and the bill.
  • resolution and ratio. Cost tracks resolution tier and duration more than portrait vs landscape. Match whatever the create UI offers (often 480p/720p and 9:16 for Shorts).
  • generate_audio. When the product ships “finished” downloads, leave audio on; creators who want a trending sound can mute later.
  • Status machine. Expect something like queued → running → succeeded / failed. Success URLs are often short-lived signed links — download/rehost on your side before handing the file to the user.
  • Decent failure. On supply_unavailable or hard failures: refund credits, show a short human message, log the detailed upstream error server-side, optionally fall back to another Seedance tier.

Rough mental model for upstream cost (illustrative only — use your own usage fields and invoices):

tokens ≈ duration_sec × width × height × fps / 1024
cost   ≈ tokens × price_per_million_tokens

Price the site after you measure a few real 720p runs with retry margin, Stripe fees, and failed-job refunds — not from a spreadsheet fantasy of 0% failure.

Booth-specific: map two reference images to left/right seats consistently; same-person clones in both seats look wrong — the UI should say so.

Credits, Stripe, and guest checkout

Demo UIs are easy. The line between toy and product is:

  1. User hits Create → check credit balance.
  2. If short → Stripe Checkout Session (guest allowed).
  3. Webhook (plus a return-URL sync check) grants credits.
  4. Pre-debit / lock credits, create upstream task, persist task_id in D1.
  5. Poll until done; succeed → show MP4; fail → refund credits.

Two books of account stay separate: USD balance at TryAllAPI (your cost) vs site credits (what you sold). Mixing them in one mental ledger is how you underprice or invent “mysterious” losses.

When several products share one Stripe account, isolate webhooks by endpoint or by metadata (site / product). Callbacks pointed at the wrong apex domain are a classic multi-site footgun.

Secrets stay in Workers: TRYALLAPI_API_KEY, STRIPE_SECRET_KEY, webhook secret, auth secrets. The browser only ever sees publishable Stripe keys if needed.

Deploy notes (Workers + D1)

Typical loop on this template family:

pnpm install
# wire D1 database_id, production env, custom domain in wrangler
pnpm cf:deploy

Before calling a deploy “done”:

  • D1 binding is correct; shared DBs use table prefixes, not a new database per micro-idea (free-tier DB counts are limited).
  • AUTH_TRUSTED_ORIGINS and Stripe return / webhook URLs match the production HTTPS origin.
  • GA id is set for a coarse funnel (land → upload → pay → wait → download).
  • One real end-to-end path on production or a staging Worker: upload → pay → render → download.

Production origin for Checkout / auth trust: https://tryhotellobby.app (alternate brand hostnames may exist — keep allowlists in sync with the URL users actually pay on).

Product rules that are not optional

Face-based generation is not “just another SaaS CRUD app”:

  • Require an explicit 18+ / rights-to-use confirmation on upload.
  • Block minors and refuse celebrity / stranger misuse in copy and policy.
  • Expect upstream safety refusals; refund and explain.
  • Keep privacy policy honest about retention; do not train on user media by default.
  • Market as an independent fan-style tool for a trend format — not as an official tie-in unless you actually have that deal.
  • Use your own sample renders in marketing.

Those constraints belong in the product, not in a footnote you add after the first dispute email.

What the UX taught me

  1. Preview-before-pay reduces “bad crop” chargebacks more than shaving another dollar off the Single pack.
  2. Locked booth layout beats free-form hotel prompts.
  3. Guest Single pack (~$8.88) matches “I need one clip tonight.”
  4. Credits with automatic refund on failed generation is table stakes.
  5. Measure land → upload → pay → wait → download before rewriting marketing adjectives.

Consumer path: tryhotellobby.app — watch the sample, upload two authorized adult faces, preview framing, pay once. Builder path: TryAllAPI, top up, prove create+poll, then polish the preview UX. Sell confidence in framing first; sell GPU second.

title: SkillMem: Compact External Skill Memory for Latent Multi-Agent Reasoning
description:
arXiv:2610.37935v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Latent multi-agent systems reduce inference cost by keeping intermediate reasoning and inter-agent communication in continuous representations.\ Reusable skills, however, are commonly supplied as text or stored as layer-wise Key-Value states or skill-specific model parameters, introducing repeated processing or substantial per-skill storage.\ We introduce \textbf{SkillMem}, which represents each reusable skill as a small external latent memory and makes it directly available during latent multi-agent reasoning.\ A role-conditioned cross-attention reader allows the same memory to guide different agents according to their roles and current hidden states.\ We train the skill memories and shared reader through behavioral distillation, matching the change in token predictions induced by a textual skill while keeping the backbone frozen.\ For our experiments, we obtain textual skills from paired successful and failed multi-agent trajectories, although existing skills can also be compiled directly.\ Across six benchmarks and Qwen3 models ranging from 4B to 14B parameters, SkillMem provides strong gains for smaller backbones while preserving efficient latent multi-agent inference across model scales.\ We use the same $8\times256$ memory configuration across all evaluated model scales, requiring 9.6\,KB of skill-specific storage per skill, including its retrieval embedding.\ For a library of 100 skills, SkillMem reduces total storage by more than $38\times$ compared with alternative skill representations and achieves up to a $4.23\times$ end-to-end inference speedup.\ These results show that compact procedural memories can be reused without sacrificing the efficiency of latent multi-agent reasoning.

title: The 1280 720 Lesson: Why a Zip Isn't Shippable Until It Has a Cover"**
description:
I had 39 finished products sitting in a folder and a zip file I was proud of. Then I opened my sales page preview and saw a gray rectangle with a filename in it. Nobody buys a gray rectangle. That was the moment I learned the 1280×720 lesson: a zip file is not a product until it has a cover.

Here is what I actually did about it, and the rules I now bake into every package.

The cover is the product page

When you sell a digital download, the buyer never touches the zip before paying. All they see is the preview image your store renders. Gumroad, Etsy, and every stock platform work the same way: the thumbnail does the selling, the file just has to not break.

So the cover is not decoration. It is the entire sales surface. I settled on 1280×720 for covers and 600×600 for thumbnails because those two sizes render cleanly everywhere I sell, and they are cheap to generate. Pillow draws one in under a second on my 1 vCPU, 2 GB server. No GPU, no image API call, no cost per cover.

Before I scripted this, I was hand-making covers in an image editor. That was twenty minutes per product, which across 39 products was thirteen hours I did not have. The script does it in one command:

python pack_product.py my-product "My Product" "A short subtitle" 9

That writes the zip, the cover, and the thumbnail in one pass. Total third-party dependencies for the whole thing: Pillow. That is it.

Stock platforms reject wrong metadata instantly, and that is a different problem

The cover lesson applies to your own products. Stock platforms have a harsher rule: they reject the upload before a human ever looks at it if the CSV header is wrong. Adobe Stock wants a 5-column header. Vecteezy wants 4 columns. Dreamstime wants 15. Get one column wrong and the whole batch bounces.

I learned this by submitting a batch and watching all of it fail for a header mismatch. Not the art, not the keywords, the header. So make_metadata.py writes the exact header each platform demands and nothing else. No clever extras, no optional columns. The platforms do not reward creativity in metadata, they reward compliance.

One honest caveat the script also enforces: if you do not supply titles, it title-cases the filename and uses that. That is fine for a first pass and bad for submission. Replace it before you hit submit. Reviewers notice lazy titles.

Double-posting is the fastest way to get flagged

The second failure I had was running a batch twice. I lost track of what I had already uploaded, re-ran the queue, and posted duplicates. On stock platforms that is a flag on your account, not a shrug. So now there is a ledger:

python upload_tracker.py pending items.txt
python upload_tracker.py done "asset-001.jpg"
python upload_tracker.py status

It is a plain text ledger, standard library only, no database. A re-run checks the ledger first. Since I added it, zero double-posts across every batch. For context on scale: I have made about 1,700 assets total, 58 are live on Adobe Stock, and my first sale was $0.99. That first dollar proved the pipeline worked. The ledger is what keeps it working at batch size.

The 2 GB server rules that make any of this possible

None of this runs on a fancy machine. The whole pipeline runs on 1 vCPU and 2 GB RAM with no GPU. That forces habits worth adopting even if you have better hardware:

  • One process at a time. Never fan out image jobs in parallel on a single core. It does not go faster, it goes OOM.
  • Call gc.collect() after each asset. Free memory between items or peak RSS climbs until the kill.
  • Measure peak RSS, not average: resource.getrusage(RUSAGE_SELF).ru_maxrss gives the real ceiling.
  • Run heavy render steps one file per subprocess so memory returns to the OS.
  • Render at the resolution you need. Inspecting a preview at 60 dpi instead of 300 is the difference between fitting in RAM and not.

Keep your research folder forever

One structural mistake I made once and will not repeat: I deleted my research folder to "clean up." Six weeks later I wanted the notes behind a product decision and they were gone. Scrapes, logs, notes, all of it is raw material for the next product. The folder layout I use now:

project/
  assets/       raw output
  output/       ready-to-submit files + metadata.csv
  packs/        finished zips + covers
  research/     never delete this
  scripts/      the tools

Where this all lives now

Everything above is now four scripts: make_metadata.py for the Adobe, Vecteezy, and Dreamstime CSVs, upload_tracker.py for the ledger, md2pdf.py for turning Markdown docs into styled PDFs, and pack_product.py for the zip, the 1280×720 cover, and the 600×600 thumbnail. Two dependencies total, Pillow and reportlab, and two of the four scripts need nothing but the standard library. These are the exact scripts that packaged those 39 products, 856 MB of output, validated on that same tiny server. They are the packaging layer of the larger system I call the digital asset factory, which is where the 1,700 assets and the 58 live Adobe listings came from. If you want the tools instead of the story, it is here:

Get digital asset factory

Building digital products? Free guides & kits for digital product sellers.

title: Converting Web Applications to Native iOS & Android Apps: Modern WebView Architectures, PWA, and Native Shell Engineering
description:
Converting Web Applications to Native iOS & Android Apps: Modern WebView Architectures, PWA, and Native Shell Engineering

One of the most frequent dilemmas for modern product teams and startups is choosing between a costly, multi-codebase native mobile development cycle (Swift/Kotlin) and delivering a cross-platform mobile experience from an existing responsive web application.

While modern Progressive Web Apps (PWAs) deliver near-native performance, businesses still require App Store and Google Play distribution for push notifications, in-app purchases, camera integration, and brand discoverability.

However, simply wrapping a web URL inside a standard webview almost always leads to Apple App Store rejection under Guideline 4.2 (Minimum Functionality), sluggish touch response times, and broken offline states.

In this technical case study, the engineering team at UCDREAMS breaks down how we architect native-shell applications that pass App Store review, achieve 60fps scrolling, and integrate native hardware bridges.

1. Why Naive "URL Wrappers" Fail App Store Review

Apple Guideline 4.2 explicitly states:

"Your app should include features, content, and UI that elevate it beyond a repackaged website. If your app is not particularly useful, unique, or 'app-like', it doesn't belong on the App Store."

Common failure modes of naive web wrappers include:

  1. White Flash on Cold Boot: Loading remote web pages causes a 1-3 second blank viewport before CSS renders.
  2. Missing Native Navigation: Hardware back buttons on Android break or exit the app unexpectedly.
  3. Viewport Bounce & Text Selection: Default Safari/WebKit bounce physics make the UI feel like a webpage rather than a compiled app.
  4. Zero Offline Capability: When connectivity drops, users see the browser's default "No Internet Connection" error.

2. The Modern Native Shell Architecture (Capacitor & WKWebView)

To deliver an authentic native experience, the web application assets (HTML, CSS, JS, WASM) must be bundled locally inside the application bundle or served through an asset bridge (capacitor://localhost or http://localhost:8080), eliminating remote HTTP latency.

// capacitor.config.ts - Enterprise Shell Configuration
import { CapacitorConfig } from '@capacitor/cli';

const config: CapacitorConfig = {
  appId: 'com.ucdreams.webapp',
  appName: 'UCDreams Mobile App',
  webDir: 'dist',
  bundledWebRuntime: false,
  server: {
    androidScheme: 'https',
    cleartext: false,
    allowNavigation: ['ucdreams.com', '*.ucdreams.com']
  },
  plugins: {
    SplashScreen: {
      launchShowDuration: 1800,
      launchAutoHide: true,
      backgroundColor: '#0F172A',
      androidSplashResourceName: 'splash',
      showSpinner: true,
      spinnerColor: '#2563EB'
    },
    PushNotifications: {
      presentationOptions: ['badge', 'sound', 'alert']
    }
  }
};

export default config;

3. High-Performance Bridge & Hardware Acceleration

Eliminating Webview Clutter

In CSS, lock down mobile browser physics to ensure native tactile response:

/* Native App CSS Normalization */
html, body {
  overscroll-behavior-y: none;
  -webkit-touch-callout: none;
  -webkit-user-select: none;
  user-select: none;
  -webkit-tap-highlight-color: transparent;
  touch-action: pan-x pan-y;
}

/* Enable hardware-accelerated GPU layer compositing */
.mobile-view-container {
  transform: translateZ(0);
  will-change: transform, opacity;
  overflow-y: auto;
  -webkit-overflow-scrolling: touch;
}

Bi-directional Native Bridge (WKScriptMessageHandler)

In iOS (Swift), establish secure, zero-overhead asynchronous bridge communication between JavaScript and the native runtime:

// Swift WKScriptMessageHandler Implementation
import WebKit

class BridgeController: NSObject, WKScriptMessageHandler {
    func userContentController(_ userContentController: WKUserContentController, didReceive message: WKScriptMessage) {
        guard let dict = message.body as? [String: Any],
              let action = dict["action"] as? String else { return }

        switch action {
        case "hapticFeedback":
            let impact = UIImpactFeedbackGenerator(style: .medium)
            impact.impactOccurred()
        case "biometricAuth":
            authenticateUser()
        default:
            break
        }
    }
}

4. Test the Live In-Browser Web-to-App Generator

To simplify this configuration process for developers and business owners, we released UCDREAMS Free Web to App Converter.

The tool allows you to input any web URL or PWA manifest and immediately generate ready-to-build Xcode (iOS) and Android Studio project configurations, complete with app icons, splash screens, permission manifests, and Capacitor scaffolding.

Try it directly in your browser:
👉 Open UCDREAMS Web to App Converter

5. Enterprise Custom Mobile & Web Application Engineering

While automated shells work great for basic web utilities, high-traffic SaaS platforms and enterprise applications require custom native bridge engineering, background geolocation, offline SQLite synchronization, and dedicated App Store review consulting.

Our senior engineering team at UCDREAMS designs and builds bespoke full-stack web applications, React Native architectures, and high-performance WordPress systems guaranteed to achieve 95+ PageSpeed scores.

title: Cryptopals: CBC bitflipping attack
description:
• CBC block cipher mode
  • CBC bitflipping attack
    • Setup
    • Attack
      • Get block size
      • Craft the input to the oracle
      • Flip ciphertext bits
    • Code
  • Conclusion

Today, we will learn about the CBC block cipher mode, how it works, and the bitflipping attack. This post is related to https://cryptopals.com/sets/2/challenges/16.

CBC block cipher mode

Cipher Block Chaining (CBC) is a block cipher mode of operation. Data is encrypted in blocks of fixed size and with the same key. Also, some bytes are added when the plaintext doesn't have a length that is a multiple of the block size, known as padding.

Let p be the plaintext, c the ciphertext, k the key, IV the
initialization vector (later explained), ^ the XOR operation, E any encryption algorithm and D its decryption counterpart. Assume that the ciphertext can be divided into blocks of length equal to l, without any leftover bytes. For the first block, the encrypted version is computed as c[0] = E(IV ^ p[0], k). For all the other blocks, we have that c[i] = E(p[i] ^ c[i - 1], k). From these equations, we can derive the decryption. We have that p[i] = D(c[i], k) ^ c[i - 1] and p[0] = D(c[0], k) ^ IV.

The IV is a unique, non-repeating, random binary sequence that we use to randomize the encryption. As opposed to ECB, identical plain blocks won't result in identical encrypted blocks. Furthermore, the same message will return different encrypted messages.

It still has some issues. Encryption can't be parallelized, even though decryption can be, and it's vulnerable to attacks.

CBC bitflipping attack

Setup

For this exercise, we assume that we have access to two functions.

The first function takes some userdata as input and builds the
following string
comment1=cooking%20MCs;userdata{};comment2=%20like%20a%20pound%20of%20bacon. It then encodes and encrypts the data.

pub fn encrypt_user_data(data: &str) -> Vec<u8> {
    let data = format!(
        "comment1=cooking%20MCs;userdata={};comment2=%20like%20a%20pound%20of%20bacon",
        data
    );
    let url_encoded_data = data
        .replace('=', "%3D")
        .replace(';', "%3B")
        .replace(' ', "%20");

    encrypt_aes_128_cbc(url_encoded_data.as_bytes(), &KEY, Some(IV.to_vec()))
}

The second function decrypts the data and checks if the user is admin. However, the data is not decoded. That means that = won't appear. Therefore, it's impossible to get admin=true by inputting the data into the first function. We need to break the cryptography.

pub fn is_admin(data: &[u8]) -> bool {
    let plain = decrypt_aes_128_cbc(data, &KEY, Some(IV.to_vec()));
    plain.contains(";admin=true;")
}

Attack

The goal of the exercise is to get the is_admin function to return true.

Get block size

As in a previous ECB blog, we need to detect the block size.

let encrypt_fn = |data: &[u8]| encrypt_user_data(&String::from_utf8_lossy(data));
let (block_size, _) = compute_block_size_and_padding_length(encrypt_fn);

Craft the input to the oracle

We need to compute the prefix length, including the blocks it takes, and how many bytes of the last prefix block are dedicated to the prefix.

let full_prefix_length = prefix_length(encrypt_fn, block_size);
let block_prefix_length = block_size - (full_prefix_length % block_size);

Now, we can craft the input. The trick here is to make sure that our ;admin=true; string ends up all together on one block. Not spilled over two different blocks. With the prefix length, we can make sure that happens. One last detail, ; and = are encoded. On decryption, they won't be decoded. We are going to use some placeholder characters instead. In this case, X for ; and Y for =. We will see why in the next section.

let mut crafted_input = vec!["a"; block_prefix_length].join("");
crafted_input.push_str("XadminYtrueX");

Flip ciphertext bits

We send the crafted input to the oracle, we get the ciphertext, and it's time to get into the offense!

In CBC, encrypting a block requires doing XOR between the previous
encrypted block and the current plaintext block. Any bit we modify in the ciphertext will modify the final value that gets decrypted because of the XOR operation. We can take advantage of that.

Imagine we have the two following plaintext blocks (I'm using shorter block size to simplify things):

|            p1           |            p2           |
| 00 01 02 03 04 05 06 07 | 08 09 10 11 12 13 14 15 |
| a  a  a  a  a  a  a  a  | a  a  a  a  a  a  a  X  |

Where X is the value we want to modify. We want to get ;. And the final encrypted form is:

|            c1           |            c2           |
| 00 01 02 03 04 05 06 07 | 08 09 10 11 12 13 14 15 |
| b  b  b  b  b  b  b  b  | b  b  b  b  b  b  b  Z  |

Assume the decrypted value of Z is Y. Thus, Y is the result of X ^ b.

We know that on decryption, c2 will be decrypted then XORed with c1. The idea then, is to modify the last byte of c1 in such a way that when XORing, X will turn into ;. In that case, we can do c1[7] = b ^ X ^ ;. That way, during decryption, when it XORs D(c2) with c1, the following operation is performed Y ^ c1[7] = Y ^ (b ^ X ^ ;) = (X ^ b) ^ (b ^ X ^ ;) = ;.

That's the attack. That's all we are doing. We take the byte from the previous block at the same position as the byte that we want to attack, and XOR it with both the plaintext character and the character we want to obtain.

In this case, we applied that theory to the three characters we wanted to modify.

let ciphertext = encrypt_user_data(&crafted_input);

let mut crafted_ciphertext = ciphertext;
crafted_ciphertext[2 * block_size] ^= b';' ^ b'X';
crafted_ciphertext[2 * block_size + 6] ^= b'=' ^ b'Y';
crafted_ciphertext[2 * block_size + 11] ^= b';' ^ b'X';

With that, we accomplished the task.

Code

You can check the whole implementation https://github.com/danielorihuela/cryptopals/blob/main/src/set2/challenge16.rs.

Conclusion

The CBC cipher is simple but insecure. It's an improvement over ECB. It doesn't leak patterns. However, it's still vulnerable to attacks.

title: DORA Metrics for AI Agents: How We Built an Observability Engine in Pure Go
description:
The first phase of AI coding was dominated by awe at token generation speed: how many lines of code could Claude, Devin, or Antigravity produce in 60 seconds?

However, once autonomous coding agents enter production-grade engineering workflows, the fundamental question asked by Tech Leads and CTOs shifts dramatically:

"Are AI agents genuinely accelerating software delivery, or are they simply amplifying technical debt, rework rates, and pull-request chaos?"

To answer this question quantitatively rather than intuitively, we don't need to invent new software metrics. We need to leverage the gold standard of modern engineering: DORA Metrics (DevOps Research and Assessment).

In this article — consolidating releases DEL-020 through DEL-027 (v0.9.0) of the Pipeline-AI framework —, I share how we redesigned and implemented the four DORA metrics specifically for autonomous AI agents, building a zero-dependency telemetry engine in pure Go 1.24 stdlib, hardened with fuzz testing, rendered via an Interactive Generative UI Dashboard, and exposed directly to agents via the Model Context Protocol (MCP).

1. Why DORA Metrics for AI Agents?

Developed by Google Cloud / DORA, the four key metrics balance two essential software delivery forces: Throughput and Stability.

When human keystrokes are replaced by a team of specialized AI agents (Triage, Architecture, Test Writer, Dev Implementation, Code Review, Security, and QA), the four DORA metrics take on an entirely new meaning at machine speed:

DORA Metric Human Engineering Meaning Adaptation for Autonomous Agents (Pipeline-AI)
Deployment Frequency (DF) How often code reaches production (weekly or monthly). Number of fully validated micro-deliveries shipped per day at machine speed.
Lead Time for Changes (LT) Time from first commit to production deployment (days/weeks). Time elapsed from initial issue triage (pm-triage) to validated PR creation in git-delivery (measured in minutes).
Change Failure Rate (CFR) Percentage of deployments causing a production failure. Percentage of pipeline runs blocked by deterministic AI quality gates (doctor, sensor, validate) and calibrated semantic sensing (Jev / eval).
Time to Restore Service (MTTR) Mean time to recover from a downtime or production defect. Time required for the agent pipeline to resolve a blocked gate (STATUS: bloqueado) and restore a passing state (ok).

If an autonomous agent churns out 5,000 lines of code per hour but exhibits a 60% Change Failure Rate on test and security gates, it is not delivering velocity: it is creating cognitive pollution for human reviewers.

2. Telemetry Architecture in Pure Go (internal/metrics)

In Pipeline-AI, we maintain a strict invariant: Zero external dependencies. Introducing third-party telemetry collectors or SaaS vendor SDKs would increase supply chain risk and compromise air-gapped or containerized execution.

We implemented internal/metrics exclusively with the Go 1.24 standard library:

// internal/metrics/metrics.go
type DORAMetrics struct {
    DeploymentFrequency float64       `json:"deployment_frequency"` // Deploys per day
    DeploymentsTotal    int           `json:"deployments_total"`
    LeadTimeForChanges  time.Duration `json:"lead_time_for_changes"` // Average lead time
    ChangeFailureRate   float64       `json:"change_failure_rate"`   // Percentage (0.0 to 100.0)
    FailedDeployments   int           `json:"failed_deployments"`
    TimeToRestore       time.Duration `json:"time_to_restore"` // Mean time to recovery
    RestoresTotal       int           `json:"restores_total"`
}

Atomic & Fail-Safe Persistence

Agent telemetry must be fault-tolerant: if a process aborts midway through a write, metrics files must never become corrupt.

We enforce atomic file writes using temporary files and os.Rename, synchronized via sync.Mutex:

func Save(rootDir string, data *MetricsData) error {
    mu.Lock()
    defer mu.Unlock()

    stateDir := filepath.Join(rootDir, DirName)
    _ = os.MkdirAll(stateDir, 0755)

    tmpFile := filepath.Join(stateDir, fmt.Sprintf("%s.tmp.%d", FileName, time.Now().UnixNano()))
    if err := os.WriteFile(tmpFile, payload, 0644); err != nil {
        return err
    }
    // Atomic filesystem swap
    return os.Rename(tmpFile, targetFile)
}

If the metrics database is missing or empty, Load gracefully initializes default state structures. Telemetry must never fail the build.

3. Hardened with Native Fuzzing: 1.1M+ Executions

In LLM workflows, structured outputs can be interrupted, truncated, or injected with malformed tokens. To ensure our JSON parser never panics or triggers denial-of-service vulnerabilities, we built a native Go Fuzz Target:

// internal/metrics/metrics_fuzz_test.go
func FuzzParseMetrics(f *testing.F) {
    f.Add([]byte(`{"version":1,"events":[],"stages":[],"deliveries":[]}`))
    f.Add([]byte(`{"version":1,"deliveries":[{"delivery_id":"DEL-001","success":true,"lead_time":600000000000}]}`))
    f.Add([]byte(``))
    f.Add([]byte(`null`))
    f.Add([]byte(`{"corrupted": true`))

    f.Fuzz(func(t *testing.T, data []byte) {
        md, err := ParseMetrics(data)
        if err != nil {
            return // Handled errors are expected for corrupt input
        }
        if md == nil {
            t.Fatalf("ParseMetrics returned nil without error on valid input")
        }
    })
}

We verified the parser across 1,132,000+ continuous executions (go test -fuzz=FuzzParseMetrics -fuzztime=10s), confirming zero panics or unhandled edge cases.

4. Transparent Pipeline Runner Instrumentation

Rather than relying on agents to self-report when they begin or complete tasks, we instrumented the Pipeline Runner (internal/runner) at the engine level:

// Excerpt from internal/runner/runner.go
docStart := time.Now()
docResults, docOK := doctor.Collect(absRoot)
_ = metrics.RecordStageDuration(absRoot, deliveryID, "doctor", time.Since(docStart), docOK)

sensorStart := time.Now()
sensorRes, err := sensor.Run(absRoot)
_ = metrics.RecordStageDuration(absRoot, deliveryID, "sensor", time.Since(sensorStart), sensorStep.Status == StatusPass)

valStart := time.Now()
valStep := validate.Run(...)
_ = metrics.RecordStageDuration(absRoot, deliveryID, "validate", time.Since(valStart), validateStep.Status == StatusPass)

// Record overarching gate outcome
_ = metrics.RecordEvent(absRoot, metrics.Event{
    Type:       metrics.EventGate,
    DeliveryID: deliveryID,
    Timestamp:  time.Now().UTC(),
    Duration:   time.Since(runStart),
    Success:    allOK,
    Stage:      "runner",
})

This delivers zero-overhead passive observability: agents execute their assigned skills while telemetry data is persisted in real time.

5. CLI, Model Context Protocol (MCP) & Interactive Dashboard (Generative UI)

Telemetry data is immediately queryable via terminal CLI, an interactive visual HTML5 dashboard, and AI agents over MCP:

Terminal CLI: 

$ pipeline-ai metrics summary
Métricas DORA do Pipeline:
  Deployment Frequency:    3.50 deploys/dia (total: 20)
  Lead Time for Changes:   8m 42s
  Change Failure Rate:     5.0% (falhas: 1)
  Time to Restore Service: 4m 15s (restaurações: 1)

Structured JSON for Grafana, Datadog, or GitHub Actions:

$ pipeline-ai metrics summary -json
{
  "deployment_frequency": 3.5,
  "deployments_total": 20,
  "lead_time_for_changes": 522000000000,
  "change_failure_rate": 5.0,
  "failed_deployments": 1,
  "time_to_restore": 255000000000,
  "restores_total": 1
}

Native MCP Tool (pipeline_get_metrics):

AI agents invoke the MCP tool directly:

{
  "name": "pipeline_get_metrics",
  "arguments": {
    "dir": "."
  }
}

If an agent detects its Change Failure Rate climbing, it can autonomously adapt: allocating more reasoning tokens to test generation (test-writer), running calibrated semantic evaluations (pipeline-ai eval / pipeline_eval_semantic), or requesting additional guardrail checks.

Interactive Visual Dashboard (pipeline-ai dashboard & pipeline_render_dashboard):

Built in internal/dashboard (DEL-022), the framework also renders a self-contained HTML5/CSS3/SVG executive cockpit (dark mode, zero external JS dependencies, and XSS-safe):

$ pipeline-ai dashboard -output dashboard.html

Or inline in the IDE via the pipeline_render_dashboard MCP tool, visualizing the 4 DORA KPI cards, proportional stage latency bars, delivery timelines, and agent handoff inspection.

The Takeaway: Agent Reliability Engineering (ARE)

Generating code without telemetry is like driving a supercar with a disabled dashboard: you might feel fast, but you won't know the engine is overheating until it blows up.

By implementing DORA Metrics for AI Agent Pipelines, engineering teams achieve:

  1. Bottleneck Visibility: Concrete latency data per skill (TDD Red vs. Dev Green vs. Code Review).
  2. Defeating the Speed Mirage: Fast code that fails gates is immediately surfaced in the CFR metric.
  3. Auditable Industrial AI: Shifting from casual AI prototyping to hardened, measurable Agent Reliability Engineering (ARE).

title: Ng-News 26/23: Pangular Inspector and Angular Compilation at ViteConf
description:
Pangular Inspector brings source scans and live inspection to Angular devtools. Alex Rickabaugh’s ViteConf talk, “Angular Compilation Past & Future,” covers Angular’s compiler history and its Rust/Oxc work. Also in brief: Julian Jandl’s production SSR recording.

Pangular Inspector

Devframe is a framework for writing devtools, already used by several tools outside Angular. It was created by Anthony Fu, the creator of Vitest and Slidev, and a core team member of Vue.js, Vite, and Nuxt.

Anthony announced Devframe in September 2026.

Pluggable, Extensible, and Playful DevTools | Devframe

Introduction to Devframe, a framework for building pluggable, extensible, and playful DevTools.

devfra.me

Now, Angular has a new tool built on it: Pangular Inspector, maintained by Erkam Yaman and Santosh Yadav.

Santosh has been around the Angular community for quite some time. He is a GitHub Star, Nx Champion, and Google Developer Expert.

Erkam maintains the Turkish translation of the Angular documentation and has recently contributed extensively to Angular Native - which we covered last episode - including its integration with Analog’s file-based routing.

Pangular aims to become the unified devtools for Angular. Built on Devframe, it can scan the source code of an Angular app and inspect its live state.

It shows components, signals, NgRx stores, services, forms, and routes. Source scans tell you what is declared in your project; live inspection shows the instances and values in the running application.

That information is available through its inspector panel and to your coding agent through MCP.

Pangular Inspector | The unified Angular devtools

Inspect Angular components, signals, dependency injection, routes, forms and stores. In the page, from the CLI, or through a coding agent over MCP.

pangular-inspector.dev

Erkam’s Analog integration for Angular Native

Angular Compilation Past & Future

Alex Rickabaugh also spoke at the online ViteConf. His talk, “Angular Compilation Past & Future,” starts with Angular’s compilation history before moving into the current work involving Rust and Oxc, which we discussed last episode as well.

Alex described splitting Angular’s compiler into two parts. The expensive analysis would move to a native implementation written in Rust, while code generation would remain in Node.js.

The choice of Rust is closely tied to Oxc, VoidZero’s JavaScript toolchain. Alex points to its adoption across modern JavaScript tools, including Vite, as a reason to build on it for the long term.

Compilation would still start with a tsconfig. The Oxc-based Angular analyzer would extract metadata and pass it to the Node.js code generator, which he calls the preprocessor. That would produce either TypeScript with runtime code or a different file containing code for type checking and the language service.

The following link includes a timestamp that takes you straight to Alex’s talk.

Production SSR with Julian Jandl

And the recording of Julian Jandl’s talk on SSR is now available. He presents the work he and his colleagues did on a betting platform, the challenges they encountered, and their solutions using custom strategies for Incremental Static Regeneration, or ISR.

title: Learning AWS as a Beginner: A Practical Roadmap with Hands-On Projects
description:
Learning AWS as a Beginner: A Practical Roadmap with Hands-On Projects

When I started learning AWS, the biggest problem wasn't a lack of resources. It was knowing where to begin. There are 200+ services, and most tutorials make it feel like you need to learn all of them.

You don't. This article covers the order I'd recommend, the services that matter first, and the projects that actually make the concepts stick.

1. Start with the Fundamentals

Before touching services, understand the basics:

  • Regions and Availability Zones: where your resources physically live
  • Shared Responsibility Model: what AWS secures vs. what you secure
  • Pay-as-you-go pricing: why cost awareness matters from day one

A good way to validate this knowledge is the AWS Cloud Practitioner path. I used AWS Cloud Quest: Cloud Practitioner, a game-style, hands-on learning experience that earns you a badge.

2. Secure Your Account First

Do this before building anything:

  1. Create your AWS account
  2. Enable MFA on the root user
  3. Stop using root for daily work. Create an IAM user or role instead
  4. Learn the difference between IAM Users, Groups, Roles, and Policies

The key idea: use roles for services and temporary access, and follow least privilege.

3. Set Up Billing Alarms and Budgets

Surprise bills are the #1 beginner fear. Set up AWS Budgets and a CloudWatch billing alarm early so you get notified when spend crosses a threshold.

Free Tier terms have changed over time, so check the current AWS Free Tier page for what applies to your new account.

4. Learn the Core Services in This Order

Order Service What it teaches you
1 IAM Identity and access control
2 EC2 Virtual servers, security groups, key pairs
3 S3 Object storage, static website hosting
4 VPC Networking, subnets, routing
5 CloudWatch Monitoring, logs, alarms
6 SNS Notifications and alerts
7 RDS Managed databases
8 Lambda Serverless compute

Don't try to master each one. Learn enough to build something small with it.

5. Practical Projects for Beginners

Projects are where learning becomes real. Here are some that fit each stage:

Project 1: Launch and Connect to an EC2 Instance

  • Launch a free-tier-eligible instance
  • Configure a security group
  • SSH in and install a web server like NGINX
  • Skills: EC2, security groups, Linux basics

Project 2: Host a Static Website on S3

  • Create a bucket, upload HTML/CSS/JS
  • Enable static website hosting
  • Skills: S3, bucket policies, permissions

Project 3: EC2 Monitoring with CloudWatch + SNS Alerts

  • Create a CloudWatch alarm on EC2 CPU utilization
  • Connect it to an SNS topic that emails you
  • Trigger the alarm and watch it work
  • Skills: CloudWatch, SNS, monitoring workflows

Project 4: IAM Roles in Action

  • Create an IAM role with limited permissions
  • Attach it to an EC2 instance so it can access S3 without hardcoded keys
  • Skills: IAM roles, least privilege, secure access patterns

Project 5: Build a Simple VPC

  • Create a custom VPC with public and private subnets
  • Add an Internet Gateway and route tables
  • Skills: Networking fundamentals

Project 6: CI/CD with Jenkins on EC2 (Stretch Goal)

  • Run Jenkins on EC2 and connect it to GitHub
  • Build and push a Docker image to Docker Hub
  • Skills: DevOps workflows, containers, automation

6. Habits That Make Learning Stick

  • Build, then document. Writing about what you built exposes gaps in your understanding.
  • Always clean up. Terminate instances, delete buckets, and remove unused resources after each project.
  • Break things on purpose. Misconfigure a security group and see what fails. You learn faster from errors.
  • Use the console first, then automate. Understand it manually before moving to CLI or Infrastructure as Code.
  • Share your progress. Posting your learning publicly keeps you accountable and connects you with the community.

7. What to Learn Next

Once you're comfortable with the basics:

  • AWS CLI and scripting
  • Infrastructure as Code (CloudFormation or Terraform)
  • Load balancers and Auto Scaling
  • Containers (ECS/EKS)
  • An associate-level certification such as Solutions Architect or SysOps

Final Thoughts

You don't need to know everything to start. Pick one service, build one small project, document it, and repeat. Consistency beats intensity.

If you're on a similar journey, I'd love to hear which AWS project you're building next. Drop it in the comments!

Connect with me:

  • LinkedIn: Vishal Patil
  • GitHub: VishalPatil-DevOps-AWS
  • dev.to: @vishal_patil_aws

vishalcloudjourney

title: PromptSense: Sentiment-Aware Mental Health Chatbot with Dynamic Prompting
description:
arXiv:2610.38044v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Current Large Language Models (LLMs)-based mental health chatbots often lack sufficient empathy, contextual awareness, and safety mechanisms, potentially leading to ineffective or harmful interactions. This paper proposes a novel framework that integrates sentiment and depression analysis with a rule-based filtering mechanism prior to model inference. By dynamically constructing prompts based on emotional and risk-related insights, the framework aims to significantly improve the contextual relevance, empathy, and risk-aware of model-generated responses. We evaluated four model strategies and two prompt engineered variants across qualitative metrics such as empathy, helpfulness, clarity, relevance, safety, as well as toxicity assessments using the Perspective API. Experimental results indicate that the prompt engineering approaches outperforms DSFT and RLAIF by 1.8\% and 1.1\% respectively.

title: AI-Driven Digital Twin Framework for Warehouse Logistics Automation Optimization
description:
arXiv:2610.38101v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: In recent years, warehouse logistics optimization has increasingly focused on intelligent, data-driven systems to enhance operational efficiency. Conventional static product placement strategies are being progressively replaced by dynamic slotting approaches that can adapt to real-time variations in warehouse conditions. In this work, we present a novel framework that employs a reinforcement learning agent integrated within a FlexSim-based Digital Twin environment for real-time product placement optimization. The proposed agent continuously learns from streaming operational data, enabling it to reduce picking time while improving overall system throughput. The simulation environment models a four-zone warehouse layout with forklift-based material handling and leverages the Asset Administration Shell framework to ensure seamless interaction between the learning agent, physical asset, and the digital twin. Experimental evaluation demonstrates substantial performance gains, with the proposed approach achieving a 29.66\% reduction in average picking time, a 35.42\% increase in throughput, and an 18.54\% decrease in travel distance.
