title: How to Implement WhatsApp Click-to-Chat QR Codes with SVG in Web Apps
description:
In modern mobile-first web development, reducing conversion friction on landing pages is the fastest lever to increase inbound lead velocity. While desktop users can click on an inline WhatsApp link to open WhatsApp Web, mobile and cross-device visitors benefit significantly from dynamic, scannable QR codes rendered directly on screen.

Unlike raster image formats (PNG, JPEG) which blur upon zooming or increase HTTP payload sizes, generating vector SVG QR codes client-side ensures crisp rendering on retina displays with zero external image requests.

In this tutorial, we will build a lightweight, responsive WhatsApp QR code component in React and TypeScript that formats dynamic click-to-chat deep links.

Understanding the WhatsApp Deep Link Protocol

WhatsApp supports universal deep links formatted as:

https://wa.me/<PhoneNumber>?text=<EncodedMessage>

Key formatting requirements:

  1. E.164 Format: The phone number must include the international country code without plus signs, dashes, or leading zeros (e.g., 15551234567).
  2. URL Encoding: The message string must be properly URI-encoded using encodeURIComponent to handle emojis, spaces, and punctuation.

Step 1: Installing the Lightweight QR Code Generator

We will use qrcode which supports zero-dependency SVG string generation:

npm install qrcode
npm install --save-dev @types/qrcode

Step 2: Creating the Responsive React QR Component

Here is the complete implementation of our WhatsApp QR component:

import React, { useMemo } from 'react';
import QRCode from 'qrcode';

interface WhatsAppQRProps {
  phoneNumber: string; // e.g. "15551234567"
  defaultMessage: string;
  size?: number;
}

export const WhatsAppQRCode: React.FC<WhatsAppQRProps> = ({
  phoneNumber,
  defaultMessage,
  size = 220
}) => {
  const cleanPhone = phoneNumber.replace(/[^0-9]/g, '');
  const encodedText = encodeURIComponent(defaultMessage);
  const waUrl = `https://wa.me/${cleanPhone}?text=${encodedText}`;

  const [svgString, setSvgString] = React.useState<string>('');

  React.useEffect(() => {
    QRCode.toString(waUrl, {
      type: 'svg',
      margin: 2,
      color: {
        dark: '#128C7E', // WhatsApp Brand Green
        light: '#FFFFFF'
      }
    }, (err, svg) => {
      if (!err && svg) setSvgString(svg);
    });
  }, [waUrl]);

  return (
    <div style={{ display: 'inline-block', textAlign: 'center' }}>
      <div 
        dangerouslySetInnerHTML={{ __html: svgString }} 
        style={{ width: size, height: size, margin: '0 auto' }} 
      />
      <a 
        href={waUrl} 
        target="_blank" 
        rel="noopener noreferrer"
        style={{
          display: 'inline-block',
          marginTop: 12,
          padding: '8px 16px',
          backgroundColor: '#25D366',
          color: '#fff',
          borderRadius: 8,
          textDecoration: 'none',
          fontWeight: 600
        }}
      >
        Chat on WhatsApp
      </a>
    </div>
  );
};

Enhancing Conversion Tracking and Lead Routing

To measure campaign effectiveness, avoid hardcoding static numbers in your production client bundle. Instead:

  • Use UTM campaign tracking parameters within the pre-filled message string so your CRM can attribute inbound chats to specific ads or blog posts.
  • For non-technical marketing teams, you can generate instant, trackable QR links using the Free WhatsApp Link Generator on AI Soul.
  • Once prospects scan the code and start chatting, route them into a multi-agent shared workspace with Conversational CRM Features on AI Soul and deploy automated AI Chatbot Solutions to qualify inquiries immediately.

Summary

  • Generate QR codes client-side in SVG format for zero layout shift and retina crispness.
  • Sanitize phone numbers to pure numeric E.164 strings.
  • Pair QR codes with direct one-tap links to serve both desktop and mobile users seamlessly.

title: Post-Training Large Language Models with LLMON
description:
arXiv:2610.38120v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) treat all context tokens uniformly, lacking explicit separation between executable instructions and passive data. This leads to prompt injection vulnerabilities, ambiguous instruction binding, and unreliable execution control. We present a post-training methodology using LLMON (LLM Object Notation), a framework that enables separating instructions from data and requires explicit identifier-based execution. We construct a large-scale structured training corpus of 4.6B tokens spanning general, RAG (Retrieval-Augmented Generation), and tool-calling data, augmented with distractor-infused variants in which competing instructions and irrelevant data segments are present in context but not referenced. Post-training two Granite-4.1 base models (3B and 8B) through supervised fine-tuning followed by reinforcement learning, we show that LLMON-structured supervision reduces attack success rates on indirect prompt-injection benchmarks from 53-100% to 0.02-5.6% while preserving general capabilities. We further introduce attention-based interpretability metrics that diagnose failure modes at individual transformer layers for structured inputs, revealing how our approach reshapes internal attention patterns. Our results demonstrate that explicit execution semantics can be taught through standard post-training without architectural modification.

title: Rumpelstiltskin Dance AI: Locking a Tip-Toe Barn Meme Template
description:
How I shipped a 1–2 photo → tip-toe barn meme dance on Cloudflare Workers — template lock, guest Stripe, Seedance via TryAllAPI.

rumpelstiltskindance.video turns 1–2 adult photos into a tip-toe / “Wing In My Jawwdinz”-adjacent meme dance short with sound. Independent fan tool (2026), 18+. The homepage does not ask users to storyboard; it locks the motion template and sells the render.

Angle for this post: template lock done with an optional second dancer — similar family to party sites, different farm/barn beat. Prices and model ids change; treat live site / console as source of truth.

Locked motion, optional friend

Create panel pattern:

  1. Photo 1 · Lead — required, clear front face.
  2. Photo 2 · Friend — optional, only with permission.
  3. Fixed tip-toe dance motion template.
  4. 720p default messaging; pay once.

Copy on-site refuses celebrity / MV stills. That is load-bearing product policy for face tools — not a legal afterthought.

Live pricing verified: 500 credits · $8.88 · 720p, with multi-packs (e.g. $16.99, larger tiers). Guest Stripe. Always re-check the create button.

Why template lock wins on meme dances

Meme dances are recognizable moves. If you let users rewrite the choreography prompt, you get mush that does not match the sample. Locking the motion:

  • Makes demos honest.
  • Stabilizes Seedance payloads.
  • Shrinks the UX to “good photos + pay.”
  • Cuts support threads that start with “why doesn’t it look like the viral clip?”

Stack overview

Layer Choice Role
Front / SSR TanStack Start (Vite) Landing, upload panel, generation status
Runtime Cloudflare Workers Edge deploy, secrets, API routes
DB Cloudflare D1 Credits, orders, task rows (table prefixes if DBs are shared)
Payments Stripe Checkout One-time packs + optional larger packs; guest checkout
Video upstream TryAllAPI → Seedance Async create + poll
Analytics GA Funnel sanity check 
lead (+ optional friend) → tip-toe template
→ check credits (else Stripe)
→ Worker creates Seedance task via TryAllAPI
→ poll until MP4 URL → store / show
→ on failure: refund credits

Why a video API aggregator

Operational checklist after register / top-up:

  1. Confirm available USD balance in the console (not only the checkout success page).
  2. Create a token in pay-as-you-go style billing.
  3. Enable the video / Seedance-related channel group on that token. Wrong group → “no available channel” even when the model id looks right.
  4. Prefer separate keys per product (rumpel-prod vs sandbox).
  5. Put the key only in Workers Secrets (for example TRYALLAPI_API_KEY). Never in the frontend bundle or a blog post.

Conceptually the call shape looks like this (field names follow the aggregator’s v3 contents API; always re-check current docs):

POST /api/v3/contents/generations/tasks
Authorization: Bearer <TRYALLAPI_API_KEY>
Content-Type: application/json
Accept-Encoding: identity

GET /api/v3/contents/generations/tasks/{id}

I send Accept-Encoding: identity from the Worker because some gateways behave badly with transparent decompression. Model ids used in production look like Seedance 2.x family strings — treat console ids as source of truth, not this paragraph.

Seedance parameters that matter for tip-toe templates

A few details that bit me across this family of sites:

  • Pass duration as an explicit integer. Some models default to “smart length.” Omitting duration can silently lengthen the clip and the bill.
  • resolution and ratio. Cost tracks resolution tier and duration more than portrait vs landscape. Match whatever the create UI offers (often 480p/720p and 9:16 for Shorts).
  • generate_audio. When the product ships “finished” downloads, leave audio on; creators who want a trending sound can mute later.
  • Status machine. Expect something like queued → running → succeeded / failed. Success URLs are often short-lived signed links — download/rehost on your side before handing the file to the user.
  • Decent failure. On supply_unavailable or hard failures: refund credits, show a short human message, log the detailed upstream error server-side, optionally fall back to another Seedance tier.

Rough mental model for upstream cost (illustrative only — use your own usage fields and invoices):

tokens ≈ duration_sec × width × height × fps / 1024
cost   ≈ tokens × price_per_million_tokens

Price the site after you measure a few real runs with retry margin, Stripe fees, and failed-job refunds — not from a spreadsheet fantasy of 0% failure.

Map lead vs friend roles consistently. Rehost short-lived result URLs. Separate keys if you operate a matrix of dance domains.

Credits, Stripe, and the “can charge money” line

Demo UIs are easy. The line between toy and product is:

  1. User hits Create → check credit balance.
  2. If short → Stripe Checkout Session (guest allowed).
  3. Webhook (plus a return-URL sync check) grants credits.
  4. Pre-debit / lock credits, create upstream task, persist task_id in D1.
  5. Poll until done; succeed → show MP4; fail → refund credits.

Two books of account stay separate: USD balance at TryAllAPI (your cost) vs site credits (what you sold). Mixing them in one mental ledger is how you underprice or invent “mysterious” losses.

When several products share one Stripe account, isolate webhooks by endpoint or by metadata (site / product). Callbacks pointed at the wrong apex domain are a classic multi-site footgun.

Secrets stay in Workers: TRYALLAPI_API_KEY, STRIPE_SECRET_KEY, webhook secret, auth secrets. The browser only ever sees publishable Stripe keys if needed.

Deploy notes (Workers + D1)

Typical loop on this template family:

pnpm install
# wire D1 database_id, production env, custom domain in wrangler
pnpm cf:deploy

Before calling a deploy “done”:

  • D1 binding is correct; shared DBs use table prefixes, not a new database per micro-idea (free-tier DB counts are limited).
  • AUTH_TRUSTED_ORIGINS and Stripe return / webhook URLs match the production HTTPS origin.
  • GA id is set for a coarse funnel (land → upload → pay → wait → download).
  • One real end-to-end path on production or a staging Worker: upload → pay → render → download.

Production origin: https://rumpelstiltskindance.video.

Product rules that are not optional

Face-based generation is not “just another SaaS CRUD app”:

  • Require an explicit 18+ / rights-to-use confirmation on upload.
  • Block minors and refuse celebrity / stranger misuse in copy and policy.
  • Expect upstream safety refusals; refund and explain.
  • Keep privacy policy honest about retention; do not train on user media by default.
  • Market as an independent fan-style tool for a trend format — not as an official tie-in unless you actually have that deal.
  • Use your own sample renders in marketing.

Those constraints belong in the product, not in a footnote you add after the first dispute email.

What I would reuse on the next tip-toe / barn meme site

  1. Lock the recognizable move; do not open a choreography IDE.
  2. Lead required + optional friend keeps the funnel simple.
  3. Guest one-time pack from ~$8.88 beats subscribe-first.
  4. Credits with automatic refund on failed generation.
  5. Self-hosted samples sell faster than SEO adjectives.

Consumer: watch the sample on rumpelstiltskindance.video, upload authorized photos, pay once. Builders: TryAllAPI, prove create+poll, then wrap credits. Lock the tip-toe; meter the GPU.

title: Diagnosing OLED Backlight Bleeding and Subpixel Burn-in Using HTML5 Canvas and RequestAnimationFrame
description:
When developing display diagnostics or panel evaluation routines inside web environments, developers frequently encounter challenges with browser chrome intrusion, subpixel scaling artifacts, and uneven backlight bleed. In this article, we explore the algorithmic and architectural fundamentals of rendering pure black test patterns to isolate hardware display anomalies.

1. Why True Black (#000000) Matters for OLED Displays

OLED (Organic Light Emitting Diode) displays operate on an emissive pixel architecture. Unlike traditional LCDs that employ a global or zoned LED backlight shining through a liquid crystal matrix, each OLED subpixel emits its own luminance.

When an RGB value of rgb(0, 0, 0) is piped to an OLED panel:

  • The organic diode is physically unpowered (0 mA).
  • Contrast ratio theoretically approaches infinity (∞ : 1).
  • Any visible luminescence immediately indicates either:
    1. Operating system gamma misconfiguration (e.g., limited RGB range 16-235 instead of full range 0-255).
    2. Subpixel degradation or persistent charge trapping (often termed "burn-in").
    3. Panel-level mura effects or edge glow from hybrid backlight units.

2. Preventing Browser Compositor Degradation

In standard CSS layouts, declaring background-color: #000 on the body tag can be subject to browser compositing quirks, scrollbar rendering, and operating system gesture bars.

To guarantee bit-exact fullscreen coverage, we initialize a dedicated <canvas> element and handle high-DPI scaling directly:

class DisplayDiagnostics {
  constructor(canvas) {
    this.canvas = canvas;
    this.ctx = canvas.getContext('2d', { alpha: false });
    this.initResizeListener();
  }

  resize() {
    const dpr = window.devicePixelRatio || 1;
    const width = window.innerWidth;
    const height = window.innerHeight;

    this.canvas.width = Math.floor(width * dpr);
    this.canvas.height = Math.floor(height * dpr);
    this.canvas.style.width = `${width}px`;
    this.canvas.style.height = `${height}px`;

    this.render();
  }

  render() {
    this.ctx.fillStyle = '#000000';
    this.ctx.fillRect(0, 0, this.canvas.width, this.canvas.height);
  }

  initResizeListener() {
    window.addEventListener('resize', () => this.resize());
    this.resize();
  }
}

3. Burn-in Recovery and Subpixel Exercising

For panels showing minor image retention, cyclic subpixel switching (rapid alternation between primary chromatic channels) can help equalize subpixel voltage retention:

const CHROMATIC_CYCLES = ['#ff0000', '#00ff00', '#0000ff', '#ffffff', '#000000'];
let cycleIndex = 0;

function runExcitationCycle(ctx, width, height) {
  ctx.fillStyle = CHROMATIC_CYCLES[cycleIndex];
  ctx.fillRect(0, 0, width, height);
  cycleIndex = (cycleIndex + 1) % CHROMATIC_CYCLES.length;
}

Using pure frontend Canvas APIs enables hardware engineers and QA testers to validate display fidelity without installing heavy native benchmarking suites.

title: Open-weight models take 56% of token volume, Astra doubles Fable 5.1 spend
description:
AI Gateway Production Index — September 2026

Every month, AI Gateway routes tens of trillions of tokens between production applications and AI labs. That traffic gives us a view of what AI usage actually looks like in today's enterprise, and we publish it here monthly. See the Production Index reports from June, July, and August.

September 2026 summary

The September index reports on AI Gateway data collected through August 2026.

  • Open-weight models ran the majority of gateway tokens for the first time, up from 7% in December to 56% in August.

  • The average token costs less than half what it did five months ago. Price per token fell 23.2% in August, the third straight monthly drop, and the median team paid 7.6% less.

  • Fable 5, Anthropic's most capable model, lost two-thirds of its share of gateway spend in one month. Opus 5, at half the price, tripled its share. Anthropic kept 64% of all spend.

  • Gemini 3 Flash has lost 95% of its share of gateway tokens since May, and more than three-quarters of the volume it lost went to models from other labs.

Latest Index updates

The monthly report covers data through August. We add notable developments here between editions.

  • September 17: OpenAI launched Astra on September 3, and it took a third of OpenAI's spend within two days and twice Fable 5.1's share of gateway spend. Astra took 7.7% of all gateway spend in its first twelve days while Fable 5.1, launched two days earlier at the same price, took 3.7%.

  • September 18: Jev is now the fastest-adopted model in AI Gateway history. Within its first 24 hours, it was being used by nearly 13% of paid teams, 2x as many as the GPT-5.6 family and over 6x as many as Fable 5.1.

Open-weight models take a majority of token volume for the first time

In August, open-weight models ran 56% of all tokens on AI Gateway, marking the first month they took the majority of volume.

In December 2025, they processed fewer than one in ten tokens, and only eight months later, they ran more token volume than all closed-weight models combined.

Though the frontier kept the majority of spend, open-weight dollar share is accelerating. As open-weight models become more capable, customers are moving more production workloads over to them.

Growth in open-weight model adoption helped push the average price per token across the gateway down 23.2% in August, its third consecutive monthly drop and the steepest since April. Among teams running more than ten million tokens in both months, the median team paid 7.6% less per token, more than double July's 2.9% decline.

Teams can now get more inference from the same budget and reserve frontier models only for the tasks that justify the premium.

Frontier plateaus as Fable spend goes to Opus 5

Production workloads that justify a frontier model don't always need the most expensive one. They need one that’s good enough.

Fable is the most capable model Anthropic sells. Opus is the tier below it and costs roughly half of Fable’s price per token. When the US export control on Fable 5 was lifted and its access restored on July 1, its gateway spend share surged to 13.2%. At the end of that same month, Opus 5 came online.

In August, Fable 5’s share of gateway spend fell to 4.9%, and Opus 5's share rose to 22.5%. Nine in ten of the teams that ran Fable cut their usage, and more of them moved their workloads to Opus 5 than any other model. Fable’s extra capability wasn’t worth double the price.

Teams left Fable, Anthropic's most expensive and capable model, but the lab retained the lion’s share of gateway spend because those workloads stepped down to Opus 5, not a different lab.

Anthropic has taken at least 61 cents of every dollar spent through AI Gateway every month since December, and 64 cents in August. Its models have held the top two spots by spend every month since December, even as the models in those spots changed.

Customer loyalty follows the model profile, not the lab

Lab loyalty doesn’t follow brand, it follows model profile, and consistency wins.

When a new model preserves what users valued in its predecessor, the lab retains its customers. When it doesn’t, those customers fill the need through other providers.

When Claude Opus 5 launched, it gained almost twice what Fable lost, because it handled the same workloads at half the price. And within five days of Z.ai launching GLM-5.3-Flash, it was running three times GLM-5.2's daily volume.

Google struggled to retain customers with its new models. Because the new offerings didn’t provide a relative advantage on capability or price, a majority of Gemini 3 Flash’s workloads moved to OpenAI, Anthropic, and DeepSeek.

About half of the volume that left Gemini 3 Flash went to cheaper models, led by GPT-5.6 Luna, which costs less than half as much per token. Most of the other half went to higher-priced models, led by Claude Opus 5 and Sonnet 5, which cost roughly nine and three times as much as Gemini 3 Flash, respectively.

The flight to better-fit models meant that over the same period, Google’s share of gateway token volume fell from 30% to 5%, with Gemini 3 Flash accounting for 22 of the 25 percentage points lost.

Special report: Astra took a third of OpenAI spend within 48 hours and outpaced Fable 5.1 two to one at launch

GPT-6 Astra launched on the AI Gateway on September 3 at the same price as Fable 5.1 and two and a half times the price of GPT-5.6 Sol. Two days later, it accounted for one in every three dollars spent on OpenAI models through the gateway. Its share of spend has held, hovering between 28% and 39% since.

Within OpenAI’s model lineup, Astra and Sol processed 27% of OpenAI’s tokens but accounted for 71% of its spending from September 4 through 16. Luna and Nano processed more than twice as many tokens for about one-ninth as much spending.

Anthropic launched Fable 5.1 on September 1, two days before Astra. Over each model's first twelve days on the gateway, Astra took 7.7% of all gateway spend, more than twice Fable 5.1's share of 3.7%, and was used by twice as many teams.

OpenAI’s cheaper models carry its volume, while Astra’s early lead over Fable shows it can also attract teams at the highest price point. Together, they let OpenAI compete with other frontier labs for both scale and premium spend.

Stay tuned for more in next month's report.

Also in August’s data

  • Google's Nano Banana took the lead in image spend for the first time, at 50% to GPT Image's 44%, even as GPT Image took back the lead in images generated, 46% to 39%.

  • Google's Veo rose to second in video spend, at 20%, up from 15% in July. Seedance remained in first on both videos generated and video spend.

  • The share of videos generated by xAI’s Grok Imagine has more than halved since June, from 42% to 31% to 19%.

Previous AI Gateway Production Index reports

  • May 2026

  • June 2026

  • July 2026

  • August 2026

About this report

This report uses anonymized, aggregate traffic routed through Vercel AI Gateway through August 2026.

A few notes on measurement:

  • Token volume includes input, output, reasoning, cached-input, and cache-creation tokens.

  • Spending is estimated using labs’ published list prices; actual bills may differ. Average price per token is estimated spending divided by token volume.

  • Statements about where volume moved compare changes among the same teams. They do not trace individual tokens between models.

  • Open-weight classifications follow the current AI Gateway model list, which is broader than the definition used in earlier reports.

  • All figures use the most recent data available; prior months may be revised as methodology is updated.

title: Website Redesign: What to Change and How to Measure It
description:
A website redesign is a project hypothesis: changing a page or journey should help people complete a defined task without damaging what already works. New colors and components may be part of the answer, but they do not tell you whether visitors can find delivery terms, complete a form, or navigate on a phone.

The practical work starts before a designer opens a canvas. Define the problem, capture a baseline, choose the smallest change that can test your idea, and plan how to protect existing URLs and data. This guide walks through the decisions and the measurements.

Start with the user task

Replace a vague objective such as "make the site modern" with a description of a job someone needs to complete. For a service page, that could be understanding the conditions and sending an inquiry. For a shop, it might be choosing the right product variant and completing checkout. For a publication, it might be finding and reading a relevant article.

Write down the business objective, the user task, a primary measure, and a guardrail. A shorter form, for example, may increase submissions while removing information the team needs to help the customer. Track the quality of inquiries alongside the submission rate.

Also decide who owns the decision, how long the team will observe the result, and what would trigger a rollback. That makes the project easier to evaluate when opinions differ after launch.

Audit the existing experience

Make an inventory of important landing pages, navigation routes, forms, search, product pages, contact information, and integrations. For each important page, record its purpose, current URL, relevant traffic sources, and the action it supports. Include content that people already rely on, not only the elements you intend to replace.

Then inspect real journeys on both mobile and desktop. Test with long headings, empty search results, error messages, unavailable products, and slower connections. Try keyboard navigation and check whether the focused control remains visible. Verify that images with a meaningful role have appropriate text alternatives.

Ask a few people who resemble your intended audience to complete specific tasks without coaching. Record where they hesitate, what they expect, and whether they succeed. A small qualitative study is useful for finding problems; it does not estimate how often every visitor experiences them. Avoid collecting unnecessary personal data and use agreed test accounts.

Support tickets, sales questions, and internal feedback can add useful clues. Treat each clue as a starting point for investigation rather than proof that one design change will fix the issue.

Capture a baseline before changing anything

Save the definitions of your analytics events and the values for a comparable period. Check that a form success event represents a successful submission rather than a button click, and compare it with processed inquiries where possible. Record the denominator you plan to use: sessions, users, or another clearly defined population.

Segment the baseline by device, important landing pages, and major traffic sources. Document relevant context such as campaigns, prices, stock availability, or changes in the team. If several of these change at launch, a shift in conversion cannot automatically be attributed to the design.

Make a note of any known measurement gaps. If a consent choice, integration, or duplicate event affects the data, investigate it before treating the chart as an exact description of customer behavior.

Prioritize changes as testable hypotheses

For every issue, write four short statements:

  1. Observation: what did people do, or what did the team see?
  2. Possible explanation: why might that be happening?
  3. Proposed change: what will you alter?
  4. Check: what evidence would support or challenge the idea?

For instance: mobile test participants did not find the delivery conditions. The team suspects the link is too far from the price. Move a relevant link closer and check task completion and related support questions. The explanation remains a hypothesis until you have evidence.

Prioritize by impact on a key task, frequency or strength of the evidence, implementation risk, and the cost of checking the idea. A broken order form usually deserves attention before a decorative detail. If the evidence is weak, test a focused prototype before rebuilding the entire site.

Changes may involve clearer labels, more useful content, navigation, responsive layouts, form validation, or a consistent visual system. Test components with realistic copy and edge cases rather than only with ideal demonstration content.

Protect content, URLs, and recovery

A redesign can accidentally remove a useful page, break an internal link, or change a URL that people have bookmarked or found in search. Before launch, map important existing addresses to their intended destinations. Preserve the current URLs where practical; when an address must change, plan relevant redirects and verify them after deployment.

Do not redirect every old page to the homepage merely to avoid an error. A relevant destination is more useful to visitors. Check internal links, indexability settings, and key pages in your search tools after launch. Search data may take time to reflect a change, so record the launch context and keep monitoring.

Prepare backups of data, files, and configuration according to the project's process. Test the recovery procedure and agree on rollback criteria before deployment. Check forms, notifications, payment flows, and integrations in an agreed test environment without exposing real payment details.

Measure outcomes without overclaiming

Choose metrics that reflect the goal, keep their definitions stable, and pair them with guardrails. A form project might track successful submissions per eligible session, processed inquiry quality, and errors. A shop might look at completed orders alongside cancellations and average order value. Technical performance is also worth monitoring, but a faster page alone does not prove that sales improved.

Consider a hypothetical example. Before the redesign, 100 successful inquiries came from 2,000 comparable sessions: a 5% rate. In a later sample, 120 successful inquiries came from 2,000 sessions: 6%. The difference is one percentage point, or a 20% relative increase from the original rate.

That arithmetic describes the observed samples; it does not prove that the redesign caused the difference. A new ad campaign, a change in the visitor mix, duplicate tracking, seasonality, or ordinary variation could contribute. Check the data quality, segment the results, and avoid drawing a confident conclusion from a small number of events.

Choose an evaluation method

A before-and-after comparison can be useful when an experiment is impractical. Compare similar periods and segments, and document other changes that could explain the result. Looking at mobile and desktop, or major traffic sources, separately can reveal patterns hidden by an overall average.

Where feasible, a controlled A/B test compares versions with visitors allocated during the same period. Define the main metric, allocation, stopping rules, and evaluation approach in advance. Check that exposure and success events are recorded correctly. A short test or a small sample may not support a reliable conclusion, so report uncertainty instead of declaring a winner at the first favorable movement.

For either method, investigate guardrails: did more inquiries translate into useful conversations? Did errors rise for a particular device? Did an important search landing page disappear? A measured improvement in one number can coexist with a problem elsewhere.

A launch checklist

Before launch, review the goal, baseline, prototype findings, important URLs, redirects, event definitions, backups, and rollback owner. Test key journeys across devices, keyboard navigation, form feedback, notifications, and integration responses.

After launch, repeat those checks on the live site using agreed test data. Confirm that analytics events fire once, old addresses lead to relevant pages, and important content remains accessible. Record issues and assign owners. During the observation period, review outcomes and context together, then decide whether to keep, refine, or revert each major change.

A good redesign produces evidence that a defined task is easier to complete while preserving the functions and information people depend on.

title: GARDEN: Generalist Autonomous Reward Design Through Evidence Navigation for Cooperative Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning
description:
arXiv:2610.37926v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Cooperative multi-agent reinforcement learning (MARL) enables teams of agents, such as robots and autonomous vehicles, to learn coordinated behavior, but what such teams learn is largely determined by their reward function. Because task success alone provides too little guidance for learning, intermediate rewards are usually designed by hand, and this effort must often be repeated whenever the environment or the team changes. Large language models (LLMs) can automate the effort by writing reward functions as code, yet the resulting rewards are typically designed and tested in a single setting. To enable their reuse across settings, GARDEN (Generalist Autonomous Reward Design through Evidence Navigation) is proposed, in which one reward program is developed for a family of related scenarios and transferred, unchanged, to scenarios that were not available during its design. During development, environment code, training records, and agent behavior are investigated by an LLM reward engineer, and draft rewards are tested in trial training runs, while the learning algorithm and the rule for selecting the final reward are held fixed. On unseen scenarios of the Overcooked and SMAX benchmarks, task returns were increased by 58.2% and 52.5% over the default rewards on two kitchen layouts, and the mean win rate in two combat scenarios was raised from 51.0% to 89.9%. Under matched candidate and probe budgets, this exceeded the 84.2% and 79.2% obtained with fixed diagnostic feedback and Eureka-inspired reward reflection. These results show that a single autonomously engineered reward can be reused effectively across related cooperative scenarios.

title: Giving an AI assistant a memory of your Google search traffic that does not go stale
description:
Picture this.

You ask your AI assistant which pages bring in the most search traffic. It answers with confidence. The numbers are from three months ago, for a site you stopped managing in August.

Nothing crashed. The assistant just kept a memory of data that is no longer true.

I wanted a memory of Google search traffic that stays current, and that forgets what it should. So for Mergetober I built a Google Search Console connector for Cognee. The code lives in PR #584 for issue #4793.

What it does

Cognee turns documents into a knowledge graph that an agent can search. The connector feeds it from Search Console. You sign in with Google, pick your properties, and it syncs how they perform in search.

Search Console gives you numbers, not prose. One row per date, query and page would be millions of documents, and an LLM would read every one. So the connector groups the data by calendar month. Each month of a property becomes:

  • an overview: totals, devices, top countries, top queries and top pages;
  • one document per top page, with the queries that led to it.

All of a property's documents share one node set. The same query in two months becomes one entity in the graph, so you can ask how it changed.

source = google_search_console_source(
    sites=["sc-domain:example.com"],  # leave it out for every verified property
    months=3,
)
await cognee.remember(source, dataset_name="search_console",
                      primary_key="id", write_disposition="merge")

Sign-in is OAuth 2.0 with the read-only scope. Run login.py once, in the browser, and the token is cached in a private file.

Data that is late and sampled

Two things make Search Console different from a normal source.

First, the newest data is late and preliminary. Google publishes final numbers about two days behind, and it can still revise the last days. So the connector reads final data only. A month stays open until it is a few days older than that lag. An open month is read again on every run. Then it is read one last time and closed, and a closed month is never read again. Only documents whose text changed are sent on, so an unchanged run makes no LLM call.

Second, the data is sampled. Google returns the top rows by clicks and leaves out rare queries for privacy. That means a query that disappears from a response is not a deleted query, and the rows never add up to the totals. Every document says so.

What gets forgotten

A property you remove, deselect, or lose verification on is forgotten whole, with its documents. I added a few safety rules, because a wrong delete is worse than a missed one:

  • A failed request never deletes anything. The run stops and the next one starts from the same spot.
  • A month that suddenly comes back empty keeps its documents. Google having a bad moment is more likely than every click vanishing.
  • If Google throttles the sync, it stops cleanly and keeps the months it already read. It waits a minute at most at a time, because a sync holds Cognee's lock. The next run picks up where it stopped.
  • If the account suddenly sees no verified property, the run stops instead of forgetting everything.

The real test

First I tested against a fake: an in-memory copy of the Search Console API. It aggregates real fact rows, sorts by clicks, hides the newest days, and withholds rare queries. 110 tests pass on Python 3.10 and 3.12, and on Cognee 1.6.4 and 1.6.6. They include a run of the whole Cognee pipeline with a mocked LLM. The 106 that skip that pipeline run also pass on Python 3.14. But a fake only proves what you thought to fake.

So I signed in with a real Google account. I created an OAuth client, went through the browser consent, and listed my properties. Google returned my one property, with siteOwner permission. I then ran the connector against it twice.

Here is the honest part. My only property is a personal portfolio, and it had no search traffic in the last 80 days. So the real sync found no data. It created no documents and raised no errors. The second run skipped the two closed months:

run 1  {'sites': 1, 'periods': 3, 'closed': 0, 'documents': 0, ...}
run 2  {'sites': 1, 'periods': 1, 'closed': 2, 'documents': 0, ...}

The bug only a real Google could find

That empty property showed me something my fake got wrong.

When there is no data, I expected Google to answer with an empty response. It does not. For a query with no dimensions, it returns one row of zeros: {'clicks': 0, 'impressions': 0, ...}.

My code read "one row" as "there is data". It would have written an overview that says "0 clicks" for every empty month. Worse, it would have walked straight past my own safety rule. A month that had real documents and then got a zero row back would have been overwritten with zeros, instead of being kept.

Now a row with zero impressions counts as no data. I changed the fake to behave the way Google does, so a test fails if this comes back.

The same run settled a smaller question. Google accepts the lowercase type and dataState values that I send.

What I did not test

I did not test any of this against real traffic: documents built from real queries and pages, a recall on real data, a changed month, or forgetting a real property. Those paths are covered by the fake-API tests and the mocked-LLM pipeline test, not by a live account. I also never saw a real 429 from Google.

Rare queries are left out of the lists by design. A long tail of low-click pages shows up in the totals only. Sitemaps and URL inspection are not ingested. The README lists these.

Try it

The example is in packages/connector/google-search-console/examples/. You need a Google Cloud project with the Search Console API enabled, an OAuth client of type Desktop app, and a verified property. The README walks through it.

If you point it at a property with real traffic, I would love to hear what breaks.

title: How to send transactional emails from Next.js App Router (Server Actions, route handlers and after())
description:
Almost every Next.js app needs to send a few emails: a welcome email after signup, a magic link or password reset, a receipt. The App Router gives you several places to put that code, and they don't behave the same way when something is slow or fails.

This guide covers where the send should live, how to keep the API key off the client, how to avoid making users wait for your email provider, and the mistakes that lead to missing or duplicate emails. The examples use a generic sendEmail() helper so you can plug in whichever provider you use.

1. Keep the send on the server, always

Your email provider's API key can send mail as your domain. If it reaches the browser, anyone can use it.

  • Read it from process.env.EMAIL_API_KEY (no NEXT_PUBLIC_ prefix, which would inline it into client bundles).
  • Put the helper in a module that only server code imports, and mark it so a mistaken client import fails the build: 
// lib/email.ts
import "server-only";

type SendEmailInput = {
  to: string;
  subject: string;
  html: string;
  idempotencyKey?: string;
};

export async function sendEmail(input: SendEmailInput) {
  const res = await fetch("https://api.your-email-provider.com/send", {
    method: "POST",
    headers: {
      Authorization: `Bearer ${process.env.EMAIL_API_KEY}`,
      "Content-Type": "application/json",
    },
    body: JSON.stringify(input),
  });

  if (!res.ok) {
    throw new Error(`Email send failed: ${res.status} ${await res.text()}`);
  }
  return res.json();
}

The server-only package (npm i server-only) makes the build fail if a Client Component imports this file.

2. Pick the right entry point

Trigger Where to send from
A form in your own UI (signup, invite a teammate, contact form) A Server Action
An external system calls you (Stripe webhook, auth provider hook, cron) A route handler (app/api/.../route.ts)
Something that happens later (trial ending in 3 days, weekly digest) A queue or scheduled job, not a request handler

Server Action: invite a teammate 

// app/team/actions.ts
"use server";

import { after } from "next/server";
import { auth } from "@/lib/auth";
import { db } from "@/lib/db";
import { sendEmail } from "@/lib/email";
import { renderInviteEmail } from "@/emails/invite";

export async function inviteTeammate(formData: FormData) {
  const session = await auth();
  if (!session) throw new Error("Not signed in");

  const email = String(formData.get("email") ?? "").trim().toLowerCase();
  if (!email.includes("@")) return { error: "Enter a valid email" };

  const invite = await db.invite.create({
    data: { email, teamId: session.teamId, invitedBy: session.userId },
  });

  // Respond to the user now; send the email after the response is done.
  after(async () => {
    await sendEmail({
      to: email,
      subject: `${session.name} invited you to ${session.teamName}`,
      html: await renderInviteEmail({ invite, inviter: session.name }),
      idempotencyKey: `invite-${invite.id}`,
    });
  });

  return { ok: true };
}

Two things to notice:

  • Authorization happens inside the action. Server Actions are public HTTP endpoints. Anyone can call them with any form data, so check the session and validate input in the action itself, not only in the UI.
  • after() (from next/server, stable since Next.js 15.1) runs the callback once the response has been sent. The user doesn't wait on your email provider's latency, and a slow provider doesn't hold the form in a pending state.

Route handler: a webhook from your auth provider 

// app/api/webhooks/auth/route.ts
import { sendEmail } from "@/lib/email";
import { renderWelcomeEmail } from "@/emails/welcome";
import { verifyAuthWebhook } from "@/lib/auth-webhooks";

export async function POST(request: Request) {
  const payload = await verifyAuthWebhook(request); // throws on a bad signature
  if (payload.type !== "user.created") {
    return Response.json({ ignored: true });
  }

  await sendEmail({
    to: payload.user.email,
    subject: "Welcome to Acme",
    html: await renderWelcomeEmail({ name: payload.user.firstName }),
    idempotencyKey: `welcome-${payload.user.id}`,
  });

  return Response.json({ ok: true });
}

Webhook senders retry when you return an error or time out, which is good for reliability and bad for duplicate emails. That's what the idempotencyKey is for (section 5).

3. Don't send from Client Components or useEffect

It's tempting to fire a "send welcome email" request from the client after signup succeeds. Don't:

  • The browser tab can close before the request goes out.
  • React Strict Mode runs effects twice in development, so you'll see double emails locally and might "fix" the wrong thing.
  • You need a public endpoint for it, which anyone can call to make you send email.

Send from the server code that created the user, or from the webhook your auth provider calls.

4. Templates: React Email or plain HTML

Email clients are not browsers. Outlook on Windows still renders with Word's engine, Gmail strips <style> blocks in some contexts, and flexbox and grid are unreliable. Two sane options:

  • React Email (@react-email/components + @react-email/render): write templates as React components using email-safe primitives (Section, Row, Column, Button) and render them to an HTML string on the server.
  • Provider-side templates: design the email in your provider's editor and send a template ID plus variables. Non-developers can then edit copy without a deploy. 
// emails/welcome.tsx
import { Html, Body, Container, Heading, Text, Button } from "@react-email/components";
import { render } from "@react-email/render";

function WelcomeEmail({ name }: { name: string }) {
  return (
    <Html>
      <Body style={{ fontFamily: "Arial, sans-serif", backgroundColor: "#ffffff" }}>
        <Container style={{ maxWidth: 560, padding: 24 }}>
          <Heading as="h1">Welcome, {name}</Heading>
          <Text>Your workspace is ready. The fastest way to get value is to connect your data first.</Text>
          <Button href="https://app.acme.com/onboarding" style={{ backgroundColor: "#111", color: "#fff", padding: "12px 20px" }}>
            Finish setup
          </Button>
        </Container>
      </Body>
    </Html>
  );
}

export function renderWelcomeEmail(props: { name: string }) {
  return render(<WelcomeEmail {...props} />); // returns a Promise<string>
}

Whichever you choose, also send a plain-text version if your provider doesn't generate one, and keep the important action in a real link rather than only in an image.

5. Make sends idempotent

Duplicates come from retries: a webhook delivered twice, a user double-submitting a form, a serverless function retried after a timeout. The fix is to give every logical email a stable key:

  • welcome-${userId}, invite-${inviteId}, receipt-${invoiceId}, password-reset-${tokenId}

Then either pass it to your provider as an idempotency key (many APIs accept one and return the original result for a repeated key), or record it in your database with a unique constraint and skip the send when the insert conflicts:

const inserted = await db.sentEmail.createMany({
  data: [{ key: `welcome-${user.id}` }],
  skipDuplicates: true,
});
if (inserted.count === 0) return; // already sent

6. Know what after() doesn't do

after() is great for "don't make the user wait". It is not a job queue:

  • If the send throws, nothing retries it. Log the error, and alert on it for important emails.
  • On serverless platforms the work is tied to the lifetime of that invocation. Short sends are fine; long work belongs elsewhere.
  • It can't schedule anything for later.

For emails that must arrive (password resets, receipts), either retry inside the callback with a short backoff, or enqueue a job (BullMQ, Inngest, QStash, Trigger.dev, your provider's own scheduling) and let the queue retry. For anything time-based (trial reminders, onboarding drips), use a scheduler or an email platform's automation instead of request handlers.

7. Before you go live

  • [ ] Send from your own domain with SPF, DKIM and DMARC set up, not the provider's shared test domain
  • [ ] Separate sending subdomains for transactional and marketing email, if you send both
  • [ ] API key only in server env vars, server-only on the email module
  • [ ] Server Actions check the session and validate input
  • [ ] Every email has an idempotency key
  • [ ] Failures are logged and alerted, not swallowed
  • [ ] Test rendering in Gmail, Outlook and Apple Mail (or a rendering preview tool)

Using Sequenzy for this

Here is how this looks with Sequenzy, an email platform for SaaS. The sendEmail helper above becomes:

import "server-only";
import Sequenzy from "sequenzy";

const sequenzy = new Sequenzy({ apiKey: process.env.SEQUENZY_API_KEY });

export function sendWelcome(to: string, firstName: string) {
  return sequenzy.transactional.send({
    to,
    slug: "welcome-email", // template designed in the dashboard
    variables: { firstName },
  });
}

The same account also runs the onboarding and trial sequences from section 6, so time-based emails don't need their own queue. The quick start takes about five minutes. Everything else in this guide applies whichever provider you choose.

title: Vercel and Shopify make agents first-class shoppers
description:
Agents already shop on the web, but they often use pages and tools originally built for people and search engines. Building a better shopping experience for agents means treating them as first-class shoppers, with product information they can read directly and tools designed for agents to shop.

Today, Vercel Shop, our open source Next.js storefront template for Shopify, is generally available. Teams can launch storefronts optimized for how people, search engines, and agents interact with them.

Vercel Shop is built on Shopify’s Hydrogen SDK. The SDK gives teams access to the store’s product catalog, cart and order management, payments, and checkout to build custom storefronts. Earlier this year, Vercel and Shopify announced plans to rebuild Hydrogen to work across JavaScript frameworks. Today, the rebuilt SDK is generally available.

Give agents the information and tools they need

Vercel Shop makes product pages available as machine-readable content, including price, availability, and options. The same product URL can serve a visual page to people or product information that agents can read without interpreting the page’s layout. The template also includes structured data embedded in pages and sitemaps to help search and answer engines discover and understand the products.

Shopify co-developed the Universal Commerce Protocol (UCP), which gives agents a standard way to search a store’s catalog, read product details, check availability, build a cart, and get a checkout link. Vercel Shop makes these capabilities discoverable at the merchant’s own domain, so agents can use MCP to search products and build carts without navigating the site.

Customize the experience for all customers

Vercel Shop brings the store’s product catalog, cart, and checkout together with a Next.js storefront, product information and shopping tools for agents, and a shopping assistant powered by eve. The storefront and assistant live in the same codebase, so teams can customize the store’s design and how the assistant helps shoppers.

Skills included in the template guide coding agents through setup, customization, and template updates. Teams can create an experience where shoppers browse product pages or ask the assistant to find products and add them to their cart. Both share the same cart, so shoppers keep what they’ve added as they move between experiences.

Storefronts built with Shopify and Vercel

Today, we launched our merch store at vercel.store with limited-edition drops. It’s built on Vercel Shop. The store’s shopping agent helps shoppers find products, add them to their cart, and continue to checkout.

Shopify, Next.js, and Vercel already power storefronts for brands including AG1, Bombas, and PAIGE. When PAIGE re-architected its ecommerce platform, it saw a 22% increase in revenue and a 76% increase in conversion over Black Friday and Cyber Monday, with no downtime.

Get started with Vercel Shop

Create a storefront:

Get started with Vercel Shop. Check the documentation to connect your Shopify store and configure the storefront.

title: Why Some of My Google Play Closed Testers Didn't Count (and How I Check Every Opt-In Before Day 1)
description:
You can have more than 12 names on your list and still watch the Play Console Dashboard sit below 12. Every one of those Google Play testers says they joined. Some did. Others did something that felt like joining on their phone and meant nothing on Google's side.

I stopped trusting "yes, I'm in" a while ago. Now I treat the opt-in as its own small project and verify every tester before the 14-day clock starts to matter. This post is that audit, cause by cause, with the check I use for each one.

Two kinds of "didn't count"

The rule for personal developer accounts created after November 13, 2023 fits in one line: when you apply for production access, at least 12 testers must have been in your closed test without a break for the previous 14 days.

In practice, a tester can fail you in two different ways:

  • They never become an opted-in tester at all. Play Console simply doesn't see them.
  • They opt in and then do nothing. On paper they count. But Google's help page says it may ask for more testing if engagement was too low, and a tester who never opened the app gives you nothing to write on the application form.

Most of the causes below are the first kind. Two of them are the second kind, and I think those are the sneakier ones.


The five gates I walk each tester through. If someone stalls, I know which gate to look at instead of guessing.

Cause 1: their email isn't where you think it is

Closed tests take testers from an email list or from a Google Group. Both fail quietly.

With an email list, the usual problem is a typo or a second address. Someone gives me their work email, then uses their personal Gmail on their phone. The list has one address, the phone has another, and the opt-in page usually tells them they can't join.

One more trap: uploading a CSV to an email list replaces the addresses that were already there. Upload a "new testers" file and the first batch is gone.

With a Google Group, the person has to be a member of the group before they opt in. Getting the invite email isn't the same as joining. I check the group's member list myself rather than taking "yes, I joined" at face value.

Cause 2: the wrong Google account on the phone

This one gets its own heading because it's the first thing I check when a name is missing.

Plenty of people carry a personal Gmail, a work account and maybe an old one on the same phone. Joining happens in a browser, signed in as whoever Chrome last remembered. Installing happens in Play, signed in as whoever is selected there right now. If those are two different people, the tester has joined as account A and is trying to install as account B.

What I ask now, before sending any link: "Open Play Store, tap your profile picture, and tell me the email at the top." That email is the one I put on the list.

Cause 3: opted in on the web, never installed

Some testers tap "Become a tester", see the confirmation, and close the tab. They think they're done.

Technically the opt-in is what Google counts. But a tester with no install has no sessions, no crashes, no feedback. If half your 12 look like that, you're the developer Google's help page has in mind when it mentions insufficient engagement.

So my audit has two columns, not one: opted in, and installed. I only tick the second when the tester sends me something from inside the app, like a screenshot of the home screen or the version name from the settings page.

Cause 4: the opt-in link vs the Play Store link

There are two links and people mix them up.

  • The opt-in link comes from Play Console, on the closed track's Testers tab. It's where the tester joins.
  • The Play Store link is your app's normal listing URL. It's where they install, after joining.

Sending only the Play Store link to someone who hasn't opted in usually lands them on a page saying the app isn't available. Sending only the opt-in link usually works, since the page links onward to Play, but testers stop at the confirmation more often than you'd expect. I send both, in that order, and say which is which.

Timing matters too. Play Console won't show the opt-in link until the release is published, and after a first publish Google warns it may be hours before the link works for testers. Send it too early and people hit an error, then assume they did something wrong.

Cause 5: country availability

If a tester lives in a country your app isn't distributed to, the Play listing won't let them install. It's easy to set countries for the launch market you have in mind and forget that your testers are spread across a few others.

Check the countries and regions for the closed track before day 1, and compare them against where your testers actually are, not where your future users will be.

Cause 6: uninstalling halfway through

People tidy their phones. A test app they opened twice is an easy candidate.

From what I can find in Google's docs, uninstalling isn't the same as opting out. The opt-out is a separate action. But an uninstalled app produces no usage either, so for the engagement side it's almost as bad. And testers who uninstall sometimes go one step further and leave the program, which resets their 14 days if they rejoin, since Google wants the days consecutive.

I ask testers to keep the app installed for the whole window and tell them why. Plain reasons work better than reminders.

Reading the count in Play Console

The Dashboard is where Play Console shows your progress toward applying for production, and that's where I watch the opted-in number. What I haven't found is a screen that tells me which emails opted in. You get a number, not names.

That's why I keep my own roster. When the Dashboard number and my roster disagree, the gap is my to-do list.

tester | on list/group | account confirmed | opted in | installed | country ok | day 3 check
-------+---------------+-------------------+----------+-----------+------------+------------
T01    | yes           | yes (Play email)  | yes      | yes       | yes        | opened app
T02    | yes           | no  <- ask again  | ?        | ?         | yes        |
T03    | group invite  | yes               | no       | no        | yes        | <- join group

A plain text file or a sheet is enough. The point is that every column has an owner, and a blank means "go find out", not "probably fine".


What testers report, what it usually means, and the one question I ask to confirm it.

My day 0 routine

The night before I care about the clock, I go down the roster and make sure each row is full. Anyone who can't be confirmed gets replaced, not chased for three more days. I'd rather start with 14 confirmed Android app testers than 16 maybes.

On day 3 I do the same pass for the "opened the app" column. That's early enough to swap someone in without losing much time.

When the roster itself is the problem

All of this assumes you have people to audit. If finding them is where you're stuck, we run Google Play closed testing at TestMyApps: 14 testers for 16 days, which gives some room above Google's minimum, and testers join within 6 hours. Plans start from $15. Our track record across 400+ apps tested is a 99.9% approval rate. Google still makes the final call, so if production access isn't approved you get a free retest, and if that still isn't approved, a refund (terms at testmyapps.app/guarantee). The setup is on our 12 testers for 14 days page.


The live testmyapps.app page for the 12 testers for 14 days setup, captured 31 Oct 2026.

Either way, do the account check first. If I could keep only one habit from this post, it would be that single question about the Play Store profile picture.

title: One brand color, three platforms: what actually changes
description:
A while back I inherited a design system that had been ported from web to a mini program. The primary color made it. Almost nothing else did.

The tokens were all there. primaryHover, primaryActive, border, surface, textSub. Someone had copied them into the mini program stylesheet in good faith. Then, one at a time, they became dead weight. border had no consumer, because the mini program draws dividers instead. primaryHover sat there doing nothing, because a finger cannot hover.

The usual explanation is "the port was sloppy." I don't think that's it. The three platforms genuinely have different shapes, and almost nobody writes those shapes down. So I did.

I maintain a palette library with 100 palettes across the three platforms (31 app, 34 web, 35 mini program). Every palette has exactly ten color roles. I compared the role sets, the state transitions and the contrast behavior. All figures below are computed from those 100 palettes, so they describe one particular library and not the industry.

Here's what came out.

Ten roles each, and one shared field name

Put the three lists side by side and the intersection is one field name: bg. That's it. Everything else is named differently, or exists on one platform and not the others.

Purpose App Web Mini program
Primary primary primary theme
Darker / interaction primaryDark primaryHover + primaryActive btn
Lighter version primaryLight none tag
Secondary secondary none none
Accent accent accent + link price
Text levels text (one) textMain + textSub textMain + textSub
Divider none border divider
Container none surface card
Status success / warning / danger none none
Disabled none none btnDisabled

Ten roles on each platform. Same count, different sets. Which explains the dead tokens: the mini program had no place to put success, warning or danger, and no consumer for border. Meanwhile it was missing three roles it actually needed, price, tag and divider, because nobody had added them.

So "one brand color across three platforms" is true of exactly one role. The primary can stay. The other nine have to be rewritten per platform, and someone has to decide what they become.

Web darkens along one line, the app spreads to both sides

Web carries two interaction states. The app carries none, and the reason is the input device rather than the screen. A mouse pointer can hover. A finger has no middle state between pressing and lifting.

Measured across the web palettes here, primaryHover sits 13.9 lightness points below the primary (range 5.3 to 14.2), and primaryActive sits 26.1 points below. The second is about 1.9x the first.

The app does something structurally different. It gives the primary two flanks:

  • primaryDark: 14.0 points darker than the primary
  • primaryLight: 32.0 points lighter

The rise on the light side is 2.3x the drop on the dark side. That asymmetry is not arbitrary. The dark variant only ever marks a press. The light variant gets used as a tag background and as the fill of a selected area, which are large surfaces, and a fill that isn't light enough leaves no contrast headroom for dark text sitting on it. The dark side can move a little. The light side cannot.

Working numbers if you're setting these by hand: darken hover by 10 to 14 points, take active to roughly twice that, and push the light variant about twice as far as the dark one in the opposite direction. Narrower than that and the press is invisible. Wider and one tap looks like a different brand.

The mini program hides its accent behind a business word

Web and app both call their accent accent, and it is decorative: badges, highlights, anything that should be noticed without carrying information. The mini program has no accent. It has price.

That rename is the most useful thing in the whole comparison, because it exposes the rule underneath. In a mini program the accent serves a transaction, and price is its only job. Measured here, price sits at a median 4.50:1 against the background, with a low of 3.65:1. Compare that to the decorative accent on the other platforms, which in many palettes sits far below the body text threshold and is fine there.

The generalizable version: whether a color needs to clear a contrast threshold depends on whether it carries information or atmosphere. A decorative accent may sit low. An accent carrying a price, a count or a status may not. Same hue position, two uses, two standards, and the field name is doing the work of telling you which one you're looking at.

Each platform drops what it doesn't need, and the drops are the tell

The omissions are not random. They line up with how each platform organizes a screen.

Web has surface and border, and no status colors. Long pages divide with hairlines and faint fills. A form can run two thousand pixels tall, and a rule tells you something changed.

The mini program has card, divider and tag, and no status colors either. The page is a card stack, one card per unit of information, and the gaps between cards do most of the dividing.

The app has success, warning and danger, and neither surface nor border. Actions on a phone have consequences. A delete or a submit cannot be taken back, so state has to be explicit.

Which settles the first question when porting: don't move colors first. Look at what establishes hierarchy on the target platform. Carrying web colors into a mini program without its spacing gives you cards that collapse into a smear. Carrying app colors to the web leaves three status roles with nowhere to live.

The exception worth knowing about

The primaryLight figure above (32 points lighter) is a median. One palette in the library goes the other way: a primary of #4c8df6 at lightness 63, and a primaryLight of #1e3a63 at lightness 25, darker by 38 points.

That palette is a dark theme. Some dark implementations read primaryLight as "the tinted container for the primary" and return a darkened surface instead of a lightened one. The name didn't change. The value did.

The failure is concrete: if you treat primaryLight as a light fill because of its name, that palette gives you dark navy behind dark text, and the contrast collapses.

So the rule is one line: measure before you trust the name. Compare the lightness of primaryLight against the primary. Lighter, and it's a fill. Darker, and in this palette it's a deep container that wants light text on it. Same check applies to any palette you import and any design system you inherit.

If you only ship one platform, you need four roles

Most projects ship one platform, or ship one and expand later. You do not need thirty roles for that. Each platform has a minimum set, and four roles carry a page:

Platform Minimum set What breaks first without it
Web primary + bg + textMain + border No border and tables and forms lose their structure, leaving spacing to do all the work
Mini program theme + bg + textMain + card No card and the card stack flattens into one long column of text
App primary + bg + text + primaryDark No primaryDark and pressing a button produces no feedback at all

Four roles get a usable interface out the door, with three gaps: no secondary text, no accent, and no disabled state. None of that blocks a launch. All of it shows up afterward, one "why does this look off" at a time.

The order to fill the gaps is not a matter of taste. Secondary text first, then disabled states, then accent. The first affects legibility, the last affects looks, and the middle one decides whether people think a button can be pressed.

The short list

If you're doing the port this week:

  1. Leave the primary alone. Recognition depends on it and it has to match across platforms.
  2. Web: add primaryHover (10 to 14 points darker), primaryActive (about double), border, surface, textSub. No status colors.
  3. Mini program: replace the accent with price and hold it to the text standard. Add card, divider, tag, btnDisabled.
  4. App: add primaryDark (14 points darker), primaryLight (32 points lighter, and verify it is actually lighter), secondary, and the three status colors. No surface, no border.
  5. Dark themes: check the direction of every variant. Names lie at the edges.

Where the numbers come from

Every ratio in this post is computed with the WCAG 2.1 relative luminance formula, not estimated by eye, and every figure is regenerated at build time from the palette data rather than typed into the page. The full write-up, the datasets these figures come from, and two more pieces on secondary text contrast and on why card and border colors are nearly invisible, live at paletteget.com/guides. The thresholds and the method are documented at paletteget.com/method.

If you want to check one of your own palettes, the contrast numbers for all three platforms are listed on each palette page, so you don't have to work them out by hand.

One caveat worth stating plainly: this is 100 palettes from one library, curated by one person. It is a decent sample for spotting structural patterns in how the three platforms differ, and it is not a survey of what the industry does. Treat the ratios as evidence that the difference exists, not as targets to hit.

title: Amortized Localized Posterior Inference for Model Calibration with Application to an Ocean Turbulence Closure
description:
arXiv:2610.37731v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Model discrepancy may prevent a single calibration parameter from reproducing a physical response across the context domain. In addition, uncertainties in observations and contexts affect calibration and must be accounted for and quantified. We construct a family of localized posteriors by weighting observation likelihoods according to their proximity to a target context. Gaussian localization weights incorporate context uncertainty through covariance inflation, with reflection at domain boundaries and an optional correction for uneven context sampling. A conditional normalizing flow approximates the family of posteriors through amortized variational inference. Integrating the localized posteriors under a prescribed context measure gives the marginalized parameter distribution. In a twin experiment with the Branin-Hoo model, we compare global and localized inference under uniform and skewed context distributions. Localization reduces the reported aggregate predictive errors relative to the global posterior. An application to the k-$\epsilon$ turbulence closure in a single-column ocean model, with atmospheric surface forcing as context, shows that localized posterior calibration reduces temperature and zonal-velocity errors relative to deterministic and global-posterior calibration. Both twin experiments are constructed to admit local compensation.
