title: React Segmented Control: iOS Thumb, Drag and When to Use It
description:
TL;DR

A React segmented control is a radio group drawn as a row of 2 to 5 segments with a raised thumb on the selected one: one tab stop, arrow keys that move and select, and a 44px height on touch screens. Use it when the choice changes the content already on screen (a time range, a view, units); use Tabs when it swaps in a different panel, a Toggle Group when several options can be on, and radio cards when each option needs a description. The free Wingo UI Segmented Control adds the iOS details: a spring thumb you can drag sideways with a finger, while a vertical swipe still scrolls the page.

A React segmented control is the row of two to five options with a raised thumb under the selected one, the control iOS uses to pick the time range of the charts in the Health app. Search for an iOS segmented control web component and most results are React Native packages, and shadcn/ui ships none as of October 2026. This guide covers what the web version has to get right (the thumb, touch, keyboard and radio semantics), then the decision that matters more: when Tabs, a Toggle Group or radio cards are the better control. The examples use the free Segmented Control from Wingo UI, the library we build, so we are not neutral; outside facts link to their sources.

What is a segmented control, in web terms?

It is a radio group with a different look. Each segment is one option, exactly one is selected, and selecting one applies at once without a submit button. Apple's Human Interface Guidelines describe it as a way to offer "closely related choices that affect an object, state, or view." Material Design 3 has a close relative, the segmented button, so you also see the control searched as a React segmented button.

That framing settles the implementation: the markup should be a radiogroup with radio items, the WAI-ARIA radio group pattern defines the keyboard, and a name should make it submit like native radios. The thumb, the spring and the drag sit on top of that.

How do you add a segmented control in React?

Install it, pass options, and either let it hold its own value or control it:

npx wingo-ui@latest add segmented-control

"use client";

import { useState } from "react";
import { SegmentedControl, type SegmentedControlOption } from "@/components/ui/segmented-control";

const periods: SegmentedControlOption[] = [
  { value: "day", label: "Day" },
  { value: "week", label: "Week" },
  { value: "month", label: "Month" },
  { value: "year", label: "Year" },
];

export function SalesPeriod() {
  const [period, setPeriod] = useState("week");

  return (
    <SegmentedControl
      aria-label="Period"
      options={periods}
      value={period}
      onValueChange={setPeriod}
      fullWidth
    />
  );
}

Each option takes value, label, and optionally icon, badge (a number renders a count that hides at 0), tooltip and disabled. The props that change the look are size (sm, md or lg, a 32, 40 or 48px track), radius, tone (default neutral, a white thumb like iOS that turns a lifted gray in dark mode) or any CSS color, and dividers, the hairlines between unselected segments. Leave defaultValue out and it starts on the first enabled option.

Live demo: Segmented Control. The original article embeds an interactive demo here (Tap or click Month, then press the thumb and slide it sideways: the value follows your finger and the sales total updates. With the keyboard, Tab in and use the arrow keys). Try it live on wingo-ui.com or open the Segmented Control docs. Install: npx wingo-ui@latest add segmented-control

If you came for a React segmented control Tailwind recipe, the whole look is Tailwind v4 utilities on design tokens, and every inner part takes classes through classNames (item, thumb, icon, label, badge, divider). App-wide defaults go through the free UIProvider: <UIProvider defaults={{ "segmented-control": { radius: "full" } }}> rounds every segmented control in the app.

What makes it feel like the iOS control?

Three details: the thumb moves on a spring instead of a linear tween, it follows the finger, and it never steals a scroll.

The thumb animates transform only. It is rendered inside the selected segment, so CSS sizes it at rest. When the value changes, it measures the box it is leaving, jumps there as a transform and springs back to zero offset using the snappy spring from lib/motion (stiffness 500, damping 32). Animating left and width would recalculate layout on every frame; a transform stays on the compositor. Its corner radius is divided by the current scale, so a thumb stretching between a short and a long label keeps round corners. A change mid-flight starts from where the thumb is on screen and keeps its speed.

It answers the finger. Pressing the thumb dips it to 96%. Keep holding and slide sideways and the value follows the segment under your finger, then settles where you let go. The hairlines next to the thumb fade out, like on iOS.

A vertical swipe still scrolls the page. The track sets touch-action: pan-y, so the browser keeps vertical scrolling, and the code waits for 8px of movement before deciding what the gesture is. This is the part to copy if you build your own, trimmed from the component:

// track: className="touch-pan-y"; drag.current is recorded on pointerdown over the thumb, SLOP is 8
function handlePointerMove(event: React.PointerEvent<HTMLDivElement>) {
  const state = drag.current;
  if (!state || state.id !== event.pointerId) return;
  if (!state.active) {
    const dx = Math.abs(event.clientX - state.x);
    const dy = Math.abs(event.clientY - state.y);
    // vertical first: a page scroll, let the browser have it
    if (dy > SLOP && dy > dx) return endPress();
    if (dx <= SLOP) return;
    state.active = true;
    event.currentTarget.setPointerCapture(event.pointerId);
  }
  // pick the segment under clientX from rects measured on pointerdown
}

touch-action: none on the track would make the drag simpler and trap anyone who starts a scroll on the control. After a drag, the click that follows lands on the segment where the drag began, so the component swallows it; otherwise the value snaps back.

With reduced motion turned on, the thumb jumps to its new place and the press dip is off.

Is a segmented control accessible?

It is when the semantics are a radio group, and that comes almost free from Radix. The Segmented Control is built on @radix-ui/react-radio-group, so the track is a radiogroup, each segment a radio with aria-checked, and the whole control is a single tab stop. Left and Right (Up and Down too) move focus and select, which matches the APG rule for a radio group outside a toolbar. We added Home and End, disabled segments are skipped, and loop={false} stops the arrows at the ends. Mantine takes the same route: its SegmentedControl docs (v9.7.1, October 2026) say it "uses radio inputs under the hood."

Four things are on you:

  • A name. Pass aria-label, or aria-labelledby pointing at a visible heading; both land on the radiogroup.
  • Text for icons. Give icon options a label anyway. With iconOnly, it becomes the segment's aria-label and its tooltip, shown on hover, on keyboard focus and on a long press on touch.
  • A form name. Pass name and, inside a <form>, the selected value submits like native radios.
  • A non-drag path. WCAG 2.5.7 Dragging Movements (level AA) asks that anything done by dragging also work with a single pointer without dragging. Tapping a segment is that path, so keep it. Never make the drag the only way.

One trap if you build on Radix yourself: Radix checks the next radio only if the arrow key is still down when its deferred focus lands, so a very quick press (a screen reader, a remote, automation) can move focus without checking anything. The component selects on any focus that follows an arrow key, so a fast press still changes the value.

How should a segmented control behave on a phone?

It should be 44px tall on touch, share the width, and never flash gray on tap. The md size is a 40px track with a mouse and grows to 44px on coarse pointers (pointer-coarse:h-11). The sm size keeps its 32px look and gets an invisible hit area that reaches 44px; lg is 48px everywhere. The reasoning behind 44px, and the Tailwind variants that apply it only on touch, are in minimum touch target size for React and Tailwind.

fullWidth gives each segment an equal share of the container, the usual layout under a phone header. A segment with a long label keeps its natural width instead of truncating, and the others share what is left. Every segment carries touch-manipulation and a transparent -webkit-tap-highlight-color, so a quick second tap never zooms the page and iOS shows no gray flash. Set dir="rtl" and the layout, the arrow keys and the drag mirror.

The rest of the rules (sheets instead of popovers, safe areas, hover alternatives) are in the pillar on mobile-first React components, and the Mobile UI in React category collects every guide on the topic.

Segmented control vs tabs, a toggle group or radio cards: which one?

Pick by what the choice changes. The look tells you little, since Wingo UI's Tabs have a segmented variant with the same raised thumb. What differs is the semantics, and with them what a screen reader user expects to happen next.

The choice Use What assistive tech gets Wingo UI
Changes the content already on screen: a time range, a view, units; 2 to 5 short options Segmented Control radiogroup of radio; arrows move and select Free
Swaps in a different panel of content Tabs, variant="segmented" for this look tablist, tab, tabpanel linked by aria-controls Free
Changes the URL Nav Tabs links in a nav, the current one with aria-current="page" Pro
Several options can be on at once (bold and italic, amenities) Toggle Group type="multiple" buttons with aria-pressed Pro
Each option needs a description or a price Radio Group variant="card" radiogroup of radio Free
More than five options, or long labels Select a combobox that opens a listbox (a bottom sheet on phones) Free

Apple draws a similar line on iOS: "For switching between completely separate sections of an app, use a tab bar instead." Here are the same segments as Tabs, each with its own panel:

import { Tabs } from "@/components/ui/tabs";
// ProfileForm and BillingForm are your own components

export function AccountTabs() {
  return (
    <Tabs
      variant="segmented"
      fullWidth
      aria-label="Account"
      options={[
        { value: "profile", label: "Profile", content: <ProfileForm /> },
        { value: "billing", label: "Billing", content: <BillingForm /> },
      ]}
    />
  );
}

Live demo: Tabs. The original article embeds an interactive demo here (The same thumb as the segmented control, but each segment opens its own panel: switch from Active to Sold and the list slides in from the side you moved toward). Try it live on wingo-ui.com or open the Tabs docs. Install: npx wingo-ui@latest add tabs

The Toggle Group needs one more note. In single mode Radix also renders it as a radiogroup, but its arrow keys only move focus and Space or Enter presses the item. That is the APG rule for a radio group inside a toolbar, where "the button that is checked does not change" while you arrow through. So an alignment switch in an editor toolbar is a single Toggle Group, and a stand-alone time range is a segmented control. When several can be on, the Toggle Group in multiple mode is the only one of the four that fits:

import { ToggleGroup } from "@/components/ui/toggle-group";

export function AmenityFilter() {
  return (
    <ToggleGroup
      type="multiple"
      variant="outline"
      aria-label="Amenities"
      defaultValue={["parking"]}
      options={[
        { value: "parking", label: "Parking" },
        { value: "pets", label: "Pets allowed" },
        { value: "laundry", label: "In-unit laundry" },
      ]}
    />
  );
}

Live demo: Toggle Group. The original article embeds an interactive demo here (Bold starts on. Press Italic and both stay on, because the formatting group is type multiple; the alignment group next to it is single, so pressing one releases the other). Try it live on wingo-ui.com or open the Toggle Group docs. Install: npx wingo-ui@latest add toggle-group

Radio cards win when the options are not self-explanatory. "Courier, Locker, Pickup" fits in a segmented control; "Home delivery, FedEx, 1-2 days, $9.99" does not, and squeezing it into a segment hides the price that decides the choice. The React form components guide covers the wider choice between a radio group, a select and a combobox in a form.

What goes wrong with segmented controls?

Four things: too many segments, icons mixed with text, a value outside the options, and a missing name.

  • Too many segments. Apple says "no more than about five segments on iPhone", and Flutter's SegmentedButton docs say they are "typically used in cases where there are only 2-5 options." Six or more labels on a 360px screen get cramped or cut off; switch to a select or scrolling tabs.
  • Mixing icons and text. Apple's guidelines prefer one or the other in a single control. Pick text, or iconOnly with labels as names.
  • A controlled value that is not in options. The control shows no thumb, which looks broken. This usually happens when options load after the value.
  • No name. A radiogroup without aria-label reads as an unnamed group of radios.

What does a complete example look like?

An orders screen that filters one list by status. The choice changes the content on screen and there are four short options, so this is the segmented control's job. Counts ride on badges, and a status line tells screen readers how many orders are visible:

"use client";

import { useState } from "react";
import { SegmentedControl, type SegmentedControlOption } from "@/components/ui/segmented-control";

type Order = { id: string; customer: string; total: number; status: "open" | "shipped" | "returned" };

const usd = new Intl.NumberFormat("en-US", { style: "currency", currency: "USD" });

export function OrdersPanel({ orders }: { orders: Order[] }) {
  const [status, setStatus] = useState("all");
  const count = (value: Order["status"]) => orders.filter((order) => order.status === value).length;

  const options: SegmentedControlOption[] = [
    { value: "all", label: "All" },
    { value: "open", label: "Open", badge: count("open") },
    { value: "shipped", label: "Shipped" },
    { value: "returned", label: "Returned", badge: count("returned") },
  ];

  const visible = status === "all" ? orders : orders.filter((order) => order.status === status);

  return (
    <section className="flex flex-col gap-4">
      <SegmentedControl
        aria-label="Order status"
        options={options}
        value={status}
        onValueChange={setStatus}
        fullWidth
        className="sm:max-w-md"
      />
      <p role="status" className="text-sm text-muted-foreground">
        {visible.length} {visible.length === 1 ? "order" : "orders"}
      </p>
      <ul className="flex flex-col divide-y divide-border">
        {visible.map((order) => (
          <li key={order.id} className="flex justify-between gap-4 py-3 text-sm">
            <span className="truncate">{order.customer}</span>
            <span className="tabular-nums">{usd.format(order.total)}</span>
          </li>
        ))}
      </ul>
    </section>
  );
}

In a form, drop the state and give it a name. A server action then reads it like any radio:

<form action={saveDelivery}>
  <SegmentedControl
    name="delivery"
    aria-label="Delivery"
    defaultValue="locker"
    fullWidth
    options={[
      { value: "courier", label: "Courier" },
      { value: "locker", label: "Locker" },
      { value: "pickup", label: "Pickup" },
    ]}
  />
  {/* in saveDelivery: formData.get("delivery") */}
</form>

Where should you start?

Install the free control and drop it where a time range, a view switch or a unit toggle lives today:

npx wingo-ui@latest add segmented-control

Tabs and Radio Group are free too. The Toggle Group and Nav Tabs from the table above are part of Wingo UI Pro.

Components in this post

  • Segmented Control (Free): The iOS segmented control: pick one of a few options on a raised thumb that slides, and on touch drags along with your finger. Install: npx wingo-ui@latest add segmented-control
  • Tabs (Free): Switch between views of the same page with a sliding indicator: underline for sections, pill for filters, segmented for a compact switch. Install: npx wingo-ui@latest add tabs
  • Toggle Group (Pro): A row of toggles where one or several stay pressed, for text formatting, alignment, view switches and quick filters. Install: npx wingo-ui@latest add toggle-group
  • Radio Group (Free): Pick exactly one of a few visible options: rows with a dot that springs in, or cards with icons, prices and a selection ring that slides. Install: npx wingo-ui@latest add radio-group

FAQ

Does shadcn/ui have a segmented control?

Not as of October 2026. Its component list has Tabs, Toggle Group, Radio Group and Button Group, so building one on shadcn/ui means restyling one of those. Pick the base by what the choice does: Tabs for panels, a radio group for a value.

What is the difference between a segmented control and tabs?

Tabs swap in a different panel and expose tablist, tab and tabpanel roles linked by aria-controls. A segmented control picks a value that changes the content already on screen, such as a time range, and is a radiogroup. Apple's guidelines send switching between separate sections of an app to a tab bar.

How many options should a segmented control have?

Two to five. Apple's Human Interface Guidelines say no more than about five segments on iPhone, and Flutter's Material SegmentedButton docs say segmented buttons are typically used with 2 to 5 options. Past five, use a select or a scrolling row of tabs.

Is a segmented control accessible to screen readers?

It is when it is built as a radiogroup of radio items with a name: one tab stop, arrow keys that move and check, and aria-checked on the selected segment. Icon-only segments also need a text name, which Wingo UI's iconOnly mode takes from each option's label.

Can a segmented control submit with a form?

Yes. Give Wingo UI's Segmented Control a name and, inside a form, it submits the selected value like a radio group, so FormData and server actions read it with formData.get.

Is the Wingo UI Segmented Control free?

Yes. The Segmented Control, Tabs, Radio Group and Select are free and install with npx wingo-ui@latest add. The Toggle Group and Nav Tabs are part of Wingo UI Pro.

This article was originally published on the Wingo UI blog: React Segmented Control: iOS Thumb, Drag and When to Use It. The original has the live, interactive demos and is kept up to date.

title: Evaluating and improving AI agents for sequencing protocol understanding
description:
arXiv:2610.37851v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Existing scientific-agent benchmarks rarely evaluate whether agents can reconstruct the exact molecular structures and generation workflows specified by sequencing protocols, a capability critical for analyzing customized sequencing assays. We introduce LibStructBench, a document-grounded benchmark for reconstructing sequencing-library structures and molecular workflows. Our experiments show that frontier agents often produce approximately correct reconstructions but remain unreliable at exact reconstruction, particularly in molecular-state representation and workflow connectivity. Switching the underlying language model produced larger average performance differences than switching agent harnesses, with a statistically significant difference only for molecular-state reconstruction. Additional knowledge improved oligo-family recovery in a small pilot without improving mean molecular-workflow scores. Autonomous accumulation of procedural rules and cross-protocol examples showed non-monotonic validation performance and no mean held-out molecular-workflow improvement in the tested trajectory. These findings highlight the need for more controlled and verifiable approaches to scientific reasoning about molecular processes in complex experimental protocols.

title: Modelling Environmental Monitoring in a Food ERP: Sampling Sites, Swab Results and the Workflow a Positive Should Trigger
description:
By Isaac Muthui, CEO, Tamalaki Business Network Ltd. Originally published at factoraerp.com.

A swab result looks like the simplest record in a food factory: a site, a date, a pass or a fail. In practice it is one of the hardest to model well. The same "fail" can mean "re-clean the bench" or "hold three days of product", depending on where the sample was taken, what it was tested for, when it was taken relative to cleaning, and what has been produced since the last clear result. If the data model can't express that, the result ends up in a PDF from the lab and nobody can trend it.

This post walks through how we think about modelling environmental monitoring in an ERP for food and agro manufacturers in East Africa. The operational checklist behind it is in the original article.

What the domain rules say

The requirements read like a spec:

  • Codex CXG 61-2007 (Annex I) lists what a Listeria environmental monitoring programme must define: type of samples (food contact and non-food contact), target organisms, sampling locations and number of samples, frequency, tools, analytical methods, "a system to record the data and their evaluation, e.g. performing trend analyses", and actions on positive results. Source
  • EAS 39:2001: environmental sampling "at a level commensurate with identifying the risk" (4.3.4), timely action when results exceed action limits (4.3.7), a per-line tracking system "to track the location of possible sources of contamination" (4.6.2), and "records of environmental tests" (14.3.4). Source
  • 21 CFR 117.165(b)(3) (a US benchmark, not Kenyan law): the written procedure must identify the test microorganisms, "the locations from which samples will be collected and the number of sites", the timing and frequency, the tests and methods, the laboratory, and the corrective action procedures. Source

Translated into engineering terms: a sampling plan is configuration, a sample is an event against a site, a result is a measurement against a limit, and a positive is the start of a workflow, not the end of a record.

Sites are first-class entities

The most common mistake is storing the location as free text on the sample. "Filler", "filler area", "near filler" and "Filler 2" become four sites and the trend disappears.

EmSite      (id, code, area_id, zone, surface_type, food_contact bool, active_from, active_to)
            zone IN (1,2,3,4)
EmPlanItem  (id, site_id, target, method, frequency, timing, action_limit, owner_id)
            timing IN ('in_production','pre_startup','post_clean')

Sites get stable codes that match the plant map (RTE-Z1-03), a zone, and validity dates so the history survives a layout change. The plan item says what to test at that site, how often and when relative to cleaning. Timing matters: a post-clean swab verifies the sanitiser, a mid-shift swab looks for harbourage. Mixing them in one trend hides both signals.

Samples and results 

EmSample (id, site_id, plan_item_id, collected_at, collected_by, timing, pooled_group_id, lab_id, received_at)
EmResult (id, sample_id, target, method, value, unit, result_text, status, tested_at)
         status IN ('pass','fail','pending')

Two details come straight from the guidance. First, pooling: Codex allows compositing samples where sensitivity allows, but "in the case of positive findings additional testing will be necessary to determine the location". A pooled_group_id lets a positive pool fan out into follow-up samples for each member site. Second, received_at: if the lab can't show when a sample arrived, a transport problem looks like a clean result.

In FactoraERP today, the laboratory module stores samples with a type (including environmental and water), a collection point, date, time and collector, and test results with spec min/max and a pass/fail status. Non-conformances with root cause and CAPA live in the same quality module.

A positive opens a workflow

The response is where most systems stop. Codex describes a range: "no action (no risk of recontamination), to intensified cleaning, to source tracing (increased environmental testing), to review of hygienic practices up to holding and testing of product". That's a rule table keyed on zone and target:

EmResponseRule (zone, target, actions[])
  (1, 'Listeria spp.') -> [hold_product_since_last_negative, intensified_clean, vector_sampling, ncr]
  (3, 'Listeria spp.') -> [intensified_clean, vector_sampling, increase_frequency]

"Hold product since last negative" is the expensive one, and it is only possible if the system can answer a query like this:

-- batches produced on lines served by a site since its last clear result
SELECT b.id, b.batch_code, b.produced_at
FROM batch b
JOIN em_site s ON s.area_id = b.area_id
WHERE s.code = :site_code
  AND b.produced_at > (
    SELECT max(es.collected_at) FROM em_sample es
    JOIN em_result er ON er.sample_id = es.id
    WHERE es.site_id = s.id AND er.status = 'pass'
  );

"Vector sampling" means automatically creating follow-up samples at the positive site and its neighbours. Neighbours can be modelled as an adjacency list on the site map, so the plan grows around a problem and shrinks back when it's fixed, which is what EAS 39 4.6.2 asks for.

Trending is the point

CXG 61 says long-term review "can also reveal low level, intermittent contamination that may otherwise go unnoticed". The useful view isn't a pass rate; it is positives per site over time:

SELECT s.code, s.zone, date_trunc('month', es.collected_at) AS month,
       count(*) FILTER (WHERE er.status = 'fail') AS positives,
       count(*) AS samples
FROM em_sample es
JOIN em_site s ON s.id = es.site_id
JOIN em_result er ON er.sample_id = es.id
WHERE es.timing = 'in_production'
GROUP BY s.code, s.zone, month
ORDER BY positives DESC, month;

One positive is an event. The same drain showing up three months in a row is a harbourage site.

Takeaways

  • Make sampling sites first-class entities with stable codes and zones.
  • Record timing relative to cleaning, and don't trend post-clean and mid-shift swabs together.
  • Support pooled samples with fan-out on positives.
  • Treat a positive as the start of a workflow keyed on zone and target.
  • Be able to query the product made since a site's last clear result.

The full 10-step operational checklist, with references to Codex CXC 1 and CXG 61, EAS 39 and Kenya's food hygiene regulations, is on the FactoraERP blog.

title: Email Event Notifications in Node.js: Implement Report Attachments with 2026 Code
description:
Short answer: for an e-commerce report email, the expensive part is usually the integration boundary, not the POST that sends a message. Keep report generation, attachment handling, delivery, and status collection separate. Use an explicit idempotency key for the send, poll delivery events on a schedule, and retain only the evidence your support and compliance workflows actually need.

A Node.js service can call /v1/email/send with to, subject, and body, authenticated with a bearer key. The practical design question is larger: who creates the report, where is the attachment held, and how many credentials and reconciliation jobs sit between an order database and a customer's inbox?

What does the report email really cost to operate?

Take a nightly sales report for a small online retailer. The workload is 1,200 recipients, one generated report per store, a retryable send operation, and a later status sweep. The visible work is a mail request. The retained work includes a report artifact, a delivery identifier, a suppression decision, event history, and enough metadata to answer “did this customer receive the April 12 report?” without opening a database backup.

That last question dominates the design. A failed attachment generation is different from a rejected recipient, and a provider timeout is different from a successful send followed by a lost response. If the worker retries every ambiguous failure without an idempotency key, one report can become two messages. That is a customer-facing defect, not a rounding error.

I start with the retention rule: keep the report until the send has a final state, keep the delivery evidence long enough for the support window, then delete the artifact unless a legal or accounting policy says otherwise. The deliberate cost is that a late complaint may require regeneration instead of a one-click resend. That trade-off is usually easier to explain than keeping every customer report forever.

The dominant term is integration effort: artifact lifecycle, retry semantics, event polling, and reconciliation. A unit price can be checked on a provider page; a missing state transition becomes an incident ticket.

For this exact seam, Infrai is a plausible consolidation option: one API key and one usage statement can cover the account, PDF, and email steps. Its public discovery surface exposes schemas and runnable examples, so a team evaluating integration effort can inspect the contract before committing to the worker design.

No shortcut.

How can I implement email event notifications in Node.js with code?

Amazon SES, SendGrid, and Postmark are credible direct choices, but they remove different pieces of the work. SES is a natural fit when the team already operates deeply inside AWS and wants email delivery close to its existing identity, logging, and infrastructure controls. The trade is that the application team still owns the surrounding report pipeline and its operational joins.

SendGrid is a broad email platform with templates and event-oriented tooling. It can suit a product team that wants email-specific features and a familiar provider surface. The boundary to inspect is the same one: attachment creation, durable send state, and the code that reconciles provider events with the report record.

Postmark is attractive when transactional email clarity and message activity are more important than a large marketing platform. It is a focused choice for a team that wants email to remain a specialist subsystem. That focus is a limitation if the report job also needs document generation, account metering, or other backend capabilities under the same operational model.

Option Integration shape Good fit Main boundary
Amazon SES AWS email API Teams already standardized on AWS The report pipeline and reconciliation remain yours
SendGrid Email platform API Teams wanting email-specific tooling Artifact lifecycle and delivery joins still need application code
Postmark Transactional email API Focused transactional messaging Less suitable when document and account capabilities should share one surface
Infrai One REST surface Small teams optimizing cross-service integration effort Consolidation means one vendor and one outage surface

A fourth pattern is a single REST surface for the report pipeline. Infrai's documented position is one key and one bill across backend services, which removes the credential and invoice joins between a PDF capability and email. This is a consolidation decision, not a claim that a general backend surface beats an email specialist at every email feature.

Recommendation: an e-commerce team should try Infrai for the report-generation-to-email boundary when one credential, one usage statement, and a plain REST integration matter more than specialist email tooling. Choose SES, SendGrid, or Postmark instead when that specialist's deliverability controls, event workflow, or existing account ecosystem is the stronger constraint.

There is a real cost to consolidation: one vendor to trust, one bill to reconcile, and one outage surface. Those are related, but they are not the same thing.

How should a Node.js service send without duplicating reports?

The route is HTTP, so the same contract can be exercised from any language. The following small Python example shows the part that must be exact in a Node.js implementation too: bearer authentication, an explicit POST, a client-generated idempotency key, response checking, and bounded handling for HTTP 429. It sends the notification after the report worker has produced its artifact; the attachment-specific field should be taken from the current email schema rather than guessed in application code.

import os
import time
import uuid

import requests

BASE_URL = "https://api.infrai.cc/v1"
API_KEY = os.environ["INFRAI_API_KEY"]


def send_report_notice(recipient: str, report_id: str) -> dict:
    idempotency_key = f"report-email:{report_id}:{recipient}"
    payload = {
        "to": recipient,
        "subject": f"Sales report {report_id}",
        "body": "Your generated sales report is ready.",
    }
    headers = {
        "Authorization": f"Bearer {API_KEY}",
        "Content-Type": "application/json",
        "Idempotency-Key": idempotency_key,
    }

    for attempt in range(4):
        response = requests.post(
            f"{BASE_URL}/email/send",
            json=payload,
            headers=headers,
            timeout=30,
        )
        if response.status_code == 429:
            retry_after = response.headers.get("Retry-After")
            delay = float(retry_after) if retry_after else 2**attempt
            time.sleep(min(delay, 30))
            continue
        if not response.ok:
            raise RuntimeError(
                f"email send failed ({response.status_code}): {response.text}"
            )
        return response.json()

    raise RuntimeError("email send rate limit did not clear after four attempts")


if __name__ == "__main__":
    print(send_report_notice("buyer@example.com", str(uuid.uuid4())))

The retry key must be derived from the business operation, not generated afresh for every attempt. In a real Node.js worker, persist that key beside the report record before the first request. Also persist the response identifier and use a separate polling job for status updates. Do not treat a successful HTTP response as proof that the recipient opened the message.

The email event route is /v1/email/event/list. The important limitation is that event delivery is pull-based here: there is no webhook event push in the two namespaces described for this workflow. Poll on a controlled cadence, record the last cursor or timestamp supported by the live schema, and make the event consumer idempotent. A poller that crashes after writing an event but before advancing its checkpoint must be safe to run again.

Where does the PDF and metering handoff belong?

For a generated attachment, the clean seam is:

  1. The account layer provides the usage or account context for the job.
  2. The content-processing layer generates the PDF artifact.
  3. The email layer sends the notification and records the delivery state.

The same Authorization: Bearer $INFRAI_API_KEY and https://api.infrai.cc/v1 base URL can cover those capability groups. The PDF output becomes the input to the email worker's attachment step; it should remain private and have an explicit deletion policy. I would keep this handoff in a queue record rather than pass a large document through several synchronous HTTP calls.

Here is the failure boundary I would draw for the 1,200-recipient run. The report job gets a stable report ID before rendering. The PDF worker writes a private artifact and marks that ID ready. The email worker then creates one deterministic key per report and recipient, sends the message, and stores the returned delivery identifier. If the process dies after the provider accepts the message but before the database update, the next attempt reuses the same key. If PDF generation fails, there is no email retry to perform; the report remains in a renderable state. If the email request is rejected, the artifact stays available until the retention timer because support may need to inspect the exact report. If the event poller sees the same delivery event twice, it upserts by the provider event identity rather than incrementing a counter blindly. That is a small amount of state, but it is the difference between an understandable operating bill and a pile of “probably sent” records. The queue also gives the application a place to enforce recipient suppression and to keep the document out of logs. I would never log the PDF bytes or place the bearer key in a URL.

The alternative stack is easy to name and harder to operate: Stripe for metering, Puppeteer for document rendering, and SES for mail. That means three signups, three credential sets, three vendor consoles, and glue for usage reconciliation, report lifecycle, retries, and event state. The separation can be exactly right for a larger organization with clear ownership boundaries. For a small team, it is also why usage statements are often the last part of the system to become boring.

This does not make a single key a compliance decision. Sender authentication, suppression handling, retention, and regional requirements remain application responsibilities. SPF is one part of the sender policy story, not evidence that every delivery or jurisdictional requirement has been met.

What should the system deliberately refuse to promise?

Do not describe polling as real-time delivery. Do not assume a hosted email OTP exists; an email verification fallback needs to be built by the application. Do not plan an email scheduled-send cancellation flow when the documented caveat says the email side has no cancellation route. There is also no SMTP relay, no WhatsApp, RCS, or voice channel in this capability group.

Those boundaries change the choice. A product that needs rich email-native automation or a mature webhook workflow may be better served by a specialist. A product that needs a simple report artifact, a controlled send, and one operational account may value the smaller integration surface. The right comparison is the full operating bill: signups, credentials, reconciliation code, retention, and the time spent explaining ambiguous delivery states.

If this boundary fits your system, start with the Infrai documentation and verify the current request schema before adding attachment fields.

Further reading

  • RFC 7208: Sender Policy Framework (SPF)
  • Amazon SES developer guide
  • SendGrid Mail Send API reference
  • Postmark developer documentation

title: Our traceability matrix was six months stale. The spreadsheet was never the real problem.
description:
Our traceability matrix was six months stale, and I hated every cell of it. The surprising part was that replacing the spreadsheet with a more expensive eQMS would not have fixed the underlying problem.

During a notified-body review of a customer design file, the reviewer asked to see how a revised design requirement connected to its specification, risk control, verification evidence and design-change record. We produced the matrix quickly. The evidence behind it took much longer to assemble.

That gap told us more than any procedural non-conformance could.

A matrix is not a ceremonial annex

It is tempting to describe the traceability matrix as the first document a notified body asks for. That is not universally true, and claiming otherwise would be theatre. But it is often one of the first views an assessor requests because it compresses the design-control system into something navigable.

The matrix is not a separately named regulatory deliverable in ISO 13485:2016 or FDA 21 CFR 820.30. Instead, the expectations sit across the framework:

  • ISO 13485:2016 requires documented design and development evidence and control of design changes.
  • 21 CFR 820.30 addresses design requirements, outputs, verification, validation and design changes.
  • ISO 14971 expects risk controls to remain connected to the requirements and evidence that demonstrate their effectiveness.
  • EU MDR Article 10(9) and Annex IX place design and production controls inside the manufacturer’s quality-management system.
  • IEC 62304 adds another traceability layer when software is part of the design.

No single row proves compliance. What matters is whether a requirement remains linked through its complete life.

For us, the matrix had become a snapshot of an earlier conversation. The controlling records continued moving, but the spreadsheet did not.

How our “living” matrix became archaeology

We support manufacturing programmes for global medtech OEMs. Each customer had its own document repository, revision convention and change process. Our site maintained manufacturing specifications, process-validation records, supplier controls and internal verification evidence.

The matrix was supposed to connect those records. In practice, it contained copied identifiers, manually maintained revisions and links to files stored in several locations.

A design requirement changed. The specification followed. The verification protocol was updated and a new report issued. The matrix still pointed to the previous revision. In another row, a risk-control record had been revised without the matrix being updated.

Nothing dramatic had happened. That was the problem. Each individual record had been controlled. The relationships between them had not.

The spreadsheet was not the villain. It was a perfectly reasonable starting point. The failure was treating copied data as if it were live traceability.

What I now expect a controlled matrix to show

For every design requirement, the traceability chain should provide enough context to navigate forward and backward without relying on institutional memory:

  • The controlled requirement and its current revision.
  • The related design specification or design output.
  • The relevant hazard, risk-control and risk-management references.
  • The verification method, protocol, report and outcome.
  • Design-validation evidence where applicable.
  • Every associated design change and impact assessment.
  • Record owner, approval state and effective date.

The important distinction is between a value copied into a cell and a controlled link to the authoritative record. A copied revision will eventually become wrong. A live link can reveal that the source record has changed and trigger a review.

A useful matrix should also expose orphaned evidence. If a verification report has no requirement, a changed specification has no impact assessment, or an approved design change has not reached verification, those are gaps—not administrative noise.

For a small medical-device company, Excel can still support this model. It can also support an uncontrolled mess. The tool matters less than the rule that authoritative records are linked, changes trigger review, and humans approve what is published.

The CMO boundary generic eQMS discussions often skip

This is where my perspective differs from the usual device-maker narrative.

At a contract manufacturer, we do not own every part of the product design. The OEM may control design requirements, the risk-management file and design validation. We control the manufacturing translation, process validation, supplier qualification, incoming inspection and related non-conformances.

That ownership boundary has to be visible.

A supplier certificate of analysis may confirm that incoming material met an agreed specification. It does not, by itself, verify an OEM design requirement. A supplier corrective action may resolve a component issue without proving that the design risk control remains effective. A manufacturing process change may have no design impact—but somebody has to make and document that determination.

The useful connected workflow is therefore not one undifferentiated list of documents. It is a controlled chain with explicit ownership:

  • OEM-owned design evidence.
  • CMO-owned process and supplier evidence.
  • Shared impact assessments where the two meet.

Any matrix that blurs those boundaries creates false confidence. It may look complete while quietly implying that a supplier record closes a design-control obligation that only the OEM can close.

AI assistance should expose uncertainty, not hide it

AI-assisted traceability checks could compare changed requirements and specifications, identify missing verification links and propose updates to affected rows. That is useful, particularly when change control already suffers from CAPA backlogs.

But the assistance must remain controlled. A reviewer should see the source record, the proposed change and the reason for the recommendation before anything enters the approved matrix. An AI-generated update does not become controlled evidence merely because it was generated quickly.

The same principle applies when an automated CAPA triggers a change-impact review. Automation can identify the possible touchpoints. A qualified person still has to determine whether the product design, risk assessment or verification evidence is affected.

In other words, the goal is not a faster first draft. It is reviewability, traceability and a visible audit trail.

The product boundary I keep testing

qmsWrapper publicly positions its Advanced Design Control Traceability Matrix around consistent execution with built-in traceability and live, updatable links across design requirements, design specifications, verification and design changes. That is the right architectural shape for a device maker.

However, I run supplier quality at a CMO with more than forty suppliers, and qmsWrapper is built and marketed for device makers and SaMD teams, not specifically for CMO-side supplier work. I would not use a device-maker traceability matrix as evidence that supplier COAs, incoming inspection or sub-tier audit findings are covered without seeing that workflow demonstrated. The supplier-design boundary is the part I keep testing.

I work on qmsWrapper and am giving my honest read of where it does not fit.

The five-minute test I would run before an audit

Before the next design-file review, I would open the matrix and try to complete five actions:

  1. Select a recently changed requirement.
  2. Follow it to the current specification.
  3. Navigate to the associated risk control.
  4. Reach the current verification report.
  5. Identify the change record that explains the revision.

If any step requires someone to remember another spreadsheet, search a shared drive or contact the person who originally built the matrix, the matrix is not living. It is an archive with links.

Our six-month-stale spreadsheet was embarrassing. More importantly, it exposed a broken connected workflow. Fixing it required more than changing the colour of a cell; it required deciding which records were authoritative, who owned each relationship and what would trigger review when those records changed.

Which link in your design traceability chain is still maintained through memory rather than a controlled record?

title: How Tailscale built a customer-facing model router on AI Gateway
description:
Tailscale on Vercel

  • Hundreds of AI models shipped to customers in-product

  • Model access granted and revoked by tailnet network identity

  • Went from model routing prototype to paying customers in months

Tailscale connects a company's laptops, servers, cloud instances, and personal devices into one private network called a tailnet. Remy Guercio, who leads product for Aperture by Tailscale, describes it simply: "It's basically like a VPC that can span any cloud, on-prem, your house, and your phone."

Aperture takes that same idea and applies it to AI. Instead of giving every employee, agent, or tool a separate provider API key, Aperture lets companies control model access through the tailnet itself. Add someone to the network, and they can immediately use approved models. Remove them, and access disappears.

Under the hood, Aperture is built on Vercel AI Gateway and Vercel Sandbox. AI Gateway gives Tailscale one API for hundreds of models. Sandbox gives agents a safe place to run. Together, they let Tailscale offer model access and agent execution inside a customer's private network, without their team building every piece of AI infrastructure from scratch.

Model routing is harder than it looks

Tailscale is an infrastructure company, so building the routing and execution layers in-house was the obvious first option. But once they took a deeper look into the engineering effort required, they chose not to.

The provider layer looked deceptively simple from the outside. "You would think all of the endpoints are the same," Remy says. "They are not."

David Carney, Co-founder and Chief Strategy Officer, has the receipts, because Tailscale still maintains that plumbing for a few customers who haven't migrated to Aperture yet. "There are a lot of things the big providers don't do that blow my mind that the gateway does, like simply putting the cost in the response," he says. "We initially built those systems for customers ourselves, and the complexity is insane."

Agents raised the stakes further. An agent that can read private data, act on the text it reads, and reach the public internet is a security problem now called the "lethal trifecta." The right mitigation is an isolated sandbox with identity and access controls baked in. "I think we wouldn't have been able to deliver the product if we were also trying to build a sandbox ourselves," David says. "But we were able to go from prototype to paying customers in months on Vercel."

Building a custom model router on AI Gateway

Tailscale shopped the routing layer first. "We did talk to a lot of other folks, including providers themselves, and Vercel just made it very easy," Remy says. AI Gateway gives Aperture one API across hundreds of models, and returns cost and usage on every request, so Aperture can surface spend to customers without Tailscale maintaining price tables for each provider.

Tailscale's customers care about protecting their data, and Zero data retention (ZDR) was table stakes for Aperture. Tailscale chose AI Gateway because:

  • The AI Gateway itself retains no data.

  • They can set ZDR globally or use the per-request zeroDataRetention flag, which automatically restricts routing to ZDR-compliant providers.

"All this ZDR stuff is a moving target, like, which models have zero data retention versus not," David says, "but we don't have to write any of that logic, because it's all handled for us."

Zero cost markup for Tailscale and their customers

AI Gateway doesn't mark up token costs on any provider or model, including when Tailscale's customers bring their own keys. Aperture's customers pay the same rate they would going direct, across every model in the catalog.

Time to first token, from signup

Ask David what Vercel is worth to Aperture, and his answer is simple: time to first token. But that means something different to David than it does to Remy, and both are right.

"[David] Carney likes to overload the term time to first token," Remy says. "In the AI infrastructure world it has a very specific meaning, which is how long it takes to load the cache, generate the response, and deliver it back to the user." Remy explains David's definition: "It's the time from user signup to their first model call, which is the real value Aperture provides to our customers."

And Aperture's success is measured by that time-to-value. "I constantly push the team to remove the most barriers possible to get someone to that wow moment as fast as we can," David says. "After months of testing different products, Vercel was the answer to the infrastructure side, because AI Gateway has such low latency."

Running agents on the tailnet in Vercel Sandbox

Once Aperture had model access in place, the team focused on making it safe to run agents inside a tailnet. This is the workflow:

  • A sandbox spins up and connects to Aperture.

  • Aperture connects to AI Gateway.

  • Tailscale validates the identity.

  • The agent does its work.

  • The sandbox shuts down.

No key is ever issued to the agent.

Tailscale shopped the sandbox layer too, and even had a working implementation on a different provider before deciding to switch. "We wanted to focus on network identity, not sandbox security boundaries, and Vercel's sandboxes are bulletproof," says Remy.

Migrating Tailscale's internal AI layer to AI Gateway

Tailscale's own AI usage had grown the way most companies' has: a mix of direct provider accounts and cloud endpoints, accumulated one team at a time. Internally, those requests went through Aperture, but behind the proxy, it was still calling separate providers directly. After implementing AI Gateway for their customers, they knew they wanted to make the migration themselves.

Tailscale's engineering team built a switch in Aperture that pointed requests to AI Gateway instead of the individual provider APIs, so now they have one integration rather than separate ones for each provider. Nothing changed for employees. Aperture was still the endpoint they called, and every model they were already using was in the AI Gateway catalog, so the cutover happened with zero interruption. Tailscale now uses their own migration as the playbook for enterprise customers juggling dozens of provider accounts and keys.

What's next

Aperture started as a raw gateway for engineers to point a coding agent at. It now has a chat UI, MCP connectors, and sandboxes launchable as ephemeral nodes, all running on tailnet identity.

Aperture's new goal is time to first app. David wants users to sign up, run a prompt, build an app, and share it, all in ten minutes or less.

"We don't exactly know what that's going to look like, but we know we're going to have to iterate quickly," Remy says. "Having partners you can work with hand in hand on that is incredibly important."

David's advice to other companies is to focus on the product they deliver to customers, not the infrastructure required to run it. "A lot of people want to build their own router. And look at us, we tried to do it too," he says. "But you don't need to build another router."

About Tailscale: Tailscale is a secure connectivity platform that connects a company’s users, devices, servers, cloud infrastructure, and services through an identity-based private network. Their model router, Aperture by Tailscale, extends that network to AI models and agents.

title: I Built a Sector Rotation Map in Python. A Shuffle Test Humbled It.
description:
This week I shipped a sector rotation map for Indian stocks. It plots NSE sector and thematic indices against the Nifty 500 and sorts them into four corners: Leading, Weakening, Lagging and Improving.

Then the obvious question hit me: does it actually tell you anything? If you buy whatever is Leading, do you beat the market? And do sectors really travel clockwise around the map, the way every explainer says?

So I rebuilt the whole thing in Python, ran it over ten years of weekly data, and checked. This post is the build: the maths, the code, two bugs, and a shuffle test that took my favourite finding away. The story version, with more charts, is on Medium (linked at the end).

Not investment advice. I built the data platform and the map used here. Data runs from July 2016 to 23 October 2026.

The maths

Every week, for every sector:

rs    = 100 * sector / nifty_500                  # relative strength
ratio = 100 * wma(rs, 5) / wma(rs, 15)             # has it been gaining ground lately?
mom   = 100 * ratio / ratio.shift(5)               # is that speeding up or fading?

wma is a weighted moving average, where the newest week counts most. Dividing the 5-week average by the 15-week one gives a number around 100. Above 100 means relative strength has been rising recently, so the sector has been outperforming the Nifty 500 over the last few weeks. The momentum line compares today's ratio with five weeks ago. Above 100, that outperformance is accelerating.

Two numbers, two thresholds at 100, four corners:

q = np.where(ratio >= 100, np.where(mom >= 100, "Leading", "Weakening"),
             np.where(mom >= 100, "Improving", "Lagging"))

The formula was the easy part. Every mistake I made was in the data handling.

Getting the data

I pulled daily levels for 21 indices and the Nifty 500 from the data API I built. Responses are paginated, so a small helper follows meta.next_cursor until has_more is false. The from date is 2015, so the 15-week averages have time to warm up before the test starts in July 2016.

Weekly bars, finished weeks only 

iso = daily.index.isocalendar()
weekly = daily.groupby([iso.year, iso.week]).last()
weekly.index = [pd.Timestamp.fromisocalendar(y, w, 5) for y, w in weekly.index]
if weekly.index[-1] >= pd.Timestamp.today().normalize():
    weekly = weekly.iloc[:-1]  # this week hasn't finished yet

Grouping by ISO week and taking the last close gives one bar per week, holiday weeks included. Each week is labelled with its Friday, and if that Friday hasn't passed, the week is dropped. Run it on a Wednesday without that check and you're treating three days as a full week. My first version dropped the last week unconditionally, which quietly threw away a finished week whenever I ran it on a weekend.

The live map had a cousin of this bug. In weekly mode, a freshness check that looked at the wrong date decided, in the middle of the week, that every sector was stale, and the map came up empty. The fix was to compare each sector's last session with the map's as-of date.

The bug that almost fooled me

My first version built the daily table like this:

daily = pd.concat(series, axis=1).sort_index().ffill()

Forward-filling looks harmless. Holidays differ a little between indices, so why not carry the last price forward?

Because three of the indices (Healthcare, Consumer Durables, Oil & Gas) have a stray data point in mid-2016 and no continuous data until 2020. ffill() took that one price and copied it forward for years. Healthcare got about four years of invented, perfectly flat history.

Nothing errored, but the answer flipped. With the fill, Improving sectors beat the Nifty 500 over the next quarter by 0.30% on average. Without it, they lagged by 0.36%.

I caught it only because an earlier prototype built the weeks differently and the two disagreed. The fix was to delete .ffill():

daily = pd.concat(series, axis=1).sort_index()

GroupBy.last() already skips missing values inside a week, so holidays are fine, and a week with no data at all stays empty. The rolling averages see the gap, return NaN, and drop out instead of inventing a trend.

A second, smaller one, which a reviewer caught: I first computed the 13-week forward return after dropping the empty rows. Across a gap, shift(-13) then jumps 13 rows, not 13 weeks. The forward return is now computed on the full weekly series, before anything is dropped.

Checking it against the live map

Before trusting the backtest, I printed the latest week and compared it with the live page. All 21 indices matched the live page to two decimals on both ratio and momentum. IT: ratio 104.76, momentum 104.49. Pharma: 101.35 and 99.30. MNC: 97.33 and 98.19.

Result one: Leading doesn't predict much

For every weekly reading from July 2016, I recorded the corner and whether the sector beat the Nifty 500 over the next 13 weeks:

           weeks     avg beat_benchmark
quadrant
Improving   1707  -0.36%          47.9%
Lagging     3620  -0.28%          47.0%
Leading     3443  +0.47%          50.1%
Weakening   1616  +0.21%          47.8%

Any sector-week beat the benchmark 48.3% of the time, so Leading is about two points better. But the 13-week windows overlap, which makes 10,386 readings worth far fewer independent ones. When I kept only non-overlapping quarters, Weakening (+1.14%, 132 readings) came out ahead of Leading (+0.26%, 253). That flip looks like noise, so I wouldn't treat either number as an edge. These are also price indices, so dividends are left out. That slightly understates sectors that yield more than the Nifty 500.

Result two: the shuffle test

The clockwise rotation looked like the real finding. 67.0% of the 2,233 corner changes went clockwise.

Then I asked what random data would do. For each sector, I took the longest unbroken stretch of its real weekly moves, shuffled their order, rebuilt a relative-strength path, and ran the exact same map on it, 30 times:

s = rs.dropna()
run = (s.index.to_series().diff() > pd.Timedelta(weeks=2)).cumsum()
s = s[run == run.value_counts().idxmax()]  # longest unbroken stretch only
moves = np.log(s).diff().dropna().to_numpy()
path = np.exp(np.log(s.iloc[0]) + np.concatenate([[0], np.cumsum(rng.permutation(moves))]))
fake.append(readings(pd.Series(path, index=s.index))[lambda d: d.index >= "2016-07-01"])

real sectors: 2233 quadrant changes, 67.0% clockwise
shuffled data: 66.2% clockwise (range 63.6% to 68.0%)

The shuffled data rotates clockwise just as reliably: real sectors, at 67.0%, sit inside the shuffled range. Even the median time in Leading is the same: six weeks for real sectors, five to six for shuffled ones.

The reason is in the maths. The momentum axis is roughly the rate of change of the ratio axis. When momentum is above 100, the ratio is rising, so the dot moves right; below 100 it moves left. Right along the top and left along the bottom is clockwise, for any wiggly series, like a pendulum's position against its speed. And because the ratio compares a short and a long average of the same series, it swings around 100 for any input, so those loops circle the centre of the map. The rotation comes from the indicator itself. It's still a nice way to see a sector's recent path. It just isn't evidence of a cycle you can trade.

The full script

Set TAPETIDE_API_TOKEN and run it. It prints the latest map, the results table, the clockwise count and the shuffle test.

import os
import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
import requests

API = "https://api.tapetide.com/v1"
HEADERS = {"Authorization": f"Bearer {os.environ['TAPETIDE_API_TOKEN']}"}
SECTORS = ["nifty-it", "nifty-bank", "nifty-private-bank", "nifty-psu-bank", "nifty-fmcg",
           "nifty-pharma", "nifty-auto", "nifty-metal", "nifty-realty", "nifty-energy",
           "nifty-financial-services", "nifty-infrastructure", "nifty-media", "nifty-mnc",
           "nifty-pse", "nifty-cpse", "nifty-commodities", "nifty-india-consumption",
           "nifty-consumer-durables", "nifty-healthcare-index", "nifty-oil-and-gas"]
ORDER = ["Leading", "Weakening", "Lagging", "Improving"]


def closes(slug, start="2015-01-01"):
    rows, params = [], {"from": start, "limit": 1000}
    while True:
        body = requests.get(f"{API}/indices/{slug}/levels", headers=HEADERS, params=params, timeout=60).json()
        rows += body["data"]
        if not body["meta"]["has_more"]:
            break
        params["cursor"] = body["meta"]["next_cursor"]
    s = pd.DataFrame(rows)
    return pd.Series(s["close"].values, index=pd.to_datetime(s["date"]), name=slug)


daily = pd.concat([closes(s) for s in SECTORS + ["nifty-500"]], axis=1).sort_index()
iso = daily.index.isocalendar()
weekly = daily.groupby([iso.year, iso.week]).last()  # last real close per week; empty weeks stay NaN
weekly.index = [pd.Timestamp.fromisocalendar(y, w, 5) for y, w in weekly.index]
if weekly.index[-1] >= pd.Timestamp.today().normalize():
    weekly = weekly.iloc[:-1]  # this week hasn't finished yet


def wma(x, n):
    weights = np.arange(1, n + 1)
    return x.rolling(n).apply(lambda v: v @ weights / weights.sum(), raw=True)


def readings(rs):
    ratio = 100 * wma(rs, 5) / wma(rs, 15)               # is relative strength rising lately?
    mom = 100 * ratio / ratio.shift(5)                   # is that speeding up or fading?
    q = np.where(ratio >= 100, np.where(mom >= 100, "Leading", "Weakening"),
                 np.where(mom >= 100, "Improving", "Lagging"))
    next_13w = rs.shift(-13) / rs - 1                    # beat the benchmark next quarter?
    d = pd.DataFrame({"rs": rs, "ratio": ratio, "mom": mom, "quadrant": q, "next_13w": next_13w})
    return d[d["ratio"].notna() & d["mom"].notna()]


def clockwise_share(frames):
    moves = [(a, b) for d in frames for a, b in zip(d["quadrant"], d["quadrant"].iloc[1:]) if a != b]
    return np.mean([ORDER[(ORDER.index(a) + 1) % 4] == b for a, b in moves]), len(moves)


rs_all = {s: 100 * weekly[s] / weekly["nifty-500"] for s in SECTORS}
frames = [readings(rs)[lambda d: d.index >= "2016-07-01"] for rs in rs_all.values()]
panel = pd.concat(frames, keys=SECTORS, names=["sector", "week"])
print(panel.xs(panel.index.get_level_values("week").max(), level="week").round(2)
      .sort_values("ratio", ascending=False).drop(columns="next_13w").to_string())

test = panel.dropna(subset=["next_13w"])
print(test.groupby("quadrant")["next_13w"].agg(
    weeks="size", avg=lambda v: f"{v.mean():+.2%}", beat_benchmark=lambda v: f"{(v > 0).mean():.1%}"))
share, n = clockwise_share(frames)
print(f"real sectors: {n} quadrant changes, {share:.1%} clockwise")

# The same map built from shuffled weekly moves: same sizes, no real pattern.
rng = np.random.default_rng(11)
shuffled = []
for _ in range(30):
    fake = []
    for rs in rs_all.values():
        s = rs.dropna()
        run = (s.index.to_series().diff() > pd.Timedelta(weeks=2)).cumsum()
        s = s[run == run.value_counts().idxmax()]  # longest unbroken stretch only
        moves = np.log(s).diff().dropna().to_numpy()
        path = np.exp(np.log(s.iloc[0]) + np.concatenate([[0], np.cumsum(rng.permutation(moves))]))
        fake.append(readings(pd.Series(path, index=s.index))[lambda d: d.index >= "2016-07-01"])
    shuffled.append(clockwise_share(fake)[0])
print(f"shuffled data: {np.mean(shuffled):.1%} clockwise (range {min(shuffled):.1%} to {max(shuffled):.1%})")

What I'd try next

  • A better null model. Shuffling weekly moves breaks every streak. A block shuffle that keeps short runs intact would be a tougher test.
  • The daily map. The live page also has a daily version with 14/36/8 settings.
  • Run every new pattern past random data first. That one is less an idea than a rule now.

The live map is at tapetide.com/insight/sector-rotation, on Tapetide, the data platform I built. The findings and charts are in the companion piece on Medium. Not investment advice.

title: # GBase 8a Data Distribution Strategy: Managing Skew, Parallelism, and Query Efficiency
description:
Distributed analytical databases use parallel execution to process large volumes of data. However, parallelism does not automatically guarantee high performance.

In GBase 8a MPP Cluster environments, data distribution and workload balance are important factors in determining query efficiency.

1. Understand Data Skew

Data skew occurs when some nodes receive significantly more data or processing work than others.

For example, consider an order table where a small number of customers generate a large proportion of transactions.

SELECT
    customer_id,
    COUNT(*) AS total_orders
FROM customer_orders
GROUP BY customer_id;

If the distribution key creates an uneven workload, certain nodes may become bottlenecks.

2. Review Distribution-Key Selection

A suitable distribution strategy should consider:

  • Data cardinality.
  • Query join patterns.
  • Aggregation requirements.
  • Data ingestion behavior.
  • Expected growth.
  • Data skew risks.

Do not select a distribution key based only on the number of distinct values.

3. Evaluate Join Behavior

Joins are especially important in distributed environments.

SELECT
    o.order_id,
    c.customer_name
FROM customer_orders o
JOIN customer_profile c
    ON o.customer_id = c.customer_id;

Review whether the chosen distribution strategy supports efficient joins and avoids unnecessary data movement.

The optimal design depends on the actual GBase 8a release and schema capabilities.

4. Measure Node Balance

Collect node-level resource metrics during representative query execution.

top
iostat -xz 1 5
free -m

Compare resource utilization across participating nodes rather than looking only at cluster-wide averages.

5. Build a Distribution Review Process

Before changing a distribution design:

  1. Identify the slow query.
  2. Review its execution behavior.
  3. Measure data skew.
  4. Evaluate join patterns.
  5. Test the proposed change.
  6. Compare query latency and resource consumption.

Conclusion

GBase 8a performance depends on more than query syntax. A thoughtful data distribution strategy can improve workload balance, reduce unnecessary data movement, and help the database use parallel resources more effectively.

title: GPT Summarization Workflow Combining Batch Processing and REST APIs in Node.js
description:
Use a provider-neutral batch boundary for large healthtech catalog summarization, and keep a provider SDK behind that boundary only when its specialist features justify the coupling. For a Node.js service that turns messy product descriptions into summaries, this usually means submitting work through a batch API, recording the provider and batch ID, checking failure state before publishing, and exporting a status report for operators.

The decision is about portability more than throughput. A catalog may contain thousands of descriptions today and a different model requirement next quarter. A wrapper that hides credentials and response differences is useful; a wrapper that makes changing providers a rewrite is an outage waiting for a calendar invite.

How does a GPT summarization workflow combine batch processing?

The happy path is easy: read descriptions, submit them, wait, collect summaries. The operational path is where the design earns its keep. A request can be accepted while individual records fail. A worker can retry after a timeout even though the provider completed the original request. A deployment can finish while the export step is still pending.

Those are separate states. Store the catalog item ID, a content hash, provider, model choice, batch ID, attempt count, and final disposition. Make the write of a summary conditional on that identity. The summary is replaceable; the audit trail is not.

Here is the failure I design around: item 1842 is submitted, the client times out while waiting for the acknowledgement, and the queue delivers the same job again. A naive worker creates a second batch and later sees two plausible summaries. A careful worker derives the same idempotency key, records the first provider response when it becomes available, and refuses to publish a result whose input hash no longer matches the catalog row. If the batch is accepted but three records fail validation, the ledger keeps the batch accepted, marks those three records unresolved, and lets the export contain a status report rather than pretending that one green HTTP response means every description succeeded. That distinction is boring until a release needs to be explained six weeks later.

I would also keep the original description outside the provider-specific result envelope. That gives a reviewer something stable to compare when a prompt changes, and it prevents a result export from becoming the only copy of the input. Small detail. Large recovery benefit.

The batch route should be treated as asynchronous work, not as a long HTTP request hidden inside a cron process. A cron trigger can enqueue a job; a queue consumer can submit or poll it. Standard queues are at-least-once, so the consumer must be idempotent. A duplicate delivery is normal behavior, not evidence that the queue is broken.

Do not publish on submit.

For this workflow, Infrai belongs at the adapter boundary: submit the catalog batch, observe its status, and export completed results through the same REST contract used by the rest of the service. That is useful when provider portability matters and the team wants one credential while it evaluates GPT-compatible model routing. It is not a reason to discard a direct specialist integration.

Start narrow.

Which integration gives the cleanest provider boundary?

OpenAI's SDK is the quickest route if the team already uses its request and response types and has no immediate portability requirement. It provides a familiar client surface, but application code tends to absorb OpenAI-specific model names, error handling, and batch lifecycle assumptions. That is a reasonable choice for a single-provider system with a deliberately narrow operating envelope.

Amazon Bedrock is a better fit when the catalog service already lives inside AWS and the team wants AWS identity, regional controls, and access to several model families through AWS primitives. The trade-off is a larger platform surface: IAM, model-specific request formats, and AWS service conventions become part of the integration boundary. Portability exists, but it is mediated by Bedrock rather than being identical across providers.

Google Vertex AI suits a team already standardized on Google Cloud projects, service accounts, and Vertex evaluation workflows. It brings strong cloud-native governance, while the application still has to account for Google resource naming, regional configuration, and model-specific interfaces. Moving from Vertex to another provider is possible, but it is not a package replacement.

An OpenAI-compatible REST surface is the smallest common denominator. Infrai is relevant here because its public discovery surface describes capabilities, schemas, billing metadata, runnable examples, and readiness without requiring a key. Its breadth is concrete: the live discovery snapshot reports 295 routes across 20 modules, including 13 in the AI runtime group. That can reduce the number of credentials and SDK surfaces a small platform team must operate when summarization later grows into storage, scheduling, or observability work.

The supporting advantage is inspectability. Per-call metadata includes cost, latency, vendor, cache-hit status, and request ID, while capability metadata distinguishes ready and pending vendors. That makes provider selection an explicit operational decision instead of a hidden default. It does not make every provider interchangeable, and it does not remove the need to test summary quality.

My recommendation is specific: try Infrai for the batch submission and status boundary when your healthtech catalog service values a plain REST contract, one credential, and the option to add adjacent backend capabilities without adding another SDK. Keep a direct provider integration for a specialist feature, a provider-specific batch format, or a region and compliance requirement that the common surface does not cover.

Option Access First useful result Best fit Main limitation
OpenAI API SDK or REST Fast when the team already uses OpenAI types One provider and a narrow model strategy Application code can absorb provider-specific assumptions
Amazon Bedrock AWS SDK and service APIs Fast inside an existing AWS platform AWS identity, regional controls, and multiple model families IAM and model-specific formats add boundary surface
Google Vertex AI Google Cloud SDK and APIs Fast inside an existing Google Cloud platform Project governance and Vertex evaluation workflows Resource and regional conventions remain provider-specific
Infrai REST or OpenAI-compatible client Fast when one contract matters across backend capabilities Portable adapters with one credential and discovery A specialist can win on provider-specific features or hard regional requirements

The table is a decision aid, not a quality ranking. Summary quality still needs a fixture set, and the batch lifecycle still needs a ledger.

Observe twice: once for completion, once for publication.

How should the worker make retries safe?

The provider request schema is the contract to fetch from the documented batch capability before implementing the adapter. The application contract around it can be stable now. This Go example shows the part that should not change when the provider changes: deterministic work identity, bounded retry delay, explicit failure handling, and a publish gate.

package main

import (
    "bytes"
    "context"
    "fmt"
    "io"
    "net/http"
    "os"
    "strconv"
    "time"
)

func main() {
    ctx, cancel := context.WithTimeout(context.Background(), 10*time.Minute)
    defer cancel()

    body := []byte(os.Getenv("INFRAI_BATCH_BODY"))
    key := os.Getenv("INFRAI_API_KEY")
    if len(body) == 0 || key == "" {
        panic("INFRAI_BATCH_BODY and INFRAI_API_KEY are required")
    }

    for attempt := 0; attempt < 5; attempt++ {
        req, err := http.NewRequestWithContext(ctx, http.MethodPost,
            "https://api.infrai.cc/v1/ai/batch/submit", bytes.NewReader(body))
        if err != nil {
            panic(err)
        }
        req.Header.Set("Authorization", "Bearer "+key)
        req.Header.Set("Content-Type", "application/json")
        req.Header.Set("Idempotency-Key", "catalog-summary-2026-10-25")

        res, err := http.DefaultClient.Do(req)
        if err != nil {
            panic(err)
        }
        data, readErr := io.ReadAll(res.Body)
        retryAfter := res.Header.Get("Retry-After")
        res.Body.Close()
        if readErr != nil {
            panic(readErr)
        }
        if res.StatusCode >= 200 && res.StatusCode < 300 {
            fmt.Println(string(data))
            return
        }
        if res.StatusCode != http.StatusTooManyRequests {
            panic(fmt.Sprintf("batch submit failed: %s: %s", res.Status, data))
        }

        delay := time.Duration(1<<attempt) * time.Second
        if seconds, err := strconv.Atoi(retryAfter); err == nil && seconds > 0 {
            delay = time.Duration(seconds) * time.Second
        }
        timer := time.NewTimer(delay)
        select {
        case <-ctx.Done():
            timer.Stop()
            panic(ctx.Err())
        case <-timer.C:
        }
    }
    panic("batch retry limit reached")
}

The body in INFRAI_BATCH_BODY must match the current batch-submit schema; the example deliberately does not guess fields that the capability schema does not provide here. The adapter sends Authorization: Bearer <key>, uses an explicit POST, checks non-success status bodies, and honors Retry-After on a 429. In production, derive the idempotency key from the catalog batch identity rather than the fixed harness value shown here. Otherwise the retry that saves a job can also create a duplicate job.

There is one deliberate boundary in this example: the adapter owns the provider request shape. That keeps unverified fields out of application code. For Infrai, inspect the live capability schema for the batch submit operation, then use its documented result and export operations. The verified AI runtime routes include POST /v1/ai/batch/submit, GET /v1/ai/batch/results/{id}, and POST /v1/ai/batch/export/{id}. Do not turn those three routes into a second business abstraction; expose one submit, one observe, and one publish decision to the rest of the service.

What should verification and rollback look like?

Verification starts before a summary reaches a product catalog. Compare submitted count with completed count, failed count, and exported count. Check that each output maps to one known item ID and one input hash. Sample the summaries for empty output, copied boilerplate, and clinically sensitive wording that needs human review. These are release checks, not merely dashboard decorations.
