Export a status report even when the batch has failures. A partial report lets an operator retry only unresolved items; a single opaque "batch failed" status encourages resubmitting everything. The latter is how duplicate work and confusing audit histories accumulate.

Rollback should mean stopping publication and retaining the raw inputs and provider result, not deleting evidence. Mark the affected batch as withheld, route failed records to a review queue, and resume from the last item whose identity and content hash have been verified. If the provider changes, replay a small fixture set through both adapters before moving the catalog cursor.

For scheduled work, cap a cron trigger at 900 seconds and hand longer processing to a queue worker. Keep queue delays at or below 604800 seconds and retention at or below 30 days. Those limits force a useful design question: what is the durable source of truth after the queue message expires? The answer should be the batch ledger, not an operator's memory.

The specialist wins when it offers a capability your common boundary cannot express, or when its regional, governance, or quality controls are a hard requirement. The portable boundary wins when the main risk is integration friction: credential sprawl, incompatible SDKs, hidden retry behavior, and a painful provider change. For a healthtech catalog, that is a meaningful decision rule.

If this boundary fits the system, start with the Infrai API discovery documentation and verify the batch schema before writing the adapter.

References

  • Infrai API discovery
  • Cohere Rerank overview
  • OpenAI API documentation
  • Amazon Bedrock documentation
  • Vertex AI documentation

title: drizzle-kit migrate fails with "relation users already exists" after push
description:
TL;DR

drizzle-kit migrate fails on its very first file with relation "users" already exists when the tables were created by drizzle-kit push. Push compares your schema with the database and changes the database directly. It never writes to Drizzle's migration log, drizzle.__drizzle_migrations. migrate reads only that log, finds it empty, and replays 0000_*.sql from the top.

Do not add IF NOT EXISTS to the files. Insert a row into the log for the newest migration the database already matches, using the file's sha256 and its when value from the journal. migrate then skips everything up to that point and applies only what is new. After that, use one workflow per database: push or generate + migrate, never both.

The error

The report is drizzle-orm issue #2825, on SQLite (Turso). The reporter generated a migration, ran drizzle-kit push, changed the schema, generated again and pushed again. Then everything failed "with an error that the table already exists", and the reporter asked for IF NOT EXISTS in the generated CREATE TABLE. A Drizzle maintainer closed it with the answer that matters: drizzle-kit push "is not applying any migrations. It will just find the difference between your schema and database and apply those. To apply all generated migrations you should use drizzle-kit migrate".

The reproduction ran the sequence the maintainer points to, push and then migrate, on PostgreSQL. It used drizzle-kit 0.31.11 and drizzle-orm 0.45.4 on Windows 11 with Node v26.7.0. The database was PGlite 0.5.13, which is PostgreSQL 18.6 compiled to WebAssembly and run in-process (driver: "pglite" in drizzle.config.ts), not a PostgreSQL server. The reporter's own sequence, push twice with a generate in between, completed without any error there: the second push simply added the new column. That matches the maintainer's statement that push applies no migration files. The failure came from migrate. push created users from the first schema, a second generate wrote ALTER TABLE "users" ADD COLUMN "email_verified", and then drizzle-kit migrate ran:

$ npx drizzle-kit migrate
No config path provided, using default 'drizzle.config.ts'
Reading config file '<app>\drizzle.config.ts'
[⣷] applying migrations...[⣷] applying migrations...exit=1

The CLI printed only its spinner and exited with code 1. That silence is a separate drizzle-kit behaviour, covered in the page on drizzle-kit migrate stopping with no error. To see the database error, call the same migrator from a script (migrate() from drizzle-orm/pglite/migrator here; use drizzle-orm/node-postgres/migrator for pg):

$ node migrate.mjs
migration failed: relation "users" already exists (SQLSTATE 42P07)
exit=1

Why migrate replays your first migration

The two commands keep state in different places. The drizzle-kit push docs describe push as reading your schema, introspecting the database, generating the SQL for the difference and applying it. No migration file and no log row are involved. The drizzle-kit migrate docs describe the other side: migrate fetches entries from the migrations log table, then "Based on previously applied migrations it will decide which new migrations to run". By default that table is __drizzle_migrations in the drizzle schema.

The decision itself is short. In pg-core/dialect.ts at drizzle-orm 0.45.4, the migrator creates the schema and the log table if missing, outside any transaction. Then it reads one row: order by created_at desc limit 1. Inside a transaction it runs every journal entry whose when is greater than that row's created_at, or every entry when the table is empty. The hash comes from migrator.ts, a sha256 of the .sql file. It is stored but never compared.

On a database built by push, there is no log yet. The reproduction checked right after the failure:

$ node q.mjs select id, hash, created_at from drizzle.__drizzle_migrations
[]
exit=0
$ node q.mjs select column_name from information_schema.columns where table_name = 'users' order by ordinal_position
[{"column_name":"id"},{"column_name":"email"}]
exit=0

The log table now exists, because it was created before the transaction, and it is empty. users is untouched, because the failed transaction rolled back.

Two controls confirm the mechanism. On an empty database, migrate alone applied both files and wrote two rows. A second run changed nothing. The generated files themselves are fine. And a second push after generate added email_verified directly. Afterwards drizzle.__drizzle_migrations did not exist at all (relation "drizzle.__drizzle_migrations" does not exist (SQLSTATE 42P01)), so push never reads or writes the migrations folder's history.

Fix: baseline the migrations the database already has

The idea is the same as supabase migration repair --status applied, which the Supabase db push page uses after a 42P07: record a migration as applied without running it. Drizzle has no command for this, so you write the row yourself. Back up the database first if it holds data you care about.

1. Find the newest migration the database already matches

Open each file in drizzle/ in order and compare it with the live database. In the reproduction, the database had id and email but no email_verified. It matched 0000 and not 0001. If push ran after your latest generate, the database usually matches the last file.

2. Read that migration's when and compute its hash

when is in drizzle/meta/_journal.json:

{
  "idx": 0,
  "version": "7",
  "when": 1793381648727,
  "tag": "0000_zippy_giant_girl",
  "breakpoints": true
}

The hash is the sha256 of the file, exactly as the migrator computes it:

node -e 'console.log(require("crypto").createHash("sha256").update(require("fs").readFileSync(process.argv[1])).digest("hex"))' drizzle/0000_zippy_giant_girl.sql

3. Insert one row into the log

Run this with psql or your SQL client, with your own hash and when. The first two statements are the ones the migrator itself runs, so they are harmless if the table already exists:

CREATE SCHEMA IF NOT EXISTS drizzle;
CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS drizzle.__drizzle_migrations (
  id SERIAL PRIMARY KEY,
  hash text NOT NULL,
  created_at bigint
);
INSERT INTO drizzle.__drizzle_migrations (hash, created_at)
VALUES ('c9dc9641b6c6f4bdc644fcf1e6ea8b5fed2405ef127db1d46948f5f5800c98af', 1793381648727);

If drizzle.config.ts sets migrations.table or migrations.schema, use those names instead. The migrate docs show both options.

The SQL above is the PostgreSQL form, and only PostgreSQL was reproduced. On SQLite and Turso, as in the issue, the table has no schema prefix. It is plain __drizzle_migrations, with created_at declared numeric. The selection rule is the same: newest created_at first, then every journal entry with a later when. The source shows this in sqlite-core/dialect.ts and in the libSQL driver's libsql/migrator.ts.

4. Run migrate again 

$ npx drizzle-kit migrate
No config path provided, using default 'drizzle.config.ts'
Reading config file '<app>\drizzle.config.ts'
[⣷] applying migrations...[✓] migrations applied successfully!exit=0

Only 0001 ran. The log now holds both timestamps and the column exists:

$ node q.mjs select id, created_at from drizzle.__drizzle_migrations order by id
[{"id":1,"created_at":1793381648727},{"id":2,"created_at":1793381668028}]
exit=0
$ node q.mjs select column_name from information_schema.columns where table_name = 'users' order by ordinal_position
[{"column_name":"id"},{"column_name":"email"},{"column_name":"email_verified"}]
exit=0

If push had already applied every file, baseline only the last one. The migrator reads just the newest row, so there is no need to insert one row per file. In the reproduction, a database where push had added email_verified got a single row for 0001, created by hand together with the table. migrate then exited 0 and applied nothing.

Verify the fix

Two checks change nothing. Run drizzle-kit migrate a second time: it should exit 0 and add no row to drizzle.__drizzle_migrations. Then query the columns of each table the last migration touched, as above, and compare them with that migration's SQL.

On a development database or a copy, you can also let push compare the whole schema with the database. Run it as npx drizzle-kit push --verbose --strict. With nothing to change it stops at once, as on the baselined database in the reproduction (run there without --strict):

$ npx drizzle-kit push --verbose
No config path provided, using default 'drizzle.config.ts'
Reading config file '<app>\drizzle.config.ts'
[⣷] Pulling schema from database...
[✓] Pulling schema from database...
[i] No changes detected
exit=0

Keep --strict in that command: according to drizzle-kit push --help it makes push "Always ask for confirmation". Without it, a database that is behind does not get a report. Push prints the statements and applies them. On the database from the failing run, it added email_verified itself, which brings you back to the mixed state this page fixes. If it lists statements, decline them and finish with migrate.

When IF NOT EXISTS seems like the answer

The issue asks Drizzle to emit CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS, and a comment there links a script that rewrites the generated files with a regular expression. Drizzle removed this on purpose. The drizzle-kit 0.30.0 release notes (9 December 2024) say the PostgreSQL dialect "will no longer include IF NOT EXISTS, $DO, or similar statements, which could cause incorrect DDL statements to not fail when an object already exists in the database and should actually fail."

The reproduction shows why the rewrite only moves the failure. With CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS "users" in 0000 and an empty log, the migrator passed on the database where push had applied only the first schema. On the database where push had also added the column, it stopped at the next file:

$ node migrate.mjs ./drizzle-ine
migration failed: column "email_verified" of relation "users" already exists (SQLSTATE 42701)
exit=1

ALTER TABLE ... ADD COLUMN, constraints and foreign keys have no clause that covers every case. The rewrite also skips a table whose definition differs from the file without saying so. The baseline row records the true state and leaves the generated SQL as it is.

Keep push and migrate on separate databases

The migrations overview presents push and generate + migrate as separate options. Mixing them on one database is what creates this state. A common split is push on a throwaway local database and generate + migrate everywhere else. If a development database is already mixed and holds nothing you need, resetting it is quicker than a baseline. Dropping every table covers public, but drop the drizzle schema too, or the old log rows will make migrate skip files on the empty database. The issue itself was on Turso, where the CLI talks to SQLite. Push also has dialect-specific failures there, such as the run()/get() TypeError on libSQL.

If migrate exits 1 again after the baseline with no message, it is hitting a different SQL error. Run the migrator script to print it, as described in the silent drizzle-kit migrate page. If the error names a table you did not expect, check the log's newest created_at against the journal before you insert anything else. A row with a later timestamp than the database really has will make migrate skip work without any error.

Originally published on iloveblogs.blog. Drafted with AI assistance; the reproduction (drizzle-kit 0.31.11, drizzle-orm 0.45.4, PGlite) was run and logged before publishing.

title: Read-Only Postgres Role for AI Agents: 7 Gaps to Close
description:
A read-only Postgres role for AI agents is the right first step. It is also not enough on its own.
Most guides stop at GRANT SELECT. We ran the usual setup on PostgreSQL 16, tried to get around it the way a manipulated agent or a careless query would, and found seven places where "read-only" doesn't mean what people assume. Each one comes with the SQL to reproduce it and the fix.
Quick answer
A read-only Postgres role for an AI agent should be a dedicated login role with no superuser or BYPASSRLS, SELECT granted only on the columns the agent needs, and timeouts set. But default_transaction_read_only and statement_timeout are defaults that a session can change, a SECURITY DEFINER function can still write, and anything you grant can still be read by a manipulated agent. The real barrier is what the role is allowed to do, so grant as little as possible and never give the agent a raw SQL session.
In this post

  1. How we tested
  2. The baseline setup
  3. Gap 1: the read-only setting is a default, not a lock
  4. Gap 2: your timeout can be switched off
  5. Gap 3: a SECURITY DEFINER function can write for you
  6. Gap 4: table names stay visible
  7. Gap 5: SELECT * fails, and the error blames the table
  8. Gap 6: row-level security with no policy returns nothing
  9. Gap 7: everything you grant can be read
  10. The hardened setup in one block
  11. FAQ How we tested Everything below ran on PostgreSQL 16.15 in a clean database, with each statement sent from a normal login role. The results are copied from the terminal. Nothing needs an extension, and you can paste each block into psql and compare. The sample schema has three tables: customers, orders and secrets. The agent should reach only some columns of the first two, and nothing in the third. The baseline setup This is the setup most guides describe, plus the settings people add to make it "read-only". CREATE TABLE public.customers (id serial PRIMARY KEY, name text, email text); CREATE TABLE public.orders ( id serial PRIMARY KEY, customer_id int REFERENCES customers(id), status text, total numeric, internal_notes text ); CREATE TABLE public.secrets (id serial PRIMARY KEY, token text);

CREATE ROLE claix_agent WITH LOGIN PASSWORD 'use-a-secret-manager'
NOSUPERUSER NOCREATEDB NOCREATEROLE NOINHERIT NOREPLICATION NOBYPASSRLS;

GRANT CONNECT ON DATABASE mydb TO claix_agent;
GRANT USAGE ON SCHEMA public TO claix_agent;
GRANT SELECT (id, name) ON public.customers TO claix_agent;
GRANT SELECT (id, customer_id, status, total) ON public.orders TO claix_agent;

ALTER ROLE claix_agent SET default_transaction_read_only = on;
ALTER ROLE claix_agent SET statement_timeout = '2s';

Two things to avoid at this stage. Don't use GRANT SELECT ON ALL TABLES, which also covers tables you didn't mean to expose. And don't use the built-in pg_read_all_data role for an agent: it grants read access to every table in the database, which is far more than an agent needs.
Gap 1: the read-only setting is a default, not a lock
The assumption: default_transaction_read_only = on means the role can't write.
What happens: it means new transactions start read-only. The session can change that. To see it, we made a second role that does have INSERT and the same read-only default:
INSERT INTO orders(customer_id, status, total) VALUES (1, 'x', 1);
ERROR: cannot execute INSERT in a read-only transaction

SET default_transaction_read_only = off;
INSERT INTO orders(customer_id, status, total) VALUES (1, 'x', 1);
-- succeeded
The same happened with BEGIN READ ONLY; followed by SET TRANSACTION READ WRITE; as the first statement: the write went through.
What stopped the write in the real agent role was something else. After SET default_transaction_read_only = off;, an INSERT from claix_agent failed with:
ERROR: permission denied for table orders
The fix: treat the setting as a safety net and the privileges as the barrier. Grant SELECT only. If you can, connect the agent to a read replica, because a standby server rejects writes whatever the session sets (we didn't test this one).
Gap 2: your timeout can be switched off
The assumption: ALTER ROLE ... SET statement_timeout = '2s' caps every query.
What happens: it sets the starting value. The session can raise it or remove it:
SHOW statement_timeout;
2s

SELECT pg_sleep(3);
ERROR: canceling statement due to statement timeout

SET statement_timeout = 0;
SELECT pg_sleep(3);
-- ran to completion
The fix: the timeout protects you only if the agent can't send a SET. So never give the agent a raw SQL session. Your code should run a single validated SELECT, set the limits itself for each transaction (SET LOCAL statement_timeout = '5s') and add its own timeout around the call. A pooler or proxy that cancels long queries is a second layer, and you should check its documentation for the exact setting.
Gap 3: a SECURITY DEFINER function can write for you
The assumption: a role with only SELECT can't change data.
What happens: functions declared SECURITY DEFINER run with the privileges of their owner, and by default Postgres lets everyone execute functions. We created one that inserts into secrets, a table claix_agent can't touch:
CREATE FUNCTION public.archive_orders() RETURNS void
LANGUAGE sql SECURITY DEFINER AS $$
INSERT INTO public.secrets(token) VALUES ('written-by-function')
$$;
With the read-only default on, the call failed. After the session switched it off (gap 1), it worked, and secrets went from one row to two.
The fix: find these functions and remove public execute access from the ones that write:
SELECT p.oid::regprocedure
FROM pg_proc p JOIN pg_namespace n ON n.oid = p.pronamespace
WHERE n.nspname = 'public' AND p.prosecdef;

REVOKE EXECUTE ON FUNCTION public.archive_orders() FROM PUBLIC;
After the revoke, the same call returned permission denied for function archive_orders. Give EXECUTE back to the roles that need it. You can also run ALTER DEFAULT PRIVILEGES IN SCHEMA public REVOKE EXECUTE ON FUNCTIONS FROM PUBLIC; so that future functions aren't public by default, but that affects every function created afterwards by the same role, so check your application first.
Gap 4: table names stay visible
The assumption: if the role can't read a table, it can't see it.
What happens: it can't read the contents, but the catalog still lists the name:
SELECT tablename FROM pg_tables WHERE schemaname = 'public';
customers
orders
secrets

SELECT table_name FROM information_schema.tables WHERE table_schema = 'public';
customers
orders

SELECT * FROM secrets;
ERROR: permission denied for table secrets
information_schema shows only what the role has privileges on. pg_catalog shows everything.
The fix: don't put anything sensitive in a table or column name. And when you build the description of your schema for an agent, read it with the agent's own role through information_schema, so the agent is told about the tables it can use and nothing else.
Gap 5: SELECT * fails, and the error blames the table
The assumption: with a column-level grant, SELECT * returns the allowed columns.
What happens: it fails, and the message names the table, not the column:
SELECT * FROM orders;
ERROR: permission denied for table orders

SELECT id, status, total FROM orders ORDER BY id LIMIT 2;
1|shipped|10
2|pending|20

SELECT internal_notes FROM orders;
ERROR: permission denied for table orders
That is useful: an agent can't get a column you didn't grant by accident. It is also confusing when you debug, because the table looks denied even though only one column is.
The fix: make your agent list its columns, and reject SELECT * in your validator so the failure is a clear message from your code and not a database error. A view with only the safe columns is a simple alternative:
CREATE VIEW public.order_status WITH (security_invoker = true) AS
SELECT id, status FROM public.orders;

GRANT SELECT ON public.order_status TO claix_agent;
The security_invoker option (PostgreSQL 15 and later) makes the view use the privileges and row-level security of the caller, not the view's owner.
Gap 6: row-level security with no policy returns nothing
The assumption: enabling row-level security on a table limits what the agent sees.
What happens: if the role is not the owner and no policy applies to it, it sees zero rows. That fails safe, and it looks like an empty table:
ALTER TABLE public.customers ENABLE ROW LEVEL SECURITY;

SELECT count(*) FROM customers; -- as claix_agent
0

CREATE POLICY agent_read ON public.customers FOR SELECT TO claix_agent USING (true);

SELECT count(*) FROM customers;
2
The fix: if you use row-level security, write a policy for the agent role with the narrowest condition that works, and check that the role is not the table owner and does not have BYPASSRLS. If an agent suddenly "finds nothing", look at the policies first.
Gap 7: everything you grant can be read
The assumption: once the role is read-only, the data is safe.
What happens: a read-only role protects what it can't reach. It doesn't protect what you gave it. Instructions hidden in a user message, a document or a database field can change what an agent asks for, and the role will answer any query for data it was granted. Supabase's own documentation names prompt injection as the main risk of connecting an agent to your data, and says its MCP server is designed for development and testing.
A role also can't tell a useful query from a pointless or expensive one, or a correct query from one that is valid and wrong, and it doesn't separate one person's rows from another's.
The fix: grant less, and add layers outside the database:
• Validate every query with a real SQL parser before it runs: one SELECT, approved tables, an allowlist of functions.
• Add a row limit, a timeout and a cost check.
• Treat query results as untrusted data.
• Log every request: the question, the query and the result.
• Keep per-user rules in row-level security or in your application.
The hardened setup in one block
This is the baseline plus the fixes that belong in the database. We ran the whole block on a clean cluster and checked that granted columns work and others don't.
-- 1. A dedicated role, not your app user and not postgres
CREATE ROLE claix_agent WITH LOGIN PASSWORD 'use-a-secret-manager'
NOSUPERUSER NOCREATEDB NOCREATEROLE NOINHERIT NOREPLICATION NOBYPASSRLS
CONNECTION LIMIT 10;
GRANT CONNECT ON DATABASE mydb TO claix_agent;
GRANT USAGE ON SCHEMA public TO claix_agent;

-- 2. Columns, not whole tables
GRANT SELECT (id, name) ON public.customers TO claix_agent;
GRANT SELECT (id, customer_id, status, total) ON public.orders TO claix_agent;

-- 3. Guardrails (defaults the session can change)
ALTER ROLE claix_agent SET default_transaction_read_only = on;
ALTER ROLE claix_agent SET statement_timeout = '5s';
ALTER ROLE claix_agent SET idle_in_transaction_session_timeout = '10s';

-- 4. Find functions that run with their owner's privileges
SELECT p.oid::regprocedure AS security_definer_function
FROM pg_proc p JOIN pg_namespace n ON n.oid = p.pronamespace
WHERE n.nspname = 'public' AND p.prosecdef;

-- 5. Remove public execute access from any that write
REVOKE EXECUTE ON FUNCTION public.archive_orders() FROM PUBLIC;
-- GRANT EXECUTE ON FUNCTION public.archive_orders() TO app_user;
Then add what a database role can't: validation, limits, logging, and a controlled way for the agent to ask.
Where Claix fits
Claix is a managed service between your agent and your database. You connect Postgres or Supabase with a read-only role like the one above, choose the tables and columns each agent can use, and write a short guide with your rules. Your agent sends questions to its own endpoint and gets typed answers back, so it never holds a database connection or sends raw SQL. Every request is traced.
It doesn't replace the role. Claix connects with a role like this one, and what that role can read is still the ceiling. You can try it in the Sandbox and read the docs at claix.dev.
FAQ
Is a read-only user enough to secure a database for an AI agent? No. It is the first layer. A session can change settings such as default_transaction_read_only and statement_timeout, a SECURITY DEFINER function can still write, and a manipulated agent can read anything you granted. Add query validation, limits and logging.
How do I create a read-only user in Postgres? Create a login role without superuser or BYPASSRLS, grant CONNECT on the database and USAGE on the schema, and grant SELECT only on the tables or columns it needs. The block in this post does that.
Can a read-only Postgres user still modify data? It can if it can call a SECURITY DEFINER function that writes, or if the session lifts the read-only default and the role has write privileges. With only SELECT privileges and no public execute access to writing functions, it can't.
How do I limit an AI agent to certain columns in Postgres? Use column-level grants, such as GRANT SELECT (id, status) ON orders TO claix_agent, or expose a view with only the safe columns.
Should an AI agent connect to a read replica? It is a good extra layer, because a standby server rejects writes whatever the session sets, and it keeps heavy queries away from your main database. It doesn't replace limiting what the role can read.
Does this work on Supabase? Yes. Supabase is Postgres, so the same SQL works in its SQL editor. Supabase's MCP server has a read-only option that runs queries as a read-only Postgres user, and its documentation says the server is designed for development and testing.
How do I stop an AI agent's long-running queries? Set a statement_timeout for the role, set it again in your code for every transaction, and make sure the agent can't send SET statements. A pooler or proxy that cancels long queries adds another layer.
Sources and further reading
• PostgreSQL documentation, GRANT: https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/sql-grant.html
• PostgreSQL documentation, CREATE FUNCTION and SECURITY DEFINER: https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/sql-createfunction.html
• PostgreSQL documentation, client connection defaults: https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/runtime-config-client.html
• PostgreSQL documentation, row security policies: https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/ddl-rowsecurity.html
• PostgreSQL documentation, predefined roles: https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/predefined-roles.html
• Supabase documentation, MCP server: https://supabase.com/docs/guides/getting-started/mcp
SEO notes (not part of the post)
Why this angle. I searched the main phrase, how to connect an AI agent to a database safely, and the results are crowded: a dev.to post from September 2026 on giving an agent safe, read-only access, a hoop.dev guide, an Airbyte guide on connection patterns, Microsoft's SQL MCP Server documentation and several open-source projects. A generic how-to would compete with all of them. This post targets a narrower phrase with the same intent, read-only Postgres role for AI agents, and brings something those results don't: tested results, with the SQL to reproduce them. That is your best chance to rank and to be linked. I can't give you search volumes, so check the phrase in a keyword tool before you commit.
Keyword placement
Element
What it contains
Title
Read-Only Postgres Role for AI Agents (primary keyword first)
First sentence
The primary keyword, with a clear claim
Description (front matter)
Primary keyword and the numbers 7 and PostgreSQL 16
Quick answer
A direct answer in about 90 words, for featured snippets and answer engines
H2 headings
Each gap, plus FAQ questions in the words people use
Secondary keywords
AI agent database access, Postgres read-only user, default_transaction_read_only, statement_timeout, SECURITY DEFINER, row-level security, Supabase, MCP, prompt injection
Tags
postgres, ai, security, database (dev.to allows four

title: Test Step Functions with the TestState API
description:
For a long time, I treated the question of how to test Step Functions as something for “later”. You check the happy path anyway, because you see it while trying things out. The Retry and Catch blocks, however, are a piece of JSON that only really runs for the first time when something goes wrong in production. That is exactly the wrong place to find out that an error name has a typo.

With the TestState API, there is now a tool I would use in every Step Functions project. It lets you test a single state of your state machine in the cloud without deploying it. Since mocks are supported, you do not even need real Lambda functions or an IAM role. In this article, we build the whole thing with a small example: a bike rental with a retry for throttling, a catch for “no bike available” and tests with node:test in TypeScript.

In short

The TestState API runs exactly one state of your Step Functions definition and reports whether it succeeded, would be retried or ends up in a catch. With mocked results and errors, you can test retry and catch paths in a targeted way, without a deployment and without an IAM role. The biggest pitfall: the API only ever tests one state, so for a run through the whole machine with real permissions you also need a short test after deployment.

What you will learn in this article

  • What the TestState API can do and where its limits are
  • How to check retry, backoff and catch with mocked errors
  • How tests and the CDK stack share the same ASL file
  • Which guardrail tests run without any AWS access
  • Which typical mistakes happen when testing

Why teams rarely test Step Functions properly

AWS Step Functions is the orchestration service of AWS. You describe a workflow as a state machine in the Amazon States Language (ASL), a JSON format, and Step Functions runs the steps, waits, branches and retries. This is practical, because error handling lives declaratively in the definition instead of being scattered across code. However, that is also where the testing problem starts.

A Retry block is configuration. For example, it says: on Lambda.TooManyRequestsException, try three times, start with a two second pause and double the wait each time. Whether the error names are right, whether the order of the catchers fits and whether the error ends up in the right next state is something you will not notice during normal testing. After all, the error case simply does not happen.

For years, the answer was Step Functions Local, an emulator in a Docker container. AWS now states very clearly in the documentation that Step Functions Local does not provide feature parity and is unsupported. Instead, AWS explicitly recommends the TestState API. That matches my view: an emulator that lags behind the real service creates false confidence. A test against the real execution logic in the cloud is more honest.

What the TestState API does

The TestState API takes an ASL definition and runs exactly one state. You either pass only that single state or the complete state machine plus the name of the state in the stateName field. No state machine is created or changed. In response, you get the status, the output, the next state and, if you ask for it, details about data processing.

The four statuses at a glance

The status is the heart of your tests. It tells you what Step Functions would do with the result of the state:

Status Meaning Typical test
SUCCEEDED The state completed, nextState names the following state. Happy path, shaping data with ResultSelector and ResultPath
RETRIABLE The error matches a retrier and attempts are left. Throttling, short service errors
CAUGHT_ERROR A catcher handled the error. Business errors, exhausted retries
FAILED Neither retry nor catch apply, the execution would fail. Spotting missing error handling

With inspectionLevel, you control the level of detail. INFO is the default and only returns the result. With DEBUG, you also see the intermediate values after InputPath, Parameters, ResultSelector and ResultPath, and in case of an error the fields retryIndex, retryBackoffIntervalSeconds and catchIndex. TRACE adds the full HTTP request and response for HTTP tasks.

Mocks instead of real Lambda calls

The most important building block is the mock field. For Task, Map or Parallel states, it lets you provide either a result (mock.result) or an error (mock.errorOutput with error and cause). Both at once are not allowed. As soon as a mock is set, roleArn becomes optional according to the documentation. You then test pure workflow logic, and no service is called at all.

In addition, Step Functions validates the mock against the API model of the service. With fieldValidationMode, you choose how strict this is: STRICT (default) checks names, types and required fields, PRESENT only checks the fields in the mock, and NONE turns validation off. I would stay with STRICT, because a mock that can never exist in reality tests nothing.

For retry tests, there is also stateConfiguration.retrierRetryCount. It simulates how many retries have already happened for the matching retrier. For Map and Parallel states, errorCausedByState names the inner state the error came from.

Fast and cheap on the left, realistic on the right: each layer catches different mistakes.

The example: a bike rental with retry and catch

As an example, we take renting a bike, a deliberately small, fictional domain. The state machine first checks whether the rider is verified. After that, a Lambda function reserves a bike at the station, and a second function unlocks it. Two kinds of errors are interesting:

  • Throttling by Lambda (Lambda.TooManyRequestsException) is temporary and should be retried with backoff.
  • The business error BikeUnavailable (“no bike available”) should not be retried, but lead directly to a hint about another station.

Everything else ends up in the RentalFailed state via States.ALL. The placeholders ${ReserveBikeFunctionArn} and ${UnlockBikeFunctionArn} are replaced by CloudFormation through DefinitionSubstitutions on deployment, while the tests replace them with dummy ARNs. This way, tests and infrastructure share the same file.

{
  "Comment": "Bike rental: check rider, reserve bike, unlock bike",
  "StartAt": "CheckRider",
  "States": {
    "CheckRider": {
      "Type": "Choice",
      "Choices": [
        { "Variable": "$.rider.verified", "BooleanEquals": true, "Next": "ReserveBike" }
      ],
      "Default": "RejectRental"
    },
    "ReserveBike": {
      "Type": "Task",
      "Resource": "arn:aws:states:::lambda:invoke",
      "Parameters": {
        "FunctionName": "${ReserveBikeFunctionArn}",
        "Payload.$": "$"
      },
      "ResultSelector": { "reservationId.$": "$.Payload.reservationId" },
      "ResultPath": "$.reservation",
      "Retry": [
        {
          "ErrorEquals": ["Lambda.TooManyRequestsException", "Lambda.ServiceException"],
          "IntervalSeconds": 2,
          "MaxAttempts": 3,
          "BackoffRate": 2
        }
      ],
      "Catch": [
        { "ErrorEquals": ["BikeUnavailable"], "ResultPath": "$.error", "Next": "OfferOtherStation" },
        { "ErrorEquals": ["States.ALL"], "ResultPath": "$.error", "Next": "RentalFailed" }
      ],
      "Next": "UnlockBike"
    },
    "UnlockBike": {
      "Type": "Task",
      "Resource": "arn:aws:states:::lambda:invoke",
      "Parameters": {
        "FunctionName": "${UnlockBikeFunctionArn}",
        "Payload.$": "$"
      },
      "ResultPath": null,
      "Retry": [
        {
          "ErrorEquals": ["Lambda.TooManyRequestsException", "Lambda.ServiceException"],
          "IntervalSeconds": 1,
          "MaxAttempts": 2,
          "BackoffRate": 2
        }
      ],
      "Catch": [
        { "ErrorEquals": ["States.ALL"], "ResultPath": "$.error", "Next": "RentalFailed" }
      ],
      "End": true
    },
    "OfferOtherStation": {
      "Type": "Pass",
      "Parameters": {
        "status": "NO_BIKE",
        "stationId.$": "$.stationId",
        "hint": "Try a nearby station"
      },
      "End": true
    },
    "RejectRental": {
      "Type": "Fail",
      "Error": "RiderNotVerified",
      "Cause": "The rider has not been verified yet"
    },
    "RentalFailed": {
      "Type": "Fail",
      "Error": "RentalFailed",
      "Cause": "Reservation or unlock failed"
    }
  }
}

One detail that is often overlooked: States.ALL must always be the last catcher. Step Functions checks the catchers in order, so an early catch-all would swallow the specific BikeUnavailable case. We will check exactly that automatically in a moment.

🎬 How a TestState test runs – this animated diagram only runs on my site: watch it on sascha-ms.de

How to test Step Functions step by step with TypeScript

Now let us build the tests. I use the built-in test runner of Node.js (node:test) and the AWS SDK for JavaScript v3. Node.js 22.18 and later runs TypeScript files directly as long as they only contain type annotations. So the tests need no extra build step.

Prerequisites

You need Node.js 22.18 or later, an AWS account with credentials on the command line (for example via aws sso login) and the AWS CDK for deployment. The identity you test with needs the states:TestState permission. For tests without a mock, you also need iam:PassRole for the execution role.

Step 1: Create the project 

mkdir bike-rental && cd bike-rental
npm init -y
npm pkg set type=module
npm install @aws-sdk/client-sfn aws-cdk-lib constructs
npm install -D typescript @types/node aws-cdk esbuild
mkdir statemachine src test lib bin

Then save the ASL file from above as statemachine/bike-rental.asl.json. The tsconfig.json is only used for type checking, which is why noEmit is set to true:

{
  "compilerOptions": {
    "target": "ES2022",
    "module": "nodenext",
    "moduleResolution": "nodenext",
    "strict": true,
    "noEmit": true,
    "allowImportingTsExtensions": true,
    "verbatimModuleSyntax": true,
    "types": ["node"],
    "skipLibCheck": true
  },
  "include": ["bin", "lib", "src", "test"]
}

Step 2: Guardrail tests without AWS access

Before we ask the cloud, a quick look at the structure pays off. These tests run completely offline and finish in milliseconds. They check rules I want to see in every review: every Lambda task retries throttling, has a catch-all, and that catch-all comes last. In addition, all transitions point to existing states.

// test/asl-guardrails.test.ts
import { test } from "node:test";
import assert from "node:assert/strict";
import { loadDefinition } from "./test-state.ts";

interface AslState {
  Type: string;
  Resource?: string;
  Retry?: { ErrorEquals: string[]; MaxAttempts?: number }[];
  Catch?: { ErrorEquals: string[]; Next: string }[];
  Next?: string;
  Default?: string;
  Choices?: { Next: string }[];
}

const definition = JSON.parse(loadDefinition()) as { StartAt: string; States: Record<string, AslState> };
const states = Object.entries(definition.States);

test("every Lambda task retries throttling and has a catch-all", () => {
  for (const [name, state] of states.filter(([, s]) => s.Type === "Task")) {
    const retried = (state.Retry ?? []).flatMap((r) => r.ErrorEquals);
    assert.ok(retried.includes("Lambda.TooManyRequestsException"), `${name}: Retry for throttling is missing`);
    const caught = (state.Catch ?? []).flatMap((c) => c.ErrorEquals);
    assert.ok(caught.includes("States.ALL"), `${name}: Catch with States.ALL is missing`);
  }
});

test("States.ALL is always the last catcher", () => {
  for (const [name, state] of states) {
    const catchers = state.Catch ?? [];
    const index = catchers.findIndex((c) => c.ErrorEquals.includes("States.ALL"));
    if (index >= 0) assert.equal(index, catchers.length - 1, `${name}: States.ALL must come last`);
  }
});

test("every transition points to an existing state", () => {
  const known = new Set(Object.keys(definition.States));
  assert.ok(known.has(definition.StartAt));
  for (const [name, state] of states) {
    const targets = [state.Next, state.Default, ...(state.Choices ?? []).map((c) => c.Next), ...(state.Catch ?? []).map((c) => c.Next)];
    for (const target of targets.filter(Boolean)) {
      assert.ok(known.has(target as string), `${name}: unknown target ${target}`);
    }
  }
});

test("all placeholders are replaced", () => {
  assert.doesNotMatch(loadDefinition(), /\$\{\w+\}/);
});

Step 3: A small helper for the TestState API

The helper loads the definition, replaces the placeholders and calls TestStateCommand. Without a mock, it requires a role from the SFN_TEST_ROLE_ARN environment variable, so nobody calls real Lambda functions by accident.

// test/test-state.ts
import { readFileSync } from "node:fs";
import { SFNClient, TestStateCommand, type TestStateCommandOutput } from "@aws-sdk/client-sfn";

const client = new SFNClient({});

// Replace the CDK placeholders with dummy ARNs, just like DefinitionSubstitutions does on deploy.
const placeholders: Record<string, string> = {
  ReserveBikeFunctionArn: "arn:aws:lambda:eu-central-1:123456789012:function:reserve-bike",
  UnlockBikeFunctionArn: "arn:aws:lambda:eu-central-1:123456789012:function:unlock-bike",
};

export function loadDefinition(file = "statemachine/bike-rental.asl.json"): string {
  const raw = readFileSync(file, "utf8");
  return raw.replace(/\$\{(\w+)\}/g, (match, key: string) => placeholders[key] ?? match);
}

export const hasAwsCredentials = Boolean(
  process.env.AWS_PROFILE || process.env.AWS_ACCESS_KEY_ID || process.env.AWS_WEB_IDENTITY_TOKEN_FILE,
);

export interface RunOptions {
  input: unknown;
  mockResult?: unknown;
  mockError?: { error: string; cause: string };
  retrierRetryCount?: number;
}

// Runs exactly one state of the full definition via the TestState API.
export async function runState(stateName: string, opts: RunOptions): Promise<TestStateCommandOutput> {
  const mocked = opts.mockResult !== undefined || opts.mockError !== undefined;
  const roleArn = process.env.SFN_TEST_ROLE_ARN;
  if (!mocked && !roleArn) {
    throw new Error(`State ${stateName} is tested without a mock: please set SFN_TEST_ROLE_ARN`);
  }
  return client.send(
    new TestStateCommand({
      definition: loadDefinition(),
      stateName,
      input: JSON.stringify(opts.input),
      inspectionLevel: "DEBUG",
      roleArn: mocked ? undefined : roleArn,
      mock: mocked
        ? {
            result: opts.mockResult !== undefined ? JSON.stringify(opts.mockResult) : undefined,
            errorOutput: opts.mockError,
          }
        : undefined,
      stateConfiguration:
        opts.retrierRetryCount !== undefined ? { retrierRetryCount: opts.retrierRetryCount } : undefined,
    }),
  );
}

Step 4: Test retry and catch

Now for the actual tests. Each test simulates a result or an error of the Lambda function and checks what Step Functions does with it. The second test is my favourite: it recalculates the backoff. With IntervalSeconds 2, BackoffRate 2 and one retry already done, the next pause is 2 × 2¹ = 4 seconds. This calculation matches the example in the AWS documentation.

// test/reserve-bike.test.ts
import { test } from "node:test";
import assert from "node:assert/strict";
import { hasAwsCredentials, runState } from "./test-state.ts";

const input = { rentalId: "r-42", stationId: "harbour-3", rider: { id: "u-7", verified: true } };
const skip = hasAwsCredentials ? false : "no AWS credentials – TestState runs in the cloud";

test("happy path: reservation lands in $.reservation", { skip }, async () => {
  const res = await runState("ReserveBike", {
    input,
    mockResult: { StatusCode: 200, Payload: { reservationId: "res-1001" } },
  });
  assert.equal(res.status, "SUCCEEDED");
  assert.equal(res.nextState, "UnlockBike");
  assert.deepEqual(JSON.parse(res.output ?? "{}").reservation, { reservationId: "res-1001" });
});

test("throttling is retried with backoff", { skip }, async () => {
  const res = await runState("ReserveBike", {
    input,
    mockError: { error: "Lambda.TooManyRequestsException", cause: "Rate exceeded" },
    retrierRetryCount: 1,
  });
  assert.equal(res.status, "RETRIABLE");
  assert.equal(res.inspectionData?.errorDetails?.retryIndex, 0);
  // IntervalSeconds 2 x BackoffRate 2 ^ 1 retry so far = 4 seconds
  assert.equal(res.inspectionData?.errorDetails?.retryBackoffIntervalSeconds, 4);
});

test("after the last retry the catch-all takes over", { skip }, async () => {
  const res = await runState("ReserveBike", {
    input,
    mockError: { error: "Lambda.TooManyRequestsException", cause: "Rate exceeded" },
    retrierRetryCount: 3,
  });
  assert.equal(res.status, "CAUGHT_ERROR");
  assert.equal(res.nextState, "RentalFailed");
  assert.equal(res.inspectionData?.errorDetails?.catchIndex, 1);
});

test("no bike available leads to another station, without retries", { skip }, async () => {
  const res = await runState("ReserveBike", {
    input,
    mockError: { error: "BikeUnavailable", cause: "Station harbour-3 is empty" },
  });
  assert.equal(res.status, "CAUGHT_ERROR");
  assert.equal(res.nextState, "OfferOtherStation");
  const output = JSON.parse(res.output ?? "{}");
  assert.equal(output.error.Error, "BikeUnavailable");
  assert.equal(output.rentalId, "r-42");
});

test("unverified riders are rejected", { skip: hasAwsCredentials && process.env.SFN_TEST_ROLE_ARN ? false : "needs SFN_TEST_ROLE_ARN" }, async () => {
  const res = await runState("CheckRider", { input: { ...input, rider: { id: "u-8", verified: false } } });
  assert.equal(res.status, "SUCCEEDED");
  assert.equal(res.nextState, "RejectRental");
});

The Choice check in the last test has no mock, because mocks only exist for Task, Map and Parallel states. The examples in the AWS documentation pass a role for it, so this test only runs when you set SFN_TEST_ROLE_ARN. Since a Choice state calls no service, a role without further service permissions should be enough.

Step 5: Run the tests

Add the scripts to package.json and start the tests. The region matters, otherwise the SDK stops with “Region is missing”.

npm pkg set scripts.typecheck="tsc --noEmit" scripts.test="node --test test/*.test.ts"
export AWS_REGION=eu-central-1
npm run typecheck
npm test

With valid credentials, all tests run against the TestState API. Without credentials, the guardrail tests still run and the cloud tests are skipped cleanly. The expected result then looks like this:

ok 1 - every Lambda task retries throttling and has a catch-all
ok 2 - States.ALL is always the last catcher
ok 3 - every transition points to an existing state
ok 4 - all placeholders are replaced
ok 5 - happy path: reservation lands in $.reservation # SKIP no AWS credentials – TestState runs in the cloud
...
# pass 4
# fail 0
# skipped 5

Step 6: Deploy the same definition with CDK

For deployment, the CDK stack reads exactly the file the tests use. DefinitionBody.fromFile uploads it as an asset, and definitionSubstitutions inserts the real function ARNs. The Lambda functions are deliberately simple. What matters is that BikeUnavailable arrives as the error name, which is why the error class sets this.name.

// src/reserve-bike.ts
class BikeUnavailable extends Error {
  constructor(stationId: string) {
    super(`No bike available at station ${stationId}`);
    this.name = "BikeUnavailable"; // becomes the error name in Step Functions
  }
}

interface RentalRequest {
  rentalId: string;
  stationId: string;
}

// Demo stock instead of a real database
const stock: Record<string, number> = { "harbour-3": 2, "old-town-1": 0 };

export const handler = async (event: RentalRequest) => {
  const free = stock[event.stationId] ?? 0;
  if (free < 1) throw new BikeUnavailable(event.stationId);
  return { reservationId: `res-${event.rentalId}` };
};

// src/unlock-bike.ts
export const handler = async (event: { rentalId: string; reservation: { reservationId: string } }) => {
  console.log(JSON.stringify({ msg: "unlock", rentalId: event.rentalId, reservationId: event.reservation.reservationId }));
  return { unlocked: true };
};

// lib/bike-rental-stack.ts
import * as path from "node:path";
import { Duration, Stack, type StackProps } from "aws-cdk-lib";
import { Runtime } from "aws-cdk-lib/aws-lambda";
import { NodejsFunction } from "aws-cdk-lib/aws-lambda-nodejs";
import { DefinitionBody, StateMachine, StateMachineType } from "aws-cdk-lib/aws-stepfunctions";
import type { Construct } from "constructs";

export class BikeRentalStack extends Stack {
  constructor(scope: Construct, id: string, props?: StackProps) {
    super(scope, id, props);

    const common = { runtime: Runtime.NODEJS_22_X, memorySize: 256, timeout: Duration.seconds(10) };
    const reserveBike = new NodejsFunction(this, "ReserveBike", { ...common, entry: "src/reserve-bike.ts" });
    const unlockBike = new NodejsFunction(this, "UnlockBike", { ...common, entry: "src/unlock-bike.ts" });

    const rental = new StateMachine(this, "BikeRental", {
      stateMachineType: StateMachineType.STANDARD,
      // The same ASL file that the tests read
      definitionBody: DefinitionBody.fromFile(path.join("statemachine", "bike-rental.asl.json")),
      definitionSubstitutions: {
        ReserveBikeFunctionArn: reserveBike.functionArn,
        UnlockBikeFunctionArn: unlockBike.functionArn,
      },
    });

    reserveBike.grantInvoke(rental);
    unlockBike.grantInvoke(rental);
  }
}

// bin/app.ts
import { App } from "aws-cdk-lib";
import { BikeRentalStack } from "../lib/bike-rental-stack.ts";

const app = new App();
new BikeRentalStack(app, "BikeRentalStack");

echo '{ "app": "node bin/app.ts" }' > cdk.json
npx cdk synth
npx cdk deploy

In the synthesized template, you will find the AWS::StepFunctions::StateMachine resource with DefinitionS3Location and both substitutions. If you prefer the Serverless Framework, the serverless-step-functions plugin gets you to the same place. The tests stay unchanged, because they only know the ASL file.

Typical mistakes when testing with TestState

A few pitfalls stood out while I worked through the documentation and built the example:

  • Missing region: The SDK needs a region. Set AWS_REGION or add it to your profile.
  • No mock, no role: Without a mock, the TestState API has to call real services and needs a role with matching permissions. The helper above deliberately stops with a clear message in that case.
  • Mock does not match the API model: In STRICT mode, Step Functions rejects mocks with wrong field names or types. For .sync integrations, the mock must also match the response of the polling API, so for startExecution.sync:2 it must look like DescribeExecution.
  • Map and Parallel: A mock is required here. The test covers input and output processing of the outer state, not the individual iterations. You test the inner state separately via stateName.
  • Console instead of code: According to the documentation, the console does not support mocks or Map and Parallel tests yet. For everything in this article, you need the CLI or an SDK.
  • Exhausted retries: retrierRetryCount counts the retries that have already happened. If the value equals MaxAttempts, no attempts are left and the catcher takes over. If your test shows something else, look at the inspection data with DEBUG.

Cost and security when testing

The TestState API creates no state machine and starts no execution. The Step Functions pricing page does not list TestState as a separate item. What it bills are state transitions of real executions: for Standard workflows in US East (N. Virginia), 0.000025 US dollars per transition, with 4,000 free transitions per month. Still, check the current pricing page for your region before using it in large CI pipelines.

For security, the rule is simple: mocked tests only need states:TestState. Give your CI role exactly this permission and no iam:PassRole as long as you only work with mocks. Only tests with real calls need an execution role, which you should scope tightly as well. Leave out the revealSecrets parameter in CI pipelines, so no credentials from HTTP tasks end up in test logs.

My take

For me, the TestState API with mocks is the most useful testing tool Step Functions has received so far. It tests the real execution logic instead of a replica, and it makes exactly those parts testable that otherwise only run in an emergency. Especially with patterns like the saga pattern with Step Functions, correctness depends on catch rules and compensations. Those should not only be right on a whiteboard.

Still, TestState does not replace a test after deployment. The API checks one state after another, mocked and without real IAM permissions. Whether the role of the state machine is really allowed to invoke the Lambda function is something you will not see this way. So my split would be: guardrail tests offline on every commit, TestState tests with mocks in CI and, after deployment, a single real execution as a smoke test.

One point where I disagree with some teams: they try to test every combination of errors and states. That quickly turns into a test suite nobody understands anymore. Instead, test the decisions that matter for the business. For the bike rental, these are “throttling is retried”, “no bike available goes to another station” and “everything else fails in a controlled way”. By the way, I wrote about how long the pauses between retries should be in more detail in exponential backoff with jitter.

FAQ

Can I test Step Functions locally?

Step Functions Local still exists, but AWS calls it unsupported and without feature parity. For tests before deployment, AWS recommends the TestState API. You can additionally check the structure of the ASL file offline with your own tests.

Does the TestState API need an IAM role?

Only without a mock. As soon as you mock a result or an error, roleArn is optional. The caller always needs the states:TestState permission.

Can TestState run a whole state machine?

No, each call tests exactly one state. However, you can chain tests by using the output and nextState of one call as the input for the next.

Does TestState work with Map and Parallel states?

Yes, with a mock. The test covers input and output processing of the outer state. For Parallel, the mock must be an array with one element per branch, and for errors you name the inner state that caused them with errorCausedByState.

Your next step

Pick the state machine in your setup with the most error handling. Write exactly one test with a mocked error for each catcher and run it in CI. If you are still deciding whether Step Functions is the right service for your workflow at all, the AWS service finder helps you sort it out.

And now I am curious: how do you test your Step Functions workflows today, and which error path surprised you most recently in production?

title: Verification-Guided Retrosynthesis: Reaction Feedback and Evidence Timing
description:
arXiv:2610.38245v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Retrosynthesis planning seeks synthesis routes from purchasable starting materials to a target molecule. Search over predicted reactions can connect a target to available materials, yet an infeasible reaction can invalidate the resulting route. Evaluating route quality only after search has finished cannot correct errors made during search. We introduce Verification-Guided Reflow (VGR), incorporating reaction verification as a decision action in AND/OR search. Verification results are represented as binary verdicts; queries are scheduled from the search structure, and acquired verdicts exclude reactions or adjust search priorities. We define verified solvability as the fraction of targets for which a complete route accepted stepwise by the verifier is found. On Retro190, feeding verification results into search increases verified solvability from 51.1% to 62.6% relative to route evaluation without feedback. Further controlled experiments show that earlier verification and immediate prioritization of accepted reactions each improve route discovery, yet combining them performs worse than either change alone. We therefore propose early pruning and delayed guidance: rejected reactions are pruned immediately, while accepted reactions gain search priority when processed as part of a complete candidate route. In a separate comparison with the verification scheduling rule fixed, this strategy increases verified solvability from 61.1% with immediate guidance to 71.1%, using fewer proposal calls and unique verifier queries.

title: Why I Built yesh: Linux Automation You Can Explain
description:
Small Linux automation scripts tend to grow in a predictable way: they start as a few commands and gradually accumulate validation, quoting, branching, file replacement, service restarts, and error handling.

Bash is a remarkable tool. It is fast to start, available on almost every
Linux system, and excellent when the job is shell work: interactive commands, short glue, and composition of existing Unix tools. I use it and respect it.

The job changes when a script becomes an operational procedure. A small script that combines preflight checks, file publication, service changes, and failure handling must also explain what it will check, change, and leave untouched. That is where Bash's historical rules can make the script harder to review than the underlying commands themselves.

I built yesh for that gap: scripts that stay close to Linux commands while making their arguments, ordering, failure boundaries, and planned changes easy to review.

The goal is not to replace Bash, Python, or Ansible. Each tool has a different job. yesh is for the awkward middle: a small administrative script that is too important to hide behind shell tricks, but too close to the Linux command line to justify a larger automation framework.

The question is not “can it run?”

For operational code, a successful exit status is only one part of the story.

Before running a script, an operator should be able to answer:

  • What does it check first?
  • What exact arguments reach each external process?
  • Which files or services can change?
  • What happens if a command fails halfway through?
  • What remains unchanged after a failed run?

That is the standard behind yesh. The rest of the design follows from it: keep Linux utilities visible, make the surrounding procedure explicit, and make the failure boundary reviewable before execution.

The same intent, with a visible boundary

Consider a configuration update:

set -euo pipefail

if grep -q '^mode=production$' config.next; then
    install -m 0640 -- config.next /etc/myapp.conf.next
    mv -T /etc/myapp.conf.next /etc/myapp.conf
    systemctl restart myapp.service
    systemctl is-active --quiet myapp.service
fi

Here is the same operational intent in yesh:

if grep -q '^mode=production$' config.next:
    install -m 0640 -- config.next /etc/myapp.conf.next
    publish /etc/myapp.conf.next to /etc/myapp.conf
    service restart myapp.service until active within 10s

The yesh version earns its keep because the sequence reads like an operational procedure: validate, prepare, publish, restart, and verify a bounded postcondition. It does not need to be dramatically shorter. This is the kind of procedure yesh is designed to make readable.

publish uses a same-filesystem rename and does not silently fall back to
copying. The typed service operation has a finite deadline and checks that the exact unit becomes active. The script shows these boundaries directly instead of leaving a reviewer to reconstruct them.

Bash is excellent when the job is shell work

Bash remains excellent for interactive work, one-off commands, and the
enormous body of existing Unix tooling. yesh is not an argument against using Bash for those jobs.

The boundary appears when the main risk is not writing the command, but
reviewing what the procedure will do. Bash's flexibility can make that review harder: implicit word splitting, multiple quoting rules, several rounds of shell expansion, several condition syntaxes, and failure behavior that depends on context.

yesh makes a narrower set of choices to reduce that review burden:

message = "backup finished"
hosts = [web-1, web-2]

echo $message

for host in $hosts:
    echo $host

A string remains one value. A list expands into separate arguments. A variable is expanded only with the explicit $name form; a bare word remains a literal. Values are not reparsed as code and are not split implicitly by whitespace.

Those rules remove a category of shell reasoning from the review. They do not make the external command safe or guarantee that it will succeed.

Python solves a different problem

Python is often the right answer when the problem needs data structures,
libraries, APIs, concurrency, or substantial application logic. But many Linux administration tasks are primarily sequences of existing commands:

check a mount
inspect a directory
run rsync with explicit arguments
publish a completed result
restart one service
verify its state

For this class of task, a language that keeps Linux commands visible can be easier to audit than a Python wrapper that recreates process execution,
quoting, timeouts, and error reporting around every command.

That does not make Python a poor choice. It means yesh has a different center of gravity: a small language surface and a command-oriented runtime for procedures built from existing Linux tools.

Ansible coordinates a different layer

Ansible is an orchestration system with inventory, modules, roles, and a
desired-state model for many hosts. yesh is a small Linux runbook and preflight language for transparent local workflows and command-level steps inside larger automation.

yesh keeps ssh, rsync, systemctl, and other tools visible instead of
hiding them behind a new module model. Use Ansible for fleet orchestration and idempotent desired state. Use yesh when a Bash-like Unix workflow needs clearer syntax, explicit arguments, and reviewable execution.

The relationship is complementary. Ansible can select hosts and coordinate a rollout; a yesh script can perform or inspect one carefully bounded Linux operation on a host. An administrator can also run that runbook directly when a full inventory and role model would add more machinery than the task needs.

With that boundary established, the important question becomes: what does
yesh make visible inside one procedure?

Commands remain commands

yesh does not turn a line into one shell string and pass it to sh -c.
Commands are parsed into an argument vector and executed directly by the Go runtime.

install -m 0640 -- config.next /etc/myapp.conf.next

The process receives these separate arguments:

["install", "-m", "0640", "--", "config.next", "/etc/myapp.conf.next"]

This keeps argument boundaries visible when values contain spaces, commas, or characters that would have a special meaning to a shell. It also means that yesh does not reinterpret a value as a new command or operator.

Linux tools remain visible and retain their native semantics. rsync is still rsync; systemctl is still systemctl; ssh is still ssh. yesh provides the surrounding checks, ordering, and failure behavior.

--plan makes review practical

The argument boundary is only half of the review problem. Before a script
changes state, yesh can also show the expanded work:

./yesh --plan examples/service-restart.yesh

The plan shows expanded external commands and possible branches without
starting processes or opening redirect files:

PLAN ["grep" "-q" "^mode=production$" "config.next"]
PLAN ["install" "-m" "0640" "--" "config.next" "/etc/myapp.conf.next"]
PLAN publish "/etc/myapp.conf.next" to "/etc/myapp.conf"
PLAN ["systemctl" "restart" "myapp.service"] until active within 10s

Bracketed lines are external argv. Named lines are yesh operations with
their own semantics. The output is not a transaction and does not eliminate races between checking and acting. It is a concrete description of the work the script would attempt, suitable for review.

Failure is part of the design

The plan describes intended work. Execution still needs a clear failure rule. An ordinary command failure stops the script by default. A non-zero result used as an external condition can select an explicit else branch. A missing executable, startup failure, cancellation, signal, or timeout remains an execution error; yesh does not quietly turn it into a normal branch.

source = "/srv/releases/current"

if exists $source:
    echo "release is present"
else:
    echo "release is missing"
    exit 2

If any pipeline stage fails, the pipeline fails. On POSIX systems, cancellation terminates the owned process group and waits for child processes instead of only killing the first visible process.

This is not a claim that external programs are safe. rsync can still delete data if given destructive arguments. systemctl can still interrupt a service. Direct argument execution prevents shell reinterpretation; it does not give an arbitrary executable good intentions.

The runtime has to earn that promise

The runtime is written in Go, so the hard part is not only parsing commands. It is also making cancellation and cleanup predictable when several processes and goroutines are involved.

The project has been tested with more than 200 automated tests and four fuzz targets. The POSIX/Linux tests cover pipeline failure, SIGPIPE, process groups, timeouts, cancellation, child-process reaping, redirect cleanup, and repeated cancellation. The race-instrumented lifecycle tests also watch for file-descriptor and goroutine leaks after interrupted jobs.

I also ran ten integration tests in disposable Debian and Rocky Linux environments. These tests exercised the documented Linux workflows under controlled conditions. The results support the tested systems and scenarios; they do not prove universal compatibility.

That work matters because killing the first process is not the same as stopping a pipeline. Returning an error is not enough if a child or a cleanup goroutine remains behind. The runtime must stop the work it owns and wait for the processes it started.

A backup makes the boundary concrete

Backups expose whether a language makes failure boundaries clear. “The command returned zero” is not enough. The sysadmin also needs to know whether the source existed, whether the archive was complete, whether a partial result became visible, and whether a rerun remains understandable.

source = "source"
partial = "backup.tar.gz.partial"
archive = "backup.tar.gz"

if exists $source:
    tar -cf - -- $source | gzip > $partial
    mv -- $partial $archive
else:
    echo "source directory is missing"
    exit 2

The producer writes the private name first. The published name changes only after the producer succeeds. That is a visible publication boundary, not a claim of power-loss durability.

The same reasoning applies to incremental snapshots. yesh can make the
preflight, lock, staging, and publication sequence explicit while leaving
rsync and rsnapshot semantics alone. It does not silently add --delete, rewrite their option models, or pretend that a backup engine has become part of the language.

What yesh does not promise

yesh is not an interactive shell, a Bash-compatible replacement, a Python
competitor, an Ansible alternative, or a backup engine.

There is no command substitution, implicit background execution, eval,
unbounded while loop, hidden sudo, or general-purpose object model in the small core. Those omissions are deliberate. A feature belongs only when it makes an administrative script easier to read, review, and safely repeat.

The current prototype supports assignments, strings, lists, control flow,
pipelines, redirections, bounded process execution, locks, same-filesystem
publication, --plan, read-only storage inspection, and bounded systemd and journal operations. Practical Linux scenarios cover backup, restore, rsync, rsnapshot, SSH, services, processes, and configuration publication.

It is still a prototype, not a production safety boundary. External programs, privileges, paths, filesystems, kernels, remote hosts, and service behavior remain real operational concerns.

The narrower claim is the useful one: yesh makes a script's intent and failure boundaries easier to inspect.

That is why I built it.

Explore yesh on GitHub
