title: MongoDB TTL Collections vs. Application-Layer Expiry: Mechanics, Index Contention, and the Data Lifecycle Trap
description:
The Problem Nobody Audits Until It Hurts

Data expiry is infrastructure, not cleanup. The choice between MongoDB's built-in TTL mechanism and application-managed expiry determines your write amplification budget, index contention profile, oplog pressure, and what happens to your query plans at 3 AM when the TTL thread wakes up hungry.

This article dissects both approaches at the mechanical level—how TTL indexes actually execute, where they contend with your hot write path, and what application-layer expiry costs you in exchange for control. The tradeoffs are not symmetric and the defaults will bite you in high-throughput services.

How MongoDB TTL Actually Executes

TTL deletion is driven by the TTLMonitor background thread, which runs on a fixed 60-second interval by default (ttlMonitorSleepSecs). Each pass performs a collection scan over every TTL-indexed collection, issues range deletes for documents where the indexed field is older than expireAfterSeconds, and writes those deletes to the oplog.

The key mechanics:

  • TTL uses a regular BSON Date index. Under the hood it is a single-field ascending index with a expireAfterSeconds property. Reads against that index compete with TTL's own range scans.
  • Deletes are not batched as a single operation. MongoDB issues individual document deletes per expired document internally—each one acquires a document-level write lock, writes a delete to the oplog, and updates all secondary indexes on that collection.
  • Oplog amplification is proportional to secondary indexes. A collection with five secondary indexes generates six oplog entries per TTL delete (one delete plus five index key removals). At scale, this taxes replication bandwidth and secondary apply throughput.
  • The TTL thread is not throttled by default before MongoDB 7.0. On 7.0+, ttlMonitorBatchDeletes and the associated batch size controls allow the thread to yield between batches, which reduces lock contention but extends the actual expiry window beyond the configured expireAfterSeconds.

What Contention Looks Like

Imagine a session store: a sessions collection with a TTL index on createdAt (expire after 3600 seconds), plus secondary indexes on userId and deviceId. Write throughput is 8,000 inserts/second during peak.

At second 3600, the TTL thread wakes and begins deleting the cohort from an hour ago. If that cohort represents 500,000 documents, the thread issues 500,000 individual deletes, each touching three index structures. Your oplog rate spikes. Secondary apply lag creeps up. Replica read preferences that route to secondaries start returning stale session data—not expired data, just old data—which can masquerade as authentication bugs.

Meanwhile, your Go service is hammering the same userId index with session lookups. WiredTiger's document-level locking prevents a hard bottleneck there, but index-level operations still share B-tree page locks. At high concurrency, TTL-driven index page splits on the createdAt index cause insert latency spikes precisely when write load is highest: when sessions are being created because users are active.

Application-Layer Expiry: What You Buy and What You Pay

Application-layer expiry means your Go service is responsible for identifying and deleting expired documents, typically via a background goroutine with controlled concurrency.

func runExpiryWorker(ctx context.Context, coll *mongo.Collection) {
    ticker := time.NewTicker(30 * time.Second)
    defer ticker.Stop()

    for {
        select {
        case <-ctx.Done():
            return
        case <-ticker.C:
            if err := deleteExpiredBatch(ctx, coll); err != nil {
                log.Printf("expiry batch error: %v", err)
            }
        }
    }
}

func deleteExpiredBatch(ctx context.Context, coll *mongo.Collection) error {
    cutoff := time.Now().UTC().Add(-1 * time.Hour)
    filter := bson.D{{Key: "createdAt", Value: bson.D{{Key: "$lt", Value: cutoff}}}}

    opts := options.Delete().SetHint(bson.D{{Key: "createdAt", Value: 1}})
    result, err := coll.DeleteMany(ctx, filter, opts)
    if err != nil {
        return fmt.Errorf("deleteMany: %w", err)
    }

    metrics.ExpiredDocumentsDeleted.Add(float64(result.DeletedCount))
    return nil
}

This is not simply "the same thing in Go." The behavioral differences are significant:

Scheduling control. You decide when deletion runs and can suspend it during peak traffic windows—something the TTL thread cannot do without changing a global server parameter.

Batching semantics. DeleteMany with a query is still multiple document-level deletes internally, but you control how often you call it. You can implement cursor-based pagination over the expired cohort and delete in capped batches with time.Sleep between iterations, giving WiredTiger checkpoints time to flush and replication time to catch up.

Partial expiry signals. Before deletion, your Go worker can emit metrics, publish events to an SQS queue for audit, or write to an archive collection. TTL gives you nothing between "exists" and "gone."

The cost you pay: you now own the liveness of this goroutine. If the service restarts during a large expiry batch and does not complete it, documents accumulate until the next run. You need observability: a counter on DeletedCount, a gauge on the oldest document age, and an alert when that gauge exceeds 2 * expireAfterSeconds.

Index Design Pressure from Both Approaches

The createdAt index required for TTL (or for application-layer range queries) sits in your hot index set. Consider what this means for insert throughput:

Every insert must update the createdAt B-tree. If createdAt values are monotonically increasing (they almost always are for timestamps), the rightmost leaf of the B-tree is the only page being written to. WiredTiger handles this reasonably with its MVCC design, but at very high insert rates you still observe right-edge contention on that leaf page.

A compound index {userId: 1, createdAt: 1} may serve reads better but is ineligible as a TTL index (TTL requires single-field). This forces you to maintain a separate single-field {createdAt: 1} TTL index alongside your compound read index—two index writes per insert instead of one. Application-layer expiry can use the compound index for its batch deletes, eliminating the redundant single-field index entirely.

Oplog and Replication: The Underestimated Factor

In replica sets with cross-region secondaries (common in AWS multi-AZ or multi-region deployments), oplog apply rate is your replication ceiling. TTL-driven deletes that generate millions of oplog entries in a short window can push secondary apply lag into the tens of seconds. If your service reads from secondaries with readPreference: secondary for scale, those reads will operate on a meaningfully stale view of the data—stale not just by seconds but by the depth of the oplog backlog.

This is a correctness issue when expired documents are security-relevant (sessions, tokens, capability grants). A secondary that is 15 seconds behind oplog apply will serve session documents that the TTL thread already deleted on the primary. Your Go service reading from that secondary considers the session valid.

Application-layer expiry using w: majority write concern for deletes ensures all nodes acknowledge the delete before your worker proceeds—at the cost of latency per batch. The tradeoff: slower expiry, stronger consistency guarantees on cross-node reads.

Decision Framework

Use this matrix when evaluating which approach fits your workload:

Dimension TTL Index Application-Layer Expiry
Operational overhead Low — fire and forget High — goroutine lifecycle, alerting
Scheduling control None (60s global thread) Full — pause during peak, batch size tuning
Secondary index count Forces extra createdAt index Can reuse compound read index
Oplog pressure High — uncontrolled burst Controlled — sized by batch frequency
Pre-delete actions None Audit, archive, event emission
Replication lag risk High at scale Low with batching and sleep
Correctness under secondary reads Risk of stale-valid documents Controllable with write concern

Choose TTL when: the collection has at most two secondary indexes, write throughput is below 1,000 documents/second, no pre-delete processing is needed, and replication lag on secondaries is not a correctness concern.

Choose application-layer expiry when: the collection is high-write, carries security-relevant data (sessions, tokens), has three or more secondary indexes, serves reads from secondaries, or requires any audit trail before deletion.

Hybrid approach: Use the TTL index as a safety net with a very long expireAfterSeconds (e.g., 7 days) to prevent unbounded collection growth in case the application worker fails. Set the application worker to delete at the true business expiry window (1 hour). The TTL index almost never fires, eliminating its contention profile while preserving a backstop against worker failure.

Observability Requirements for Application-Layer Expiry

If you own the expiry loop, you own its failure modes. Minimum instrumentation:

  • Gauge: oldest document age in the collection (sampled, not a full scan—use find({}).sort({createdAt: 1}).limit(1)).
  • Counter: documents deleted per batch run. A sudden drop to zero means the query plan changed or the index was dropped.
  • Histogram: batch duration. Spikes indicate lock contention or oplog backpressure.
  • Alert: oldest document age > 2× expiry window. This is your canary for a stalled worker.

Without these, application-layer expiry fails silently and you discover the problem when your collection has grown by an order of magnitude and your index scans have regressed.

Data lifecycle decisions compound. A TTL index that looks free on day one has a compounding cost profile as collection size, secondary index count, and write throughput grow. Model the oplog amplification factor before you ship to production. The hybrid backstop pattern costs almost nothing and eliminates the worst failure mode of application-managed expiry. That is the baseline.

title: BridgeRouter: Gain-Aware Instance Routing over Cross-Modal Bridge Portfolios
description:
arXiv:2610.38152v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Lightweight representation bridges make pretrained, task-adapted EEG foundation models executable on other biosignal modalities without retraining their backbones. However, selecting a single bridge pathway globally assigns every instance to the same transfer route and ignores complementary errors across routes. We therefore formulate multi-bridge transfer as an instance-level algorithm-selection problem and introduce BridgeRouter, a gain-aware router over a portfolio of frozen cross-modal pathways. A validation-selected Single Best Solver (SBS) serves as a protected default route. During training, task labels are used to compute the reduction in negative log-likelihood provided by each alternative route relative to the SBS, and a lightweight MLP predicts these route-specific gains from a target-modality representation extracted by a frozen encoder. At inference, BridgeRouter observes only the target modality, requires neither EEG, task labels, nor predictions from all candidate routes, and executes exactly one bridge pathway: the route with the largest predicted gain when that gain exceeds a validation-calibrated threshold, and the SBS otherwise. We evaluate seven EEG foundation-model bridge pathways for EMG-based freezing-of-gait detection on FOG and ECG-based sleep classification on ISRUC. Across five seeds, BridgeRouter achieves $81.38\pm1.11\%$ balanced accuracy on FOG, improving over the BIOT SBS by $11.49$ percentage points, and $62.92\pm2.17\%$ on ISRUC, improving over the CBraMod SBS by $3.83$ points. Per-instance bridge oracles reach $99.96\%$ and $78.61\%$, respectively, revealing substantial remaining portfolio headroom. These results show that anchor-relative gain prediction can convert complementary cross-modal bridge behavior into deployable instance-level routing improvements while retaining single-route inference.

title: I Built a Self-Hosted WhatsApp Gateway Using Node.js, Docker and PostgreSQL
description:
Building Puffx WhatsApp Gateway: A Self-Hosted WhatsApp Messaging API with Node.js, Docker and PostgreSQL

Author: Nitin Mehta

Project: Puffx WhatsApp Gateway

GitHub Repository: https://github.com/puffxhost/puffx-whatsapp-gateway

Website: https://puffxhost.com

Introduction

What if developers could run their own WhatsApp messaging gateway instead of depending entirely on a third-party hosted messaging service?

That question inspired me to build Puffx WhatsApp Gateway, an open-source, self-hosted messaging gateway designed to connect a WhatsApp account with applications through a REST API.

The project brings together a web dashboard, WhatsApp account pairing, API key authentication, PostgreSQL, and Docker-based deployment.

The main idea is simple:

  • Run the gateway on your own computer or VPS.
  • Connect a WhatsApp account using QR pairing or a phone pairing code.
  • Manage the connected session through a web dashboard.
  • Generate an API key.
  • Send text messages from your own backend applications using HTTP requests.

I built this project under Puffx Host to explore backend development, API architecture, self-hosted infrastructure, and messaging integrations.

The project is currently in its initial beta stage.

Explore the source code:

https://github.com/puffxhost/puffx-whatsapp-gateway

1. What Is Puffx WhatsApp Gateway?

Puffx WhatsApp Gateway is a self-hosted application that exposes a REST API for sending text messages through a paired WhatsApp Web session.

Instead of using a gateway hosted by someone else, developers can deploy the application on infrastructure they control.

The application provides a web dashboard for managing sessions and API credentials.

Main Features

1. QR Code Pairing

Connect a WhatsApp account by scanning a QR code using WhatsApp's Linked Devices feature.

2. Phone Pairing Code

The project also supports an alternative phone pairing code flow.

3. Web Dashboard

Manage your account, create WhatsApp sessions, check connection status, and generate API keys.

4. REST API

Send text messages programmatically through an HTTP endpoint.

5. API Key Authentication

The API uses Bearer token authentication to authorize message requests.

6. PostgreSQL Database

PostgreSQL stores application data.

7. Docker Deployment

Docker Compose provides a convenient way to run the gateway and its database together.

8. Persistent Session Storage

Docker volumes preserve database data and WhatsApp authentication state across normal container restarts.

2. Technology Stack

I used the following technologies and tools to build the project.

Technology Purpose
Node.js Backend runtime
TypeScript Application development
PostgreSQL Database
Docker Containerization
Docker Compose Service orchestration
REST API Application integration
Baileys WhatsApp Web connectivity

Why Docker?

A self-hosted application should be relatively straightforward to deploy and maintain.

Docker makes it easier to package the gateway and database into a consistent environment.

Instead of manually configuring every dependency, developers can start the application using Docker Compose.

Why PostgreSQL?

The project needs persistent application data. PostgreSQL provides a relational database for managing that information.

3. Understanding the Architecture

At a high level, the application has four important parts:

  1. Dashboard: The interface used to manage accounts, sessions, and API keys.
  2. Backend API: Handles authentication, session management, and message requests.
  3. PostgreSQL: Stores persistent application data.
  4. WhatsApp Web integration: Handles the paired WhatsApp session and communication.

The basic message flow looks like this:

Your Application
       |
       | HTTP Request
       v
Puffx REST API
       |
       | Bearer Token Authentication
       v
Session Validation
       |
       v
WhatsApp Integration
       |
       v
WhatsApp Network

This architecture allows another backend application to communicate with the gateway without directly managing the WhatsApp session itself.

4. Installing the Project with Docker

One of the main goals was to make local setup accessible to developers.

Requirements

Before starting, install:

  • Docker Desktop or Docker Engine.
  • Docker Compose.
  • Git.
  • A WhatsApp account that can use Linked Devices.

For Windows users, Docker Desktop should be installed and running.

Step 1: Clone the Repository

Open Windows CMD, PowerShell, or a terminal on Linux/macOS.

git clone https://github.com/puffxhost/puffx-whatsapp-gateway.git

cd puffx-whatsapp-gateway

Step 2: Configure Environment Variables

Copy the example environment configuration.

On Windows CMD:

copy .env.example .env

On Linux/macOS:

cp .env.example .env

Open the .env file and configure the required secrets.

POSTGRES_PASSWORD=your_strong_database_password
SESSION_SECRET=your_random_session_secret
API_KEY_PEPPER=your_random_api_key_pepper

Use unique, randomly generated values.

The session secret and API key pepper should be different from each other.

Important: Never commit your real .env file to a public repository.

Step 3: Start Docker Compose

Run:

docker compose up -d --build

Docker Compose will build and start the gateway and database services.

Step 4: Open the Dashboard

After the services start, open:

http://127.0.0.1:3000

You can also check the readiness endpoint:

http://127.0.0.1:3000/api/v1/ready

The endpoint should report that the application is ready.

Step 5: Check Container Status

Run:

docker compose ps

To view gateway logs:

docker compose logs -f gateway

To restart the gateway:

docker compose restart gateway

To stop the services while preserving data:

docker compose down

Be careful with docker compose down -v. It removes the associated named volumes and can permanently delete the database and WhatsApp login data.

5. Connecting a WhatsApp Account

After opening the dashboard, follow these steps:

  1. Create an account in the dashboard.
  2. Select Add session.
  3. Give your WhatsApp session a name.
  4. Choose QR pairing or phone pairing code.
  5. For QR pairing, open WhatsApp on your phone.
  6. Navigate to Settings → Linked Devices → Link a Device.
  7. Scan the displayed QR code.
  8. Wait until the session status becomes connected.

Once connected, the session is available for API integration.

Security note: Never share QR codes, pairing codes, WhatsApp authentication files, or session backups with anyone.

6. Generating an API Key

After connecting your WhatsApp session:

  1. Open the connected session in the dashboard.
  2. Select Create API key.
  3. Copy the generated key immediately.
  4. Store it securely on your backend server.

The key is displayed only once.

If you lose it, revoke it and generate a new key.

The API key is associated with the session selected when it was created.

The session UUID is also required when making a message request. Use the dashboard's Copy ID option to obtain it.

7. Sending Your First WhatsApp Message Through the REST API

This is one of the most important parts of the project.

Once the gateway is running and a WhatsApp session is connected, another application can send a text message using an authenticated HTTP request.

API Endpoint 

POST /api/v1/messages/send

Authentication 

Authorization: Bearer YOUR_API_KEY

Request Body 

{
  "sessionId": "YOUR_SESSION_UUID",
  "to": "919876543210",
  "type": "text",
  "message": "Hello from Puffx WhatsApp Gateway!"
}

Replace the example phone number with the recipient's number, including the country code and digits only.

Complete cURL Example 

curl -X POST "http://127.0.0.1:3000/api/v1/messages/send" \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer YOUR_API_KEY" \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{
    "sessionId": "YOUR_SESSION_UUID",
    "to": "919876543210",
    "type": "text",
    "message": "Hello from Puffx WhatsApp Gateway!"
  }'

Replace the API key and session UUID with your actual values.

The API returns HTTP 202 when the provider accepts the message request.

An important distinction: HTTP 202 does not guarantee successful delivery or confirm that the recipient has read the message.

Delivery and read receipts are not currently implemented in this beta.

8. Integrating with Other Programming Languages

The gateway is designed to be accessed through HTTP, so a developer can integrate it with a backend written in different programming languages.

Examples and integration guidance are included in the repository's API documentation.

Potential client applications include:

  • Node.js applications.
  • PHP applications.
  • Python applications.
  • Internal business tools.
  • Backend automation systems.

For example, a PHP application could make an HTTP POST request to the gateway with its API key stored in a server-side environment variable.

Never expose an API key in frontend JavaScript, a public GitHub repository, or a mobile application's publicly accessible configuration.

For detailed examples, refer to:

https://github.com/puffxhost/puffx-whatsapp-gateway/blob/main/docs/api-reference.md

9. Can It Run on a VPS?

Yes. The application is designed for self-hosted deployment on a Linux VPS or cloud virtual machine.

A typical deployment needs:

  • Linux server.
  • Docker Engine.
  • Docker Compose.
  • PostgreSQL.
  • Persistent storage.
  • Domain name.
  • HTTPS reverse proxy.
  • Outbound WebSocket connectivity.

For public deployments, the gateway should run behind an HTTPS reverse proxy such as Nginx.

The repository includes deployment documentation and an example Nginx configuration.

A typical deployment workflow:

Domain
  |
  v
HTTPS Reverse Proxy
  |
  v
Puffx WhatsApp Gateway
  |
  +------ PostgreSQL
  |
  +------ Persistent WhatsApp Session Data

The Docker Compose configuration binds the gateway to localhost on port 3000. The reverse proxy forwards HTTPS requests to that local service.

Ordinary shared hosting and static website hosting are generally unsuitable because the application requires continuously running services and persistent writable storage.

For additional information:

  • Docker deployment: https://github.com/puffxhost/puffx-whatsapp-gateway/blob/main/docs/docker-deployment.md
  • VPS deployment: https://github.com/puffxhost/puffx-whatsapp-gateway/blob/main/docs/vps-deployment.md
  • Installation guide: https://github.com/puffxhost/puffx-whatsapp-gateway/blob/main/docs/installation.md

10. Security Considerations

Self-hosting gives developers control over their infrastructure, but it also means they are responsible for securing it.

Some important considerations:

Environment Secrets

Use strong, unique secrets for the database password, session secret, and API key pepper.

HTTPS

Never expose a public dashboard or API over unencrypted HTTP. Configure a valid TLS certificate.

API Key Protection

Keep API keys in backend environment variables or a secret manager.

Session Data

WhatsApp authentication state is stored on disk and is not encrypted by the application. Protect the Docker volume and its backups.

Database Backups

Back up PostgreSQL and the WhatsApp authentication volume. Treat both as sensitive data.

Access Restrictions

Do not expose internal database ports or unnecessary services to the public internet.

Read the full security documentation before deploying publicly:

https://github.com/puffxhost/puffx-whatsapp-gateway/blob/main/docs/security.md

11. Current Beta Status and Limitations

I want to be transparent about the current state of the project.

Puffx WhatsApp Gateway is an initial beta implementation.

Currently supported functionality:

  • WhatsApp QR pairing.
  • Phone pairing code.
  • Web dashboard.
  • Session management.
  • API key creation.
  • REST API authentication.
  • Text message sending.
  • Docker Compose deployment.

Current limitations:

  • Only text messages are supported.
  • Media messaging is not implemented.
  • Webhooks are not implemented.
  • Message queues are not implemented.
  • Delivery and read receipts are not implemented.
  • There is no separate admin console.
  • Real WhatsApp pairing and delivery behavior have not been verified by automated tests.

These limitations are important. The project should not be treated as a fully production-ready messaging platform.

12. Why I Started This Project

I enjoy exploring how software systems work beyond the frontend.

Working on this project has given me an opportunity to explore:

  • Backend architecture.
  • REST API design.
  • Database integration.
  • Docker-based deployment.
  • Authentication and secrets management.
  • Persistent application data.
  • VPS infrastructure.
  • WhatsApp Web connectivity.

I also wanted to build a practical tool that other developers could inspect, run, and experiment with.

This is an ongoing learning and development project under Puffx Host.

13. Open Source and Community Feedback

The project is publicly available on GitHub.

I welcome feedback from developers who work with:

  • Node.js.
  • TypeScript.
  • PostgreSQL.
  • Docker.
  • REST APIs.
  • Backend development.
  • Self-hosted infrastructure.

You can explore the source code, read the documentation, report issues, and contribute improvements.

GitHub Repository:

https://github.com/puffxhost/puffx-whatsapp-gateway

If you find a bug or have a technical suggestion, please open an issue in the GitHub repository.

Conclusion

Puffx WhatsApp Gateway is my attempt to build a self-hosted messaging gateway with a practical REST API and Docker-based deployment.

It is still in beta, and there is plenty of room for improvement.

Building this project has been a useful experience in backend engineering, infrastructure, and API development.

I would love to hear your feedback:

What would you improve in a self-hosted WhatsApp messaging gateway?

Would you focus on better session management, more API capabilities, monitoring, or deployment improvements?

Explore the project:

https://github.com/puffxhost/puffx-whatsapp-gateway

title: Repo Séance 👻 — Giving Abandoned Repositories a Second Life
description:
Repo Séance 👻 — Giving Abandoned Repositories a Second Life

This is a submission for the Hacktoberfest Open-Source AI Challenge Week 4: Ghost in the Machine

What I Built

Every abandoned repository has a story.

Some projects stop after a single commit. Others contain months of development, unfinished features, confusing dependencies, and code that nobody has touched in years. When the original developer disappears, the repository is left behind — almost like a digital ghost.

That's the idea behind Repo Séance.

Repo Séance is a local-first AI-powered tool that helps developers understand abandoned or unfamiliar codebases. Instead of simply generating a summary, it lets you interact with a repository as if you were interviewing its past.

You can ask questions such as:

  • What was this project originally trying to achieve?
  • Which parts of the application were actively developed?
  • What was the last major change?
  • Which modules depend on this file?
  • What should I work on first to bring this project back to life?

The tool analyzes source code, project structure, dependencies, and Git history to build an evidence-backed picture of the repository.

I interpreted Ghost in the Machine as the digital remains of software projects: code that still exists, even when the people and context behind it are gone.

The goal is simple: help developers understand what was left behind and make it easier to continue the work.

The project is designed for local execution, so the demo can also showcase the application running on a developer's machine.

Code

🔗 GitHub Repository:

ansh-rajpoot / repo-ghost

Repo Séance

Every repository leaves a ghost. Some still have something to say.

Repo Séance is a local archaeological tool for forgotten software. You open a ZIP or a checkout the backend can already see. It reads the tree, the git history when one exists, and the Python import graph. Then you question an entity called the Ghost. Every factual claim is tied to a file, a line, or a commit that was actually retrieved. When the record is silent, the ghost says so.

Summon the past. Understand the code. Revive what was forgotten.

What it does

  • Cinematic threshold, then a three-pane archive: catacombs, memory topology, and the medium.
  • ZIP upload with path-traversal, symlink, size, and secret-filename checks. Uploaded code is never executed.
  • Local-directory mode limited to configured roots. The browser cannot send an arbitrary path.
  • Git history through the git CLI: hashes, author timestamps with their original offsets, file…
View on GitHub

How I Built It

Repo Séance combines traditional code analysis with local AI inference.

The planned architecture uses:

  • React + TypeScript + Vite for the frontend.
  • FastAPI + Python for the backend.
  • Python AST to inspect Python source files and extract structural information.
  • Git history analysis to understand commits and reconstruct the project's development timeline.
  • Ollama to run an open-weight language model locally.
  • A repository retrieval layer to provide relevant code and history as context for AI-generated answers.

One important design decision was to avoid relying on a hosted AI API. Repository code can contain private implementation details, credentials, or intellectual property. Keeping inference local gives developers greater control over where their code goes.

I also wanted the application to distinguish between verified facts, reasonable inferences, and unknown information. For example, a repository may show that development stopped after a particular commit, but it cannot reliably tell us why the developer stopped working on it.

Repo Séance should never invent that story.

The AI helps interpret the evidence; the repository itself remains the source of truth.

Why Does Open Innovation Matter?

A project like Repo Séance makes much more sense when built with open-source technologies.

Local inference through Ollama and open-weight models makes it possible to experiment with AI without sending an entire repository to an external API. Open-source frameworks also let developers inspect, modify, and extend the system according to their own requirements.

title: Zero Code Execution: Building a Safe Jupyter Notebook Connector for Cognee GraphRAG
description:
In modern data science organizations, Jupyter Notebooks (.ipynb) serve as the primary medium for exploratory data analysis (EDA), model training, hypothesis validation, and architectural experiments. However, standard enterprise knowledge graphs and LLM retrieval pipelines have historically struggled to ingest notebooks safely and meaningfully:

  1. Security Vulnerabilities (OWASP LLM02): Ingesting external notebooks that contain untrusted Python or shell magics (!curl, os.system) risks accidental code execution if runtime environments (ipykernel, exec(), eval()) are triggered during parsing.
  2. Noise & Bloat: A single uncleaned notebook can contain tens of megabytes of raw Base64 PNG plots, ANSI color codes from failed stack traces, and verbose progress bar outputs.
  3. Stale Knowledge & Orphaned Entities: When a data scientist deletes or refactors a notebook, stale entity nodes and outdated embeddings often remain indefinitely in vector and graph storage.

As part of the WeMakeDevs × Cognee Mergetober Hackathon, I engineered and submitted the official Jupyter Notebook data-source connector (cognee-community-connector-jupyter) for Cognee.

In this article, I will break down how we solved these challenges through zero code execution passive parsing, pre-ingestion secret redaction, and Cognee’s native forget-on-delete graph lifecycle.

Architecture: From Raw .ipynb to Knowledge Graph

Here is the high-level ingestion pipeline from disk to Cognee's GraphRAG engine:

flowchart TD
    A[".ipynb File on Disk"] --> B["Passive JSON Parser (nbformat v3/v4)"]
    B --> C["Cell Content Extractor"]

    subgraph Sanitization ["Pre-Ingestion Sanitization"]
        C --> D["Markdown Cells (Structured Prose)"]
        C --> E["Code Cells (Fenced Code Blocks)"]
        C --> F["Outputs (stdout / text/plain)"]
        F --> G["Noise Filter (Strip ANSI, Drop Base64 Images)"]
        D & E & G --> H["Regex Redactor (Bearer, API Keys, PATs)"]
    end

    H --> I["dlt Document Generator (cognee_document_source='jupyter')"]
    I --> J["Cognee Ingestion Engine"]

    subgraph Cognify ["Cognify Graph Processing"]
        J --> K["Entity & Relationship Extraction (LLM)"]
        K --> L["Knowledge Graph (NetworkX / FalkorDB)"]
        K --> M["Vector Store (Qdrant / LanceDB)"]
    end

    J --> N["write_disposition='replace' (Forget-on-Delete Orphan Cleanup)"]

1. Zero Code Execution: Passive JSON AST Parsing

A critical security requirement when building data pipelines for AI memory is never executing untrusted code. Many naive notebook parsers inadvertently import kernel execution utilities or evaluate expressions.

Under the hood, every .ipynb file is simply a structured JSON document conforming to the Jupyter nbformat schema. Our connector treats notebooks strictly as passive data using Python's standard library:

import json
from pathlib import Path

def parse_notebook_statically(file_path: Path) -> dict:
    """Statically parse .ipynb as raw JSON with zero kernel interaction."""
    with open(file_path, "r", encoding="utf-8") as f:
        nb_data = json.load(f)

    # Validate nbformat version
    nbformat_ver = nb_data.get("nbformat", 4)
    cells = nb_data.get("cells", [])
    return {"version": nbformat_ver, "cells": cells}

By decoupling extraction from ipykernel, the pipeline can ingest thousands of notebooks across legacy versions (nbformat v3 and v4) with zero CPU execution risk and zero dependency overhead.

2. Noise Suppression & Output Filtering

Raw notebook outputs are notoriously noisy. To keep LLM context windows efficient and prevent embedding pollution:

  1. Base64 Image Suppression: Base64-encoded PNG/JPEG plots (image/png, image/jpeg) are stripped entirely from outputs.
  2. ANSI Color Stripping: Terminal escape sequences generated by Python tracebacks (\u001b[0;31m) are removed with compiled regex patterns.
  3. Character Caps: Verbose stdout logs are capped to configurable lengths (max_output_chars=2000) with explicit truncation markers. 
import re

ANSI_REGEX = re.compile(r"\x1B(?:[@-Z\\-_]|\[[0-?]*[ -/]*[@-~])")

def clean_traceback_output(text: str) -> str:
    """Remove ANSI terminal color escape sequences from traceback strings."""
    return ANSI_REGEX.sub("", text)

3. Pre-Ingestion Credential & Secret Redaction

Data scientists frequently forget hardcoded test credentials in scratch cells before saving notebooks. Emitting unredacted API tokens into shared vector databases or external LLM inference endpoints violates enterprise privacy boundaries.

The connector runs a compiled regex redaction pipeline over all Markdown prose, code blocks, and output buffers before records leave the local connector sandbox:

  • OpenAI Keys: sk-[A-Za-z0-9]{20,}
  • GitHub PATs: ghp_[A-Za-z0-9]{36}
  • AWS Access Keys: AKIA[0-9A-Z]{16}
  • Bearer Tokens: Bearer [A-Za-z0-9\-\._~\+\/]+=* 
REDACTION_RULES = [
    (re.compile(r"Bearer\s+[A-Za-z0-9\-._~+/]+=*", re.IGNORECASE), "Bearer [REDACTED_TOKEN]"),
    (re.compile(r"ghp_[A-Za-z0-9]{36}"), "[REDACTED_GITHUB_PAT]"),
    (re.compile(r"sk-[A-Za-z0-9]{20,}"), "[REDACTED_API_KEY]"),
    (re.compile(r"AKIA[0-9A-Z]{16}"), "[REDACTED_AWS_KEY]"),
]

def redact_secrets(content: str) -> str:
    for pattern, replacement in REDACTION_RULES:
        content = pattern.sub(replacement, content)
    return content

4. The Cognee Graph Invariant: "Forget-on-Delete"

In GraphRAG architectures, handling deletions and moves is just as important as handling additions. If a team removes an obsolete experimentation notebook, its graph nodes shouldn't mislead the LLM.

To solve this, the connector integrates directly with Cognee's internal DOCUMENT_SOURCE_ATTR mechanism:

from cognee.tasks.ingestion.dlt_utils import DOCUMENT_SOURCE_ATTR

# 1. Flag the source for document routing
setattr(source, DOCUMENT_SOURCE_ATTR, "jupyter")

# 2. Use full snapshot replacement disposition
@dlt.resource(name="notebooks", write_disposition="replace")
def notebooks_resource():
    for notebook in discover_and_parse_notebooks():
        yield notebook

Why this matters:

  1. Bypasses Relational Flattening: DOCUMENT_SOURCE_ATTR = "jupyter" signals to Cognee that incoming items are rich documents rather than relational database tables, automatically routing them to the Cognify entity-extraction pipeline.
  2. Automated Graph Pruning: Setting write_disposition="replace" allows Cognee's background orphan cleanup job to compute differences between sync snapshots and automatically prune removed notebooks from both vector collections and the FalkorDB/NetworkX knowledge graph.
  3. Content Deduplication: Unchanged notebooks retain identical deterministic data_id content hashes, skipping redundant LLM inference calls on subsequent runs.

In Action: Ingesting Notebooks and Querying the Knowledge Graph

Using the connector in a Cognee pipeline takes just a few lines of asynchronous Python:

import asyncio
import cognee
from cognee_community_connector_jupyter import jupyter_source

async def main():
    # 1. Initialize connector pointing to data science repositories
    source = jupyter_source(
        workspace_dir="./analytics_workspace",
        include_outputs=True,
        max_output_chars=2000,
        redact_secrets=True,
    )

    # 2. Add source to Cognee staging and cognify into knowledge graph
    print("Ingesting notebooks...")
    await cognee.add(source)

    print("Extracting entities and building graph relationships...")
    await cognee.cognify()

    # 3. Query the unified notebook knowledge graph
    query = "What data preprocessing steps and evaluation metrics were used for customer churn?"
    print(f"\nQuerying: '{query}'")
    results = await cognee.search(query)

    for idx, match in enumerate(results, 1):
        print(f"\n[Result {idx}]:\n{match}")

if __name__ == "__main__":
    asyncio.run(main())

When Cognee processes the notebooks, it identifies concepts like RandomForestClassifier, AUC-ROC, and data_leakage_mitigation, creating cross-notebook edges that connect experimental hypotheses with quantitative findings.

Verification & Maintainer Standards

Following the Cognee core maintainer review standards:

  • 100% Offline Testing: 27 unit tests pass offline with zero external network or kernel dependencies (tests/test_source.py, tests/test_parser.py, tests/test_redaction.py).
  • Dependency Hygiene: Clean separation using modern pyproject.toml configuration with flexible bounds (cognee>=1.6.3,<2).
  • DCO Certified: Verified Developer Certificate of Origin (git commit -s).

Conclusion & What's Next

By combining passive JSON parsing, pre-ingestion redaction, and Cognee's GraphRAG lifecycle, data science teams can safely turn their institutional notebook repositories into interactive, searchable memory.

You can inspect the connector and open PR under the Cognee community repository:

  • Pull Request: topoteretes/cognee-community#373
  • Cognee Core: topoteretes/cognee

Have questions about GraphRAG, Cognee connector architecture, or notebook sanitization? Drop a comment below or connect on GitHub!

title: Why We Built PaperTrail: Moving from AI Paper Summaries to Continuous Scientific Intelligence
description:
Every few months, a new "AI research tool" hits the front page of Hacker News or Product Hunt. Almost without exception, they all do the same thing:

  1. Ingest a PDF.
  2. Chunk it into embeddings.
  3. Feed the chunks into a vector database.
  4. Put a conversational chatbot in front of it that summarizes what the authors said.

Here's the fundamental problem: Science is not a collection of static text summaries. Science is an evolving, adversarial debate.

A paper published in 2023 demonstrating a 4x inference speedup for 4-bit quantized language models on Apple Silicon is not an absolute truth. It is a finding contingent on specific hardware, quantization algorithms, precision levels, and thermal conditions. When a 2024 paper reports severe degradation under continuous workloads on Qualcomm Snapdragon chips, they aren't necessarily contradicting each other—they're operating in completely different experimental contexts.

And when a seminal paper gets retracted or contradicted six months later, your vector database doesn't know. It happily continues serving obsolete claims as ground truth.

We built PaperTrail to fundamentally rethink how software interacts with scientific literature.

Instead of another paper summarizer, PaperTrail is an autonomous, continuously evolving scientific intelligence engine.

In this article, I want to walk through the technical architecture, design philosophy, and lessons learned building PaperTrail with Next.js 14, TypeScript, local Ollama models, and a local-first SQLite/Supabase hybrid storage engine.

The Core Proposition

PaperTrail is built around a single thesis:

"Discover what research has established, what it challenges, what remains unexplored, and how the scientific evidence changes over time."

To deliver on this, we established ten non-negotiable architectural capabilities:

  1. Grounded Scientific Claim Extraction: Never extract an assertion without an exact, verbatim passage and paper citation.
  2. Context-Aware Disagreement Investigation: Never label two differing findings as a contradiction without examining differences in hardware, precision, quantization bitwidth, context length, or thermal states.
  3. Candidate Research-Gap Discovery: Automatically identify blind spots and uninvestigated parameter intersections across literature.
  4. Adversarial 6-Stage Gap Falsification: Never present a research gap as valid until an automated red-team agent attempts to aggressively falsify it against counter-evidence.
  5. Practical Experiment Feasibility & Protocol Planning: Convert validated gaps into runnable, resource-evaluated empirical protocols with compute hour calculations and step-by-step checklists.
  6. Continuous Research Tracking & Evidence Evolution: Monitor topics and incoming preprints to compute how evidence shifts over time.
  7. Preprint-to-Publication Lineage Mapping: Trace preprints from arXiv to peer-reviewed venues, isolating shifts in methodology and benchmarks.
  8. Retraction & Correction Intelligence: When papers are retracted or corrected, flag dependent claims and recalculate conclusions without silently erasing historical evidence.
  9. Accessible Dataset Discovery: Find benchmark datasets on Hugging Face, Zenodo, and Figshare with verified licenses.
  10. Cross-Domain Hypothesis Transfer: Formulate principled transfer hypotheses connecting primary research with adjacent fields (e.g., neuroscience synaptic pruning $\leftrightarrow$ LLM weight quantization).

1. Grounded Claim Extraction & Schema Validation

One of our strictest engineering rules is: No hallucinated consensus.

Every claim extracted by PaperTrail must adhere to a strict Zod schema. If the model cannot provide the exact supporting passage from the abstract or text, the extraction fails validation and falls back to a deterministic semantic parser.

Here is a snippet of our claim validation contract:

export const ClaimExtractionSchema = z.object({
  claims: z.array(
    z.object({
      claim_text: z.string().min(10),
      claim_type: z.enum([
        'FINDING',
        'HYPOTHESIS',
        'METHODOLOGY',
        'LIMITATION',
        'BENCHMARK_RESULT',
        'THEORETICAL_BOUND',
      ]),
      section: z.enum(['Abstract', 'Introduction', 'Evaluation', 'Conclusion']),
      supporting_passage: z.string().min(15),
      page_number: z.number().int().positive().optional(),
      extraction_confidence: z.number().min(0).max(1),
    })
  ),
  experimental_context: z.object({
    model: z.string().default('Unspecified'),
    hardware: z.string().default('Unspecified'),
    dataset: z.string().default('Unspecified'),
    quantization: z.string().default('FP16'),
    precision: z.string().default('Unspecified'),
    metrics: z.record(z.string()).default({}),
    variables: z.record(z.string()).default({}),
  }),
  limitations: z.array(z.string()).default([]),
});

By extracting both the claim and its experimental condition matrix (hardware, precision, model scale, metrics), we create the foundation for intelligent, context-aware comparison.

2. Context-Aware Disagreement Investigation: Beyond Binary "Contradictions"

Traditional NLP pipelines treat contradiction detection as an NLI (Natural Language Inference) task: Premise vs. Hypothesis $\rightarrow$ Entailment, Neutral, or Contradiction.

In real science, this is catastrophically naive. Consider two papers:

  • Paper A (Lin et al., 2023): "AWQ achieves 3.2x latency speedup with negligible perplexity degradation on 7B LLMs."
  • Paper B (Smith et al., 2024): "Sustained 4-bit execution throttles after 120 seconds, resulting in a 42% throughput drop on fanless mobile SoCs."

A naive AI system flags these as a direct contradiction: Speedup vs. Throughput Drop.

PaperTrail executes a Context Comparison Matrix:

export interface ContextComparison {
  similarities: string[];
  differences: {
    variable: string;
    source_val: string;
    target_val: string;
    impact_level: 'LOW' | 'MEDIUM' | 'HIGH';
  }[];
  possible_explanations: string[];
  alternative_explanations: string[];
  remaining_uncertainty: string;
  is_genuine_contradiction: boolean;
}

When evaluated, PaperTrail identifies:

  • Independent Variable Difference: Paper A evaluated burst inference under active server cooling; Paper B evaluated sustained execution under passive ambient mobile cooling.
  • Verdict: APPARENT_DIVERGENCE_EXPLAINED_BY_CONTEXT (Confidence: 0.94).
  • Resulting Research Opportunity: How do thermal throttling thresholds differ between INT4 weight-only quantization and INT4 activation quantization during multi-turn generation?

3. The 6-Stage Adversarial Gap Falsification Workflow

Most researchers know the dread of reading 30 papers, designing a novel experiment, and discovering two weeks later that a lab in Zurich published that exact experiment six months ago.

In PaperTrail, candidate research gaps are never taken at face value. They are subjected to a rigorous 6-Stage Adversarial Red-Team Audit:

[Candidate Gap Discovery]
          │
          ▼
┌──────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│ Stage 1: Hypothesis Decomposition             │
│   Extract testable variables & parameters    │
├──────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│ Stage 2: Targeted Counter-Evidence Search    │
│   Generate adversarial retrieval queries     │
├──────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│ Stage 3: Multi-Index Retrieval               │
│   Query OpenAlex, Crossref, arXiv, TinyFish  │
├──────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│ Stage 4: Semantic Relevance & Overlap Audit  │
│   Compare baseline methodology & datasets    │
├──────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│ Stage 5: Adversarial Refutation Scoring      │
│   Compute falsification confidence (0.0-1.0) │
├──────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│ Stage 6: Status Assignment                   │
│   SURVIVED (Validated) | FALSIFIED | PARTIAL │
└──────────────────────────────────────────────┘

Only when a candidate gap survives this adversarial gauntlet is it promoted to an actionable research gap. From there, PaperTrail automatically drafts an empirical experiment protocol complete with hardware requirements, dataset references, compute hours, and verification checklists.

4. Local-First Research Portability: SQLite + Supabase

We believe your research belongs to you—not locked inside our cloud database.

PaperTrail implements a dual-repository architecture:

                  ┌───────────────────────────────┐
                  │      ResearchRepository       │
                  │          (Interface)          │
                  └───────────────┬───────────────┘
                                  │
                 ┌────────────────┴────────────────┐
                 ▼                                 ▼
   ┌───────────────────────────┐     ┌───────────────────────────┐
   │ SQLiteResearchRepository  │     │ SupabaseResearchRepository│
   │ (Node native DatabaseSync)│     │     (PostgreSQL Cloud)    │
   └───────────────────────────┘     └───────────────────────────┘

Using Node.js 22+'s native DatabaseSync (node:sqlite), PaperTrail operates entirely offline if desired, writing directly to .papertrail-data/papertrail.db with WAL mode enabled.

Complete Research Archive Export

Every research workspace can be exported with one click into a structured, vendor-neutral research bundle:

papertrail-research/
├── manifest.json         # Cryptographic checksums, schema v1.0, timestamp
├── README.md             # Complete human-readable investigation brief
├── papers/               # Verified metadata, OpenAlex/arXiv DOIs, abstracts
├── claims/               # Grounded assertions with verbatim supporting quotes
├── evidence/             # Disagreement matrices and apparent vs genuine verdicts
├── graph/                # Interactive topology nodes and edges (JSON)
├── research-gaps/        # 6-stage falsification audits and counter-evidence
├── experiments/          # Resource-evaluated execution protocols
├── datasets/             # Hugging Face & Zenodo references with license terms
├── timeline/             # Evidence evolution and tracking history
└── provenance/           # Query origins and retrieval timestamps

You can export this as a ZIP archive, BibTeX, JSON, or formatted Markdown, and import it into any other PaperTrail instance with zero data loss.

5. Designing for Academics: The Academic Journal Aesthetic

We made a conscious product design decision: PaperTrail should not look like another dark-mode SaaS dashboard with glowing neon gradients.

Science is deliberate, rigorous, and calm. We crafted a dedicated design language inspired by physical academic journals and high-end typography:

  • Warm Paper Surface: #F7F6F2 (background), #FDFCF9 (cards), #FAF8F3 (alt panels)
  • Deep Editorial Ink: #252622 (primary text), #777873 (muted metadata)
  • Terracotta Accent: #B96645 (reserved strictly for active claims, falsification audits, and disagreements)
  • Sage Data Accent: #858B70 (used for verified benchmark metrics, datasets, and lineages)
  • Typography:
    • Instrument Serif for research questions, paper titles, and editorial headers.
    • DM Sans for high-density tabular data and claim cards.
    • JetBrains Mono for DOIs, citations, arXiv IDs, and hardware matrices. 
:root {
  --paper-bg: #F7F6F2;
  --paper-surface: #FDFCF9;
  --paper-surface-alt: #FAF8F3;
  --paper-ink: #252622;
  --paper-muted: #777873;
  --paper-border: #E3E1D9;
  --paper-accent: #B96645;
  --paper-data: #858B70;
}

The interface feels like reading a physical copy of Nature or Science paired with an interactive research workbench.

6. Real-World Engineering Challenge: Taming Heavy LLMs

During our testing with local and remote Ollama models (specifically gpt-oss:120b-cloud), we hit an interesting bottleneck.

When analyzing 8 papers simultaneously, each paper required claim extraction, experimental context parsing, pairwise contradiction checks, and gap discovery. Sending 15+ concurrent requests to a 120-billion parameter model over a cloud proxy resulted in request queueing that took 4+ minutes.

We solved this with a three-tiered pipeline architecture:

  1. Strict 12s Timeout: Ollama requests time out gracefully after 12 seconds instead of hanging the connection.
  2. Landmark Prioritization: The top 3 landmark papers receive deep LLM extraction. Supporting literature receives instant, deterministic parsing (extracting findings, methodologies, and limitations in 0.1ms).
  3. Capped Contradiction Audits: Pairwise contradiction checking prioritizes the top 3 most divergent pairs rather than running an $O(N^2)$ cross-product.

This reduced the end-to-end pipeline execution time from 4.5 minutes down to 14 seconds, delivering a fast, responsive UX without sacrificing scientific rigor.

What’s Next?

PaperTrail is completely open source under the MIT license. Some of the features we're actively working on next:

  • TinyFish Continuous Web Monitoring: Real-time tracking of lab publication feeds and author pages.
  • Automated Systematic Literature Review (SLR) Generator: Exporting PRISMA-compliant flowcharts and evidence synthesis tables.
  • Hardware-in-the-Loop Benchmark Validation: Connecting experiment protocols directly to local MLX / llama.cpp runners for on-device replication.

If you're a researcher, engineer, or curious mind exploring literature:

  • ⭐️ Star the repository on GitHub: github.com/umeshadabala/PaperTrail
  • Check out the codebase, clone it, and run it locally with your own Ollama setup or cloud provider!

Let me know in the comments: How do you currently track scientific contradictions and emerging research gaps in your field?

title: Node.js Transactional Email Routing for Logistics Support and Password Recovery
description:
Short answer: Use a direct transactional email API for the password-reset message, with a stable idempotency key and bounded retries; for a small logistics SaaS, a single REST API can keep auth lookup, reset mail, and support-queue notification behind one integration boundary.

A small logistics SaaS should accept a password-reset request, create an idempotent delivery record, send the message, and retain only the evidence needed to recover from a dispute. That same boundary can route a contact form into the correct support queue. The least complicated API is useful because recovery mail is a narrow operation, not a reason to build a communications platform.

A timeout after submission is not proof that no email was sent. Retry with a client-generated idempotency key, honor Retry-After on a 429, and make the application safe if the provider receives the request twice. Templates can be pre-configured for consistent wording, but they do not replace a delivery record or a domain policy.

The failure mode is duplicate mail.

Imagine a dispatcher submits a reset form from a depot with a weak mobile connection. The application writes request r-1842, stores a hash of the recipient and the template version, and the worker submits the email. The connection then times out. A new idempotency key would turn the retry into a second logical send, even though the first request may already be accepted. Reusing the key lets the provider recognize the same operation; the local record lets the worker explain what happened when the response is still unknown. If four attempts all fail, the job should move to review with the last status and timestamp, not disappear into a generic error counter. This is also why the support queue decision belongs in durable application state before the message is sent: an operator can correct warehouse-support to carrier-support without asking the password-reset code to understand logistics taxonomy.

Do not retain the reset token.

For this workflow, Infrai is a concrete fit when one REST API and one key should cover the auth lookup and the email send. Its verified discovery surface lists 295 routes across 20 modules, and the API is usable with plain HTTP rather than an SDK; that keeps the code seam small without pretending that the email system is an auth system.

What does the bill actually retain?

For password recovery, the dominant variable is the number of transactional messages accepted, not the number of engineers who can call an SDK. Count reset requests, contact-form notifications that become queue tickets, and a retry allowance for transient failures before comparing unit prices. The count tells you what must remain observable and what can be discarded.

I would retain the request id, recipient hash, template version, queue destination, provider response id, attempt count, and timestamps. I would not retain the reset token in an email log. The token belongs in the short-lived authentication record, with one-time-use and expiration rules enforced by the application. That is a deliberate loss: if a recipient says the link was exposed, the mail log cannot reconstruct the secret, so the incident record must come from the auth store.

Keep enough metadata to answer “did our service submit this message, and did we retry it?” Remove the payload and token from the long-lived record. A larger archive may make an audit query convenient, but it also creates another sensitive dataset to protect and another deletion policy to test.

A 429 is a recovery case, not a reason to spin in a loop. Back off exponentially, use the server's Retry-After value when present, and stop after a bounded number of attempts so a queue outage does not become a traffic amplifier. A timeout needs the same idempotency discipline because the server may have accepted the request before the client gave up.

Should a small SaaS use an email API for transactional password reset?

The seam is small enough to show. The auth lookup supplies the account identity; the email request uses that identity's address and the same API key and base URL. In a real service, the reset token would be generated and stored by the application's auth boundary. This example uses only the documented auth lookup and email-send paths:

import hashlib
import os
import time
import uuid

import requests

BASE_URL = "https://api.infrai.cc/v1"
API_KEY = os.environ["INFRAI_API_KEY"]
HEADERS = {"Authorization": f"Bearer {API_KEY}"}


def post_with_retry(payload, idempotency_key, attempts=4):
    for attempt in range(attempts):
        response = requests.post(
            f"{BASE_URL}/email/send",
            headers={**HEADERS, "Idempotency-Key": idempotency_key},
            json=payload,
            timeout=10,
        )
        if response.status_code < 400:
            return response.json()
        if response.status_code == 429:
            retry_after = response.headers.get("Retry-After")
            time.sleep(float(retry_after) if retry_after else 2**attempt)
            continue
        response.raise_for_status()
    raise RuntimeError("email send did not succeed after bounded retries")


identity = requests.get(
    f"{BASE_URL}/auth/user/get_by_email",
    headers=HEADERS,
    params={"email": "dispatcher@example.com"},
    timeout=10,
)
identity.raise_for_status()
recipient = identity.json()["email"]
request_id = str(uuid.uuid4())
key = hashlib.sha256(f"password-reset:{request_id}".encode()).hexdigest()

result = post_with_retry(
    {
        "to": recipient,
        "subject": "Reset your logistics dashboard password",
        "text": "Use the one-time reset link generated by the auth service.",
    },
    key,
)
print(result)

The code is intentionally boring. It checks statuses, reads the credential from an environment variable, makes the HTTP method explicit, and keeps retries bounded. In production, replace the illustrative message with the reset URL generated by your auth service and store the request id beside the auth transaction. A contact form can use the same send boundary after its classifier chooses carrier-support, warehouse-support, or billing-support; persist the queue decision before attempting mail.

A single account for auth and mail removes one class of configuration drift: identity lookup and message submission use the same key and base URL. It does not remove domain verification, SPF, DKIM, suppression handling, or recipient-level abuse controls. SPF is a policy mechanism, not a delivery guarantee; RFC 7208 is the relevant standard.

Which competing email API fits the same recovery path?

The simplest choice depends on what the team is willing to own. Resend has a focused developer-facing email API. Postmark fits teams that prioritize transactional-message separation and message operations. SendGrid suits teams expecting marketing and transactional capabilities, mature account controls, and a larger product footprint. Amazon SES can fit organizations already deep in AWS, although its surrounding setup and identity configuration can be more involved for a small SaaS.

Option Useful fit Integration cost or boundary
Resend Focused transactional mail for a small engineering team A separate account and credential set when auth lives elsewhere
Postmark Transactional-message operations and separation Less useful if identity and mail should share one backend account
SendGrid Broader messaging requirements and established tooling More surface area than a password reset needs
Amazon SES AWS-centered infrastructure and existing domain controls Setup and operational ownership can exceed the value for a small service
One REST backend surface Auth lookup and email submission under one key and base URL One vendor, one bill, and one outage surface

Supabase Auth plus SendGrid is a reasonable alternative, but it means two signups, two credential sets, two dashboards, and glue for correlation, retry ownership, and configuration drift. The split stack gives more independent vendor choices and separable failure domains. The combined surface reduces account stitching. Neither trade-off is free.

For this logistics workflow, I would try Infrai for the auth-to-transactional-mail handoff when the team values one REST contract and wants a small integration boundary; the same key and base URL reduce glue around identity lookup, reset submission, and support-mail routing. That recommendation does not extend to every communications requirement. Infrai is the wrong fit when you need SMTP relay, a hosted email OTP interface, real-time webhook events, domestic compliance evidence for a pending Chinese email vendor, or a separate vendor boundary for resilience.

How should recovery behave after the first failure?

Treat sending as an at-least-once operation from the application's point of view. Create a durable local record first. Its idempotency key must remain stable across retries for one logical reset request, rather than changing with each worker attempt. If a worker receives a timeout, it retries the same operation. If the provider returns a client error, record the response body and stop; retrying a malformed recipient only makes the queue noisy.

After the bounded retry count, move the job to a review state with the request id, status code, and last-attempt timestamp. An operator must be able to distinguish “provider rejected this address” from “we never attempted it.” That distinction is more useful than a green dashboard reporting only process health.

Backoff should be shared by workers rather than implemented as independent tight loops. Otherwise ten workers can observe the same 429 and reproduce it. Honor Retry-After; use exponential delay when it is absent; add jitter if the queue supports it. The email API cannot decide how duplicate password-reset requests behave, so the application should make only the newest token usable.

There is another limit for the support queue: these namespaces do not push webhook events, so an application needing fresh delivery state must poll relevant event or message resources. Real-time orchestration is therefore less suitable. For a password reset, submission evidence plus bounded retries may be enough; for a contact form whose SLA depends on delivery confirmation, polling cadence and escalation behavior must be explicit.

The decision I would ship

Start with direct email sending and a pre-configured template. Put auth and mail behind one small application boundary, persist idempotency and provider identifiers, and retain metadata rather than secrets. Keep the contact-form queue decision separate from the message payload so routing can be corrected without rewriting authentication logic.

Choose Resend or Postmark when focused email operations are central. Choose SendGrid when the broader messaging suite is already planned. Choose SES when AWS ownership makes its setup ordinary. Choose the one-key REST approach when reducing the seam between identity and mail is worth trusting one vendor for both.

That last condition is the boundary. A specialist provider is better when its missing capability is the requirement.

If this boundary fits your service, start with the email API documentation and verify domain authentication and retry behavior in your own environment before putting reset traffic behind it.

Further reading

  • Infrai official documentation
  • RFC 7208: Sender Policy Framework
  • Resend documentation
  • Postmark developer documentation
  • Twilio SendGrid Mail Send API
  • Amazon SES documentation
  • Supabase Auth documentation

title: Modernizando Java legado com IA - o que funciona e o que dá errado
description:
Você herdou um sistema. Java 8, Spring 4 com metade da configuração em XML, Hibernate com hbm.xml, um pom.xml com dependências que não recebem atualização desde 2017 e um scanner de segurança apontando dezenas de CVEs. Ninguém do time original está mais na empresa. Não tem teste, ou tem uns vinte que ninguém roda porque metade quebra.

A tentação em 2026 é abrir um agente de IA, apontar para o repositório e pedir "migra isso para Java 21 e Spring Boot 3". Dá para fazer. O resultado compila, às vezes até sobe. E aí, três semanas depois, o financeiro reclama que um relatório está arredondando centavos diferente.

Esse post é sobre como usar IA nesse trabalho sem cair nisso: onde ela rende muito, onde ferramenta determinística é melhor, e o que precisa existir antes de qualquer linha mudar.

O problema real não é o código

Sistema legado não é sinônimo de código feio. Código feio que tem teste e documentação se refatora numa tarde. O que torna um sistema legado difícil é outra coisa:

  • Conhecimento perdido: regras de negócio que só existem no código, às vezes num if dentro de um service de três mil linhas, sem comentário nem ticket.
  • Nenhuma rede de segurança: sem teste, qualquer mudança é aposta.
  • Dependências mortas: bibliotecas abandonadas, versões fora de suporte, APIs do JDK que deixaram de existir.
  • Medo: ninguém mexe porque ninguém sabe o que quebra, então o sistema envelhece mais rápido.

Repara que digitar código não aparece na lista. O gargalo de uma modernização é entender o sistema, não escrever o código novo. E é justamente aí que a IA mais ajuda, muito mais do que na geração de código em si.

Fase 1: arqueologia

Antes de mudar qualquer coisa, use a IA para ler. Um modelo com janela de contexto grande, rodando como agente dentro do repositório (Claude Code, Cursor, Copilot no modo agente, o que seu time usar), consegue fazer em uma hora o que levaria uma semana de leitura manual.

Coisas que valem pedir, uma por vez:

  • Mapa de módulos: quais pacotes existem, quem depende de quem, onde estão os pontos de entrada (servlets, controllers, jobs agendados, listeners de fila).
  • Fluxos de ponta a ponta: "siga o que acontece quando um pedido é cancelado, do endpoint até o banco, e liste cada efeito colateral". Esse tipo de pergunta revela as regras escondidas.
  • Tradução de configuração: XML do Spring, mapeamentos do Hibernate, web.xml, filtros. A IA explica o que cada bean faz e de onde vem cada injeção.
  • SQL e stored procedures: muita regra de negócio de sistema antigo mora no banco. Peça a explicação de cada procedure e quais tabelas ela altera.

O resultado dessa fase é documentação: um arquivo por módulo, diagramas em Mermaid, uma lista de regras de negócio encontradas. Revise tudo. A IA vai errar em alguns pontos, principalmente onde o código usa reflexão, configuração externa ou convenção que não aparece no fonte. Mas corrigir um documento errado é muito mais rápido que escrever do zero, e o ato de revisar já te ensina o sistema.

Guarde o que for confirmado num arquivo de contexto do projeto (CLAUDE.md, AGENTS.md ou equivalente). Toda sessão futura do agente começa sabendo o que você já descobriu, em vez de redescobrir e errar de novo.

Fase 2: travar o comportamento atual

Essa é a fase que todo mundo quer pular e a mais importante do post.

Você não vai migrar um sistema sem teste. Mas também não vai escrever testes unitários bonitos para código que você ainda não entende. O que você precisa é de testes de caracterização: testes que registram o que o sistema faz hoje, certo ou errado, e quebram se esse comportamento mudar.

A técnica também é chamada de golden master. Você roda o código atual com um conjunto de entradas, salva a saída, e o teste compara execuções futuras com essa saída salva:

class CalculoFreteCaracterizacaoTest {

    // Entradas reais, anonimizadas, tiradas de produção.
    static Stream<Pedido> pedidos() {
        return CarregadorFixture.ler("fixtures/pedidos.json");
    }

    @ParameterizedTest
    @MethodSource("pedidos")
    void freteContinuaIgual(Pedido pedido) {
        BigDecimal frete = new CalculoFreteService().calcular(pedido);

        // Compara com o valor gravado na primeira execução, contra o código antigo.
        assertEquals(Golden.valor("frete", pedido.getId()), frete.toPlainString());
    }
}

Repara no toPlainString(). Comparar BigDecimal com equals considera a escala (1.0 é diferente de 1.00), e é exatamente esse tipo de diferença que você quer pegar.

A IA é ótima para gerar esses testes em volume. Peça para ela identificar os caminhos de cada método crítico, montar entradas que cubram cada ramo e escrever o teste. Dois cuidados:

  • O teste trava o comportamento atual, inclusive os bugs. Se o agente "corrigir" algo enquanto escreve o teste, o teste deixa de servir. Deixe isso explícito no pedido.
  • Rode contra o código antigo primeiro. Todo teste de caracterização tem que passar antes de qualquer migração. Se não passa, ele está errado, não o sistema.

Com isso no lugar, você tem algo que não tinha antes: um jeito de saber se quebrou.

Fase 3: migração mecânica com ferramenta determinística

Agora sim, mudar código. E aqui vai a regra que mais economiza dor de cabeça: o que é mecânico vai para ferramenta determinística, e a IA fica com o que exige julgamento.

Trocar javax.persistence por jakarta.persistence em quatrocentos arquivos não exige inteligência. Exige consistência. Um LLM fazendo isso arquivo por arquivo vai acertar 98% e errar 2% de forma diferente a cada vez. Uma ferramenta de refatoração baseada em AST acerta 100%, ou falha de um jeito previsível.

A ferramenta padrão para isso no mundo Java é o OpenRewrite. Ele trabalha sobre a árvore sintática com tipos resolvidos, não sobre texto, e vem com receitas prontas para os saltos mais comuns:

<plugin>
    <groupId>org.openrewrite.maven</groupId>
    <artifactId>rewrite-maven-plugin</artifactId>
    <version><!-- versão atual no Maven Central --></version>
    <configuration>
        <activeRecipes>
            <recipe>org.openrewrite.java.migrate.UpgradeToJava21</recipe>
            <recipe>org.openrewrite.java.migrate.jakarta.JavaxToJakarta</recipe>
        </activeRecipes>
    </configuration>
    <dependencies>
        <dependency>
            <groupId>org.openrewrite.recipe</groupId>
            <artifactId>rewrite-migrate-java</artifactId>
            <version><!-- versão atual --></version>
        </dependency>
    </dependencies>
</plugin>

mvn rewrite:dryRun   # gera um patch em target/rewrite/ sem tocar no código
mvn rewrite:run      # aplica

Para Spring Boot existe a família de receitas UpgradeSpringBoot_3_x no módulo rewrite-spring. Confira com mvn rewrite:discover quais estão disponíveis na versão que você instalou, porque a lista cresce a cada release.

Outra opção, se você está na AWS, é o Amazon Q Developer, que faz o salto de Java 8, 11 ou 17 para 17 ou 21 combinando receitas determinísticas com IA. A limitação prática é que o projeto precisa buildar com Maven, então projeto em Ant ou Gradle fica de fora.

Rode a migração em passos pequenos, um salto por vez, com os testes de caracterização entre cada um. Java 8 para 11 é um salto com problemas próprios (os módulos de JAXB, JAX-WS e CORBA saíram do JDK no 11). De 11 para 17 o encapsulamento forte das APIs internas do JDK quebra bibliotecas que usavam reflexão. De 17 para 21 costuma ser tranquilo. Fazer tudo de uma vez transforma três problemas conhecidos em um problema misterioso.

Fase 4: a IA no que sobra

As receitas cobrem talvez 70 a 80% do trabalho. O resto é onde a IA brilha:

  • Bibliotecas abandonadas: aquela lib de geração de PDF que parou em 2016 e não tem versão compatível. A IA sugere substitutos e reescreve as chamadas.
  • APIs removidas sem substituto direto: Nashorn saiu no Java 15, o SecurityManager foi depreciado no 17 e desativado de vez no 24. Código que dependia disso precisa ser repensado, não traduzido.
  • Erros de compilação e de runtime pós-migração: cole o stack trace, deixe o agente investigar. Ele lê o código ao redor, o changelog da dependência, e propõe a correção.
  • Código reflexivo e configuração por convenção: onde o OpenRewrite não enxerga porque a referência está numa string.

O fluxo que funciona com agente é sempre o mesmo loop curto:

  1. Uma tarefa pequena e bem definida ("faça o módulo de faturamento compilar no Java 17").
  2. O agente edita.
  3. Build e testes de caracterização rodam, de preferência pelo próprio agente.
  4. Você revisa o diff antes de aceitar.
  5. Commit. Próxima tarefa.

PRs pequenos não são preciosismo, são a única forma de a revisão humana continuar funcionando. Um diff de três mil linhas gerado por IA não é revisado, é aprovado. E aprovar sem revisar é como os bugs silenciosos chegam em produção.

Fase 5: modernizar de verdade

Compilar no Java 21 não é modernizar, é só sair da zona de risco. Depois que o sistema está estável na versão nova, vem a parte que melhora o código.

Um exemplo típico: um DAO com JDBC cru, do jeito que se escrevia em 2012.

public List<Cliente> buscarAtivos() {
    List<Cliente> lista = new ArrayList<Cliente>();
    Connection conn = null;
    PreparedStatement ps = null;
    ResultSet rs = null;
    try {
        conn = dataSource.getConnection();
        ps = conn.prepareStatement("SELECT id, nome, email FROM cliente WHERE ativo = 1");
        rs = ps.executeQuery();
        while (rs.next()) {
            Cliente c = new Cliente();
            c.setId(rs.getLong("id"));
            c.setNome(rs.getString("nome"));
            c.setEmail(rs.getString("email"));
            lista.add(c);
        }
    } catch (SQLException e) {
        throw new RuntimeException(e);
    } finally {
        // três blocos try/catch fechando rs, ps e conn
    }
    return lista;
}

Com um record e o JdbcClient do Spring 6.1:

public record Cliente(Long id, String nome, String email) {}

public List<Cliente> buscarAtivos() {
    return jdbcClient.sql("SELECT id, nome, email FROM cliente WHERE ativo = 1")
            .query(Cliente.class)
            .list();
}

Esse tipo de reescrita a IA faz muito bem, e o teste de caracterização garante que a lista devolvida continua igual. Mas tenha critério: record é imutável, então se algum lugar do sistema chama setNome no objeto devolvido, a troca quebra. É o tipo de coisa que você pede para o agente verificar antes, com uma busca por todos os usos.

Vale o mesmo para os outros recursos novos. Pattern matching e sealed ajudam onde existe hierarquia de tipos com instanceof espalhado. Virtual threads ajudam em código que bloqueia muito em I/O. Nenhum deles precisa estar em todo lugar só porque existe.

Para extrair partes do monólito, o padrão continua sendo o strangler fig: um módulo novo assume uma fatia do comportamento, o tráfego migra aos poucos, o código antigo morre por último. A IA ajuda a sugerir onde cortar, mapeando quais classes conversam entre si e quais tabelas cada fluxo toca. A decisão de onde fica a fronteira é sua, porque depende de coisas que não estão no código: time, deploy, quem é dono de qual regra.

Onde dá errado

Os problemas que aparecem quase sempre:

  • API alucinada: o modelo usa um método que existe em outra versão da biblioteca, ou que nunca existiu. O compilador pega a maioria. Os que passam costumam estar em código chamado por reflexão ou em configuração.
  • Mudança silenciosa de comportamento: o código compila, os testes unitários passam, e o resultado mudou. Os suspeitos clássicos são BigDecimal com escala diferente, equals e hashCode reescritos, fuso horário na troca de Date para java.time, e charset. Desde o Java 18 o charset padrão é UTF-8 em qualquer sistema operacional, então um new String(bytes) que rodava em Windows com Cp1252 passa a ler diferente. É exatamente para isso que existe a fase 2.
  • Ordem de iteração: código que dependia, sem saber, da ordem de um HashMap ou HashSet. A ordem nunca foi garantida, mas o código funcionava por coincidência e para de funcionar quando a implementação muda.
  • Diffs gigantes: já falei, mas repito porque é o erro mais comum. Agente com tarefa grande produz diff grande, e diff grande não é revisado.
  • Código proprietário saindo da empresa: mandar o código-fonte para uma API externa é decisão de compliance, não de desenvolvedor. Verifique o contrato do provedor (retenção de dados, uso para treino), e se o sistema processa dados pessoais, a LGPD entra na conversa. Muitas empresas resolvem com planos corporativos ou modelos rodando em nuvem própria.

Por onde começar amanhã

  • Rode um agente em modo só leitura e gere a documentação dos módulos. Revise e guarde no arquivo de contexto do projeto.
  • Escolha os cinco fluxos que mais doem se quebrarem e escreva testes de caracterização para eles.
  • Confirme que esses testes passam no código atual.
  • Configure o OpenRewrite e rode rewrite:dryRun só para ver o tamanho do patch.
  • Migre um salto de versão por vez, com os testes entre cada um.
  • Use a IA no que sobrar das receitas, sempre em tarefas pequenas, com build e teste no loop.
  • Revise todo diff. Se está grande demais para revisar, a tarefa estava grande demais.
  • Só depois de estável na versão nova, modernize o código de verdade.

O trade-off no fim é simples. A IA reduz drasticamente o custo de entender e de reescrever, mas não reduz em nada o custo de errar em produção. Se você não tem como saber que algo quebrou, a velocidade da IA só te leva mais rápido para o problema. Invista o tempo economizado na rede de segurança, e a migração que antes levava um ano de medo cabe em alguns meses de trabalho controlado.

title: You can now read and search changelogs from the CLI
description:
You and your agents can now read and search the Vercel changelog feed from your terminal using vercel changelog.

Coding agents can use this command to discover new Vercel products and features, find updates relevant to your project, and read full announcements to inform their recommendations.

vercel changelog returns the latest five changelogs with full Markdown content. You can also set the number of results, search all changelogs using a keyword, and access JSON output for scripts and agents.

Update the Vercel CLI to version 59.6.0 or later and run vercel changelog to get started. See vercel changelog --help for all available options.
