title: How to Choose 2026 Object Storage Service for Tenant Documents: Recovery Boundaries
description:
How to Choose 2026 Object Storage Service for Tenant Documents: Recovery Boundaries

Short answer: for property-management training documents, choose private object storage with idempotent writes and signed delivery; use a specialist for versioning, WORM retention, replication, or self-managed browser CORS, and consider Infrai when one REST API and one credential across AI generation and storage reduce integration glue.

Private object storage is the least complex answer for training documents: keep every object private, make retries idempotent, and deliver short-lived signed URLs only after authorization. The cheapest-looking service is a poor choice if a failed upload can silently overwrite a compliance artifact or if a browser cannot be configured for its upload path.

Infrai belongs in the early comparison for one narrow reason: its plain REST API lets a Go service call storage without installing or versioning a storage SDK, while the same key and base URL can cover an adjacent AI runtime handoff. The limitation is equally important: this is an application-owned recovery design, not a replacement for storage primitives it does not expose.

The page that fires first

The alert should not begin with “the vendor is down.” It should begin with an application symptom: training-artifact-write-failures > 0 for five minutes, split by region and tenant. The on-call sees the tenant, object key, request ID, HTTP status, retry count, and whether the write was acknowledged.

Work backward from that page. A timeout is not proof that the object was absent; the server may have committed it before the client lost the response. Retrying with a new key creates a duplicate. Retrying the same write without an idempotency key can overwrite a document. The recovery record therefore needs the tenant ID, a deterministic object key, a client-supplied idempotency key, and a status transition that can be checked by a worker.

I initially treated the storage bill as the decision. The operational boundary changed my mind: access control and recovery behavior decide whether a low monthly GB figure is useful for this workflow.

The duplicate is the incident.

The recovery record should live longer than the retry loop. Infrai documents a 24-hour default deduplication window for idempotent operations, so the worker should retain its logical operation ID and payload digest for at least that window, then reconcile any request that ended in an unknown state before allowing a new upload. A 429 is a scheduling event, not permission to spin: parse Retry-After, apply exponential backoff, and let queue age feed the SLO. If the response is a 4xx validation or authorization error, preserve the response body for the operator and stop retrying; if the network failed after the server may have accepted the write, query the application's status record before deciding to submit again.

No magic timeout.

What should the retry worker actually do?

The worker should retry transient failures, honor Retry-After on HTTP 429, and stop on a clear authorization or validation error. It should never pass the platform authorization header to a returned presigned URL. A private object and a signed delivery URL are different credentials with different audiences.

Here is the small part of the write path that is safe to reason about in Go. It uses the verified object-write route, an explicit method, a private ACL, and an idempotency key; the application still owns the queue, durable status record, and authorization decision.

package main

import (
    "bytes"
    "fmt"
    "io"
    "net/http"
    "os"
    "time"
)

func putTrainingArtifact(bucket, key, idempotencyKey string, body []byte) error {
    apiKey := os.Getenv("INFRAI_API_KEY")
    if apiKey == "" {
        return fmt.Errorf("INFRAI_API_KEY is required")
    }

    url := fmt.Sprintf("%s/storage/object/put/%s/%s", "https://api.infrai.cc/v1", bucket, key)
    for attempt := 0; attempt < 5; attempt++ {
        req, err := http.NewRequest(http.MethodPut, url, bytes.NewReader(body))
        if err != nil {
            return err
        }
        req.Header.Set("Authorization", "Bearer "+apiKey)
        req.Header.Set("Content-Type", "application/octet-stream")
        req.Header.Set("Idempotency-Key", idempotencyKey)
        req.Header.Set("X-Object-ACL", "private")

        resp, err := http.DefaultClient.Do(req)
        if err != nil {
            time.Sleep(time.Duration(1<<attempt) * time.Second)
            continue
        }
        responseBody, readErr := io.ReadAll(resp.Body)
        resp.Body.Close()
        if readErr != nil {
            return readErr
        }
        if resp.StatusCode >= 200 && resp.StatusCode < 300 {
            return nil
        }
        if resp.StatusCode == http.StatusTooManyRequests && attempt < 4 {
            delay := time.Duration(1<<attempt) * time.Second
            if retryAfter := resp.Header.Get("Retry-After"); retryAfter != "" {
                if seconds, parseErr := time.ParseDuration(retryAfter + "s"); parseErr == nil {
                    delay = seconds
                }
            }
            time.Sleep(delay)
            continue
        }
        return fmt.Errorf("object write failed: status=%d body=%s", resp.StatusCode, string(responseBody))
    }
    return fmt.Errorf("object write exhausted retries")
}

The threshold matters. A one-minute alert can page for a single overloaded edge; a fifteen-minute alert can leave a property manager without a required course record. Measure the queue age and the percentage of writes with an unknown final state, then set the page against the service-level objective for document availability. False positives spend the same scarce resource as incidents: attention.

Which object storage service should I use for storing user documents?

For US/EU projects, compare storage per GB-month, upload and retrieval calls, lifecycle operations, free-tier limits, access time, and redundancy together. API compatibility is part of the cost because every special client, presign rule, and recovery script becomes an on-call surface.

Service Where it fits Boundary to verify before choosing
Amazon S3 Broad ecosystem, mature redundancy choices, and deep lifecycle controls More account and policy surface; model request, retrieval, and replication charges rather than storage alone
Cloudflare R2 S3-compatible applications that prioritize an alternate egress model Check its regional behavior, redundancy expectations, and the exact lifecycle and consistency assumptions your recovery plan needs
Backblaze B2 Straightforward object storage for teams willing to keep the surrounding control plane simple Validate latency, replication design, API compatibility, and recovery tooling for the target US/EU deployment
Infrai storage A workflow that wants a plain REST API, one key, and the same account for the adjacent AI runtime and private document write It has no public-read ACL, object versioning, object lock, cross-region automatic replication, or self-service CORS route; lifecycle expiration starts at one day, metadata is not server-searchable, and trial credit cannot pay for persistent writes

That last row is a fit only when private delivery and application-owned recovery are acceptable. The trade-off is concrete: it is not a fit for static hosting, permanent public links, image hosting, WORM retention, strict If-Match concurrency, or browser-direct uploads that require a self-managed CORS rule. S3 or another specialist is the better choice when those are hard requirements.

The useful Infrai distinction here is operational glue: it exposes a plain REST API, so a Go service can call it without installing or versioning a storage SDK, and its discovery surface documents capabilities and runnable examples. That can reduce integration branching for a small platform team. It does not remove the need to own authorization, queue idempotency, retention policy, or a restore plan.

Can one credential carry generation into storage?

For training content generated by an AI step, the seam is worth testing separately from the storage decision. An OpenAI-images-plus-S3 design means two signups, two credential sets, and glue for handing the generated bytes across vendors, translating errors, and correlating bills. A single-account design uses one Authorization: Bearer $INFRAI_API_KEY credential and the same https://api.infrai.cc/v1 base URL for the AI runtime and the private object write.

The handoff should be explicit in the worker: receive the AI response bytes, derive the tenant-scoped key, then call the private object-write route with the same idempotency key family. The AI route and its request schema should be obtained from the public discovery document rather than guessed fields, because capability schemas are the contract. The storage write remains the durable boundary.

That consolidation has a cost: one vendor to trust, one bill, and one outage surface. Keep an exportable manifest of object keys and source records so a later migration is a controlled project; there is no cross-cloud bulk migration tool here.

The decision rule

Choose the service whose failure behavior matches the document’s consequence. If training artifacts must be immutable, publicly reachable, browser-uploaded with self-managed CORS, or automatically copied across regions, use a specialist with those primitives. If the application can keep objects private, authorize delivery itself, coordinate strict concurrency in a database or queue, and accept application-owned recovery, a REST-only storage boundary can be a practical fit.

For a property-management platform, I would pilot the write path with a small set of synthetic tenant documents, inject timeouts and 429 responses, and verify three outcomes: one logical artifact, one durable status, and one auditable delivery decision. Storage price is an input. It is not the recovery plan.

Recommendation: try Infrai for the private document-write portion when the team values one REST interface and one credential across AI generation and storage, while keeping S3, R2, or B2 in the evaluation for versioning, WORM retention, replication, or browser-delivery requirements.

If that boundary fits your system, start with the storage documentation.

Further reading

  • MDN: Cross-Origin Resource Sharing (CORS)
  • Amazon S3 documentation
  • Cloudflare R2 documentation
  • Backblaze B2 documentation

title: One plugin, two surfaces: putting an image editor inside an agent's composer
description:
Most "chat with images" flows assume the image is already finished when you send it. Mine usually isn't: I want to circle a face and say "this expression, but warmer", or mask a product and say "re-shoot it on a wooden table". Typing that description is slower than pointing at it.

So the plugin I built for DeepSeek Harness, dsh-img2img-config, adds a full-screen editor that opens on the images already staged in the composer. The editing itself was the easy part — canvas, markers, brush mask, resize. The interesting problem was the hand-off: how do the edits reach the model without turning the composer into a JSON dump?

This post is about that hand-off, plus the two surfaces the plugin ships and the host half that wires it to real provider credentials.

Two surfaces, one bundle

The package is one npm artifact with a browser half and a host half:

  • Browser half (./client): the composer dock + editor, and a Settings panel.
  • Host half (./index.js): the provider store and HTTP routes behind /dsh-img2img-config/*.

Installation is a bundle patch — the profile gets a row pointing at the package:

# cordis.patch.yml
- insert:
    - id: dsh-img2img-config
      name: 'dsh-img2img-config'

and package.json declares both halves:

{
  "dsh": {
    "bundle": { "patch": "./cordis.patch.yml" },
    "client": {
      "inject": [
        "@deepseek-ai/dsh-client-locale",
        "@deepseek-ai/dsh-client-ui-slots",
        "@deepseek-ai/dsh-client-ui-conversation",
        "@deepseek-ai/dsh-client-ui-session",
        "@deepseek-ai/dsh-client-ui-settings",
        "@deepseek-ai/dsh-client-ui-theme"
      ],
      "platform": "web"
    }
  }
}

That dsh.bundle field is the part people forget. A plugin that only declares dsh.client is not installable — the client half has nowhere to attach. (I learned this the hard way; more in the last section.)

The dock renders nothing most of the time

The editor is a dock entry on conversation.input.dock. The rule that matters for a crowded composer: the strip renders nothing while the session holds no image drafts, so it never competes with the queue / todo / goal docks that may already be there. When there are image drafts, each one gets a chip; clicking a chip opens the editor.

Confirming the editor does three things:

  1. exports the edited files (edited.png, plus marked.png when markers exist, plus a binary brush mask when strokes exist),
  2. stages them as draft attachments, replacing the edited source,
  3. hands the brief to the composer.

Step 3 is where the design questions are.

Hand-off, three options

If you read the image plus the instructions as "one message to the model", there are three shapes:

  1. Write the instructions into the draft as text. Simple, but users hate it: a wall of coordinates in the input box they have to scroll past.
  2. Attach the images and say nothing. The model gets pixels, not intent. "Warmer" doesn't survive.
  3. Carry the instructions out-of-band and attach them as a file. The model still reads them; the human still gets a clean composer.

I went with a variant of 3 plus a reference chip. The composer shows one chip labelled with the edit summary. The chip owns a payload — the full brief text — and the model never sees the chip: at submit, the chip's codec expands it.

// src/client/brief-source.ts (trimmed)
export function briefSource(): TriggerSourceFace {
  return {
    trigger: '@',
    name: 'img2img-brief',
    order: 900,
    showGroupTitle: false,
    candidates: () => Promise.resolve([]),   // no menu rows
    onPick: () => undefined,
    codec: {
      // Projection used for copy, draft persistence, and "flatten to text"
      clipboardText: (ref) => {
        const first = ref.split('\n', 1)[0]
        return first === undefined || first === '' ? BRIEF_MARK : first
      },
      // The payload already IS the model text
      serialize: (ref) => Promise.resolve(ref),
    },
  }
}

Two details make this work in practice:

  • The first line is the marker. Every brief starts with [img2img] 图片编辑请求 · img2img-studio. That line is short, language-neutral as an identifier, and is exactly what the chip flattens to when the draft is persisted or copied. The rest of the brief never enters the draft.
  • Re-editing replaces, it doesn't stack. mergeDraft() removes the previous [img2img] … [/img2img] block (and the legacy <!-- img2img-editor:begin --> block from an older version), then appends the new brief. Your own typed text is left alone.

The same facts are also attached as a machine-readable file, img2img-manifest.json, next to the exported PNGs. So the model can read pixels and fields:

{
  "version": 1,
  "createdAt": "2026-10-27T09:12:44.183Z",
  "source": { "name": "table.png", "width": 1600, "height": 1200 },
  "size": { "width": 1024, "height": 1024, "mode": "cover", "changed": true },
  "bgRemove": { "requested": true, "localPreview": false, "tolerance": 18 },
  "erase": { "strokes": 2, "prompt": "replace the price tag with the same wood grain" },
  "markers": [
    { "id": 1, "x": 0.412, "y": 0.238, "text": "keep the glaze highlights here" }
  ],
  "files": { "edited": "edited.png", "marked": "marked.png", "mask": "mask.png" }
}

Marker coordinates are normalized percentages with the origin at the top-left, so a model that works in relative terms doesn't need the source resolution. And the brief closes with an explicit instruction to the generation provider:

按标记与掩码做局部重绘，再做整体 i2i；标记与掩码只用于定位，不要出现在成图里。
(Local redraw per mark and mask first, then a whole-image i2i. Marks and masks are for localisation only — never let them into the output.)

That last sentence is doing real work. Without it, models happily draw the numbered pins into the final image.

Degrading instead of crashing

The chip path depends on services owned by the harness (inputTriggers, conversation, session). Those are not guaranteed to be present, or present at the moment this plugin applies — a batched client boot can materialise a service after your apply. So the client half resolves them lazily and falls back:

  • No trigger registry (older client build, moved service): the same brief is written into the draft as text between [img2img] and [/img2img]. Re-editing replaces that block instead of stacking another one.
  • Service appears late: register the codec source in ctx.inject(['inputTriggers'], …) rather than reading it once during apply. A one-shot read on such a boot finds nothing and silently leaves an unexpandable chip behind.
  • Draft attachments unavailable: keep the dock, but the confirm path drops to the draft-line carrier.

None of these paths crash; they get less pretty. That's the trade I wanted: the editor is a convenience layer on top of the composer, not a new failure mode for it.

The settings surface: from a panel to real credentials

The second surface is a Settings panel that configures both halves of the toolchain: vision (dsh-vision-skill) and generation (this skill). The panel talks to the host half through the plugin's own routes, and the host owns a provider store at ~/.dsh/dsh-img2img-config/providers.json.

What the panel actually manages, briefly:

  • Three priority tiers (main / backup / fallback) with drag ordering — so "try ChatGPT web, then DashScope, then a local fallback" is a configuration, not code.
  • Per-channel model fallback chains — a provider can list several models; the script walks them on failure.
  • Arrears-aware probing — providers that report insufficient balance can be auto-disabled instead of retried into a wall.
  • A ChatGPT-web account store — the channel that drives a real browser session, with per-account quota state.

Saving writes each provider back into the matching skill's scripts/.env, so the skill's own scripts pick the settings up with no extra step. The mapping — which keys to write, which to delete, which to leave alone — lives in one planSync() function, which is also exported to an offline regression script (scripts/verify-catalog.mjs). That last part matters: the panel can be tested without a browser.

What shipping it actually took

The code was the fun part. Distribution was the humbling part:

  • dsh.client alone is not installable. The first version declared only the client half; the plugin resolved, but had nowhere to attach. dsh.bundle + cordis.patch.yml is what makes it a bundle.
  • Guessed peer upper bounds are a silent killer. I had >=4.0.0-rc <5 on the host package. That's a promise to be refused on the next major release — with no log line, because the harness refuses before importing your module. I dropped the upper bounds and pinned "no < in peer ranges" with a CI check instead.
  • Publishing needed three gates. Security-key 2FA, provenance (only from CI, via OIDC), and staged publishing for a brand-new package name. I wrote that one up separately: Three gates before your first npm publish.
  • Storefront metadata lives in your repo. A screenshots.json next to package.json (1–8 images, relative paths or GitHub-hosted URLs) is what gives the plugin page App Store-style screenshots; without it, the storefront falls back to scraping your README.

What I would change next

  • Make the brief locale-aware. The brief is written in Chinese today because the primary user is; a model-facing text probably should follow the session language, not the author's.
  • Version the manifest schema explicitly. version: 1 is there, but there's no migration path yet for when the editor grows a new operation.
  • Two carriers, one truth. The chip and the manifest file carry the same facts; I'd like to derive one from the other in exactly one place rather than keeping both builders in sync by hand.

The point of the plugin was to make "point at the image and describe the change" feel like part of writing, not a separate app. The dock and the chip get most of the way there; the degradation paths are what make it survive contact with a host that is still moving.

title: Why Developers & Tech Creators Are Moving Away from Flat UI Toward Tactile Motion
description:
If you’ve browsed Twitter/X, Product Hunt, or GitHub releases over the last year, you’ve likely felt it: an overwhelming wave of visual deja vu.

Every SaaS landing page features the exact same gradient blur background. Every technical blog post is decorated with the same pastel, flat-vector illustrations. Every product announcement video uses the same sterile screen recorder with an ultra-smooth floating mouse pointer.

We spent the last decade perfecting flat design, stripped of all shadows, textures, and physical references. But in our quest for clean minimalism, digital products ended up looking interchangeable.

Now, a quiet counter-revolution is happening across developer communities and tech studios: the rise of tactile, handcrafted motion.

From paper cutouts and line-boil wobble to vintage newspaper match-cuts and physical unfold reveals, creators are re-introducing texture, weight, and friction back into the digital experience.

Here is why developers and tech creators are embracing tactile motion, the psychology behind it, and how you can apply it to your own projects without needing a background in complex motion software.

1. The Great Flattening and "Corporate Memphis" Fatigue

In the early 2010s, software design rightly moved away from heavy skeuomorphic leather and glossy glass buttons toward flat, responsive UI systems. Flat design made responsive web layouts easier to build and faster to load.

However, as design systems matured, minimalism became monotone. Illustrations turned into what designers call "Corporate Memphis"—flat, stylized characters with blue skin and noodle arms that communicate nothing about the actual craft behind a software tool.

For developers and indie founders, this creates a major problem: Differentiation.

When your landing page and product demo look identical to thousands of other AI tools and developer utilities, potential users scroll past without registering what makes your product unique. Flatness conveys utility, but it rarely conveys personality or craftsmanship.

2. The Cognitive Psychology of Tactile Motion

Why do handcrafted, physical aesthetics resonate so strongly on a digital screen?

A. The Craving for Friction in a Frictionless World

Digital experiences have become friction-free to a fault. When everything is instant, glossy, and mathematically perfect, the human brain registers it as synthetic.

Tactile motion re-introduces physical principles that we understand intuitively:

  • Tear and Crumple: Shows dynamic resistance and physical transformation.
  • Line Boil / Wobble: Mimics the micro-imperfections of traditional frame-by-frame cel animation.
  • Paper Grain & Edge Depth: Gives flat 2D shapes visual mass and tactile weight.

B. High Perceived Value

When users see subtle paper cutouts, textured borders, and dimensional drop shadows, their subconscious connects it with physical printed work—like art prints, magazines, and architectural models. That physical association elevates perceived product quality.

3. High-Impact Ways Tech Teams Are Using Tactile Motion

You don’t have to redesign your entire web app into a paper craft museum. The most effective teams use tactile motion strategically in three key areas:

1. Feature Announcements & Changelogs

Instead of posting another generic screen recording on social media, founders are framing their UI screenshots inside animated paper cutout borders or revealing new features via folded-paper flip effects. It instantly stops the endless feed scroll.

2. High-Converting Landing Page Heroes

Rather than a sterile software screenshot, adding tactile depth—like layered paper-style cards with subtle animated edges—gives software an editorial, human touch that builds immediate trust.

3. Kinetic Search & Narrative Walkthroughs

When presenting research, technical documentation, or historical data, the "newspaper match-cut" (camera tracking through vintage newsprint to highlight exact phrases) has become one of the most compelling visual storytelling devices on the modern web.

4. The Tooling Barrier (And How It’s Changing)

Historically, creating authentic paper animations was notoriously difficult for developers. It typically required:

  1. Sourcing high-res paper textures and scan libraries.
  2. Opening Adobe After Effects or Blender.
  3. Manually keyframing displacement maps, drop shadows, and frame-rate reducers (e.g., locking animations to 12fps for that stop-motion feel).
  4. Dealing with massive render times and bloated video exports.

For developers who just want to ship a polished changelog or product highlight, that friction was too high.

This is why dedicated creative tools designed specifically for tactile aesthetics are emerging. For instance, PaperAnimationLab provides an intuitive, browser-based studio specifically built for this aesthetic. Instead of wrestling with keyframes, you can drop in your product screenshots or text and instantly generate realistic paper cutouts, newspaper phrase searches, line-boil animations, and textured reveals—all running client-side with transparent GIF and video export ready for your docs and marketing pages.

5. Practical Checklist for Adding Tactile Polish

If you want to experiment with tactile motion in your next release, keep these four principles in mind:

  1. Limit Framerates for Character: Smooth 60fps linear motion looks digital. Lowering animation steps to 12fps or 24fps instantly gives graphics a stop-motion, handcrafted texture.
  2. Prioritize Performance & Transparency: For web embeds and dark-mode sites, ensure your assets support transparent backgrounds (transparent WebM or alpha-ready GIFs) so they sit naturally over your existing CSS layouts.
  3. Use Imperfection with Purpose: Add subtle edge jitter or torn paper margins to callouts and screenshots, but keep typography crisp and readable.
  4. Context Matters: Use tactile reveals for milestones, celebrations, and core feature explanations where human connection and attention matter most.

Conclusion:

In an era where AI can generate endless flat landing pages and generic vector graphics in seconds, intentional craft and tactile warmth have become a true competitive advantage.

When you show that care and personality were poured into the visual presentation of your software, users naturally assume the same level of care was poured into the codebase beneath it.

title: Draku: Exorcising the Ghosts in Your Camera Roll with Offline Open-Weight AI 🦇
description:
This is a submission for the Hacktoberfest Open-Source AI Challenge Week 4: Ghost in the Machine

What I Built

You are standing at the pharmacy counter. The pharmacist asks for your prescription. You know it is on your phone—somewhere between 4,000 WhatsApp forwards, food photos, and old boarding passes. You scroll past IMG-20261011-WA0004.jpg, Screenshot_2026-09-14.png, and scan_final_v2.pdf.

Screenshots are the most-used notebook on earth that nobody calls a notebook. The problem is that a screenshot stores pixels, not meaning. And inside those pixels live four kinds of digital ghosts haunting every laptop and phone:

  1. The Ghost of a Date: A warranty receipt that expires next week, a medical lab test due for a repeat, or a coupon that dies tonight—trapped inside a flat image where your calendar can't see it.
  2. The Ghost of a Secret: A national ID number, tax form, blood test report, or Wi-Fi password sitting unredacted in a folder that any app with gallery permissions can read.
  3. The Ghost of a Place: Hidden EXIF GPS coordinates and device serials silently attached to documents you are about to email or share.
  4. The Dead Weight: Last spring's OTP screenshots, expired boarding passes, and blurry duplicates quietly haunting your storage long after their purpose has passed.

Meet Draku—a fluffy black cat with crimson bat wings and eyes full of black flames. He sees everything on your device, and he tells no one.

Draku is a 100% offline, open-source desktop application (built with Tauri) that reads every screenshot, photo, and PDF in a folder once using local PaddleOCR and Google's open-weight EmbeddingGemma, turning that single reading into four concrete outcomes:

  • Find: Turns IMG-20261011-WA0004.jpg into 2026-10-11 Dr Patel blood test prescription.jpg and embeds the semantic context so you can type "blood test" or "router password" in plain English and find it instantly.
  • Remember: Extracts dates alongside their surrounding context ("Warranty ends in 6 days", "Refill by 10 Nov") and generates a one-tap calendar reminder once you confirm.
  • Protect: Detects exposed ID numbers, card digits, and passwords at the exact pixel bounding box, burns an irreversible pixelation blur into a safe copy, and strips hidden GPS/EXIF metadata.
  • Let Go: Calculates a transparent, inspectable "dead file" score (based on age, category, passed dates, duplicate distance, and blur) to move dead OTPs and expired tickets into a rest folder—only when you press the button.

Zero bytes uploaded. Zero accounts. Zero settings screens.

Outcome Before After What produces it
Find IMG-20261011-WA0004.jpg 2026-10-11 Dr Patel blood test prescription.jpg, findable by typing "blood test" local OCR → rule-based reader → EmbeddingGemma-300M → semantic search
Remember A warranty screenshot quietly expiring A real .ics calendar reminder, one tap date extraction with surrounding words → confirm → local .ics
Protect A photo exposing an ID number and GPS A safe copy with the blur burned into pixels and location metadata stripped local OCR bounding boxes + EXIF → confirm → clean copy
Let go OTPs, dead tickets, duplicates Rested in a folder you can restore from transparent signals → an explainable dead score → "Set aside"

Demo

  • Interactive Live Web Demo & Landing Page: https://0dvsh0.github.io/draku/ (Try the interactive "One Screen" sandbox and the 4-outcome inspector right in your browser with zero setup!)
  • Desktop Release Installer (Windows x64 · 182 MiB with models bundled): Download Draku v0.1.0

Four Real Captures — Airplane Mode On the Entire Time

Every capture below is recorded directly from the real desktop application on Windows with Wi-Fi off and Airplane Mode visibly enabled—no cloud calls, no mockups, no staged telemetry. The full airplane-mode walkthrough script lives in the repo as DEMO.md.

1. Find — Search the Pixels, Not the Filename

Local PaddleOCR extracts the text, a structured rule-reader extracts human naming cues, and Google's EmbeddingGemma-300M embeds the reading into a 768-dimensional local vector. Type "internet password" and the router login surface appears immediately—pure meaning match with zero keyword overlap.

2. Remember — Trapped Deadlines Become Calendar Events

Dates are extracted alongside their surrounding contextual words, allowing Draku to recognize that "Warranty ends in 6 days" or "Refill by 10 Nov" is an actionable deadline rather than an old receipt date. One click generates an RFC-compliant .ics calendar file accepted by your system calendar—no cloud sync intermediary.

3. Protect — Permanent Burn-In Redaction & EXIF GPS Stripping

PaddleOCR returns exact pixel bounding boxes for sensitive ID numbers, card digits, and credentials. Clicking "Make a safe copy" burns irreversible pixelation blur directly into new pixel buffers and strips hidden EXIF location metadata. The original document remains untouched.

Before and after, side by side — the sensitive ID number and GPS coordinates visible in the first frame are permanently eradicated in the safe copy:

4. Let Go — Transparent Rest Scoring with One-Tap Restore

Expired boarding passes, old OTP screenshots, and blurry duplicates earn transparent, inspectable "dead file" scores with human-readable explanations. Clicking "Set aside" lays them to rest in .draku/rest/—never deleted, completely reversible with one-tap Undo.

Code

0dvsh0 / draku

Draku

Your files, finally understood.

Draku is a free, open-source, on-device AI file manager for Windows. It reads every screenshot, photo and PDF on your machine — it finds what you need warns you before a date passes, hides what should stay private, and lets go of what is dead. Nothing leaves your machine.

Built for Hacktoberfest 2026 · Week 4 — Ghost in the Machine.

  • Landing page (live): https://0dvsh0.github.io/draku/
  • Download the installer: https://github.com/0dvsh0/draku/releases/latest/download/Draku_0.1.0_x64-setup.exe
  • Read the source: https://github.com/0dvsh0/draku 
draku/
├── CONTEXT.md     ← project context: plan, stack, tokens, status (read first)
├── site/          ← the landing page (static HTML/CSS/JS + WebGL embers)
├── app/           ← the product: Tauri 2 desktop app (Rust + React/TypeScript)
│   ├── src/           One Screen UI, mascot design tokens (tokens.css)
│   ├── scripts/       bundle prep + one-time model fetch for source builds
│   └── src-tauri/     scanner · reader · OCR · embeddings · actions
└── site/About.md
…
View on GitHub
  • Repository: https://github.com/0dvsh0/draku
  • License: MIT

To build and run Draku from source (fetches the local models once, then runs completely offline forever):

git clone https://github.com/0dvsh0/draku && cd draku/app
npm install && node scripts/fetch-model.mjs
npm run tauri dev

Clean Architecture & Codebase Layout 

draku/
├── site/               ← Interactive web sandbox & landing page (vanilla HTML/CSS/JS, WebGL embers)
└── app/
    ├── src/            ← The One Screen UI (React 19 + TypeScript, mascot design tokens)
    ├── scripts/        ← Model fetchers, NSIS installer packager, automated CI smoke test
    └── src-tauri/      ← Native Rust core touching every byte
        ├── scan.rs     ← Folder walker + dHash perceptual duplicate detection
        ├── extract/    ← The READER: PaddleOCR, PDF text parser, kamadak-exif, rule reader
        ├── embed.rs    ← Bundled EmbeddingGemma-300M loader + local cosine similarity search
        ├── score.rs    ← Transparent "Let Go" arithmetic engine — weights you can read
        ├── store.rs    ← SQLite (WAL mode) — single local embedded DB, zero daemons
        └── actions.rs  ← Safe copies, .ics generation, set-aside / restore (the ONLY disk mutations)

The Embedding Model Lives Beside the Executable, and Never Talks

EmbeddingGemma's 4-bit quantized weights ship inside the installer as model_q4.onnx alongside an external initializer file. Draku's native Rust core loads both in memory directly into ONNX Runtime with DirectML hardware acceleration—without requiring CUDA or external services:

// app/src-tauri/src/embed.rs — the offline path is the only shipped path
let mut bundled = UserDefinedEmbeddingModel::new(read("model_q4.onnx")?, TokenizerFiles {
    tokenizer_file:          read("tokenizer.json")?,
    config_file:             read("config.json")?,
    special_tokens_map_file: read("special_tokens_map.json")?,
    tokenizer_config_file:   read("tokenizer_config.json")?,
})
.with_pooling(Pooling::Mean)
.with_quantization(QuantizationMode::None)
.with_external_initializer("model_q4.onnx_data".into(), read("model_q4.onnx_data")?);

TextEmbedding::try_new_from_user_defined(bundled, InitOptionsUserDefined::new())

When you search "internet password", your query is converted to a 768-dimensional vector, and cosine similarity matches against local readings in SQLite. There is no HTTP client anywhere in the crate.

The Judge is Arithmetic You Can Read

Rather than relying on an unexplainable black-box classifier, score.rs exposes a plain struct of inspectable signals. Every weight is an auditable constant with a clear rationale:

// app/src-tauri/src/score.rs
pub fn judge(s: &Signals) -> Verdict {
    let mut score = 0.10;
    score += (s.age_days / 180.0).min(0.30);
    if s.is_otp      { score += 0.44; }   // one-time codes only live once
    if s.date_passed { score += 0.50; }   // the deadline is gone; the file overstayed
    if s.is_dup      { score += 0.50; }   // a near-identical file exists
    // …the result clamps to [0, 1]; above 0.60 a file earns the Let-go card
    Verdict { dead: score.clamp(0.0, 1.0), reason: choose_reason(&s) }
}

Verified, Not Vibes

  • 42 cargo tests on the full OCR build: Covering EXIF GPS scrubbing, redaction bounding box math, and end-to-end vector queries against bundled Gemma weights. 41 tests also run on the light build (--no-default-features) for machines that cannot run PaddleOCR.
  • Automated CI Installer Lie Detector: scripts/smoke-test-installer.mjs, wired into GitHub Actions, silent-installs the NSIS package on a clean Windows runner and verifies every bundled binary: draku.exe, DirectML.dll, all 4 OCR models, and all 6 embedding files.
  • Verified Checksums: The release build is published with verifiable SHA-256 signatures: SHA256: 19473E9A5AEC88BDE82DF50CD697E7A9450A0B0EA88B49E65B57F89843E52791

How I Built It

Most AI tools bolt four separate pipelines onto four separate problems: one tool for semantic search, another for reminders, another for PII redaction, and a fourth for storage cleanup. That wastes compute and clutters the UI.

Draku is built around a single architectural rule: One reading. Four outcomes.

[ Screenshot / Photo / PDF ]
             │
             ▼
   ┌───────────────────┐
   │  Local PaddleOCR  │ ──► Extracts text + exact pixel bounding boxes + EXIF
   └─────────┬─────────┘
             │
             ▼
   ┌───────────────────┐
   │ Structured Reader │ ──► Parses dates, PII patterns, category & dead-score
   └─────────┬─────────┘
             │
             ▼
   ┌───────────────────┐
   │  EmbeddingGemma   │ ──► Generates local semantic vector embeddings
   └─────────┬─────────┘
             │
             ▼
      [ reading.json ]
             │
   ┌─────────┴──────────┬────────────────────┬───────────────────┐
   ▼                    ▼                    ▼                   ▼
[ FIND ]           [ REMEMBER ]         [ PROTECT ]         [ LET GO ]
Semantic search    Contextual .ics      Pixel-burned PII    Transparent
& smart rename     deadline alerts      & EXIF stripping    rest scoring

When Draku scans a file like IMG-20261011-WA0004.jpg, it produces a single structured internal artifact (reading.json):

{
  "name":     "2026-10-11 Dr Patel blood test prescription",
  "category": "medical / prescription",
  "dates":    [{ "refill_by": "2026-11-10" }],
  "private":  ["patient_id", "gps"],
  "dead":     0.04,
  "network":  null
}

The Stack & Design Decisions

Layer Choice Why It Earns Its Place
Shell & Core Tauri 2 · Rust Native filesystem speed, minimal memory footprint, and zero open sockets. Bundles everything into a clean 182 MiB installer instead of a bloated Electron container.
Semantic Memory Google EmbeddingGemma-300M (4-bit ONNX) Generates 768-dimensional embeddings entirely on-device from open weights, making true offline semantic search possible from the first run.
Local Runtime fastembed + ONNX Runtime + DirectML Hardware acceleration across modern Windows GPUs/NPUs with zero CUDA configuration. Loads external weight initializers directly in memory.
Vision & Text PaddleOCR PP-OCR (Apache-2.0) Detection + classification + recognition returning exact bounding boxes that directly feed Protect's pixel-burned redaction.
Duplicate & Metadata dHash + kamadak-exif 64-bit visual perceptual hashing detects rescaled copies; parses EXIF metadata to reveal hidden GPS coordinates and camera serials.
Frontend React 19 + TypeScript + Vite Type-safe IPC boundaries, crisp UI with mascot tokens, and @fontsource vendored typography (zero CDN calls).
Persistence SQLite (WAL) via rusqlite Single embedded database in the local app directory storing readings, vectors, and approved action history.
  1. Desktop Runtime (Tauri): Gives Draku native filesystem speed and a tiny memory footprint across Windows without bundling a bloated browser backend.
  2. Eyes (PaddleOCR + EXIF Parser): Instead of sending images to a multimodal cloud API, local OCR extracts raw text and exact pixel coordinates. Knowing the exact bounding box of an ID number allows Draku to burn pixelation directly into the image buffer so redactions can never be peeled off.
  3. Memory (EmbeddingGemma): Google's open-weight EmbeddingGemma embeds the structured reading locally on the user's CPU/GPU. When you search "pharmacy receipt" or "cholesterol check", EmbeddingGemma matches the meaning even if those exact words aren't in the filename.
  4. Judgment (Transparent Rule & Scoring Engine): For Let Go, I deliberately avoided a black-box classifier. Draku computes a transparent weighted score from inspectable signals—file age, category (OTP, ticket, receipt), whether the extracted date has passed, perceptual duplicate distance, blurriness, and byte size. You can read the exact reason Draku suggests letting a file rest.
  5. The 5 "No" Promises:
    • No upload: There is no cloud mode to toggle on. network is always null.
    • No silent deleting: "Let go" moves files to a rest folder you control.
    • No guessing out loud: Draku suggests; nothing changes on disk until you click confirm.
    • No accounts or subscriptions: Free, MIT-licensed, no telemetry.
    • No settings screen: If a feature needs a configuration toggle to be usable, the design isn't finished yet. One screen: three cards and a search bar.

Honest Boundaries

Windows is the primary platform where DirectML and WebView2 ensure a guaranteed, zero-friction experience out of the box. For hardware without OCR capabilities, Draku provides a lightweight build (--no-default-features): semantic search, dates, duplicate detection, and rest actions function without OCR, while Protect reports what can be discerned from names and metadata.

Why Does Open Innovation Matter?

If a tool asks to read your entire camera roll and Downloads folder, it is asking to read your life: your prescriptions, tax returns, national ID cards, bank statements, and private family photos.

You cannot build a trustworthy version of Draku on a closed, cloud-hosted API. Here is why open-weight models and open-source code are the only way this product can exist:

  1. It Reads Your Camera Roll—So You Must Be Able to Read It Back: When a proprietary cloud app claims "we don't train on your photos," you have to take their legal team's word for it. Because Draku pairs open-weight models (EmbeddingGemma and PaddleOCR) with an MIT-licensed codebase, anyone can inspect the source, unplug their Ethernet cable, switch on Airplane Mode, and verify that zero bytes ever leave the machine.
  2. No "Storage Ransom" Economics: Cloud photo organisers charge you a monthly subscription once your storage fills up—meaning they have a financial incentive for you to hoard dead screenshots. Because Draku runs on your own silicon at zero marginal cost per file, a tool that helps you clear space never tries to sell you more of it.
  3. Different Tools for Different Jobs (Not Everything Is Windows Recall): Unlike invasive background screen-recorders that capture everything you do every few seconds, Draku captures nothing on its own. It reads only the folder you hand it, executes one pass, and puts you in complete control.
  4. Built to Outlive Any Server: Closed APIs deprecate models, hike token prices, or shut down. Because the weights are bundled right inside the Draku installer (fetch-model.mjs), your personal file guardian will work identically ten years from now on an air-gapped laptop.

The Spirit of It

When I saw the Ghost in the Machine theme coinciding with Halloween and Día de los Muertos, I didn't want to build another spooky terminal chatbot pretending to be a poltergeist. I started thinking about the real ghosts that live inside our machines every single day.

Our devices are full of unfinished business: the prescription we forgot to refill, the warranty we missed by three days, the old ticket stub from a trip we took a year ago, and the dead OTP screenshots cluttering the drawer. In the spirit of Día de los Muertos, some things in our digital lives deserve to be remembered and honoured on time, our private secrets deserve to be protected, and the things whose time has passed deserve to be laid peacefully to rest.

That is why Draku is a tiny guardian familiar—eyes of black flame to read the dark pixels, bat wings to shield your secrets, and a quiet nudge to help you let go of what is dead.

Prize Categories

  • Best Use of Gemma ($200): Google's open-weights EmbeddingGemma-300M is Draku's core semantic engine, not an optional gimmick. The shipped Windows installer bundles the 4-bit ONNX weights, tokenizer, and external initializer, loaded into memory by fastembed + ONNX Runtime with DirectML acceleration. Every semantic search query ("internet password" finding router credentials, zero keyword overlap) and every human-readable filename originates from a Gemma-family model executing 100% offline.
  • Best Use of GitHub Copilot ($100): The automated build-and-verify workflow is orchestrated via GitHub Actions (ci.yml): linting and type-checking (React 19 + TypeScript + Vitest), dual cargo test suites (light and full OCR) with model caching, and a Windows runner job that builds the NSIS installer, silent-installs it in a clean environment, and verifies the integrity of every bundled model and binary.

Built with 🦇 for Hacktoberfest 2026 — Draku on GitHub · Landing page · Download the installer

title: Our copy audit read 56,462 words and found no exclamation marks. The 161 strings it could not see have two.
description:
A while ago I audited every word inside <main> on PubTrivia's 72 public pages: 56,021 words, zero exclamation marks, 855 instances of "you" against 135 of "we". Re-running the count for this post gives 56,462 words and the same zero.

That audit measured rendered HTML, which means it measured the copy that is easiest to measure, easiest to proofread, and read in the calmest moment of a customer's day. The copy people read when something has gone wrong lives somewhere else entirely, so this time I extracted every string literal assigned to an error, message, title, description, subject or label field outside the content pages and the content components.

161 distinct strings, across 52 files:

Where Strings
components 65
dashboard server actions and pages 52
API route JSON bodies 19
utils (Stripe, email, plan limits) 17
auth server actions 10
lib 6
app/manifest.ts, proxy.ts, the small standalone pages 1 to 2 each

None of them is in the sitemap. Most of them are read by somebody who is mid-task and slightly annoyed.

Two strings that arrive on a domain we do not own

The shortest and most consequential entries are in lib/pricing/plans.ts:

/** What Stripe's checkout page and the customer's invoices call each paid plan. */
export const PLAN_PRODUCT_NAMES: Record<PaidPlanType, string> = {
  pro: 'PubTrivia Pro',
  ultimate: 'PubTrivia Ultimate',
}

We deleted our Stripe Products and Prices and build every Checkout line item inline, which means the product name is not configured in a dashboard any more, it is a string in our repository. Those two strings are rendered on checkout.stripe.com, in a layout we do not control, next to the only number in this business that really matters. They also land in the invoice Stripe emails afterwards, which is a document a venue's accountant may read years from now.

For something with that reach it is a remarkably thin piece of copy. It is the right call (a plan name on a card statement should be boring and recognisable, not clever) but it is worth noticing that the words a customer reads at the moment of paying were never reviewed by anything that reviews our page copy.

Nineteen strings that arrive as JSON

Our API routes answer machines most of the time and people some of the time. The strings in them are written for both, inconsistently.

Some are purely diagnostic, which is correct, because the only caller is Stripe or Resend:

return NextResponse.json({ error: 'Missing stripe-signature header' }, { status: 400 })
return NextResponse.json({ error: 'Webhook secret not configured' }, { status: 500 })

Some are read by a person, through our own dashboard, with no page between them and a human:

return NextResponse.json({ error: "You're already on this plan." }, { status: 409 })

And one of them, in the checkout route, is the only string in the entire product that hands the reader off to a human being:

error: "Your plan is billed in a currency we can't change plans in. Email hello@pub-trivia.app and we'll change it for you."

That is a 115-character apology for a real constraint: a subscription's currency is fixed by Stripe at the moment it is created, so a venue that signed up in one currency cannot be moved to a plan priced in another one by any automated path we have. I like this string. It admits a limit, it does not pretend the limit is a feature, and it gives a next step. It is also the only one of the 161 with an email address in it.

The proxy has its own, sent to anything that trips the global rate limiter without asking for HTML:

return NextResponse.json(
    { error: 'Too many requests. Please slow down.' },
    { status: 429, headers: { 'Retry-After': '60' } }
)

Browsers get redirected to a page instead, which is a nicer experience and also means the same condition is described twice, in two voices, in two places. The same is true of the maintenance message, which is one exported constant read by the proxy for the 503 body and by four auth server actions for the form error, which is the version of this problem I would like the rest of them to look like.

The email is written twice

Our only transactional email is a host invite, and it exists as an HTML part and a plain text part, so every sentence in it is written twice by hand. They do not say the same thing:

HTML Text
a button reading "Accept invite" Accept the invite here: ${acceptUrl}
"The owner of venue has invited you to be a host on PubTrivia. Accept the invite to start running trivia nights together." "You've been invited to join venue on PubTrivia."
"This link expires in 7 days." "This link expires in 7 days."

The text part also carries a sentence the HTML part does not: "If you weren't expecting this, you can safely ignore it." That line belongs in both, and it is in the half of the email almost nobody sees.

The only exclamation mark we ship

Of the 161 strings, exactly two end a sentence with an exclamation mark. The first is a server action's success message: "Account created! Please check your email to confirm your account before logging in."

The second is in a file no copy audit of HTML would ever open:

$ curl -s https://pub-trivia.app/manifest.webmanifest
{"name":"PubTrivia","short_name":"PubTrivia",
 "description":"Live pub quiz nights, scan, join, play!", ...}

The web app manifest. That description is what an install prompt shows, and what an app-listing surface would scrape. It is one of the most widely syndicated sentences on the site, it is not HTML, it is not in <main>, and it carries the only piece of punctuation our style guide has an opinion about. The audit that found "zero exclamation marks" was telling the truth about the thing it measured.

What the other 159 look like under the same rules

I ran the house rules over the whole set:

  • Em dashes: zero. The cleanup that removed them from user-visible copy swept the source, not just the pages, so this held everywhere. One rule that actually transferred.
  • Contractions: four. All four are in the money and invite paths: "You're already on this plan", "we can't change plans in", "You've been invited", "You've reached the table limit". The page copy almost never contracts, so the error strings are, by accident, the friendliest writing in the product.
  • "Failed to": seven. Failed to create tables, Failed to update table, Failed to delete table, and four more. Seven strings that tell a host that something did not happen and nothing about what to do next. These are the worst copy in the repository and they are the copy most likely to be read at ten past eight on a Thursday with forty people waiting.
  • "Please": sixteen. Mostly in the auth and rate-limit paths. Politeness scales inversely with how much the message can actually help.
  • No terminal punctuation: 90 of 161. Roughly half our strings are sentences and half are labels, and which one a given string is was decided independently 161 times.
  • Template placeholders: ten. Strings like "You can only add N more tables on your current plan" cannot be found by grepping the live site for them, which is the practical reason an audit of rendered HTML will always miss this layer.

What I am changing

The seven Failed to strings, first, because they are the only items on this list where the words are doing actual damage. Each one should name the thing that failed and the thing to try.

Then the duplication: the rate limit and the maintenance notice each have a page version and a JSON version, and only the maintenance pair shares a constant. Hoisting the rate-limit wording next to it is a five-line change that makes two surfaces agree forever.

The structural fix is the interesting one, and I am stealing it from a test we already have. The pricing copy is protected by a list of phrases a price may never be described with, asserted against the rendered component. The same technique works on a string table: collect the user-facing strings into one module, and assert the house rules over the module rather than over the HTML. A rule that only holds where you remembered to look is not really a rule, and the places you remember to look are never the places somebody is reading at the worst moment of their evening.

Check it yourself 

# the manifest, with the exclamation mark
curl -s https://pub-trivia.app/manifest.webmanifest

# the page a browser gets when it trips the limiter, which says 429 in a 200
curl -s https://pub-trivia.app/too-many-requests | grep -o '<title>[^<]*</title>'

Then read the pricing page, which is the surface every one of those billing strings sits behind, and whose figures are shown in your own currency. The free tier needs no card, so you can sign up and meet the second exclamation mark on your way in.

title: GIF to Live Photo without leaving the tab
description:
Someone on the marketing channel drops a looping GIF and asks if we can use it as an iPhone Lock Screen. Half the team is on Linux. The other half has never heard of a .livp file. Nobody wants to install another "GIF to Live Photo" Mac app for a one-off wallpaper request.

For a while my path was: find a cloud converter, upload the GIF, download something that might open on iPhone, AirDrop it, discover Photos rejected the package, try again. That was fine for memes. It was wrong the moment the GIF included unreleased UI or a client brand mark.

These days I convert GIF → Live Photo in the browser, preview the loop in the same tab, download a .livp, and only then AirDrop to the phone. No desktop app. No account. No "we delete uploads in 24h" promise I can't verify.

Why this shows up in frontend work

Live Photos are an Apple Photos format: a still JPEG paired with a short H.264 movie, tied together with a content identifier and a still-image-time track. Designers and PMs want them for:

  • Lock Screen / wallpaper motion from an existing GIF
  • iMessage shares that feel more "Photos" than "Giphy"
  • Reaction loops that should press-and-hold like a real Live Photo
  • Demo assets for iOS marketing that started life as a Slack GIF

It's almost never a product feature. It's a format bridge between "we already have a GIF" and "Photos will accept it." Wiring FFmpeg into the app for that is usually overkill.

The upload tax (again)

Most "GIF to Live Photo online" tools still POST the bytes. The UI looks local; the Network panel says otherwise. For anything from a private beta, client work, or staging UI, that's the wrong default.

What I want for this job:

  1. Frames stay in the tab — decode → encode locally (WASM / FFmpeg-in-browser), then download
  2. Preview before download — so I catch a broken loop before AirDrop
  3. No signup before the download button works
  4. A real .livp Photos can import — not a lone MOV with "hope for the best" metadata
  5. Survives Offline in DevTools after the first WASM load

If convert dies the moment I flip Offline (after the runtime is cached), I close the tab.

A quick check before I trust the tool

Same habit as with HEIC converters:

// After dropping a redacted sample GIF and clicking Convert:
performance.getEntriesByType("resource")
  .filter((r) =>
    r.initiatorType === "fetch" ||
    r.initiatorType === "xmlhttprequest"
  )
  .map((r) => r.name);

Expect a one-time fetch for the WASM/FFmpeg core. Do not expect a POST of the GIF itself to some api.* host. Then flip Offline and convert again — if export still works, the bytes stayed local.

Always use a redacted sample first (no faces, no product chrome). Never validate the trust model with the real asset.

The loop I reuse 

1. Redacted sample GIF first
2. Open a browser-local GIF → Live Photo tool
3. Drop → convert → preview the loop in-tab
4. Download .livp
5. AirDrop to iPhone → open from Files → save to Photos
6. Confirm press-and-hold motion + still look right
7. Close the tab, then run the real GIF

Under the hood the good tools encode frames to H.264, pair a JPEG still, stamp Apple's content identifier / still-image-time metadata, and zip that into .livp. You can roll your own with ffmpeg.wasm if this is a weekly pipeline. For "someone Slack'd a wallpaper GIF," a solid tab beats a side project.

When I need that tab fast, I've used Uwarp's GIF to Live Photo tool — drop the GIF, convert in the browser, preview, download .livp. Worth trying when you don't want an App Store install or another upload site in the critical path.

Tips that actually matter for wallpaper GIFs

  • Keep it short. Live Photos only play a few seconds; trim long GIFs first.
  • Prefer clean loops. A hard cut mid-motion looks worse after H.264 than a GIF that already looped cleanly.
  • Portrait or square for Lock Screen. Wide landscape memes waste the phone chrome.
  • Finish on device. AirDrop the .livp and open it on iPhone so Photos can register the paired still + movie. Don't expect Linux to "preview" a Live Photo the way Photos does.

When you should put this in the product

Sometimes the one-off habit is wrong:

  • Users upload GIFs and your iOS app must emit Live Photos at the API boundary
  • You're building a creator tool where Live Photo export is a checked feature
  • You need batch conversion with consistent CRF / duration caps

Then own the encode path (server or WASM), test the metadata, and don't paper over failures with "please use this random website." That's product work.

For internal wallpaper requests and marketing one-offs? Keep it out of the codebase. Convert once in a tab, AirDrop, move on.

DX note: agents and media uploads

If an agent is helping with asset pipelines, constrain it: browser-local convert or local FFmpeg; no third-party upload of product or client assets. Agents default to whichever cloud converter snippet ranks first — which is often the upload path you're trying to avoid. Paste the policy into the prompt the same way you'd paste a lint rule.

What I stopped doing

  • Installing a one-purpose Mac app for a single Lock Screen request
  • Uploading unreleased UI GIFs to the first Google result for "gif to live photo"
  • Shipping a lone MOV and hoping Photos treats it as a Live Photo
  • Asking the agent to "just host the GIF somewhere and convert it"

GIF → Live Photo is a packaging problem, not a collaboration problem. Fix it in the browser, verify on the phone, close the tab. If you want a concrete starting point, the GIF → Live Photo page on Uwarp is the one I've reached for when the team is mostly on Linux and nobody wants another desktop converter.
